docs.title: Scripting FontLab
docs.text:
A year at a small type studio, told one script at a time.

This book teaches you to write Python scripts for FontLab 9. You do not need to know Python. You do not need to know much about FontLab, or about how fonts work inside. The book explains all three as it goes, in plain English.

You learn by doing small jobs. Each chapter starts with a chore that a type designer meets in a normal week: count the glyphs, find the empty ones, copy the spacing from one letter to twenty others, build the accented letters, check the kerning, export the family. You write a short script that does the chore. By the end of the chapter the script works and you keep it.

docs.title: The studio in this book
docs.text:
The chapters follow Halfmoon Type, a studio of three people, through a year of work on one typeface. The studio and its people are invented. I made them up so the chores have a setting and a deadline. FontLab, Python and everything the scripts do are real.

On your screen, the studio's typeface is played by GG Plum, a free font you can open and change without risk. Chapter 1 shows you where to get it.

docs.title: How the book is built
docs.text:
There are seven parts with twenty chapters each.

  1. First words. You run your first line of Python and learn to ask a font questions.
  2. A toolbox. You collect your own functions and learn to change a font safely.
  3. Shapes. Contours, nodes, drawing, components, anchors and accented letters.
  4. Space. Sidebearings, widths and kerning.
  5. Words. Glyph names, Unicode, OpenType features and Font Info.
  6. Families. Masters, interpolation, export, proofs and checks.
  7. Tools. Windows, panels, menus, packages and sharing your work.

Read the parts in order the first time. Later chapters use the scripts you wrote in earlier ones.

This book is being written

Chapters appear in the menu as they are finished. A chapter that is not in the menu does not exist yet.

docs.title: Part 1: First words
docs.text:
Oskar's sheet, with its eleven lines.

Oskar leaves Halfmoon Type on a Friday and hands Mira a list of eleven chores. She has never written a line of code.

In this part you sit next to her. You find the place in FontLab where Python goes, run one line, and break it on purpose so that red text stops being frightening. Then you start asking the font questions: how many glyphs it has, what each one is called, how wide it is, which ones are still empty.

You need no Python and no programming background. By the last chapter of the part you will have a script that writes a short report about any font you open, and the first four chores on Oskar's list will be done.

This part is being written. Its chapters appear in the menu as they are finished.

docs.title: 1. The list Oskar left
docs.text:
Oskar's last day at Halfmoon Type is a Friday. He waters the plant, wipes his desk and puts one sheet of paper on Mira's keyboard.

"That's everything I do that nobody sees," he says.

Mira reads the first line. Count the glyphs and tell Ines. Then the second. Find the glyphs that are still empty. There are eleven lines. Next to most of them Oskar has written the same three words in pencil: an afternoon by hand.

"Forty afternoons," Mira says.

"Forty afternoons every time the client changes something," Oskar says. "I stopped doing them by hand years ago. There's a folder called chores on the shared drive. Start there." He picks up his bag. "You draw better than I ever did. You'll be fine."

Mira has never written a line of code.

That's where this book starts, and I suspect it's close to where you start. You draw type, or you want to. And somewhere in your week there's a job that takes an afternoon, needs no talent and comes back every time something changes.

This book is about handing those jobs to FontLab.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9.
  • An internet connection, to download one practice font.
  • No Python and no programming. We start from nothing.

docs.title: What a script is
docs.text:
A script is a list of instructions in a text file. You write the instructions, FontLab follows them.

You already give FontLab instructions all day. You click a glyph, you pick a menu command, you type a number into a field. Each click is an instruction. The trouble with clicks is that FontLab forgets them. If you fix the spacing of 30 glyphs on Tuesday and the client changes the brief on Wednesday, you click 30 times again.

A script doesn't forget. You write down what you want once, in a language FontLab understands, and from then on the job costs you one click. If the brief changes, you change one line and run it again.

The language is called Python. FontLab 9 has Python built in, so there's nothing to install before you write your first line. People who have nothing to do with type use Python too: scientists, accountants, people who build websites. That's good news for you. What you learn here works elsewhere, and the world is full of free Python lessons if you ever want a second teacher.

Scripts in this book stay short. Most are under 20 lines. You'll run your first one before this chapter ends.

One thing before we go on. Halfmoon Type is invented. So are Mira, Oskar and Ines. I made them up because chores need a setting. Mira asks the questions a beginner asks, and I'm the one who answers. FontLab, Python and the fonts are real.

docs.title: Get the practice font
docs.text:
You're not going to practice on your own typeface. Not yet. You're going to practice on a font you can wreck.

In the story, Halfmoon's typeface for the publisher is called Plum. On your screen it's played by GG Plum, a real font from FontLab's GetGo Fonts collection. Its license is CC0, which means it's in the public domain. You may open it, change it and break it.

GG Plum has 205 glyphs and three weights: Light, Regular and Bold. That's small enough to see all at once and large enough to make hand work tedious, which is what we want.

To get it:

  1. Go to GetGo Fonts and download the collection for FontLab. It arrives as one ZIP file.
  2. Unpack the ZIP. Inside, open the cc0 folder, then the plum folder.
  3. You'll find a file called plum-var.vfj. That's the one we want. A .vfj file is a font in one of FontLab's own formats, with everything still editable.

docs.title: Open it and look around
docs.text:
Start FontLab 9. Choose File > Open Fonts… (Cmd+O on a Mac, Ctrl+O on Windows), find plum-var.vfj and open it.

You may know most of what follows. I go through it because I use these words in every chapter.

FontLab shows you the Font window: a grid of small boxes. Each box shows one drawing and a name. Capitals, lowercase, figures, punctuation and accented letters are all there.

What you're looking at is a font: a file that carries a typeface design to a computer. And each box holds a glyph: one drawn shape with a name. The capital A is a glyph. So is the comma. So is space, a glyph with nothing drawn in it. Find it in the grid. Its box looks empty because it is.

Read a few of the names. A, a, comma, Aacute, germandbls. Every glyph in a font has a name, and no two glyphs in one font share one. When a script wants a glyph, it asks for it by name, so you'll be reading and typing these names a lot.

Now find a and aacute, the a with an acute accent. Double-click aacute. FontLab opens the Glyph window, which is where you draw. You see the outline of the letter with the accent above it.

Here's one distinction to carry with you. A glyph isn't the same thing as a character. A character is what you type: the idea "lowercase a". A glyph is what you see: one particular drawing. One character can have several glyphs. A font may hold a normal a and a second, fancier a for the ends of words. And one glyph can stand for two characters, the way a joined fi does. FontLab keeps the two apart, so we will too.

That's all the vocabulary this chapter needs: font, glyph, name, and the difference between a glyph and a character. Widths, outlines, kerning and the rest each arrive when a chore needs them.

Every one of the things you looked at is something a script can ask about. How many glyphs? What's this one called? Is anything drawn in it? And nearly every one is something a script can change, many glyphs at a time.

docs.title: Save a copy you can break
docs.text:
Never practice on the original.

With the font open, choose File > Save Font As. Name the copy Plum-practice.vfj and put it in a folder you'll find again. I keep a folder called scripting-book on my desktop for this.

From now on you work in Plum-practice. The file you downloaded stays untouched in its folder. If a script in chapter 30 turns every glyph inside out, you open the original and save a fresh copy.

There are two more nets under you. FontLab's Undo can take back what a script did, but not always in one step. Part 2 shows you how to make a script undo cleanly. And File > Revert Font throws away everything since the last save.

Until Part 2, the copy is your net. As long as the font you're working in is Plum-practice, you can try anything.

docs.title: Run one line
docs.text:
Before Mira goes home, Oskar leans over her keyboard one last time. "You should see it work once," he says. "Then the weekend is easier."

So let's see it work once.

Choose Window > Panels > Scripting. A panel opens with a blank area, like an empty page. Then choose Window > Panels > Output. A second panel opens. Arrange them so you can see both.

Click in the blank area of the Scripting panel and type this line:

print("Hello, Mira")

Lowercase print, an opening parenthesis, a double quote mark from the plain quote key, the words, the same quote mark again, a closing parenthesis.

In the toolbar at the top of the Scripting panel there's a triangle, ▶. FontLab calls it Run script. Click it.

Look at the Output panel.

Hello, Mira

You wrote an instruction and FontLab carried it out. That was a script.

Now do what Mira does next. She changes Mira to Oskar, forgets the last quote mark, and clicks the triangle.

print("Hello, Oskar)

No greeting this time. The Output panel shows a few lines she didn't ask for, and the last one reads:

SyntaxError: unterminated string literal (detected at line 1)

"That's an error," Oskar says. "It means the line was wrong. The font's fine. Put the quote mark back."

She does, and runs it again.

Hello, Oskar

That's the whole cycle of scripting, and you've now been around it once: type, run, read, fix, run again. Chapter 2 takes the line apart. Chapter 3 is all about errors.

docs.title: Read the list
docs.text:
Mira takes Oskar's sheet home for the weekend. Here are the lines.

  • Count the glyphs and tell Ines.
  • Find the glyphs that are still empty.
  • Make a table of every glyph and its width.
  • List the glyphs that are built from other glyphs.
  • Mark every glyph that mixes its own outlines with borrowed ones.
  • Make the left sidebearing of the d, q and g match the o.
  • Rebuild the accented letters from the base letters and the accents.
  • Find kerning pairs that are larger than they should be.
  • When the small caps come: list every glyph whose name ends in .sc.
  • Put the right family name and version number into every weight.
  • Export the whole family to a dated folder every Friday.

Some of these words may be new. Each gets explained when its chore comes up.

Read the list again and notice how the lines are written. None of them needs an eye for type. Each one is a rule applied to many glyphs: every glyph, all the weights, each pair. A person gets bored and makes mistakes on glyph 140. A script does glyph 140 the way it did glyph 1.

That's the test for whether a job belongs in a script. If you can say it as "for every one of these, check this, then do that," it does. If it needs you to squint and decide whether a curve looks right, it stays yours.

By the end of Part 1 you'll have done the first few chores on that list. By the end of the book you'll have worked through the rest, and built a few tools of your own that Oskar never thought of.

On Monday, Mira opens FontLab again.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: You can now say what a script is, open a font in FontLab and name what you see: a font, its glyphs, their names. You have a copy of GG Plum that you're free to break. And you've run one line of Python, broken it and mended it.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. In the Font window of Plum-practice, open o in the Glyph window, then d. Compare the gap between the drawing and the vertical line on the left side. Does it look the same in both? Now compare the gaps on the right. Should those match? Hold on to your answers. In Part 4 a script will give you the numbers.
  2. Count the glyphs in the font by hand, or try to. Stop when you get bored and write down how far you got. Chapter 4 does it in a few lines.
  3. Write your own list. Think of three jobs from your own work that fit the sentence "for every one of these, check this, then do that." Keep the list near your desk. By the end of Part 2 you'll be able to script at least one of them.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: In chapter 2 you take the line you ran today apart, piece by piece.

docs.title: 2. Say hello to FontLab
docs.text:
Monday morning. Mira has Plum-practice open and Oskar's sheet propped against her monitor. On Friday she ran one line with Oskar leaning over her shoulder. Today the chair next to hers is empty, and she can't remember which menu he used.

"Where did he type it?" she asks the empty chair.

Her phone buzzes. Oskar, from a train: Window menu. Panels. Scripting. Type something, press the triangle. Don't think too hard yet.

It's good advice, and it's the plan for this chapter. You ran one line yesterday. Today we take it apart: where it goes, what each piece of it does, and what happens when you change the pieces. No font work yet.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9, running.
  • Plum-practice open, from chapter 1. We won't touch it today, but it's a good habit.

docs.title: The two panels, properly this time
docs.text:
Choose Window > Panels > Scripting, if the panel isn't open already.

Most of the panel is a blank area, like an empty page. It's a text editor that lives inside FontLab, and it's where you type Python. Along the top is a small toolbar. At its left end is a button with three lines, ≡, which opens the panel's own menu. Next to it is the triangle, ▶, which FontLab calls Run script.

Now choose Window > Panels > Output.

You don't type in this one. The Output panel is where FontLab talks back. When a script has something to say, it says it here. When a script goes wrong, the complaint lands here too.

Drag the two panels so you can see both, and keep both visible for the rest of this book. You write on one side. FontLab answers on the other.

Type Friday's line again and run it.

print("Hello, Mira")

Hello, Mira

Your panel may show the time in front of each line. I leave it out.

Now click Run script a second time and watch the Output panel. One of two things happens. Either a second Hello, Mira appears under the first, or the panel empties and shows one fresh greeting. Which one you get depends on a setting, and I'd like you to choose it yourself. Open the ≡ menu of the Scripting panel and find Clear Output Panel. When it's on, every run starts with a clean Output panel. Turn it on. From now on, what you see in the Output panel is what the last run did, with no leftovers from earlier.

If you got an error and no greeting, compare your line with mine, one character at a time. Lowercase print. An opening parenthesis straight after it. Double quote marks from the plain quote key. A closing parenthesis.

docs.title: Take the line apart
docs.text:
One line, three pieces.

print is a function. A function is a named job that Python knows how to do. This one's job is to write something to the Output panel. Python comes with dozens of functions, FontLab adds many more, and from chapter 16 on you'll write your own.

The parentheses are how you tell a function to go. Whatever sits between them is what you hand to the function to work on. Think of a letterbox: print is the box and the parentheses are the slot. You push something through the slot and the function deals with it.

"Hello, Mira" is a string. String is the programmer's word for a piece of text. The quote marks aren't part of the text. They're the fence around it, and they tell Python: everything between these two marks is text, so don't try to understand it, only carry it.

Python reads everything you type and tries to make sense of it as instructions. The quote marks are how you say "this part isn't an instruction, this is words." Inside the fence you can put anything:

print("Find kerning pairs that are larger than they should be.")

Find kerning pairs that are larger than they should be.

Python doesn't know what kerning is. The text was inside the fence, so Python carried it to the Output panel and left it there.

The fence can be built from double quote marks or single ones. Python accepts both, as long as the mark that opens the string is the mark that closes it.

print("Halfmoon Type")
print('Halfmoon Type')

Halfmoon Type
Halfmoon Type

Why have two kinds? Because sometimes the text has a quote mark in it.

print("Oskar's list")
print('Ines says "Friday"')

Oskar's list
Ines says "Friday"

The first string has an apostrophe inside, so it gets double quotes outside. The second has double quotes inside, so it gets single quotes outside. Python sees the opening mark and treats everything as text until it meets the same mark again. In this book I use double quotes unless the text forces me to do otherwise.

docs.title: More than one line
docs.text:
A script can have as many lines as you want. Python reads them from the top down, one after another, the way you read a recipe.

Replace what's in the Scripting panel with this:

print("Count the glyphs and tell Ines.")
print("Find the glyphs that are still empty.")
print("Make a table of every glyph and its width.")

Run it.

Count the glyphs and tell Ines.
Find the glyphs that are still empty.
Make a table of every glyph and its width.

Three instructions, three lines of output, in the same order. Each print starts a fresh line in the Output panel.

Swap the first and last lines of the script and run it again. The output swaps too. The order of your lines is the order of events. The computer does what you wrote, in the order you wrote it, and nothing else.

docs.title: Numbers, alone and in company
docs.text:
Text goes in quotes. Numbers don't.

print(205)

205

That's the number of glyphs in GG Plum. Without quotes, Python understands 205 as a quantity, something it can do arithmetic with:

print(205 * 3)

615

The star means "times". GG Plum has 205 glyphs and three weights, so there are 615 drawings in that file. Python worked it out before printing.

Now put the same thing inside quotes and see what changes.

print("205 * 3")

205 * 3

No arithmetic. Inside the fence it's text, and Python carries text without reading it. So 205 and "205" are different things. The first is a number. The second is a picture of a number. You'll mix them up one day, and chapter 3 shows you what Python says when you do.

The other arithmetic signs are what you'd guess: + to add, - to subtract, / to divide.

print(1000 - 742)
print(600 / 2)

258
300.0

Look at the 300.0. Division gives an answer with a decimal point, even when it comes out even. Python keeps two kinds of numbers, whole ones and ones with a decimal point, and chapter 11 explains why a type designer should care. For today, 300.0 is 300.

You can also push more than one thing through the slot. Put a comma between them.

print("Plum has", 205, "glyphs")

Plum has 205 glyphs

Three things went in: a string, a number, a string. print wrote them on one line and put a space between each. You didn't have to type the spaces.

Most reports in this book have this shape. Some words to say what the number is, then the number. At the moment you're typing the 205 yourself. In chapter 4 FontLab supplies it, and the line looks much the same.

You can do the sum inside the print, too:

print("That makes", 205 * 3, "drawings in three weights")

That makes 615 drawings in three weights

docs.title: An old habit that no longer works
docs.text:
Sooner or later you'll find a FontLab script on the internet, or in a forum post from years ago, that prints like this:

print "Hello, Mira"

No parentheses. Type that into the Scripting panel and run it. Go on, do it on purpose.

No greeting. The Output panel shows an error, and its last line reads:

SyntaxError: Missing parentheses in call to 'print'. Did you mean print(...)?

Nothing is damaged. Python read the line, couldn't follow it, and told you why. It even suggests the fix.

The reason is history. Python has had two major versions. In the old one, Python 2, print was written without parentheses. FontLab Studio 5 used Python 2, and many scripts from those years are still around. FontLab 9 uses Python 3, where print is a function like any other and needs its parentheses.

So when an old script fails on its first print, you know what happened and how to mend it. Put the parentheses back and run it again.

docs.title: Keep your script
docs.text:
What you type into the Scripting panel isn't saved anywhere until you save it. Let's keep today's work.

Put this in the panel:

print("Hello, Mira")
print("Plum has", 205, "glyphs")
print("That makes", 205 * 3, "drawings in three weights")

Run it once to be sure it works.

Hello, Mira
Plum has 205 glyphs
That makes 615 drawings in three weights

Then open the ≡ menu and choose Save Script As…. Go to the scripting-book folder you made in chapter 1, name the file hello.py and save.

Open the folder in Finder, or in File Explorer on Windows, and look at the file. A Python script is a plain text file whose name ends in .py. There's nothing else to it. You could open hello.py in any text editor and read it. You could email it to a friend, who would run it in their FontLab and get the same three lines.

To get it back later, use the same menu and choose Open Script. To start with a clean page, choose New Script.

In chapter 18 we move your scripts to a place where FontLab lists them in its Scripts menu, so you can run them without opening the panel at all. A folder on your desktop is fine until then.

Going deeper: the Console

The Scripting panel's toolbar has a toggle called Console panel. Turn it on and you get a prompt that looks like py>. Type a line of Python there, press Enter (Enter on Windows), and it runs at once. The Console is handy for one-line questions. This book uses the main editor, because a script you can save is a script you can run again.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: You know where Python goes in FontLab and where the answers come out. You can print text and numbers, on one line or several, and let Python do the arithmetic on the way. And you have a first script, hello.py, saved as a file you can open and run again.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Write a script that prints your name, the name of a typeface you're working on and how many weights it has, each on its own line.
  2. A font has 420 glyphs and four weights. Make Python print the sentence That is 1680 drawings, with Python doing the multiplication.
  3. Print this line, quote marks and apostrophe included: "Oskar's" list. Try double quotes on the outside, then single ones. If neither works, good. Bring the error text with you to chapter 3.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: In chapter 3 you make mistakes on purpose and learn to read what Python says about each one.

docs.title: 3. Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Tuesday. Mira types a line from memory, clicks the triangle, and the Output panel fills with text she didn't write.

She pulls her hands off the keyboard as if it were hot.

"I broke it," she tells Ines, who's passing with coffee.

Ines looks at the screen. "Is the font still there?"

It is. Plum-practice sits in its window, every glyph in place.

"Then you didn't break it," Ines says. "You got a letter of complaint. Read it."

That text is called an error, and an error is Python telling you what kind of problem it found, where, and often how to fix it. People who script for a living get these letters many times a day. They don't make fewer mistakes than a beginner. They've stopped being afraid of the letter, and they read it. So today you make mistakes on purpose, one at a time, with me standing next to you.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with the Scripting and Output panels open, as in chapter 2.
  • Clear Output Panel turned on in the Scripting panel's ≡ menu, so each run starts clean.

docs.title: Names Python doesn't know
docs.text:
Start with a line that works.

print("Oskar")

Oskar

Now take the quote marks away and run it again.

print(Oskar)

No Oskar this time. Read what you got from the bottom, because the last line is the one that counts:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
NameError: name 'Oskar' is not defined

The lines above the last one may look a little different in your Output panel. Here's how to read the whole thing.

The top line, Traceback, means "here's the path I was on when I fell over." You can skip it.

The middle line says where. The part to look for is line 1. Python counts the lines of your script from the top, starting at 1, and tells you which one it was reading when things went wrong.

The last line says what. It has two halves with a colon between them. NameError is the kind of problem. name 'Oskar' is not defined is the explanation, in something close to English.

So what happened? Remember the fence from chapter 2. Inside quote marks, text is only text. Without the fence, Python tries to understand the word. It reads Oskar and assumes this must be the name of something it has been told about. It looks through everything it knows, finds no Oskar and gives up. Name not defined means "you're talking about something as if I should know it, and I don't."

Put the quotes back. The error goes away.

NameError nearly always means one of two things: you forgot the quotes around some text, or you mistyped a name.

Here's the mistyped kind. Run this.

Print("Oskar")

NameError: name 'Print' is not defined

From here on I show only the last line of each error, since that's where the news is.

Same kind of error, different cause. Python is case-sensitive. To Python, print, Print and PRINT are three different words, the way a and A are two different glyphs to you. Python knows print. It has never heard of Print.

Your message may be a little longer than mine. Some versions of Python add a guess at the end, such as Did you mean: 'print'? When Python offers a guess, try it. So read every message to its end before you start hunting.

Glyph names are case-sensitive too. A and a are different glyphs, Aacute and aacute are different glyphs, and a script that asks for germandbls won't find Germandbls. A lot of scripting is spelling.

docs.title: A string with no end
docs.text:
Now take away only the closing quote mark. You met this one on Friday.

print("Oskar)

SyntaxError: unterminated string literal (detected at line 1)

A new kind: SyntaxError. Syntax is grammar. A NameError means Python understood your sentence but didn't know one of the words. A SyntaxError means Python couldn't make out the sentence at all.

In plain words, "unterminated string literal" says: a piece of text was opened and never closed. Python saw the opening quote, started treating everything after it as text, and ran off the end of the line still waiting for the closing mark. The fence has no second post.

These two kinds of error behave differently, and you can test it. Run this three-line script, where the mistake is on the last line:

print("one")
print("two")
print(Oskar)

one
two
NameError: name 'Oskar' is not defined

Python ran the first two lines, printed their output and stopped at the third. Now change the last line to the broken string:

print("one")
print("two")
print("Oskar)

SyntaxError: unterminated string literal (detected at line 3)

No one, no two. Nothing ran. Before Python runs a script, it reads the whole thing to check the grammar. If the grammar is wrong anywhere, it refuses to start.

Keep that in mind when you begin changing fonts. A SyntaxError means nothing happened. Any other error means the script got some of the way and stopped, so some of your glyphs may be changed and others not. Part 2 shows you how to make that safe.

A quote mark inside the quotes

At the end of chapter 2 I asked you to print "Oskar's" list. Whichever mark you put on the outside, the same mark inside ended the string too early. The way out is the backslash. \' means "this apostrophe is part of the text", so print('"Oskar\'s" list') works. The backslash itself isn't printed.

docs.title: The quotes a type designer loves
docs.text:
Copy this line from the page and paste it into the Scripting panel. Don't retype it.

print(“Oskar”)

SyntaxError: invalid character '“' (U+201C)

To your eye, those are the correct quote marks. They're the ones you draw with care and kern against the A and the T. Python can't use them.

This message speaks your language. It shows you the character it stopped at, and then its Unicode value, U+201C. That's the left double quotation mark. Python wants U+0022, the plain straight one, or U+0027, the plain apostrophe.

You get curly quotes when code passes through a program that tries to help with typography: a word processor, an email, some chat apps, a note-taking tool. They see straight quotes and curl them. The fix is to retype the quote marks yourself, from the plain quote key.

The same thing happens with dashes. A minus sign that has been turned into an en dash gives you the same error with a different number. When you see invalid character, look at the number and you'll know what crept in.

docs.title: The parenthesis that never closed
docs.text:
Leave off the last parenthesis.

print("Oskar"

SyntaxError: '(' was never closed

Every opening parenthesis needs a closing one. The same holds for the square brackets and curly braces you'll meet later.

A close cousin turns up when you leave out a comma between two things:

print("Plum has" 205)

SyntaxError: invalid syntax. Perhaps you forgot a comma?

"Invalid syntax" is the vaguest thing Python says. It means "this isn't a sentence, and I can't tell you more." Here it adds a guess, and the guess is right. When it adds nothing, look for what's missing: a comma, a parenthesis, a quote mark.

docs.title: Text plus a number
docs.text:
One more, and this one is a different sort of trouble. The grammar is fine, and every name is known.

In chapter 2 you joined things with commas inside print. A plus sign can join two strings as well:

print("Half" + "moon")

Halfmoon

The plus glues the two strings end to end. Now try gluing a string to a number.

print("Plum has " + 205)

TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

A TypeError means you asked for something that doesn't make sense for the kind of thing you have. "Concatenate" is a long word for "glue end to end." str is short for string. int is short for integer, a whole number. So the message says: I can glue a string only to another string, and you handed me a whole number.

Python won't guess. Should "Plum has " + 205 glue, or add? It refuses to pick, and tells you so.

There are two ways out. The first you already know: use a comma, and let print handle it.

print("Plum has", 205)

The second is to turn the number into a string yourself, with a function called str:

print("Plum has " + str(205))

Both print Plum has 205. In this book I use the comma for quick reports. Chapter 12 shows a third way, the one I use for tables.

docs.title: How to read any error
docs.text:
Every error in this chapter gave way to the same routine, so here it is in one place. When the Output panel shows an error:

  1. Go to the last line. That's the message.
  2. Read the word before the colon. It tells you the kind of problem. SyntaxError: the grammar is wrong, and nothing ran. NameError: Python met a word it doesn't know. TypeError: wrong kind of thing for the job.
  3. Read the rest of that line, to the end. If Python offers a guess, try it.
  4. Find the line number, in the message or in the lines above it, and look at that line in your script, one character at a time.
  5. Change one thing, and run again. One thing. If you change three things and the error goes away, you won't know which one mattered.

Here's the list Mira pins to the wall next to Oskar's sheet.

The last line starts with In plain words Look for NameError: name '…' is not defined Python doesn't know this word missing quotes, a typo, a wrong capital letter SyntaxError: unterminated string literal a string was opened and not closed a missing or mismatched quote mark SyntaxError: invalid character a character Python can't use curly quotes or a dash pasted from elsewhere SyntaxError: '(' was never closed a parenthesis is missing count the opening and closing ones SyntaxError: invalid syntax Python can't follow the line a missing comma or other small mark SyntaxError: Missing parentheses in call to 'print' an old Python 2 script put parentheses around what print gets TypeError: can only concatenate str text glued to a number with + use a comma, or str()

Later chapters add rows to this table as new kinds of trouble turn up. Chapter 19 comes back to errors with a font open and real work at stake.

One last thing. Sometimes you'll meet an error whose message you can't make sense of, however slowly you read it. Copy the last line and paste it into a search engine. Somebody has had it before you, and somebody else has explained it. Every programmer does this.

Mira reads her letter of complaint again, from the bottom this time. NameError: name 'Print' is not defined. She looks at her line, fixes the capital P and clicks the triangle.

"Complaint withdrawn," she says.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: You can read an error now: last line first, the kind before the colon, then the line number. You know that a SyntaxError means nothing ran, and that any other error means the script stopped part of the way through. The table above is your summary. Keep it where you can see it.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Each of these three lines has one mistake. Run them one at a time. Before you run a line, say out loud which error you expect, then see if you were right.

    print("Regular", "Bold)

    print(Light)

    pront("Bold")

  2. Write a three-line script where the second line has a NameError. Run it and note which lines printed. Then change the mistake into a SyntaxError and run it again. What printed this time, and why?

  3. Open hello.py from chapter 2 and add one of these lines at the end: print(10 / 0) or print("Plum" * "3"). Run it and read the message. Then add your own row to the table above.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: In chapter 4 you install the toolbag that Oskar's scripts depend on, and FontLab counts the glyphs for you.

docs.title: 4. Pack the toolbag
docs.text:
Wednesday. Mira finds a folder on the studio server called chores. Inside are Oskar's scripts, dozens of them, with names like width_report.py and mark_empty.py.

She opens the first one in the Scripting panel. The top line reads:

from fly import fl

She clicks the triangle. An error. This time she reads it from the bottom, the way she learned yesterday.

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'fly'

She messages Oskar: What is fly and why don't I have it?

The answer comes an hour later. My fault. Fly is the toolbag. Every script I wrote reaches into it. It was on my machine, not yours. Install it once and forget about it.

Today you install things. No glyph gets counted until the last five minutes. But every chapter after this one starts with the line that failed on Mira's screen, so this is the day that makes the rest possible. Put the kettle on.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9, and Plum-practice from chapter 1.
  • An internet connection.
  • About twenty minutes.

docs.title: Why a toolbag at all
docs.text:
In chapter 2 you used print. Nobody installed it. print is part of Python, in the same way that the letter a is part of every text font.

FontLab adds its own words to Python: words for fonts, glyphs, contours, kerning. They are built into the app too. But they were made for the programmers who build FontLab, and they show it. Asking for a simple thing in those words can take five lines and some knowledge of how FontLab is put together inside.

So over the years, people who script FontLab have written friendlier words on top. One line where there were five. Sensible names. Protection against the usual accidents. These friendly words live in packages. A package is a folder of Python files that somebody else wrote, tested, and gave a name, so that your script can borrow from it.

There are several of these packages, written by different people for different jobs. That could mean learning ten names and remembering which word lives where. Fly solves that. Fly is one small package that holds the door to all the others. You ask Fly, and Fly fetches.

Here is what is in the bag. You don't need to remember any of it today.

You write You get Good for fl FontLab's own words fonts, glyphs, layers, the app itself fg FontLab's font storage names, Unicode values, kerning, font info ap the FontLab app helpers everyday chores done safely, with Undo tr TypeRig work on outlines and nodes qt the window-building kit dialogs, buttons, panels qs a second window-building kit the same, with different spelling pr the command bridge driving FontLab's own commands gp a Glyphs-style dialect running scripts written for Glyphs fp a UFO-style dialect running scripts written for RoboFont and friends pens the drawing pens drawing outlines from numbers

For most of this book you will use three or four of them. The others wait in the bag until a chore needs them.

docs.title: Step 1: Install the installer
docs.text:
FontLab brings its own Python, but no package installer. Instamix supplies that missing piece. It sets up uv, the program that fetches Python packages, and a separate Python environment with the same version and architecture as FontLab. Both read the same package folder.

Download the current install.vfpy from the Instamix documentation site. You need version 1.0.9 or newer. In FontLab, choose File > Open and select that file. You can also double-click it if your system opens .vfpy files with FontLab.

This file works before Instamix is installed. It fetches and checks the package, including its distribution metadata. Keep the internet connection open and read the Output panel. Once it finishes, check in the Scripting panel:

from importlib.metadata import version

print(version("fontlab-python-instamix"))

You need 1.0.9 or a later version. This matters if you have an older installation: 1.0.8 had a failed-upgrade bug that could remove other files recorded by an old installer. Use the current standalone installer before upgrading those tools. A current generated installer also checks that its provider has the corrected rollback support.

You do not need to install uv separately. Instamix finds or downloads it when a package needs it.

docs.title: Step 2: Put the packages side by side
docs.text:
Make a new folder somewhere you won't delete it by accident. Your home folder is a good place. Call it fontlab-scripting.

Into that folder you will put eight packages, each in its own folder. Seven come from the fontlabcom account on GitHub. TypeRig comes from its author's account, kateliev.

Folder What it is fontlab-fly Fly, the door to the rest fontlab-echopy lets Fly reach fl, fg and pr fontlab-fontlabapp the app helpers, ap fontlab-python-pens drawing tools that the app helpers use TypeRig tr pythonqtside qs fontlab-glyport gp fontlab-fontport fp

For each one, open its page on GitHub, click the green Code button, and choose Download ZIP. Unzip it and drag the folder into fontlab-scripting. GitHub adds -main to the folder name. You can leave that or remove it. The installer doesn't go by folder names.

What matters is that the eight folders are neighbors, all directly inside fontlab-scripting, like this:

fontlab-scripting/
    fontlab-echopy/
    fontlab-fly/
    fontlab-fontlabapp/
    fontlab-fontport/
    fontlab-glyport/
    fontlab-python-pens/
    pythonqtside/
    TypeRig/

Here is why. When you install Fly in the next step, it looks at the folders next to its own and installs every neighbor it needs. One step, eight packages. If a folder is nested one level too deep, or sitting on your desktop, Fly won't see it.

If you know Git, clone the eight repositories into the folder. The result is the same, and updating later takes one command per folder.

docs.title: Step 3: Run the installer
docs.text:
Open the fontlab-fly folder. Near the top is a file called install.vfpy.

A .vfpy file is a Python script that belongs to FontLab. It is a plain text file like hello.py, but macOS knows to hand it to FontLab when you open it.

Make sure FontLab is running and the Output panel is visible. Then double-click install.vfpy, or drag it onto the FontLab window.

The script starts at once. Watch the Output panel. Lines appear, one group for each package, as Fly works through its neighbors:

Installing dependency fontlab-echopy>=0.1.0 from /Users/mira/fontlab-scripting/fontlab-echopy

A dependency is a package that another package needs. You will see that word a lot in the next minute. FontLab may stop responding while this runs. Leave it alone. A script and the FontLab window take turns, and while a script is busy, FontLab can't redraw itself or answer your clicks.

Read the final result in the Output panel. A successful install records Fly under com.fontlab.fly; Scripts > Instamix provides the list and uninstall commands. Use Refresh Scripts if that submenu is not visible yet.

An error is a reason to read the named requirement or path before trying again. A missing or incompatible neighbor, an unavailable dependency version, or a file you edited can stop installation. Keep your edited files. Corrected Instamix restores the project's earlier files and receipts if its replacement fails; dependencies installed separately may remain. If restoration itself fails, the error names a retained recovery folder. Keep it.

A timeout does not tell you whether work stopped. Check the output and installed records before repeating the operation.

docs.title: Step 4: Restart FontLab
docs.text:
Do what the last line says. Quit FontLab and start it again.

FontLab reads its list of packages once, when it starts. Until you restart, it doesn't know that anything new arrived.

Open Plum-practice again, and bring back the Scripting and Output panels if they aren't showing.

docs.title: Step 5: Reach into the bag
docs.text:
Now type the line that failed for Mira this morning.

from fly import fl

Run it.

Nothing happens. The Output panel stays empty.

That's the result you want. In Python, no news is good news. The line asked for something, got it, and had nothing to report.

Read the line as an English sentence: from Fly, import fl. Import means "bring this in so that I can use it." Before this line runs, your script knows Python and nothing else. After it, your script also knows fl, and fl knows FontLab.

You will type some version of this line at the top of every script from now on. If a chore needs the app helpers too, you ask for both, with a comma:

from fly import fl, ap

Now make the mistake Mira would make.

from fly import fontlab

ImportError: cannot import name 'fontlab' from 'fly'

There may be a folder path at the end of your message. A new kind of error for the list on the wall, and it reads plainly: Fly has no tool by that name. The tools have the short names from the table near the top of this chapter. Fix the line and run it again.

docs.title: One extra package
docs.text:
Some later scripts need a package from the Python Package Index, PyPI. Once Instamix is installed, a script can ask for one directly:

from fontlab_instamix import install_packages

install_packages("fonttools>=4")

The requirement uses the distribution's PyPI name. Its Python import name can differ: fonttools is imported as fontTools. Instamix refreshes import caches after installation; it does not reload a module that is already running. Compiled packages must match FontLab's Python and architecture. Don't use Terminal's unrelated Python as a substitute.

docs.title: The first question
docs.text:
You have earned something for all that installing. Put this in the Scripting panel, with Plum-practice open:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
print("This font has", len(font), "glyphs")

Run it.

This font has 205 glyphs

In chapter 2 you typed that 205 yourself. This time you didn't. FontLab looked at the font in front of you and counted.

Open a different font and run the same four lines. The number changes. You didn't change the script. That's the moment where a script stops being a typing exercise and starts being a tool: the same words, pointed at a different font, give a different and correct answer.

I have used two things here without explaining them: the font = line, and the dots. The next two chapters are about them. For today, read the script like this. Line 1 opens the bag. Line 3 asks FontLab for the font you are working on. Line 4 counts its glyphs and prints the count.

Save the script as count.py in your scripting-book folder.

Mira runs it, reads the number, and crosses out the first line on Oskar's sheet: Count the glyphs and tell Ines.

"Two hundred and five," she calls across the room.

"I know," says Ines. "But now you know how you know."

Going deeper: where it all went

The installer uses FontLab's data folder. On a Mac its default is ~/Library/Application Support/FontLab/FontLab 9; on Windows it is normally Documents/FontLab/FontLab 9. The packages are in python/3.11/site-packages there. Instamix keeps extension payloads under Extensions/Library and ownership records in Extensions/.instamix.

Scripts > Instamix contains List Extensions and uninstall commands. Uninstall removes recorded unchanged files and reports files it keeps because you changed them. Separately installed shared Python dependencies remain.

If you cloned the repositories with Git, the installer links to your folders and does not copy them. Move or delete fontlab-scripting and the packages stop working, so keep the folder where it is.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: You can now install a FontLab package: open its install.vfpy in FontLab, then restart. Fly is the one package your scripts ask, and from fly import fl is how they ask. You also know two new errors apart: ModuleNotFoundError means the package isn't installed, and ImportError means the package is there but the name you asked for isn't.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Choose Scripts > Instamix > List Extensions and read the Output panel. Look for a line that mentions Fly. I haven't seen this list myself, so I can't tell you how many lines to expect.
  2. Run from fly import fl, ap, tr as a one-line script. Then change tr to tR and run it again. Which error do you get, and which rule from chapter 3 did you break?
  3. Open another font you have, any font, and run count.py. Write the number down. Then check it against what the Font window says. If the two numbers differ, look at how the Font window is filtered before you blame the script.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 5 takes the four lines of count.py apart and shows you what a font looks like from Python's side: a list of glyphs.

docs.title: 5. A font is a list of glyphs
docs.text:
Thursday. Ines stops at Mira's desk with a coffee in each hand.

"The publisher wants to know what's first and what's last in the font. Don't ask me why. Somebody there has a spreadsheet."

Mira opens count.py. Four lines. She ran them yesterday and they worked, and she still can't say what the third one does.

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
print("This font has", len(font), "glyphs")

So today we take those four lines apart. By the end you'll have answered the publisher's question, and you'll have the one idea that the rest of this book stands on.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, from chapter 4.
  • Plum-practice open, and your count.py.

docs.title: Step 1: Put a number in a box
docs.text:
Start a new script. Leave FontLab's words out of it for a minute and type this:

glyph_count = 205
print(glyph_count)

Run it.

205

Look at the second line. There are no quotes around glyph_count, so Python doesn't print the word. It prints what the word stands for.

Here's the picture I use. The first line takes the value 205, puts it in a box, and sticks a label on the box that says glyph_count. From then on, whenever Python meets that label, it opens the box and uses what's inside.

The box with its label is called a variable. The = sign does the putting, and it works from right to left: the value on the right goes into the box named on the left. It doesn't mean "equals" the way it does in arithmetic. Read it as "becomes" and you won't go wrong.

You choose the label. A few rules come with that freedom. A label has no spaces, so people write an underscore where the space would go. It can't start with a digit. And capitals count, as they did in chapter 3: glyph_count and Glyph_count are two different boxes.

Now use the box for something.

glyph_count = 205
masters = 3
print(glyph_count * masters)

615

In chapter 2 you got that 615 by typing 205 * 3. The answer hasn't changed. What's changed is that the script now says what the numbers are. Come back to it in a month and glyph_count * masters still makes sense. 205 * 3 won't.

docs.title: Step 2: Ask for a box that isn't there
docs.text:
Delete the first line, so the script is this:

masters = 3
print(glyph_count * masters)

Run it.

NameError: name 'glyph_count' is not defined

You met NameError in chapter 3, when Python didn't know Print. It's the same complaint here. Python went looking for a box labeled glyph_count and nobody had made one.

If it ran without an error

FontLab can remember boxes from the script you ran a minute ago. If you got 615 again, open the Scripting panel's menu, choose Clear Python Context, and run the script once more. It's a good habit when a script behaves as if it knows something it shouldn't.

The order matters. Python reads your script from the top, one line at a time, and a box exists only after the line that fills it has run. Put the line back.

One more thing a box can do: take a new value.

glyph_count = 205
glyph_count = glyph_count + 4
print(glyph_count)

209

The middle line looks like nonsense if you read = as "equals". Read it right to left. Python opens the box, finds 205, adds 4, and puts 209 back in the same box. The old value is gone.

docs.title: Step 3: Put a font in a box
docs.text:
Now go back to line 3 of count.py.

font = fl.CurrentFont()

Right to left again. fl.CurrentFont() asks FontLab a question: which font is the person working on right now? FontLab hands back the font, and = puts it in a box labeled font.

So a box doesn't have to hold a number or a piece of text. It can hold a whole font. It's still a box with a label, and the next line can use the label.

Why bother with the box? Because without it you'd ask FontLab the same question on every line. You can call the box anything you like. font is what most people call it, and when I'm in a hurry I call it f. Stay with font for now, since it says what's inside.

The current font is the one in the Font window you clicked last. If you've got two fonts open, click the one you mean before you run the script.

docs.title: Step 4: Count without a font
docs.text:
Before we count the font, try len on something smaller. Start a new script:

names = ["A", "B", "C"]
print(len(names))

3

The square brackets make a list: several values in a row, separated by commas, kept in order. This one holds three pieces of text. len is short for length. Hand it a list and it tells you how many things are in it.

len is a function, like print. It has the same slot for you to push something through. The difference is what comes out. print writes to the Output panel. len hands a number back to your script, and what you do with that number is up to you. You can print it, put it in a box, or multiply it by three.

Not everything has a length. Try this:

print(len(205))

TypeError: object of type 'int' has no len()

int is Python's word for a whole number. A number isn't a row of things, so Python refuses to count it.

docs.title: Step 5: A font is a list of glyphs
docs.text:
Here's line 4 of count.py again, split in two so you can see the box:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph_count = len(font)
print("This font has", glyph_count, "glyphs")

This font has 205 glyphs

len worked on the font. That tells you something. A number has no length, but a font does, because to Python a font is a row of things kept in order. The things are glyphs.

That's the idea the title names. A font is a list of glyphs. Nearly every chore on Oskar's sheet comes down to going through that list and doing something with each glyph. Later you'll find lists inside the glyphs too. Once you can handle one list, you can handle them all.

Now for the publisher. Go back to the small list first, because it's easier to see what's going on.

names = ["A", "B", "C"]
print(names[0])
print(names[2])

A
C

Square brackets after a list mean "give me the one at this position". And Python starts counting at zero. The first thing in a list is at position 0, the second at position 1. I won't defend this. Every programmer trips over it for a week and then stops noticing.

It has one consequence you need today. A list of three things has positions 0, 1 and 2. There's no position 3.

print(names[3])

IndexError: list index out of range

Index is the word for the position number. The last thing in a list is always at the length minus one.

So, for the font:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph_count = len(font)
first = font[0]
last = font[glyph_count - 1]
print("Glyphs:", glyph_count)
print("First:", first)
print("Last:", last)

Run it.

Glyphs: 205
First: <fgGlyph '.notdef'>
Last: <fgGlyph 'tilde'>

Look at the top-left cell of the Font window, then scroll to the very last cell. The names match.

The odd wrapping, <fgGlyph '...'>, is what you get when you print a whole glyph. first isn't a piece of text. It's the glyph itself, with its drawing and its width and everything else, and all of that can't go on one line. So Python prints a short tag: the kind of thing it is, and its name. fgGlyph is the name FontLab's storage uses for a glyph. Tomorrow you'll reach inside and take out the name on its own.

Notice that I didn't type 204 for the last position. I wrote glyph_count - 1 and let the script work it out. Tomorrow somebody adds a glyph to the font, and the script is still right.

Save it over count.py.

Mira copies the three lines into a message to Ines. Ines forwards them to the publisher without comment, which at Halfmoon counts as praise.

docs.title: Step 6: When there's no font
docs.text:
One last experiment. Save Plum-practice and close its window, along with any other font you have open, so that FontLab has no font at all. Run count.py.

TypeError: object of type 'NoneType' has no len()

You saw this shape of message a few minutes ago, with 'int' in it. This time the thing without a length is a NoneType.

Here's what happened. Line 3 asked FontLab for the current font. There wasn't one. FontLab didn't complain. It handed back a special value called None, which is Python's way of saying "nothing here". The box labeled font got None in it, and the script carried on. It was line 4 that fell over, when len tried to count nothing.

So the error is on line 4, and the cause is on line 3. That happens a lot, and it's worth remembering the pattern: when a message mentions NoneType, look back up the script for the place where you asked for something and didn't get it.

Open Plum-practice again. In chapter 19 you'll teach your scripts to check for None themselves and say something kinder.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A variable is a labeled box: = puts the value on the right into the box named on the left, and the label then stands for whatever's inside. A list keeps things in order, len counts them, and square brackets pick one by position, starting at zero. To Python, a font is a list of glyphs, so the same two tools tell you how many glyphs a font has and which one sits where.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add two lines to count.py that print the second glyph in the font and the one before the last. Check both against the Font window.
  2. Make a list of the names of five glyphs you'd put in a test word, and print its length, its first item and its last item. Use len for the last one, not a number you counted yourself.
  3. In the names script, change names[0] to names[1.5] and run it. Read the message from the bottom. What does Python want between the brackets? Two words in the message are new; the first half is enough.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 6 opens up one glyph and asks it questions: its name, its Unicode value, its width.

docs.title: 6. Ask a glyph its name
docs.text:
Friday. The publisher's spreadsheet person has a name now, Tomas, and Tomas has a follow-up.

Thanks for first and last. Could I also get the Unicode value and the width of the capital A? I'm testing my import.

Mira could open the glyph and read both numbers off the screen. She knows that. She also knows Tomas will ask about another glyph on Monday, and another after that.

Yesterday's script printed a glyph as <fgGlyph 'tilde'>: a tag on a closed door. Today you open the door.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • count.py from chapter 5, for reference.

docs.title: Step 1: Take one glyph out by name
docs.text:
Yesterday you picked glyphs by position: font[0], font[glyph_count - 1]. That's fine for first and last. It's no use for the A, unless you want to count cells in the Font window.

A font lets you ask by name too. Start a new script:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph = font["A"]
print(glyph)

Run it.

<fgGlyph 'A'>

Same square brackets, but with a piece of text between them where the number was. The quotes matter. font[A] without them would send Python looking for a box labeled A, and you know which error that gives.

The glyph is now in a box labeled glyph. Printing the box gives you the tag again. So far, nothing new.

docs.title: Step 2: Open a drawer
docs.text:
Change the last line:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph = font["A"]
print(glyph.name)

A

No tag this time. You got the name, as plain text.

The new thing is the dot. Here's the picture, and we'll keep it for the rest of the book. A glyph is a wardrobe with labeled drawers. One drawer is labeled name, and the glyph's name is in it. Another is labeled width. The dot means "open this drawer": glyph.name is the name drawer of whatever is in the glyph box.

A thing with drawers is called an object. The font is an object. Each glyph is an object. A number like 205 is too plain to need drawers, but nearly everything FontLab hands you has them.

You've been writing dots since chapter 4. fl.CurrentFont() is a dot: fl is a wardrobe, and CurrentFont is one of its drawers.

Why does that one end in parentheses when glyph.name doesn't? Because the two drawers hold different kinds of thing. The name drawer holds a value, and you take it out. The CurrentFont drawer holds a function, and a function does nothing until you push something through its slot. Even when you have nothing to push, the empty parentheses are what make it go.

Leave them off and see what you get. Change the last line to this:

print(fl.CurrentFont)

No error. Python prints a tag in angle brackets, like the one you got for a glyph. That's the function itself, sitting in its drawer, not doing its job. If one of your scripts ever prints a tag where you expected an answer, look for missing parentheses. Put the line back the way it was.

docs.title: Step 3: Answer Tomas
docs.text:
Two more drawers.

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph = font["A"]
print("Name:", glyph.name)
print("Unicode:", glyph.unicode)
print("Width:", glyph.width)

Name: A
Unicode: 65
Width: 596.0

Both numbers need a word.

Unicode: 65. In chapter 1 we kept glyph and character apart. The glyph is the drawing. The character is the thing a person types. Unicode is the worldwide list that gives every character a number, and a font connects each glyph to the number of the character it draws. Capital A is number 65.

If you look at the glyph in FontLab, you'll see 0041 where the script says 65. They're the same number. FontLab writes it the way Unicode charts do, in a counting system with sixteen digits, and Python writes it the way you'd count on your fingers. Chapter 23 sorts this out. Until then, there's a function that translates:

print(hex(65))

0x41

Ignore the 0x in front. That's Python's way of saying "sixteen-digit number coming up".

Width: 596.0. This is the glyph's advance width: how far the cursor moves when somebody types an A. It's the drawing plus the space on its left and right. The unit is the font unit. Plum is drawn on a grid 1,000 units tall, so an A that's 596 wide is a bit more than half as wide as the grid is tall.

Plum comes in three weights, and the A is 596 wide in Regular and Bold and 554 in Light. If you get 554, you're looking at the Light. Part 6 is about weights. Until then, stay on Regular.

The .0 is Python telling you this number is allowed to have a fractional part, even though this one doesn't use it. Chapter 11 is about that.

Mira sends Tomas three lines. He replies with a thumbs-up and, as predicted, a second glyph.

docs.title: Step 4: Change one word, ask again
docs.text:
Tomas wants the n now. Change one line:

glyph = font["n"]

Name: n
Unicode: 110
Width: 523.0

One word changed, three correct answers. Try space. Try tilde.

Then try the very first glyph, the one called .notdef:

Name: .notdef
Unicode: None
Width: 500.0

There's None again, the "nothing here" value from yesterday. It isn't an error this time. .notdef is the glyph a font shows when somebody types a character the font doesn't have. No character belongs to it, so its unicode drawer is empty, and Python says so.

Now put two glyphs side by side. Mira does this by eye a hundred times a day: is the n wider than the o, and by how much? With two boxes the script can say.

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
n_width = font["n"].width
o_width = font["o"].width
print("n:", n_width)
print("o:", o_width)
print("Difference:", n_width - o_width)

n: 523.0
o: 520.0
Difference: 3.0

Look at font["n"].width. That's two steps on one line, read from left to right: take the n out of the font, then open its width drawer. You don't have to put the glyph in a box of its own first. When you only want one thing from it, you can reach straight through.

Three units. Mira would have guessed more. The round o looks narrower than the n on screen, and in Plum it nearly isn't. That's the kind of thing a script is good for: it doesn't replace your eye, but it tells you when your eye is guessing.

Some glyphs draw more than one character. For those there's a second drawer, unicodes with an s, which holds a list.

glyph = font["A"]
print(glyph.unicodes)

For the A that prints [65]: a list with one thing in it. You know lists from yesterday.

docs.title: Step 5: Ask for a glyph that isn't there
docs.text:
Tomas's third request is the small-cap A. Glyph names for small caps usually end in .sc, so:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph = font["a.sc"]
print("Name:", glyph.name)

Run it.

AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'name'

That's the last line of the message. From here on I'll often show only that line, because it's the one to read first. Attribute is Python's word for a drawer. So: something called NoneType has no drawer called name.

You saw NoneType yesterday, and the rule from yesterday holds. Look back up the script for the place where you asked for something and didn't get it. It's the line above. Plum has no small caps yet. You asked the font for a.sc, there was no such glyph, and the font handed back None. Then the last line tried to open a drawer on nothing.

This is the error you'll meet more than any other in this book. You'll get it from a typo in a glyph name. You'll get it from a wrong capital, because font["a"] and font["A"] are two different glyphs. Whenever you see 'NoneType' object has no attribute, the fault is almost never in the line Python points at. Something a little earlier came back empty.

Put "A" back.

docs.title: Step 6: The glyph in front of you
docs.text:
Typing a name into the script is one way to choose a glyph. Here's another. In the Font window, double-click the o so that it opens in the Glyph window. Then run this:

from fly import fl

glyph = fl.CurrentGlyph()
print("Name:", glyph.name)
print("Unicode:", glyph.unicode)
print("Width:", glyph.width)

Name: o
Unicode: 111
Width: 520.0

fl.CurrentGlyph() is the cousin of fl.CurrentFont(). It asks FontLab which glyph you're working on and hands it back. There's no name in the script at all now. Go to another glyph, run the script, and it reports on that one.

Save this as this_glyph.py. It's the first script in this book that you can use without editing it: go to a glyph, run, read.

If you run it with no glyph open, you'll get the NoneType message from step 5, for the same reason.

Going deeper: two kinds of glyph object

The glyph you get from fl.CurrentGlyph() or font["A"] is the one FontLab's storage keeps. It's called fgGlyph, and it's good for reading names, Unicode values and widths. FontLab has a second, richer glyph object for work on layers and outlines. The friendly tools in the bag hand you that one when a chore needs it, starting in chapter 8.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: An object is a wardrobe with labeled drawers, and a dot opens a drawer: glyph.name, glyph.unicode, glyph.width. You can take a glyph out of a font by name with font["A"], or ask FontLab for the one you're working on with fl.CurrentGlyph(). When either comes back as None, the next dot fails with 'NoneType' object has no attribute, and the cause sits a line or two above.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Use this_glyph.py to find the widest of these in Regular: m, w, M, W. Write the four widths down. You'll check them against a script in chapter 12.
  2. Add a line to this_glyph.py that prints the Unicode value the way FontLab shows it, using hex. Test it on A and on space.
  3. Change font["A"] to font["a"] in the script from step 3 and run it. Then try font["Å"]. One of these works and one doesn't. Find the name Plum uses for that glyph by looking at its cell in the Font window.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 7 stops asking one glyph at a time and puts the same three questions to all 205.

docs.title: 7. Do it to all of them
docs.text:
Monday of the second week. Tomas has stopped asking for one glyph at a time.

Can I have all of them? Name, Unicode, width. Whenever suits.

Mira does the sum. this_glyph.py takes about ten seconds a glyph if she's quick with the mouse. Two hundred and five glyphs. Half an hour of clicking, and she'd lose her place twice.

She messages Oskar. The reply comes from what looks like a train.

Don't click. Loop. Line 3 of my sheet has wanted doing for a year.

Line 3 of the sheet says: Make a table of every glyph and its width.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • this_glyph.py from chapter 6.

docs.title: Step 1: Say it once, run it three times
docs.text:
Start with the small list from chapter 5. Type this, and when you get to the second line, press Tab once before print:

for name in ["A", "B", "C"]:
    print(name)

Run it.

A
B
C

One print in the script, three lines in the Output panel.

Here's what Python did. It took the first thing in the list, "A", and put it in a box labeled name. Then it ran the pushed-in line, which printed what's in the box. Then it went back up, put "B" in the same box, and ran the pushed-in line again. Then "C". Then the list ran out, and Python stopped.

This is called a loop, and it's the reason scripting pays. You describe the job once. The computer does it for every item, in order, and doesn't lose its place.

Read the first line as a sentence: for each name in this list, do what follows. for and in are Python's words and you can't change them. name is a label, and labels are yours. The loop would work the same with x or banana there. Pick a word that says what one item is.

docs.title: Step 2: The colon and the push
docs.text:
Two small things on those two lines carry the whole meaning: the colon at the end of the first, and the space at the start of the second. Take each away in turn.

First the colon. Delete it and run.

    for name in ["A", "B", "C"]
                               ^
SyntaxError: expected ':'

That's about as plain as Python gets. The little arrow points at the spot. The colon says "a block of lines belongs to this one, and here it comes". Put it back.

Now the push. Delete the space in front of print so both lines start at the left edge, and run.

    print(name)
    ^^^^^
IndentationError: expected an indented block after 'for' statement on line 1

Indentation is the word for that space at the start of a line. In most writing it's a matter of taste. In Python it's grammar. The pushed-in lines are the ones the loop repeats. A line that isn't pushed in isn't in the loop, and a loop with nothing in it makes no sense, so Python stops.

The custom is four spaces. The Scripting panel puts them in for you when you press Tab, and after a line that ends in a colon it pushes the next line in on its own. To come back out, press Backspace at the start of the line.

docs.title: Step 3: What's inside and what's outside
docs.text:
A loop can repeat more than one line. Everything pushed in by the same amount belongs to it.

for name in ["A", "B", "C"]:
    print("Glyph:", name)
    print("Done")

Glyph: A
Done
Glyph: B
Done
Glyph: C
Done

Three times "Done" is probably not what the writer meant. Pull the last line back to the left edge:

for name in ["A", "B", "C"]:
    print("Glyph:", name)
print("Done")

Glyph: A
Glyph: B
Glyph: C
Done

Same words, different script. The only thing that changed is four spaces. When a loop does something too often, or only once when you wanted it every time, look at the left edge of your lines before you look at anything else.

The spaces have to line up exactly, too. If one line in the block is pushed in by four and another by two, Python complains that the indentation "does not match", and it's right.

docs.title: Step 4: Every glyph in the font
docs.text:
Now the real list. In chapter 5 I said a font is a list of glyphs. A font object keeps that list in a drawer called glyphs.

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    print(glyph.name)

Run it and watch the Output panel.

.notdef
A
Aacute
Abreve
Acircumflex
Adieresis

It goes on for 205 lines and ends with grave, ring, tilde. That's every glyph in Plum, in the order of the Font window, and it took less time than reading this sentence.

Go through the loop line the way you did in step 1. For each glyph in the font's list of glyphs: put it in a box labeled glyph, then run the pushed-in line. The first time around, glyph holds .notdef. The second time it holds A. Inside the loop you never say which glyph you mean. You say glyph, and the loop sees to it that the box holds the right one.

That's why the body of the loop can be the body of this_glyph.py, unchanged. Everything you learned to ask one glyph on Friday, you can now ask all of them.

Save this as list_names.py.

docs.title: Step 5: Tomas's table
docs.text:
Three questions, one line per glyph. Put the three answers into one print, separated by commas:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    print(glyph.name, glyph.unicode, glyph.width)

.notdef None 500.0
A 65 596.0
Aacute 193 596.0
Abreve 258 596.0
Acircumflex 194 596.0
Adieresis 196 596.0

And so on to the end:

grave 96 500.0
ring 730 500.0
tilde 732 500.0

There's the None for .notdef at the top, where you'd expect it from chapter 6.

Click in the Output panel, select everything, copy, and paste it into a message. Mira does. Tomas pastes it into his spreadsheet and writes back that the columns don't line up and the widths have a .0 he doesn't want. He's right on both counts. Chapters 11 and 12 fix them, and then line 3 of Oskar's sheet gets crossed out properly. For now Tomas has his numbers.

docs.title: A list of your own
docs.text:
The loop doesn't care where its list comes from. The font's list has 205 glyphs in it. You can write a shorter one yourself.

Type designers have glyphs they look at before any others. For Latin it's often H, O, n and o: a straight capital, a round capital, a straight lowercase and a round lowercase. If those four sit well together, the rest of the alphabet has something to follow. Mira checks them every morning.

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for name in ["H", "O", "n", "o"]:
    glyph = font[name]
    print(name, glyph.width)

H 672.0
O 708.0
n 523.0
o 520.0

This loop walks through four pieces of text, not through glyphs. So the first pushed-in line does what you did by hand in chapter 6: it uses the name to take the glyph out of the font. The second line prints. Two lines in the block, both run four times.

Notice the two kinds of square brackets, because they'll keep turning up together. The ones in the for line make a list. The ones in font[name] pick from a list. And name has no quotes in font[name], because it's a box this time. The quotes are already inside it.

Change the four names to the glyphs you check first in your own work. If you mistype one, you'll get the NoneType message from chapter 6, and it'll arrive partway through the output, after the names that were spelled right. That tells you which name to look at: the one after the last line that printed.

docs.title: Step 6: Count as you go
docs.text:
One more thing a loop is good for. Suppose you want to know how many times it went around. Make a box before the loop, and add to it inside:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
count = 0
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    count = count + 1
print("Counted", count, "glyphs")

Counted 205 glyphs

You know this move from chapter 5's glyph_count = glyph_count + 4: open the box, add one, put it back. Here it runs once per glyph. The last line sits at the left edge, so it runs once, after the loop has finished.

Yes, len(font) gives you 205 without the trouble. But this version can do something len can't. Tomorrow you'll add one line so that it counts only the glyphs you care about, and that's line 2 of Oskar's sheet.

Try the mistake that everybody makes once. Push the print line in by four spaces and run it. You get 205 lines, counting up from 1. Nothing's broken. The line moved inside the loop, so it runs every time around. Pull it back out.

Going deeper: the font itself as a list

You can count a font with len(font) and pick from it with font[0], so you might expect for glyph in font: to work as well. It may; I haven't tried it. Use font.glyphs in a loop. It's the form the tools in the bag use themselves, and it says what you mean.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A for loop takes the things in a list one at a time, puts each in a box you name, and runs the indented lines below it once for each. The colon opens the block and the indentation marks what's in it, so four spaces decide whether a line runs 205 times or once. With for glyph in font.glyphs: every question you can ask one glyph becomes a question you can ask the whole font.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Change list_names.py so that each line shows the glyph's width first and its name second.

  2. A piece of text is a row of characters, so a loop can walk through it. Run this, then put a glyph name from Plum in place of "Plum":

    for letter in "Plum":
    print(letter)

  3. Before the loop in step 6, make a second box called total and set it to 0. Inside the loop, add each glyph's width to it. After the loop, print it. You've measured how wide a line would be if somebody typed every glyph in the font once. With the Regular master showing, Plum-practice gives 102107.0.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 8 teaches the loop to be choosy: do something for a glyph only if it passes a test.

docs.title: 8. Only the ones I want
docs.text:
Tuesday. Ines forwards a one-line message from the publisher:

Before we plan the proofs: which glyphs in Plum are still empty?

Mira laughs, because she was about to make that answer longer. The small caps start today. Her plan is to add the glyph cells first, with nothing in them, and draw into them over the next weeks. So the honest answer to the publisher changes this morning, and it'll change again every time she finishes a letter.

It's also the second line on Oskar's sheet: Find the glyphs that are still empty.

Yesterday's loop treats every glyph the same way. It prints all 205 of them. Today the loop learns to ask a question about each glyph and to act only when the answer is yes.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open in a Font window.
  • list_names.py from chapter 7. You won't change it, but today's script starts the same way.

docs.title: Step 1: Ask a question that has two answers
docs.text:
Clear the Scripting panel, type this and run it:

print(5 > 3)
print(5 > 8)

True
False

You asked Python two questions. Is 5 greater than 3? Is 5 greater than 8? It answered each with one word.

Now ask about the font:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
print(font["A"].width)
print(font["A"].width > 600)

596.0
False

The A is 596 units wide, so "is it wider than 600?" gets a no.

A line like 5 > 3 is called a comparison. The two answers, True and False, are values, like 205 or "Plum". They aren't strings: there are no quotes around them, and the capital letter matters. Python knows True. It has never heard of true.

There are six comparison signs. You'll use all of them before the year is over:

You type It asks a > b is a greater than b? a < b is a less than b? a >= b is a greater than b, or equal to it? a <= b is a less than b, or equal to it? a == b are a and b equal? a != b are a and b different?

Look twice at the fifth one. Two equals signs. Step 3 is about what happens when you type one.

docs.title: Step 2: Do it only if the answer is yes
docs.text:
A question by itself prints True or False and that's all. To make the answer decide something, put the word if in front of it:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.width > 800:
        print(glyph.name, glyph.width)

AE 852.0
M 840.0
OE 989.0
W 859.0
Wacute 859.0
Wcircumflex 859.0
Wdieresis 859.0
Wgrave 859.0
oe 824.0
emdash 1000.0
at 848.0
