Eleven lines instead of 205. The loop still visits every glyph. For each one it asks "is your width greater than 800?", and it runs the print line only when the answer is True. The other 194 glyphs pass by in silence.

Read the shape of the if line. It's the shape of the for line from yesterday: a word, then something to work on, then a colon. And like for, it owns the indented lines below it. The print line is now indented twice, eight spaces. Four of them say "I belong to the loop". Four more say "and inside the loop, I belong to the if".

Press Tab twice to get there, or let the Scripting panel do it: after you type the colon and press Enter, the next line may start at the right depth already. Count the spaces if you aren't sure.

Change 800 to 900 and run it again. Two glyphs are left, the OE and the em dash. Change > to < and 900 to 200. One glyph is left: quotesingle, the straight quote, 190 units wide. You're asking the font questions now, and it takes about a second each.

docs.title: Step 3: One equals sign too few
docs.text:
In Plum, the O is 708 units wide. Which other glyphs have that same width? Type this, with one equals sign, and run it:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.width = 708:
        print(glyph.name)

  File "<string>", line 5
    if glyph.width = 708:
       ^^^^^^^^^^^
SyntaxError: cannot assign to attribute here. Maybe you meant '==' instead of '='?

Read the letter of complaint from the bottom, the way you learned in chapter 3. The last line says what went wrong and, this time, even offers the fix.

Here's the reason. In chapter 5 you learned to read = as "becomes". glyph_count = 205 puts 205 into a box. So glyph.width = 708 means "the width becomes 708". That's an order. After if, Python wants a question, and it got an order, so it stops before running anything. Nothing in your font changed.

The question is spelled with two signs. == reads "is equal to":

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
count = 0
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.width == 708:
        print(glyph.name)
        count = count + 1
print("Same width as O:", count)

O
Oacute
Ocircumflex
Odieresis
Ograve
Oslash
Otilde
Q
Same width as O: 8

The O, six accented versions of it, and the Q. That's a type designer's decision made visible: in Plum the Q is an O with a tail, and it takes up the same room.

Two more things happened in that script. First, the counter from chapter 7 moved inside the if. It used to count every glyph. Now it counts only the ones that pass the test, because the line that adds 1 is indented under the if. Second, there's one = and one == three lines apart, and they do different jobs. count = count + 1 gives an order. glyph.width == 708 asks a question.

Everybody types = where == belongs. I still do it. Python catches it every time, so it costs you five seconds.

docs.title: Step 4: What does empty mean?
docs.text:
Back to the publisher's question. A glyph cell is empty when nothing is drawn in it: no outline of its own, and nothing borrowed from another glyph either. The Aacute in Plum has no outline of its own, but it isn't empty. It's built from the A and the acute accent, and it shows up in text like any other letter.

The space glyph is the opposite case. It has a width of 230 units and nothing at all in it. It's empty on purpose.

The glyph you get from font.glyphs doesn't have a drawer that says "empty". It's the plain kind of glyph: name, Unicode value, width. For this question you need a second tool from the bag you packed in chapter 4. Type this and run it:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()
print(pGlyph(font, font["space"]).isEmpty())
print(pGlyph(font, font["A"]).isEmpty())
print(pGlyph(font, font["Aacute"]).isEmpty())

True
False
False

There's the answer for three glyphs: the space is empty, the A isn't, and the Aacute isn't either.

I owe you an explanation for two lines, and I'm going to pay only part of it today.

The second line is long. Treat it as a magic line for now: copy it exactly, dots and all. It fetches a tool called pGlyph from deep inside the toolbag. The path is long because the bag has many pockets, and this tool lives four pockets down. In Part 2 you'll learn to read such a line piece by piece.

pGlyph(font, glyph) takes two things through the slot: the font and one plain glyph from it. It hands back a richer version of the same glyph, one that knows more about its own drawing. One of the things it knows is isEmpty(). The parentheses at the end are there because isEmpty isn't a drawer with a value lying in it. It's a question the glyph works out when you ask, the way len() works out a count. Nothing goes through the slot, but the slot has to be there.

And what comes back is True or False. That's the kind of answer if wants.

docs.title: Step 5: Mira adds three cells, and the script finds them
docs.text:
Before the script runs over the whole font, give it something to find. Mira starts her small caps with three placeholders, and you'll do the same.

  1. Click the Font window of Plum-practice.
  2. Choose Font > New Glyph….
  3. Type the name a.sc and confirm.
  4. Do it twice more, for b.sc and c.sc.

You now have three new cells with nothing drawn in them. The name a.sc is a convention: the part before the dot says which letter it is, and the part after the dot says which version. sc is short for small cap. The next chapter takes such names apart.

Now the script. Start a new one:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()
count = 0
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if pGlyph(font, glyph).isEmpty():
        print(glyph.name)
        count = count + 1
print("Empty:", count, "of", len(font))

space
a.sc
b.sc
c.sc
Empty: 4 of 208

Save it as empty_glyphs.py in your scripting-book folder.

Look at the if line. There's no > and no == in it. There doesn't have to be. if needs something that is True or False, and isEmpty() already hands back one of the two. You could write if pGlyph(font, glyph).isEmpty() == True: and it would work, but it says the same thing twice, like "if it is true that the glyph is empty".

The font has 208 glyphs now, not 205, and len(font) knows it without being told. That's the reason the script asks the font for the count instead of having the number typed into it.

Mira writes back to the publisher: Four. One is the space, which stays empty. Three are small caps I started this morning. There will be more of those before there are fewer. Then she takes Oskar's sheet and crosses out line 2.

When she adds twenty more cells next week, she won't count them. She'll run empty_glyphs.py again.

docs.title: Step 6: Test for nothing
docs.text:
One more question, because it uses a value you met in chapter 5. In chapter 6 you saw that the unicode drawer holds a number for most glyphs. For a glyph without a Unicode value, the drawer holds None, Python's word for "nothing here". You can compare with it:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.unicode == None:
        print(glyph.name)

.notdef
a.sc
b.sc
c.sc

Four glyphs that no key on a keyboard reaches directly. The .notdef is the box a font shows when it has no glyph for a character. The three small caps have no Unicode value because Unicode has no separate numbers for small caps: an a is an a, however you dress it. Fonts reach such glyphs through OpenType features, which is a story for Part 5.

Notice that the two lists overlap but aren't the same. space is empty and has a Unicode value. .notdef has a drawing and no Unicode value. "Empty" and "has no Unicode value" are different questions, and now you can ask either.

Going deeper: is None

When you read other people's scripts, you'll see if glyph.unicode is None: more often than == None. Both work here. is asks "is this the very same thing?", and since Python keeps exactly one None, that's the stricter and more usual way to ask. Use whichever you can read aloud more comfortably. I'll write is None from now on.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A comparison such as glyph.width > 800 is a question, and Python answers it with True or False. Put if in front of the question and a colon behind it, and the indented lines below run only when the answer is True. Inside a loop, that turns "do it to all of them" into "do it to the ones I want". One = gives an order and two ask a question, and when you mix them up, Python tells you before anything runs.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Change the script from step 2 so it prints the glyphs that are 859 units wide or wider. Use >=. You should get seven names: OE, five W's and emdash.
  2. Change the script from step 6 so it counts the glyphs that do have a Unicode value, and prints only the count after the loop. Use !=. Add your number to the four glyphs from step 6. Do you get 208?
  3. In empty_glyphs.py, the if line picks the empty glyphs. Change it so the script counts the glyphs that are not empty, by comparing the answer with False. Don't save over the original.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 9 looks inside glyph names. A name is a string, a string is made of letters, and Python can check how a name starts, how it ends and what's in the middle. That's how you find every .sc without typing the list.

docs.title: 9. Strings are made of letters
docs.text:
Wednesday. Ines stops at Mira's desk with her coat still on.

"The small caps. How many are in the font so far?"

"Three," says Mira. She knows because she made them yesterday.

"And next month, when there are sixty, and some figures with a .tf on the end, and whatever else the publisher thinks of?"

Mira looks at Oskar's sheet. Line 9: When the small caps come: list every glyph whose name ends in .sc. He saw this coming.

Yesterday's loop picked glyphs by a number: wider than 800, exactly 708. Today it picks them by their names. A glyph name looks like one solid thing, but Python sees it as a row of characters, and it can check how the row starts, how it ends and what's in the middle.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open. It should have 208 glyphs, with the three small caps from chapter 8.
  • Nothing else. Today's script starts from an empty Scripting panel.

docs.title: Step 1: Ask a name how it ends
docs.text:
No font yet. Type this and run it:

name = "a.sc"
print(name.endswith(".sc"))

True

Then change the first line to name = "Aacute" and run it again.

False

You put a string in a box called name and asked it a question: do you end with .sc? The answer is one of the two values from yesterday, True or False.

Look at how the question is written. name, a dot, endswith, and then a slot with a string in it. You know the dot from chapter 6: it opens a drawer of the thing on its left. A glyph has drawers called name and width. It turns out a string has drawers too, and endswith is one of them. Like isEmpty() yesterday, it's a question the string works out when you ask, so it ends in parentheses. This time something goes through the slot: the ending you're asking about.

The whole word is lowercase. Type it with a capital W and see what happens:

name = "a.sc"
print(name.endsWith(".sc"))

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 2, in <module>
AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'endsWith'. Did you mean: 'endswith'?

You met AttributeError in chapter 6, when you asked for a drawer that wasn't there. Same thing here. 'str' object is Python's way of saying "a string", and a string has no drawer called endsWith. Python is fussy about capitals everywhere, in the names it gives things as much as in the names you give things. Put the small w back.

docs.title: Step 2: Find the small caps
docs.text:
A glyph's name is a string. So everything you can ask "a.sc", you can ask glyph.name:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
count = 0
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.name.endswith(".sc"):
        print(glyph.name)
        count = count + 1
print("Small caps:", count)

a.sc
b.sc
c.sc
Small caps: 3

Read the if line from left to right, one dot at a time. glyph is the glyph the loop is holding. .name opens its name drawer and takes out a string. .endswith(".sc") asks that string a question. Two dots, two drawers, one inside the other. The answer goes to if, and if decides whether the two lines below it run.

Save this as find_suffix.py in your scripting-book folder.

Why ".sc" with the dot, and not "sc"? Try the shorter one on a name you make up:

print("disc".endswith("sc"))
print("disc".endswith(".sc"))

True
False

Plum has no glyph called disc, but some font will. The dot is part of the convention, so the dot belongs in the test. When you write a test, think about what else might pass it.

That last listing also shows you something new: you don't need a box. A string in quotes can be asked directly. "disc".endswith("sc") works for the same reason name.endswith("sc") works. The box only holds the string. The string answers.

docs.title: Step 3: Ask how it starts
docs.text:
The opposite question is spelled startswith. Plum has a family of quotation marks, and their names all begin the same way. Change the if line in your script and the text in the last line:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
count = 0
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.name.startswith("quote"):
        print(glyph.name)
        count = count + 1
print("Quotes:", count)

quotedbl
quotesingle
quotedblbase
quotedblleft
quotedblright
quoteleft
quoteright
Quotes: 7

Seven quotation marks, found by their first five letters. If Mira wants to check that all of them sit at the same height, that's her list.

Now a test that goes wrong in an instructive way. Which glyphs are versions of the lowercase a? Change "quote" to "a" and run it. You get sixteen names, and they start out well: a, aacute, abreve, acircumflex. Then, further down:

ae
asterisk
asciitilde
ampersand
asciicircum
at
acute
a.sc

An asterisk is not a version of the letter a. Its name happens to begin with one. Python did what you said, and what you said was "starts with a". The test is too loose for the question you had in mind. There's no error message for that. The only protection is to read the list the first time you run a new test, before you trust the count. Chapter 13 gives you ways to tighten a test like this one.

docs.title: Step 4: Ask what's inside
docs.text:
Sometimes the interesting part of a name is in the middle or could be anywhere. For that, Python has a short word: in.

print("acute" in "Aacute")
print("Acute" in "Aacute")

True
False

in isn't a drawer. It stands between two strings, like > stands between two numbers, and it asks: does the row of characters on the left appear somewhere in the row on the right? The second line says False because of the capital A. Aacute contains acute but not Acute.

You've seen the word in before, in for glyph in font.glyphs:. There it's part of the loop's grammar. After if, or between two values, it's a question. Same word, two jobs, and Python tells them apart by what comes before.

Put it in the loop:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
count = 0
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if "acute" in glyph.name:
        print(glyph.name)
        count = count + 1
print("With acute:", count)

Aacute
Eacute
Iacute
Oacute
Uacute
Wacute
Yacute
aacute
eacute
iacute
oacute
uacute
wacute
yacute
acute
With acute: 15

Seven capitals, seven lowercase letters and, at the bottom, the accent itself. That last one is the acute glyph: the bare accent that the other fourteen borrow. If you're collecting "letters with an acute", it doesn't belong. If you're collecting "everything that changes when I redraw the acute", it's the most important line. The test is the same. Whether the answer is right depends on the chore.

One more use of in. Which glyphs have a dot anywhere in their name?

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if "." in glyph.name:
        print(glyph.name)

.notdef
a.sc
b.sc
c.sc

The three small caps, and .notdef, whose name starts with a dot. Keep that odd one in mind for the next step.

docs.title: Step 5: Take a name apart
docs.text:
A name like a.sc has two parts with different meanings. The part before the dot says which letter. The part after says which version. To work with them separately, cut the string at the dot:

name = "a.sc"
parts = name.split(".")
print(parts)

['a', 'sc']

split cuts a string wherever it finds the thing you passed through the slot, throws the cutting marks away, and hands back the pieces as a list. You know lists from chapter 5: square brackets, things in a row, counted from zero. So the base name is piece number 0 and the suffix is piece number 1:

name = "a.sc"
parts = name.split(".")
print(parts[0])
print(parts[1])

a
sc

What does split do with a name that has no dot?

print("Aacute".split("."))
print(len("Aacute".split(".")))

['Aacute']
1

A list with one piece: the whole name. Nothing to cut, so nothing was cut. That gives you a second way to recognize a suffixed name: split it, and count the pieces with len. More than one piece means there was a dot.

Now the odd one:

print(".notdef".split("."))

['', 'notdef']

Two pieces, and the first is '', a string with nothing between its quotes. The dot was at the very start, so the piece before it is empty. .notdef isn't a letter with a suffix. It's a special name that begins with a dot, and a script that treats it as "base name, then suffix" gets an empty base. You'll deal with it in step 6.

docs.title: Step 6: Print the base and the suffix
docs.text:
Put the pieces together. For every glyph with a suffix, print the suffix first, then the letter it belongs to:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    parts = glyph.name.split(".")
    if len(parts) > 1:
        print(parts[1], parts[0], glyph.name)

notdef  .notdef
sc a a.sc
sc b b.sc
sc c c.sc

There's .notdef in the first line, with its empty base name showing as a gap. To leave it out, the test has to be stricter. You could count the pieces and also check the base, but you can't join two tests yet. So use a test that fails for .notdef in the first place: go back to endswith.

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.name.endswith(".sc"):
        parts = glyph.name.split(".")
        print(parts[0], "is the base of", glyph.name)

a is the base of a.sc
b is the base of b.sc
c is the base of c.sc

The order of the lines matters here. The if comes first and lets only the small caps through. The split happens inside it, so it only ever cuts names that passed the test.

Mira runs find_suffix.py once more and tells Ines: three. Then she puts a pencil dot next to line 9 on Oskar's sheet. She won't cross it out while the list is three glyphs long. But the script is ready for sixty.

Going deeper: a string is a row you can count and pick from

len("Aacute") gives 6, the number of characters. "Aacute"[0] gives A, the first one. Counting and picking work on strings the way they work on lists. In the exercises of chapter 7 you walked through a string with a for loop for the same reason: to Python, a string is a row of characters in order.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A string can answer questions about itself: endswith and startswith check its two ends, and in checks whether a shorter string appears anywhere inside it. All three give True or False, so they fit after if. split cuts a string into a list of pieces, which is how you separate a base name from its suffix. A test on names does what you spell and not what you mean, so read the list it produces before you rely on it.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Change find_suffix.py so it lists the glyphs whose names end with grave. You should get fifteen. Which one of them isn't a letter?
  2. List every glyph with tilde anywhere in its name. There are eight. One of them is neither a letter with a tilde nor the tilde accent. What is it?
  3. Glyph names with exactly one character are the plain letters. Write a loop that counts the glyphs where len(glyph.name) == 1. How many do you expect before you run it?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 10 keeps what the loop finds. So far the names scroll past in the Output panel and are gone. With a list of your own, you can collect them, count them, sort them and take the first ten.

docs.title: 10. Keep a list
docs.text:
Thursday. Mira has run the "wider than 800" loop from Tuesday four times this morning, and each time she's done the same thing afterwards: scrolled up in the Output panel, read the names and counted them on her fingers.

The publisher's proofreader wants the wide glyphs on one proof page. Ines wants them in alphabetical order, because that's how the proofreader's checklist is sorted. And Mira wants to know which three come first, so she can start drawing the proof while the rest waits.

Three wishes, and the loop can't grant any of them. It prints a name and forgets it. By the time it reaches the em dash, it no longer knows it ever saw the AE.

She writes to Oskar: How do I make it remember?

Give it somewhere to put things, he answers. An empty list. Then append.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open, with 208 glyphs.
  • The "wider than 800" loop from chapter 8. You'll type it again in step 2.

docs.title: Step 1: Start empty, then add
docs.text:
In chapter 5 you made a list by typing everything that was in it: names = ["A", "B", "C"]. Today you start with nothing in it and add things one at a time. Type this and run it:

wide = []
print(wide)
print(len(wide))

[]
0

Two square brackets with nothing between them: an empty list. It's a real list. It has a length, and the length is zero. Think of an empty row with room at the end.

Now add to it:

wide = []
wide.append("AE")
wide.append("M")
print(wide)
print(len(wide))

['AE', 'M']
2

append is a drawer that every list has, the way every string has endswith. You pass one thing through the slot and the list puts it at the end of the row. Run append twice and the list holds two things, in the order you added them.

There's a difference from everything you've asked an object so far. endswith answers a question and leaves the string alone. append changes the list. After the line has run, the list is longer than before. You don't write wide = ... in front of it. The list in the box changes where it sits.

docs.title: Step 2: Let the loop fill the list
docs.text:
Here's Tuesday's loop with one line changed. Where it said print, it now says append:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
wide = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.width > 800:
        wide.append(glyph.name)

print(wide)
print(len(wide), "wide glyphs")

['AE', 'M', 'OE', 'W', 'Wacute', 'Wcircumflex', 'Wdieresis', 'Wgrave', 'oe', 'emdash', 'at']
11 wide glyphs

The loop runs in silence now. It visits all 208 glyphs, and each time one passes the test, its name goes onto the row. When the loop has finished, the row holds eleven names, and the two lines at the left edge look at it.

Mira doesn't have to count on her fingers any more. len(wide) does it. You also don't need the counter from chapter 7 here, the box that went count = count + 1. A list knows how long it is.

The order of three lines matters. wide = [] comes before the loop, so the row exists before anything goes onto it. The append is inside the if, so only the wide glyphs go in. The print lines are outside the loop, so they run once at the end.

Take the first of them away and see. Delete the line wide = [] and run the script:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 6, in <module>
NameError: name 'wide' is not defined

Read it from the bottom. You know NameError from chapter 3: Python met a name it had never heard. You asked it to append to wide, and there's no box with that label. Python won't guess that you wanted a list. Put the line back.

If you saw no error, that's the Scripting panel remembering the wide from your last run. Choose Clear Python Context from the panel's menu and run again. You met that trick in chapter 5.

There's a quieter way to get this wrong. Put wide = [] inside the loop, indented under the for line, and run it. No error. The output is [] and 0 wide glyphs, or one name if the last glyph in the font happens to be wide. The loop makes a fresh, empty row every time around and throws the old one away. When a list comes out empty and you expected it full, look at where it was born.

docs.title: Step 3: Pick from the list
docs.text:
The names are in a list of your own now, so everything you learned about lists in chapter 5 works on them. Add these lines at the bottom of the script:

print(wide[0])
print(wide[10])

AE
at

Number 0 is the first name. The list has eleven names, counted from zero, so the last is number 10. You could work that out each time as len(wide) - 1, the way you found the last glyph of the font in chapter 5. There's a shortcut:

print(wide[-1])
print(wide[-2])

at
emdash

A negative number counts from the end. -1 is the last one, -2 the one before it. It works on any list, however long, and you don't have to know the length.

docs.title: Step 4: Take a slice
docs.text:
Mira's third wish was the first three names. You could print wide[0], wide[1] and wide[2]. Or you can ask for a stretch of the list in one go:

print(wide[0:3])

['AE', 'M', 'OE']

That's called a slice. Inside the brackets there are two numbers with a colon between them: where to start, and where to stop. The start is included and the stop isn't. So 0:3 gives numbers 0, 1 and 2. Three things, which is also 3 minus 0. That's the reason for the odd rule: the count is always the second number minus the first.

A slice is a new list. The square brackets in the output tell you so. The original stays as it was, all eleven names.

You can leave either number out. Python fills in "from the start" or "to the end":

print(wide[:3])
print(wide[8:])
print(wide[-3:])

['AE', 'M', 'OE']
['oe', 'emdash', 'at']
['oe', 'emdash', 'at']

[:3] reads "the first three". [8:] reads "from number 8 to the end". [-3:] reads "the last three", and you'll use that one most: it works without knowing that the list has eleven things in it.

Slices are forgiving. wide[5] on a list of three gives you an IndexError, as you saw in chapter 5. wide[:50] on a list of eleven gives you all eleven and no complaint. A slice hands over what's there.

docs.title: Step 5: Sort it
docs.text:
Now Ines's wish. The names came out in the order the loop met them, which is the order of the glyphs in the font. That order was chosen by whoever built the font: capitals, then lowercase, then figures and punctuation, with the accents near the end. It's a sensible order for drawing. It isn't the alphabet.

print(sorted(wide))

['AE', 'M', 'OE', 'W', 'Wacute', 'Wcircumflex', 'Wdieresis', 'Wgrave', 'at', 'emdash', 'oe']

sorted takes a list through its slot and hands back a new list in order. It's a word that stands by itself, like len and print, not a drawer after a dot.

Compare the two outputs. The first eight names didn't move. The last three did: oe, emdash, at became at, emdash, oe. And look where they ended up. After Wgrave. In your alphabet, at comes long before M.

Python's alphabet isn't yours. It puts every capital letter before every lowercase letter. All of A to Z first, then all of a to z. That's because it compares characters by their Unicode numbers, the ones you saw in chapter 6: A is 65 and a is 97, so A comes first, and so does Z at 90. For glyph names this is often what you want anyway. It keeps the capitals together. If Ines's checklist is sorted the way a dictionary is, tell her about the difference before the proofreader finds it.

sorted did not change wide. Print wide again and it's still in font order. To keep the sorted version, put it in a box:

by_name = sorted(wide)
print(by_name[:3])
print(wide[:3])

['AE', 'M', 'OE']
['AE', 'M', 'OE']

Same three here, because the capitals were already in order. Now you have both lists and can use whichever the chore needs.

Sorting works on numbers too, smallest first. Collect widths instead of names and you get the answer to a different question:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
widths = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.width > 800:
        widths.append(glyph.width)

print(sorted(widths))
print(sorted(widths)[-3:])

[824.0, 840.0, 848.0, 852.0, 859.0, 859.0, 859.0, 859.0, 859.0, 989.0, 1000.0]
[859.0, 989.0, 1000.0]

The last line sorts the widths and slices off the last three: the three largest. Sorting and slicing together answer most "top three" questions you'll ever have. What this list can't tell you is which glyph each number belongs to. The names are in one list and the widths in another. Keeping them side by side is a job for Part 2.

docs.title: Step 6: The whole script
docs.text:
Here's what Mira saves. It collects, counts, sorts and shows the start:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
wide = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.width > 800:
        wide.append(glyph.name)

by_name = sorted(wide)
print(len(wide), "glyphs are wider than 800")
print("In font order:", wide)
print("By name:", by_name)
print("First three:", by_name[:3])

11 glyphs are wider than 800
In font order: ['AE', 'M', 'OE', 'W', 'Wacute', 'Wcircumflex', 'Wdieresis', 'Wgrave', 'oe', 'emdash', 'at']
By name: ['AE', 'M', 'OE', 'W', 'Wacute', 'Wcircumflex', 'Wdieresis', 'Wgrave', 'at', 'emdash', 'oe']
First three: ['AE', 'M', 'OE']

Save it as collect_and_sort.py in your scripting-book folder.

To print the names one per line, without brackets and quotes, loop over your own list. You did this in chapter 7 with a list you typed by hand. A list the script built is no different:

for name in by_name:
    print(name)

Look at the shape of the script, because most of the scripts in this book have it. First collect: a loop goes through the font and fills a list. Then work on the list: count, sort, slice, print. The two halves don't mix. When Ines asks for the widest three, or for the list backwards, you change the second half and leave the loop alone.

Mira sends the sorted list to the proofreader, with one line about capitals coming first. Then she starts the proof page with AE, M and OE.

Going deeper: append hands nothing back

Sooner or later you'll type wide = wide.append("AE"), by analogy with count = count + 1. Don't. append changes the list and hands back None. The line then puts that None into the box, your list is gone, and the next append fails with AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'append'. A bare wide.append("AE") is the whole instruction.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: An empty list, [], is a row you can fill, and append puts one more thing at its end. With the list made before the loop and the append inside the if, a loop collects what it finds instead of printing it and forgetting it. Once the names are in a list, len counts them, sorted hands back an ordered copy with capitals before lowercase, and a slice such as [:3] or [-3:] takes a stretch from either end.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Change collect_and_sort.py so it collects the glyphs narrower than 225 units. How many are there? In Plum as it came there are 14, and your three new glyphs may add to that. Print the last three in font order.
  2. Collect every glyph name in the font, with no if, and print the first ten of the sorted list. Which name comes first, and why does it come before A? The Unicode number of the dot is 46.
  3. Collect the names that contain dieresis, as in chapter 9. Print the length of the list, then loop over the sorted list and print one name per line.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 11 looks at the numbers themselves. Every width so far has come with .0 on the end, and nobody has said what a width of 596 is 596 of.

docs.title: 11. Numbers with units
docs.text:
Friday morning. Tomas, the publisher's spreadsheet person, is on the phone. He's laying out a sample page and wants to know how much room a line of Plum takes.

"How wide is the n?"

Mira has the answer in the Output panel. "Five hundred and twenty-three."

"Five hundred and twenty-three what? Millimeters? Points?"

She looks at the number. 523.0. It has a decimal point and a zero that nobody asked for, and no unit at all.

"I'll call you back," says Mira.

Two things are wrong with that number, and this chapter fixes both. The .0 is about how Python keeps numbers. The missing unit is about how a font keeps sizes. After today a width means something you can say on the phone.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • Nothing saved from earlier chapters. You'll use font["n"] from chapter 6 and the loop over a string from the exercises of chapter 7.

docs.title: Step 1: Two kinds of number
docs.text:
Start without the font. Type this and run it:

print(523)
print(523.0)
print(7 / 2)
print(8 / 2)
print(3 * 4)

523
523.0
3.5
4.0
12

Python keeps two kinds of number. A whole number, written without a decimal point, is called an integer, or int for short. A number with a decimal point is called a float. 523 is an int. 523.0 is a float. They're worth the same, and Python still treats them as two kinds of thing, the way a designer treats a 12 pt rule and a 12 pt gap as two kinds of thing.

The last three lines show the arithmetic signs you haven't met. You know + and -. The star * multiplies, because the keyboard has no multiplication cross. The slash / divides.

Look at 8 / 2. The answer is 4, and Python prints 4.0. Division always hands back a float, even when it comes out even, because most divisions don't. Multiplying two ints gives an int. One float anywhere in a sum is enough to put a decimal point on the result.

That's where Mira's .0 comes from. FontLab keeps every width as a float, so that a width of 523.5 would be possible. Plum's widths are all whole, and Python shows the decimal point anyway to tell you which kind of number it is holding.

One rule about order, the same one you learned at school:

print(2 + 3 * 4)
print((2 + 3) * 4)

14
20

Multiplying and dividing happen before adding and subtracting. Parentheses go first of all. When you're not sure, add parentheses. They cost nothing and they show the reader what you meant.

docs.title: Step 2: Ask the font for its unit
docs.text:
Now Tomas's question. 523 what?

A font has no millimeters in it. A typeface can be printed at 9 pt or painted two meters high, and the drawing is the same drawing. So a font measures everything on a grid of its own. The grid divides the height of the type size, which typographers call the em, into a fixed number of steps. Every width, every point of every outline, every sidebearing is counted in those steps. They're called font units.

How many steps make one em is the font's decision. Ask it:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
print(font.info.unitsPerEm)

1000

Two dots again, like glyph.name.endswith in chapter 9. font.info opens a drawer of the font that holds the facts about the font as a whole: its names, its measurements. Inside that drawer, unitsPerEm is the number of units in one em. You'll hear it called UPM. You can see the same number in FontLab under File > Font Info.

Plum's em has 1000 units. So the answer for Tomas is: the n is 523 units wide, and there are 1000 units to the em. Put the other way, the n takes 523 thousandths of the type size, a little more than half.

That's the reason the widths in a font look like they do. A width of 523 isn't large or small. It's a share.

docs.title: Step 3: Turn units into points
docs.text:
Tomas sets his sample in 12 pt. At 12 pt, the em is 12 points high, and those 12 points are divided into 1000 units. To get from units to points, divide by the UPM and multiply by the size:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
upm = font.info.unitsPerEm
print(font["n"].width / upm * 12)

6.276

The n is 6.276 points wide at 12 pt. Python worked from left to right: 523.0 divided by 1000 is 0.523, and 0.523 times 12 is 6.276.

Before you go on, break it. Suppose you'd typed the UPM in by hand, and out of habit put quotes around it:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
upm = "1000"
print(font["n"].width / upm * 12)

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 5, in <module>
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for /: 'float' and 'str'

Read the last line. TypeError you met in chapter 3: the wrong kind of thing. An operand is one of the two things on either side of a sign. So the letter says: I can't divide a float by a string. Inside the quotes, "1000" is four characters behind a fence, and you can't do sums with characters. Take the quotes away, or better, go back to asking the font. Then the script is still right when you open a font with 2048 units to the em.

Now try the capital A. Change "n" to "A":

7.151999999999999

Do it on paper and you get 7.152. Python is off by a hair in the fifteenth decimal place. Nothing is broken. A float is kept in a fixed amount of room, and some decimal fractions don't fit exactly, the way one third doesn't fit into any number of decimal places. The float holds the nearest value it can.

For a type designer, an error that small doesn't matter. What matters is that you don't hand Tomas a number with fifteen decimals.

docs.title: Step 4: Tidy the number
docs.text:
Python has two words for tidying a number. Try them next to each other:

print(int(6.276))
print(int(6.9))
print(round(6.276))
print(round(6.9))

6
6
6
7

int cuts the decimals off. It doesn't care what they were: 6.9 becomes 6. round goes to the nearest whole number: 6.9 becomes 7. Both hand back an int, without a decimal point.

round has a second slot. Pass a second number and it keeps that many decimals:

print(round(6.276, 1))
print(round(6.276, 2))
print(round(7.151999999999999, 2))

6.3
6.28
7.15

Two things go through the slot, with a comma between them: the number, and how many decimals to keep. The untidy 7.151999999999999 comes out as 7.15.

Which of the two do you use? When the number is whole already and only looks like a float, use int. It says "this is a count of units, show it as one". When the number has real decimals, use round, and decide how many decimals the reader needs. For a size in points, one is plenty.

Neither word changes the number you gave it. round hands back a new, tidy number. A number you keep in a box stays as exact as it was. So calculate with the exact number and round at the last moment, when you print.

docs.title: Step 5: Print widths without the .0
docs.text:
Here are four glyphs from chapter 7's table, with the widths tidied:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for name in ["H", "O", "n", "o"]:
    glyph = font[name]
    print(name, int(glyph.width))

H 672
O 708
n 523
o 520

No .0. The widths in the font are still floats. You changed how they're shown, and nothing else.

You may wonder whether the two kinds of number get in each other's way when you compare them. They don't:

print(523.0 == 523)

True

That's why glyph.width == 708 worked in chapter 8, with a float on the left and an int on the right. Python compares what the numbers are worth.

docs.title: Step 6: Measure a word
docs.text:
Mira calls Tomas back with a better answer than he asked for. A script that takes a word and a size, and says how wide the word sets:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
upm = font.info.unitsPerEm

word = "Plum"
size = 12

total = 0
for letter in word:
    total = total + font[letter].width

print(word, "is", int(total), "units wide")
print("At", size, "pt that is", round(total / upm * size, 1), "pt")

Plum is 2025 units wide
At 12 pt that is 24.3 pt

Save it as widths.py in your scripting-book folder.

Read it in three parts. At the top it asks the font for its UPM and puts the two things you might change, word and size, into boxes with plain names. In the middle is a loop. A string is a row of characters, so for letter in word: hands you P, then l, then u, then m. Each time around, the loop looks up the glyph with that name and adds its width to total. That's the counter from chapter 7, except that it grows by a width each time and not by 1. At the bottom are the two tidying words: int for the units, which are whole, and round with one decimal for the points.

Check it by hand once. P is 492, l is 222, u is 523 and m is 788. That makes 2025. Divided by 1000 and multiplied by 12, it's 24.3.

Change size to 72 and run it again:

Plum is 2025 units wide
At 72 pt that is 145.8 pt

The units didn't change. They never do. Only the last line depends on the size.

The script has two limits, and you should know them. It adds up widths and nothing else. When FontLab sets the word, it also applies kerning, the small corrections between particular pairs of letters, so the real line can be a little shorter or longer. Kerning is the subject of Part 4. And font[letter] only works when the glyph's name is the letter itself. That's true for P and m. It isn't true for a space, whose glyph is called space, or for a comma. Put a space in word and you get the AttributeError about 'NoneType' from chapter 6. Part 2 shows how to get from any character to its glyph.

"Twenty-four point three points, at twelve," says Mira. "Before kerning."

"Before what?" says Tomas.

Going deeper: why round(2.5) is 2

Try print(round(2.5)) and print(round(3.5)). You get 2 and 4. When a number sits exactly halfway, Python rounds to the nearest even number, not always upward as you learned at school. Over many numbers, that keeps the rounding errors from piling up in one direction. It only affects exact halves, and it won't change a width report. But it explains a result that would otherwise look like a bug.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Python has whole numbers and floats, division always gives a float, and FontLab keeps widths as floats, which is where the .0 comes from. int cuts the decimals off and round goes to the nearest value, with an optional second number for how many decimals to keep. A width is counted in font units, and font.info.unitsPerEm says how many units make one em, so a width divided by the UPM and multiplied by the type size gives a real measurement.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Change word in widths.py to "Mira" and size back to 12. You should get 1852 units and 22.2 pt.
  2. How many times wider is the m than the n? Divide one width by the other and round the answer to two decimals.
  3. Print font["emdash"].width / upm. What does the result tell you about how the em dash got its name?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 12 builds the table Tomas asked for on Monday: every glyph and its width, with the names lined up on the left and the numbers lined up on the right.

docs.title: 12. The width report
docs.text:
Friday, after lunch. Tomas has been patient since Monday. He asked for every glyph and its width, and what he got was this:

.notdef None 500.0
A 65 596.0
Aacute 193 596.0
Abreve 258 596.0
Acircumflex 194 596.0
Adieresis 196 596.0

Two hundred lines of it. The numbers start wherever the name happens to stop, so the eye can't run down them. Every one has a .0 on the end. He pasted it into his spreadsheet and wrote back one line: Can the numbers be in a column?

Mira knows how to lose the .0 since this morning. The column is the last thing missing. It's also line 3 on Oskar's sheet: "Make a table of every glyph and its width." Today she crosses it out.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open, with 208 glyphs.
  • What you learned about floats in chapter 11. No saved script is needed.

docs.title: Step 1: Put a value inside a sentence
docs.text:
So far, when you wanted words and values on one line, you gave print several things with commas between them. Here's another way. Type this and run it:

name = "A"
width = 596
print(f"{name} is {width} units wide")

A is 596 units wide

Look at the string. It has an f in front of the opening quote, touching it, and it has two pairs of curly braces inside. That's called an f-string. The f stands for "formatted".

You know that quotes are a fence, and that Python doesn't read what's behind a fence. The curly braces are gates in that fence. Wherever Python finds a pair of them in an f-string, it reads what's between them as Python, works out the value and puts the value into the sentence at that spot. Everything outside the braces stays as you typed it.

The f is what opens the gates. Take it away and run the line again:

print("{name} is {width} units wide")

{name} is {width} units wide

No error. Without the f, it's an ordinary string, the braces are ordinary characters, and Python prints them. When you see curly braces in your output, look for the missing f.

Between the braces you can put more than a name. Anything that has a value will do:

print(f"{name} with 4 more units is {width + 4}")
print(f"The name has {len(name)} character")

A with 4 more units is 600
The name has 1 character

docs.title: Step 2: Say how the number should look
docs.text:
Now use a real width, which is a float:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
name = "A"
width = font["A"].width
print(f"{name} is {width} units wide")

A is 596.0 units wide

The .0 is back. This morning you'd have wrapped the width in int. An f-string has its own way. Inside the braces, after the value, you can put a colon and then a short note that says how to show it:

print(f"{name} is {width:.0f} units wide")

A is 596 units wide

Read :.0f in three pieces. The colon separates the value from the note. .0 says "no decimals". The f at the end says "this is a float, show it as an ordinary decimal number". That last f has nothing to do with the f in front of the quote. It's an unlucky coincidence of letters.

Change the digit and you get that many decimals. Here's this morning's calculation, the A at 12 pt:

print(f"{width / 1000 * 12:.1f} pt")
print(f"{width / 1000 * 12:.2f} pt")

7.2 pt
7.15 pt

The untidy 7.151999999999999 never shows. The note rounds for you, the way round did. And as with round, the value in the box doesn't change. Only what's printed does.

docs.title: Step 3: Give each value a column
docs.text:
The same note can say how much room a value gets. Run this:

name = "A"
width = 596
print(f"{name:<14}|")
print(f"{width:>6}|")

A             |
   596|

The upright bars are there so you can see where each piece ends.

:<14 says: give this value 14 characters of room and push it to the left. The name A takes one character, and Python fills the other thirteen with spaces. :>6 says: six characters of room, pushed to the right. The number takes three, and three spaces go in front.

The arrow points to the side where the value goes. < points left, > points right. Names read best pushed left, the way a list of words does. Numbers read best pushed right, so that ones sit under ones and hundreds under hundreds. That's what Tomas means by a column.

You can combine room and decimals in one note. Room first, then the decimals:

width = 596.0
print(f"{width:>6.0f}|")

   596|

Six characters wide, pushed right, no decimals, a float.

Now make the mistake that everybody makes once. Give the name the note that was meant for the number:

name = "A"
print(f"{name:>6.0f}")

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 2, in <module>
ValueError: Unknown format code 'f' for object of type 'str'

Read the letter from the bottom. ValueError is new: the kind of thing was acceptable, the particular value wasn't. Here the complaint is about the note. A "format code" is the letter at its end, and f means float. Python is telling you that name holds a str, a string, and a string has no decimals to show. Take the .0f off the name's note and it runs. When you see this message, check which note you gave to which value.

docs.title: Step 4: Line up six glyphs
docs.text:
Put the two notes on one line and try them on the six glyphs from Tomas's ragged sample:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for name in ["H", "O", "n", "o", "emdash", "quotesingle"]:
    glyph = font[name]
    print(f"{glyph.name:<8}{glyph.width:>6.0f}")

H          672
O          708
n          523
o          520
emdash    1000
quotesingle   190

Nearly. Five rows line up and the sixth doesn't. The name quotesingle has eleven characters, and you gave the names eight characters of room. Python doesn't cut a value to make it fit. When the value is longer than its room, it takes what it needs and pushes everything after it to the right.

So the name column has to be at least as wide as the longest name in the font. In Plum, the longest names have 14 characters: guillemotright and guilsinglright. Give the names 16, which leaves two spaces of air:

    print(f"{glyph.name:<16}{glyph.width:>6.0f}")

H                  672
O                  708
n                  523
o                  520
emdash            1000
quotesingle        190

Run your eye down the numbers. The 1000 sticks out to the left by one digit, and the 190 shows at once as the smallest. A column lets you see things that a ragged list hides.

docs.title: Step 5: The whole font, with a header
docs.text:
Now all the glyphs, with a line on top that says what the columns are:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()

print(f"{'Glyph':<16}{'Width':>6}")
print("-" * 22)
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    print(f"{glyph.name:<16}{glyph.width:>6.0f}")
print(f"{len(font)} glyphs")

Here's the top of the output:

Glyph            Width
----------------------
.notdef            500
A                  596
Aacute             596
Abreve             596
Acircumflex        596
Adieresis          596
Agrave             596
Aring              596

It goes on for 208 rows and ends with the line 208 glyphs.

Save it as width_report.py in your scripting-book folder.

Three details are new. In the header line, the values between the braces are strings typed on the spot: 'Glyph' and 'Width'. They're in single quotes because the f-string around them is already using double quotes, and Python needs to tell the inner fence from the outer one. The header gets the same notes as the rows, <16 and >6, so the words sit exactly above their columns.

The second line uses the star on a string. You learned this morning that * multiplies numbers. A string times a number repeats the string: "-" * 22 is 22 hyphens. Why 22? The two columns are 16 and 6 characters wide.

And the last line counts with len(font) from chapter 4, inside braces.

The table is in font order: .notdef, then the capitals with their accents. If Tomas would like it by name, you know how from chapter 10. Collect the names in a list, sort the list, then loop over the sorted names and look each glyph up with font[name]. That's exercise 2.

docs.title: Step 6: Send it
docs.text:
The table is in the Output panel. Click in the Output panel, select everything, copy, and paste it into a mail to Tomas.

One warning goes with it. The columns are made of spaces. They line up only in a typeface where every character has the same width, as in the Output panel. Pasted into a mail that's set in a proportional typeface, a typeface like Plum, the numbers wander again. A type designer doesn't need this explained. Tell Tomas to view it in a fixed-width typeface, or to split the lines at the spaces when he imports them. Writing a real spreadsheet file, one that opens with each value in its own cell, is the subject of chapter 28.

Mira sends it. The answer takes four minutes.

That's it. Thank you. Can I have this for the Bold as well?

That one has to wait. The script reads one set of widths, and asking for another weight comes in a later chapter. But the table she has sent took one run. A week ago it would have been an afternoon of clicking and typing.

Then she takes Oskar's sheet and draws a line through number 3. Three of eleven.

Going deeper: a column for a value that might be missing

You might want a third column with the Unicode number: {glyph.unicode:>6}. It stops at the first row with TypeError: unsupported format string passed to NoneType.__format__. The .notdef glyph has no Unicode value, so glyph.unicode is None, and None doesn't know what to do with a note about room. You need a way to say "if there's a number, show it, otherwise show something else". That's else, and it's in the next chapter.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: An f-string is a string with an f in front, in which every pair of curly braces is replaced by the value of what's inside. After a colon, a note says how to show the value: .0f for a float without decimals, <16 for sixteen characters of room pushed left, >6 for six pushed right. Give every row the same notes, with the name column wider than the longest name, and the output is a table.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a third column to width_report.py that shows each width in points at 12 pt, with one decimal, in eight characters of room. The row for H should end in 8.1. Give the header a third word.
  2. Print the table sorted by name. Collect the names in a list first, then loop over sorted(names).
  3. Print the table only for glyphs wider than 800. You should get 11 rows, from AE at 852 to at at 848.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 13 joins tests together. "Wider than 700" is one question and "an uppercase letter" is another, and the proofreader wants the glyphs that answer yes to both.

docs.title: 13. And, or, not
docs.text:
Monday of the third week. The width table has reached the proofreader, and the proofreader has read it. Tomas passes on her question:

She says some capitals look very wide next to the others. Can she have only the uppercase ones that are wider than 700?

Mira reads it twice. She can list the glyphs wider than 700. That's the test from chapter 8 with 700 in it, and it gives her 22 names with an em dash and a percent sign among them. She could find the capitals too, somehow. What she can't do is ask both questions about the same glyph at the same time.

Last Wednesday the same wall came up with glyph names. A test that was too loose let an asterisk in among the versions of the letter a, and there was no way to add a second condition. Today you get three small words that join tests together, and two more that say what to do when a test fails.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open, with 208 glyphs.
  • The f-string notes from chapter 12, for the table at the end.

docs.title: Step 1: Two tests joined with and
docs.text:
Start with a plain number. The O in Plum is 708 units wide. Type this and run it:

w = 708
print(w > 700)
print(w < 800)
print(w > 700 and w < 800)
print(w > 750 and w < 800)

True
True
True
False

The first two lines are comparisons, as you know them. The third joins them with the word and. The joined question is True only when both parts are True. In the fourth line the first part fails, 708 isn't greater than 750, so the whole thing is False. One no is enough.

That's how the word works in a sentence, too. "Wider than 700 and narrower than 800" describes a glyph that passes both tests.

Now write it the way you'd say it aloud:

w = 708
if w > 700 and < 800:
    print("wide")

  File "<string>", line 2
    if w > 700 and < 800:
                   ^
SyntaxError: invalid syntax

The little arrow points at the <. In speech you say "wider than 700 and narrower than 800" and the listener knows that both halves are about the same glyph. Python doesn't fill in what you left out. On each side of and it wants a whole question, one that could stand alone after if. < 800 can't stand alone: less than 800, but what is? Say w again, as in w > 700 and w < 800, and it runs.

docs.title: Step 2: Which glyphs are uppercase?
docs.text:
For the proofreader you need a second test: is this glyph a capital? A plain glyph has no drawer that says so. But its name is a string, and a string can say whether it's written in capitals:

print("A".isupper())
print("a".isupper())
print("Aacute".isupper())
print("Aacute"[0].isupper())

True
False
False
True

isupper is another question a string works out when asked, like endswith in chapter 9, with nothing to pass through the slot. It says True when the letters in the string are all capitals. So "A" passes and "Aacute" doesn't, because five of its six letters are small.

That's the wrong test for glyph names. The glyph Aacute is a capital letter. What marks it as one is the first character of its name. The fourth line asks only that character. You know [0] from lists: the first thing in the row. A string is a row of characters, so "Aacute"[0] is "A", and the question goes to that one letter.

This is a convention of glyph names, not a law. In Plum, 68 names start with a capital. Sixty-seven are capital letters, and one is Euro, the currency sign. A test on names finds what the names say. Later in the book, in Part 5, you'll ask FontLab what kind of character a glyph stands for, and that's the dependable way. For today's question the name is good enough, and you'll check the list by eye.

docs.title: Step 3: Both at once
docs.text:
Now put the two tests on one line, inside the loop:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.name[0].isupper() and glyph.width > 700:
        print(glyph.name)

AE
M
O
Oacute
Ocircumflex
Odieresis
Ograve
Oslash
Otilde
OE
Q
W
Wacute
Wcircumflex
Wdieresis
Wgrave

Sixteen names, and every one a capital. The em dash, the percent sign, the at sign and the small m are gone. Each glyph had to pass two tests, and they failed the first. The Euro passed the first and failed the second: it's 490 units wide.

Read the if line aloud. "If the first character of the glyph's name is uppercase, and the glyph's width is greater than 700." It's long, but each side of the and is a question you could have asked alone.

docs.title: Step 4: Either one will do, with or
docs.text:
and wants both. The word or is content with one:

w = 708
print(w < 200 or w > 700)
print(w < 200 or w > 900)

True
False

In the first line, 708 isn't less than 200, but it is greater than 700, and one yes is enough. In the second line both parts fail. or is False only when everything it joins is False.

Use it to collect two families of glyphs in one pass:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.name.startswith("W") or glyph.name.startswith("M"):
        print(glyph.name)

M
W
Wacute
Wcircumflex
Wdieresis
Wgrave

You can use and and or in the same line. When you do, put parentheses around the part that belongs together. Compare these two tests:

(glyph.name.startswith("W") or glyph.name.startswith("M")) and glyph.width > 850

glyph.name.startswith("W") or glyph.name.startswith("M") and glyph.width > 850

The first one says: a name that starts with W or M, and in either case a width over 850. The M is 840 units wide, so it drops out, and all five W glyphs stay. The second one has no parentheses, and Python reads and before or, the way it multiplies before it adds. So it means: starts with W, whatever the width, or else starts with M and is over 850. In Plum both versions happen to print the same five names. In a font with a narrow W they wouldn't. Don't make the reader work out which you meant. Write the parentheses.

docs.title: Step 5: Turn a test around with not
docs.text:
The third word goes in front of a test and flips its answer:

w = 708
print(w > 700)
print(not w > 700)

True
False

Here's the other half of this morning's list. The glyphs wider than 700 that aren't capitals:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.width > 700 and not glyph.name[0].isupper():
        print(glyph.name)

ae
m
oe
emdash
percent
at

Six names. Sixteen and six make 22, the number Mira's first test found for all the glyphs wider than 700. Every wide glyph is on one list or the other, and none is on both. When two lists are supposed to split a group, add them up. It's the cheapest check there is.

not also narrows a test that lets too much in. Last Wednesday's too-loose test was glyph.name.startswith("a"), and it caught asterisk, asciitilde and asciicircum. Now you can shut them out:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.name.startswith("a") and not glyph.name.startswith("as"):
        print(glyph.name)

That leaves thirteen names. It still lets through ampersand, at and the acute accent, so the test is tighter and not yet tight. You could add more conditions. At some point a short list typed by hand is the better tool, and knowing when you've reached that point is part of the craft.

docs.title: Step 6: Otherwise: else and elif
docs.text:
So far an if either does something or stays silent. Often you want it to do one thing or another. Type this:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for name in ["H", "O", "n", "m"]:
    glyph = font[name]
    if glyph.width > 700:
        print(name, "is wide")
    else:
        print(name, "is not wide")

H is not wide
O is wide
n is not wide
m is wide

else means "otherwise". It sits at the same depth as the if it belongs to, it has no test of its own, and it ends in a colon. The lines indented under it run when the if test was False. Exactly one of the two blocks runs each time around. Never both, never neither.

Two choices aren't always enough. The proofreader's real question is how the capitals compare, so sort the 26 plain capital letters into three bins:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if len(glyph.name) == 1 and glyph.name.isupper():
        if glyph.width < 500:
            label = "narrow"
        elif glyph.width <= 700:
            label = "medium"
        else:
            label = "wide"
        print(f"{glyph.name:<4}{glyph.width:>6.0f}  {label}")

Here are the rows for five of the letters:

A      596  medium
I      228  narrow
M      840  wide
Q      708  wide
W      859  wide

Over all 26 letters you get 8 narrow, 14 medium and 4 wide.

elif is short for "else if". It's an else with a test of its own. Python goes down the ladder from the top and stops at the first rung whose test is True. It runs that block and skips all the rest. That's why the second test doesn't need to say "500 or more". If a glyph arrives at the elif, the first test has already failed, so its width can't be under 500. You can have as many elif rungs as you like, and one else at the bottom to catch whatever is left.

Look at the outer if as well. It joins two tests with and: the name is one character long, and that character is uppercase. And it shows an if inside an if, each with its own depth of indentation. The print line is at the depth of the inner if, not inside any of its three blocks, so it runs once for every capital, whichever label was chosen.

docs.title: The proofreader's list
docs.text:
Here's what Mira saves, with the columns from chapter 12 and a count at the end:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()

count = 0
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.name[0].isupper() and glyph.width > 700:
        print(f"{glyph.name:<16}{glyph.width:>6.0f}")
        count = count + 1
print(f"{count} uppercase glyphs are wider than 700")

AE                 852
M                  840
O                  708
Oacute             708
Ocircumflex        708
Odieresis          708
Ograve             708
Oslash             708
Otilde             708
OE                 989
Q                  708
W                  859
Wacute             859
Wcircumflex        859
Wdieresis          859
Wgrave             859
16 uppercase glyphs are wider than 700

Save it as wide_caps.py in your scripting-book folder.

Mira sends the list with a note: the O family and the Q are round, the M and the W have four strokes, and the two ligatures are two letters each. Wide is what they should be. The proofreader writes back that she'll stop worrying about the W.

Going deeper: the column for a missing value

Chapter 12 left a table that broke on .notdef, because None can't be given a note about room. With else you can mend it. Before the print line, write if glyph.unicode is None: and under it shown = "none", then else: and under it shown = glyph.unicode. Print {shown:>6} in place of {glyph.unicode:>6}. Now the box shown always holds something that can be printed, a word or a number.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: and joins two tests into one that passes only when both pass, or makes one that passes when either does, and not flips an answer. Each side of and and or has to be a whole question. When you mix them, parentheses say which parts belong together. else gives an if a second block for the times its test fails, and elif adds further tests in between, tried from the top until one is True.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Change wide_caps.py so it lists the uppercase glyphs narrower than 300. You should get seven: the I, five accented versions of it, and the J.
  2. List the glyphs whose names start with O and whose width is not 708. Use !=, or use not with ==. There's one.
  3. In the three-bin script from step 6, add a fourth bin called very wide for widths over 850. Where in the ladder does the new rung have to go, and what happens if you put it last?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 14 is the first script that changes the font. Until now every script has looked and reported. The next one puts a red mark on the empty glyphs, so that Mira can see them in the Font window without reading a list.

docs.title: 14. Mark them red
docs.text:
Mira prints the list of empty glyphs for Ines and reads it out: space, a.sc, b.sc, c.sc. Ines nods, turns to the Font window and starts hunting for the four cells. The list is correct, but Ines still has to carry it in her head from one window to the other.

Designers solved this long before scripts. They mark glyphs with a color: red for "not drawn yet", green for "approved". The colored cells stand out in the Font window at a glance. Line 5 of Oskar's sheet even says so: Mark every glyph that mixes its own outlines with borrowed ones. That chore needs things you'll learn in Part 2. But the marking half of it you can learn today.

Every script so far has read the font. This is the first one that writes to it, so we start with a precaution.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open in a Font window.
  • empty_glyphs.py from chapter 8.

docs.title: Step 1: Save first
docs.text:
Until now, nothing you ran could harm the font. You asked questions, and the font was the same afterwards. From this chapter on, some scripts change things, and a script can change two hundred glyphs in the time it takes you to blink.

So make two habits now.

Work on a copy. You already do: Plum-practice is your copy, and the original plum-var.vfj stays untouched.

Save before you run. Choose File > Save Font. Now the file on disk holds the font as it was before the script. If the script does something you didn't want, choose File > Revert Font, and FontLab loads the font from disk again, as you saved it.

You might expect Edit > Undo to do that job. Don't count on it. Undo remembers the steps you take by hand. The changes in this chapter go into the font by a different door, and they leave no step behind for Undo to take back. Part 2 shows how a script can leave a proper Undo step. Until then, saving and reverting is your way back.

docs.title: Step 2: Read a mark
docs.text:
In chapter 8 you met the richer glyph: pGlyph(font, glyph) takes a plain glyph and hands back one that knows more about its own drawing. You asked it one question, isEmpty(). It has drawers too. One of them is called mark.

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()
rich = pGlyph(font, font["space"])
print(rich.mark)

0

The box rich holds the richer version of the space glyph, so the long line doesn't have to be typed twice. Its mark is 0, and 0 means no mark at all. If you got another number, somebody has marked the space in your copy by hand. That's fine. Read on and you'll see what the number means.

docs.title: Step 3: Change it
docs.text:
In chapter 5 you learned to read = as "becomes": the box on the left gets the thing on the right. Until now the left side was always a box of your own. It can be a drawer, too.

rich.mark = 1
print(rich.mark)

1

Add these two lines under the others and run the script. "The mark of this glyph becomes 1." Reading a drawer and writing to it use the same dot and the same name. Which one happens depends on the side of the = the drawer stands on.

Now look at the Font window and find the space. Its cell should be red. If it isn't yet, click the Font window so that FontLab draws it again.

A script changed the font for the first time in this book, and the change is as real as if you'd made it by hand. The mark is part of the font now, and if you save, the red mark is saved with it.

docs.title: Step 4: What the number means
docs.text:
Why is 1 red? FontLab stores a mark as one number, and the number is a position on the color wheel. The wheel runs through 360 degrees: red at the start, then yellow, green, cyan, blue, magenta and back to red. The mark is the position plus one, so that 0 stays free to mean "no mark".

Mark Color 0 none 1 red 61 yellow 121 green 241 blue

Try a few. Change the 1 in your script to 121 and run it, then to 241. Then set it back to 0, and the cell goes plain again.

You don't have to remember the numbers. When a script needs a color, give the number a name at the top and use the name:

RED = 1
GREEN = 121

The capitals don't mean anything to Python. They're a custom, and chapter 17 comes back to it.

docs.title: Step 5: The mistake that makes no noise
docs.text:
Now make a mistake on purpose. Type the drawer's name with a capital M:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()
rich = pGlyph(font, font["space"])
rich.Mark = 121
print(rich.mark)

0

There's no letter of complaint. The script ran to the end. And the mark is still 0.

Compare that with chapter 6. There, you asked for a drawer that didn't exist, and Python refused with an AttributeError. Reading from a drawer that isn't there is an error. Writing to one often isn't. The richer glyph is a wardrobe that lets you add drawers, so Python made a new drawer called Mark, put 121 in it, and went on. FontLab never looks in that drawer. It only knows mark.

This is the first mistake in the book that Python doesn't catch for you. From now on, when a script writes something, make it read the value back, or go and look at the font. A script can finish without an error and still not have done what you meant.

Fix the capital and run it again. Then set the mark back to 0.

docs.title: Step 6: Mark the empty ones
docs.text:
You have a loop that finds the empty glyphs, and you have a line that marks one glyph. Put the line inside the loop. Open empty_glyphs.py, change it to this, and save it as mark_empty.py:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

RED = 1

font = fl.CurrentFont()
count = 0
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    rich = pGlyph(font, glyph)
    if rich.isEmpty():
        rich.mark = RED
        count = count + 1
        print("Marked", glyph.name)
print(f"Marked {count} of {len(font)}")

Before you run it: File > Save Font. Then run.

Marked space
Marked a.sc
Marked b.sc
Marked c.sc
Marked 4 of 208

The loop makes the richer glyph once for each turn and keeps it in the box rich. Then it uses the box twice: once to ask the question, once to write the mark. The script still prints the names. A script that changes things should say what it changed, so that you can check the font against the list.

Look at the Font window. The space is red, and at the end of the font, three red cells sit in a row. Ines doesn't need the list any more.

Now practice the way back. Choose File > Revert Font. FontLab loads the saved font, and the red cells are plain again. Run mark_empty.py once more to get them back, and this time keep them.

One more thing about the space. It's marked red as "not drawn yet", and it'll never be drawn, because a space has nothing in it by design. The test says "empty". It can't tell which glyphs are supposed to be empty. Leave it for now. In chapter 13 you learned to join two tests, and exercise 2 asks you to use that here.

When Mira draws the a.sc, the cell will stay red until somebody changes it. A mark doesn't follow the drawing, and it only changes when a person or a script sets it again. That's why a marking script is one you run again and again, and why it should also clear the marks that are no longer true. Exercise 3 does that.

Going deeper: grays, and marks on layers

The numbers 1 to 360 are the color wheel. The numbers from 1001 to 1255 are a scale of grays, from dark to light, for marks that should stay quiet. Other numbers aren't valid marks.

The plain glyph you get from font["space"] has a mark drawer of its own, and it holds the same value. This book writes marks through the richer glyph, because the richer glyph is what you'll use for every other change to a glyph in parts 2 and 3. A glyph can also carry a different mark on each of its layers. Part 6 is about fonts with more than one layer.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A drawer on the left side of = gets a new value, in the same way a box does, and that's how a script changes a font. A glyph's mark is one number: 0 for none, and a position on the color wheel plus one for a color, so 1 is red and 121 is green. Marks set by a script don't go through Undo, so you save before you run and use File > Revert Font to go back. Writing to a misspelled drawer raises no error, so a script that writes should print what it did.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Mark every glyph that has no Unicode value in green. The test is in chapter 8. How many cells turn green, and which glyphs end up green that were red before?
  2. Change mark_empty.py so that it doesn't mark the space: join the empty test with a second test on the glyph's name, using and from chapter 13. It should report Marked 3 of 208.
  3. Write clear_marks.py: a loop that sets every glyph's mark to 0 and counts how many glyphs had a mark other than 0 before. Save the font first, run it, and then decide whether to revert.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 15 lets you point at glyphs with the mouse and have the script work on the ones you picked.

docs.title: 15. The selection
docs.text:
Ines is looking at a proof of Plum's lowercase and something bothers her about the rhythm. She asks Mira for the widths of ten letters, the ones with a bowl or an arch: a, b, d, e, g, h, n, o, p, q. And their average, if that's no trouble.

Mira knows two ways to do it. She can loop over the whole font and print 208 lines, then pick out ten by eye. Or she can type the ten names into a list, as in chapter 7. That works, until Ines says "and now the same for these", pointing at the screen.

Pointing is the natural way to say which glyphs you mean. You click one cell in the Font window, you hold a key and click the others, and the cells you picked are highlighted. FontLab calls that the selection. Today the script asks FontLab what you picked.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open in a Font window.
  • No Glyph window in front. The tool in this chapter reads the selection of the Font window.

docs.title: Step 1: Select ten glyphs
docs.text:
In the Font window, click the cell of a. Then hold Cmd on a Mac, or Ctrl on Windows, and click b, d, e, g, h, n, o, p and q. Ten cells are highlighted.

If you click without the key, the selection starts over with that one cell. That's fine. Start again.

docs.title: Step 2: Ask what's selected
docs.text:
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

names = scripting.names_selected_names()
print(names)

['a', 'b', 'd', 'e', 'g', 'h', 'n', 'o', 'p', 'q']

The square brackets tell you what came back: a list. The quotes tell you what's in it: strings. FontLab handed your script the names of the ten glyphs you clicked. If your list comes in another order, you'll put it in order yourself in a moment.

The first line is a new kind of import, so let's read it slowly. Until now you've written from fly import fl: from the toolbag, take one tool. This line says: import a whole pocket of the bag, the one at fly.ap.core.scripting, and as scripting gives it a short label so you don't have to write the long path every time you use it. The pocket holds many tools. You reach each one with a dot: scripting.names_selected_names().

The tool's name is long, and it tells you what you get: the names of the selected glyphs. The parentheses are empty because the tool needs nothing from you. You've been calling tools that hand something back since len in chapter 5. This one hands back a whole list, and you can do with it everything chapter 10 taught you:

print(len(names))
print(names[0])
print("o" in names)
print("z" in names)

10
a
True
False

The last two lines use in on a list. In chapter 9 it asked whether one string sits inside another. Between a thing and a list, it asks whether the thing is one of the list's items.

docs.title: Step 3: Names are not glyphs
docs.text:
Now ask the first selected glyph for its width.

print(names[0].width)

AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'width'

Read the complaint. A 'str' object is a string. The list holds names, and a name is text: it has the drawers that strings have, like endswith, and no width. The glyph has the width. The name is only the label on the wardrobe.

You know how to get from the name to the glyph. You did it in chapter 6:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph = font[names[0]]
print(glyph.name, glyph.width)

a 471.0

font[...] takes a name and hands back the glyph. Here the name comes out of the list, where in chapter 6 you typed it in quotes. This two-step move, ask for names and then look each one up in the font, is how most scripts in this book get from "what the designer pointed at" to "the glyphs to work on".

docs.title: Step 4: Loop over the selection
docs.text:
One glyph works, so do all ten. Start a new script:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
names = scripting.names_selected_names()

total = 0
for name in sorted(names):
    glyph = font[name]
    total = total + glyph.width
    print(f"{name:<10}{glyph.width:>6.0f}")
print(f"{len(names)} glyphs, average width {total / len(names):.0f}")

a            471
b            543
d            543
e            470
g            543
h            523
n            523
o            520
p            543
q            543
10 glyphs, average width 522

Nothing in the loop is new. It's the loop over a list of names from chapter 7, with the running total from that chapter's exercise, the columns from chapter 12 and sorted from chapter 10. What's new is where the list comes from. You didn't type it and the script didn't build it. You pointed.

Mira sends the table to Ines. The four letters with a bowl and a stem, b, d, p and q, are all 543 wide, and so is g. The two arches are 523. The outsiders are a and e, about fifty units narrower than the o. Ines says that's what she saw.
