Now click a different set of cells in the Font window, say the figures, and run the script again without changing a character of it. This is the point of the chapter. A script that reads the selection is one you write once and then aim with the mouse.

docs.title: Step 5: When nothing comes back
docs.text:
What does the tool hand back when you've selected one glyph and no more? Try it. Click one cell in the Font window so that only that glyph is selected, and run the script. You get one line and an average that equals the width. One is a fine number of glyphs.

The harder case is none. Close every font and run the script.

ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

With no font open, the tool hands back an empty list, []. The loop over an empty list runs zero times, without complaint, and total stays 0. The last line then divides 0 by len(names), which is also 0, and no number is the answer to that.

An empty list is not an error. It's a correct answer to "what's selected?". The script has to decide what to do with that answer, and it does so with an if:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
names = scripting.names_selected_names()

if len(names) == 0:
    print("Nothing is selected.")
else:
    total = 0
    for name in sorted(names):
        glyph = font[name]
        total = total + glyph.width
        print(f"{name:<10}{glyph.width:>6.0f}")
    print(f"{len(names)} glyphs, average width {total / len(names):.0f}")

Nothing is selected.

Everything that needs at least one glyph now sits under else:, one level further in. Save this as selected_report.py. Open Plum-practice again, select the ten letters, and check that the table is back.

Make this a habit for any list that comes from outside your script, whether from FontLab, from a file or from a person: ask how long it is before you count on its first item or divide by its length.

docs.title: Step 6: Put it to work
docs.text:
Mira has a use for this the same afternoon. She has sketched the a.sc on paper and counts it as started, and she wants to take its red mark away without touching the others. She selects the one cell and runs a short script, which is chapter 14's marking line fed by today's list:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for name in scripting.names_selected_names():
    pGlyph(font, font[name]).mark = 0
    print("Cleared", name)

Remember the rule from chapter 14: this script writes to the font, so save the font first. Then select a.sc in your own copy and run it. You should see Cleared a.sc in the output, and the cell should go plain.

There's no if for the empty list here, and none is needed. A loop over an empty list does nothing, and nothing is the right thing to do. The guard in step 5 was there because of the division, not because of the loop.

Going deeper: what counts as selected

The tool reads the selection of the Font window. If no cells are highlighted but FontLab has a current glyph, the one that fl.CurrentGlyph() handed you in chapter 6, the tool hands back a list with that one name. So a script built on it does something sensible in both situations: on the cells you picked, or on the glyph you're looking at.

The selection inside a Glyph window, where you pick nodes and contours of a drawing, is a different thing and has different tools. Part 3 gets to those. The tool also has a partner that goes the other way and makes a script select glyphs for you. You'll use it in Part 2, when a script that finds problem glyphs leaves them selected for you to look at.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: scripting.names_selected_names() hands back a list of the names of the glyphs selected in the Font window, and font[name] turns each name into its glyph. A tool can hand back a whole list, and that list can be empty, so a script checks len(names) == 0 before it divides by the length or reaches for the first item. import ... as brings in a whole pocket of tools under a short label. A script that works on the selection is written once and aimed with the mouse.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Select the ten figures, zero to nine, and run selected_report.py. All ten should be 490 wide, so the average is 490 too. Then add period and comma to the selection and watch the average drop.
  2. Change the report so that its last line also names the widest and the narrowest glyph of the selection. Chapter 10's sorted won't do it alone, because it sorts names. Keep two boxes, widest and narrowest, start both with the first glyph, and compare inside the loop.
  3. Write mark_selected.py: it marks every selected glyph green, mark 121, and prints how many it marked. Save the font before you run it.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 16 takes a script that has grown too long to read and cuts it into steps with names.

docs.title: 16. Name your steps
docs.text:
The publisher has asked for an inventory of Plum: how many glyphs are empty, how many have no Unicode value, how many are small caps. Mira has a script for each of those questions. Late on Tuesday she pastes the three into one file, runs it, and gets the right answers.

Then she scrolls up to change the heading of the second list and can't find it. The script is thirty-one lines long and it looks like the same paragraph written three times. She changes a line, runs it, and the wrong list changes.

She sends the file to Oskar with one word: Help. The answer: "You've written one thing three times. Write it once and give it a name."

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • The long script below. Type it, or build it from empty_glyphs.py and find_suffix.py. Save it as three_lists.py. One spelling in it is new: glyph.unicode is None asks the same question as == None did in chapter 8. It's the usual way to write that test, and chapter 18 explains it.
from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()

empty = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if pGlyph(font, glyph).isEmpty():
        empty.append(glyph.name)
print("Empty")
print(len(empty), "of", len(font))
for name in empty:
    print("   ", name)

no_unicode = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.unicode is None:
        no_unicode.append(glyph.name)
print("Without Unicode")
print(len(no_unicode), "of", len(font))
for name in no_unicode:
    print("   ", name)

small_caps = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.name.endswith(".sc"):
        small_caps.append(glyph.name)
print("Small caps")
print(len(small_caps), "of", len(font))
for name in small_caps:
    print("   ", name)

Its output starts like this, and goes on for two more lists:

Empty
4 of 208
    space
    a.sc
    b.sc
    c.sc

docs.title: Step 1: Give a step a name
docs.text:
Leave the long script for a moment and open a new, empty one. Type this:

def greet():
    print("Good morning, Ines.")
    print("The report is on its way.")

Run it. Nothing is printed, and nothing is wrong.

def is short for "define". The line says: here's a step, and its name is greet. The indented lines under it are what the step consists of. Python reads them, remembers them under that name, and does not carry them out. You've written a recipe, and nobody has cooked from it yet.

To carry the step out, say its name with parentheses after it. Add two lines at the bottom, against the left edge:

greet()
greet()

Good morning, Ines.
The report is on its way.
Good morning, Ines.
The report is on its way.

Each greet() runs the two lines once. A named step like this is called a function, and using it is called calling it. You've been calling functions since chapter 2: print(), len(), sorted(). Somebody wrote those with def, the same way. Now you can add your own to the set.

The shape is one you know. A def line ends with a colon and the lines that belong to it are indented, as with for and if. The first line back at the left edge is outside the function.

docs.title: Step 2: A slot for what changes
docs.text:
The greeting is always for Ines. To greet somebody else, you'd need a second function, and that's the copying we're trying to stop. So give the function a slot. In chapter 2 you put things into the slot of print. Now you build one.

def greet(name):
    print(f"Good morning, {name}.")


greet("Ines")
greet("Tomas")

Good morning, Ines.
Good morning, Tomas.

The word in the parentheses of the def line is a box that belongs to the function. Each time you call the function, whatever you put through the slot lands in that box, and the lines inside use it. The first call puts "Ines" in name and the second puts "Tomas" there. The thing you pass through the slot is called an argument.

If the function has a slot, it wants it filled. Call it with nothing:

greet()

TypeError: greet() missing 1 required positional argument: 'name'

The message names the function, says how many arguments are missing and gives the name of the box that stayed empty.

A function can have several slots, separated by commas, and the arguments go in by position: the first argument into the first box, the second into the second.

docs.title: Step 3: Hand something back
docs.text:
greet does something: it prints. Most functions you'll write should answer something, so that the rest of the script can go on working with the answer. len doesn't print the count. It hands the count back, and you decide what to do with it.

The word for handing back is return.

def half(number):
    return number / 2


print(half(596))
side = half(596) + 10
print(side)

298.0
308.0

When Python reaches return, the function is over, and the value after the word travels back to the place where the function was called. You can read half(596) in the last lines as if 298.0 stood there. You can print it, put it in a box or do arithmetic with it.

Now the mistake, and it's one everybody makes. Delete the word return and leave the rest:

def half(number):
    number / 2


print(half(596))

None

There's no complaint. The function did the division and then dropped the result on the floor, because nobody told it to hand anything back. A function that reaches its end without a return hands back None, the nothing from chapter 5. When a function of yours gives you None and you expected a value, look for the missing return first.

docs.title: Step 4: Name the test
docs.text:
Back to three_lists.py. The longest line in it is the empty test, with its two pairs of parentheses. It's a step, and it can have a name:

def is_empty(font, glyph):
    return pGlyph(font, glyph).isEmpty()

Two slots: the font and one glyph from it. The function asks the richer glyph the question and hands the answer back, True or False. Put these lines above the line font = fl.CurrentFont(), with an empty line or two around them, and change the first loop to use the new name:

for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if is_empty(font, glyph):
        empty.append(glyph.name)

Run it. The output is the same. The script isn't shorter, but the if line now reads as a sentence, and the long line exists in one place only. If Part 2 gives you a better test for emptiness, you'll change it there and every script line that asks is_empty gets the better answer.

A function that answers yes or no usually gets a name that starts with is_ or has_, so that the if line reads well.

docs.title: Step 5: Name the printing
docs.text:
Look at the three places where the script prints a list. They have the same three moves, a heading, a count and the names. Two things change from one to the next: the heading and the list. Each thing that changes becomes a slot.

def report(title, names, total):
    print(title)
    print(len(names), "of", total)
    for name in names:
        print("   ", name)

The third slot is the size of the font. The function could reach out for the box font in the script around it, and it would work. But a function is easier to trust, and to carry to another script, when everything it needs comes in through its slots.

This function has no return, and that's fine. Its job is to print, like greet.

Now the twelve printing lines of the script shrink to three calls:

report("Empty", empty, len(font))
report("Without Unicode", no_unicode, len(font))
report("Small caps", small_caps, len(font))

To change how every list looks, Mira changes one function. To change one heading, she changes one word in a line that has nothing else in it.

docs.title: Step 6: One loop, three lists
docs.text:
One more repair. The script walks through the font three times, once per list. One walk is enough: a glyph can be asked all three questions in the same turn of the loop. Here's the whole script. Save it as three_lists.py, over the old one.

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph


def is_empty(font, glyph):
    return pGlyph(font, glyph).isEmpty()


def report(title, names, total):
    print(title)
    print(len(names), "of", total)
    for name in names:
        print("   ", name)


font = fl.CurrentFont()

empty = []
no_unicode = []
small_caps = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if is_empty(font, glyph):
        empty.append(glyph.name)
    if glyph.unicode is None:
        no_unicode.append(glyph.name)
    if glyph.name.endswith(".sc"):
        small_caps.append(glyph.name)

report("Empty", empty, len(font))
report("Without Unicode", no_unicode, len(font))
report("Small caps", small_caps, len(font))

Count the lines and you'll find it's as long as the script you started with. The gain is that you can read it. The bottom third says what the script does. The top third says how each step works, for the day you need to know.

The three if lines are separate questions, not if, elif, elif from chapter 13. A glyph like a.sc belongs in all three lists, and elif would stop asking after the first yes.

The order of the parts matters. Python reads a script from the top, and it has to have read a def before the line that calls it. Move the three report lines above the def report line and you get:

NameError: name 'report' is not defined. Did you mean: 'repr'?

It's the complaint from chapter 3: Python doesn't know the name yet. So the custom is imports first, then the functions, then the work.

Going deeper: boxes inside a function

A box you make inside a function lives only while the function runs. If is_empty made a box called rich, the rest of the script couldn't see it: asking for rich afterwards gives a NameError. That's a feature. It means two functions can each have a box called name or count without disturbing each other, and that you can read a function without wondering what the rest of the script does to its boxes. The slots are the way in, and return is the way out.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: def name(slots): teaches Python a step and gives it a name; the indented lines run only when you call the function with name(...). The values you pass go into the function's own boxes by position, and return hands a value back to the caller, while a function without return hands back None. A script made of small named functions, defined above the work that calls them, says what it does in its last few lines.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Write has_unicode(glyph) that returns True when the glyph has a Unicode value. Use it in the loop, with not from chapter 13, to fill the no_unicode list.
  2. Add a fourth list to three_lists.py: glyphs wider than 800 units. You need one new list, one new if and one new report line. The count should be 11.
  3. Change report so that it prints the names on one line, separated by spaces, when there are fewer than six of them, and one per line otherwise. Only the function changes. Start with an empty string and add each name to it. Check that all four lists follow.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 17 is about the reader of your script a week from now, and what you can leave in the file for her.

docs.title: 17. Notes to yourself
docs.text:
Tomas is laying out a table for the publisher's catalog and his columns are narrow. He wants to know which glyphs in Plum are wider than 700 units, because those are the ones that will push his numbers out of line.

Mira knows she wrote that script. She wrote it some time ago, late, between two other things. She finds it in the scripting-book folder under the name w2.py, opens it, and looks at it for a while.

from fly import fl
f = fl.CurrentFont()
c = 0
for g in f.glyphs:
    if g.width > 700:
        c = c + 1
        print(g.name, g.width)
print(c)

It runs. It prints 22 glyphs and the number 22. But is 700 the number Tomas asked for, or one she tried on the way to another number? What was c for? Why is the file called w2? Was there a w1?

Nothing in the script is wrong. Python reads it without complaint. The reader it fails is Mira, eight days later.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • The eight lines above. Type them into a new script and save it as w2.py, so you have Mira's problem in front of you.

docs.title: Step 1: Lines that Python skips
docs.text:
Add one line at the top of the script, starting with the sign #:

# Lists the glyphs that are wider than 700 units.
from fly import fl
f = fl.CurrentFont()

Run it. The output is the same as before: the same 22 glyphs, the same 22 at the end.

Python saw the # and stopped reading that line. Everything from the # to the end of the line is a comment: a note for people. You can write anything there, in any language, with any punctuation, and Python won't look at it.

A comment doesn't need a line of its own. It can sit at the end of a line of code, and Python reads the code and skips the rest:

    if g.width > 700:  # Tomas's column limit, in font units

Now take the # away from your first line and run the script.

    Lists the glyphs that are wider than 700 units.
          ^^^
SyntaxError: invalid syntax

Without the sign, Python tries to read your English as Python and gives up at the second word. That's the whole job of the #: it's a fence, like the quotes around a piece of text, except that it has no closing half. The end of the line closes it. Put it back.

docs.title: Step 2: Switch a line off
docs.text:
There's a second use for the sign, and you'll use it every day. Put a # in front of a line of code, and that line stops running. Nothing is deleted. Take the sign away and the line is back.

Mira only wants the count today, not the list. She could delete the print inside the loop, and then type it again tomorrow when she wants the list. Or:

for g in f.glyphs:
    if g.width > 700:
        c = c + 1
        # print(g.name, g.width)
print(c)

22

Programmers call this "commenting out" a line. It's how you try a script with and without one of its parts. When a script misbehaves and you can't see why, switch off lines one at a time until it behaves, and you've found the line to look at.

One habit to go with it: when you're done trying, either switch the line back on or delete it. A script with a dozen switched-off lines in it is as hard to read as one with no notes at all. Take the # away from the print now.

docs.title: Step 3: Names that explain themselves
docs.text:
Look at the labels on Mira's boxes: f, c, g. They saved her a few keystrokes last week and cost her five minutes today.

You chose good labels in the earlier chapters without thinking about it, because I chose them for you: font, glyph, count. Change the short ones here. There are three, and each appears more than once, so go slowly and change every one:

# Lists the glyphs that are wider than 700 units.
from fly import fl
font = fl.CurrentFont()
wide_count = 0
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.width > 700:
        wide_count = wide_count + 1
        print(glyph.name, glyph.width)
print(wide_count)

Run it, and check that you still get 22. If you get a NameError, you missed one. The message names the label Python couldn't find, and that's the one you changed in some places and not in others.

Read the loop out loud now. For glyph in font glyphs: if glyph width is more than 700, wide count becomes wide count plus one. It's close to a sentence. That's the test for a name: read the line aloud and listen for whether it says what it does.

A few customs that Python people follow, and that this book follows:

  • Lowercase letters, with an underscore where a space would go: wide_count, not WideCount or widecount.
  • A name says what's in the box, not what kind of thing it is. wide_count is better than number.
  • One thing gets a singular name and a list of things gets a plural one. That's why the loop reads for glyph in font.glyphs.
  • Short names are fine when the box lives for one or two lines. Long-lived boxes get real names.

docs.title: Step 4: Pull the number out
docs.text:
The number 700 appears once in the script, in the middle of a line, with nothing to say what it is. Tomorrow Tomas will change his mind and ask for 800. Mira will have to find the number, and be sure she found the right one.

Give the number a name and move it to the top. The import line stays where it is; change the lines below it:

LIMIT = 700  # font units

font = fl.CurrentFont()
wide_count = 0
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.width > LIMIT:
        wide_count = wide_count + 1
        print(glyph.name, glyph.width)
print(wide_count)

LIMIT is a box like any other. The capitals are a custom, not a rule of the language: they tell the next reader "this is a setting, it's decided once at the top and the script doesn't change it afterwards". When you open a script and see a few lines of capitals near the top, you know where the knobs are. Settings like this are the one thing a function may read without a slot, as is_wide will do in the finished script.

Change 700 to 800 and run.

AE 852.0
M 840.0
OE 989.0
W 859.0
Wacute 859.0
Wcircumflex 859.0
Wdieresis 859.0
Wgrave 859.0
oe 824.0
emdash 1000.0
at 848.0
11

Eleven. One number changed, in a place you could find with your eyes shut. Set it back to 700.

Remember that Python cares about capitals. LIMIT, Limit and limit are three different labels. If you write the box as LIMIT and ask for limit further down, you get the NameError you met in chapter 3.

docs.title: Step 5: A header, some air and a template
docs.text:
Three more changes and the script is finished.

A header. The first lines of a script are the first thing you see when you open it, so that's where the answers to Mira's questions go: what the script is called, what it does and who wanted it. Two or three comment lines are enough.

Air. Python ignores empty lines, and people don't. Put one between the parts of a script the way you'd put space between paragraphs: the imports, the settings, the functions, the work.

The function. In chapter 16 you learned to give a step a name with def. The test in the middle of the loop is a step, and it deserves one.

Here's the whole thing. I've also used what chapter 12 taught about lining up columns, and given the last line some words.

# wide_glyphs.py
# Lists every glyph in the current font that is wider than LIMIT,
# then says how many there are. Written for Tomas's column check.

from fly import fl

# Settings. Change these, leave the rest alone.
LIMIT = 700  # font units


def is_wide(glyph):
    return glyph.width > LIMIT


font = fl.CurrentFont()
wide_count = 0

for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if is_wide(glyph):
        wide_count = wide_count + 1
        print(f"{glyph.name:<14}{glyph.width:>6.0f}")

print(f"{wide_count} glyphs are wider than {LIMIT}")

The output ends like this:

emdash          1000
percent          798
at               848
22 glyphs are wider than 700

Save it as wide_glyphs.py. The file name is the last piece of naming, and the same rule holds: it says what the script does. Then delete w2.py. Mira does, with some feeling.

Compare the two versions. They do the same work. The first is eight lines and the second is about twenty, and the second is the shorter read.

Look at the shape of it once more, because every script from here on has the same one:

  1. A header: name, purpose, who it's for.
  2. The imports.
  3. The settings, in capitals.
  4. The functions.
  5. The work.

Make yourself a blank copy of that shape. Take wide_glyphs.py, cut it down to the five parts with a comment line in each, and save it as template.py. When you start a new script, open the template, save it under the new name, and fill it in. Starting from a shape is quicker than starting from an empty panel, and the header gets written while you still know what the script is for.

docs.title: Step 6: A title for the menu
docs.text:
There's one comment that FontLab itself reads. If the very first line of a script starts with #FLM: followed by a space, FontLab takes the rest of that line as the script's title when it lists the script in its Scripts menu.

Add it above the header:

#FLM: Wide Glyphs
# wide_glyphs.py
# Lists every glyph in the current font that is wider than LIMIT,

To Python this is one more comment, and the script runs as before. You won't see the title anywhere yet, because the script isn't in the menu. Putting it there is the next chapter's job. Without the line, FontLab makes a title out of the file name, which is one more reason to name files well.

Add the same line to template.py, with a title you'll remember to change.

Going deeper: how much to comment

Write a comment where the code can't speak for itself: why 700, who asked, what a number's unit is, which chapter of the style guide a rule comes from. Don't write one that repeats the code. count = count + 1 # add one to count tells the reader nothing and has to be kept up to date. Good names do most of the explaining, and comments do the rest.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A # starts a comment, which Python skips to the end of the line, so you can leave notes for the next reader and switch a line off without deleting it. Names carry most of a script's meaning: lowercase words joined by underscores for boxes and functions, capitals for the settings at the top, and a file name that says what the script does. A script laid out as header, imports, settings, functions and work can be read by someone who has never seen it, and that someone is usually you.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Open list_names.py from chapter 7 and give it the full treatment: header, air, a #FLM: title. It has no settings and no functions. Decide whether it needs them, and leave the empty parts out if it doesn't.
  2. Add a second setting to wide_glyphs.py, SHOW_LIST = True, and change the script so that it prints the list only if SHOW_LIST:. Set it to False and check that you get only the last line. You've replaced the # trick from step 2 with a knob.
  3. Find the worst name in any script you've written for this book so far. Change it everywhere it appears, run the script, and read the changed lines aloud.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 18 moves a script out of the Scripting panel and into FontLab's Scripts menu, where it's two clicks away every Friday.

docs.title: 18. Save it, run it again
docs.text:
On Wednesday Ines stops at Mira's desk with a request that sounds small. Every Friday, before the weekly call with the publisher, she wants five lines about Plum: the family name, the date, how many glyphs there are, which ones have no Unicode value yet, and the widest glyph. Tomas keeps asking about the last one.

Mira can write that. She has all the pieces. What bothers her is the word "every". Every Friday she'd open the Scripting panel, find the file, open it and press the button. Four steps aren't many, but they're four steps she has to remember on the busiest morning of the week.

She messages Oskar. The answer comes back before lunch: "Put it in the menu. Then it's a command, like any other."

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • template.py from chapter 17. If you skipped it, an empty script will do.

docs.title: Step 1: Write the report
docs.text:
Start from the template and save it under a new name, friday_report.py, in your scripting-book folder. You'll move it later.

Two of the five lines need a loop, so they get a function each. Type the first one and try it on its own before you go on:

from fly import fl


def widest_glyph(font):
    widest = font[0]
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if glyph.width > widest.width:
            widest = glyph
    return widest


font = fl.CurrentFont()
print(widest_glyph(font))

<fgGlyph 'emdash'>

Read the function from the top. It puts the first glyph of the font into a box called widest. Then it walks through all the glyphs, and each time it meets one that's wider than the glyph in the box, it puts that one in the box in its place. When the loop is done, the box holds the widest glyph of all, and return hands it back.

This is a pattern you'll use for the tallest, the narrowest, the longest name, the largest kerning pair: start with the first one, compare it with each of the others, keep the winner.

The second function collects names in a list, the way you did in chapter 10:

def names_without_unicode(font):
    names = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if glyph.unicode is None:
            names.append(glyph.name)
    return names

You saw in chapter 6 that a glyph with no Unicode value has None in that drawer. is None is how you ask whether a box holds that nothing. Chapter 19 has more to say about it.

docs.title: Step 2: Borrow today's date
docs.text:
The report needs a date, and Mira isn't going to type it in by hand each week. Python can read the computer's calendar. The tool for it doesn't come from Fly. It comes with Python itself, in a package called datetime.

from datetime import date

print(date.today())

2026-11-13

You'll get your own day, in the same year-month-day order. That order sorts well in a file list, which matters in Part 6 when you export a family to a dated folder.

The import line has the shape you know from chapter 4: from a package, import a tool. Python arrives with a few hundred packages like this one, for dates, file names, math and much else. You've been inside FontLab so far, and here you reach past it for the first time.

Now make the mistake. Python cares about capitals, and so do package names:

from datetime import Date

ImportError: cannot import name 'Date' from 'datetime'

The real message goes on to name the file where Python looked. It's the same error you got in chapter 4 when you asked Fly for a tool it doesn't have: the package is there, the name inside it isn't. Change Date back to date.

docs.title: Step 3: Put it together
docs.text:
Here's the whole script, in the shape from chapter 17. There are no settings this time, so that part is left out.

#FLM: Friday Report
# Friday Report.py
# Prints a short status report on the current font for Ines:
# family name, date, glyph count, glyphs without a Unicode value,
# and the widest glyph.

from datetime import date

from fly import fl


def widest_glyph(font):
    widest = font[0]
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if glyph.width > widest.width:
            widest = glyph
    return widest


def names_without_unicode(font):
    names = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if glyph.unicode is None:
            names.append(glyph.name)
    return names


font = fl.CurrentFont()
print("Friday report:", font.info.familyName)
print("Date:", date.today())

no_unicode = names_without_unicode(font)
widest = widest_glyph(font)
print("Glyphs:", len(font))
print("Without Unicode:", len(no_unicode), no_unicode)
print(f"Widest: {widest.name} ({widest.width:.0f})")

Friday report: GG Plum
Date: 2026-11-13
Glyphs: 208
Without Unicode: 4 ['.notdef', 'a.sc', 'b.sc', 'c.sc']
Widest: emdash (1000)

One line reaches into font.info, the drawer of facts about the whole font that gave you the units per em in chapter 11. familyName is another drawer in the same wardrobe, next to the style name and a few dozen more. Part 6 opens most of them. Today you need one.

The em dash is the widest glyph in Plum, 1,000 units, which is the full height of the grid turned sideways. That's where its name comes from. Tomas will be pleased to have that settled.

docs.title: Step 4: Find the Scripts folder
docs.text:
FontLab keeps a folder of its own for the things you add to it. It's called the user data folder, and Fly's installer put its packages there in chapter 4. Inside it is a folder named Scripts. Every Python file in that folder shows up in FontLab's Scripts menu.

The quickest way there:

  1. Open Preferences. On a Mac, press Cmd+,.
  2. Go to the General page.
  3. Click Open user data folder in Finder. On Windows the button says in Explorer.

A file window opens. On a Mac the folder sits at ~/Library/Application Support/FontLab/FontLab 9. Look inside for Scripts. You'll find that it isn't empty: Fly's installer left a folder called Extensions there, and you met its List Extensions command in chapter 4 without knowing where it lived.

A folder inside Scripts becomes a submenu. Use that. Make a new folder inside Scripts and call it Halfmoon. Everything the studio writes will go there, apart from what other people's installers bring.

docs.title: Step 5: Move the script and refresh the menu
docs.text:
In FontLab, choose Save Script As… from the Scripting panel's menu, go to your new Halfmoon folder, and save the script there as Friday Report.py.

Then choose Scripts > Refresh Scripts. FontLab reads the folder again and rebuilds the menu.

Open the Scripts menu. There's a Halfmoon submenu, and in it one command: Friday Report. Choose it. The five lines appear in the Output panel. The Scripting panel doesn't need to be open, and nothing needs to be loaded into it.

Where did the command's name come from? From the first line of the file. You met #FLM: at the end of chapter 17: when the first line of a script starts with it, FontLab uses the rest of that line as the title in the menu. If the line isn't there, FontLab builds a title out of the file name.

Try it. Change the first line to #FLM: Friday Report for Ines, save, and choose Scripts > Refresh Scripts again. The command has a new name, and the file doesn't. Change it back when you've seen it.

Two copies

You now have friday_report.py in scripting-book and Friday Report.py in the Scripts folder. The menu runs the second. Delete the first, or one Friday you'll improve the wrong one and wonder why nothing changed.

docs.title: Step 6: Run it on another font
docs.text:
Open the original plum-var.vfj next to your practice copy, so that it's the font in front. Choose Scripts > Halfmoon > Friday Report.

Friday report: GG Plum
Date: 2026-11-13
Glyphs: 205
Without Unicode: 1 ['.notdef']
Widest: emdash (1000)

The script isn't about Plum-practice. It never names a file. It asks FontLab for the current font, whichever font that is at the moment you choose the command, and reports on that. When there's more than one font to report on, the same command will do for each of them.

Now close every font and choose the command once more. You get a letter of complaint, and its last line is one you've seen:

AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'info'

With no font open, fl.CurrentFont() hands back None, and None has no drawers. A command that sits in a menu will sooner or later be chosen at the wrong moment, by you or by somebody else in the studio. It should say something better than this. That's the next chapter.

On Friday morning Mira chooses the command, copies five lines out of the Output panel and pastes them into a message to Ines. It takes her less time than finding the file would have.

Going deeper: what else lives in that folder

The user data folder is where FontLab keeps everything that's yours and not part of the app: scripts, the packages Fly installed under python/3.11/site-packages, and a good deal that has nothing to do with Python. You can add other script folders too, anywhere on your disk, from the sidebar of the Scripting panel with Add scripts folder. A studio can keep one shared folder on a server that way, and Part 7 comes back to that idea.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A script saved in the Scripts folder of FontLab's user data folder becomes a command in the Scripts menu after Scripts > Refresh Scripts; a folder there becomes a submenu, and a first line starting with #FLM: sets the command's title. Python ships with packages of its own, such as datetime, that you import the same way you import from Fly. A script that asks for the current font works on whichever font is in front, and the pattern "start with the first, compare with the rest, keep the winner" finds the largest or smallest of anything.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Save wide_glyphs.py from chapter 17 into the Halfmoon folder, refresh, and run it from the menu. It already has its #FLM: line.
  2. Write narrowest_glyph(font) by changing one character in a copy of widest_glyph, and add a line for it to the report. In Plum as it came, that's quotesingle, the straight single quote, at 190 units. If you get a.sc, that tells you what width FontLab gave your new glyphs.
  3. Make a second folder inside Scripts, called Scratch, and save any small script there. Refresh and look at the menu. Then delete the folder in the file window, refresh again, and check that the submenu is gone.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 19 takes the complaint from step 6 and teaches the script to check for trouble before it starts.

docs.title: 19. When it goes wrong
docs.text:
On Friday afternoon Ines tries the new command herself. She has FontLab open and no font in it, because she's between two jobs. She chooses Scripts > Halfmoon > Friday Report and gets a block of text she can't read. She copies the last line into a message to Mira:

AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'info'. Is Plum broken?

Plum is fine. The script met a situation Mira didn't plan for, and it answered in Python's words, not in hers. You saw this complaint at the end of chapter 18. Today you teach the script to notice trouble and to say something a person can act on.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • Friday Report.py from chapter 18, in the Halfmoon folder inside FontLab's Scripts folder.

docs.title: Step 1: Find where the nothing came from
docs.text:
Read the complaint the way chapter 3 taught you: from the bottom. The last line names the kind of error and gives the detail. 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'info' means: you asked for the drawer info, and the thing you asked wasn't a font. It was None.

The line that failed is this one:

print("Friday report:", font.info.familyName)

That line isn't where the trouble began. It began further up, here:

font = fl.CurrentFont()

With no font open, FontLab has nothing to hand back, so the box font holds None. Python doesn't mind. Putting nothing in a box is allowed. The complaint comes later, at the first line that tries to use the nothing as if it were a font. You met the same delay in chapter 5, when len(font) failed one line below the line that caused it.

So when a complaint mentions 'NoneType', don't stare at the line it points to. Look upward for the box that was filled with nothing.

docs.title: Step 2: Ask before you open the drawer
docs.text:
The fix is a question. Before the script touches the font, it asks whether there is one. Try it in the Scripting panel first, in a new script, with every font closed:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
if font is None:
    print("Open a font first.")
else:
    print("Glyphs:", len(font))

Open a font first.

Open Plum-practice and run it again:

Glyphs: 208

is None is the test you've used since chapter 16, for glyphs without a Unicode value. It asks: does this box hold the nothing? Its opposite is is not None. You could write font == None and get the same answer here, but Python people write is for this one question, and every script you read will too.

An if that stands at the door of a script and turns away the cases it can't handle is called a guard.

docs.title: Step 3: Leave early
docs.text:
The guard works, but look at what it did to the shape of the script. Everything that used to be the work now has to live under else:, pushed four spaces to the right. Add a second guard and the work moves right again.

There's a tidier way, and it uses what you learned in chapter 16. Put the work inside a function called main. Inside a function, return means "stop here and go back". It doesn't have to hand anything back. So the guard can say its piece and leave, and the rest of the function stays flat against the left edge:

def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        print("Friday Report: open a font first.")
        return

    no_unicode = names_without_unicode(font)
    widest = widest_glyph(font)

    print("Friday report:", font.info.familyName)
    print("Date:", date.today())
    print("Glyphs:", len(font))
    print("Without Unicode:", len(no_unicode), no_unicode)
    print(f"Widest: {widest.name} ({widest.width:.0f})")


main()

Change Friday Report.py so that its last part looks like this. The header, the imports and the two functions above it stay as they were. Don't forget the last line. def only teaches Python the step, and main() is what performs it. Leave that line out and the command does nothing at all, without any complaint, which is harder to diagnose than an error.

Save, close every font, and choose the command from the menu.

Friday Report: open a font first.

The message starts with the name of the command. When you have ten commands in the menu and a line appears in the Output panel, you'll want to know who is talking.

The script template from chapter 17 gets a sixth habit: the work goes in main(), and main() starts with its guards. Open template.py and add that now.

docs.title: Step 4: The glyph that isn't there
docs.text:
A missing font is one kind of nothing. A missing glyph is the other, and you'll meet it more often. Ask Plum for a small cap that nobody has drawn yet:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph = font["Q.sc"]
print(glyph)
print(glyph.width)

None
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'width'

Asking a font for a name it doesn't have is not an error. The font hands back None, and the error waits for the next line. It's the same delay as in step 1, and the same guard cures it. Here it is inside a loop, where it earns its keep:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for name in ["a.sc", "b.sc", "Q.sc", "n"]:
    glyph = font[name]
    if glyph is None:
        print(name, "is not in this font")
    else:
        print(name, glyph.width)

The first two lines of output depend on the widths your .sc glyphs got in chapter 8. The last two are the same for everybody:

Q.sc is not in this font
n 523.0

Without the guard, the loop would stop at Q.sc and never reach n. With it, one missing glyph costs one line of output and the loop goes on. Any time a script works from a list of names that a person typed, some name in the list will be wrong sooner or later. Guard the lookup.

docs.title: Step 5: Try it, and catch what falls
docs.text:
A guard works when you can ask beforehand. Sometimes you can't. Then you let Python try, and you catch the complaint yourself.

Tomas sends Mira a column of numbers copied out of his spreadsheet, and she wants the total. Text copied from a spreadsheet arrives as strings, so each cell has to go through int(). In chapter 11 it cut floats down. It also reads a number out of a string. Two of his cells aren't numbers:

cells = ["596", "672", "n/a", "708", "", "520"]

total = 0
for cell in cells:
    total = total + int(cell)
print(total)

ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'n/a'

A ValueError means the tool got the right kind of thing, a string, with the wrong contents. Could you guard against it? You'd have to describe every string that isn't a number: letters, empty cells, a stray comma, two minus signs. It's less work to let int() decide, since it already knows.

cells = ["596", "672", "n/a", "708", "", "520"]

total = 0
skipped = 0
for cell in cells:
    try:
        total = total + int(cell)
    except ValueError:
        skipped = skipped + 1
        print("Not a number:", repr(cell))
print("Total:", total)
print("Skipped:", skipped)

Not a number: 'n/a'
Not a number: ''
Total: 2496
Skipped: 2

Read it as two instructions. try: says: do the indented lines, and watch. except ValueError: says: if one of them raises a ValueError, don't stop the script. Do these lines, then carry on after the whole block. If nothing goes wrong, the except part is skipped.

Two details. repr(cell) prints a string with its quotes on, so an empty cell shows up as '' and not as a blank you could miss. And the script counts what it skipped and says so. A script that drops things without a word is worse than one that stops, because you'll believe its total.

docs.title: Step 6: Don't catch everything
docs.text:
Now the mistake, and it's one that experienced people make. You can leave the error's name out and write a bare except:. It catches every complaint there is. Watch what that does when the script has a typo in it:

cells = ["596", "672", "n/a", "708", "", "520"]

total = 0
skipped = 0
for cell in cells:
    try:
        total = totl + int(cell)
    except:
        skipped = skipped + 1
print("Total:", total)
print("Skipped:", skipped)

Total: 0
Skipped: 6

No complaint. The script ran to the end and reported that all six cells were bad. They weren't. Look at the line under try:. The box is spelled totl. Every turn of the loop raised a NameError, the bare except: swallowed it, and the script told a confident lie.

Put the name back, except ValueError:, and run it again.

NameError: name 'totl' is not defined. Did you mean: 'total'?

That's the letter of complaint you needed. It names the typo and even suggests the spelling. An error message is the most useful thing Python gives you, so catch only the one error you expect and can do something about. Let every other error through.

Going deeper: guard or try?

The two tools overlap, and you'll see both styles in other people's scripts. In this book the habit is: guard when a cheap question answers it (is None, len(font) == 0, name in names), and use try when the only way to find out is to attempt the thing: turning text into a number, opening a file, asking a server. Keep the try block short, one or two lines. The more lines it holds, the more unrelated mistakes it can hide.

One more guard belongs in Friday Report.py. A new font with no glyphs in it isn't None, and I haven't tried what font[0] in widest_glyph does there. A second guard after the first, if len(font) == 0:, with its own message and its own return, covers that.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: None travels quietly from the line that produced it to the first line that uses it, so when a complaint mentions 'NoneType', look upward for the box that was filled with nothing. A guard, if font is None: followed by a message and return, stops a script at the door with words a colleague can act on, and the same test keeps a loop alive when one glyph name is missing. When you can't ask beforehand, try: and except ValueError: let the script attempt something and handle the one failure you expect, and a bare except: hides the failures you didn't.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Give wide_glyphs.py in the Halfmoon folder the same treatment: a main() with a guard that prints "Wide Glyphs: open a font first." Close every font and choose it from the menu.
  2. Add the cell "12.5" to Tomas's list and run the script from step 5. int() refuses it, because it isn't a whole number. Check that the report says so and that the total hasn't changed.
  3. Write a function glyph_width(font, name) that returns the glyph's width, or None when the font has no glyph of that name. Try it with "A" and with "Q.sc".

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 20 puts three weeks of small scripts together into one inventory of the font, and closes the first part of the book.

docs.title: 20. The first chore, done
docs.text:
It's Friday afternoon, three weeks after Mira found Oskar's sheet. The publisher's inventory is due on Monday, and Ines has added a condition: she wants to be able to produce it herself, for any font that's open, without calling anybody.

Mira has every piece of it. three_lists.py from chapter 16 finds the empty glyphs, the ones without a Unicode value and the small caps. Friday Report.py knows the family name and the date, lives in the Scripts menu and no longer falls over when no font is open. The width report from chapter 12 knows how to line up a column.

No Python is new today. The chapter is about putting the pieces together in an order that keeps working at every stage, which is a skill of its own.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • three_lists.py from chapter 16 and template.py from chapter 17.
  • The Halfmoon folder inside the Scripts folder, from chapter 18.

docs.title: Step 1: Say what the script answers
docs.text:
Before you write a line, write down what the reader of the output wants to know. Tomas, at the publisher, asked five questions:

  • How many glyphs are in the font?
  • How many of them are empty?
  • How many have a Unicode value, and how many don't?
  • How many small caps are there?
  • Which glyphs are behind each of those numbers?

That list is the plan. Each line of it will become one or two lines of the script, and when the output answers all five, you're done. Without the list, a script like this tends to grow a sixth and seventh answer that nobody asked for.

Open template.py, save it as inventory.py in your scripting-book folder, and turn the plan into the header:

#FLM: Inventory
# Counts what is in the current font: all glyphs, empty glyphs,
# glyphs with and without a Unicode value, and small caps.
# Reads only. Changes nothing in the font.

The last comment line tells whoever runs the script what it leaves alone. Ines doesn't need to save the font first, as she would for the marking script of chapter 14. It's worth one line to say so.

docs.title: Step 2: Collect, in one walk
docs.text:
Bring in the working part of three_lists.py, and wrap it the way chapter 19 showed: a main function with a guard at the top.

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

SMALL_CAP_SUFFIX = ".sc"


def is_empty(font, glyph):
    return pGlyph(font, glyph).isEmpty()


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        print("Inventory: open a font first.")
        return

    empty = []
    no_unicode = []
    small_caps = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if is_empty(font, glyph):
            empty.append(glyph.name)
        if glyph.unicode is None:
            no_unicode.append(glyph.name)
        if glyph.name.endswith(SMALL_CAP_SUFFIX):
            small_caps.append(glyph.name)

    print(len(font), len(empty), len(no_unicode), len(small_caps))


main()

208 4 4 3

The print line is scaffolding. It's ugly and it will go, but it tells you now that the collecting works, before you've spent any time on the looks. You know these four numbers from earlier chapters: 208 glyphs, four empty, four without a Unicode value, three small caps. If one of them is off, the mistake is in the thirty lines you have, and not somewhere in the forty you'll have later.

The suffix sits in a setting at the top, in capitals, like LIMIT in chapter 17. Another studio might name its small caps .smcp, and then one line changes.

docs.title: Step 3: Count what you didn't collect
docs.text:
Tomas asked how many glyphs have a Unicode value. The script has no list of those. Does it need a fourth list and a fourth if?

It doesn't. Every glyph either has a Unicode value or doesn't have one, so the two counts add up to the size of the font. You have the size and you have one of the counts. Inside main, indented like the lines around it, add:

with_unicode = len(font) - len(no_unicode)
print(with_unicode)

204

This is cheaper than a fourth list. The more important gain is that the two numbers can never disagree with each other, because one is made from the other. When a report has numbers that must add up, calculate one of them from the rest.

docs.title: Step 4: Line up the numbers
docs.text:
Five labels and five numbers make a small table. Chapter 12 gave you the tool: an f-string with a width for each column. Since the same pattern is needed five times, it gets a name.

def line(label, count):
    print(f"{label:<18}{count:>5}")

Put it under is_empty. Then replace the scaffolding line in main with the real output:

    print(f"Inventory of {font.info.familyName}, {date.today()}")
    print()
    line("Glyphs", len(font))
    line("Empty", len(empty))
    line("With Unicode", len(font) - len(no_unicode))
    line("Without Unicode", len(no_unicode))
    line("Small caps", len(small_caps))

Run it.

NameError: name 'date' is not defined

That's the deliberate mistake of the chapter, though you may have made it for me. The heading line came from Friday Report.py, and the import it depends on stayed behind. When you carry lines from one script to another, look at every name in them and ask where it comes from. Add the missing line at the top, above the Fly imports:

from datetime import date

Inventory of GG Plum, 2026-11-13

Glyphs              208
Empty                 4
With Unicode        204
Without Unicode       4
Small caps            3

Your date will be your own. The numbers stand in a column with their last digits aligned, which is how people expect to read counts.

docs.title: Step 5: Name the glyphs
docs.text:
The fifth question was "which ones?". report from chapter 16 printed a title, a count and the names. The counts are in the table now, so the function gets simpler, and it gets two improvements.

def name_list(title, names):
    if len(names) == 0:
        return
    print()
    print(f"{title}:")
    for name in sorted(names):
        print("   ", name)

The first improvement is the guard. A finished font has no empty glyphs, and a heading with nothing under it looks like a script that broke. If the list is empty, the function leaves early and prints nothing. The table above already says 0.

The second is sorted. The lists were filled in glyph order, which is the order of the Font window. Tomas doesn't have the Font window. Alphabetical order is the one he can find things in.

Three calls at the end of main:

    name_list("Empty", empty)
    name_list("Without Unicode", no_unicode)
    name_list("Small caps", small_caps)

docs.title: Step 6: Hang it in the menu
docs.text:
Here's the whole script.

#FLM: Inventory
# Counts what is in the current font: all glyphs, empty glyphs,
# glyphs with and without a Unicode value, and small caps.
# Reads only. Changes nothing in the font.

from datetime import date

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

SMALL_CAP_SUFFIX = ".sc"


def is_empty(font, glyph):
    return pGlyph(font, glyph).isEmpty()


def line(label, count):
    print(f"{label:<18}{count:>5}")


def name_list(title, names):
    if len(names) == 0:
        return
    print()
    print(f"{title}:")
    for name in sorted(names):
        print("   ", name)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        print("Inventory: open a font first.")
        return

    empty = []
    no_unicode = []
    small_caps = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if is_empty(font, glyph):
            empty.append(glyph.name)
        if glyph.unicode is None:
            no_unicode.append(glyph.name)
        if glyph.name.endswith(SMALL_CAP_SUFFIX):
            small_caps.append(glyph.name)

    print(f"Inventory of {font.info.familyName}, {date.today()}")
    print()
    line("Glyphs", len(font))
    line("Empty", len(empty))
    line("With Unicode", len(font) - len(no_unicode))
    line("Without Unicode", len(no_unicode))
    line("Small caps", len(small_caps))
    name_list("Empty", empty)
    name_list("Without Unicode", no_unicode)
    name_list("Small caps", small_caps)


main()

Below the table, it prints:

Empty:
    a.sc
    b.sc
    c.sc
    space

Without Unicode:
    .notdef
    a.sc
    b.sc
    c.sc

Small caps:
    a.sc
    b.sc
    c.sc

Read the output the way Tomas will. The space glyph is empty, and it should be: a space has a width and no drawing. The .notdef glyph has no Unicode value, and it shouldn't have one: it's the box a font shows for a character it doesn't have. The script can't know either of those things. It reports what it finds, and a person who knows fonts decides what's a problem. Mira writes two lines to Tomas explaining the two exceptions, which takes less time than teaching them to the script.

Use Save Script As… to put a copy in the Halfmoon folder as Inventory.py, choose Scripts > Refresh Scripts, and run Scripts > Halfmoon > Inventory. Then close every font and run it once more, to see the guard speak:

Inventory: open a font first.

Mira shows Ines where the command is. Ines opens a font Mira has never seen, an old Halfmoon display face, and runs it. Sixty lines of Python count a font they weren't written for.

Going deeper: what the inventory doesn't know yet

The script calls a glyph a small cap when its name ends in .sc. That's a convention, not a fact about the drawing: a glyph named a.sc that holds a lowercase a would be counted all the same. It also counts a glyph as having a Unicode value without asking whether it's the right one, and it treats a glyph built entirely from other glyphs as not empty, without saying that it borrows. Lines 4 and 5 of Oskar's sheet are about that last point. Each of these is a chapter of Part 2.

docs.title: Where you are
docs.text:
Three weeks ago the first chapter asked you to type one line and press a button. Look at the script above. You can read every line of it and say what it does and why it's there, and you wrote most of those lines yourself, in earlier chapters, before you put them together today.

On Oskar's sheet, line 1 was crossed out in chapter 4, line 2 in chapter 8 and line 3 in chapter 12. Line 9, "list every glyph whose name ends in .sc", has had a pencil dot next to it since chapter 9. The inventory lists them on demand, for any font. Mira crosses it out. Seven lines are left, and every one of them asks the script to know more about a font than names, widths and Unicode values.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A larger script is assembled from small ones that already work: write down the questions it answers, get the numbers right with one plain print, and only then make the output readable. A count that can be calculated from two others should be, so that the report can't contradict itself. Lines carried from another script bring their imports and settings along as a debt, and the complaint that follows names what's missing. The script reports and the person reading decides what the numbers mean.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a line to the table for glyphs wider than 800 units, with the limit as a setting at the top, and a name list for them. On Plum-practice the count is 11.
  2. Add a line for the widest glyph, using widest_glyph(font) from Friday Report.py. The line function wants a number in its second slot, so decide how to show a name and a width: write a second small function, or use a plain print with an f-string.
  3. Make a new empty glyph by hand with Font > New Glyph…, name it d.sc, and run the inventory again. Predict all five numbers before you look. Then check your prediction against the output.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Part 2 begins with a question the loop answers slowly, "what's the width of adieresis?", and a new kind of container that answers it at once.

docs.title: Part 2: A toolbox
docs.text:
A box for the things you'll want again.

The chores pile up. Mira builds a toolbox of her own.

In Part 1 you asked a font questions, one glyph at a time, and read the answers in the Output panel. That is enough for a count. It isn't enough when Ines wants the answer as a file, when the publisher sends a list of characters, or when a change has to be taken back.

This part gives you the tools for that. You learn the dictionary, which looks things up by name, and use it to count and to find the glyph for a letter. You write a report to a file, read a list from a file, and make tables a spreadsheet can open. You change a glyph and undo the change, rename with care, and tag and mark glyphs so that people can find them.

Then you start keeping what you write. You learn how Python finds modules, and you gather your best functions into a set of snippets that you can paste into any script. You sort tables by any column, read a traceback without alarm, and make a script ask before it acts.

Oskar's sheet waits through these four weeks. The chores come from Ines, from Tomas and from the publisher, and the sheet still has four lines crossed out and seven open when the part ends. What changes is that you now have the tools for the seven.

You need the practice copy of Plum from Part 1 and Fly installed in FontLab 9.

docs.title: 21. Look it up
docs.text:
Monday, the fourth week. Ines is on the phone with the publisher's proofreader, and she's covering the receiver with her hand.

"Mira. How wide is the a-umlaut?"

Mira has this_glyph.py. She could have the answer in five seconds, if she knew what to type. Plum has no glyph called a-umlaut. She scrolls the Font window, finds the cell and reads the name under it: adieresis.

"471."

"And the sharp s?"

That one is germandbls. Then "the a-e, the stuck-together one", which is ae. Three questions, three trips to the Font window. The proofreader talks like a person and the font is named like a font, and Mira is the translator.

A translator needs a dictionary. Python has one.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open. Since chapter 8 it has 208 glyphs.
  • Nothing else. This chapter starts a new script.

docs.title: Step 1: A list where you choose the labels
docs.text:
You know lists. A list keeps things in a row, and you get one back by its position: names[0], names[1]. Position is the only handle a list gives you.

A dictionary keeps things in pairs. You choose a label for each thing, and you get the thing back by its label. Type this:

nicknames = {
    "a-umlaut": "adieresis",
    "sharp s": "germandbls",
    "a-e": "ae",
}
print(nicknames["sharp s"])

Run it.

germandbls

Look at how it's built. Curly braces go around the whole thing, where a list has square brackets. Inside are three pairs. Each pair is a label, a colon and a value, and commas keep the pairs apart. I've put one pair per line because that's how you'd write a word list on paper. Python doesn't mind the line breaks inside the braces.

The label is called a key and the thing it leads to is called a value. You ask with square brackets, the way you ask a list, but the key goes between them where the position would be.

You've done this already without the name. font["A"] in chapter 6 was a lookup by key. A font behaves like a dictionary of glyphs whose keys are the glyph names. Today you're making a dictionary of your own.

docs.title: Step 2: Two lookups in a row
docs.text:
Now use the translation. The nickname leads to the glyph name, and the glyph name leads to the glyph.

from fly import fl

nicknames = {
    "a-umlaut": "adieresis",
    "sharp s": "germandbls",
    "a-e": "ae",
}

font = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph_name = nicknames["sharp s"]
glyph = font[glyph_name]
print(f"sharp s is {glyph.name}, width {int(glyph.width)}")

sharp s is germandbls, width 569

Follow the boxes. nicknames["sharp s"] gives the text germandbls, and it goes in the box glyph_name. font[glyph_name] gives the glyph. There are no quotes around glyph_name in that line, because you want what's in the box and not the word on its label.

Change "sharp s" to "a-e" in both places and run again. 753. Mira could have answered Ines without leaving the keyboard.

Save this as lookup.py.

docs.title: Step 3: Ask for a word that isn't in the dictionary
docs.text:
Ines's next question is the e-acute. Put "e-acute" between the brackets and run.

KeyError: 'e-acute'

A new letter of complaint, and a short one. KeyError means: you asked for a key, and this dictionary has no such key. The key you asked for is right there in the message.

Compare that with what the font did in chapter 6. When you asked a font for a glyph it didn't have, it handed back None and said nothing, and the trouble started one line later. A dictionary of your own is stricter. It stops on the spot and names the missing key. That's the better behavior. You find out where the problem is, not where it ended up.

A KeyError is also what you get from a capital in the wrong place. "Sharp S" and "sharp s" are two different keys.

docs.title: Step 4: Check first, and add a word
docs.text:
You can ask a dictionary whether it has a key before you use it. The word is in, the same in you used on text in chapter 9.

nicknames = {
    "a-umlaut": "adieresis",
    "sharp s": "germandbls",
    "a-e": "ae",
}

ask = "e-acute"
if ask in nicknames:
    print(nicknames[ask])
else:
    print(f"I don't know '{ask}' yet")

I don't know 'e-acute' yet

No error. The script took the else road and told you what's missing in words you chose.

To teach the dictionary a new word, put a value in under a new key. Add this line above ask = "e-acute":

nicknames["e-acute"] = "eacute"

Run it again and you get eacute. It's the same move as putting something in a box, except this box has many drawers and you say which one. If the key is new, the dictionary grows by one pair. If the key was there already, the old value is thrown out and the new one takes its place. That second case will catch you one day: two pairs with the same key don't give you two answers. The later one wins, and Python doesn't warn you.

len works here as it does on a list. len(nicknames) is now 4: four pairs.

The keys here are pieces of text. A key can be a number too, and tomorrow's will be.

docs.title: Go through the whole dictionary
docs.text:
A for loop works on a dictionary too. It hands you the keys, one at a time, in the order they went in.

for nickname in nicknames:
    print(nickname)

a-umlaut
sharp s
a-e
e-acute

The keys come out and the values stay behind. Mira expected pairs, a nickname and a name on each line. But a key is all you need, because with the key in your hand you can look the value up inside the loop. And sorted, which you used on a list in chapter 10, puts the keys in alphabetical order first:

for nickname in sorted(nicknames):
    print(nickname, "means", nicknames[nickname])

a-e means ae
a-umlaut means adieresis
e-acute means eacute
sharp s means germandbls

That's the word list printed the way a paper dictionary would have it. Mira pins a copy next to the phone, so Ines can see which nicknames the script knows. Notice that a dictionary has no positions. nicknames[0] doesn't mean "the first pair". It means "the value under the key 0", there's no such key, and you get KeyError: 0.

docs.title: Step 5: Let the font fill a dictionary
docs.text:
Typing pairs by hand is fine for a dozen nicknames. For anything about every glyph, let a loop do the typing.

Start with an empty dictionary, which is a pair of curly braces with nothing between them. Then go through the font and put one pair in for each glyph: the name as the key, the width as the value.

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
widths = {}
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    widths[glyph.name] = int(glyph.width)

print(len(widths))
print(widths["adieresis"])
print(widths["germandbls"])

208
471
569

The loop ran 208 times and each time around it added one pair. After the loop, widths is a little table you made: every glyph name in Plum, each with its width next to it.

Why bother, when font["adieresis"].width gives the same 471? Two reasons.

The first is that the table is yours. You decided what goes in it. Today it's the width. It could be the width with the left side taken off, or the width compared with another weight, or a yes-or-no for "has Ines approved this glyph". The font only stores what a font stores. A dictionary stores whatever you work out.

The second is that the table keeps still. Suppose a script changes widths, and afterwards you want to say which glyphs changed and by how much. If you filled widths before the change, the old numbers are still in it.

docs.title: Step 6: Put the two dictionaries together
docs.text:
Now Ines can ask in her own words, about several glyphs at once.

from fly import fl

nicknames = {
    "a-umlaut": "adieresis",
    "sharp s": "germandbls",
    "a-e": "ae",
    "e-acute": "eacute",
}

font = fl.CurrentFont()
widths = {}
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    widths[glyph.name] = int(glyph.width)

for ask in ["a-umlaut", "sharp s", "o-slash", "a-e"]:
    if ask in nicknames:
        glyph_name = nicknames[ask]
        print(f"{ask}: {glyph_name}, {widths[glyph_name]}")
    else:
        print(f"{ask}: not in my list yet")

a-umlaut: adieresis, 471
sharp s: germandbls, 569
o-slash: not in my list yet
a-e: ae, 753

Three answers and one honest "not yet". The script didn't stop at o-slash, because the if checked before the lookup.

Mira's first run looked different in one line. She had typed the dictionary a second time for this script, and in her hurry she wrote "a-e": "a-e". Her last line read:

KeyError: 'a-e'

The complaint came from widths[glyph_name], and it's a fair one: Plum has no glyph called a-e. She found the typo in a minute. She was lucky that the wrong value led nowhere. If she had typed "a-e": "a", the script would have printed a-e: a, 471 and nobody would have complained at all.

That's the limit of a dictionary. It tells you when a key is missing. It can't tell you that a value is wrong, and a wrong value that leads somewhere gives a wrong answer with a straight face. When you type a table by hand, read it back once, the way you'd read back a phone number.

Save the script over lookup.py. The list on the for ask in line is the part you change when the phone rings.

Going deeper: what can be a key

Keys are usually pieces of text, and in this book they nearly always are. Numbers work as keys too, which is how chapter 24 looks a glyph up by its Unicode value. A list can't be a key, because a key must not be able to change after it goes in. Values can be anything at all: text, numbers, lists, glyphs, other dictionaries.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A dictionary holds pairs of key and value in curly braces, and d[key] gives you the value back. A missing key stops the script with KeyError, so check with in first when you aren't sure. You can add a pair with d[key] = value, and a loop that does this for every glyph turns the font into a lookup table that holds whatever you decide to put in it.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add three nicknames of your own to lookup.py for glyphs in Plum. Look their real names up in the Font window, then ask for all three in the last loop.
  2. Build a second dictionary in the loop from step 5, called codes, with the glyph name as key and glyph.unicode as value. Print codes["germandbls"] and codes[".notdef"]. One of them prints something you met in chapter 6.
  3. Make a dictionary with the same key twice and different values, for example {"a": 1, "a": 2}. Print it, and print its len. Say in one sentence what happened to the first pair.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 22 uses a dictionary to count: how many glyphs of each kind does the font have?

docs.title: 22. Counting things
docs.text:
Tuesday. The publisher prints price lists, and the proofreader has a question that sounds small.

Do Plum's figures line up in columns? If the 1 is narrower than the 8, our tables wobble.

Mira knows what she's being asked. Figures that all share one width are called tabular figures, because they stack up cleanly in a table. To answer, she could open ten glyphs and read ten numbers.

Ines, reading over her shoulder, makes it bigger. "While you're in there. How many different widths does that font have, anyway?"

Nobody at Halfmoon knows. It's the kind of question you don't ask when the only way to answer it is by hand.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • lookup.py from chapter 21, for the dictionary moves.

docs.title: Step 1: A tally sheet
docs.text:
Think about how you'd count the cars on your street by color, with a pencil. You write a color the first time you see it and put one stroke next to it. Every time that color comes by again, you add a stroke. You don't know before you start which colors will turn up.

A dictionary can be that sheet. The key is the thing you're counting. The value is the number of strokes.

Try it on a short list first, with no font. This counts glyph names by their first letter:

names = ["A", "Aacute", "B", "a", "adieresis", "b", "a.sc"]

tally = {}
for name in names:
    first = name[0]
    tally[first] = tally[first] + 1
print(tally)

name[0] is the first character of the name, the same square brackets you used on lists and on text in Part 1. The line after it is the pencil stroke: open the drawer for this letter, add one, put it back. Run it.

KeyError: 'A'

You met KeyError yesterday. Python is right again. The first name is A. The script tries to open the drawer "A" to add one to it, and the sheet is still blank. You can't add a stroke next to a color you haven't written down.

docs.title: Step 2: Ask politely with get
docs.text:
What you want to say is: "give me the count for this letter, and if there isn't one yet, call it zero." A dictionary has a tool for exactly that sentence. It's called get.

tally = {"A": 2}
print(tally.get("A", 0))
print(tally.get("B", 0))

2
0

get sits in a drawer of the dictionary, so there's a dot in front of it, and it's a function, so it has a slot. Two things go through the slot: the key you're asking about, and the answer you want if the key isn't there. For "A" the dictionary has a value, and you get it. For "B" it has nothing, and you get your zero. No error either way.

Square brackets are the strict way to ask, and get is the polite way. Use the strict way when a missing key means something has gone wrong, as it did with Mira's typo yesterday. Use the polite way when a missing key is normal, and on a tally sheet it's normal every time something turns up for the first time.

Put get into the tally:

names = ["A", "Aacute", "B", "a", "adieresis", "b", "a.sc"]

tally = {}
for name in names:
    first = name[0]
    tally[first] = tally.get(first, 0) + 1
print(tally)

{'A': 2, 'B': 1, 'a': 3, 'b': 1}

Seven names, four different first letters. Go through it for "A". The first time, get answers 0, the script adds 1, and the pair "A": 1 goes on the sheet. The second time, get answers 1, and the pair becomes "A": 2. You'll write that one line many times. Capital A and small a are counted apart, as they should be.

While we're counting, here's a shorter way to write something you've typed since chapter 7. count = count + 1 has a short form, count += 1. It means the same thing: take what's in the box, add 1, put it back.

count = 0
count += 1
count += 1
print(count)

2

It works with any number on the right, so total += 20 adds 20. From here on the book uses the short form for a plain counter. The tally line keeps its long form, because get has to supply the 0 for a key that's new.

docs.title: Step 3: Tally the font
docs.text:
Now the real question. The thing to count is the width, so the width is the key.

One decision first. The three small caps from chapter 8 are empty, and .notdef isn't a character anybody types. I'd leave those four out, so that the count is about glyphs a reader of the price list can meet. They have one thing in common: no Unicode value. You know how to test for that.

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
tally = {}
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.unicode is not None:
        width = int(glyph.width)
        tally[width] = tally.get(width, 0) + 1

print(len(tally), "different widths")

84 different widths

There's Ines's answer. Plum has 204 glyphs with a Unicode value, and between them they use 84 different widths.

Is that a lot? It's about what you'd expect from a text face. Each letter gets the width its shape needs, and an m needs more than an i. But it isn't 204 either, so many glyphs share a width with others. The interesting part is which ones.

Notice that the keys are numbers this time. I said yesterday that numbers can be keys, and here they are. tally[596] doesn't mean position 596. It means "the count filed under the width 596".

docs.title: Step 4: Read the sheet, pair by pair
docs.text:
Print tally and you get one long line with 84 pairs between curly braces. It's all there and it's hard to read. You want one pair per line.

Yesterday's loop over a dictionary gave you the keys. There's a second way that gives you the key and the value together:

for width, count in tally.items():
    print(width, count)

596 8
852 1
517 1
621 2
665 1
485 5

And 78 more lines. items hands the loop one pair at a time, and the loop puts the two halves in two boxes. That's why there are two labels between for and in, with a comma. The first box gets the key and the second gets the value. I've called them width and count because that's what they are on this sheet. On another sheet you'd pick other words.

The first line says eight glyphs are 596 wide. That's the A and its seven accented versions, which you saw at the top of Tomas's table. An accent doesn't change how much room a letter takes, so the whole group shares the width of its base letter.

docs.title: Check that the strokes add up
docs.text:
Before you trust a tally, add it up. If you counted cars for an hour and a hundred went by, the strokes on your sheet should come to a hundred. If they come to ninety, you missed some. If they come to a hundred and ten, you counted some twice.

Here the strokes should come to the number of glyphs that have a Unicode value. Add this under the loop from step 3:

total = 0
for width, count in tally.items():
    total = total + count
print(total, "glyphs counted")

204 glyphs counted

Your font has 208 glyphs. Take away .notdef and the three empty small caps, and 204 is what should be left. It is, so the sheet and the font agree.

It takes four lines, and it catches a wrong tally before anyone else sees it. A script that counts will always give you a number, and a wrong number looks as tidy as a right one. Whenever you can think of a second way to arrive at a figure, spend the four lines. The day the two don't match, you've found a mistake before Ines did.

docs.title: Step 5: Only the busy widths
docs.text:
Eighty-four lines is still a lot to look at, and half of them say 1. Put a test inside the loop, and tidy the line with an f-string:

for width, count in tally.items():
    if count >= 8:
        print(f"{width}: {count} glyphs")

596: 8 glyphs
708: 8 glyphs
523: 9 glyphs
471: 8 glyphs
490: 14 glyphs
500: 10 glyphs

Six widths do a lot of the work. One of them stands out: fourteen glyphs at 490. Ten of those could be the figures. If they are, what are the other four?
