The tally knows how many. It doesn't know who, because you only asked it to count. For that, go back to the font with the number in your hand.

docs.title: Step 6: Who is 490 wide?
docs.text:
from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if int(glyph.width) == 490:
        print(glyph.name)

zero
one
two
three
four
five
six
seven
eight
nine
numbersign
dollar
yen
Euro

All ten figures, at one width. Plum's figures are tabular, and the price lists won't wobble.

The other four are the number sign, the dollar, the yen and the euro. Whoever drew Plum gave the currency signs the same width as the figures, so that a column of prices lines up from the sign to the last digit. Nobody at Halfmoon had noticed that. It was sitting in the font, and a count found it.

Mira writes back: Yes. All ten figures are 490 units wide, and so are $, ¥, € and #. Then she changes 490 to 708 and runs it again, for fun, and gets the O family and the Q.

One note. who_is.py doesn't test for a Unicode value, so it looks at every glyph, the empty small caps from chapter 8 included. If your new glyphs show up in one of its lists, that's why.

Put the script from step 3 together with the loop from step 5 and save it as width_tally.py. Keep the script from this step as who_is.py. The number on its if line is the part you change.

Going deeper: sorting the sheet by count

The lines in step 5 come out in the order the widths first turned up in the font, so 490 isn't at the top even though it's the biggest group. sorted on a dictionary sorts the keys, which here would sort by width. Sorting by the count takes one more idea, and chapter 36 has it.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A dictionary makes a tally sheet: the thing you count is the key and the count is the value. d.get(key, 0) asks for a value and takes 0 when the key is new, so d[key] = d.get(key, 0) + 1 adds one stroke without tripping over the first one. for key, value in d.items(): goes through the pairs. A count tells you how many, and a second pass over the font tells you which.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Change the script from step 3 so that it tallies by the first letter of the glyph name, as in step 2, and take the Unicode test out so that every glyph counts. How many glyph names in your font start with a small a? Count the cells in the Font window to check.
  2. In width_tally.py, change the test to count == 1 and print only the count of such widths, not the widths themselves. You'll need a counter from chapter 7 inside the loop.
  3. Run who_is.py for 523 and for 500. One of the two groups has an odd member that doesn't share a shape with the rest. Which glyph is it, and can you think why the designer gave it that width?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 23 looks hard at the number you've been using to tell real characters from the rest: the Unicode value.

docs.title: 23. Unicode is a number
docs.text:
Wednesday. The proofreader has stopped phoning and started writing, and what she writes looks like this:

Please confirm Plum covers U+00E9, U+0153 and U+20AC.

Mira looks at her own list, the one from chapter 7 with its Unicode numbers. It says things like 233 and 8364. Nothing in it starts with U+, and nothing in it has a letter in the middle of a number.

"Is she using a different Unicode?" Mira asks.

She isn't. There's one Unicode, and two ways of writing its numbers down. Today you learn to read both, and you teach your scripts to speak the proofreader's.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • this_glyph.py from chapter 6. You'll improve it.

docs.title: Step 1: Every character has a number
docs.text:
Start with no font at all. Python knows Unicode by itself, and it has a function that tells you the number of any character.

print(ord("A"))
print(ord("a"))
print(ord("é"))
print(ord("€"))

65
97
233
8364

ord is short for "ordinal", which is a number that says where something stands in a row. Unicode is that row: one long numbered list of every character people write with, kept by a group called the Unicode Consortium. Capital A stands at place 65. The euro sign stands at place 8,364. The list has room for more than a million characters, and so far it holds about 150,000.

You saw 65 in chapter 6, when you asked the glyph A for its unicode drawer. It's the same 65. The font didn't make that number up. A font says "my glyph named A is the drawing for character number 65", and that's how a computer that receives the character 65 from a keyboard knows which drawing to show.

The trip works in the other direction too:

print(chr(233))
print(chr(8364))

é
€

chr is short for "character". Give it a number and it hands you the character at that place.

Capital and small letters are different characters with different numbers. A is 65 and a is 97. To Unicode they've no more to do with each other than A and €.

docs.title: Step 2: One character, please
docs.text:
ord has a slot for exactly one character. Give it two:

print(ord("ab"))

TypeError: ord() expected a character, but string of length 2 found

That's a clear letter of complaint. The reason I'm showing it is what it tells you about text. To you, "ab" and "a" are the same kind of thing, a bit of typing. To Python, a piece of text is a row of characters, and a row with one character in it is the only kind ord will take. When you want the numbers for a whole word, you loop:

for letter in "Plum":
    print(letter, ord(letter))

P 80
l 108
u 117
m 109

docs.title: Step 3: The other way to write the number
docs.text:
Now the proofreader's version. She wrote U+00E9 for the é. Your script says 233. These are the same number, and here's the idea in a few lines.

The way you count has ten digits, 0 to 9. When you run out, you start a new column: after 9 comes 10. There's a second way of counting that has sixteen digits. It uses 0 to 9 and then, because we've no more digit shapes, the letters A to F. In that system A means ten, B eleven, and so on up to F for fifteen. Only after F do you start a new column. It's called hexadecimal, or hex.

Why would anyone do that? Because computers store numbers in a way that sixteen fits neatly and ten doesn't. Unicode charts were laid out by people who think in sixteens, with sixteen characters to a row. So the charts, FontLab and every proofreader in the business write Unicode values in hex, and put U+ in front so you can tell.

Take the proofreader's E9. It has two columns. The right one counts ones, as you're used to, and holds 9. The left one doesn't count tens. It counts sixteens, and it holds E, which is fourteen. Fourteen sixteens are 224, and 9 more makes 233. Same number, written in a different system, the way 233 and CCXXXIII are.

One trap comes with this. A hex number that happens to use no letters looks like an everyday number and isn't. U+0041 is the capital A, and you know that as 65, not 41. When a number arrives from a type person without a label, ask which kind it is.

You don't have to do the sums. Python translates. You met hex in chapter 6:

print(hex(233))

0xe9

That's e9, with Python's own "hex coming up" mark in front. It's the right number in the wrong clothes. The custom is capital letters, at least four digits, zeros in front if it's short, and U+ at the start. An f-string can dress it properly:

number = 233
print(f"U+{number:04X}")

U+00E9

In chapter 12 you put things after a colon inside the curly braces to line up columns. This is the same slot with a different order in it. X means "write this in hex, with capitals". 04 means "at least four digits, and fill with zeros". The U+ in front is plain text. Copy :04X as it stands. You'll type it the same way every time.

And back the other way, from the proofreader's digits to your number:

print(int("00E9", 16))

233

In chapter 11 int cut a float down to a whole number. It also reads text: int("523") gives 523. With a second thing in the slot, 16, it reads the text as hex. Leave the U+ off. int doesn't know that part.

docs.title: Step 4: A better this_glyph.py
docs.text:
Open this_glyph.py. It prints the Unicode value in the plain form. Make it print both forms and the character too.

from fly import fl

glyph = fl.CurrentGlyph()
number = glyph.unicode
print("Name:", glyph.name)
print("Unicode:", f"U+{number:04X}", "which is", number)
print("Character:", chr(number))
print("Width:", int(glyph.width))

Go to the eacute glyph and run it.

Name: eacute
Unicode: U+00E9 which is 233
Character: é
Width: 470

Now try it on Euro. You get U+20AC, 8364 and €. Try fi, the ligature: U+FB01, 64257. That's one of the two highest numbers in the whole font.

Then go to .notdef and run it.

TypeError: unsupported format string passed to NoneType.__format__

The script got as far as the name and stopped on the next line. Read the complaint from its end. NoneType is the name you learned to look for in chapter 19: somewhere a box holds the nothing. __format__ is the part of a value that an f-string asks to do the dressing. So the complaint says: I was handed a format, 04X, and the thing I was to dress in it was None.

Which box? .notdef has no Unicode value, so number is None, and the f-string was asked to write nothing as four hex digits. It couldn't. Notice that the plain version of the script never had this trouble. print("Unicode:", None) prints the word None and goes on. The complaint arrived on the day you asked for more than plain printing. That's how a script that ran for weeks fails on a glyph it has seen before.

The fix is the guard from chapter 19:

from fly import fl

glyph = fl.CurrentGlyph()
number = glyph.unicode
print("Name:", glyph.name)
if number is None:
    print("Unicode: none")
else:
    print("Unicode:", f"U+{number:04X}", "which is", number)
    print("Character:", chr(number))
print("Width:", int(glyph.width))

Save it as what_unicode.py. Leave this_glyph.py as it was. You'll want to remember where you started.

docs.title: Step 5: The glyph name is not the character
docs.text:
There are now three things on Mira's screen for one letter, and it's worth keeping them apart.

eacute is the glyph name. It's a label inside the font, made of plain letters so that every program can handle it. People chose it. It could have been e_with_stroke_on_top and the font would work the same.

233, or U+00E9, is the Unicode value. It's the link from the font to the outside world. Change it and the keyboard's é shows a different drawing, or none.

é is the character, the thing the reader types and sees.

Scripts get these mixed up all the time, and so do people. Here's a way to see that they're separate:

print(len("eacute"))
print(len("é"))

6
1

Six letters in the name. One character. When a script asks the font for font["é"], it's using a character where a glyph name belongs, and it gets None. You found that in an exercise in chapter 6. Now you know why.

docs.title: Step 6: Answer the proofreader
docs.text:
She asked about three values. You can now read them: 00E9 is 233, the é. What's 0153, and what's 20AC?

for code in ["00E9", "0153", "20AC"]:
    number = int(code, 16)
    print(f"U+{code} is {number}, the character {chr(number)}")

U+00E9 is 233, the character é
U+0153 is 339, the character œ
U+20AC is 8364, the character €

So she wants the é, the œ and the euro sign. Notice the script hasn't touched the font yet. It only translated. Whether Plum has a glyph for each of those numbers is a different question, and you can't answer it with font[...], because that looks up names, not numbers.

Mira scrolls the Font window. The é is there. The euro is there. She can't see an œ anywhere near the o, but with 208 cells she isn't sure she hasn't missed it.

She writes: é and € yes. œ I can't find. I'll confirm tomorrow.

Going deeper: glyphs with no number, and numbers above FFFF

Not every glyph needs a Unicode value. Small caps, alternates and the parts of ligatures are reached through OpenType features, which Part 5 covers, and they usually have none. Going the other way, Unicode values can be longer than four hex digits. Emoji and many historic scripts sit above U+FFFF and are written with five or six digits. :04X handles them: four is the least it writes, not the most.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Every character has a place in Unicode's list: ord("é") gives the number 233 and chr(233) gives the character back. Type people write that number in hex with U+ in front, and you translate with f"U+{number:04X}" in one direction and int("00E9", 16) in the other. A glyph name, a Unicode value and a character are three different things, and a font is what ties them together.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Find the number and the U+ form for these characters without opening FontLab: ß, ?, a space, and the first letter of your own name.
  2. ord("a") - ord("A") gives a number. Work it out, then check whether ord("z") - ord("Z") gives the same. Use what you find to print the small letter for "Q" with chr and ord and a sum.
  3. Run what_unicode.py on the space glyph. The line that starts with Character: looks unfinished. Why isn't it? Change that line so that the character is printed between two quote marks.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 24 answers the question Mira couldn't: given a number, does the font have a glyph for it?

docs.title: 24. Find the glyph for a letter
docs.text:
Thursday. Mira owes the proofreader an answer about the œ, and before she's had coffee there's a second question on top of it. The publisher is thinking about a Hungarian novel.

Do we have ő? That's an o with two long accents, not an ö.

Mira scrolls the Font window again. She's hunting through 208 cells for one small letter, and then for its capital. I stop her.

"You know its number," I say. "Yesterday you learned how to get the number of any character. Ask the font by number."

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • What you know about dictionaries from chapters 21 and 22, and about def from chapter 16.

docs.title: Step 1: The slow way first
docs.text:
Start with what you can already write. You have a number, 339, the œ. Every glyph has a unicode drawer. Go through all the glyphs and look in each drawer.

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.unicode == 339:
        print(glyph.name)

oe

There it is. Plum has an œ, and its glyph is named oe. It sits a few cells after the o, behind the accented ones, and Mira went past it twice. That's no shame. After a hundred cells of small black shapes, an œ looks a lot like an o followed by an e. The loop doesn't get tired. It looked in all 208 drawers and compared numbers, and a number can't look like its neighbor.

Change 339 to 337, the ő, and run it again. Nothing prints. Is that a "no"?

It is, but it's a quiet one. A script that prints nothing when the answer is no looks the same as a script that's broken. Mira looks at the empty Output panel and isn't sure which she's got. You want a script that says no out loud.

docs.title: Step 2: Turn the font inside out
docs.text:
The loop also does more walking than it needs to. For every question, it visits every glyph. Ask about ten characters and it makes ten trips through the font.

You've seen the cure. In chapter 21 you built widths, a dictionary from glyph name to width, by going through the font once. After that, every lookup was instant. Build the same kind of table, but file each glyph under its Unicode value:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
by_number = {}
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.unicode is not None:
        by_number[glyph.unicode] = glyph.name

print(len(by_number))
print(by_number[339])

204
oe

The keys are numbers and the values are names. In chapter 21 I said numbers can be keys, and in chapter 22 you used them to count. Here they're doing the job a dictionary was made for: you hold a number, you want the thing filed under it.

The if keeps the four glyphs without a Unicode value out. If you left it off, all four would try to file themselves under the key None, each one replacing the last, and you'd have one useless pair in your table.

Now the question about ő:

print(by_number[337])

KeyError: 337

That's a loud no, at least. But it's a letter of complaint, and you don't want to forward one of those to a proofreader. You know two polite ways to ask. One is in. The other is get:

print(by_number.get(339))
print(by_number.get(337))

oe
None

In chapter 22 you gave get a second thing through the slot, the 0 to use when the key was new. Leave it off and get answers None for a key it doesn't have. You've met None before: it's what Python says when there's nothing there.

docs.title: Step 3: Give the question a name
docs.text:
You're going to ask this question often. Wrap it in a function, so that the question has a name.

def glyph_for(character):
    number = ord(character)
    return by_number.get(number)

Three lines. It's a recipe with one slot, as in chapter 16, and the slot takes a character. The first line inside turns it into its number. The second looks the number up and hands back what it found.

return is the word that hands something back. You used it in chapter 16, and here's a closer look at it, because it's what makes this function useful. A function with return is a question that has an answer. When Python gets to return, the function is over, and the answer goes back to the place where the function was called. You can put that answer in a box, test it, or print it:

print(glyph_for("œ"))
print(glyph_for("ő"))
print(glyph_for("é"))

oe
None
eacute

Mira types the character she's been asked about, straight from the proofreader's message. No numbers, no hex, no scrolling.

Remember the three things from yesterday: the character, the Unicode value and the glyph name. This function is the whole chain in one go. A character goes in, ord makes it a number, the table makes the number a glyph name. It's the same trip a computer makes when someone presses a key and a letter of Plum appears on the screen, except that the computer goes on to fetch the drawing.

docs.title: Step 4: Print is not return
docs.text:
Here's a mistake that almost everybody makes once. Write the function with print where return should be:

def glyph_for(character):
    number = ord(character)
    print(by_number.get(number))

answer = glyph_for("œ")
print("The answer is", answer)

oe
The answer is None

Look at the two lines. The function did show oe, in the Output panel, for a person to read. But it handed nothing back. So the box answer got None, which is what every function hands back when it has no return.

This is the difference between a colleague who says the number out loud as they walk past your desk and one who writes it on a slip and puts it in your hand. If all you wanted was to hear it, both will do. If you need to do something with it next, you need the slip. print is for people. return is for the rest of your script.

Put the return back.

docs.title: Step 5: Say yes or no in words
docs.text:
Now use the answer. The function hands back a name or None, and an if turns that into a sentence:

character = "ő"
name = glyph_for(character)
if name is None:
    print(f"No. There is no glyph for {character} (U+{ord(character):04X}).")
else:
    print(f"Yes. {character} (U+{ord(character):04X}) is the glyph {name}.")

No. There is no glyph for ő (U+0151).

Change the first line to "œ":

Yes. œ (U+0153) is the glyph oe.

Both answers are out loud now, and both come with the U+ form the proofreader likes, thanks to yesterday's :04X.

Notice what the function doesn't do. It doesn't print, and it doesn't decide how the answer is worded. It finds a glyph name and that's all. The wording lives outside. That split is worth keeping. Next week you may want the same answer in a file, or in a count, and a function that only finds things can serve all of those. One that also talks can only talk.

docs.title: Step 6: A whole word at a time
docs.text:
The proofreader won't stop at one letter. A piece of text is a row of characters, so loop over it. Here's the Hungarian sentence that typesetters use to test accents, the way English speakers use the quick brown fox:

text = "Árvíztűrő tükörfúrógép"
for character in text:
    if glyph_for(character) is None:
        print(f"Missing: {character} (U+{ord(character):04X})")

Missing: ű (U+0171)
Missing: ő (U+0151)

Twenty-two characters, two gaps. Plum has the Á, the í, the ö, the ú and the rest. It lacks exactly the two letters that Hungarian has and its neighbors don't: the o and the u with the double acute accent.

That's a much better answer than "no". Mira writes: œ yes, it was hiding under the name oe. For Hungarian we're two letters short, ő and ű, plus their capitals I expect. Everything else is there. Ines reads it and says the two letters are a morning's drawing, not a reason to turn a book down.

Here's the whole script. Save it as have_we_got.py.

from fly import fl


def glyph_for(character):
    number = ord(character)
    return by_number.get(number)


font = fl.CurrentFont()
by_number = {}
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.unicode is not None:
        by_number[glyph.unicode] = glyph.name

text = "Árvíztűrő tükörfúrógép"
for character in text:
    if glyph_for(character) is None:
        print(f"Missing: {character} (U+{ord(character):04X})")
print("Checked", len(text), "characters.")

The last line is there for the reason from step 1. When nothing is missing, the script still says something, so you can tell a clean result from a script that didn't run.

The function sits at the top and uses by_number, which is filled further down. That works because Python only reads a function when it's defined. It looks for by_number later, at the moment the function is called, and by then the table exists.

Going deeper: FontLab can look up a Unicode value itself

The font object has its own way to find a glyph by Unicode value, and chapter 81 uses it when the book gets to encoding in earnest. I've built the table by hand here for two reasons. It's four lines you fully understand, and a table you built is one you can also loop over, count and compare, which is what chapter 25 does with it.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: To find things fast, go through the font once and file each glyph under the thing you'll search by, here its Unicode value. d.get(key) hands back None when the key isn't there. A function with return hands its answer to the rest of the script, which print can't do, and a function that only finds something is easier to reuse than one that also reports. A script should say something when the answer is no.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Check your own name with have_we_got.py, then the sentence Zażółć gęślą jaźń, which is the Polish test sentence. Which characters does Plum lack for Polish?
  2. The loop in step 6 reports a missing character once for every time it appears. Try the text "őőő". Then fix it: keep a list of the characters you've already reported, and report a character only if character in reported is false. You need append, and an if with an else: do nothing much in the first branch, and report in the second.
  3. Write a second function, number_for(name), that goes the other way: give it a glyph name, get its Unicode value, or None. You'll need a second dictionary, filed by name. What does it hand back for "a.sc", and for "nosuchglyph"? The two answers look the same. Do they mean the same?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 25 takes a whole language's worth of characters and subtracts the font from it, with a new kind of container made for that sum.

docs.title: 25. The missing list
docs.text:
Friday. Yesterday's answer about Hungarian went down well, and it has had the usual effect of a good answer, which is more questions. The publisher's rights person has sent Ines a list of five languages they sell books in: French, German, Hungarian, Polish and Czech.

"She wants to know what's missing for each one," Ines says. "And I want to know how many letters that is in total, because I'm the one who has to say when they'll be drawn."

Mira could run have_we_got.py five times with five test sentences. But a sentence isn't a language. The Hungarian one happened to have no capital Ő in it. What she needs is to take everything a language needs, take away everything the font has, and see what's left.

That's a subtraction. Python has a container you can subtract.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • have_we_got.py from chapter 24.

docs.title: Step 1: A bag with no doubles
docs.text:
Type this, with no font involved yet:

letters = set("banana")
print(letters)
print(len(letters))

{'b', 'n', 'a'}
3

Your three letters may come out in a different order. That's the first thing to know about what you've made.

This is a set. Picture a cloth bag. You can drop things in and you can ask whether something's in there, but the things have no order, and the bag won't hold two of the same. "banana" has six letters and three different ones, and the bag kept the three.

A list is a row. It has a first and a last, and it can hold the same thing twice. A set has no first and no last, and holds each thing once. You can check that it has no first:

print(letters[0])

TypeError: 'set' object is not subscriptable

"Subscriptable" is Python's word for "you can use square brackets on it". You can't. There's no place number 0 in a bag.

When you want to read a set, put it in order on the way out with sorted, which you know from chapter 10. It hands you a list:

print(sorted(letters))

['a', 'b', 'n']

You can also write a set out by hand, with curly braces and no colons: {"a", "b", "n"}. Curly braces with colons make a dictionary. Curly braces without make a set. One trap: empty curly braces, {}, make an empty dictionary, as you saw in chapter 21. For an empty set you write set().

docs.title: Step 2: Take one bag from another
docs.text:
Here's what sets are for. Two small ones:

need = set("äöüß")
have = set("abcäö")

print(sorted(need - have))

['ß', 'ü']

The minus sign between two sets means "everything in the first that isn't in the second". German needs four special letters, this pretend font has two of them, and the two left over are the missing list. You wrote no loop and no if. The subtraction is the whole question.

There are two more signs, and you'll want both today.

print(sorted(need & have))
print(sorted(need | have))

['ä', 'ö']
['a', 'b', 'c', 'ß', 'ä', 'ö', 'ü']

& means "in both". Read it as "and": in need and in have. | is the upright bar, on most keyboards near the Return key, and it means "in either". Read it as "or". It pours both bags into one, and because a set won't hold doubles, the ä and the ö show up once.

The three have names from school math that you may remember: difference, intersection and union. You don't need the names to use the signs.

Notice that the order matters for minus and not for the other two. have - need is a different question: what does the font have that the language doesn't need? Here that's a, b and c.

docs.title: Step 3: Everything the font has
docs.text:
Now the real font. Yesterday you built by_number, a dictionary filed by Unicode value. Today you want something simpler, the bag of characters that Plum can show.

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
have = set()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.unicode is not None:
        have.add(chr(glyph.unicode))

print(len(have))

204

add is to a set what append is to a list: it drops one more thing in. chr turns each glyph's number back into its character, as in chapter 23. So have holds 204 characters: A, B, é, €, the space and all the rest.

Asking a set whether it holds something uses in, the same word as for lists and dictionaries:

print("é" in have)
print("ő" in have)

True
False

docs.title: Step 4: Everything a language needs
docs.text:
Next, the other bag. Hungarian writes with the plain letters a to z plus nine accented ones. The plain ones Plum has, so I'll only list the nine:

letters = "áéíóöőúüű"
need = set(letters)
print(sorted(need - have))

['ő', 'ű']

The same two as yesterday. But yesterday's sentence had no capitals in it apart from the first letter, and a book has chapter titles. A function that lives in a drawer of an object is called a method. You've used several without the word: append on a list, split on text. Text has one called upper, which hands back the same text in capitals:

print(letters.upper())

ÁÉÍÓÖŐÚÜŰ

Pour both into one bag with the "or" sign, then subtract:

need = set(letters) | set(letters.upper())
missing = need - have
print(len(need), "needed,", len(missing), "missing:", sorted(missing))

18 needed, 4 missing: ['Ő', 'ő', 'Ű', 'ű']

Four, not two. Mira guessed at the capitals in her message yesterday. Now she knows.

One caution about upper. It follows the rules of Unicode, and for a few letters those rules are odd. The German ß has no capital in everyday spelling, so "ß".upper() hands back SS, two letters. Your set of German capitals ends up with an S in it and no capital ß. For this job that does no harm, since Plum has an S. It does mean that "German: complete" below leaves out the capital sharp s, ẞ, which Plum doesn't have. Keep it in mind when a count looks odd.

docs.title: Step 5: Five languages at once
docs.text:
You have five languages and one question to ask of each. That's a dictionary and a loop. The keys are the language names and the values are the special letters:

languages = {
    "French": "àâæçéèêëîïôœùûüÿ",
    "German": "äöüß",
    "Hungarian": "áéíóöőúüű",
    "Polish": "ąćęłńóśźż",
    "Czech": "áčďéěíňóřšťúůýž",
}

for language, letters in languages.items():
    need = set(letters) | set(letters.upper())
    missing = need - have
    if len(missing) == 0:
        print(f"{language}: complete")
    else:
        missing_text = " ".join(sorted(missing))
        print(f"{language}: {len(missing)} missing: {missing_text}")

French: complete
German: complete
Hungarian: 4 missing: Ő ő Ű ű
Polish: 16 missing: Ą ą Ć ć Ę ę Ł ł Ń ń Ś ś Ź ź Ż ż
Czech: 18 missing: Č č Ď ď Ě ě Ň ň Ř ř Š š Ť ť Ů ů Ž ž

There's one new thing in that listing, " ".join(...). It's the opposite of split from chapter 9. split cuts a string into a list. join glues a list into one string, and the string in front of the dot is the glue. Here the glue is a single space. It makes the missing letters print as a neat row and not as a list with brackets and quote marks, which Ines would have to explain to the rights person.

I typed those five alphabets from a reference book. They're the letters each language needs beyond a to z, and nothing more: no quote marks, no special punctuation. A real check would add those. This one answers the question that was asked.

Look at what the result says about Plum. It's a font for Western Europe. French and German are done, down to the œ and the ÿ. Hungarian is nearly done. Polish and Czech have hardly been started: Polish has only its ó, and Czech only the acute accents it shares with everyone else.

docs.title: Step 6: How many to draw
docs.text:
Ines wanted a total. You might add 4 and 16 and 18 and say 38. Are you sure no letter is on two lists? Polish and Czech are neighbors, and neighbors share.

Don't guess. Pour every missing list into one bag and count the bag. A set won't hold doubles, so anything shared gets counted once:

to_draw = set()
for language, letters in languages.items():
    need = set(letters) | set(letters.upper())
    to_draw = to_draw | (need - have)

print(len(to_draw), "characters to draw")

38 characters to draw

Thirty-eight after all. This time the plain sum was right, because the letters these languages share, like á and ó, are ones Plum already has. Add Slovak to the dictionary and it stops being right: Slovak wants č, ď, ň, š, ť and ž as well, and the sum would count them twice. The set never does.

to_draw = to_draw | ... is the pattern from the counter in chapter 7, count = count + 1, done with bags. Take what's in the box, pour more in, put the result back in the same box.

Mira sends Ines three lines and a number. Ines does her own sum: thirty-eight letters, most of them a base letter with an accent the font partly has. "Two weeks," she tells the rights person, "if nothing else comes in." Something else always comes in.

Put the pieces together and save them as missing_chars.py: the lines that fill have from step 3, the languages dictionary and its loop from step 5, and the total from step 6.

Going deeper: where real language lists come from

Nobody types alphabets from memory for production work. The Unicode Consortium publishes a free database called CLDR that lists the characters each language uses, and several font tools ship ready-made lists built from it. In chapter 27 you read such a list from a text file, so that the next language is a file somebody sends you and not a line you type.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A set is a bag that holds each thing once and keeps no order. With two sets, - gives what's in the first and not the second, & what's in both and | everything in either, and that turns "what's missing?" into one subtraction. add puts one thing in, sorted lays a set out for reading, and ' '.join(...) glues a list of strings into one line.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add Turkish to the dictionary with the letters çğıöşü and run the script. Then look at what "ı".upper() and "i".upper() give you, and say why a careful Turkish check needs one more capital than upper provides.
  2. Turn the subtraction around. Which characters does Plum have that none of the five languages asked for and that aren't plain letters a to z or A to Z? Build one big need set first. You'll get figures and punctuation, and some letters. Which languages might those letters be for?
  3. Use & to find which special letters Hungarian and Czech have in common. Then find the letters that Polish and Czech share. Does the answer fit what step 6 said about the total?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: In chapter 26 the report stops living in the Output panel. Ines wants a file she can attach to an email.

docs.title: 26. Write it to a file
docs.text:
Still Friday, four o'clock. The language question is answered, and now the weekly report is due. Mira picks Scripts > Halfmoon > Friday Report, five lines appear in the Output panel, and she does what she's done every Friday since chapter 18: drags the mouse across them, copies, switches to her mail, pastes.

Today she drags one line short. Ines gets a report with no widest glyph and writes back: Where's the last line? And could this be an attachment? I keep them in a folder.

Copying from a panel by hand is a small job, and small jobs done by hand are where the slips happen. The script already knows every word of the report. It can put them in a file.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • Friday Report.py from chapter 18.
  • The scripting-book folder where your practice font lives.

docs.title: Step 1: Where is the font?
docs.text:
A file has to go somewhere. The natural place for a report about a font is next to the font. So the first question is where the font file sits on the disk, and the font can tell you:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
print(font.path)

/Users/mira/Documents/scripting-book/Plum-practice.vfj

Yours will show your own name and wherever you put the folder. On Windows it starts with a drive letter and uses backslashes.

That string is a path: the route from the top of the disk down to one file. Read it like an address written backwards, biggest thing first. Users, then the person mira, then her Documents, then the folder scripting-book, and at the end the file. The slashes separate the stops.

You want the same address with a different last stop: same folder, but report.txt in place of the font. You could cut the string up yourself with split. Don't. Python comes with a tool that knows how addresses work, on a Mac and on Windows:

from pathlib import Path

font_file = Path(font.path)
folder = font_file.parent
print(folder)
print(font_file.name)

/Users/mira/Documents/scripting-book
Plum-practice.vfj

Path comes from pathlib, which ships with Python the way datetime does. You hand it the string and get back a path object: a wardrobe again, with drawers that make sense for an address. parent is the folder the file sits in. name is the last stop on its own.

To add a stop to a path, you use a slash. That's odd the first time you see it, because a slash between numbers means divide. Between a path and a string it means "and then, inside that":

report_file = folder / "report.txt"
print(report_file)

/Users/mira/Documents/scripting-book/report.txt

Nothing has been written yet. You've made an address. There's no house there.

docs.title: Step 2: Open, write, close
docs.text:
Writing a file takes three moves. You open it, you put text in, you close it. Python has a way of writing this so that the third move can't be forgotten:

with open(report_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Friday report: GG Plum")

Run it. The Output panel stays empty. Go to the scripting-book folder in the Finder, or in Explorer on Windows. There's a new file, report.txt. Open it with a double-click, and there's your line.

Take the first line of the listing apart, because you'll type it for the rest of your scripting life.

open(...) opens a file and hands you something to write with. Three things go through the slot. The first is the address. The second, "w", says what you're there to do: w for write. The third, encoding="utf-8", I'll come back to in a moment.

as f puts the opened file in a box labeled f.

with and the colon and the indented block say: the file is open for as long as these indented lines run. When the indentation ends, Python closes it for you. You know this shape from for and if. Inside the block is "while the file is open". Outside is "afterwards".

Why does closing matter? Until a file is closed, some of your text may still be waiting in memory and not yet on the disk. Open the file too early from another program and you can find it half-written or empty. with makes sure the file gets closed even when a line inside the block goes wrong.

And encoding="utf-8". A file on disk holds numbers, not letters. Chapter 23 showed you that every character has a number. An encoding is the rule for storing those numbers in a file, and UTF-8 is the rule that can store all of them and that nearly every program now expects. Leave it off and Python picks whatever your computer's system prefers, which on some Windows machines can't store an ő. This morning's report was full of such letters. Type the encoding every time and you won't have to think about it again.

docs.title: Step 3: Three things that go wrong
docs.text:
Break it on purpose, three ways. First, write a second line:

with open(report_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Friday report: GG Plum")
    f.write("Glyphs: 208")

Open the file again.

Friday report: GG PlumGlyphs: 208

The line from step 2 hasn't been kept and added to. It's been replaced. "w" means write from the start: if the file exists, its old contents are thrown away the moment you open it. Python doesn't ask. Keep that in mind before you aim "w" at a file you care about.

And the two pieces of text sit on one line. print has been ending every line for you since chapter 2. write doesn't. It puts down what you give it and nothing more. To end a line you write the line-ending character yourself. In Python you type it as \n, a backslash and an n, inside the quotes:

    f.write("Friday report: GG Plum\n")
    f.write("Glyphs: 208\n")

Second mistake. Hand write a number:

    f.write(208)

TypeError: write() argument must be str, not int

print takes anything and turns it into text. write takes text and only text. An f-string is the handy way to make text out of anything, and you already know those.

Third mistake. Send the file to a folder that isn't there:

report_file = folder / "reports" / "report.txt"
with open(report_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Friday report\n")

FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/Users/mira/Documents/scripting-book/reports/report.txt'

That reads strangely. You weren't looking for a file, you were making one. What's missing is the folder reports. open will make a file. It won't make folders. Either make the folder by hand, or let the path make it, which you'll do in step 5.

docs.title: Step 4: Let print do the writing
docs.text:
Ending every line with \n and turning every number into text is a nuisance, and you have a tool that already does both. print can write to a file. You tell it which one with file=:

with open(report_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print("Friday report:", font.info.familyName, file=f)
    print("Glyphs:", len(font), file=f)

Friday report: GG Plum
Glyphs: 208

That text is in the file now, not in the Output panel. Everything you know about print still holds: commas between the pieces, a space put between them, any kind of thing accepted, a new line at the end. The only change is where the words land. Leave file=f off one line and that line goes to the Output panel as before. That's a slip anyone can make, and one you spot quickly.

This is why I held file writing back until you were comfortable with print. A report that prints is one small change away from a report that saves.

docs.title: Step 5: A name with the date in it
docs.text:
Ines keeps the reports in a folder, so each needs its own name, or every Friday will wipe out the last. The date belongs in the name. You have the date from chapter 18, and an f-string builds the name:

from datetime import date

today = date.today()
reports = folder / "reports"
reports.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
report_file = reports / f"plum-report-{today}.txt"
print(report_file.name)

plum-report-2026-11-13.txt

mkdir is short for "make directory", and directory is an older word for folder. exist_ok=True tells it not to complain when the folder is already there, which from the second Friday on it will be.

The date comes out as year, month, day. Leave it that way. File names that start with the year sort themselves into date order in any folder window, and no one has to wonder whether 11-12 is November or December.

docs.title: Step 6: The Friday report, saved
docs.text: Now change the real script. Open Friday Report.py from the Halfmoon folder inside FontLab's Scripts folder. Three things change. Two imports join the one at the top. Four lines in main work out where the file goes. And the five print lines move into a with block and gain file=f. The two functions and the guard from chapter 19 stay as they are.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Friday Report
# Friday Report.py
# Saves a short status report on the current font for Ines,
# as a text file in the folder "reports" next to the font.

from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

from fly import fl


def widest_glyph(font):
    widest = font[0]
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if glyph.width > widest.width:
            widest = glyph
    return widest


def names_without_unicode(font):
    names = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if glyph.unicode is None:
            names.append(glyph.name)
    return names


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        print("Friday Report: open a font first.")
        return

    no_unicode = names_without_unicode(font)
    widest = widest_glyph(font)

    today = date.today()
    reports = Path(font.path).parent / "reports"
    reports.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    report_file = reports / f"plum-report-{today}.txt"

    with open(report_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        print("Friday report:", font.info.familyName, file=f)
        print("Date:", today, file=f)
        print("Glyphs:", len(font), file=f)
        print("Without Unicode:", len(no_unicode), no_unicode, file=f)
        print(f"Widest: {widest.name} ({widest.width:.0f})", file=f)

    print("Saved", report_file)


main()

Save, and run it from the Scripts menu. One line appears in the Output panel:

Saved /Users/mira/Documents/scripting-book/reports/plum-report-2026-11-13.txt

The last line of the script has no file=f and sits outside the with block, so it goes to the panel, after the file is closed. It's the script saying out loud that it did something, and where. A script that writes a file and says nothing leaves you hunting through folders.

Mira attaches the file. All five lines are in it, because nobody dragged a mouse. Ines files it and replies with one word, which from Ines is praise.

The script has one weak spot, and you should know about it. A font that's never been saved has no file, so it has no path to stand next to. Make a new font with File > New Font, run the report on it, and see what the complaint says. Then close that font without saving. In chapter 19 you learned to guard against a missing font with if font is None:. A guard for a font with no path is the first exercise.

Going deeper: letting the user pick the folder

The script decides where the file goes, and for a weekly report that's what you want. For a tool that other people use, you'd let them choose, with the same Save window every program shows. FontLab scripts can open that window. It needs a few ideas you haven't met, so it waits for chapter 39, where your scripts start asking questions.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: font.path is where the font file lives, and Path from pathlib takes that address apart and builds new ones with /. A file is written inside with open(address, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:, which closes the file for you. "w" replaces whatever was there. print(..., file=f) sends a line to the file and not the Output panel, so any report you can print is a report you can save.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Run the report on a new, unsaved font and read the error. Then add a guard above the line that builds reports: if the font has no path, print a sentence asking the user to save the font first, and don't write anything. Print font.path for the unsaved font first, so you know what to test for.
  2. Open a file with "a" where the script has "w". Run it three times and look at the file. What does "a" stand for, and when would Ines want it?
  3. Change missing_chars.py from chapter 25 so that it saves the language report as plum-languages.txt in the reports folder. Open the result. Are the ő and the ž there? Then take encoding="utf-8" out and try again. On a Mac you'll likely see no difference. Put it back anyway.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 27 goes the other way. Somebody sends Mira a text file with a list of glyph names, and the script has to read it.

docs.title: 27. Read a list from a file
docs.text:
Monday of the fifth week. Over the weekend the publisher's art director decided which small caps the first book needs, and she's sent Ines a text file. Ines forwards it with one line: Which of these do we have?

Mira opens smallcaps.txt. It's a list of glyph names, one to a line. There are some blank lines in it, and two lines that start with #, where the art director has left herself notes.

She could type the names into a Python list, quotes and commas and all. For ten names that's five minutes. But the art director has said this is the first batch. There'll be a second file, and a third, and each time Mira would be retyping somebody else's list and adding her own typos to it.

The names are already in a file. Last chapter the script wrote one. Today it reads one.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • A plain text file to read. Make it now: open a text editor, type the lines below, and save the file as smallcaps.txt in your scripting-book folder, next to the font. On a Mac, TextEdit needs Format > Make Plain Text first.
# Small caps for Plum, first batch
a.sc
b.sc
c.sc
d.sc
e.sc
f.sc
g.sc
h.sc

# figures
zero.sc
one.sc

Leave the blank line in. And put two spaces after one.sc, where nobody will see them. Real files that people send you have such things in them, and the script has to cope.

docs.title: Step 1: Read the whole thing
docs.text:
Opening a file to read looks like opening it to write, with one piece missing:

from pathlib import Path

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
list_file = Path(font.path).parent / "smallcaps.txt"

with open(list_file, encoding="utf-8") as f:
    text = f.read()

print(text)

The Output panel shows the file, line for line, as you typed it.

The "w" is gone. Leave the second thing out and open assumes you've come to read, which is the safe guess, since reading can't damage anything. f.read() takes everything in the file and hands it over as one string. The with block closes the file as before.

Notice where print(text) sits: outside the block, after the file is closed. That works because the text is in the box labeled text by then. You don't need the file open any longer than it takes to get the words out of it.

One string holding thirteen lines isn't much use yet. Ask how long it is:

print(len(text))

103

A hundred and three characters. Count the letters you typed and you'll come up short, because some of those characters are ones you can't see: the line endings, one at the end of every line, and the two spaces after one.sc. Last chapter you typed the line ending as \n when you wrote a file. Here it is coming back.

docs.title: Step 2: One line at a time
docs.text:
You want a list of names, and the file has one name to a line. Python lets you loop over an open file as if it were a list of lines:

wanted = []
with open(list_file, encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        wanted.append(line)

print(len(wanted))
print(wanted[:3])

13
['# Small caps for Plum, first batch\n', 'a.sc\n', 'b.sc\n']

Thirteen items, one for each line in the file. Now look hard at the second line of output, because the trouble for the rest of the chapter is in it. Each string ends in \n. When Python hands you a line from a file, it hands you all of it, the line ending included.

Printing a list shows you its strings in their raw form, quotes and backslashes and all. That's why I printed the list and not the lines one by one. When something read from a file misbehaves, print it inside a list and look for what's hiding at the ends.

docs.title: Step 3: The name that isn't there
docs.text:
Does it matter? Ask the font about the second line of the file. You know from chapter 6 that font[name] gives you the glyph, or None when there's no glyph by that name. I couldn't run this one in FontLab, so take the None below as what I expect from chapter 6. And you know a.sc is in the font, because Mira added it in chapter 8.

name = wanted[1]
print(name)
print(font[name])

a.sc

None

Printed, the name looks right. There's an empty line under it, which is your only hint. And the font says it has no such glyph.

The font is correct. It has a glyph named a.sc, four characters. You asked for a.sc\n, five characters. To a person those are the same name. To a computer they're as different as a.sc and a.scx. Nothing complains. The name with an invisible line end on it isn't in the font, and that's all you're told. You get a quiet wrong answer: every name in the art director's list would be reported missing.

Text has a method for this, strip. It hands back the string with everything invisible trimmed off both ends: line endings, spaces and tabs.

print([name.strip()])
print(font[name.strip()])

['a.sc']
<fgGlyph 'a.sc'>

strip only trims the ends. A space in the middle of a string stays where it is. And like upper in chapter 25, it doesn't change the string in the box. It hands you a new one, and it's up to you to keep it.

So strip every line you read from a file, as a habit.

docs.title: Step 4: Skip what isn't a name
docs.text:
Strip each line on the way into the list and print the result:

wanted = []
with open(list_file, encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        wanted.append(line.strip())

print(wanted)

['# Small caps for Plum, first batch', 'a.sc', 'b.sc', 'c.sc', 'd.sc', 'e.sc', 'f.sc', 'g.sc', 'h.sc', '', '# figures', 'zero.sc', 'one.sc']

Better. The line endings are gone, and so are the two spaces after one.sc. Three items still aren't glyph names. Two are the art director's notes. One is '', two quote marks with nothing between them: that's the blank line, which was nothing but a line ending, and stripped down to an empty string.

You need an if that lets names through and keeps the rest out. Both tests are ones you have. An empty string equals "". A note starts with #, and startswith is from chapter 9.

wanted = []
with open(list_file, encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        name = line.strip()
        if name != "" and not name.startswith("#"):
            wanted.append(name)

print(len(wanted), "names")
print(wanted)

10 names
['a.sc', 'b.sc', 'c.sc', 'd.sc', 'e.sc', 'f.sc', 'g.sc', 'h.sc', 'zero.sc', 'one.sc']

Ten names, clean. Read the if line aloud: "if the name isn't empty and doesn't start with a hash". Strip first, then test. A line of spaces is blank only after you've stripped it.

Using # for notes isn't a rule of text files. It's a habit the art director picked up somewhere, and it happens to be Python's own comment mark. When you write a script that reads lists, you decide what counts as a note. Whatever you decide, say so in a comment at the top of the script, so the next person knows what they may put in the file.

docs.title: Step 5: Which do we have?
docs.text:
Now Ines's question. For each wanted name, is there a glyph? You could ask the font ten times with font[name]. I'd sooner build the bag of all glyph names once, as in chapter 25, and ask the bag. It keeps the question in plain sight:

in_font = set()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    in_font.add(glyph.name)

have = []
missing = []
for name in wanted:
    if name in in_font:
        have.append(name)
    else:
        missing.append(name)

print(f"Asked for: {len(wanted)}")
print(f"In the font: {len(have)}: {' '.join(have)}")
print(f"Still to make: {len(missing)}: {' '.join(missing)}")

Asked for: 10
In the font: 3: a.sc b.sc c.sc
Still to make: 7: d.sc e.sc f.sc g.sc h.sc zero.sc one.sc

I kept have and missing as lists and not sets on purpose. The art director wrote her names in an order that means something to her, letters first and figures after. Lists keep that order. A set would shuffle it.

There's a second question hiding here, and it's worth one more line. "In the font" means a glyph by that name exists. Mira made a.sc, b.sc and c.sc as empty glyphs, with nothing drawn in them. A glyph that exists and a glyph that's finished aren't the same, and you have the test for empty from chapter 8. Exercise 2 asks you to put the two together.

docs.title: Step 6: The file that isn't there
docs.text:
One more mistake before you save. Change the file name in the script to smalcaps.txt, with one l, and run it.

FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/Users/mira/Documents/scripting-book/smalcaps.txt'

Last chapter this error meant a missing folder. Here it means what it says. Read the path in the message letter by letter. It's the exact address Python tried, and nine times out of ten the mistake is visible in it: a misspelled name, a file saved as smallcaps.txt.rtf by an editor that wasn't in plain-text mode, or a file that's sitting in Downloads and not next to the font.

Fix the name, and save the script as read_glyph_list.py. Here's the whole thing:

# Reads a list of glyph names from a text file next to the font.
# One name per line. Blank lines and lines starting with # are skipped.
from pathlib import Path

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
list_file = Path(font.path).parent / "smallcaps.txt"

wanted = []
with open(list_file, encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        name = line.strip()
        if name != "" and not name.startswith("#"):
            wanted.append(name)

in_font = set()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    in_font.add(glyph.name)

have = []
missing = []
for name in wanted:
    if name in in_font:
        have.append(name)
    else:
        missing.append(name)

print(f"Asked for: {len(wanted)}")
print(f"In the font: {len(have)}: {' '.join(have)}")
print(f"Still to make: {len(missing)}: {' '.join(missing)}")

Mira sends the three lines to Ines. Ines reads "still to make: 7" and asks whether the script could make them. It could. But making glyphs is a change to the font, and changes need more care than questions do. That care starts in chapter 29.

docs.title: A language in a file
docs.text:
Chapter 25 said the next language would be a file somebody sends you. Here it is. The rights person has added Slovak, and Ines has typed its special letters into slovak.txt, one line:

áäčďéíĺľňóôŕšťúýž

Reading it takes what you learned in step 1 and step 3: read the whole file, strip it. Then it's chapter 25 again.

have_characters = set()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.unicode is not None:
        have_characters.add(chr(glyph.unicode))

with open(Path(font.path).parent / "slovak.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    letters = f.read().strip()

need = set(letters) | set(letters.upper())
missing = need - have_characters
missing_text = " ".join(sorted(missing))
print(f"Slovak: {len(need)} needed, {len(missing)} missing: {missing_text}")

Slovak: 34 needed, 18 missing: Č č Ď ď Ĺ ĺ Ľ ľ Ň ň Ŕ ŕ Š š Ť ť Ž ž

The first four lines fill the bag of characters as missing_chars.py did. That script called the bag have. I've renamed it here because this chapter already uses have for something else. Two boxes can't share a label. Add the lines at the end of read_glyph_list.py, where font and Path are already known, or try them on their own with the two imports on top.

f.read().strip() is two steps in one line. Read it left to right: read the file, then strip what came back. The dot after the closing parenthesis works on whatever the first call handed over.

Take encoding="utf-8" away and this is the file that suffers. A file of plain glyph names holds nothing but a to z, dots and digits, and reads the same under almost any rule. A file of Slovak letters doesn't. Read with the wrong rule, each ľ comes back as two characters of nonsense, and the script reports missing letters that no language has.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: open(address, encoding="utf-8") with no "w" opens a file for reading, f.read() gives you all of it as one string, and for line in f: gives you one line at a time. Every line arrives with its line ending attached, so strip it before you compare it with anything. After that, an if decides which lines are data and which are blanks or notes.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add the line A.sc to smallcaps.txt and run the script. Then add a.sc a second time. What does the report say in each case? Change the script so that a name listed twice is reported once. A set can help, but check what it does to the order.
  2. Split "in the font" in two: glyphs that exist and are still empty, and glyphs that exist and have something in them. Use the test for empty from chapter 8. For the art director's list, all three existing glyphs should land in the first group.
  3. Put chapters 26 and 27 together. Read smallcaps.txt, and write the names that are still to make into smallcaps-todo.txt in the reports folder, one name to a line. Then point read_glyph_list.py at the file you wrote. A list your script wrote should be a list your script can read.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Tomas is back in chapter 28. He's tired of pasting text into his spreadsheet and getting everything in one column.

docs.title: 28. Tables for spreadsheets
docs.text:
Tuesday. Tomas, who keeps the publisher's spreadsheet, has been patient since chapter 6. Every week Mira sends him the width report, and every week he pastes it into a sheet and gets all of it in column A: name and width in one cell, 208 times. Then he splits the cells by hand.

Today he writes: Could you send it as CSV? Then it opens in columns by itself.

Mira doesn't know what CSV is. She does know how to write a file, as of Friday. That's most of it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • The reports folder next to your font, which the Friday report made in chapter 26.
  • A spreadsheet program to open the result: Numbers, Excel, LibreOffice or Google Sheets.

docs.title: Step 1: Commas between the cells
docs.text:
CSV stands for comma-separated values, and it's as plain as it sounds. A CSV file is a text file. Each line is one row of the table. Inside a line, commas mark where one cell stops and the next starts. This is a table of three rows and three columns:

Glyph,Unicode,Width
A,U+0041,596
n,U+006E,523

Every spreadsheet program opens such a file and puts each piece in its own cell. That's all Tomas is asking for.

You could build such a line yourself. Chapter 25 used " ".join(...) to glue a list of strings together with spaces. Glue with a comma and you have a row:

row = ["A", "U+0041", "596"]
print(",".join(row))

A,U+0041,596

Now put a real width in the list, a number and not a string:

row = ["A", "U+0041", 596]
print(",".join(row))

TypeError: sequence item 2: expected str instance, int found

join glues strings and nothing else. "Sequence item 2" is the third thing in the list, since counting starts at zero, and it's an int. You'd have to turn every number into text first. That's a chore, but it's not the real problem. The real problem is in the next step.

docs.title: Step 2: The comma that breaks the table
docs.text:
Tomas's sheet has a notes column. Suppose one note reads wide, check. Glue it in:

row = ["W", "859", "wide, check"]
print(",".join(row))

W,859,wide, check

Count the commas. Three commas make four cells. The spreadsheet will put wide in the third column and check in a fourth, and every row with such a note will be one cell longer than the rest. The comma inside the note looks, to the spreadsheet, like any other comma.

CSV has a fix for this: a cell that holds a comma goes inside double quotes. Then a cell that holds a double quote needs a fix of its own. There are a few more such rules, and they're tedious to get right by hand.

So don't write CSV by hand. Python ships with a module, which is a file of ready-made Python, that knows the rules.

docs.title: Step 3: Let the csv module write the row
docs.text:
import csv
from pathlib import Path

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
table_file = Path(font.path).parent / "reports" / "test.csv"

with open(table_file, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["Glyph", "Width", "Note"])
    writer.writerow(["W", 859, "wide, check"])

print("Saved", table_file)

Open test.csv in a plain text editor first, not in the spreadsheet. You want to see what was written:

Glyph,Width,Note
W,859,"wide, check"

The note got its quotes, and you didn't put them there. The number 859 went in without complaint and without you turning it into text. Now open the same file in your spreadsheet program. Two rows, three columns, and the note in one cell with its comma.

Three new things are in that listing.

csv.writer(f) takes the open file and hands back a writer. Think of it as a clerk who sits between you and the file. You give the clerk rows. The clerk knows where commas and quotes go, and writes the line.

writer.writerow([...]) hands over one row. A row is a list, one item for each cell. You don't write \n and you don't use print. The clerk ends the line.

newline="" in the open call is a magic line, and I'll say so plainly. The clerk writes its own line endings, and without newline="" Python on Windows adds a second one, which shows up in the spreadsheet as a blank row after every row. On a Mac you'd never notice the difference. Type it anyway, every time you open a file for the csv module, and your tables will open properly on Tomas's machine as well as yours.

docs.title: Step 4: A row is a list
docs.text:
Here's the mistake nearly everybody makes once. Hand the clerk a bare string where it expects a list:

    writer.writerow("Aacute")

No error. Look in the file:

A,a,c,u,t,e

Six cells, one letter in each. You know why if you think back to chapter 9: a string is a row of characters, and a for loop will walk through it letter by letter. The clerk asked for a row of things, got a string and took each letter for a cell. For a row with one cell, you still need the square brackets: writer.writerow(["Aacute"]).

Hand it a bare number and the clerk does complain, because a number isn't a row of anything:

    writer.writerow(596)

_csv.Error: iterable expected, not int

The _csv. in front is the module's own name for itself.

"Iterable" is Python's word for anything a for loop can walk through: a list, a string, a set, a dictionary, an open file. You'll see the word in error messages from now on. When you do, read it as "something I can go through one at a time", and check whether you forgot the brackets.

docs.title: Step 5: The whole font as a table
docs.text:
Now the real table. One row for the headings, then one row for each glyph. This is the loop from chapter 7 with writerow where print was:

table_file = Path(font.path).parent / "reports" / "plum-metrics.csv"

with open(table_file, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["Glyph", "Unicode", "Width"])
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        writer.writerow([glyph.name, glyph.unicode, glyph.width])

print("Saved", table_file)

The first lines of the file:

Glyph,Unicode,Width
.notdef,,500.0
A,65,596.0
Aacute,193,596.0
Abreve,258,596.0

It works, and Tomas would find two flaws in a minute. First, something that looks like a flaw and isn't.

Look at .notdef. Between its two commas there's nothing. Its Unicode value is None, and the clerk writes None as an empty cell. That's the right thing to do, and it's one decision you don't have to make.

The Unicode values are plain numbers, 65 and 193. Tomas and the proofreader think in the U+0041 form, and you built that in chapter 23 with f"U+{number:04X}". But that format falls over on None, as you also saw in chapter 23, so the .notdef row needs an if.

And the widths carry their .0. Chapter 11 dealt with that: round(glyph.width) gives a whole number.

Build each cell in a box of its own before you make the row. It's three more lines and far easier to read:

    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if glyph.unicode is None:
            code = ""
        else:
            code = f"U+{glyph.unicode:04X}"
        width = round(glyph.width)
        writer.writerow([glyph.name, code, width])

Glyph,Unicode,Width
.notdef,,500
A,U+0041,596
Aacute,U+00C1,596
Abreve,U+0102,596

There's a reason beyond taste for the U+ in front. A spreadsheet tries to be helpful with anything that looks like a number. Give it a bare 0041 and it may store 41 and throw the zeros away. Give it 00E9 and it may decide that's zero in scientific notation. U+0041 doesn't look like a number to any spreadsheet, so it's left alone.

docs.title: Step 6: Read it back
docs.text:
A file your script wrote should be a file your script can read. The module has a reader to match the writer:

with open(table_file, encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    for row in reader:
        print(row)

['Glyph', 'Unicode', 'Width']
['.notdef', '', '500']
['A', 'U+0041', '596']
['Aacute', 'U+00C1', '596']

And so on for all 209 lines. You loop over the reader as you looped over the file in chapter 27, but each turn gives you a list of cells and not a raw line. No strip, no splitting at commas, and a note with a comma in it comes back as one cell.

Look at the widths. They went out as the number 596. They've come back as the string '596', in quotes. The empty cell came back as '' and not as None. A CSV file is text and nothing but text. It can't remember what was a number. If you read a table and want to do arithmetic with a column, you turn each cell back into a number yourself with int(...), as you did with int("00E9", 16) in chapter 23. And you skip the heading row first, because int("Width") is an error.

Mira sends plum-metrics.csv. Tomas opens it, gets three columns, and sorts by width before he's finished reading her message. He writes back that emdash is 1000 units wide and asks whether that's a mistake. It isn't. An em dash is as wide as the em, and Plum's em is 1,000 units. But it's the first time the publisher's spreadsheet person has asked a question about the design.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Save this as metrics_csv.py:

# Writes one row per glyph to reports/plum-metrics.csv next to the font.
import csv
from pathlib import Path

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
reports = Path(font.path).parent / "reports"
reports.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
table_file = reports / "plum-metrics.csv"

with open(table_file, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["Glyph", "Unicode", "Width"])
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if glyph.unicode is None:
            code = ""
        else:
            code = f"U+{glyph.unicode:04X}"
        width = round(glyph.width)
        writer.writerow([glyph.name, code, width])

print("Saved", table_file)
Going deeper: semicolons, tabs and Excel

In countries that write decimal numbers with a comma, some spreadsheet programs expect a semicolon between cells. If Tomas's copy of Excel shows everything in one column, that's why. The writer takes a second argument for it: csv.writer(f, delimiter=";"). For a tab between cells, use delimiter="\t". And if accented names look wrong in an older Excel, open the file with encoding="utf-8-sig", which adds a mark at the start of the file that Excel looks for.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A CSV file is text with one row to a line and commas between the cells, and the csv module writes and reads it so that you never place a comma or a quote yourself. csv.writer(f).writerow([...]) takes a list and writes a row. csv.reader(f) gives the rows back as lists of strings. Open the file with newline="" both ways, and remember that everything read from a CSV is text until you turn it into a number.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a fourth column, Letter, that holds the character itself: A, Á, n. You have chr from chapter 23. What goes in that cell for .notdef? Open the result in your spreadsheet and look at the row for comma. Then look at the same row in a text editor.
  2. Read plum-metrics.csv back and add up the Width column. Skip the heading row. For Plum with the three small caps left out, the total of the Regular widths is 102107. What do your three empty small caps add?
  3. Tomas sends a CSV with two columns, Glyph and Note. Make one by hand with five rows, and put a comma in one of the notes. Write a script that reads it and prints, for each row, the glyph name, its width from the font and the note.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Every script so far has only asked the font questions, or painted a mark on a cell. In chapter 29 a script changes Mira's real work, and she wants to be sure she can take it back.

docs.title: 29. Change one thing, and take it back
docs.text:
Wednesday. Ines has the first proofs from the publisher on her desk, and she's drawn a pencil line under one paragraph. The word space is tight. Try twenty units more.

Mira could do it by hand in ten seconds. Click space, type 250 where it says 230. But there are three masters, and next week Ines will say "try ten less", and the week after that it'll be the figures. This is a job for a script.

It's also a job she's been putting off. In four weeks, her scripts have counted, listed, looked up and written files. They've painted a mark on a cell. Not one of them has changed a shape or a width. Today's script will reach into real work and move something.

So before she lets a script do that, she wants an answer to one question. If it goes wrong, can she take it back?

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open. The practice copy, not the real font. That's what a practice copy is for.
  • The Font window in front, with the space cell clicked so that space is the current glyph.
  • The Regular master showing. If you aren't sure, look at the Layers & Masters panel.

Save the font before you start. A script that changes things should always begin from a saved font, the way a haircut should begin with a photo of what you had before.

docs.title: Step 1: Look before you touch
docs.text:
From chapter 5 on, you've met the font through fl.CurrentFont(). That's the plain view: names, numbers, widths. To change a glyph properly you need the richer view of it, the one that knows about masters and about the Edit menu. You met it briefly in chapter 8, when you asked a glyph whether it was empty. It's called pGlyph, and the book keeps it in a box named rich, for the rich view:

from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

rich = pGlyph()
print(rich.name, rich.getAdvance())

space 230

The import line is long, and it's a magic line. It says: inside Fly, in the part called tr, down four drawers, there's a thing named pGlyph. Copy it. You'll type it often enough in Part 3 that it'll stop looking strange.

pGlyph() with an empty slot means "the glyph I'm on right now". That's why you clicked space first. getAdvance() asks for the advance width, which is the full name of what you've been calling the width: how far the pen advances before the next glyph starts.

You've changed nothing yet. Good scripts that edit things open with a line like this one. If it had printed A 596, you'd know you had the wrong cell clicked, and you'd know it before anything moved.

docs.title: Step 2: A function you hand to someone else
docs.text:
Here's the idea the whole chapter rests on, and it has nothing to do with fonts. Type this plain Python:

def say_hello():
    print("Hello")

def twice(job):
    job()
    job()

twice(say_hello)

Hello
Hello

Read twice slowly. It takes one thing, which it calls job. Then it writes job() two times. Parentheses after a name mean "run this", as they have since chapter 2. So twice expects to be handed something it can run.

And look at the last line: twice(say_hello). No parentheses after say_hello. You aren't running the function there. You're handing it over, the way you'd hand someone a recipe card. twice takes the card and cooks from it, twice, when it chooses to.

A function is a thing you can put in a box, like a number or a string. Print it and Python shows you the box's contents:

print(say_hello)

<function say_hello at 0x104f92480>

Your number at the end will differ. The point is that there's something there, and that it isn't the word Hello.

Now make the mistake. Add the parentheses:

twice(say_hello())

Hello
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable

One Hello, then a complaint. Follow what happened. Python works from the inside out, so it ran say_hello() first. That printed Hello. say_hello has no return line, and you know from chapter 24 that a function with nothing to return hands back None. So twice was given None, tried to run it, and couldn't. "Not callable" means "you put parentheses after something that isn't a function."

Keep the two apart. say_hello() is the dish, cooked now. say_hello is the recipe card. When a function asks you for a job to do later, hand over the card.

docs.title: Step 3: Why anyone would want that
docs.text:
Why would a function want your recipe and not the dish? Because it wants to do something before your steps and something after them.

That's the situation with Undo. When you move a node by hand, FontLab remembers the glyph as it was, a snapshot, lets you make the move, and adds a line to its history. Edit > Undo puts the snapshot back. A script that changes a width directly skips both ends. No snapshot is taken and no line is written, so as far as I can tell from Fly's source there's nothing for Undo to undo.

Fly has a helper that does the two ends for you. You hand it your change as a function. It takes the snapshot, runs your function, and writes the line. The helper is called commit.

To commit, in plain English, is to stop saying "maybe" and make it official. A pencil sketch isn't committed. Ink is. In scripting, to commit a change is to hand it over as one sealed package: all of it happens, and it goes on the record under one name. You'll meet the word again if you ever use Git, where it means much the same.

docs.title: Step 4: Commit the change
docs.text:
Here's the script. Type it under your Step 1 lines and read it before you run it:

import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

rich = pGlyph()
layer = rich.activeLayer()
print("Before:", rich.name, rich.getAdvance())

def widen():
    layer.advanceWidth += 20

package = scripting.current_package()
facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
history.commit("Widen", [layer], [rich.fl], widen, operation="geometry", facts=facts)

print("After:", rich.name, rich.getAdvance())

Before: space 230
After: space 250

That's a lot of new lines at once, so take them in three groups.

The thing to change. rich.activeLayer() gives you the layer of this glyph that's showing now. A glyph in Plum is three drawings stacked up, one for each master, and the width lives on each drawing separately. With Regular showing, layer is the Regular drawing of space.

The change itself. widen is your recipe card, and it's one line long. layer.advanceWidth += 20 is the += from chapter 22: take what's in the drawer, add 20, put it back. Defining widen changes nothing. It's a card in a box until somebody runs it.

The hand-over. The commit line has six things in its slot. Here's what each is for.

  • "Widen" is the title, the words that'll show in the Edit menu.
  • [layer] is the list of layers your function will change. The helper needs it to take the right snapshot.
  • [rich.fl] is the list of glyphs those layers belong to. The .fl is a part I'm not opening yet: it's the glyph in the form FontLab's history wants.
  • widen is the recipe card. No parentheses.
  • operation="geometry" says what kind of change this is. A width counts as geometry, along with outlines.
  • facts=facts hands over what the line above collected. That line, with package = scripting.current_package() before it, is a magic line. package is Fly's word for the open font file as FontLab's history knows it. scan_auto_facts looks through the font for glyphs that FontLab builds automatically, because changing those by script is asking for trouble, and commit will refuse to.

The two lists look fussy for one glyph. They're lists because the next script will change sixty.

docs.title: Step 5: Take it back
docs.text:
Now the part Mira asked for. Open the Edit menu. The first item should read Undo Widen: your title, in FontLab's own menu, next to the things you've done by hand. Choose it, or press Cmd+Z on a Mac and Ctrl+Z on Windows. Then check:

print(rich.getAdvance())

230

Back where it was. And Edit > Redo puts the 250 back again.
