One line in the menu is the point. Suppose widen had changed sixty glyphs in a loop. It would still be one line, and one Undo would take all sixty back. Without the helper you'd have sixty changes and nothing to undo them with.

Two limits, so you don't lean on Undo harder than it can bear. Undo lasts only while the font is open. Close the font and the history goes with it, which is why you saved first. And Undo covers the font, not the files your script wrote. Nothing will un-write last Friday's report.

docs.title: Step 6: When the helper says no
docs.text:
Leave something out on purpose. Delete operation="geometry", from the commit line and run:

TypeError: commit() missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'operation'

"Keyword-only" means the helper insists you write the name and the equals sign, operation=..., and won't accept the value on its own. That's deliberate. A line that changes your font should say in words what it's doing.

Put it back, but misspell the kind:

history.commit("Widen", [layer], [rich.fl], widen, operation="width", facts=facts)

ValueError: Unknown operation 'width'; use one of ['geometry', 'metadata', 'rename', 'unicode'].

That's a helpful letter of complaint. It tells you the four words it knows. You'll use "rename" in the next chapter.

In both cases, check the width afterward. It's still 230 or 250, whichever it was. The helper checks everything it can before it takes the snapshot, and if it doesn't like what it sees, it stops without touching the font. A refusal starts with the word Refused and names the glyph and the reason. If you ever see has auto layers in one, you've pointed the script at a glyph that FontLab builds for you, and the answer is to leave that glyph alone.

There's one more refusal you may meet. If you run the script from a Glyph window on glyphs that the window isn't showing, the helper tells you to Switch to the Font window first. Do as it says. It knows about a case where FontLab would undo only part of the change.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Save this as safe_edit.py. The amount has a box of its own at the top, in capitals, because next week it'll be a different number:

# Widens the current glyph on the current master by AMOUNT units.
# One step in Edit > Undo.
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

AMOUNT = 20

rich = pGlyph()
layer = rich.activeLayer()
print("Before:", rich.name, rich.getAdvance())

def widen():
    layer.advanceWidth += AMOUNT

package = scripting.current_package()
facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
history.commit("Widen", [layer], [rich.fl], widen, operation="geometry", facts=facts)

print("After:", rich.name, rich.getAdvance())

Mira runs it on Regular, switches to Bold and runs it again, then Light. Bold goes from 230 to 250. Light goes from 234 to 254, which tells her something she hadn't noticed: the Light space was already a little wider. She prints a paragraph and puts it on Ines's desk next to the proof. Ines looks at both for a while and says, "Fifteen."

Mira changes one number at the top, presses Undo three times, and runs it again.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A function is a thing you can hand to another function, and you hand it over by name, without parentheses. Fly's history.commit takes your change as such a function, and runs it so that the whole change is one named step in Edit > Undo. It refuses before it touches anything if what you asked for looks unsafe. Print the value before and after, work on a saved font, and remember that Undo can't reach files on disk.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Change the title from "Widen" to "Widen space by 20" and run the script. What does the Edit menu show? Then set AMOUNT = -20. Is "Widen" still an honest title? Build the title from AMOUNT with an f-string so that it can't lie.
  2. Write a narrow function next to widen that subtracts AMOUNT. Commit widen, then commit narrow. How many Undo steps are there now, and in what order do they come back?
  3. Add a third line to twice from Step 2 so that it becomes three_times, and hand it a function of your own that prints the name of the current glyph. Then hand it print. What happens, and why is that not an error?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: About sixty glyphs in the real Plum carry the old suffix .alt, and the publisher's files want .ss01. In chapter 30, a script renames them.

docs.title: 30. Rename with care
docs.text:
Thursday. The publisher's production notes have arrived, four pages of them, and item 11 is one line: Alternates must be named .ss01, not .alt.

Ines says sixty glyphs in the real Plum end in .alt. That Plum, the one Halfmoon ships, belongs to the story. Yours is the free one from chapter 4, and it has none, which is why you'll add four in a moment. Oskar named them that way years ago, when .alt was what everybody wrote. The publisher's layout software looks for stylistic set names, and .ss01 is the name for set number one.

Sixty renames by hand is an afternoon: double-click, select four letters, type five, press Return, next. And somewhere around the fortieth she'd type .ss10.

A name is the handle that everything else in the font holds a glyph by. Changing sixty handles at once is the riskiest thing a script of Mira's has done yet. So this chapter goes slowly, and the script shows its plan before it touches anything.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open and saved.
  • Four glyphs to rename. The practice font has no alternates, so make some, as you made the small caps in chapter 8: click the Font window, choose Font > New Glyph…, and type a.alt. Do it three more times for g.alt, y.alt and ampersand.alt.
  • The Font window in front when you run the scripts.

Four glyphs will do. A script that renames four correctly renames sixty the same way.

docs.title: Step 1: Replace part of a string
docs.text:
Start with plain Python. Strings have a method for swapping one piece of text for another:

old = "a.alt"
new = old.replace(".alt", ".ss01")
print(old)
print(new)

a.alt
a.ss01

replace takes two things through the slot: what to look for, and what to put there. It hands back a new string. The first line of output shows that old still says a.alt. You saw the same with upper and strip: a string never changes in place. If you want the result, catch it in a box.

What if the thing you're looking for isn't there?

print("A".replace(".alt", ".ss01"))

A

No error, and no change. replace hands back the string as it was. That's convenient, and it's also a trap. A replace with a typo in it runs happily and does nothing, and nothing looks like success if you aren't checking.

docs.title: Step 2: Build the list of renames
docs.text:
Now the font. You want every glyph whose name ends in .alt, and for each one the old name and the new name, side by side. endswith is from chapter 9, and a list of lists is a list whose items are small lists:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()

pairs = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.name.endswith(".alt"):
        old = glyph.name
        new = old.replace(".alt", ".ss01")
        pairs.append([old, new])

print(len(pairs), "to rename")
for pair in pairs:
    print(pair)

4 to rename
['a.alt', 'a.ss01']
['ampersand.alt', 'ampersand.ss01']
['g.alt', 'g.ss01']
['y.alt', 'y.ss01']

Your four may come in a different order, depending on how the Font window sorts them.

Each item in pairs is a little list of two strings, old then new. Call each one a pair. A list whose items are lists is a shape of its own, and chapter 35 looks at it properly. Nothing has been renamed. You've written down what you intend to do, the way you'd write a list before going to the shops. That list is the most useful thing in this chapter. You can read it, count it and check it, and the font is exactly as it was.

Do read it. Four lines you can check by eye. With sixty, read the first few, the last few, and the count. If the count says 61 when you expected 60, stop and find out why before going on.

docs.title: Step 3: Ask for a plan
docs.text:
Your list says what you want. It doesn't say whether the font can take it. What if there's already a glyph called a.ss01? What if a new name has a character in it that glyph names don't allow?

Fly has a helper that checks every pair against the font and tells you, line by line, whether the rename is safe. It changes nothing. Add this under your loop:

import fly.ap.glyphs.names.model as names
from fly.ap.glyphs.identity_tools.glyph_identity.batch_rename import plan_renames

facts = names.scan()
plan = plan_renames(facts, pairs)

for old, new, status in plan:
    print(f"{old:<16}{new:<16}{status}")

a.alt           a.ss01          ok
ampersand.alt   ampersand.ss01  ok
g.alt           g.ss01          ok
y.alt           y.ss01          ok

The two import lines are magic lines, and the second is the longest in the book so far. Copy them. They say where in Fly the two helpers live.

names.scan() reads the whole font once and remembers what it found: every glyph name, and which glyphs FontLab builds automatically from others. I've called the box facts because that's what's in it.

plan_renames(facts, pairs) goes through your pairs and hands back a list of rows. Each row has three things in it: the old name, the new name and a verdict. The for old, new, status in plan: line takes each row apart into three boxes at once, the way for key, value in ...items() took two in chapter 22.

ok means the helper found nothing against that rename. Now give it something to object to. Change the replacement so the new suffix has a space where the dot should be:

        new = old.replace(".alt", " ss01")

a.alt           a ss01          invalid name
ampersand.alt   ampersand ss01  invalid name
g.alt           g ss01          invalid name
y.alt           y ss01          invalid name

Still no error, and the font is still untouched. The plan tells you what would have gone wrong. A glyph name may hold letters without accents, digits, the dot, the underscore and the hyphen. It can't start with a digit, it can't be longer than 63 characters, and it can't hold a space. Put the dot back.

These are the other verdicts you may see, from the helper's source:

Verdict What it means exists in font There's already a glyph with the new name. duplicate target Two of your pairs want the same new name. reserved glyph You tried to rename .notdef or space. Don't. has auto layers FontLab builds this glyph automatically. base of auto ... Some other glyph is built automatically from this one.

A row with any verdict but ok is skipped when you apply the plan. The rest go through.

docs.title: Step 4: Apply it
docs.text:
When every row says ok, and you've read the rows, add the lines that do the work:

from fly import qt
from fly.ap.glyphs.identity_tools.glyph_identity.batch_rename import apply_renames

renamed = apply_renames(None, qt.QtCore, facts.package_id, pairs)

print(len(renamed), "renamed")

4 renamed

Look at the Font window. The four cells carry their new names. Now open the Edit menu. There should be one Undo entry for the whole job, with the helper's own title, Batch Rename. Choose it and all four names go back. Choose Edit > Redo and they're .ss01 again.

The same deal as yesterday's commit: all or nothing. In fact apply_renames calls a commit of its own inside. You don't write a function and hand it over this time, because the helper already knows what a rename is.

It takes four things. Two of them are parts I'm not opening yet. I'll say what they are and leave it there.

  • None means "use the FontLab I'm running in". There's a slot there because the helper's own tests pass in something else.
  • qt.QtCore hands the helper a clock. Every glyph it renames gets stamped with the time of the change.
  • facts.package_id is a number that identifies the font you scanned. Suppose you scan Plum, wander off, click on a different font and come back to run the last line. The helper notices that the front font isn't the one the plan was made for and refuses with The scanned font is no longer current; reload.
  • pairs is your list.

Notice what you didn't pass: the plan. apply_renames scans the font again and makes a fresh plan of its own the moment before it writes. The plan you printed was for you to read. The helper doesn't trust a plan that might be a minute old, and neither should you.

docs.title: Step 5: Run it twice
docs.text:
Run the whole script again, now that the glyphs are renamed.

0 to rename
0 renamed

Nothing ends in .alt any more, so pairs is empty, the plan is empty, and the helper has nothing to do. No error and no damage.

A script that changes things should be safe to run twice. People do run scripts twice: by accident, or because they aren't sure the first run worked, or because a colleague ran it yesterday and didn't say. A script that finds its targets by looking at the font, and not by counting on what it did last time, behaves properly on the second run.

docs.title: Step 6: What a rename doesn't reach
docs.text:
The glyphs have new names. The rest of the font may not have heard.

A glyph's name gets written down in other places. OpenType features refer to glyphs by name: the real Plum has a line that says, more or less, "when the reader turns on the stylistic set, swap a for a.alt". Kerning classes list their members by name. The notes at the top of Fly's rename helper say plainly that kerning and features keep the old names after a rename. So the feature line would still ask for a.alt, and there'd no longer be such a glyph.

There's no error for that today. It shows up later, when the font is exported, or worse, when the alternates quietly stop working in the publisher's layout.

So a rename has three parts, and the script does only the first:

  1. Rename the glyphs.
  2. Open the Features panel, search for the old suffix and fix what you find. Mira finds one line and fixes it by hand.
  3. Look at your kerning classes for the old names.

Part 5 of this book deals with features and Part 4 with kerning, and by then you'll have scripts that check both. Until then, check by hand, and write the three parts in a comment at the top of the script so that the next person does too.

The other thing a rename can disturb is glyphs built from other glyphs. That's what the has auto layers and base of auto verdicts are about. When FontLab builds aacute automatically from a and acute, it finds the pieces by name. Rename a and the recipe breaks. The helper refuses those rows and leaves you to sort them out with your eyes open. I think that's the right call.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Save this as rename_suffix.py. The two suffixes sit in boxes at the top:

# Renames every glyph that ends in OLD_SUFFIX so that it ends in NEW_SUFFIX.
# One step in Edit > Undo. Run it with the Font window in front.
# Afterward, by hand: fix the old names in Features and in kerning classes.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.glyphs.names.model as names
from fly.ap.glyphs.identity_tools.glyph_identity.batch_rename import (
    apply_renames,
    plan_renames,
)

OLD_SUFFIX = ".alt"
NEW_SUFFIX = ".ss01"

font = fl.CurrentFont()

pairs = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.name.endswith(OLD_SUFFIX):
        old = glyph.name
        new = old.replace(OLD_SUFFIX, NEW_SUFFIX)
        pairs.append([old, new])

facts = names.scan()
for old, new, status in plan_renames(facts, pairs):
    print(f"{old:<16}{new:<16}{status}")

renamed = apply_renames(None, qt.QtCore, facts.package_id, pairs)
print(len(renamed), "renamed")

The import with parentheses around two names is one line folded in two so that it fits the page. Python reads it as one.

Mira reads the script through and is nearly ready to run it on the real Plum. Then she notices that it prints the plan and applies it in the same breath. On four glyphs she can read the plan afterward and press Undo. On sixty, in the font she ships, she'd like the script to stop after the plan and wait until she says go.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: replace hands back a string with one piece of text swapped for another, and hands back the string unchanged when there's nothing to swap. To rename glyphs, build a list of old and new names first, read it, ask plan_renames what the font thinks of it, and only then call apply_renames, which does the whole job as one Undo step. A rename changes glyph names and nothing else: features and kerning classes still hold the old names until you fix them.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Undo the rename so that you have .alt glyphs again. Add a glyph named g.ss01 by hand, then run the script. What does the plan say for g.alt, and how many glyphs get renamed? Delete g.ss01 afterward.
  2. Change the two suffixes so that the script turns .ss01 back into .alt, and run it. You've written your own Undo. When would that be useful, given what you know from chapter 29 about how long Edit > Undo lasts?
  3. Before you run anything, work out on paper what "a.alt.sc".replace(".alt", ".ss01") gives, and what "salt".replace("alt", "ss01") gives. Then try both. One of them is fine. The other is a bug in waiting, and it's the subject of the next chapter.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Mira nearly renames the wrong sixty. Chapter 31 adds a switch to the script: plan only, or plan and apply.

docs.title: 31. Look before you leap
docs.text:
Friday morning. Mira opens the real Plum, the one that ships, and opens rename_suffix.py next to it. Sixty glyphs, one click. Her finger is over the Run button.

She doesn't press it. Yesterday's script prints its plan and carries the plan out in the same run. By the time she's read the first line of the plan, the sixtieth glyph is already renamed. There's Undo, and she trusts Undo more than she did on Wednesday morning. But "do it, then see whether it was right" is a poor way to treat a font that goes to a publisher on Monday.

What she wants is a rehearsal. The script should go through every motion except the last one, show her what it would have done, and stop. People who write scripts call that a dry run, after the fire brigade's drills with no water in the hose.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open and saved.
  • rename_suffix.py from chapter 30.
  • The four .alt glyphs from chapter 30. If you renamed them and didn't undo it, run exercise 2 of that chapter, or rename them back by hand.
  • One more glyph: choose Font > New Glyph… and add zero.alt. You'll see why in Step 4.

docs.title: Step 1: A switch in a box
docs.text:
You've had True and False since chapter 8. They're what a question hands back: name.endswith(".alt") is one or the other, and if acts on it. Until now they've always come out of a question. But True and False are values like 20 and "Plum". You can type one yourself and put it in a box:

DRY_RUN = True

if DRY_RUN:
    print("Dry run. Nothing changed.")
else:
    print("This is where the renaming would happen.")

Dry run. Nothing changed.

Change the first line to DRY_RUN = False and run it again:

This is where the renaming would happen.

That's a switch. One box at the top of the script, holding yes or no, and an if further down that goes one way or the other. To change what the script does, you change one word at the top and touch nothing else.

if DRY_RUN: reads oddly the first time, since there's no == in it and no question. It doesn't need one. if wants a True or a False, and the box already holds one. You could write if DRY_RUN == True:, and it would work, but it says "if yes is yes".

True and False are spelled with a capital letter and no quotes. Both matter, and the next step shows why.

docs.title: Step 2: The switch that's stuck
docs.text:
Put quotes around the word, as if it were a string:

DRY_RUN = "False"

if DRY_RUN:
    print("Dry run. Nothing changed.")
else:
    print("This is where the renaming would happen.")

Dry run. Nothing changed.

You wrote False and got the dry run. There's no error message.

"False" in quotes isn't the value False. It's a string of five letters that happens to spell an English word. And when if is handed something that isn't True or False, it doesn't complain. It applies a rule of its own: empty things count as no, and everything else counts as yes. An empty string "" counts as no. So do the number 0, an empty list and None. A string with five letters in it has something in it, so it counts as yes, whatever the letters say.

That rule is handy in places. if pairs: is a neat way to say "if the list has anything in it". But for a switch it means a typo can jam the switch in one position.

Notice which position, though. With the switch jammed, the script did the harmless thing. That isn't luck. It follows from a decision about names and defaults:

Name the switch after the safe behavior, and ship it switched on.

DRY_RUN = True is the safe state. Someone who opens the script cold and presses Run gets a rehearsal. To get a real rename they must do something deliberate: find the line, read it and type False. Had Mira called the switch APPLY and set it to True, the script would do damage by default, and a jammed switch would do damage too.

Take the quotes off again.

docs.title: Step 3: Plan always, apply sometimes
docs.text:
Now put the switch into the real script. The plan is printed whichever way the switch is set, because a plan costs nothing and you always want to see it. Only the last step sits behind the if:

DRY_RUN = True

facts = names.scan()
plan = plan_renames(facts, pairs)

ok = 0
problems = 0
for old, new, status in plan:
    print(f"{old:<16}{new:<16}{status}")
    if status == "ok":
        ok += 1
    else:
        problems += 1
print(f"{ok} ok, {problems} with problems")

if DRY_RUN:
    print("Dry run. Nothing changed. Set DRY_RUN = False to rename.")
elif problems > 0:
    print("Nothing changed. Fix the problems first.")
else:
    renamed = apply_renames(None, qt.QtCore, facts.package_id, pairs)
    print(len(renamed), "renamed")

Everything above DRY_RUN = True is as it was in chapter 30: the imports, the two suffixes and the loop that builds pairs. Run it.

a.alt           a.ss01          ok
ampersand.alt   ampersand.ss01  ok
g.alt           g.ss01          ok
y.alt           y.ss01          ok
zero.alt        zero.ss01       ok
5 ok, 0 with problems
Dry run. Nothing changed. Set DRY_RUN = False to rename.

Look at the Font window. The names are as they were, and the Edit menu has nothing new in it.

Two things were added besides the switch.

The first is the count. The loop that prints the plan also keeps two tallies, with the += from chapter 22. On five rows you can see at a glance that every row says ok. On sixty you can't, and a single exists in font in row 37 would scroll past. The last line of the table says it in numbers.

The second is the middle branch, elif problems > 0. Yesterday I told you that the helper skips rows that aren't ok and renames the rest. That's a fair thing for a helper to do. For Mira's job it's the wrong policy. A font with 59 glyphs named .ss01 and one still named .alt is worse than a font with none renamed, because it looks finished. So her script is stricter than the helper: all or nothing. If the plan has one problem in it, nothing is renamed, and she goes and finds out why.

Read the three branches as a ladder. Is this a rehearsal? Then stop. If not, are there problems? Then stop. Only when both answers are no does the script reach the line that changes the font.

docs.title: Step 4: Read the plan
docs.text:
A dry run only helps if you read what it prints. So read it. Five rows. Every one says ok.

And one of them is wrong.

zero.alt isn't a stylistic alternate. It's the zero with a slash through it, the one programmers like, and OpenType has a feature of its own for that, called zero. Oskar gave it the suffix .alt years ago because that was his suffix for everything. If it becomes zero.ss01, then turning on stylistic set 1 in the publisher's layout would slash every zero in the book along with changing the a's and g's.

This is what happened to Mira on the real font. The count at the bottom of her plan said 63 ok, and she'd been told sixty. She didn't shrug. She went through the rows and found three that didn't belong: the slashed zero and two old ampersands that Ines wants in a different set.

The helper said ok to all 63, and it was right to. ok means the font will accept the rename. It doesn't mean the rename is a good idea. No helper can know which of Oskar's .alt glyphs belong in which set. You know that, or Ines does. The script checks what can be checked by machine, and the dry run is where you check the rest yourself.

Now tell the script. A set, from chapter 25, holds the names to leave alone:

SKIP = {"zero.alt"}

pairs = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.name.endswith(OLD_SUFFIX) and glyph.name not in SKIP:
        old = glyph.name
        new = old.replace(OLD_SUFFIX, NEW_SUFFIX)
        pairs.append([old, new])

a.alt           a.ss01          ok
ampersand.alt   ampersand.ss01  ok
g.alt           g.ss01          ok
y.alt           y.ss01          ok
4 ok, 0 with problems
Dry run. Nothing changed. Set DRY_RUN = False to rename.

Four rows, and they're the right four. not in is the opposite of in. The if line now reads: "if the name ends in the old suffix and isn't one of the names to skip".

docs.title: Step 5: Tighten the replace
docs.text:
One more thing to fix while the switch is still on. The last exercise of chapter 30 asked what these give:

print("a.alt.sc".replace(".alt", ".ss01"))
print("salt".replace("alt", "ss01"))

a.ss01.sc
sss01

replace doesn't know about ends. It swaps the text wherever it finds it, and it swaps every occurrence. The endswith test picks glyphs whose names end in the suffix. Then replace is let loose on the whole name. Those two lines don't say the same thing. They agree for every name in Plum today. One day somebody will name a glyph so that they don't.

Python has a method that means exactly what you mean:

print("a.alt".removesuffix(".alt") + ".ss01")
print("a.alt.sc".removesuffix(".alt"))

a.ss01
a.alt.sc

removesuffix takes the text off the end and only off the end. If the string doesn't end that way, it hands the string back untouched. Then + glues the new suffix on. In the script:

        new = old.removesuffix(OLD_SUFFIX) + NEW_SUFFIX

Run the dry run again. The same four rows come back, as they should. You've changed how the new name is made, not what it comes out as. Running the rehearsal after every edit, and seeing the same plan, is how you know an edit was harmless.

docs.title: Step 6: Throw the switch
docs.text:
The plan is right and you've read it twice. Change one word:

DRY_RUN = False

a.alt           a.ss01          ok
ampersand.alt   ampersand.ss01  ok
g.alt           g.ss01          ok
y.alt           y.ss01          ok
4 ok, 0 with problems
4 renamed

Then, before you do anything else, change the word back to True and save the script. That's the part people forget. A script left with its safety off will rename things for the next person who runs it out of curiosity. In a month, that next person is you.

Mira runs it on the real Plum. Sixty ok, none with problems, sixty renamed. She fixes the one line in the Features panel, exports, and sends the fonts that evening.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
rename_suffix.py, second version:

# Renames every glyph that ends in OLD_SUFFIX so that it ends in NEW_SUFFIX.
# Prints a plan first. With DRY_RUN = True it stops there.
# Afterward, by hand: fix the old names in Features and in kerning classes.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.glyphs.names.model as names
from fly.ap.glyphs.identity_tools.glyph_identity.batch_rename import (
    apply_renames,
    plan_renames,
)

DRY_RUN = True
OLD_SUFFIX = ".alt"
NEW_SUFFIX = ".ss01"
SKIP = {"zero.alt"}

font = fl.CurrentFont()

pairs = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.name.endswith(OLD_SUFFIX) and glyph.name not in SKIP:
        old = glyph.name
        new = old.removesuffix(OLD_SUFFIX) + NEW_SUFFIX
        pairs.append([old, new])

facts = names.scan()
plan = plan_renames(facts, pairs)

ok = 0
problems = 0
for old, new, status in plan:
    print(f"{old:<16}{new:<16}{status}")
    if status == "ok":
        ok += 1
    else:
        problems += 1
print(f"{ok} ok, {problems} with problems")

if DRY_RUN:
    print("Dry run. Nothing changed. Set DRY_RUN = False to rename.")
elif problems > 0:
    print("Nothing changed. Fix the problems first.")
else:
    renamed = apply_renames(None, qt.QtCore, facts.package_id, pairs)
    print(len(renamed), "renamed")

The shape of this script matters more than its subject. It has four parts: collect what you mean to change, make a plan, show the plan, and apply it only if the switch allows and the plan is clean. You'll use this shape again: collect, plan, show, apply. A script that moves anchors can have it, and so can one that deletes kerning pairs.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: True and False are values you can keep in a box, and a box like that works as a switch for an if. Name the switch after the safe behavior and leave it on, so that a careless run and a typo both end in a rehearsal. A dry run prints the plan and stops, and it only works if you read the plan: ok means the font will accept a change, not that the change is the one you wanted.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add g.alt to SKIP and run the dry run. Then put a name in SKIP that isn't in the font at all, such as q.alt. Does the script mind? Should it? Add two lines that print a warning for any name in SKIP that the font doesn't have. Set subtraction from chapter 25 will do it.
  2. Go back to safe_edit.py from chapter 29 and give it a DRY_RUN switch. In a dry run it should print the glyph name, the width now and the width it would become, and change nothing.
  3. Make the plan say something a person can act on. When problems is more than 0, print only the rows that aren't ok, under a heading, after the full table. Test it by adding a glyph called a.ss01 by hand before the dry run.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Ines keeps track of which glyphs are finished by painting their cells green. Chapter 32 teaches the script to read her colors, and to paint some of its own.

docs.title: 32. Tags and marks
docs.text:
Monday of the sixth week. Ines has a system, and she's had it for longer than Mira has worked here. A green cell is a glyph she's approved. Yellow means "I've looked, and it needs work". Red means not drawn yet. Nobody ever wrote the system down. It lives in Ines's head and in the Font window.

This morning the publisher asks how far along the small caps are, and Ines asks Mira, and Mira looks at a Font window full of colored cells and starts counting greens with her finger on the screen.

You marked cells red in chapter 14. Today you go the other way: the script reads the colors that are already there and says what they mean. Then it meets the limit of colors, and you find out what FontLab offers in their place.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open and saved.
  • A font with some colors in it. Your practice copy has whatever earlier chapters left behind, so start from a known state. Run this once:
from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

RED = 1
YELLOW = 61
GREEN = 121

paint = {}
for name in ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "H", "O", "n", "o"]:
    paint[name] = GREEN

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    pGlyph(font, glyph).mark = paint.get(glyph.name, 0)

Nothing in it is new. It builds a dictionary from glyph name to color number, then walks the font and gives every glyph its color from the dictionary, or 0 for "no mark" when the name isn't there. That's get with a fallback, from chapter 22. The Font window should now show nine green cells and nothing else in color.

Now add the rest. Put these lines under the green loop, above font = fl.CurrentFont(), and run it again:

for name in ["a", "g", "s"]:
    paint[name] = YELLOW
for name in ["a.sc", "b.sc", "c.sc"]:
    paint[name] = RED
paint["Q"] = 200

Nine green cells, three yellow, three red and one Q in a color that isn't one of your three.

That Q is there to cause trouble. Somebody was trying out colors one afternoon and never cleared it. Real fonts are full of such leftovers.

As chapter 14 warned, marks set by a script leave no step in Edit > Undo. That's why you saved first.

docs.title: Step 1: Names for numbers
docs.text:
Look at the top of that listing:

RED = 1
YELLOW = 61
GREEN = 121

You've been writing boxes in capitals since chapter 17, and AMOUNT, DRY_RUN and OLD_SUFFIX joined them last week. It's time to say what the custom is for.

A box whose value is set once at the top and never changed afterward is called a constant. Python doesn't enforce that. You could write GREEN = 5 on line 40 and nobody would stop you. The capitals are an agreement between people: this is a fixed fact of the script, look for it at the top, don't assign to it anywhere else.

Constants buy you two things. The first is reading. rich.mark = 121 tells you nothing, and rich.mark = GREEN tells you what's going on. The second is changing. If Ines decides that approved glyphs should be a bluer green, there's one line to edit, and every place that says GREEN follows.

A number that sits bare in the middle of a script, with no name, has a nickname among programmers: a magic number. It works, and nobody remembers why it's 121. Give it a name.

docs.title: Step 2: A legend
docs.text:
Ines's system is a mapping: this color means that. You know what holds a mapping. A map has a legend in its corner that says what the colors stand for, and this dictionary does the same job:

LEGEND = {
    0: "untouched",
    RED: "not drawn",
    YELLOW: "needs work",
    GREEN: "done",
}

The keys are the constants, so the dictionary reads like the sentence in Ines's head. It's in capitals for the same reason they are: it's set once and never changed. And for the first time, her system is written down somewhere.

Now ask it about one glyph. Click the A cell and run:

rich = pGlyph()
print(rich.name, rich.mark, LEGEND[rich.mark])

A 121 done

docs.title: Step 3: The color nobody planned
docs.text:
Now the whole font. Walk the glyphs, look up each mark in the legend, and print what you find:

for glyph in font.glyphs:
    rich = pGlyph(font, glyph)
    print(glyph.name, LEGEND[rich.mark])

It prints for a while and then stops:

Otilde untouched
OE untouched
P untouched
KeyError: 200

You know KeyError from chapter 21. The script asked the legend for a key it doesn't have. The last line printed was P, so the glyph that broke it is the next one: the odd-colored Q, with a mark of 200 that isn't in anybody's system.

The legend describes what Ines intended. The font holds what people did, and a script that reads other people's work has to expect values outside the plan. get gives the legend a fallback, and while you're at it, count and don't print 213 lines:

tally = {}
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    rich = pGlyph(font, glyph)
    status = LEGEND.get(rich.mark, "unknown color")
    tally[status] = tally.get(status, 0) + 1

for status in LEGEND.values():
    print(f"{status:<14}{tally.get(status, 0):>4}")
print(f"{'unknown color':<14}{tally.get('unknown color', 0):>4}")

untouched      197
not drawn        3
needs work       3
done             9
unknown color    1

Your first number depends on how many practice glyphs you've added along the way. Mine has 213 glyphs in all.

That's the counting pattern from chapter 22, used twice: once to build the tally and once, with a fallback of 0, to print a line for a status that no glyph has. LEGEND.values() is new. items() gave you keys and values in pairs. values() gives the values alone, in the order you wrote them. So the report comes out in the legend's order, which is the order Ines thinks in.

One honest caution. I've set these marks from a script, with exact numbers. When a person picks a color from FontLab's own menu, I can't tell you which number is stored for "green". It may be 121 and it may be a neighbor. So before you trust a legend on a font that people have colored by hand, print the marks that are really in it:

seen = set()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    seen.add(pGlyph(font, glyph).mark)
print(sorted(seen))

[0, 1, 61, 121, 200]

Then write the legend from what you see.

docs.title: Step 4: One color isn't enough
docs.text:
Mira reports: nine done, three need work, three not drawn. Ines nods and then says the thing that breaks the system. "The a is drawn and I like it. It needs kerning. And the g needs work and Tomas found it in a proof."

A cell has one color. a can be green or yellow. It can't be "drawn, approved, not yet kerned", and it certainly can't carry two facts at once. Studios work around this with more colors, until there's an orange that means "approved except for the kerning" and nobody but Ines remembers it.

FontLab has a second way to label a glyph: tags. A tag is a word you stick on a glyph. A glyph can carry several tags, and they don't show as a color. Put two on a:

font = fl.CurrentFont()
rich = pGlyph(font, font["a"])
rich.tag("drawn")
rich.tag("needs-kerning")
print(rich.getTags())

['drawn', 'needs-kerning']

tag sticks one word on the glyph. getTags() hands back the glyph's tags as a list of strings. I've written needs-kerning with a hyphen and no space. I don't know how FontLab treats a space inside a tag, so I keep clear of the question.

This is how the two compare:

Mark Tag What it is one number, shown as a color a word How many on a glyph one as many as you like Where you see it at a glance, in the cell when you search or filter for it Good for one status that people scan by eye several facts that scripts and searches use

Neither replaces the other. Ines isn't going to give up her colors, and she shouldn't. Colors are for eyes. Tags are for questions.

docs.title: Step 5: Ask by tag
docs.text:
A tag is useful when you can ask for it. getTags() gives a list, and in asks a list whether it holds something, as it has since chapter 10:

print("Needs kerning:")
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if "needs-kerning" in pGlyph(font, glyph).getTags():
        print(" ", glyph.name)

Needs kerning:
  a

Now do it for the whole of Ines's system: read each glyph's color, look up the word in the legend and stick that word on as a tag. First, the words need to be fit for tags, so the legend gets hyphens: "not-drawn", "needs-work".

There's one trap here, and it's the lesson of chapter 30 over again. A script should be safe to run twice. If the script tags a with needs-work today and you run it again tomorrow, does a get the tag a second time? I don't know what FontLab does with a repeated tag, and I'd sooner not find out on a real font. So ask first:

        if status not in rich.getTags():
            rich.tag(status)

Then the script doesn't depend on the answer.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Save this as status_marks.py. It has last week's switch at the top. With DRY_RUN = True it reports and changes nothing:

# Reads Ines's mark colors and reports how many glyphs have each status.
# With DRY_RUN = False it also tags each marked glyph with its status word.
# Marks and tags set by a script leave no Undo step: save the font first.
from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

DRY_RUN = True

RED = 1
YELLOW = 61
GREEN = 121
LEGEND = {
    0: "untouched",
    RED: "not-drawn",
    YELLOW: "needs-work",
    GREEN: "done",
}
UNKNOWN = "unknown-color"

font = fl.CurrentFont()

tally = {}
tagged = 0
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    rich = pGlyph(font, glyph)
    status = LEGEND.get(rich.mark, UNKNOWN)
    tally[status] = tally.get(status, 0) + 1
    if status == UNKNOWN:
        print("Unknown color", rich.mark, "on", glyph.name)
    elif rich.mark != 0 and not DRY_RUN:
        if status not in rich.getTags():
            rich.tag(status)
            tagged += 1

for status in LEGEND.values():
    print(f"{status:<14}{tally.get(status, 0):>4}")
print(f"{UNKNOWN:<14}{tally.get(UNKNOWN, 0):>4}")

if DRY_RUN:
    print("Dry run. No tags added.")
else:
    print(tagged, "glyphs tagged")

Unknown color 200 on Q
untouched      197
not-drawn        3
needs-work       3
done             9
unknown-color    1
Dry run. No tags added.

The script names the glyph with the unknown color. A count of 1 tells Mira there's a problem. on Q tells her where to click.

Untouched glyphs get no tag, because of the rich.mark != 0 test. A tag that says "nobody has looked at this" on 197 glyphs is noise.

And UNKNOWN is a constant too, though it's used in only four places. The word appears in the lookup, in a comparison and in two print lines. Typed four times by hand, it would sooner or later be unknown-colour in one of them, and the comparison would quietly never match.

Set DRY_RUN = False, run it, and the last line reads 15 glyphs tagged. Run it again and it reads 0 glyphs tagged, because every glyph already has its word. Then set the switch back.

Ines looks at the report and says she didn't know the Q had a color at all. Then she asks the question that's been coming all month: could the Friday report include this?

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A constant is a box you set once at the top of a script and write in capitals, so that numbers get names and there's one place to change them. A small dictionary can serve as a legend that turns a stored value into a word, and get with a fallback keeps it from breaking on values nobody planned. A mark is one color on a glyph, for eyes. Tags are words, as many as you need, for scripts and searches.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a fifth status to Ines's system: blue, number 241, meaning "waiting for the publisher". Which lines of status_marks.py do you have to change? If the answer is more than two, look again.
  2. Write a script that prints the names of all glyphs tagged done, on one line, with spaces between them. join is from chapter 25. Then make it answer Ines's real question: which glyphs are tagged done and also tagged needs-kerning?
  3. The tags describe the colors on the day you ran the script. On Tuesday Ines repaints g from yellow to green. What does g carry after you run status_marks.py again? Describe in words what the script would have to do to keep tags and colors in step. You don't have to write it. Taking a tag off needs a call this chapter hasn't shown.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: pGlyph(font, glyph), the legend and the tally loop are now in several of Mira's scripts, pasted from one to the next. Chapter 33 puts them in one file that all her scripts can share.

docs.title: 33. Your own module
docs.text:
Tuesday. Ines changes her mind about green. The approved glyphs are hard to tell from the yellow ones on her laptop, so from today "done" is a bluer green, number 151.

Mira opens status_marks.py and changes one line, which is what constants are for. Then she remembers that mark_empty.py has a GREEN in it too, and so does the script from the exercise in chapter 14, and so does something she wrote on a Friday afternoon and called test2.py. She pasted the same three lines into each of them. Now she has four copies of one fact, and three of them are out of date.

The same has happened to widest_glyph and is_empty. Every script that needs them carries its own copy, and the copies have started to differ.

Python's answer to copying between scripts is the module: one file that holds the shared parts, which other scripts borrow from. You've used modules since chapter 4 without calling them that. Today you find out how they work, write a small one, and see what it costs.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • status_marks.py from chapter 32.
  • Your Friday Report.py from chapter 18, for the first exercise.

docs.title: Step 1: You've been doing this since chapter 4
docs.text:
Look at the first line of nearly every script you've written:

from fly import fl

In chapter 4 I asked you to type this line on trust. Here's what it does. Somewhere on your disk there's a folder called fly with Python files in it. Somebody wrote functions and boxes in those files, exactly as you write them. import finds the files, runs them once and hands you what they define.

A Python file that's meant to be borrowed from, and not run by itself, is called a module. csv is a module. So is pathlib. Neither is part of the language. They're files that came with Python, written by people, and you can open them and read them.

docs.title: Step 2: Two ways to borrow
docs.text:
There are two shapes of import, and you've met both. Here they are side by side, with two modules that come with Python:

import json
from pathlib import Path

print(json.dumps({"done": 9}))
print(Path.home())

{"done": 9}
/Users/mira

import json hands you the whole module under its own name. You reach inside it with a dot: json.dumps opens the drawer called dumps and calls what's in it. The dot is the same dot as always. A module is an object, and its drawers are the names its file defined.

from pathlib import Path reaches in once, takes out one name and puts it on your desk. After that you write Path and not pathlib.Path. That's the shape of from fly import fl, which you can now read in full: from the module fly, take the name fl.

A module can hold other modules, the way a folder holds folders. The long line from chapter 8 is a path of that kind:

from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

Read it from the left. In fly there's tr, which is TypeRig. In TypeRig there's proxy, in that there's fl, then objects, and in that a file called glyph.py. From that file, take pGlyph. Every dot is one step into a folder, and the last step is a file.

When the path is long and you want the whole module and not one name from it, you can give it a short name with as. Chapter 15 did this:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

That's the module scripting, four folders down inside FontLab's own app code, called scripting from here on.

Which shape is better? Use the dot when the name alone wouldn't tell a reader where it came from. json.dumps says it's JSON's. A bare dumps in line 60 of a script would send you hunting. Use from when the name is clear by itself, like Path or pGlyph, or when the dotted path is too long to write twice.

docs.title: Step 3: Where Python looks
docs.text:
When you write import csv, Python doesn't search your whole disk. It has a short list of folders, and it looks in each one in turn. You can read the list:

import sys

for folder in sys.path:
    print(folder)

sys is one more module that comes with Python, and sys.path is a plain list of strings. Your list will differ from mine in its details. On a Mac it has lines like these in it:

/Applications/FontLab 9.app/Contents/Resources/python3.11/lib/python3.11
/Users/mira/Library/Application Support/FontLab/FontLab 9/python/3.11/site-packages

Find the line that ends in site-packages and sits inside your own user folder. That's where the installer put Fly in chapter 4. It's a folder that belongs to you, FontLab's Python looks in it, and a FontLab update shouldn't empty it.

To open that folder without hunting for it, print it so you can copy it:

import sys

for folder in sys.path:
    if folder.endswith("site-packages"):
        print(folder)

If that prints two lines, take the one with your name in it. On a Mac, copy the line, switch to the Finder, choose Go > Go to Folder… and paste. On Windows, paste it into the address bar of an Explorer window.

If Python goes through every folder on the list and finds nothing, you get this:

import jsno

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'jsno'

Read the name in quotes first. Nine times in ten it's a typing slip. The tenth time, the module really isn't in any folder on the list.

docs.title: Step 4: Write a small one
docs.text:
A module is a text file whose name ends in .py, in one of those folders. To see how that works from the inside, write a small one. In the Scripting panel, start a new script and type this:

# Ines's status colors, for trying out modules.
RED = 1
YELLOW = 61
GREEN = 151

LEGEND = {
    0: "untouched",
    RED: "not-drawn",
    YELLOW: "needs-work",
    GREEN: "done",
}

Save it with the name studio_marks.py in the site-packages folder from Step 3. The name matters: all lowercase, no spaces, no hyphen, and not a name Python already uses. Call it csv.py and import csv will go on giving you Python's own, because that folder comes first in the list. Yours would never be found.

Now run it. Nothing is printed, and that's correct. The file defines three boxes and a dictionary, and then it ends. A module is a shelf, and running it only puts things on the shelf.

Start another new script and borrow from it:

import studio_marks

print(studio_marks.GREEN)
print(studio_marks.LEGEND[studio_marks.GREEN])

151
done

That's all a module of your own is. Nothing about studio_marks.py is different from json or fly, apart from who wrote it.

docs.title: Step 5: The edit that doesn't take
docs.text:
Ines's question from yesterday was whether the Friday report could count statuses. That's the tally loop from chapter 32. Open studio_marks.py, add two lines at the top and a function at the bottom, so that the whole file reads:

# Ines's status colors, for trying out modules.
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

RED = 1
YELLOW = 61
GREEN = 151

LEGEND = {
    0: "untouched",
    RED: "not-drawn",
    YELLOW: "needs-work",
    GREEN: "done",
}


def status_tally(font):
    tally = {}
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        status = LEGEND.get(pGlyph(font, glyph).mark, "unknown-color")
        tally[status] = tally.get(status, 0) + 1
    return tally

Notice the import at the top. A module does its own importing. status_tally needs pGlyph, so the module says so, and a script that borrows from it doesn't have to know.

Save it. Go back to the other script and use the new function:

from fly import fl
import studio_marks

font = fl.CurrentFont()
print(studio_marks.status_tally(font))

AttributeError: module 'studio_marks' has no attribute 'status_tally'

The function is in the file. You can see it. You saved. And Python says it isn't there.

Everybody who writes a module walks into this in the first hour. I said in Step 1 that import runs the file once. It means once. The first import studio_marks read the file and built the module. Every later import studio_marks, in this script or any other, gets the module that's already built. Python doesn't look at the file again. It does this for speed, and it's a sound rule for json, which doesn't change while you work. For a module you're in the middle of writing, it means FontLab is still holding the old copy.

A script in the Scripting panel is read each time you run it. A module isn't. That's why you've never met the problem before.

There are two ways out. Quitting FontLab and starting it again always works, since a new session has nothing built. The quicker way is to ask for a fresh read:

from fly import fl
import importlib
import studio_marks

importlib.reload(studio_marks)

font = fl.CurrentFont()
print(studio_marks.status_tally(font))

{'untouched': 197, 'unknown-color': 10, 'needs-work': 3, 'not-drawn': 3}

importlib.reload(studio_marks) reads the file again and rebuilds the module in place. importlib is one more module that comes with Python. Keep that line in while you're working on a module, and take it out when the module has settled.

The function is found. Now read what it found: ten glyphs in an unknown color and none done. That's correct too. The module says done is 151, and the nine green cells in your practice font were painted 121 in chapter 32. Ines's new green is a decision for the studio's Plum, where somebody will repaint the cells. Your practice font keeps the old one.

Change GREEN back to 121 in studio_marks.py, save, and run the script again. The reload line is still in it, so the change takes:

{'untouched': 197, 'done': 9, 'unknown-color': 1, 'needs-work': 3, 'not-drawn': 3}

The pairs come in the order the font first showed each status: A is green and comes before the odd Q, which comes before the yellow a.

Going deeper: lines that run only when a module is run directly

A module can hold a few lines that run only when you run the file directly, and not when another script imports it. You'll see them in other people's modules, looking like this:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(LEGEND)

Python puts the name of each module in a box called __name__. For the file you ran, the box holds "__main__". For a file that was imported, it holds the module's own name. People use those lines for a quick test of the module. You can leave them alone for now.

docs.title: Step 6: What a module of your own costs
docs.text:
Now look at what's left of status_marks.py when the module does the shared work:

# Reports how many glyphs have each of Ines's statuses.
from fly import fl
import studio_marks

font = fl.CurrentFont()
tally = studio_marks.status_tally(font)

for status in studio_marks.LEGEND.values():
    print(f"{status:<14}{tally.get(status, 0):>4}")
print(f"{'unknown-color':<14}{tally.get('unknown-color', 0):>4}")

untouched      197
not-drawn        3
needs-work       3
done             9
unknown-color    1

Seven lines and a comment. It's short, and the green lives in one place.

Now Mira sends this script to Ines, who runs it on her laptop:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'studio_marks'

Of course. studio_marks.py is in Mira's site-packages folder, not in Ines's. The thin script only works on a machine that has the module, and the module is a file you have to remember to copy along with it, and to copy again every time it changes. The same goes for anyone who picks up one of your scripts a year from now on a new computer.

So there's a trade. A module of your own keeps a fact in one place, and a script that carries its own copy runs anywhere Fly is installed. For a few scripts on one machine, the copies are easier. For a set of tools that a whole studio uses, a module is right, and chapter 133 shows how to pack one up properly so that it travels.

This book takes the first side until then. Every listing from here on carries the functions it needs, so you can open any chapter and run its scripts without anything from an earlier one. When a function comes back, I'll say where you first wrote it, and paste it again. Chapter 40 gathers the most useful ones in one place, ready to paste.

studio_marks.py was for learning. No later chapter imports it, and you can delete it from site-packages whenever you like.

In the studio's copies Mira changes GREEN = 151 in four places, puts the constants at the top of each script where she'll see them next time, and repaints nine cells. Yours stay at 121, to match the cells you painted. Then she deletes test2.py.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A module is a Python file that other scripts borrow from with import. import json hands you the whole module and you reach in with a dot. from pathlib import Path takes one name out. Dots in an import path are steps into folders, and as gives a long path a short name. Python looks for modules only in the folders listed in sys.path, and says ModuleNotFoundError when it finds nothing. It reads each module once per session, so a module you've edited needs importlib.reload or a restart of FontLab, or you get an AttributeError for the name you just added. A module of your own has to travel with every script that imports it.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Copy names_without_unicode(font) from your Friday report into studio_marks.py, reload, and call it from a new script as studio_marks.names_without_unicode(font). The output should match the report's line for line. Then ask yourself what Ines would need on her laptop to run that new script.
  2. Add a constant UNKNOWN = "unknown-color" to the module and use it in status_tally. Then use studio_marks.UNKNOWN in the thin script too. How many places hold that word now?
  3. Rename studio_marks.py to Studio Marks.py and run import studio_marks again. Why does it still work? Now run importlib.reload(studio_marks) and read the error. Then try import Studio Marks and read that one. Which of the two errors comes from Python looking for a file, and which comes before it looks at all? Put the name back when you're done.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: widest_glyph(font) always looks at every glyph. Mira wants it to look at only the selected ones, sometimes. Chapter 34 gives functions arguments that you may leave out.

docs.title: 34. Arguments you can leave out
docs.text:
Wednesday. Mira is spacing the capitals, and she has A, H, M and W selected in the Font window. She wants to know which of those four is the widest. She has a function for the widest glyph. It tells her emdash, as it does every time, because it looks at the whole font and the em dash is the widest thing in it.

She could write a second function, widest_selected_glyph, with the same loop and one line changed. Then a third for "widest glyph that's wider than some number", and by Friday she'd be pasting six functions into every script that all do nearly the same thing.

What she wants is one function with a knob on it. Most days the knob stays where it is and she doesn't think about it. Now and then she turns it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • An empty window in the Scripting panel. Today's functions and the calls that test them all go in that one script. Save it as widest.py so you can come back to it. Each new call goes at the bottom, below the functions.
  • The selection helper, names_selected_names, from chapter 15.

docs.title: Step 1: A slot with something already in it
docs.text:
You've thought of a function's parentheses as slots since chapter 16. widest_glyph(font) has one slot, and you must fill it. A slot can also come with a value already in it. You write the value into the def line, after an equals sign:

from fly import fl


def wider_than(font, limit=700):
    names = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if glyph.width > limit:
            names.append(glyph.name)
    return names

Call it two ways, below the function:

font = fl.CurrentFont()
print(len(wider_than(font)))
print(len(wider_than(font, 800)))

22
11

The first call fills one slot and leaves the second alone. Python uses the value that was already there, 700, and finds 22 glyphs wider than that. The second call fills both, and 800 takes the place of 700 for that one call. The 700 isn't gone. The next call that leaves the slot empty gets it again.

The value in the def line is called a default. It's what the function uses when you don't say otherwise.

A good default is the answer you'd give nine times in ten. In chapter 17 the limit lived in a constant, LIMIT = 700, and that was right for a single script. In a function that several scripts use, a default is better: every call gets 700 without asking, and the one script that needs 800 can say so without changing anything for the others.

docs.title: Step 2: Say the name
docs.text:
Look at this call as a stranger would:

wider_than(font, 800)

What is 800? You know today, because you wrote the function ten minutes ago. Python lets you say which slot you're filling, by name:

wider_than(font, limit=800)

It does the same thing, and it explains itself. You've already written calls like this. open(path, "w", newline="") in chapter 28 and history.commit(..., operation="geometry", facts=facts) in chapter 29 both fill slots by name. I asked you to copy them then, and now you can see how they work.

So there are two ways to fill a slot. By position: the first value goes in the first slot, the second in the second. Or by name: limit=800 goes in the slot called limit, wherever it sits in the line. The habit I'd recommend is the one those two calls follow. Fill the one or two obvious slots by position and name the rest.

If you get the name wrong, Python tells you at once:

wider_than(font, limt=800)

TypeError: wider_than() got an unexpected keyword argument 'limt'

"Keyword argument" is Python's term for a slot filled by name. The message says there's no slot called limt. Compare that with chapter 14, where a misspelled drawer name on the left of = was accepted in silence. A misspelled slot name is refused.

docs.title: Step 3: A yes-or-no knob
docs.text:
Now Mira's problem. The knob she wants has two positions: the whole font, or only what's selected. That's a True or False, like the switch in chapter 31, except that it sits in a slot. Here's widest_glyph from chapter 33 with the knob added. Replace the old one in your script with it:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting


def widest_glyph(font, only_selected=False):
    if only_selected:
        glyphs = []
        for name in scripting.names_selected_names():
            glyphs.append(font[name])
    else:
        glyphs = font.glyphs

    widest = None
    for glyph in glyphs:
        if widest is None or glyph.width > widest.width:
            widest = glyph
    return widest

The import goes at the top of the script, below from fly import fl. Select A, H, M and W in the Font window and run:

font = fl.CurrentFont()
print(widest_glyph(font).name)
print(widest_glyph(font, only_selected=True).name)

emdash
W

The first half of the function decides which glyphs to look at. With the knob on, it builds a list from the selected names, as chapter 15 did. With the knob off, it takes all of them. Either way the result lands in a box called glyphs, and the second half of the function doesn't care which way it was filled. That's the trick to adding an option: branch once at the start to settle what you're working on, and write the real work once.

The default is False, so every call that already says widest_glyph(font) goes on working exactly as it did. Paste this version into Friday Report.py and its old call doesn't need to change. It doesn't know the knob exists. This is what makes defaults so useful: you can teach an old function something new without breaking the lines that call it.

The knob is named after the unusual behavior, so that False is the ordinary case and a call that says nothing gets the ordinary case. Chapter 31's switch worked the other way round, and for a reason: a switch that guards a change should default to safe, while an option on a report should default to ordinary.

docs.title: Step 4: When there's nothing to hand back
docs.text:
Two lines of that function changed for a reason I haven't given yet. The old version began with widest = font[0]: start with the first glyph and let the others challenge it. The new one begins with widest = None.

Click an empty spot in the Font window so that nothing is selected, and run the second call again:

AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'name'

You met this message in chapter 19, where the font itself was missing. Here the font is fine. The selection is empty, so the list of glyphs is empty, so the loop never runs, so widest is still the None it started as, and the function hands that back. Then the calling line asks None for its name.

The function did the honest thing. Asked for the widest of no glyphs, it can't hand back the first glyph of the font, which is what the old opening line would have done. That would be a wrong answer that looks like a right one. None means "there isn't one", and it's the caller's job to ask:

widest = widest_glyph(font, only_selected=True)
if widest is None:
    print("Select some glyphs first.")
else:
    print(widest.name, widest.width)

Select some glyphs first.

is None is the test from chapter 19.

The line inside the loop needs the same care: if widest is None or glyph.width > widest.width. The first glyph the loop meets wins by default, because there's no champion yet. After that, a glyph has to be wider than the champion. The order of the two tests matters. Python reads an or from the left and stops as soon as one side is true, so when widest is None it never gets as far as asking None for a width.

docs.title: Step 5: The order of the slots
docs.text:
Now the mistake. Mira decides that only_selected is the more important slot and moves it to the front:

def widest_glyph(only_selected=False, font):

Run the script, and none of it runs:

SyntaxError: non-default argument follows default argument

A SyntaxError means Python couldn't read the script at all, so nothing in it runs until it's fixed, not even the lines above the mistake. The rule it's quoting: slots that must be filled come first, and slots with defaults come after them.

Think about why. Suppose Python allowed that line, and you called widest_glyph(font). One value, two slots. Does the value go in the first slot, because it's first? Then only_selected holds a font and font holds nothing. Or should Python skip the first slot because it has a default? It would have to guess, and Python refuses to guess. With the required slots at the front, a call by position always fills them first and whatever's left over goes into the optional ones.

Put the line back as it was.

Two more messages belong to this family, and you'll see both sooner or later:

widest_glyph()
widest_glyph(font, True, 800)

TypeError: widest_glyph() missing 1 required positional argument: 'font'
TypeError: widest_glyph() takes from 1 to 2 positional arguments but 3 were given

The first says a slot without a default was left empty. The second says you brought more values than there are slots, and "from 1 to 2" is Python counting for you: one required, one optional.

docs.title: Step 6: Two knobs
docs.text:
A function can have several optional slots. Give wider_than the same knob, and move the choosing of glyphs into a small function of its own, since two functions now need it:

def glyphs_of(font, only_selected=False):
    if not only_selected:
        return font.glyphs
    glyphs = []
    for name in scripting.names_selected_names():
        glyphs.append(font[name])
    return glyphs


def wider_than(font, limit=700, only_selected=False):
    names = []
    for glyph in glyphs_of(font, only_selected):
        if glyph.width > limit:
            names.append(glyph.name)
    return names

With A, H, M and W selected again:

print(wider_than(font, only_selected=True))
print(wider_than(font, limit=600, only_selected=True))
print(len(wider_than(font, limit=900)))

['M', 'W']
['H', 'M', 'W']
2

The first call skips limit and sets the knob after it. You can only do that by name. By position you'd have to write wider_than(font, 700, True), repeating a default you didn't want to think about, and leaving a bare True that tells a reader nothing. Naming the slot is the only good way to write that call.

glyphs_of shows something else. A function can have more than one return. The first one hands back the whole font and leaves at once, and the rest of the function is only reached when the knob is on.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is widest.py as it stands by this evening, with the test calls at the bottom. It needs nothing but Fly.

from fly import fl
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting


def glyphs_of(font, only_selected=False):
    if not only_selected:
        return font.glyphs
    glyphs = []
    for name in scripting.names_selected_names():
        glyphs.append(font[name])
    return glyphs


def widest_glyph(font, only_selected=False):
    widest = None
    for glyph in glyphs_of(font, only_selected):
        if widest is None or glyph.width > widest.width:
            widest = glyph
    return widest


def wider_than(font, limit=700, only_selected=False):
    names = []
    for glyph in glyphs_of(font, only_selected):
        if glyph.width > limit:
            names.append(glyph.name)
    return names


font = fl.CurrentFont()
widest = widest_glyph(font, only_selected=True)
if widest is None:
    print("Select some glyphs first.")
else:
    print(widest.name, widest.width)
print(wider_than(font, limit=700, only_selected=True))

widest_glyph is shorter than it was in Step 3, because glyphs_of took over its first half.

Mira selects her four capitals and gets her answer: W, at 859 units. Then she selects all 26 and asks which are wider than 700. The old calls in her other scripts still mean what they meant, because a call that says nothing gets the ordinary case.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A slot in a def line can carry a default, written name=value, and a call that leaves the slot empty gets that value. You can fill any slot by name, which makes a call explain itself and lets you skip the optional slots you don't care about. Slots that must be filled come before slots with defaults. A function that has nothing to hand back should return None, and its caller should ask is None before using the result.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Copy status_tally and LEGEND from chapter 33 into widest.py, and give status_tally an only_selected=False slot, using glyphs_of. Select the capitals and print the tally for them alone. Which line of the function did you have to change, besides the def line?
  2. Write narrower_than(font, limit=300, only_selected=False). Then look at it next to wider_than. They differ in one character. Is that worth a single function with a third knob, or are two functions clearer? There's no right answer, but decide, and say why in a comment.
  3. Call wider_than(font, only_selected=True, limit=600), with the two named slots the other way around. Does it work? Then call wider_than(limit=600, font=font). What does that tell you about slots filled by name?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: wider_than hands back names, and Mira wants the widths beside them. Chapter 35 builds rows: lists that hold lists.

docs.title: 35. Rows
docs.text:
Thursday. Yesterday's function told Mira that M and W are wider than 700 units. This morning that isn't enough. She's spacing, and a spacer wants to see three numbers for every glyph: how much white is on its left, how wide it is in all, and how much white is on its right. She wants them side by side, for six glyphs at once, so that she can compare the n with the o and the H with the O.

That's a table, with one line per glyph and the same kinds of things in each line. You built a table in chapter 28 and sent it straight to a file, row by row, without keeping it. In chapter 30 you kept a small one, the list of rename pairs, without looking hard at its shape. Today you keep it, because in the next chapter you'll want to sort it, and you can't sort what you've already printed.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • glyphs_of from chapter 34. It's repeated below, so you don't need the old script open.
  • Six glyphs selected in the Font window: H, O, A, n, o and v.

docs.title: Step 1: The white on each side
docs.text:
A glyph sits in a box as wide as its advance width. The black shape doesn't touch the edges of the box. The gap between the left edge and the leftmost point of the shape is the left sidebearing. The gap on the other side is the right sidebearing. When two glyphs stand next to each other, the right sidebearing of the first and the left sidebearing of the second add up to the white between them. Spacing a font is, for the most part, choosing those two numbers for every glyph.

The rich glyph from chapter 14 knows both. Ask it about the n:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph = font["n"]
rich = pGlyph(font, glyph)
print(rich.getLSB(), glyph.width, rich.getRSB())

70 523.0 66

LSB and RSB are the left and right sidebearings, and getLSB() and getRSB() ask for them. Type people shorten the words that way all day, so the names are worth knowing. The n has 70 units of white on its left, 66 on its right, and 523 in all. The black part must be 387 units wide, since the three have to add up.

I worked these numbers out from the font file. If FontLab gives you a unit more or less, trust FontLab.

The sidebearings come back as whole numbers and the width with .0 after it. Use int(glyph.width) from chapter 11 so that they match.

docs.title: Step 2: A list is a row
docs.text:
Put the four facts about the n into one list:

row = [glyph.name, rich.getLSB(), int(glyph.width), rich.getRSB()]
print(row)

['n', 70, 523, 66]

A list doesn't have to hold things of one kind. This one holds a string and three numbers, and it's one line of Mira's table. In chapter 30 you made small lists of two, [old, new], and kept a list of them. It's the same idea here with four.

Now do it for every selected glyph, and keep the rows in a list of their own:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

rows = []
for name in scripting.names_selected_names():
    glyph = font[name]
    rich = pGlyph(font, glyph)
    rows.append([glyph.name, rich.getLSB(), int(glyph.width), rich.getRSB()])

print(rows)

[['H', 76, 672, 70], ['O', 36, 708, 36], ['A', 13, 596, 11], ['n', 70, 523, 66], ['o', 38, 520, 38], ['v', 8, 455, 3]]

Your rows may come in a different order, depending on how you selected the cells. Your numbers may differ from mine by a unit, too. I worked mine out from the font's source file.

Count the brackets at the start: two. The outer pair is the table and each inner pair is a row. A list of lists is the simplest way Python has to hold a table, and you'll meet it wherever data has rows.

docs.title: Step 3: Two numbers to find a cell
docs.text:
One number in brackets picks a row. A second picks a cell in it:

print(rows[0])
print(rows[0][2])
print(rows[3][0])

['H', 76, 672, 70]
672
n

Read rows[0][2] from left to right. rows[0] is the first row, which is itself a list. Then [2] asks that list for its third item. It's a street and a house number.

It works, and it reads badly. Nothing about [2] says "width". If you write row[1] when you meant row[3], the script gives you a left sidebearing where you wanted a right one, and no error will ever tell you. The next step is the cure.

docs.title: Step 4: Unpack
docs.text:
You've written loops like this since chapter 30 without my explaining them properly:

for name, lsb, width, rsb in rows:
    print(f"{name:<6}{lsb:>5}{width:>6}{rsb:>5}")

H        76   672   70
O        36   708   36
A        13   596   11
n        70   523   66
o        38   520   38
v         8   455    3

Each time around, the loop takes one row and deals its four items into four boxes, in order. That's called unpacking. It isn't special to loops. It works anywhere there's an equals sign:

name, lsb, width, rsb = rows[3]
print(name, width)

n 523

Four names on the left, a row of four on the right, and each name gets its item. After that line you never write [2] again. You write width.

That's the table Mira wanted, and it's worth a look as a type designer and not only as a programmer. The O and the o have the same white on both sides, as round letters should. The n has more on its left, where the straight stem is, than on its right, where the arch is. The A and the v have almost none, because their diagonals make their own white. And the H has 76 on one side and 70 on the other, which a symmetrical letter shouldn't. Mira writes that down.

Now the mistake. Suppose you decide the table doesn't need the right sidebearing and take rsb out of the loop line, but leave the rows as they are:

for name, lsb, width in rows:
    print(name, lsb, width)

ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 3)

Python had four items and three boxes, and it won't throw one away without being told. The other way around, with five names and four items, reads:

ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 5, got 4)

The count is checked every time, so a row that's the wrong shape stops the script. A wrong index number would have gone on quietly and printed nonsense.

docs.title: Step 5: Rows that can't be changed
docs.text:
There's a second kind of row. Write it with parentheses where the list has square brackets:

row = ("n", 70, 523, 66)
print(row[2])
name, lsb, width, rsb = row
print(name, width)

523
n 523

It's called a tuple, and so far it behaves like a list. You can index it, loop over it, unpack it and ask its len. The difference shows when you try to change it:

row[1] = 75

TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

A tuple is fixed once it's made. You can't replace an item, and there's no append.

Why have the weaker one? Think of a row as a record of a measurement. The n measured 70, 523 and 66 at ten o'clock this morning. A script further down that changes the 70 by accident has spoiled the record, and with a tuple that accident is an error message, where with a list it would be a silent wrong number in a report. The table itself is another matter. It grows as you add rows, so it has to be a list.

By habit, people use a list for a collection that grows and shrinks, with items of one kind, and a tuple for a record with a fixed number of fields. A list of tuples is a table.

You've held tuples already. The plan rows in chapter 30 were tuples of (old, new, status), and tally.items() in chapter 22 handed you pairs that were tuples too. When Python prints parentheses around a row, that's what you're looking at.

docs.title: Step 6: Zip two lists together
docs.text:
Sometimes the columns arrive separately. Tomas sends two lists by message, some glyph names and the widths the publisher's old font had for them:

names = ["H", "O", "A"]
old_widths = [680, 700, 600]

To compare them with Plum you need them as rows. zip takes two lists and pairs their items off, first with first, second with second, the way the two sides of a zipper meet:

for name, old in zip(names, old_widths):
    now = int(font[name].width)
    print(f"{name:<4}{old:>5}{now:>5}{now - old:>5}")

H     680  672   -8
O     700  708    8
A     600  596   -4

zip hands you tuples of two, and the loop unpacks them. If you want the pairs as a table you can keep, wrap it in list:

print(list(zip(names, old_widths)))

[('H', 680), ('O', 700), ('A', 600)]

One thing to know about zip: if the lists are of different lengths, it stops at the end of the shorter one and says nothing. Three names and two widths give two pairs, and the third name is dropped. When the two lists come from somebody else, compare their len first.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
The row-making goes in a function of its own, because the next three chapters will use it. Here is metrics_rows.py in full, with glyphs_of from chapter 34 repeated at the top so that the script runs by itself:

# Prints left sidebearing, width and right sidebearing
# for the glyphs selected in the Font window.
from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting


def glyphs_of(font, only_selected=False):
    if not only_selected:
        return font.glyphs
    glyphs = []
    for name in scripting.names_selected_names():
        glyphs.append(font[name])
    return glyphs


def metrics_rows(font, only_selected=False):
    rows = []
    for glyph in glyphs_of(font, only_selected):
        measured = pGlyph(font, glyph)
        if not measured.isEmpty():
            rows.append((glyph.name, measured.getLSB(), int(glyph.width), measured.getRSB()))
    return rows


font = fl.CurrentFont()
rows = metrics_rows(font, only_selected=True)

if not rows:
