    print("Select some glyphs with shapes in them first.")
else:
    print(f"{'glyph':<8}{'LSB':>5}{'width':>7}{'RSB':>5}")
    for name, lsb, width, rsb in rows:
        print(f"{name:<8}{lsb:>5}{width:>7}{rsb:>5}")

glyph     LSB  width  RSB
H          76    672   70
O          36    708   36
A          13    596   11
n          70    523   66
o          38    520   38
v           8    455    3

There are two things to notice in metrics_rows. Each row is a tuple, so there are double parentheses in the append line: the outer pair belongs to append and the inner pair makes the tuple. And empty glyphs are left out by the if not measured.isEmpty() test, which is the question chapter 8 asked. A space has a width, but with no shape in it there's no leftmost point to measure a sidebearing from, and I'd sooner leave the row out than print a number that means nothing.

if not rows: is the truthiness rule from chapter 31 at work. An empty list counts as no, so the line reads "if there are no rows".

Mira prints the table for all the capitals, finds two more with lopsided sidebearings and fixes them by hand before lunch. Then she asks for the obvious next thing, which is the table with the widest glyph at the top.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A table is a list of rows, and a row is a small list or tuple with the same fields in the same order every time. Unpack a row into named boxes in place of using index numbers, and Python will check the count for you. A tuple is a row that can't be changed after it's made, which suits a record. zip pairs off two lists into rows and stops without warning at the end of the shorter one.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a fifth field to each row in metrics_rows: the width of the black part, which is the width minus both sidebearings. Which other lines of the script have to change? Run metrics_rows.py before you fix them and read the error.
  2. Print only the rows whose two sidebearings differ by more than 4 units. For the six glyphs in this chapter that should leave one or two rows. abs() turns a negative number into a positive one, so abs(lsb - rsb) is the size of the difference whichever side is bigger.
  3. Send the rows to a CSV file with the writer from chapter 28, with a header row. Then open the file in a spreadsheet. A writer takes a tuple as happily as a list.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The table comes out in whatever order the glyphs were selected. Chapter 36 sorts it by any column you like.

docs.title: 36. Sort by anything
docs.text:
Friday. Mira has her table of sidebearings and widths, and it comes out in whatever order she clicked the cells. She wants the widest glyph at the top. Ines wants the most lopsided at the top. Tomas has asked for the whole font in alphabetical order, and he means his alphabet, where a comes after A and not after Z.

That's three orders for the same rows. You've had sorted since chapter 10, and it knows one order. Today you teach it the others. In chapter 29 you handed a function to commit. Today you hand one to sorted.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • metrics_rows and glyphs_of from chapter 35. They're repeated below, so you don't need the old script.
  • The same six glyphs selected: H, O, A, n, o and v.

Start every listing in this chapter with these lines. They are the two functions from chapter 35, copied in so that each listing runs by itself:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting


def glyphs_of(font, only_selected=False):
    if not only_selected:
        return font.glyphs
    glyphs = []
    for name in scripting.names_selected_names():
        glyphs.append(font[name])
    return glyphs


def metrics_rows(font, only_selected=False):
    rows = []
    for glyph in glyphs_of(font, only_selected):
        measured = pGlyph(font, glyph)
        if not measured.isEmpty():
            rows.append((glyph.name, measured.getLSB(), int(glyph.width), measured.getRSB()))
    return rows


font = fl.CurrentFont()
rows = metrics_rows(font, only_selected=True)

docs.title: Step 1: What sorted does to rows
docs.text:
Hand the table to sorted as it is:

for row in sorted(rows):
    print(row)

('A', 13, 596, 11)
('H', 76, 672, 70)
('O', 36, 708, 36)
('n', 70, 523, 66)
('o', 38, 520, 38)
('v', 8, 455, 3)

It worked, and you can see the rule it used. sorted compares rows by their first field. The names are the first field, so the table is in name order, capitals first, as chapter 10 warned. If two rows had the same first field, sorted would go on to the second to break the tie, and then to the third. That's how you'd sort a pile of index cards: by the top line, and by the next line when the top lines match.

So one way to sort by width would be to build the rows with the width in front. But then the table is in the wrong shape for everything else, and the day Ines wants a different order you'd have to rebuild it again. The rows should stay as they are. What needs to change is what sorted looks at.

docs.title: Step 2: Tell it what to look at
docs.text:
sorted has an optional slot called key. You fill it by name, as chapter 34 showed. What goes in it is a function: one that takes a row and hands back the thing to sort by.

def by_width(row):
    return row[2]


for row in sorted(rows, key=by_width):
    print(row)

('v', 8, 455, 3)
('o', 38, 520, 38)
('n', 70, 523, 66)
('A', 13, 596, 11)
('H', 76, 672, 70)
('O', 36, 708, 36)

by_width is as small as a function gets. Give it a row and it hands back the third field. sorted calls it once for every row, lines the rows up by the numbers it gets back, and hands you the rows. The numbers are thrown away afterward. They were only for comparing.

Picture a teacher lining up a class by height. She doesn't rearrange the children's heights, she rearranges the children. Height is what she looks at to decide who stands where. The key function tells sorted what to look at.

Now look hard at this part of the line:

sorted(rows, key=by_width)

There are no parentheses after by_width. You've seen that once before. In chapter 29 you handed widen to history.commit without parentheses, and I compared it to handing over a recipe card. This is the same thing. With parentheses, by_width(row) runs the function now and gives you a number. Without them, by_width is the function itself, handed to sorted for sorted to use when it needs it.

A function is a value. It lives in a box with a name on it, as a number does. You can put it in a slot or hand it to another function.

docs.title: Step 3: The parentheses that don't belong
docs.text:
Your fingers have learned that a function's name is followed by parentheses, so sooner or later you'll type this:

for row in sorted(rows, key=by_width()):
    print(row)

TypeError: by_width() missing 1 required positional argument: 'row'

You know this message from chapter 34: a slot that must be filled was left empty. The parentheses told Python to call by_width right there, before sorted had started, and with nothing in its slot. Python never got as far as sorting.

Read the message for what it's really telling you. You don't call a key function yourself. sorted does that, once per row, and it supplies the row. You only hand it over, so take the parentheses off.

docs.title: Step 4: Biggest first
docs.text:
Mira wanted the widest at the top, and so far it's at the bottom. sorted has a second optional slot for that:

for name, lsb, width, rsb in sorted(rows, key=by_width, reverse=True):
    print(f"{name:<6}{lsb:>5}{width:>6}{rsb:>5}")

O        36   708   36
H        76   672   70
A        13   596   11
n        70   523   66
o        38   520   38
v         8   455    3

reverse=True turns the order around. Its default is False, so you've been using this knob since chapter 10 without knowing it was there.

If you only want the top few, slice the sorted list. The slice comes from chapter 10. To get the five widest glyphs in the whole font, leave only_selected out so that the rows cover every glyph with a shape:

rows = metrics_rows(font)
for name, lsb, width, rsb in sorted(rows, key=by_width, reverse=True)[:5]:
    print(f"{name:<12}{width:>5}")

emdash       1000
OE            989
W             859
Wacute        859
Wcircumflex   859

That makes the plain widest_glyph from chapter 18 a special case. The widest glyph is the first row of the table sorted by width, biggest first. If you only want the single winner, Python has a shortcut that takes the same kind of key: max(rows, key=by_width) hands back the one row with the largest width, and min hands back the smallest.

docs.title: Step 5: Sort by something that isn't a column
docs.text:
The key function doesn't have to pick a field. It can work something out. Ines wants the most lopsided glyphs first, and lopsidedness is the difference between the two sidebearings:

def lopsided(row):
    name, lsb, width, rsb = row
    return abs(lsb - rsb)


rows = metrics_rows(font, only_selected=True)
for row in sorted(rows, key=lopsided, reverse=True):
    print(row, lopsided(row))

('H', 76, 672, 70) 6
('v', 8, 455, 3) 5
('n', 70, 523, 66) 4
('A', 13, 596, 11) 2
('O', 36, 708, 36) 0
('o', 38, 520, 38) 0

abs(-6) is 6: the size of a number without its sign. Inside lopsided the row is unpacked into named boxes, as chapter 35 recommended, so the sum reads as what it is.

The H is at the top, where Mira's note from yesterday said it would be. The two round letters share the bottom with a difference of 0. Look at their order: O before o. Neither is more lopsided than the other, so sorted had nothing to go on, and it left them in the order they came in. It always does that with ties. Rows that the key can't tell apart keep their original order, and you can rely on it.

Tomas's alphabet is the same trick. He wants a next to A, so the key is the name with its capitals flattened:

def by_name_like_a_person(row):
    return row[0].lower()


names = []
for row in sorted(rows, key=by_name_like_a_person):
    names.append(row[0])
print(" ".join(names))

A H n O o v

lower() is new: it hands back the string in small letters. sorted compares "a", "h", "n", "o", "o" and "v", and then hands back the real names with their capitals intact. O and o tie, so they stay in the order they came.

docs.title: Step 6: Sort the tally from chapter 22
docs.text:
In chapter 22 you counted glyphs by width and got a dictionary. Chapter 22 left the tally unsorted. In chapter 32 you got another, the tally of statuses. A dictionary can't be sorted where it stands, but items() hands you its pairs, and pairs are rows of two:

status_tally is the counter from chapter 33. Here it is again, with the colour numbers it needs, so that this listing runs after the starter lines:

RED = 1
YELLOW = 61
GREEN = 121

LEGEND = {
    0: "untouched",
    RED: "not-drawn",
    YELLOW: "needs-work",
    GREEN: "done",
}


def status_tally(font):
    tally = {}
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        status = LEGEND.get(pGlyph(font, glyph).mark, "unknown-color")
        tally[status] = tally.get(status, 0) + 1
    return tally


tally = status_tally(font)


def by_count(pair):
    return pair[1]


for status, count in sorted(tally.items(), key=by_count, reverse=True):
    print(f"{status:<14}{count:>4}")

untouched      197
done             9
needs-work       3
not-drawn        3
unknown-color    1

Each pair is (status, count). The key picks the count, and reverse=True puts the biggest first. That's the pattern for every "top ten" you'll ever be asked for: count into a dictionary, take the items, sort by the second field, slice.

Going deeper: key functions in one line

When you read other people's scripts you'll see key functions written in one line, with no def and no name:

sorted(rows, key=lambda row: row[2])

lambda makes a small function on the spot. The part before the colon is its slot and the part after is what it returns. It does what by_width does. I've used def in this chapter because a name like by_width tells you what the sort is for, and because you can test a named function by itself. Use whichever you find easier to read.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Save this as widest_first.py. It carries its own copies of glyphs_of and metrics_rows, plus the two key functions, so it needs nothing but Fly:

#FLM: Widest First
# Prints the metrics of the selected glyphs, widest first,
# and then the three most lopsided of them.
from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

HOW_MANY = 3


def glyphs_of(font, only_selected=False):
    if not only_selected:
        return font.glyphs
    glyphs = []
    for name in scripting.names_selected_names():
        glyphs.append(font[name])
    return glyphs


def metrics_rows(font, only_selected=False):
    rows = []
    for glyph in glyphs_of(font, only_selected):
        measured = pGlyph(font, glyph)
        if not measured.isEmpty():
            rows.append((glyph.name, measured.getLSB(), int(glyph.width), measured.getRSB()))
    return rows


def by_width(row):
    return row[2]


def lopsided(row):
    name, lsb, width, rsb = row
    return abs(lsb - rsb)


font = fl.CurrentFont()
rows = metrics_rows(font, only_selected=True)

if not rows:
    print("Select some glyphs with shapes in them first.")
else:
    print(f"{'glyph':<8}{'LSB':>5}{'width':>7}{'RSB':>5}")
    for name, lsb, width, rsb in sorted(rows, key=by_width, reverse=True):
        print(f"{name:<8}{lsb:>5}{width:>7}{rsb:>5}")

    print()
    print("Most lopsided:")
    for row in sorted(rows, key=lopsided, reverse=True)[:HOW_MANY]:
        print(f"  {row[0]:<6}{lopsided(row):>3}")

glyph     LSB  width  RSB
O          36    708   36
H          76    672   70
A          13    596   11
n          70    523   66
o          38    520   38
v           8    455    3

Most lopsided:
  H       6
  v       5
  n       4

key=by_width has no parentheses. You're handing the function on unopened, and sorted calls it for you. And the bare print() in the middle, with nothing in its slot, prints an empty line.

Mira will want this one every time she spaces, so put it in the menu, as you did with the Friday report in chapter 18. The first line, #FLM: Widest First, is the name the menu will show. Save a copy as Widest First.py in the Halfmoon folder inside FontLab's Scripts folder, and choose Scripts > Refresh Scripts. Select a few cells and pick it from the menu.

One caution about "lopsided". The n is meant to be lopsided, because a stem and an arch need different amounts of white. The script can't tell which differences were intended. It puts them in order so that a person who knows can look at the top of the list first. That's the limit you met in chapter 31, where ok meant the font would accept a rename and not that the rename was wise.

Ines looks at the list, says the v is fine and the H isn't, and Mira fixes the H.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: sorted takes an optional key, a function that it calls on each item to get the thing to compare, and an optional reverse=True to put the biggest first. You hand the function over by name without parentheses, because a function is a value like any other. The key can pick a field or work something out, and items that tie keep the order they came in. To sort a dictionary, sort its items().

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Sort the six rows by right sidebearing, smallest first. Then write a key function black_width(row) that returns the width minus both sidebearings, and sort by that. Which of the six glyphs has the widest black shape?
  2. The digits in Plum all have the same width, 490. Select them and sort by width, then sort by name. In what order do they come out the first time, and why? Now write a key function that returns (row[2], row[0]), a tuple of width and name. What does sorted do with a key that's a tuple? Step 1 has the answer.
  3. Print the ten most common advance widths in the whole font, most common first, using the width tally from chapter 22 and the pattern from Step 6.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: metrics_rows takes six lines to build a list. Python has a way to say the same thing in one. Chapter 37 shows it, and shows when not to use it.

docs.title: 37. One line that builds a list
docs.text:
Monday of the seventh week. Mira is reading one of Oskar's old scripts in the chores folder, to see how he exported the kerning, and she gets stuck on the third line:

wide = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs if glyph.width > 800]

She can read every word in it. There's a for, an in, an if. But they're inside square brackets, in an order she's never seen, with no colons and no indents. She messages Oskar: Is this a typo?

He answers within the minute. No. It's the four lines you'd write, folded into one. Unfold it and you'll see.

Oskar's scripts are full of lines like that one, and so are the scripts you'll find on the web. You need to be able to read them, and after today you'll write a few yourself. I'll also show you where I think they stop being a good idea.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • The functions from chapters 33 to 36: is_empty, glyphs_of and wider_than. Where a listing needs one, it's shown.

Every listing in this chapter starts with the usual two lines:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()

docs.title: Step 1: The loop you've written forty times
docs.text:
Here's the pattern from chapter 10, the one for building a list:

names = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    names.append(glyph.name)

print(names[:6])

['.notdef', 'A', 'Aacute', 'Abreve', 'Acircumflex', 'Adieresis']

Make an empty list. Walk through something. Each time around, work out one value and append it. You've written those three lines in nearly every chapter since, and your scripts from the last few chapters have them three times over.

When people write the same three lines often enough, the language grows a shorter way to say them. This is it:

names = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs]

print(names[:6])

['.notdef', 'A', 'Aacute', 'Abreve', 'Acircumflex', 'Adieresis']

It's the same list. The square brackets say "this makes a list", as they always have. Inside them, read from the middle outward: for glyph in font.glyphs is the loop line you know, minus its colon, and glyph.name in front of it is what goes into the list each time around.

It's called a list comprehension. The name isn't a helpful one. Read the line aloud as "the name of each glyph in the font", which is close to how you'd say it to Ines.

The part in front can be anything that produces a value, as the argument to append could:

widths = [int(glyph.width) for glyph in font.glyphs]
small_caps = [name + ".sc" for name in ["a", "b", "c"]]

print(widths[:6])
print(small_caps)

[500, 596, 596, 596, 596, 596]
['a.sc', 'b.sc', 'c.sc']

docs.title: Step 2: Only some of them
docs.text:
The other half of the pattern is the filter from chapter 8, a loop with an if inside:

wide = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.width > 800:
        wide.append(glyph.name)

Folded up, the if goes at the end:

wide = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs if glyph.width > 800]

print(wide)

['AE', 'M', 'OE', 'W', 'Wacute', 'Wcircumflex', 'Wdieresis', 'Wgrave', 'oe', 'emdash', 'at']

That's Oskar's line. Put the two versions side by side and you can see where each piece went:

In the loop In the comprehension wide = [] and wide.append(...) the square brackets for glyph in font.glyphs: for glyph in font.glyphs, in the middle if glyph.width > 800: if glyph.width > 800, at the end glyph.name glyph.name, at the front

So the order is: what you want, where it comes from, which ones. "The name of each glyph in the font, if it's wider than 800." The loop says the same things in the order a machine does them. The comprehension says them closer to the way you'd say the sentence.

When you meet one in somebody's script and can't read it, do what Oskar said. Unfold it into the four lines, in your head or on paper.

docs.title: Step 3: The if in the wrong place
docs.text:
Here's the mistake. It's the natural place to put the if. In the sentence I wrote a moment ago, the "if" comes last. It's tempting to put it where it sits in the loop, right after the thing it guards:

wide = [glyph.name if glyph.width > 800 for glyph in font.glyphs]

SyntaxError: expected 'else' after 'if' expression

Python doesn't say "the if is in the wrong place". It says it expected an else, which is a strange thing to want. The message makes sense once you know there are two different ifs that can appear in a comprehension, and you've only met one.

The if at the end is a filter. It decides whether a glyph gets into the list at all.

An if at the front is something else, and it must have an else. It doesn't filter. Every glyph gets in, and the if chooses which of two values goes in for it:

notes = ["wide" if glyph.width > 800 else "ok" for glyph in font.glyphs]

print(notes[:4])
print(len(notes))

['ok', 'ok', 'ok', 'ok']
205

That list has one entry for every glyph in the font, "wide" or "ok". My 205 is the count of Plum as it came in chapter 4, and so are the totals in the next step. Your practice font has grown since, so your counts run a little higher: 213 if you've followed every step. The piece "wide" if glyph.width > 800 else "ok" is a value with a choice built in: this, if the test is true, or else that. It works outside comprehensions too, anywhere a value can go.

So when you see that error, you put a filter at the front. Move it to the end.

docs.title: Step 4: Hand it straight on
docs.text:
Often you build a list only to hand it to something. There's no need to give it a name first:

print(len([glyph for glyph in font.glyphs if glyph.width > 800]))
print(sum([int(glyph.width) for glyph in font.glyphs]))
print(max([len(glyph.name) for glyph in font.glyphs]))

11
102107
14

Eleven glyphs are wider than 800. sum adds up a list of numbers, and here it gives the total of all the widths, the figure from exercise 2 of chapter 28. The longest glyph name has 14 characters. Your total will be larger than mine if the glyphs you've added have widths.

Each of those took you three or four lines in Part 1. That's the real gain: a question you can ask in one line is a question you'll ask more often. You can type a line like these into the Scripting panel, run it, read the answer and delete it, the way you'd use a calculator.

A comprehension is also a natural thing to hand to sorted:

print(sorted([glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs if glyph.name.endswith("acute")])[:5])

['Aacute', 'Eacute', 'Iacute', 'Oacute', 'Uacute']

Read it from the inside out, as you read nested parentheses in arithmetic: the names that end in acute, sorted, and then the first five.

docs.title: Step 5: Dictionaries and sets fold too
docs.text:
The same fold works for the other two containers. With curly brackets and a colon, it builds a dictionary:

width_of = {glyph.name: int(glyph.width) for glyph in font.glyphs}

print(width_of["A"], width_of["emdash"])

596 1000

That's the lookup dictionary from chapter 21 in one line. Before the for there's a key, a colon and a value, the same three things you'd write inside {} by hand.

With curly brackets and no colon, it builds a set:

distinct = {int(glyph.width) for glyph in font.glyphs}

print(len(distinct))
print(sorted(distinct)[:6])

84
[190, 212, 217, 222, 224, 228]

A set keeps one of each, as chapter 25 showed, so this answers a question a spacer does ask: how many different advance widths does the font have? The untouched Plum has 84 in its Regular master, and the six narrowest start at 190. Your practice glyphs may add one or two. A font with a tidy rhythm has few. If that number were 180 for 205 glyphs, somebody had been nudging widths one at a time.

Curly brackets mean a dictionary or a set, depending on whether there's a colon, and that's the same rule as in chapters 21 and 25.

docs.title: Step 6: When to unfold it again
docs.text:
Now the other side. Here's metrics_rows from chapter 35, as a loop:

def metrics_rows(font, only_selected=False):
    rows = []
    for glyph in glyphs_of(font, only_selected):
        if not is_empty(font, glyph):
            measured = pGlyph(font, glyph)
            rows.append((glyph.name, measured.getLSB(), int(glyph.width), measured.getRSB()))
    return rows

And here it is as a comprehension:

def metrics_rows(font, only_selected=False):
    return [(glyph.name, pGlyph(font, glyph).getLSB(), int(glyph.width), pGlyph(font, glyph).getRSB()) for glyph in glyphs_of(font, only_selected) if not is_empty(font, glyph)]

It works. It's also 170 characters long, you have to scroll sideways to find the for, and it makes the pGlyph twice for every row because there's nowhere to keep it. The loop had a box called measured for that. Nobody will thank you for the second version, and that includes you, in a month.

My rule is this. Use a comprehension when you can say it in one breath: "the name of each glyph that's wider than 800". Use a loop when:

  • the line won't fit on the screen without scrolling;
  • you need a box in the middle to hold something you'll use twice;
  • there's more than one if, or an if with an else and a filter as well;
  • the loop does something, as opposed to building something.

A comprehension is for making a list. It isn't for marking glyphs red or renaming them or printing. You can write [print(glyph.name) for glyph in font.glyphs], and it will print, and it will also build a list of Nones, one for each glyph, and throw it away. A line that changes the font should look like one. A for loop with an indented body does, and a pair of square brackets doesn't.

wider_than passes the test:

def wider_than(font, limit=700, only_selected=False):
    return [g.name for g in glyphs_of(font, only_selected) if g.width > limit]

Five lines became one, and you can read it aloud. The short name g is fine in a comprehension, because it lives and dies within the line. In a loop with ten lines in its body, I'd spell it out.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
This is empty_glyphs.py from chapter 8, rewritten with today's tool and the is_empty function from chapter 33:

# Lists the glyphs that have no shapes in them.
from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph


def is_empty(font, glyph):
    return pGlyph(font, glyph).isEmpty()


font = fl.CurrentFont()

empty = [g.name for g in font.glyphs if is_empty(font, g)]

print(len(empty), "of", len(font), "glyphs are empty:")
print(" ".join(empty))

9 of 213 glyphs are empty:
space a.sc b.sc c.sc a.ss01 ampersand.ss01 g.ss01 y.ss01 zero.alt

Yours will list whichever practice glyphs you've added and not yet drawn. In chapter 8 this script was a loop with a counter and a print inside it. Now it has three parts that each say one thing: find the font, build the list, report. The comprehension holds the question, and the lines after it decide what to do with the answer. Scripts tend to settle into that shape once comprehensions are available.

And two functions from chapter 34 get shorter. Paste these over the old versions wherever you use them:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting


def glyphs_of(font, only_selected=False):
    if not only_selected:
        return font.glyphs
    return [font[name] for name in scripting.names_selected_names()]


def wider_than(font, limit=700, only_selected=False):
    return [g.name for g in glyphs_of(font, only_selected) if g.width > limit]

metrics_rows and status_tally stay as loops. Put the new glyphs_of into widest_first.py from last week, run it, and check that its output hasn't changed by a character. That's the test from chapter 33 again: if you rewrote a function without changing what it does, its callers can't tell.

Mira goes back to Oskar's kerning script. The third line reads like a sentence now. The fourth line has two fors in one pair of brackets. She unfolds it on paper, as he told her to, and gets through it.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A list comprehension folds the make-a-list loop into one line: what you want, then where it comes from, then an optional if that filters. An if at the front needs an else and picks between two values without filtering. Curly brackets make a dictionary or a set the same way. Use a comprehension to build something you can describe in one breath, and go back to a loop when the line gets long, needs a box in the middle or changes the font.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Write each of these as one line, and check the count against a loop you trust: the names of all glyphs with no Unicode value; the widths of all glyphs whose names start with a capital letter (the test is in chapter 13); a set of all the marks used in the font, which is the listing from chapter 32 in a single line.

  2. Unfold this line of Oskar's into a loop, then say in words what pairs holds:

    pairs = [(name, name + ".sc") for name in names if name + ".sc" not in font_names]

  3. status_tally from chapter 33 builds a dictionary with a loop. Try to write it as a dictionary comprehension. You'll find that you can't, at least not with what you know. Say why. What does the loop do on each pass that a comprehension has no way to do?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Mira's scripts now call her own functions, which call Fly, which calls FontLab. When something breaks, the error message runs to eight lines and names more than one file. Chapter 38 reads one from end to end.

docs.title: 38. Read the traceback
docs.text:
Tuesday. On Monday evening Mira did exercise 1 of chapter 35. She added a fifth field to every row, the width of the black shape, and she was pleased with it. This morning she runs widest_first.py, and after the table the panel fills with a traceback:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 51, in <module>
  File "<string>", line 40, in report
  File "<string>", line 45, in print_lopsided
  File "<string>", line 33, in lopsided
ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 4)

In chapter 3 an error message was three lines long, and you learned to read the last one. This one has six lines and four line numbers. Mira's first instinct is to scroll to line 33 and stare at it, and line 33 is fine. It hasn't changed since Friday.

Error messages got longer when you started writing functions, and they got longer for a good reason. Today you learn to read all of one. It tells you a story if you read it in the right order.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • widest_first.py from chapter 36.
  • Step 1 below replaces it. Do it whether or not you did the exercise in chapter 35, so that your script matches mine line for line.

docs.title: Step 1: Break it the way Mira did
docs.text:
Replace widest_first.py with the listing below. It's the script as Mira has it this week. metrics_rows now gives each row a fifth field, the width of the black shape: the width gets a box of its own, and the append line uses it. She also split the printing into two functions so that each job has a name. I've left out the heading row and the check for an empty list, to keep today's trail short. Paste it exactly, blank lines included, so that the line numbers match mine.

#FLM: Widest First
# Prints the metrics of the selected glyphs, widest first.
from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

HOW_MANY = 3


def glyphs_of(font, only_selected=False):
    if not only_selected:
        return font.glyphs
    return [font[name] for name in scripting.names_selected_names()]


def metrics_rows(font, only_selected=False):
    rows = []
    for glyph in glyphs_of(font, only_selected):
        measured = pGlyph(font, glyph)
        if not measured.isEmpty():
            lsb = measured.getLSB()
            rsb = measured.getRSB()
            width = int(glyph.width)
            rows.append((glyph.name, lsb, width, rsb, width - lsb - rsb))
    return rows


def by_width(row):
    return row[2]


def lopsided(row):
    name, lsb, width, rsb = row
    return abs(lsb - rsb)


def report(rows):
    for name, lsb, width, rsb, black in sorted(rows, key=by_width, reverse=True):
        print(f"{name:<8}{lsb:>5}{width:>7}{rsb:>5}{black:>7}")
    print_lopsided(rows)


def print_lopsided(rows):
    print("Most lopsided:")
    for row in sorted(rows, key=lopsided, reverse=True)[:HOW_MANY]:
        print(f"  {row[0]:<6}{lopsided(row):>3}")


font = fl.CurrentFont()
rows = metrics_rows(font, only_selected=True)
report(rows)

She remembered to unpack five names in report. Select a few glyphs and run it. You get the table, the words Most lopsided:, and then the traceback from the top of this chapter. FontLab's Output panel may lay the lines out a little differently. The parts are the same.

docs.title: Step 2: The last line first
docs.text:
You already know this part. The last line is the complaint itself:

ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 4)

It has the kind of error, a colon and the detail. You met this exact message in chapter 35: a row had more items than there were boxes to put them in. Four boxes were waiting, so the row had five or more.

Always read this line first, and read all of it. It's tempting to see the word Error and start changing things. Often the last line is enough.

docs.title: Step 3: The lines above are a trail
docs.text:
Now the middle. Each line that begins with File is one step on the way to the accident, and they're in the order things happened. Read them from the top down:

  File "<string>", line 51, in <module>

"In the script you ran, at line 51, at the top level." <string> is the name you saw in chapter 3: it stands for the script in the Scripting panel's window. <module> means the line isn't inside any function. Line 51 is report(rows). So the script called report.

  File "<string>", line 40, in report

"In the same script, line 40, inside the function report." Line 40 is print_lopsided(rows). So report called print_lopsided.

  File "<string>", line 45, in print_lopsided

Line 45, inside print_lopsided. That's the sorted line with key=lopsided. So print_lopsided asked sorted to do its work, and sorted called the key function.

  File "<string>", line 33, in lopsided

"Line 33, inside the function lopsided." That's name, lsb, width, rsb = row, and that's where it fell over. Python doesn't print the line for you here, because <string> isn't a file on disk that it can read back. Count down in the Scripting panel's window, or turn on its line numbers if your version has them. Later in this chapter you'll see a trail through a file that is on disk, and there Python shows the line.

So the story reads: the script called report, which called print_lopsided, which had sorted call lopsided, and inside lopsided a row wouldn't fit into four boxes. Each function was waiting for the next one to finish when the last one failed. That chain of waiting functions is what the first line, Traceback (most recent call last), announces. It says the calls are listed in order, with the newest at the bottom.

In chapter 3 I called an error message a letter of complaint. A traceback is the same letter with the route on the envelope. Picture a relay team. The baton passes from runner to runner, and the fourth runner drops it. The traceback names all four in order, so that you can ask whether the fourth was clumsy or was handed a baton too slippery to hold.

docs.title: Step 4: Where it fell isn't where the mistake is
docs.text:
In this case the baton was slippery. Line 33 is the place where Python noticed the problem. It isn't the place where the problem was made.

Line 33 says "unpack a row into four boxes". That was correct on Friday and it's correct in itself today. What changed is the rows. metrics_rows now makes them with five fields. Mira changed the maker and forgot one of the users.

The traceback can't tell you that directly, because metrics_rows isn't in it. It ran and finished long before the error. It handed back a perfectly good list of rows with five fields, and by the time lopsided choked on one, metrics_rows was no longer waiting for anything. A traceback only lists the functions that were still in the middle of their work.

What the traceback does give you is the right question: where did this row come from? Walk the trail backward. lopsided got the row from sorted. sorted got its rows from print_lopsided, which got them from report, which got them from line 50 of the script: rows = metrics_rows(font, only_selected=True). That's the maker. Scroll up to it, and the fifth field is there to see on line 24.

You met this pattern in chapter 19, in a smaller form. A box was filled with None on one line, and the complaint came from a later line that tried to use it. "Don't stare at the line it points to. Look upward for the box that was filled with nothing." This is the same rule on a larger scale: when the line it points to looks innocent, follow the data back to where it was made.

The fix is one line in lopsided:

def lopsided(row):
    name, lsb, width, rsb, black = row
    return abs(lsb - rsb)

There's a habit that would have saved the morning, too. When you change what a function hands back, look for everybody who uses it before you run anything. In chapter 35, exercise 1 asked "which other lines of the script have to change?" Now you know why I asked.

docs.title: Step 5: Whose file is it?
docs.text:
Your scripts now stand on a stack of other people's work. Your functions call Fly's helpers, which call FontLab. When something fails low in the stack, the trail runs through files you didn't write. Close every font, and run these three lines:

import fly.ap.glyphs.names.model as names

facts = names.scan()

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 3, in <module>
  File "/Users/mira/.../site-packages/fontlabapp/glyphs/names/model.py", line 94, in scan
    raise ValueError("Open a font first.")
ValueError: Open a font first.

The trail has two steps. The first is yours: line 3 of your script. The second is in a file called model.py, deep in a folder you've never opened, and the line it shows begins with the word raise.

raise is how a piece of Python code makes an error on purpose. Somebody who wrote that helper thought about what should happen when no font is open, decided the helper couldn't go on, and wrote a line that stops with a message for you. So this isn't a crash. It's a refusal, and you've seen these before: Refused. in chapter 29, and the statuses in chapter 30.

The rule for a trail that runs through other people's files is simple. Find the last line of the trail that's in a file of yours. Start there.

The error was noticed in model.py, but model.py has been run by many people, and line 94 of it is doing exactly what its author meant. The newest thing in the whole stack is your script, written this morning. That's where to look first. What did line 3 ask for, and what was true at that moment? It asked for a scan, and no font was open.

Only when your own line is beyond suspicion is it worth reading the stranger's file. You're allowed to. The path is right there in the message, the file is plain Python, and reading the ten lines above a raise often tells you exactly what the helper wanted. But read your own line first.

docs.title: Step 6: Errors that come from FontLab
docs.text:
So far, every message has been Python's or a Python helper's. FontLab itself is not written in Python, and when you reach it directly, problems can look different. I haven't been able to run these on FontLab 9 for you, so take this step as a description of what to expect and not as a transcript.

Sometimes FontLab does what Python does and you get an ordinary traceback whose last line names a kind of error.

Sometimes the last line is a TypeError with a long list of what the call would have accepted. That means you put the wrong kind of thing in a slot of one of FontLab's own functions, and FontLab is showing you every way the function can be called. Read the first lines of it, find your call among them and compare the slots one by one.

And sometimes nothing is printed at all. The script runs to its end, no error appears, and the font hasn't changed. Chapter 14 showed you one cause: a misspelled drawer name on the left of an equals sign. Chapter 29 showed you another: a change made without telling FontLab's history, so that the windows didn't know to redraw. A script that fails without a message is harder to fix than one that prints twenty lines of traceback, because it gives you no trail to follow. That's a strong reason to prefer the helpers that refuse out loud.

If FontLab itself closes while a script runs, that isn't an error message, and it isn't your fault in the ordinary sense. Write down the last thing the script did and tell FontLab's support. Meanwhile, the font you saved before running the script is still on disk, and saving first was for exactly this.

docs.title: A field guide
docs.text:
You've now met most of the errors you'll see in a year of scripting. Here they are in one place, with what each usually means in a font script:

Last line starts with What it usually means First thing to check SyntaxError, IndentationError Python couldn't read the script, and nothing ran the line it names and the one above: a missing colon, bracket or quote, or crooked indents NameError a word Python doesn't know spelling, a missing import, or quotes left off a string ModuleNotFoundError import found no such file the file's name and its folder (chapter 33) AttributeError: 'NoneType' ... a box holds None where you expected an object where the box was filled: no font open, no glyph by that name, empty selection AttributeError: ... has no attribute no drawer by that name spelling and capitals; for your own module, a stale copy that needs a reload TypeError the wrong kind of thing, or the wrong number of things, in a slot count the slots; look for a string where a number belongs ValueError the right kind of thing with an unusable value unpacking counts; int("wide"); a helper's refusal, which says why KeyError a dictionary has no such key print the keys; use get with a fallback (chapter 22) IndexError a list is shorter than you thought print its len; an empty list has no [0] FileNotFoundError no file at that path print the path; is the font saved? (chapter 26) ZeroDivisionError you divided by zero a count that came out 0, often from an empty selection

Look how often an empty selection or a missing font turns up in the right-hand column. Most errors in font scripts aren't about Python at all. The script assumed the world was in a certain state and it wasn't. That's why chapter 19 taught you to check for a font at the top, and why chapter 36's script checked that rows wasn't empty before it printed anything.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A traceback is a trail of calls in the order they happened, and each File line names a file, a line number and the function that was waiting there. Read the last line first for the complaint, then the trail from the top for the story. The line where Python fell over often isn't where the mistake was made, so follow the data back to its maker. When the trail runs through other people's files, start at the last line that's in a file of yours.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. In widest_first.py, change HOW_MANY = 3 to HOW_MANY = "3", with quotes. Before you run it, predict the kind of error, and how many File lines the trail will have. Then run it and compare. Put the number back.
  2. In widest_first.py, change only_selected=True to only_selected=False. Close every font and run it. I expect a trail that ends inside glyphs_of with an AttributeError about NoneType, though I haven't seen FontLab print it. Read whatever you get aloud as a story, in the manner of Step 3: who called whom, and where did it fall? Then say where the fix belongs. It isn't in the line the trail ends on. Put True back.
  3. Put a print("start") as the first line of widest_first.py, below the #FLM: line. Take the colon off the end of any def line and run it. Does start print? Put the colon back. Now misspell lopsided as lopsidded in the sorted line of print_lopsided and run again. Does start print this time? Why the difference? Put the spelling back.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Mira's scripts refuse when something's wrong, and they print when something's right. What they can't do yet is ask. Chapter 39 puts a question on the screen and waits for the answer.

docs.title: 39. Ask before you act
docs.text:
Wednesday. The publisher has changed its mind again about the alternates, and this time Mira is at the dentist. Ines opens rename_suffix.py, looks at the two lines at the top that say OLD_SUFFIX = ".alt" and NEW_SUFFIX = ".ss01", looks at DRY_RUN = True, and closes it without touching anything. When Mira gets back there's a note on her keyboard: I don't open the hood. Can't it ask me?

It's a fair request. Until now, every script in this book has taken its orders from lines you edit before you run it. That's fine for the person who wrote the script. For anyone else, a script should ask its questions on the screen, in a small window with buttons, as every other program does.

Today's script asks three things: which suffix, what to change it to, and "Rename 4 glyphs?" It does nothing until the answer is Yes.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • rename_suffix.py from chapter 31.
  • An empty window in the Scripting panel for Steps 3 to 5. Save it as questions.py. Each step adds functions to the top and a test to the bottom.
  • The four glyphs that chapter 30 renamed: a.ss01, g.ss01, y.ss01 and ampersand.ss01. Today the publisher wants them to end in .ss02. When the finished script asks, type .ss01 over the first suggestion and .ss02 over the second, and the count in the last question will be 4. zero.alt is still in the font from chapter 31, and the script goes on leaving it alone.

I couldn't run these windows on FontLab 9 while writing this chapter. The calls are taken from the helper's own source and from scripts that use it, so I describe what the windows should look like, and I show no pictures of them.

docs.title: Step 1: Say something in a window
docs.text:
Start with the simplest window there is, one that says a thing and waits for you to click OK:

from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox

run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), "Halfmoon", "Hello, Ines.", "Information", box.Ok)

Run it. A small window should appear over FontLab with the words Hello, Ines. and an OK button. Nothing else in FontLab responds until you click it. Then the script goes on, and as this was its last line, it ends.

That call has six slots, which is a lot. Take them in order.

qt is new in the first line. It's another of Fly's short names, like fl. It stands for the kit of parts that FontLab's own windows are built from: buttons, text fields, checkboxes, whole windows. The helper needs to be handed the kit, so you pass it in the first slot.

fl.MainWindow() is FontLab's main window. The message window needs a parent, which is the window it belongs to and sits in front of. Give it the main window and it will appear over FontLab and not behind it.

Then there are two pieces of text. "Halfmoon" is the title of the small window, and "Hello, Ines." is the message. On a Mac the title may not be shown, so don't put anything important in it.

"Information" picks the little picture beside the message. The other words you can use here are "Question", "Warning" and "Critical".

And box.Ok says which buttons the window has. box is a short name I made on the line above for qt.QtGui.QMessageBox, which is the part of the kit that knows about message windows, and Ok is one of its drawers.

You typed all that to make a window say hello. In Step 3 we'll wrap it so you never have to type it again.

docs.title: Step 2: A question with two buttons
docs.text:
A message with one button tells. A message with two asks:

answer = run_standard_message_box(
    qt, fl.MainWindow(), "Halfmoon", "Rename 4 glyphs?", "Question", box.Yes | box.No
)

if answer == box.Yes:
    print("Renaming.")
else:
    print("Left alone.")

Two things changed. The buttons slot now holds box.Yes | box.No. The upright bar is the same sign that joined two sets in chapter 25. Here it joins two buttons into one value that means "both of these".

And this time we catch what the function hands back. When you click a button, the window closes and the call returns a value that says which one. Compare it with box.Yes to find out.

Run it twice, and click a different button each time.

Renaming.

Left alone.

There's a trap here that prints no error, so I'll warn you about it now. It's tempting to write this:

if answer:
    print("Renaming.")

Chapter 31 taught you that if accepts anything and treats empty things and zero as false. But the answer isn't True or False. It's a code for a button, and the code for No isn't zero either. So if answer: is true whichever button was clicked, and the script would rename the glyphs when Ines said No. Always compare the answer with the button you mean.

Notice also what the else covers. It runs for No, and it also runs for anything else that might come back, such as the window being closed with the Esc key. That's deliberate. Only an explicit Yes changes the font, and everything else leaves it alone. Write your questions so that the safe thing happens by default. It's the idea behind DRY_RUN again.

docs.title: Step 3: Wrap it once
docs.text:
Nobody wants to type six slots every time they ask a question. You know what to do about that: a function. Start questions.py with these lines:

from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box, run_text_dialog

TITLE = "Halfmoon Type"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes

Look at the last line of ask. The comparison answer == box.Yes is itself a value, True or False, as chapter 13 said, so the function can hand it straight back. All the business with button codes stays inside the function. From outside, ask takes a question and returns a yes or a no. Below the functions, the script can now say:

if ask("Rename 4 glyphs?"):
    print("Renaming.")

That reads almost like the note on Mira's keyboard, and now if on the answer is safe, because ask really does return True or False. The trap from Step 2 is dealt with in one place, and no script that uses ask can fall into it.

This is the best use of a function that I know. You find something awkward, you get it right once with care, and you give it a plain name. After that you use the plain name, and when a script needs it you paste the same few lines in. Chapter 40 keeps a clean copy of them for exactly that.

docs.title: Step 4: Ask for a word
docs.text:
A yes or a no won't tell the script which suffix. For that you need a window with a text field. Add this below ask:

def ask_text(label, start=""):
    return run_text_dialog(qt.QtGui, label, start, TITLE)

run_text_dialog takes the kit, the label beside the field, the text that's in the field to begin with, and the window's title. It returns what the person typed. Try it:

old = ask_text("Suffix to replace:", ".alt")
print(old)

A window should appear with a field that already contains .alt. Click OK and you get:

.alt

Giving the field a sensible starting value is a kindness. Most of the time Ines will only have to press Enter.

Now tidy up what comes back, because people type spaces by accident. Chapter 27 has the tool for that. Replace the test lines at the bottom of questions.py with this one:

old = ask_text("Suffix to replace:", ".alt").strip()

Run it, and this time click Cancel.

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 24, in <module>
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'strip'

Read it as chapter 38 taught you, last line first. Something was None, and the script asked it to strip. The trail has one step, and it's in your script. So what on that line could be None? It can only be whatever ask_text handed back.

That's how the helper reports a Cancel. When the person clicks OK, it returns the text, and an empty field gives an empty string "". When the person clicks Cancel, there's no text to return, so it returns None. It's the same signal font["Nope"] gave you in chapter 19, and it needs the same care: check for None before you do anything with the answer.

old = ask_text("Suffix to replace:", ".alt")
if old is None:
    print("Cancelled.")
else:
    old = old.strip()
    print("Replacing", old)

A person who clicks Cancel is telling you something clear, and the script should stop and change nothing. If it shows a traceback at that point, or carries on with a guess, it has got that wrong.

docs.title: Step 5: Choose a file
docs.text:
The third kind of question is "which file?" Every program you use asks it the same way, with the system's own file window, and your scripts can too. In chapter 27 the glyph list had to be called smallcaps.txt and sit next to the font. Now Ines can pick any list from anywhere.

Add one more import and two more functions. The import goes at the top with the others, the functions below ask_text:

from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_file_dialog


def text_files_only(kind, dialog):
    dialog.setNameFilters(["Text files (*.txt)"])


def choose_text_file(caption, folder=""):
    paths = run_file_dialog(qt.QtGui, text_files_only, caption, folder)
    if paths is None:
        return None
    return paths[0]

run_file_dialog wants the kit, then a function, then the caption for the window and the folder to start in. The function in the second slot is a recipe card, as in chapter 29. The helper makes the file window, and before it shows the window it calls your function and hands it two things: the part of the kit that knows about file windows, and the window itself. Your function gets one chance to set the window up. Ours tells it to show only files that end in .txt. It doesn't use kind at all, but the slot has to be there because the helper fills it.

The helper returns a list of paths, because a file window can allow several files to be picked, or None for Cancel. We want one file, so choose_text_file hands back the first item and passes a None along untouched.

from pathlib import Path

font = fl.CurrentFont()
folder = str(Path(font.path).parent)
path = choose_text_file("Choose a glyph list", folder)
if path is not None:
    print(Path(path).name)

smallcaps.txt

What comes back is a string that holds the full path. Wrap it in Path(...) and you have everything chapter 26 taught you about paths.

Chapter 26 said a Save dialog would come. Here's that other file window, the one that asks where to save. It's the same helper with a different recipe card, and this card does use kind:

def for_saving(kind, dialog):
    dialog.setAcceptMode(kind.AcceptSave)
    dialog.setNameFilters(["Text files (*.txt)"])


def choose_save_file(caption, folder=""):
    paths = run_file_dialog(qt.QtGui, for_saving, caption, folder)
    if paths is None:
        return None
    return paths[0]

setAcceptMode(kind.AcceptSave) turns the window into a Save window, with a field for typing a new name. Choosing a path doesn't write anything. It only gives your script a path, and the with open(...) lines from chapter 26 do the writing.

docs.title: When not to ask
docs.text:
Now that you know how to put up a window, you'll want to put up a lot of them. Hold back.

A script that asks five questions in a row is worse than one with five lines to edit. Ask only what changes from one run to the next, and give each field a good starting value. Things that never change belong at the top of the script as constants.

Never ask inside a loop. "Rename a.alt? Rename g.alt? Rename y.alt?" is how you train a person to click Yes without reading. Show the whole plan and ask once.

Don't confirm things that are harmless. A report needs no "Are you sure?" Keep the question for the moment before a script changes the font or writes over a file.

And these windows stop everything else. While one is open, Ines can't click on the font to check something. For a quick question that's right. For a tool that someone keeps open and uses all afternoon, you want a small panel that sits beside the font and stays out of the way. That's a larger piece of building, and Part 7 is where we do it.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is ask_first.py. It's rename_suffix.py from chapter 31 with the two suffixes and the dry-run switch replaced by three questions. It carries its own tell, ask and ask_text, copied from Steps 3 and 4, so it runs by itself:

#FLM: Rename Suffix
# Renames glyphs from one suffix to another, after asking.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.glyphs.names.model as names
from fly.ap.glyphs.identity_tools.glyph_identity.batch_rename import (
    plan_renames,
    apply_renames,
)
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box, run_text_dialog

TITLE = "Halfmoon Type"
SKIP = {"zero.alt"}


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def ask_text(label, start=""):
    return run_text_dialog(qt.QtGui, label, start, TITLE)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return

    old = ask_text("Suffix to replace:", ".alt")
    if old is None:
        return
    new = ask_text("Replace it with:", ".ss01")
    if new is None:
        return
    old = old.strip()
    new = new.strip()
    if not old:
        tell("Type the suffix to replace.")
        return

    pairs = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if glyph.name.endswith(old) and glyph.name not in SKIP:
            pairs.append([glyph.name, glyph.name.removesuffix(old) + new])

    if not pairs:
        tell(f"No glyph name ends in {old}.")
        return

    facts = names.scan()
    problems = 0
    for before, after, status in plan_renames(facts, pairs):
        print(f"{before:<18}{after:<18}{status}")
        if status != "ok":
            problems += 1

    if problems > 0:
        tell(f"{problems} of {len(pairs)} renames can't be done. The list is in the Output panel.")
        return

    if not ask(f"Rename {len(pairs)} glyphs from {old} to {new}?"):
        return

    done = apply_renames(None, qt.QtCore, facts.package_id, pairs)
    tell(f"Renamed {len(done)} glyphs. Edit > Undo takes it back in one step.")


main()

It has the same four parts as before: collect, plan, show, apply. What changed is where the orders come from and where the news goes.

Count the returns. There are seven ways out of this script before it touches the font, and only one way through: a font is open, two questions were answered, something matched, every status is ok, and somebody clicked Yes. Chapter 19 called these guard clauses, and a script that other people will run needs plenty of them.

Notice what it still prints. The plan goes to the Output panel and not into a window, because twenty rows of names don't belong in a message box. A window is for one sentence and a decision. Anything you'd want to read slowly, copy or keep belongs in the Output panel or a file.

And notice the final message. It says what happened, in numbers, and it says how to take it back.

Look at the guard after the two strip lines. Every name ends with the empty string, so an empty answer would have asked to rename the whole font. SKIP stays at the top, because it never changes from one run to the next.

Save it as Rename Suffix.py in the Halfmoon folder inside Scripts, and choose Scripts > Refresh Scripts. Its first line gives it its name in the menu. Ines runs it that afternoon without opening anything.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A message box tells or asks in a small window, and its answer is a button code that you compare with the button you mean. A text dialog returns what was typed, a file dialog returns a list of paths, and both return None for Cancel, which you check before anything else. The awkward calls go in a function once, behind plain names like ask, tell and ask_text, and the script carries the functions it uses. Ask once, right before the change, and let anything but Yes leave the font alone.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add warn(text) to ask_first.py. It's tell with "Warning" in the picture slot. Use it in ask_first.py for the message about renames that can't be done.
  2. Write ask_number(label, start) in questions.py. It calls ask_text, hands a None straight back, and otherwise returns int(...) of the text. Then type fifteen into its window and read the traceback. Chapter 19 showed you try and except in one simple form. Use it so that a word in place of a number makes ask_number return None as well. Then paste it, with ask_text, into safe_edit.py from chapter 29, so that Ines can type her own amount.
  3. Change read_glyph_list.py from chapter 27 so that it calls choose_text_file in place of the fixed name. Paste in text_files_only and choose_text_file from Step 5, with the imports they need. What should the script do if the answer is None? What if the chosen file turns out to be empty?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: It's Friday again, and Ines wants to know what seven weeks of this have bought the studio. Chapter 40 puts the toolbox on the table and counts.

docs.title: 40. The toolbox so far
docs.text:
Friday of the seventh week, four in the afternoon. Ines has a pad of paper and a question she asks about everything the studio spends time on: what did it buy?

Mira has an answer ready, and it's a list. Before she reads it out, though, there's one debt left from chapter 27. Back then Ines asked whether a script could make the seven missing small-cap glyphs, and I said that changing a font takes care, and the care started in chapter 29. You've had eleven chapters of it since. Today you'll write that script.

There's almost no new Python in this chapter: one conversion, tuple(...), which turns a list into a tuple. As at the end of Part 1, the work is putting together things you know. This one script uses a file from chapter 27, a set from chapter 25, a comprehension from chapter 37, a question from chapter 39 and the safety habits of chapters 29 to 31. If you can follow it, you've got Part 2.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open in the Font window.
  • The window helpers from chapter 39. They're repeated below, so you don't need the old scripts.
  • smallcaps.txt from chapter 27, in your scripting-book folder.
  • Save the font before you start. This script adds glyphs.

docs.title: Step 1: Make the reader a function
docs.text:
In chapter 27 you wrote the lines that read a list of names from a file: open it, strip each line, and skip blanks and the lines that start with #. A second script needs them now, so give them a name. Start the new script, add_from_list.py, with this function:

def read_names(path):
    names = []
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            name = line.strip()
            if name and not name.startswith("#"):
                names.append(name)
    return names

The test if name and not name.startswith("#") reads "if there's anything left and it isn't a note". An empty string counts as false, as chapter 31 said, so the blank lines drop out.

I haven't folded this into a comprehension. You could, but the line needs a box, name, to hold the stripped text that's used twice. Chapter 37's rule says that's a job for a loop.

docs.title: Step 2: Work out what's missing
docs.text:
Add these lines to add_from_list.py. The imports go at the top, the rest below read_names:

from pathlib import Path
from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
wanted = read_names(Path(font.path).parent / "smallcaps.txt")

have = {glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs}
to_make = [name for name in wanted if name not in have]

print(len(wanted), "wanted,", len(to_make), "to make:")
print(" ".join(to_make))

10 wanted, 7 to make:
d.sc e.sc f.sc g.sc h.sc zero.sc one.sc

There are two comprehensions here, and each does one job. have is a set of every name in the font. I made it a set because the only thing we'll ask of it is "is this name in there?", and chapter 25 showed that a set answers that fastest. to_make is a list and not a set, because the order of the art director's file is worth keeping: the glyphs will be added in the order she wrote them.

If you did exercise 3 of chapter 20 and made a d.sc, you'll see six to make. The script has noticed that it's there.

docs.title: Step 3: Describe the new glyphs
docs.text:
Fly has a helper that adds glyphs the way FontLab's own Font > New Glyph… command does, so that each one can be undone. It doesn't take bare names. It wants a small description of each glyph: its name and, for every master, the advance width the empty glyph should start with.

from fly.ap.glyphs.creation import NewGlyph, create_glyphs

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
WIDTH = 500

layers = tuple([(master, WIDTH) for master in MASTERS])
print(layers)

specs = [NewGlyph(name, layers) for name in to_make]
print(len(specs))

(('Light', 500), ('Regular', 500), ('Bold', 500))
7

layers is a tuple of pairs, one pair for each master: the master's name and a width. It's the rows-of-fields shape from chapter 35. The helper asks for a tuple here and not a list, so tuple(...) converts one.

NewGlyph(name, layers) makes one description. It's a filled-in form that says "a glyph called d.sc, 500 units wide in each of three masters", and nothing has been added to the font yet. The second comprehension fills in seven forms.

I've typed the three master names as a constant. That's honest for now, since this is Plum and Plum has those three, but a script that only works on one font isn't finished. Part 6 shows you how to ask a font for its masters. The width of 500 is a placeholder too. Mira will set real widths when she draws the glyphs.

docs.title: Step 4: Hand the forms over
docs.text:
The call that does the work needs four things: the font in the form FontLab's history knows it, the list of forms, a title, and a fresh set of facts for the safety checks. You met the first and the last in chapter 29.

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history

package = scripting.current_package()
facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)

made = create_glyphs(package, specs, "Add glyphs from list", facts)
print(len(made.glyphs), "glyphs added")

Before you run it, open smallcaps.txt and add d.sc a second time at the bottom, as you did with a.sc in exercise 1 of chapter 27. Now run the script.

ValueError: Refused: d.sc is listed twice.

The traceback above that line runs through a file called creation.py. Chapter 38 told you what to do with it: the last line is a refusal that somebody wrote on purpose, and the last step of the trail that's yours is the create_glyphs line. The helper looked through all the forms before it touched the font, found the same name twice, and stopped. Look at the Font window. Nothing has been added, including the six glyphs that were fine. It's the all-or-nothing rule from chapter 31, and here the helper enforces it for you.

You could fix the file. But the art director's files will always have such things in them, and the right place to cope is the reader. Change one line of read_names:

            if name and not name.startswith("#") and name not in names:
                names.append(name)

Now a name that's already in the list is skipped. Run the script again.

7 glyphs added

Scroll to the end of the Font window. There should be seven new empty cells, d.sc to one.sc, in the order of the file. In chapter 29 one run was one Undo step. This helper is different. Fly's source says it records each new glyph as its own step, so taking all seven back means seven undos. I haven't watched it do so. The quick way back is File > Revert Font, and that's why you saved first.

The helper refuses in two other cases that you should know about. If any name in the list already exists in the font, it says Refused: a.sc exists now. Check the list again. Our script can't trip that one, because to_make leaves those names out. And if you run the script while a Glyph window is the active window, it asks you to switch to the Font window first, for the same reason as in chapter 29.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Wrap it in main, add the guards and the questions, and give it a menu name. The script carries tell, ask and choose_text_file from chapter 39 and the finished read_names from Step 4, so it runs by itself:

#FLM: Add Glyphs From List
# Adds an empty glyph for every name in a text file
# that the current font doesn't have yet.
from pathlib import Path
from fly import fl
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
from fly.ap.glyphs.creation import NewGlyph, create_glyphs
from fly import qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box, run_file_dialog

TITLE = "Halfmoon Type"
MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
WIDTH = 500


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def text_files_only(kind, dialog):
    dialog.setNameFilters(["Text files (*.txt)"])


def choose_text_file(caption, folder=""):
    paths = run_file_dialog(qt.QtGui, text_files_only, caption, folder)
    if paths is None:
        return None
    return paths[0]


def read_names(path):
    names = []
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            name = line.strip()
            if name and not name.startswith("#") and name not in names:
                names.append(name)
    return names


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return

    folder = Path(font.path).parent if font.path else ""
    path = choose_text_file("Choose a glyph list", folder)
    if path is None:
        return

    wanted = read_names(path)
    have = {glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs}
    to_make = [name for name in wanted if name not in have]
    if not to_make:
        tell(f"All {len(wanted)} glyphs in the list are in the font already.")
        return

    print(f"{len(wanted)} wanted, {len(to_make)} to make:")
    print(" ".join(to_make))
    if not ask(f"Add {len(to_make)} empty glyphs, {WIDTH} units wide?"):
        return

    layers = tuple([(master, WIDTH) for master in MASTERS])
    specs = [NewGlyph(name, layers) for name in to_make]
    package = scripting.current_package()
    made = create_glyphs(package, specs, "Add glyphs from list", history.scan_auto_facts(package))
    tell(f"Added {len(made.glyphs)} glyphs. Each one is its own Undo step.")


main()

One line is new in form. folder = Path(font.path).parent if font.path else "" uses the value-with-a-choice from chapter 37: the font's folder if the font has been saved, and otherwise an empty string, which lets the file window open wherever it likes. That's the unsaved-font guard chapter 26 left you as an exercise.

Save it as Add Glyphs From List.py in Scripts/Halfmoon/. The collecting part is three lines long, and the rest is questions, guards and news. That proportion is normal for a script other people will run. About thirty of its lines are the helpers at the top, and they're the same lines every time. That's why you want a clean copy of them to paste from, which is the second thing Mira reads out.

docs.title: What's in the box
docs.text:
Here's what Mira reads out to Ines. First, the menu. These are in Scripts/Halfmoon/, and anyone in the studio can run them without opening a file:

Command What it does Changes the font? Inventory counts glyphs, empty glyphs, Unicode values and small caps no Friday Report prints the week's numbers and saves them in reports no Widest First lists metrics of the selected glyphs and the most lopsided no Rename Suffix renames one suffix to another, after asking yes, one Undo step Add Glyphs From List adds empty glyphs named in a text file, after asking yes, one Undo step each

Look at the third column. Three of the five can't hurt anything. The two that change the font ask first, check before they act, and say how to take the change back. You can now see chapters 29 to 31 and chapter 39 as one lesson spread over four days.

Second, the helpers. They aren't in a module, because a script that imports a file of yours only runs on a machine that has the file, as Ines found in chapter 33. They're a set of snippets, kept in one text file, snippets.py, in your scripting-book folder. You never import it. When a script needs a helper, you copy the block it's in, with its imports, and paste it at the top of the script. Each block below runs by itself.

The colours and the tally, from chapters 32 and 33:

from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

RED = 1
YELLOW = 61
GREEN = 121

LEGEND = {
    0: "untouched",
    RED: "not-drawn",
    YELLOW: "needs-work",
    GREEN: "done",
}


def status_tally(font):
    tally = {}
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        status = LEGEND.get(pGlyph(font, glyph).mark, "unknown-color")
        tally[status] = tally.get(status, 0) + 1
    return tally

Glyph questions, from chapters 33, 34 and 37:

from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting


def is_empty(font, glyph):
    return pGlyph(font, glyph).isEmpty()


def glyphs_of(font, only_selected=False):
    if not only_selected:
        return font.glyphs
    return [font[name] for name in scripting.names_selected_names()]


def widest_glyph(font, only_selected=False):
    widest = None
    for glyph in glyphs_of(font, only_selected):
        if widest is None or glyph.width > widest.width:
            widest = glyph
    return widest


def wider_than(font, limit=700, only_selected=False):
    return [g.name for g in glyphs_of(font, only_selected) if g.width > limit]

Tables, from chapters 35 and 36. These need pGlyph and glyphs_of from the block above:

def metrics_rows(font, only_selected=False):
    rows = []
    for glyph in glyphs_of(font, only_selected):
        measured = pGlyph(font, glyph)
        if not measured.isEmpty():
            rows.append((glyph.name, measured.getLSB(), int(glyph.width), measured.getRSB()))
    return rows


def by_width(row):
    return row[2]


def lopsided(row):
    name, lsb, width, rsb = row
    return abs(lsb - rsb)

Files, from chapter 27 and today:

def read_names(path):
    names = []
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            name = line.strip()
            if name and not name.startswith("#") and name not in names:
                names.append(name)
    return names

Windows, from chapter 39:

from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box, run_text_dialog, run_file_dialog

TITLE = "Halfmoon Type"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def ask_text(label, start=""):
    return run_text_dialog(qt.QtGui, label, start, TITLE)


def text_files_only(kind, dialog):
    dialog.setNameFilters(["Text files (*.txt)"])


def choose_text_file(caption, folder=""):
    paths = run_file_dialog(qt.QtGui, text_files_only, caption, folder)
    if paths is None:
        return None
    return paths[0]


def for_saving(kind, dialog):
    dialog.setAcceptMode(kind.AcceptSave)
    dialog.setNameFilters(["Text files (*.txt)"])


def choose_save_file(caption, folder=""):
    paths = run_file_dialog(qt.QtGui, for_saving, caption, folder)
    if paths is None:
        return None
    return paths[0]

glyphs_of and wider_than are the one-line versions from chapter 37. They do the same as the loops in chapter 34.

That's about twenty names. Every one is a thing Mira got wrong at least once before she got it right. Now she pastes the right version, and the wrong one doesn't come back.

Third, the Python. In Part 1 you learned to say things to a font one glyph at a time. In Part 2 you learned to keep what it answers and to work with other people's material. Dictionaries look things up and count them, and sets compare (chapters 21 to 25). Text files go in and out, and tables go to a spreadsheet (26 to 28). Changes can be undone, plans come before changes and switches default to safe (29 to 31). Constants, modules and functions with defaults keep the scripts short (32 to 34). Rows, sorting and one-line lists shape the answers (35 to 37). And you can read a long error from end to end and ask a person a question (38 and 39).

Ines writes for a while. Mira's own guess is that the Friday numbers used to take her most of an hour and now take a minute, and that the two renaming afternoons in week five would each be ten minutes today. Ines doesn't write down a total. She writes: Mira's chores no longer depend on Mira. Then she underlines "Inventory", which she ran herself on Tuesday on a font Mira has never opened.

docs.title: Where you are
docs.text:
Get out Oskar's sheet. It hasn't moved since chapter 20. Four lines are crossed out and seven are left:

  • List the glyphs that are built from other glyphs.
  • Mark every glyph that mixes its own outlines with borrowed ones.
  • Make the left sidebearing of the d, q and g match the o.
  • Rebuild the accented letters from the base letters and the accents.
  • Find kerning pairs that are larger than they should be.
  • Put the right family name and version number into every weight.
  • Export the whole family to a dated folder every Friday.

Part 2 crossed out none of them, and that's as it should be. The chores of these four weeks came from Ines, Tomas and the publisher. They were all about names, numbers and lists, the outside of a glyph. Every line left on the sheet is about what's inside one: outlines, borrowed shapes, sidebearings measured against other shapes, accents sitting on letters.

So far a glyph has been a name, a Unicode value, a width with its two sidebearings, a color and a tag. You've asked whether it's empty, and that's the only question you've asked about what's drawn in it. In Part 3 you'll look at the drawing.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A script that other people run is mostly guards, questions and news around a few lines of work, and a set of snippets keeps you from writing those twice.
