Adding glyphs goes through a helper that takes a description of each one, checks the whole list before it touches the font, and records each addition so that it can be undone. When a helper refuses a list, it's usually better to fix the code that makes the list than to fix the file.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Give each new glyph the width of its parent instead of 500: d.sc gets the width of d, and zero.sc the width of zero. You'll need split from chapter 9, a lookup like the one in chapter 21, and a decision about what to do when the parent isn't in the font. Use the same width in all three masters for now.
  2. Add a sixth command to the menu: Status Report, which pastes in the colours-and-tally snippet and prints status_tally(font) sorted by count, largest first, as chapter 36 showed. It's a script of about ten lines. Does it need to ask anything? Does it need a guard?
  3. Go through the scripts in your scripting-book folder from Part 1 and pick one that still has its own copy of is_empty or its own loop for the widest glyph. Replace that copy with the snippet from this chapter, and check that its output hasn't changed. Did the old copy differ from the snippet? Where?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Part 3 opens with a glyph window and a single letter. Chapter 41 asks the o what it's made of, and the answer is two closed outlines and a count of points.

docs.title: Part 3: Shapes
docs.text:
An outline is points, and the lines between them.

The client wants more letters.

Halfmoon's publisher is planning Polish and Czech editions, and Plum can't set them yet. Before Mira can add a letter with a script, she has to know what a letter is made of. So this part opens a glyph and looks inside: contours, nodes, handles, and the glyphs that are built from other glyphs.

Then you draw. You make a box with a pen, a circle with curves and a row of dots with a loop. You move, scale and copy outlines. In the second half you take components and anchors apart, and build accented letters from a list of recipes.

Oskar's sheet has eleven lines. Four were crossed out by the end of Part 2:

  • Count the glyphs and tell Ines.
  • Find the glyphs that are still empty.
  • Make a table of every glyph and its width.
  • When the small caps come: list every glyph whose name ends in .sc.

Seven are open, and this part does the first two and the fourth of them:

  • List the glyphs that are built from other glyphs.
  • Mark every glyph that mixes its own outlines with borrowed ones.
  • Make the left sidebearing of the d, q and g match the o.
  • Rebuild the accented letters from the base letters and the accents.
  • Find kerning pairs that are larger than they should be.
  • Put the right family name and version number into every weight.
  • Export the whole family to a dated folder every Friday.

You need the practice copy of Plum and Fly installed in FontLab 9. Each script in this part runs by itself: any helper it needs is written out in the chapter, even when you met it earlier.

docs.title: 41. Inside a glyph
docs.text:
Monday of the eighth week. Mira has Oskar's sheet in front of her and reads the first line that isn't crossed out: List the glyphs that are built from other glyphs. She knows what it means as a designer. The é in Plum isn't drawn. It's an e and an acute accent, borrowed and put together. What she doesn't know is how a script would tell.

For seven weeks her scripts have treated a glyph like a parcel. They've read the label: the name, the Unicode value, the width, the color. Once, in chapter 8, they shook the parcel to hear whether it was empty. They've never opened it.

Today you'll open one. Double-click the o in the Font window, so that it fills a Glyph window, and look at it for a moment as a designer does. There's an outer oval and an inner oval, with small squares and circles sitting on them. Now let's find out what a script sees.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and Plum-practice open.
  • The o open in a Glyph window, with the Regular master showing.
  • Nothing else. The scripts in this chapter only read.

The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel. The calls come from the helpers' source.

docs.title: Step 1: Which drawing?
docs.text:
In chapter 29 you met the box that holds the glyph you're working on:

from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

glyph = pGlyph()
layer = glyph.activeLayer()
print(glyph.name, layer.name)

o Regular

pGlyph() with empty parentheses means "the glyph in the window I'm looking at". And activeLayer() hands you the layer that's showing.

It's time to say properly what a layer is. Plum comes in three weights, and so every glyph in it is drawn three times: a light o, a regular o and a bold o. Each of those drawings is a layer, and it carries the name of its master. All three live under the one name o. When you asked for glyph.width in Part 1, you were getting the width of one of them.

So "what's inside the glyph?" means "what's inside this layer of the glyph?" Every outline you read, from here to the end of Part 3, belongs to one layer. For now it's the one on your screen.

docs.title: Step 2: Contours
docs.text:
Ask the glyph for its contours:

contours = glyph.contours()
print(len(contours))

2

A contour is one closed line, the kind you could trace with a pencil without lifting it, ending where you began. The o has two: the outer oval and the inner one. What's black on the page is the space between them. contours is an ordinary list, so everything you know about lists works on it.

Be careful with the parentheses. Leave them off and see what happens:

print(len(glyph.contours))

TypeError: object of type 'method' has no len()

glyph.name has no parentheses, because it's a drawer with a value in it. glyph.contours() has them, because it's an action: go and collect the contours. Without the parentheses you're holding the action itself and not its result. That's the "function is a value" idea from chapter 36, and here it gets in your way. Python's complaint is exact: the thing you gave to len is a method, which is its word for a function that lives in an object's drawer, and a method has no length.

There's no rule that tells you which names want parentheses. This box, pGlyph, mostly wants them: contours(), activeLayer(), getLSB(). The plain glyph from font.glyphs mostly doesn't. When you get an error that mentions 'method', add the parentheses.

Now ask each contour two things:

for contour in contours:
    print(contour.closed, len(contour.nodes()))

True 12
True 12

closed is True when the line comes back to where it started. In a finished font every contour should be closed, and chapter 44 goes looking for the ones that aren't.

nodes() hands you the contour's points as a list, and it wants parentheses too. Each oval has twelve.

Look at the outer oval in the Glyph window and count the points that sit on the line. There are four: bottom, right, top and left. The script says twelve. Hold that thought until Step 3.

docs.title: Step 3: Nodes
docs.text:
Take the first contour and walk its nodes:

outer = contours[0]
for node in outer.nodes():
    print(f"{node.x:>5.0f}{node.y:>5.0f}")

  260  -10
  396  -10
  482   90
  482  239
  482  388
  396  488
  260  488
  124  488
   38  388
   38  239
   38   90
  124  -10

Each node is a point with two numbers. x is how far it is from the left edge of the glyph's space, and y is how far it is above the baseline. Both are in font units, the same units as the width. A negative y is below the baseline.

Read the list against the picture. The first node is at 260, −10: the bottom of the oval, a little below the baseline. The fourth is at 482, 239, which is the right side. The seventh, 260, 488, is the top. The tenth, 38, 239, is the left. Those are the four points you counted, and the list goes around the oval from one to the next.

The other eight are in between, two after each of the four. Look at 396, −10 and 482, 90. Neither is on the oval. In the Glyph window they're the small handles that stick out from a point when you click on it, the ones you drag to change how the curve bends. A script sees them as nodes like any other. So a simple round shape is four points on the line and eight handles off it, twelve in all.

Chapter 42 teaches the script to tell the two kinds apart. For today, a node is a node.

One more thing in that listing. The :>5.0f in the braces is from chapter 12: five characters of room, pushed right, no decimals. I used it because these numbers are the kind with a decimal point, and without the note you'd see 260.0 and -10.0.

docs.title: Step 4: A loop inside a loop
docs.text:
You've walked the contours, and you've walked the nodes of one contour. To see everything, do the second walk inside the first:

for contour in glyph.contours():
    print("contour")
    for node in contour.nodes():
        print(f"  {node.x:>5.0f}{node.y:>5.0f}")

contour
    260  -10
    396  -10
    482   90

And so on, for twenty-six lines: the word contour, twelve nodes, the word again, twelve more.

This is a nested loop, one loop inside another. Read the indentation as chapter 7 taught you. The second for is indented once, so it belongs to the first loop and runs once for each contour. The print under it is indented twice, so it belongs to the second loop and runs once for each node of the contour that the first loop is holding at that moment.

Here's a picture for it. The outer loop is the hour hand of a clock and the inner loop is the minute hand. The minute hand goes all the way round, and only then does the hour hand move one place. Then the minute hand goes all the way round again.

Nested loops have one classic mistake, and I'd like you to make it now. Let's count the nodes in each contour by hand, with a counter as in chapter 7:

count = 0
for contour in glyph.contours():
    for node in contour.nodes():
        count = count + 1
    print("nodes:", count)

nodes: 12
nodes: 24

There's no error. The first line is right and the second is wrong, because the second contour has twelve nodes and not twenty-four. The counter was set to zero once, before everything, so it never started again for the second contour. It kept running.

Where a line sits decides how often it happens. count = 0 sits outside both loops, so it happens once. Move it inside the outer loop:

for contour in glyph.contours():
    count = 0
    for node in contour.nodes():
        count = count + 1
    print("nodes:", count)

nodes: 12
nodes: 12

Now it's set to zero once for each contour. With one loop a line can be in two places, before the loop or inside it. With two loops there are three places, and you have to decide which one you mean for every line. When a nested loop gives a wrong number and no error, check where the counters are set to zero before you check anything else.

You didn't need the counter, since len(contour.nodes()) already told you. I used it because the mistake is easier to see on something small.

docs.title: Step 5: Elements
docs.text:
There's one level I skipped. Between the layer and its contours sits another kind of object, which FontLab calls an element. An element is a group of contours that belong together and can be moved, scaled or reused as one thing. The layer holds elements, and each element holds contours.

print(len(layer.shapes))

1

The drawer is called shapes, which was FontLab's older word for elements, and the name stuck in scripts. The o has one element, and both ovals are in it. Most glyphs in Plum are like that. When you asked for glyph.contours(), the box went through the elements for you and handed back the contours in one flat list. That's why you could ignore elements until now.

They matter today for one reason. Go back to the Font window, double-click eacute, and run this:

glyph = pGlyph()
layer = glyph.activeLayer()
print(glyph.name, len(layer.shapes), len(glyph.contours()))

eacute 2 0

It has two elements and no contours. The é has nothing drawn in it. Its two elements aren't groups of contours at all. Each one is a pointer to another glyph, one to e and one to acute, and each says "draw that one here". FontLab calls such an element a component.

That's the answer to Mira's question, or the start of it. Most glyphs built from other glyphs have elements but no contours of their own. Chapter 52 takes components apart properly and finds the exceptions, and Oskar's line gets crossed out there. First you need to be at home with ordinary outlines, and that's the next ten chapters.

So the whole address of a point in a font has five parts, like a postal address read from the bottom up: font, glyph, layer, element and contour. The node comes last, as the name on the envelope. You'll rarely write all five. The boxes take shortcuts for you, as glyph.contours() does.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here's anatomy.py. It describes whatever glyph is in front of you:

# Describes the outline of the current glyph, in the layer that's showing.
# Reads only.
from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph


def main():
    if fl.CurrentGlyph() is None:
        print("Open a glyph first.")
        return

    glyph = pGlyph()
    layer = glyph.activeLayer()
    print(f"{glyph.name}, layer {layer.name}")
    print(f"  elements: {len(layer.shapes)}")

    number = 0
    total = 0
    for contour in glyph.contours():
        number = number + 1
        nodes = contour.nodes()
        total = total + len(nodes)
        state = "closed" if contour.closed else "open"
        print(f"  contour {number}: {state}, {len(nodes)} nodes")

    print(f"  total: {number} contours, {total} nodes")


main()

With the o in front:

o, layer Regular
  elements: 1
  contour 1: closed, 12 nodes
  contour 2: closed, 12 nodes
  total: 2 contours, 24 nodes

With the n:

n, layer Regular
  elements: 1
  contour 1: closed, 20 nodes
  total: 1 contours, 20 nodes

Look at where the two counters are set to zero. number and total both describe the whole glyph, so both are set once, before the loop. That's the right place for them here, and it was the wrong place for count in Step 4. What matters is what the counter counts.

This script has only one loop. len(nodes) does the inner walk for us, which is usually the better choice when all you want is how many. You'll write the inner loop out when you need to look at each node, and from the next chapter on you will.

Mira runs it on the n, then the g, then the ampersand, and guesses the number of contours each time before she presses the button. She gets the g wrong.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
A glyph holds one layer for each master, a layer holds elements, an element holds contours, and a contour holds nodes, each with an x and a y in font units. A loop inside a loop walks two of those levels at once, and where you put a line, outside both loops, inside one or inside both, decides how often it runs. A round shape has more nodes than you'd count by eye, because the handles are nodes too. A glyph with elements and no contours is built from other glyphs.

What a glyph holds, from the outside in.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Before you run anatomy.py on each of these, write down how many contours you expect: i, g, ampersand, at. Then run it. Which one surprised you, and can you see why in the Glyph window?
  2. Add a line to anatomy.py that prints where each contour starts: the x and y of its first node. nodes[0] gets you the node. On the i, which contour comes first, the stem or the dot?
  3. Switch the Glyph window to the Bold master and run anatomy.py on the o again. The first line should now say layer Bold. Do the contour and node counts change? Print the first node of the outer contour in both masters and compare. Keep your answer in mind: chapter 58 depends on it.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Twelve nodes for an oval with four points. Chapter 42 sorts the nodes into the ones on the line and the ones off it, and finds out which glyph in Plum has the most.

docs.title: 42. Count the nodes
docs.text:
Tuesday. Mira is still thinking about the g she guessed wrong yesterday, and about something a teacher told her years ago: a point you don't need is a point that can go wrong. Every node in an outline is a place where a curve can kink, where two masters can disagree, where a hand can slip. Good outlines are economical.

"So which glyph in Plum has the most?" she asks. "I'd like to look at it."

Nobody at Halfmoon knows the answer. To find it, a script has to open every glyph in the font, which is one more level than yesterday. And before it counts, it has to deal with what we left hanging: of the twelve nodes in an oval, four sit on the line and eight are handles. A count that mixes them up tells you little.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The functions and loops from Part 2.
  • Yesterday's idea of layer, contour and node.

The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel. Treat what the calls return as what the helpers' source says they return.

docs.title: Step 1: On the line or off it
docs.text:
Open the o in a Glyph window and ask each node of the outer contour one question:

from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

glyph = pGlyph()
outer = glyph.contours()[0]
for node in outer.nodes():
    print(f"{node.x:>5.0f}{node.y:>5.0f}  {node.isOn()}")

  260  -10  True
  396  -10  False
  482   90  False
  482  239  True
  482  388  False
  396  488  False
  260  488  True
  124  488  False
   38  388  False
   38  239  True
   38   90  False
  124  -10  False

isOn() answers True for a node that sits on the outline and False for a handle. It's a question with a yes or no answer, like isEmpty() in chapter 8, and it wants its parentheses.

Look at the rhythm: one True, two False, and again. Each curved piece of the outline runs from one on-line node to the next, and it needs two handles to say how it bends, one for leaving and one for arriving. So a curve costs three nodes, and a straight piece costs one. A glyph made of straight lines is cheap, and a round one is expensive.

docs.title: Step 2: A mistake that says nothing
docs.text:
Count the two kinds for the whole glyph. glyph.nodes() hands you every node of the layer in one flat list, so you don't need the loop inside a loop for this:

on = 0
off = 0
for node in glyph.nodes():
    if node.isOn:
        on = on + 1
    else:
        off = off + 1
print(on, off)

24 0

That's wrong, and nothing complained. The o has eight nodes on the line and sixteen handles. This says twenty-four and none.

Did you see it? The parentheses are missing after isOn. Yesterday, the same slip with len(glyph.contours) earned you an error. Today it earns you nothing, and that's worse. Remember truthiness from chapter 31: if will take any value at all and decide whether it counts as true. node.isOn without parentheses is the method itself, not its answer, and a method is a thing that exists, so it counts as true. Every time. The script asked "is there such a question?" where it meant to ask the question.

This is one of the few mistakes in Python that a beginner and an old hand make equally often. You can't make Python catch it. What you can do is know what the result should look like. You knew the o has handles, so 24 0 looked wrong to you at once. Before you trust a count from a script, run it on one glyph where you already know the answer.

Put the parentheses in:

    if node.isOn():

8 16

docs.title: Step 3: A function with two answers
docs.text:
We'll want this again, so make it a function. Define it in this script:

from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph


def node_counts(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    on = len([node for node in nodes if node.isOn()])
    return on, len(nodes) - on

There are three things to notice.

The first line uses pGlyph again, but this time you hand it the font and the glyph, so it doesn't depend on what's on screen. Then it calls nodes(master), with something in the slot this time. Yesterday pGlyph() and nodes() with empty parentheses meant "the glyph on screen, the layer that's showing". That's fine for one glyph you're looking at. A script that walks the whole font isn't looking at anything, so it should say which layer it wants by name: "Regular". The name goes in as a default argument, the way chapter 34 showed, so you can ask for another master when you need to.

The second line is a comprehension with a filter, from chapter 37: collect the nodes that are on the line, and take the length of the collection.

The third line returns two values with a comma between them. You've seen this from the other side. In chapter 35 you unpacked a row with name, lsb, width, rsb = row. A comma between values makes a tuple, with or without parentheses around it, so return on, len(nodes) - on hands back one tuple of two numbers. The caller unpacks it the same way:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
on, off = node_counts(font, font["o"])
print(on, off)

8 16

Try a few more by hand. H gives 12 0: it's all straight lines. l gives 4 0, a plain rectangle. n gives 12 8, which is four curved pieces with two handles each, and the rest straight.

docs.title: Step 4: Every glyph
docs.text:
Now walk the font. For each glyph we want a row with its name and its counts, as in chapter 35:

rows = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    on, off = node_counts(font, glyph)
    rows.append((glyph.name, on, off, on + off))
print(len(rows))
print(rows[1])

220
('A', 11, 0, 11)

There's a row for each of the 220 glyphs in the practice font (the 205 that Plum came with, and the 15 you've added since chapter 8), and the second one is the A: eleven nodes on the line, no handles, because Plum's A is all straight. Check that against the Glyph window, as Step 2 told you to. The outer shape has eight corners and the triangle inside has three.

If your A says something else, don't doubt the arithmetic yet. Print what you're measuring:

print(font.info.familyName, len(font))

fl.CurrentFont() means the font in front, and when a second font is open behind your back it will answer for that one. Mira lost ten minutes to this in the morning, with one of Oskar's old files sitting in front of the practice font. It's the oldest trap in this book and it doesn't go away.

Many of the rows are all zeros: glyphs built from other glyphs, like eacute, and the empty ones waiting to be drawn. They'd only clutter the answer, so keep the rows that have something in them:

rows = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    on, off = node_counts(font, glyph)
    if on + off > 0:
        rows.append((glyph.name, on, off, on + off))
print(len(rows))

121

Of the 220 glyphs in the practice font, 121 have an outline of their own in the Regular master. The other 99 are borrowed or empty. That number alone tells you something about how Plum was made: fewer than six glyphs in ten were drawn.

docs.title: Step 5: The most, and the average
docs.text:
Sort the rows by the total, largest first, with a key function as in chapter 36:

def by_total(row):
    return row[3]


for name, on, off, total in sorted(rows, key=by_total, reverse=True)[:5]:
    print(f"{name:<12}{on:>4}{off:>5}{total:>6}")

ae            27   42    69
at            23   40    63
oe            20   34    54
ampersand     22   32    54
percent       20   32    52

There's Mira's answer. The æ has the most, 69 nodes, and that makes sense: it's two letters fused, with three contours. The at sign is next. Nothing here looks like a mistake. These are the glyphs you'd expect to be the most complicated, and that's a good sign for the font.

Now the average. Add up the totals and divide by the number of rows:

total_nodes = sum([row[3] for row in rows])
print(total_nodes, total_nodes / len(rows))

2585 21.363636363636363

So Plum's Regular master holds 2,585 nodes, about 21 for each drawn glyph. If you'd like to know how curvy a glyph is, you could divide its handles by its on-line nodes. Try that on a row:

name, on, off, total = rows[0]
print(name, off / on)

That works for every row, because we kept only glyphs with nodes. But suppose you'd done it inside the first loop, before the filter, for every glyph in the font:

for glyph in font.glyphs:
    on, off = node_counts(font, glyph)
    print(glyph.name, off / on)

.notdef 0.0
A 0.0
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 3, in <module>
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

The third glyph is Aacute. It has no nodes of its own, so on is zero, and you can't divide by zero in Python any more than on paper. The script stops there.

It's an error you should expect whenever you divide by something you counted. A count can be zero, and one day it will be. The cure is to ask first:

if on > 0:
    print(glyph.name, off / on)

The same goes for the average. total_nodes / len(rows) fails on a font where nothing is drawn, so the finished script checks that rows isn't empty before it divides.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is node_count.py:

# Lists the glyphs with the most nodes in one master, and the font's totals.
# Reads only.
from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTER = "Regular"
HOW_MANY = 5


def node_counts(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    on = len([node for node in nodes if node.isOn()])
    return on, len(nodes) - on


def by_total(row):
    return row[3]


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        print("Open a font first.")
        return

    rows = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        on, off = node_counts(font, glyph, MASTER)
        if on + off > 0:
            rows.append((glyph.name, on, off, on + off))

    if not rows:
        print("No outlines in", MASTER)
        return

    print(f"{font.info.familyName}, {MASTER}")
    print(f"{'glyph':<12}{'on':>4}{'off':>5}{'total':>6}")
    for name, on, off, total in sorted(rows, key=by_total, reverse=True)[:HOW_MANY]:
        print(f"{name:<12}{on:>4}{off:>5}{total:>6}")

    all_on = sum([row[1] for row in rows])
    all_off = sum([row[2] for row in rows])
    print()
    print(f"{len(rows)} glyphs with outlines")
    print(f"{all_on + all_off} nodes: {all_on} on the line, {all_off} handles")
    print(f"{(all_on + all_off) / len(rows):.1f} nodes a glyph")


main()

GG Plum, Regular
glyph         on  off total
ae            27   42    69
at            23   40    63
oe            20   34    54
ampersand     22   32    54
percent       20   32    52

121 glyphs with outlines
2585 nodes: 1413 on the line, 1172 handles
21.4 nodes a glyph

The script names the master in a constant at the top and prints it with the font's name, so nobody has to guess what was measured. Two guards stand before the work: no font, and nothing to count. And it stays short because the counting lives in the module.

Mira opens the ae and looks at it for a long time. Then she opens the at. "Forty handles," she says. "I'd have said twenty."

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: isOn() tells a node on the outline from a handle, and a curve costs three nodes where a straight line costs one. A method without its parentheses counts as true in an if, and Python won't warn you, so test a new count on a glyph whose answer you know. A function can return two values with a comma, and the caller unpacks them. Before you divide by a count, check that it isn't zero.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Change MASTER to "Bold" and run node_count.py again. Compare the totals with Regular. What does that tell you about how the three masters of Plum were drawn?
  2. Turn the list upside down: show the glyphs with the fewest nodes, leaving out the ones with none. Several tie for last place, so show ten. You need to change one word. Which glyphs are they, and what shape do they share?
  3. Add a fifth field to each row: handles divided by on-line nodes, to one decimal. Sort by it, largest first. The glyphs at the top are the roundest in the font. Is o among them? What's the largest value a glyph can have, and why can't it go higher?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Every node has an x and a y, and so far you've only printed them. Chapter 43 uses them to measure: how tall is the H, how far does the o dip below the baseline, and does every capital reach the same height?

docs.title: 43. Coordinates
docs.text:
Wednesday. Mira has two glyphs side by side in a Glyph window, the H and the O, and she's zoomed in on their tops. The O pokes up a little above the H. She knows why. A round shape that stops at the very height of a flat one looks too short, so every type designer lets the rounds go a touch over. It's called overshoot.

"How much is it in Plum?" she asks. "And is it the same everywhere?"

She could click on the top node of the O, read its position, write it down, click on the H, and so on through the alphabet. That's fifty-two clicks for the capitals alone. You already know a better way. Every node carries an x and a y, and for two chapters you've only printed them. Today you'll do arithmetic with them.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The node_counts function from the last chapter, for the pattern it uses.

The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel.

docs.title: Step 1: Highest and lowest
docs.text:
Start with the H. Collect the y of every node in the Regular master, and ask for the smallest and the largest:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()
nodes = pGlyph(font, font["H"]).nodes("Regular")
ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
print(min(ys), max(ys))

0.0 688.0

The line that starts with nodes is the pattern from chapter 42: the plain glyph goes into the well-equipped box, and the box hands over the nodes of a layer you name. The line after it is a comprehension that keeps one number from each node. min and max you met in chapter 36. Given a list of numbers, they need no key.

So the H stands on the baseline, at 0, and reaches 688. Change "H" to "O" and run it again:

-10.0 698.0

There's Mira's answer for one pair. The O goes 10 units over at the top and 10 under at the bottom. Its overshoot is 10.

Notice what kind of measuring this is. y counts up from the baseline, so a height is a y, and a depth is a negative one. You didn't have to subtract anything.

docs.title: Step 2: The box
docs.text:
Do the same for x, and you have four numbers:

xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
print(min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys))

For the H:

76.0 0.0 602.0 688.0

Left, bottom, right, top. Those four numbers describe the smallest upright rectangle that the glyph's outline fits inside. It's called the bounding box, and you'll meet it everywhere in font work.

Look at the first number, 76. In chapter 35 you asked the H for its left sidebearing and got 76. That's no coincidence. The left sidebearing is the distance from the left edge of the glyph's space, where x is 0, to the leftmost point of the outline. The right sidebearing is what's left over on the other side: the H is 672 wide, the outline ends at 602, and 672 − 602 is 70, the number chapter 35 gave you. So the sidebearings you've been reading since Part 2 are computed from the box and the width. There's nothing more to them.

A word of caution about what goes into the box. We used every node, handles too. A handle can stick out beyond the outline it controls, and then this box would be a little too big. In a carefully drawn font each curve has a node on the line at its highest, lowest, leftmost and rightmost point, and then the handles never stick out. Plum is drawn that way. I checked every glyph, and the box of all nodes and the box of on-line nodes are the same.

docs.title: Step 3: When there's nothing to measure
docs.text:
Make it a function, so that a script can ask for any glyph's box. Define it in this script:

def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)

Run the definition and try it on a glyph that's built from others:

print(box(font, font["eacute"]))

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
  File "<string>", line 5, in box
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)
ValueError: min() arg is an empty sequence

Read it from the bottom, as chapter 3 taught you. min was given an empty list. The é has no nodes of its own, so xs is empty, and there's no smallest number among none. It's the same kind of trouble as dividing by zero yesterday: a question that has no answer when the count is zero.

What should box do with such a glyph? It can't invent four numbers. Zeros would be a lie, because a glyph with a box at 0, 0, 0, 0 is not the same as a glyph with no box. Python has a value for "there isn't one", and you've used it since chapter 6: None.

def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)

Now the function gives either a tuple of four numbers or None, and every caller has to be ready for both. Chapter 39 made the same bargain when a dialog could be cancelled. The caller checks before it unpacks:

found = box(font, font["eacute"])
if found is None:
    print("no outline")
else:
    left, bottom, right, top = found
    print(top)

no outline

docs.title: Step 4: What the font says
docs.text:
So the H is 688 tall. Is that what it's supposed to be?

A font keeps a few heights written down, apart from any glyph: the cap height, the x-height, how far ascenders rise and descenders drop. You see them in the Glyph window as horizontal lines across the drawing. They belong to a master, since a bold may be a little taller than a light. A script can read them:

from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.font import pFont

metrics = pFont().fontMetrics()
print(metrics.getCapsHeight("Regular"))
print(metrics.getXHeight("Regular"))
print(metrics.getAscender("Regular"))
print(metrics.getDescender("Regular"))

688
478
765
-235

pFont() is the well-equipped box for the font in front, the big brother of pGlyph(). Its fontMetrics() hands you a smaller box that holds only these heights, and each question takes a master's name. If one of the four calls complains, check its spelling against the TypeRig reference before you doubt the idea.

These questions have a side effect, which I read in TypeRig's source. Asking with a master's name makes that master the current one in FontLab, and it stays the current one afterwards. We ask about the Regular only, so if you were looking at the Bold, the Font window may show the Regular when the script has finished. Nothing in the font has changed. Switch back to the master you were working in.

The cap height is 688, and the H reaches 688. Good. The x-height is 478. Try the lowercase x with the first listing and you'll get a top of 478, and o gives 488: ten units over again.

Now you can say what overshoot is in numbers. It's the top of a glyph minus the height it's measured against:

left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font["O"])
print(top - metrics.getCapsHeight("Regular"))

10.0

docs.title: Step 5: All the capitals
docs.text:
Mira's second question was whether it's the same everywhere. Let's ask all twenty-six capitals how far above or below the cap height they end.

We need to walk the alphabet. A string is a row of characters, and for walks it one character at a time, as it did in chapter 7:

for letter in "ABC":
    print(letter)

A
B
C

For each capital we'll compute the difference. Then we want the letters grouped by that difference: all the ones at 0 together, all the ones at 10 together. In chapter 22 you counted things with a dictionary, where each key held a number that went up by one. Here each key will hold a list that grows by one name. The shape is the same:

CAPITALS = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"

cap_height = metrics.getCapsHeight("Regular")
groups = {}
for letter in CAPITALS:
    found = box(font, font[letter])
    if found is None:
        print(letter, "has no outline")
    else:
        left, bottom, right, top = found
        over = top - cap_height
        if over not in groups:
            groups[over] = []
        groups[over].append(letter)

for over in sorted(groups):
    print(f"{over:>4.0f}  {' '.join(groups[over])}")

  -4  E F T Z
   0  A H I J K L M N U V W X Y
  10  B C D G O P Q R S

Go through the new parts slowly. if over not in groups: asks whether this difference has been seen before. If it hasn't, the next line starts an empty list for it. Either way, the line after that adds the letter to the list for its difference. A dictionary whose values are lists is how you sort things into piles, and you'll use it more often than almost anything else in this book.

sorted from chapter 10 takes a dictionary too, and hands back its keys in order. And ' '.join(...) is the glue from chapter 25: it makes one string out of a list of strings, with a space between each pair.

Now read the result as a designer. The bottom line is what Mira expected: nine round capitals, all 10 over. The middle line is the flat ones, at cap height. U is there because its top is two flat stems.

The top line nobody expected. E, F, T and Z stop 4 units short of the cap height. They're the four capitals whose top is a long horizontal bar.

Is that a mistake? The script can't say. It can only say that four letters differ from the rest, and that they have something in common. Some designers do lower a long flat top by a hair, because a wide bar at full height can look heavier than a stem end. It could also be an accident that got copied from the E to its relatives. Mira sends Oskar a message. The answer comes after lunch: "No idea. It was like that when I got it. Proof it before you touch it."

You'll see this again and again. A script finds what's different, and a person has to decide whether different is wrong.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
bounds.py puts the pieces together and does the same for the lowercase against the x-height. It defines box from Step 3 near the top, so it runs by itself.

# Groups letters by how far their tops end above or below a font height.
# Reads only.
from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.font import pFont
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTER = "Regular"
CAPITALS = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"
SMALL = "acemnorsuvwxz"


def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


def groups_by_top(font, letters, height):
    groups = {}
    for letter in letters:
        glyph = font[letter]
        if glyph is None:
            print(f"  {letter} is not in the font")
        else:
            found = box(font, glyph, MASTER)
            if found is None:
                print(f"  {letter} has no outline")
            else:
                left, bottom, right, top = found
                over = top - height
                if over not in groups:
                    groups[over] = []
                groups[over].append(letter)
    return groups


def show(title, height, groups):
    print(f"{title}: {height}")
    for over in sorted(groups):
        print(f"{over:>6.0f}  {' '.join(groups[over])}")


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        print("Open a font first.")
        return

    metrics = pFont().fontMetrics()
    cap_height = metrics.getCapsHeight(MASTER)
    x_height = metrics.getXHeight(MASTER)

    print(f"{font.info.familyName}, {MASTER}")
    show("cap height", cap_height, groups_by_top(font, CAPITALS, cap_height))
    show("x-height", x_height, groups_by_top(font, SMALL, x_height))


main()

GG Plum, Regular
cap height: 688
    -4  E F T Z
     0  A H I J K L M N U V W X Y
    10  B C D G O P Q R S
x-height: 478
    -4  z
     0  u v w x
     8  r
    10  a c e m n o s

The lowercase tells the same story as the capitals, with one extra. The z is 4 short, like its big sister. The flat-topped letters sit at the x-height. The round ones are 10 over, and m and n are among them because their arches are round on top. And the r is 8 over, alone. Mira adds it to her list for Oskar.

SMALL leaves out the letters with ascenders and the dotted ones on purpose. Their tops belong to a different height, and measuring them against the x-height would only make noise. Exercise 2 is about them.

In groups_by_top an if sits inside an else that sits inside another else, which is as deep as I like to go. Each else holds the rest of the work. Tomorrow you'll learn a word that flattens that staircase.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A node's y is a height above the baseline and its x is a distance from the glyph's left edge, so min and max over a layer's nodes give the bounding box, and the sidebearings follow from the box and the width. A function that may have nothing to return should return None, and its callers should check for it. The font's own heights can be read for each master and compared with what's drawn. A dictionary of lists sorts things into piles.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Do the bottoms. Change groups_by_top into a function that groups by the bottom of the box against a height of 0, and run it on the capitals. Leave J and Q aside; they have tails. One round capital goes deeper below the baseline than the others. Which one, and by how much?
  2. Measure b d f h k l against the ascender height, metrics.getAscender(MASTER). Do they reach it? What does that tell you about what the ascender line in this font is for?
  3. Add the bounding box to anatomy.py from chapter 41: one line that says box: 76 0 602 688 for the H, or box: none for a glyph without an outline.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Three ifs nested like stairs is a sign that the loop wants a way to say "this one's no good, on to the next". Chapter 44 teaches that word, and uses it to hunt for contours that were never closed.

docs.title: 44. Open contours
docs.text:
Thursday. Ines tells a story at the coffee machine. Some years ago Halfmoon delivered a font in which the comma, in one weight, had a contour that wasn't closed. On screen at the studio it looked fine. In the exported font it was gone, and nobody noticed until a cookbook came back from the printer with every list of ingredients run together.

A contour is supposed to come back to where it started. One that doesn't is called open. It's a line with two loose ends and nothing inside it to fill with black. Open contours get into fonts in ordinary ways: a sketch you forgot to finish, a guideline drawn with the wrong tool, two nodes that look joined and aren't.

"Can a script find them?" Mira asks. She already knows what I'll say. In chapter 41 you printed contour.closed and it said True twice. Today you'll look for the ones that say False, in every glyph and every master, and on the way you'll learn two small words that make loops easier to read.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • anatomy.py from chapter 41.
  • The seven small-cap glyphs you added in chapter 40. They're still empty.

Plum's source file has no open contours. So in Step 1 you'll plant one. The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel.

docs.title: Step 1: Plant one
docs.text:
Open the empty d.sc in a Glyph window, with the Regular master showing. Take the Pen tool and click three times, anywhere, to make three corners of a triangle. Don't click on the first point again to close it. Press Esc to put the pen down. You have a line with two bends, which is a contour that's open.

Run anatomy.py on it:

d.sc, layer Regular
  elements: 1
  contour 1: open, 3 nodes
  total: 1 contours, 3 nodes

If yours says closed, the pen closed the shape for you. Undo and try again, or draw the three points and stop after the third.

Now there's one open contour in a font of 220 glyphs, in one master of three. Let's go and find it as if we didn't know where it was.

docs.title: Step 2: On to the next
docs.text:
First, a helper. Define it in this script. For two chapters we've asked for a layer's nodes. Today we need its contours, since closed belongs to a contour and not to a node:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()


def contours_of(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    return pGlyph(font, glyph).contours(master)

Now walk the font. Most glyphs will have nothing for us: the ones built from other glyphs and the empty ones have no contours at all. Yesterday we handled cases like that with an if and an else, and the real work ended up three levels deep, like a staircase. Here's another way to write it:

for glyph in font.glyphs:
    contours = contours_of(font, glyph)
    if not contours:
        continue
    print(glyph.name, len(contours))

continue means: I'm done with this one, go on to the next. When Python meets it, it skips whatever is left in the body of the loop for this round and goes straight back to the for line to pick up the next glyph. So the print only happens for glyphs that got past the if.

You've seen the same move before. In chapter 19, main() began with a guard: if there's no font, say so and return. The guard turned away the hopeless case at the door, and the rest of the function didn't have to be indented under an else. continue is that guard for one round of a loop. return leaves the whole function. continue leaves only this round.

The two get mixed up, and Python will tell you when you do. Suppose you write the guard at the top of main() with the wrong word:

def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        continue

  File "<string>", line 4
SyntaxError: 'continue' not properly in loop

There's no loop there to continue. It's a SyntaxError, so Python found it while reading the script, before running a single line.

docs.title: Step 3: Is any of them open?
docs.text:
For each glyph that has contours, we want to know whether at least one of them is open. You can already write that, with a switch like DRY_RUN from chapter 31, only this one is flipped by the loop:

contours = contours_of(font, font["d.sc"])
has_open = False
for contour in contours:
    if not contour.closed:
        has_open = True
print(has_open)

True

The switch starts at False, and the first open contour flips it. Nothing ever flips it back. After the loop it tells you whether there was one.

Once it's flipped, the rest of the contours don't matter. On a glyph with fifty contours you could stop looking after the first open one. There's a word for that too:

for contour in contours:
    if not contour.closed:
        has_open = True
        break

break leaves the loop altogether. The loop is over, and Python carries on with the line after it. So there are three ways out, each a size bigger than the last. continue ends this round, break ends the loop, and return ends the function.

This pattern, a switch and a loop and a break, is so common that Python has it built in:

has_open = any([not contour.closed for contour in contours])

Read it aloud: is any of these true? The comprehension makes a list with one True or False for each contour, and any answers True if at least one item is true. That's the five-line loop in one line, and it says what it means.

any has a sibling, all, which answers True only if every item is true:

all_closed = all([contour.closed for contour in contours])

For a glyph with contours, all_closed is the opposite of has_open, and you can use whichever reads better.

But try both on a glyph with no contours:

print(any([]), all([]))

False True

any of nothing is False, which sounds right: there's no open contour in an empty glyph. all of nothing is True, and that one can fool you. "Are all the contours closed?" Yes, says Python, all none of them. It's sound logic. If you fire everyone on the team who was late, and nobody was late, you've done it. But a report that says "220 glyphs have all contours closed", when 99 of them have no contours, is saying less than it seems to. When you use all, think about what it does with an empty list, and whether you should have turned the empty cases away first. That's what the continue in Step 2 was for.

docs.title: Step 4: Every master
docs.text:
The cookbook comma was open in one weight. A check that looks only at Regular would have missed it. So for each glyph we have to look at three layers, and that's a loop inside a loop again:

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]

for glyph in font.glyphs:
    for master in MASTERS:
        contours = contours_of(font, glyph, master)
        if any([not contour.closed for contour in contours]):
            print(glyph.name, master)

d.sc Regular

There it is. Think of the clock from chapter 41: the glyph is the hour hand, the master is the minute hand, and the script looks at 660 layers to find one.

The list of masters is typed in as a constant, as it was in chapter 40, and it's right for Plum only. Asking the font for its masters is still to come.

Here continue would add nothing, because any of an empty list is False and the if takes care of the empty layers on its own. Use continue when it saves you a level of indentation or a wrong answer, and leave it out when it doesn't.

One more thing would help Mira when she goes to fix what the script finds: how many open contours a layer has, and how big they are. A stray open contour with two or three nodes is usually a slip of the pen. One with thirty is a real shape that somebody forgot to close, and it needs care. So let's collect the open ones, with a filter:

loose = [contour for contour in contours if not contour.closed]

If loose is empty, the layer is fine. If it isn't, its length is the count, and each contour in it can be asked for its nodes.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is find_open.py. It defines contours_of from Step 2 at the top, so it runs by itself.

# Lists every open contour in the font, in every master.
# Reads only.
from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]


def contours_of(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    return pGlyph(font, glyph).contours(master)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        print("Open a font first.")
        return

    found = 0
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        for master in MASTERS:
            contours = contours_of(font, glyph, master)
            loose = [contour for contour in contours if not contour.closed]
            if not loose:
                continue
            found = found + 1
            sizes = [str(len(contour.nodes())) for contour in loose]
            print(f"{glyph.name:<12}{master:<9}open: {len(loose)}  nodes: {' '.join(sizes)}")

    if found == 0:
        print("No open contours.")
    else:
        print(f"{found} layers with open contours.")


main()

d.sc        Regular  open: 1  nodes: 3
1 layers with open contours.

Look at how the inner loop reads now. It gets the contours, keeps the open ones, and if there are none it moves on. What comes after the continue is the part that only happens for the rare bad layer, and it isn't indented any deeper than the rest. A reader can see at a glance which lines are the normal path and which are the exception.

The sizes line uses ' '.join from yesterday, and join insists on strings, so each count goes through str first, the cure chapter 3 gave for gluing text to a number.

"1 layers" is bad grammar. You know enough to fix it, and exercise 1 asks you to.

Mira runs it. One line. She opens d.sc, deletes the three-point sketch, runs it again, and gets No open contours. Delete your sketch too, and run the script once more to see the same line. Later chapters count layers, and their counts assume that no sketch is left behind. Then she saves the script in the Halfmoon folder with a #FLM: Find Open Contours line at the top, the way chapter 18 showed, because this is one she'll want before every delivery.

Ines reads the output over her shoulder. "That would have saved us a cookbook," she says.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: continue ends one round of a loop and goes on to the next, break ends the loop, and return ends the function. any asks whether at least one item in a list is true and all asks whether every one is, and all of an empty list is True, so turn the empty cases away before you trust it. A check that matters has to look at every master, which means a loop inside a loop. An open contour has closed equal to False.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Fix the grammar: make the last line say 1 layer with open contours. or 2 layers with open contours. as needed. The a if test else b form from chapter 37 fits in one line.
  2. Plant a second open contour, in the Bold master of e.sc, with two points only. Run the script. Delete both points when you're done. Then change it so that it prints the word stray at the end of the line when every open contour in the layer has fewer than four nodes. Which of any and all do you need?
  3. Rewrite groups_by_top in yesterday's bounds.py with continue, so that nothing in the loop is indented more than two levels. Run it and make sure the output hasn't changed. Which version would you rather read in six months?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: A closed contour still has a property you can't see by looking at the black shape: the way round it runs. Chapter 45 finds out why the hole in the o is a hole, and what happens when it isn't.

docs.title: 45. Direction matters
docs.text:
Friday of the eighth week. Mira asks a question that sounds childish and isn't: "How does the o know it has a hole?"

Think about what the font holds. It holds two closed lines, a big oval and a small oval. Nothing in either says "I'm the outside" or "I'm the hole". If you filled both with black, you'd get a black disc with a blacker disc in the middle, which is to say a blob. Yet the o prints with white in its center, every time, on every machine.

The answer is a property of a contour that you can't see in the finished letter. A contour runs in a direction. Its nodes come in an order, as you saw in chapter 41 when the list went from the bottom of the oval to the right, the top and the left. That order goes round the shape one way or the other. Today you'll read it, break it on purpose, and write a check for the kind of damage that your eyes won't catch.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • box and contours_of from the last two chapters. You'll write them out again here.
  • The o open in a Glyph window, Regular master.

The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel. The directions quoted for Plum were worked out the same way. The drawer that reports direction, clockwise, is taken from FontLab's list of names.

docs.title: Step 1: Which way round
docs.text:
Ask the two contours of the o:

from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

glyph = pGlyph()
for contour in glyph.contours():
    print(len(contour.nodes()), contour.clockwise)

12 False
12 True

The outer oval doesn't run clockwise, so it runs the other way, which is called counter-clockwise. The inner oval runs clockwise. They go in opposite directions.

You can check the first with the node list from chapter 41. The outer contour went from the bottom, at 260, −10, to the right side, at 482, 239, then to the top and then to the left. Trace that with a finger on the o: bottom, right, top, left. Your finger moves against the clock.

clockwise is a drawer and not an action, so it takes no parentheses. If you add them out of habit from the last few chapters, you'll get the opposite of the complaint in chapter 41:

print(contour.clockwise())

TypeError: 'bool' object is not callable

contour.clockwise is already the answer, True or False. Python calls those two values bool. Putting parentheses after an answer asks Python to run it as if it were a function, and "not callable" means it can't be run. So now you know both halves. A method without parentheses gives you 'method' trouble, and a value with parentheses gives you not callable.

docs.title: Step 2: Why opposite makes a hole
docs.text:
Here's the rule the machine uses to decide what's black. Imagine walking across the letter in a straight line from far outside, keeping a number in your head that starts at zero. Each time you cross a contour that runs one way, add one. Each time you cross a contour that runs the other way, take one away. Wherever your number isn't zero, the page is black.

Walk across the o. You cross the outer oval: the number becomes 1, and you're in black. You cross the inner oval, which runs the other way: back to 0, and you're in white. You cross the inner oval again on your way out of the middle, and the number is 1 again. Then you cross the outer oval and return to 0.

So a hole isn't a kind of contour. It's what happens when a contour sits inside another and runs against it.

Now you can guess what goes wrong. If the inner oval ran the same way as the outer one, the number in the middle would be 2, not 0, and the middle would be black.

docs.title: Step 3: Break it
docs.text:
Try it. In the Glyph window, click on the inner oval of the o to select that contour alone. Then find the command that reverses a contour. In my copy it's in the Contour menu and it's called Reverse Contour. Look at the letter in the preview: the hole should have filled in.

Run the listing from Step 1 again and you should get False twice.

Press Cmd+Z on a Mac, or Ctrl+Z on Windows, to put it back.

That damage shows at once, because the letter looks wrong. Now do the other experiment. Select the whole o, both contours, and reverse them together. Look at the preview.

Nothing should have changed. The hole is still a hole, because the two contours still run against each other. Run the listing: True, then False. Both have flipped.

So is that a problem at all? It is, and it's the worse kind, because you can't see it. The rule about adding and taking away doesn't care which direction is which. But fonts follow a convention on top of the rule. In the kind of outlines Plum has, the outside of a shape runs counter-clockwise and the holes run clockwise. Other software relies on that. Tools that make a letter bolder, remove overlaps or add an outline work out which side of a line is "inside" from its direction, and a glyph that runs backwards can come out thinner where it should be bolder, or lose its counters. Some of the tools that turn your font into the files you deliver are sensitive to it too.

How does a whole glyph end up backwards? Usually by flipping. Mirror a b to start a d, and every contour in it reverses, because a mirror turns clockwise into counter-clockwise. The letter looks perfect and runs the wrong way.

Leave your o reversed for now. We'll use it to test the script.

docs.title: Step 4: Which one is the outside?
docs.text:
To check a glyph, a script has to know which contour is the outside one, and nothing in the contour says so. But there's a simple test that's right nearly always: the outside is the biggest. The contour whose bounding box covers the most ground is an outer contour, and it should run counter-clockwise.

In chapter 43, box worked out the box of all the nodes in a layer. Now we need the box of the nodes in one contour. It's the same arithmetic on a different list, so split the function in two. Define this pair in this script, in place of the old box:

from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph


def box_of(nodes):
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    return box_of(pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master))

box still does what it did, and every call to it still works. All of its arithmetic has moved into box_of, which will take any list of nodes. This is how your code should grow. When you need half of a function somewhere else, cut that half out and give it a name, and let the old function call it. Don't copy the lines.

Add one more, for the ground a contour covers:

def box_area(contour):
    left, bottom, right, top = box_of(contour.nodes())
    return (right - left) * (top - bottom)

A width times a height. Try it on the o:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph


def contours_of(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    return pGlyph(font, glyph).contours(master)


font = fl.CurrentFont()
contours = contours_of(font, font["o"])
for contour in contours:
    print(box_area(contour))

221112.0
96624.0

The outer oval's box is 444 by 498, and the inner one's is 264 by 366. Now pick the biggest, with max and a key as in chapter 36:

outer = max(contours, key=box_area)
print(outer.clockwise)

True

max hands back the contour itself, the one for which box_area gave the largest number. And since you left your o reversed, its outside runs clockwise. That's the check, in two lines.

Notice key=box_area, with no parentheses. It's the "function is a value" idea, put to work this time: you're handing max the function, for it to call on each contour.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is check_direction.py. It writes out contours_of, box_of and box_area at the top, so it runs by itself. It doesn't need box.

# Reports layers whose largest contour runs clockwise.
# Reads only.
from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]


def contours_of(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    return pGlyph(font, glyph).contours(master)


def box_of(nodes):
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


def box_area(contour):
    left, bottom, right, top = box_of(contour.nodes())
    return (right - left) * (top - bottom)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        print("Open a font first.")
        return

    checked = 0
    wrong = 0
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        for master in MASTERS:
            contours = contours_of(font, glyph, master)
            if not contours:
                continue
            checked = checked + 1
            outer = max(contours, key=box_area)
            if outer.clockwise:
                wrong = wrong + 1
                print(f"{glyph.name:<12}{master:<9}outside runs clockwise")

    print(f"{checked} layers checked, {wrong} wrong.")


main()

With the o still reversed in Regular:

o           Regular  outside runs clockwise
363 layers checked, 1 wrong.

Go back to the o and undo the reversal, or reverse both contours again. Run the script once more:

363 layers checked, 0 wrong.

Plum has 121 drawn glyphs in each of three masters, 363 layers, and in every one of them the largest contour runs counter-clockwise. I worked that out from the source file too, and it's what you'd hope for from a font that's been through a foundry's hands.

Here continue earns its place. max of an empty list fails with the same ValueError that min gave you in chapter 43, so the empty layers have to be turned away before the max line, and continue does that.

Be clear about what this script doesn't do. It looks at one contour in each layer, the biggest. It will catch a glyph that's backwards as a whole, which is the damage you can't see. It won't catch a single hole that runs the wrong way inside a good glyph, as in your first experiment. To find that, a script would have to work out which contours lie inside which, and that's real geometry, more than a box can tell you. An i has two contours and neither is a hole. A percent sign has five, and two are holes. I don't mind the gap much, because a filled-in hole is the one you'll see in any proof. And FontLab has its own command that sets every direction in a glyph by the proper geometry. Look in the Contour menu for it. Use your script to find the glyphs that need it.

Mira saves the script in the Halfmoon folder with #FLM: Check Direction. That's two delivery checks this week. She takes the sheet of chores, reads down the seven lines that are left, and finds that neither check is on it. Oskar never ran them.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A contour runs clockwise or counter-clockwise, and contour.clockwise tells you which. What's black is decided by counting crossings, so a hole is a contour that runs against the one around it, and a glyph reversed as a whole still looks right while breaking the convention that other tools depend on. The largest contour in a layer is an outside one and should run counter-clockwise in a font like Plum. When you need part of a function elsewhere, split it and let the old one call the new one.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add the direction to anatomy.py: each contour line should end with clockwise or counter-clockwise. Run it on i, B and percent, and say for each contour whether it's an outside or a hole.
  2. Open b and d side by side. Select everything in a copy of the b (make a new glyph called b.test and paste into it), flip it horizontally with FontLab's own tools, and run check_direction.py. Did the flip reverse it? Delete b.test when you're done.
  3. check_direction.py and find_open.py have the same skeleton: two loops, a helper, a counter, a last line. Write a third script on that skeleton, find_tiny.py, that reports contours whose box_area is under 100. On Plum it should find none. Plant a tiny triangle in f.sc and find it. Delete the triangle when you're done.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Enough reading. You've spent five chapters looking at outlines that someone else drew. In chapter 46 the script picks up a pen and draws a rectangle of its own.

docs.title: 46. Draw a rectangle
docs.text:
Monday of the ninth week. The publisher's art director wants to see a page of the cookbook set with small caps, and Mira has drawn three of them. The other seven exist as names with nothing inside, and an empty glyph prints as a gap. On a proof, a gap looks like a mistake in the text. A plain box the size of a letter looks like what it is: a letter that isn't drawn yet.

So Mira wants a placeholder box in each empty small cap. She could draw seven boxes in three masters by hand, twenty-one rectangles, and she'd rather not.

For five chapters your scripts have read outlines. Today one draws. The tool for it is called a pen, and it works the way you'd tell a child to draw a square without lifting the pencil: put the point here, draw to there, to there, to there, and back home.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • anatomy.py and check_direction.py.
  • The empty e.sc open in a Glyph window. Its width is 500 in each master, from chapter 40.

The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel. The pen commands themselves ran in plain Python, with a pen that draws nowhere, and you'll meet that pen in Step 1.

docs.title: Step 1: A pen that only listens
docs.text:
A pen takes four kinds of order. moveTo puts the point down at a place, without drawing. lineTo draws a straight line from where the pen is to a new place. curveTo draws a curve, and it can wait until chapter 48. closePath draws back to the start and finishes the contour.

Before you draw in a glyph, give those orders to a pen that draws nothing and only writes down what it's told:

from fly.pens import RecordingPen

pen = RecordingPen()
pen.moveTo((60, 0))
pen.lineTo((440, 0))
pen.lineTo((440, 478))
pen.lineTo((60, 478))
pen.closePath()

for order in pen.value:
    print(order)

('moveTo', ((60, 0),))
('lineTo', ((440, 0),))
('lineTo', ((440, 478),))
('lineTo', ((60, 478),))
('closePath', ())

Four corners and a closing. The output is the pen's notebook, one tuple for each order, and its exact layout needn't concern you. What matters is that nothing in FontLab changed. A recording pen is safe to play with, and it's a good way to find out what a piece of drawing code does before you let it near a font.

Look at the double parentheses in pen.moveTo((60, 0)). The outer pair is the slot, as always. The inner pair makes a tuple, the fixed little row from chapter 35, and here it holds an x and a y. A place on the drawing is one thing, so it travels as one thing. If you write pen.moveTo(60, 0), Python will complain that moveTo was given more than it takes, because you handed it two numbers where it wanted one point.

Now read the corners in order. Bottom left, bottom right, top right, top left. Trace it with a finger: you go against the clock. That's deliberate. Friday's rule said the outside of a shape runs counter-clockwise, and a script that draws should follow the convention from its first line.

docs.title: Step 2: The same orders, in a glyph
docs.text:
To draw for real, swap the recording pen for one that writes into a layer. It needs to know which layer:

from fly.pens import FlPen, layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

glyph = pGlyph()
layer = layer_of(glyph.fl, "Regular")

with FlPen(layer, notify="Draw box") as pen:
    pen.moveTo((60, 0))
    pen.lineTo((440, 0))
    pen.lineTo((440, 478))
    pen.lineTo((60, 478))
    pen.closePath()

Run it with e.sc in the Glyph window. A rectangle should appear, 380 units wide and 478 tall, standing on the baseline with 60 units of space on each side.

There are three new things here, and the orders in the middle aren't among them. They're the ones you gave the recording pen.

layer_of(glyph.fl, "Regular") fetches a layer by its master's name. glyph.fl you used once in chapter 29: it's the plain FontLab glyph inside the rich one, which is what the pens package wants. layer_of won't guess. Give it a name that isn't there and it raises a KeyError that tells you so.

FlPen(layer, notify="Draw box") makes a pen for that layer. The notify text is the name of the Undo step. Leave it out and the pen still draws, but FontLab isn't told, and you get no Undo and perhaps no redraw. So always give it.

And with. You know it from chapter 26, where it opened a file and saw to it that the file was closed. It does the same for a pen. The pen doesn't write each line into the glyph as you give the order. It collects them, and when the with block ends it hands the finished contour to FontLab in one go. If something fails inside the block, nothing is written at all.

Check the work with last week's tools. anatomy.py should say:

e.sc, layer Regular
  elements: 1
  contour 1: closed, 4 nodes
  total: 1 contours, 4 nodes

Press Cmd+Z on a Mac, or Ctrl+Z on Windows, and the box should go. Press it only once and look. Then redo, or run the script again.

docs.title: Step 3: Forget to close
docs.text:
Take out the pen.closePath() line, undo the box and run the script:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 7, in <module>
  File ".../site-packages/fontlab_pens/fontlab.py", line 240, in __exit__
    self.close()  # raises PenError on an unfinished contour
    ^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File ".../site-packages/fontlab_pens/fontlab.py", line 229, in close
    raise PenError("Unfinished contour: call closePath() or endPath() before close()")
fontlab_pens.base.PenError: Unfinished contour: call closePath() or endPath() before close()

Read it the way chapter 38 taught. Last line first: an unfinished contour, and it even tells you the two ways to finish one. Then find the last line of the trail that's in a file of yours. It's line 7, the with line. The other frames are inside the pens package, which noticed at the end of the block that you'd started a contour and never ended it.

Then look at the glyph. Nothing was drawn. Three sides of a box would have been an open contour, the very thing you hunted on Thursday, and the pen refused to leave one behind by accident.

Sometimes you want an open contour. For that there's pen.endPath(), which finishes a contour without closing it. Whichever you mean, you have to say it.

docs.title: Step 4: A function that takes a pen
docs.text:
Twenty-one rectangles are coming, so the four corners should be a function. Here's the design question: what should the function be given? It could take a layer and do everything, making the pen and the Undo step too. But then it could never draw two rectangles in one step, or draw into a recording pen for a test. So give it a pen and let it give orders:

def rect(pen, left, bottom, right, top):
    pen.moveTo((left, bottom))
    pen.lineTo((right, bottom))
    pen.lineTo((right, top))
    pen.lineTo((left, top))
    pen.closePath()

Define it in this script. It needs no import, because it doesn't care what kind of pen it gets. Anything that understands moveTo, lineTo and closePath will do. Test it on the pen that only listens:

from fly.pens import RecordingPen

pen = RecordingPen()
rect(pen, 60, 0, 440, 478)
print(len(pen.value))

5

Five orders, with no font involved. The argument order, left, bottom, right, top, is the order box gives its answers in, so the two fit together: whatever box measures, rect can draw.

Now the three masters. Each has its own layer, and a pen writes to one layer, so you need one pen per master, in a loop:

for master in MASTERS:
    layer = layer_of(glyph.fl, master)
    with FlPen(layer, notify="Draw box") as pen:
        rect(pen, 60, 0, 440, 478)

There's one danger left, and it's a new kind for us. Run the script twice and you get two boxes, one on top of the other. They look like one. anatomy.py would say two contours, and a font with doubled outlines prints badly. A script that reads can be run a hundred times without harm. A script that draws can't, unless you make it check first. So before it draws into a layer, it should look whether anything is there:

if glyph.contours(master):
    print(master, "already has outlines, skipped")
    continue

That guard also means the script can never draw a box over a drawn letter. A glyph built from components has no contours of its own and would still get one, so keep to empty glyphs.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is draw_box.py. It defines rect from Step 4 at the top, so it runs by itself.

# Draws a placeholder box in every empty master of the current glyph.
from fly.pens import FlPen, layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
SIDE = 60
TOP = 478


def rect(pen, left, bottom, right, top):
    pen.moveTo((left, bottom))
    pen.lineTo((right, bottom))
    pen.lineTo((right, top))
    pen.lineTo((left, top))
    pen.closePath()


def main():
    glyph = pGlyph()
    drawn = 0
    for master in MASTERS:
        if glyph.contours(master):
            print(f"{master}: already has outlines, skipped")
            continue
        layer = layer_of(glyph.fl, master)
        width = layer.advanceWidth
        with FlPen(layer, notify="Draw box") as pen:
            rect(pen, SIDE, 0, width - SIDE, TOP)
        drawn = drawn + 1
    print(f"{glyph.name}: {drawn} boxes drawn")


main()

With e.sc holding the box you drew in Regular in Step 2:

Regular: already has outlines, skipped
e.sc: 2 boxes drawn

The box's right side isn't typed in. It's worked out from the layer's width, width - SIDE, so the box sits in the middle of whatever width the glyph has, with 60 units either side. layer.advanceWidth is the drawer you changed in chapter 29. TOP is the x-height from chapter 43, a stand-in until Mira decides how tall her small caps are.

Each pen makes its own Undo step, so undoing this run should take one press per master. That is how the pen is built, so see for yourself.

Finish with Friday's check. Run check_direction.py:

366 layers checked, 0 wrong.

That's three more layers than on Friday, and none of them is wrong, because rect goes round against the clock. Mira prints the cookbook page. Where the e.sc should be there's a neat black box, and the art director can see what's coming.

Now think of doing the same for f.sc, and then for g.sc, and you'll feel what's wrong with the script. It does one glyph at a time and you do the walking. Doing every empty small cap in one run is exercise 2, and you have everything you need for it.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A pen draws by orders: moveTo, lineTo and closePath, each place given as an (x, y) tuple. RecordingPen writes the orders down and touches nothing, and FlPen in a with block draws them into a layer as one Undo step, named by notify. A drawing function should take a pen, so it can be tested without a font and combined with others. A script that draws must check what's already there, because running it twice isn't harmless.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Change rect so that it goes round clockwise, draw a box in an empty glyph and run check_direction.py. Then change it back and undo. How many layers were wrong?
  2. Make draw_box.py work on the whole font: loop over font.glyphs, keep the names that end in .sc, and use pGlyph(font, glyph) in place of pGlyph(). Print one line per glyph. Run it twice and check that the second run draws nothing. Then undo the run, so that e.sc is again the only small cap with a box. Chapter 51 counts on that.
  3. Draw a box into a RecordingPen with rect, then print only the points, one per line, by taking them out of pen.value. Each order is a tuple of a name and a tuple of points. You'll need two indexes, as in chapter 35.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: A box is one contour. The glyph that fonts show when a character is missing is a box with a hole in it, and you now know what makes a hole. Chapter 47 draws it from numbers.

docs.title: 47. Draw with numbers
docs.text:
Tuesday. Every font has a glyph called .notdef. It's the one a program shows when the text asks for a character the font doesn't have, and you've seen it a thousand times as a little empty box in the middle of a word. Plum's is a box with four triangles cut out of it, like the back of an envelope.

Ines doesn't like it. Halfmoon's house style is a plain frame, a rectangle with a rectangular hole, and the frame should be as heavy as the letters around it: thin in the Light, thick in the Bold. "As heavy as the l," she says. "Exactly as heavy."

That last word is why this is a job for a script. Mira could draw a frame by eye in three masters. But the rule isn't "about that thick". It's a measurement taken from one glyph and used in another, three times. Yesterday you typed the corners of a box as numbers. Today the numbers come from the font.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • box from chapter 43 and rect from yesterday. You'll write them out again here.
  • A new empty glyph called notdef.new. Make it the way chapter 40 did: put that one name in a text file and run Add Glyphs From List. It will be 500 wide in all three masters.

We draw into a new glyph and leave the real .notdef alone, so that Mira can put the two side by side before anything is replaced.
