The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel. The arithmetic ran in plain Python with a measuring pen, which you'll use too.

docs.title: Step 1: Measure the stem
docs.text:
How heavy is the l? In Plum it's a plain rectangle of four nodes, so its bounding box is the stem itself. Chapter 43 gave you the tool. Here it is again, so this script runs by itself:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph


def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


font = fl.CurrentFont()
for master in ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]:
    left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font["l"], master)
    print(master, right - left)

Light 34.0
Regular 82.0
Bold 132.0

That's three stems and nobody had to type them. If Mira makes the Bold bolder next month, the script will measure the new stem and the frame will follow. A number you type goes out of date when the font changes, and a number you measure doesn't.

Make it a function, since "how heavy is this master" will be asked again:

def stem(font, master="Regular"):
    left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font["l"], master)
    return right - left

It leans on a fact about this font, that the l is a bare stem. In a font whose l has a tail or serifs it would give the wrong answer, and a comment above the function should say so.

docs.title: Step 2: A box inside a box
docs.text:
The frame is two rectangles. The outer one we can write down as we did yesterday: 50 units in from each side of a 500 glyph, standing on the baseline, as tall as a capital. The inner one is the same box, moved in by the stem on all four sides.

Moving in on all four sides is called an inset, and it's four small sums:

def inset(sides, amount):
    left, bottom, right, top = sides
    return left + amount, bottom + amount, right - amount, top - amount

It takes a box as one tuple and hands back a new one. The left and bottom grow by the amount, and the right and top shrink by it. Try it:

outer = (50, 0, 450, 688)
inner = inset(outer, 82)
print(inner)

(132, 82, 368, 606)

Now draw the inner box. rect wants a pen and four numbers. You have a pen and one tuple. The obvious thing fails:

Define yesterday's rect in this script first, then:

from fly.pens import RecordingPen

pen = RecordingPen()
rect(pen, inner)

TypeError: rect() missing 3 required positional arguments: 'bottom', 'right', and 'top'

Read it closely, because it tells you what Python did. It put the pen in the first slot and the whole tuple in the second, the one called left, and then found three slots with nothing in them. A tuple of four numbers is one thing, and it went into one slot.

You could unpack it yourself, with left, bottom, right, top = inner and then four names in the call. Python has a shorter way:

rect(pen, *inner)

The star in front of inner says: open this up and deal its items into the slots, one each. Picture a hand of four cards. Without the star you put the whole hand in one slot, and with it you deal one card to each of four. The call does the same as rect(pen, 132, 82, 368, 606).

The star only works inside the parentheses of a call, and the count has to fit. If you deal a tuple of three into four slots you'll get a "missing" complaint again, about one argument this time.

docs.title: Step 3: The hole runs the other way
docs.text:
On Friday you learned what makes a hole: a contour inside another, running against it. rect goes round counter-clockwise. For the hole we need one that goes clockwise. That's a job for a default argument from chapter 34. Change your rect to this:

def rect(pen, left, bottom, right, top, clockwise=False):
    corners = [(left, bottom), (right, bottom), (right, top), (left, top)]
    if clockwise:
        corners.reverse()
    pen.moveTo(corners[0])
    for corner in corners[1:]:
        pen.lineTo(corner)
    pen.closePath()

Every call written yesterday still works, because they don't mention clockwise and it stays False. The four corners are now a list of tuples. corners.reverse() turns the list back to front where it stands, and the same four corners visited in the opposite order go round the opposite way. The pen moves to the first corner and draws to the others. corners[1:] is a slice, which you've used to take the first few items of a list. With the number before the colon it means "from item 1 to the end", which is everything but the first.

Does it work? You can't see a recording, and you don't want to draw in the font to find out. There's a third kind of pen for this, one that measures. AreaPen adds up the area inside what you draw, and it counts a counter-clockwise contour as positive and a clockwise one as negative:

from fly.pens import AreaPen

outer = (50, 0, 450, 688)
inner = inset(outer, 82)

pen = AreaPen()
rect(pen, *outer)
print(pen.value)
rect(pen, *inner, clockwise=True)
print(pen.value)

275200.0
151536.0

The outer box is 400 by 688, which is 275,200 square units. Then the hole is drawn, and the total goes down, to 151,536. That's the area of the black frame alone, and it went down because the hole ran against the box.

Now take out clockwise=True and run it again:

275200.0
398864.0

The total went up. Both contours ran the same way, the pen counted the middle twice, and in a font the middle would print black. You'd have a solid box where you meant a frame. The measuring pen caught it in two lines, with no font involved.

So that's three pens now, and rect served all three without changing a word. One listens, one measures and one draws. That's what yesterday's decision bought us, the one to hand the function a pen.

docs.title: Step 4: Two contours, one pen
docs.text:
Yesterday each with block held one rectangle. A pen can take as many contours as you like before the block ends, and they all go into the glyph together, as one element and one Undo step:

with FlPen(layer, notify="Draw frame") as pen:
    rect(pen, *outer)
    rect(pen, *inner, clockwise=True)

That's the right grouping here. A frame is one thing to the designer, so one press of Undo should take all of it away, and not leave a solid box behind.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is notdef.py. It writes out box, stem, inset and the new rect at the top, so it runs by itself.

# Draws the Halfmoon frame in every empty master of the current glyph.
# The frame is as heavy as the stem of the l in that master.
from fly import fl
from fly.pens import FlPen, layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
SIDE = 50


def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


def stem(font, master="Regular"):
    left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font["l"], master)
    return right - left


def inset(sides, amount):
    left, bottom, right, top = sides
    return left + amount, bottom + amount, right - amount, top - amount


def rect(pen, left, bottom, right, top, clockwise=False):
    corners = [(left, bottom), (right, bottom), (right, top), (left, top)]
    if clockwise:
        corners.reverse()
    pen.moveTo(corners[0])
    for corner in corners[1:]:
        pen.lineTo(corner)
    pen.closePath()


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    glyph = pGlyph()
    for master in MASTERS:
        if glyph.contours(master):
            print(f"{master}: already has outlines, skipped")
            continue
        layer = layer_of(glyph.fl, master)
        cap_top = box(font, font["H"], master)[3]
        weight = stem(font, master)
        outer = (SIDE, 0, layer.advanceWidth - SIDE, cap_top)
        inner = inset(outer, weight)
        with FlPen(layer, notify="Draw frame") as pen:
            rect(pen, *outer)
            rect(pen, *inner, clockwise=True)
        print(f"{master:<9}stem {weight:>5}  hole {inner}")


main()

With notdef.new in the Glyph window:

Light    stem  34.0  hole (84.0, 34.0, 416.0, 654.0)
Regular  stem  82.0  hole (132.0, 82.0, 368.0, 606.0)
Bold     stem 132.0  hole (182.0, 132.0, 318.0, 556.0)

Only one number in the script is typed in, and that's SIDE. The frame's top is the top of the H in that master, taken from box with [3], the fourth item. Its weight is the stem of the l, and its right side comes from the glyph's own width. Everything else is worked out from those.

Check it three ways, with tools you've built. anatomy.py should report one element with two closed contours of four nodes each. check_direction.py should count three more layers and find none wrong, because the biggest contour in each runs against the clock. And your eyes: flip through the masters in the Glyph window, and the frame should thicken as you go, by the same amount that the l does.

Mira puts .notdef and notdef.new next to each other in a text and shows Ines. "The new one," Ines says. Swapping them isn't a job for this book. It means deleting outlines from a glyph that every export uses, and Mira will do it by hand, in the Glyph window, after a proof.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Numbers that come from the font stay right when the font changes, so measure what you can and type only what you must. A star in a call, *inner, deals the items of a tuple into separate slots. A pen can hold several contours, and they become one element and one Undo step. AreaPen measures what's drawn into it, positive one way round and negative the other, so you can test a drawing function without a font.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. In the Bold the hole is 136 units wide. Make the stem absurd: call inset(outer, 250) and look at the tuple. What's wrong with it? Add a check to notdef.py that refuses to draw, with a clear message, when the hole would have no width or no height.
  2. Use AreaPen to answer a designer's question: what share of the frame's outer box is black, in each master? Divide the frame's area by the box's area and print it as a percentage with one decimal. You need no font for this, only the three stems.
  3. Draw Plum's present .notdef into a RecordingPen: a box and four triangles. To do that, write triangle(pen, a, b, c) in the style of rect, taking three points. Should it take a clockwise argument, or should the caller pass the points in the order it wants? Decide, and say why in a comment.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: So far the pen has only drawn straight lines. The period at the end of this sentence is round. Chapter 48 teaches the pen its fourth order, curveTo, and draws a circle with it.

docs.title: 48. Curves
docs.text:
Wednesday. The cookbook has lists of ingredients, and the publisher's designer wants each line to start with a bullet. Plum has no bullet. It has a period, which is too small and sits on the baseline, and a designer who uses a raised period as a bullet gets a list that looks as if it's stammering.

A bullet is a filled circle. So today the pen learns its fourth order, the one I put off on Monday. A straight line needs one piece of information, which is where to stop. A curve needs three, and most of this chapter is about the other two.

By the end, your script will draw Plum's own period, node for node, from a center and a radius. Then it will draw the bullet.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • box from chapter 43. You'll write it out again here.
  • A new empty glyph called bullet, made with Add Glyphs From List as you made notdef.new yesterday.

The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel. Every number comes from running the pens in plain Python and from that file.

docs.title: Step 1: Three points for one curve
docs.text:
In chapter 42 you counted the nodes of the o and found that a curve costs three: two handles and the on-curve node where it ends. curveTo takes those three, in that order:

from fly.pens import RecordingPen

pen = RecordingPen()
pen.moveTo((0, 60))
pen.curveTo((33, 60), (60, 33), (60, 0))
pen.endPath()

for order in pen.value:
    print(order)

('moveTo', ((0, 60),))
('curveTo', ((33, 60), (60, 33), (60, 0)))
('endPath', ())

That's a quarter of a circle of radius 60, from the top, at 0, 60, round to the right side, at 60, 0. I ended it with endPath, because one arc isn't a closed shape.

Here's how to read the three points. The curve starts where the pen is. The last point, 60, 0, is where it ends. The two in the middle are the handles, and the curve never touches them. The first handle belongs to the start: the pen sets off from 0, 60 heading straight for 33, 60, which is to say due east. The second handle belongs to the end: the pen arrives at 60, 0 as if it had come from 60, 33, which is to say heading due south. In between, the curve bends from one heading to the other.

So a handle says two things. Its direction from its node says which way the curve is heading there. Its distance says how long the curve holds that heading before it gives way. If you've pulled handles in the Glyph window you know both by feel. The pen needs them as numbers.

docs.title: Step 2: How long is a handle?
docs.text:
The directions are simple for a circle. At the top it runs level, and at the side it runs straight down. The distance is the puzzle. Why 33, for a radius of 60?

Let's try other lengths and measure what comes out. Yesterday's measuring pen will do it. Here's a rough circle function with the handle length as a share of the radius, and three shares to try:

from fly.pens import AreaPen


def rough_circle(pen, radius, share):
    h = radius * share
    pen.moveTo((-radius, 0))
    pen.curveTo((-radius, -h), (-h, -radius), (0, -radius))
    pen.curveTo((h, -radius), (radius, -h), (radius, 0))
    pen.curveTo((radius, h), (h, radius), (0, radius))
    pen.curveTo((-h, radius), (-radius, h), (-radius, 0))
    pen.closePath()


for share in [0, 0.5523, 1]:
    pen = AreaPen()
    rough_circle(pen, 60, share)
    print(share, round(pen.value, 1))

0 7200.0
0.5523 11313.0
1 13680.0

Read the function before the numbers. It's four curves: from the left side down to the bottom, on to the right side, up to the top, and back to the left. That's counter-clockwise, as an outside should be. Each curve has a handle h units along from its start and another h units back from its end.

Now the numbers. A true circle of radius 60 has an area of 3.14159 times 60 times 60, which is 11,310. With handles of no length the shape has an area of 7,200. That's a diamond: with nothing to hold a heading, each curve goes straight to the next corner. With handles as long as the radius it's 13,680, a fat cushion on its way to a square. With 0.5523 it's 11,313, three square units off, in a shape of eleven thousand.

That's where 33 came from. It's 60 times 0.5523, rounded. The number 0.5523 is the handle length that brings four curves closest to a circle. Nobody works it out at the desk. Type designers know it as "a bit more than half", and programmers keep it in a constant. We'll call ours KAPPA, which is its usual name, and give it a comment.

A font's curves can't draw an exact circle at all. Four of them come within a hair of one, close enough that nobody has ever seen the difference in print.

docs.title: Step 3: Plum's period, from two numbers
docs.text:
Clean up the rough function, give it a center, and define it in this script:

KAPPA = 0.5523  # handle length for a quarter circle, as a share of the radius


def circle(pen, cx, cy, radius):
    h = radius * KAPPA
    pen.moveTo((cx - radius, cy))
    pen.curveTo((cx - radius, cy - h), (cx - h, cy - radius), (cx, cy - radius))
    pen.curveTo((cx + h, cy - radius), (cx + radius, cy - h), (cx + radius, cy))
    pen.curveTo((cx + radius, cy + h), (cx + h, cy + radius), (cx, cy + radius))
    pen.curveTo((cx - h, cy + radius), (cx - radius, cy + h), (cx - radius, cy))
    pen.closePath()

Plum's period in the Regular master has a box from 41 to 161 across and from −10 to 110 up, as box from chapter 43 will tell you. So its center is at 101, 50 and its radius is 60. Draw that into a recording pen and look at the first curve:

pen = RecordingPen()
circle(pen, 101, 50, 60)
print(pen.value[1])

('curveTo', ((41, 16.862000000000002), (67.862, -10), (101, -10)))

There's a mistake in the function, and nothing complained about it. Look at the handles: 16.862000000000002 and 67.862. Those would go into the font as they are. A font can hold fractions, but a designer's master drawing shouldn't have them by accident. They make nodes that refuse to line up with anything, and some of the formats you'll export to round them anyway, each in its own fashion. The long tail of digits is the computer's own trouble with decimal fractions. It stores numbers in twos, not tens, and most decimal fractions have no exact form there, as a third has none in tens. So a sum that should end in .862 can come back a hair off.

Round the handle length once, where it's made:

    h = round(radius * KAPPA)

Run it again and print all the orders:

('moveTo', ((41, 50),))
('curveTo', ((41, 17), (68, -10), (101, -10)))
('curveTo', ((134, -10), (161, 17), (161, 50)))
('curveTo', ((161, 83), (134, 110), (101, 110)))
('curveTo', ((68, 110), (41, 83), (41, 50)))
('closePath', ())

Now ask Plum for its period:

for node in pGlyph(font, font["period"]).nodes("Regular"):
    print(node.x, node.y)

41.0 50.0
41.0 17.0
68.0 -10.0
101.0 -10.0
134.0 -10.0
161.0 17.0
161.0 50.0
161.0 83.0
134.0 110.0
101.0 110.0
68.0 110.0
41.0 83.0

Compare the two lists. They hold the same twelve points in the same order. The last curve of the recording comes back to 41, 50, which is the first node, so it isn't listed twice.

I didn't arrange that. I wrote the function, ran it and then looked at the font. Whoever drew Plum's period used a circle with handles at a bit more than half, rounded to whole units, starting at the left and going round against the clock. You've rebuilt a glyph of a published typeface from a center and a radius.

docs.title: Step 4: The bullet
docs.text:
A bullet is a bigger circle, higher up. How much bigger is Mira's call, and she says one and a half times the period, sitting at half the height of the lowercase. Both of those can be measured, per master, with the tools from chapter 43 and yesterday:

left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font["period"], master)
radius = round((right - left) / 2 * 1.5)
cy = box(font, font["x"], master)[3] / 2

The period's box is as wide as its circle, so half of that is the radius. The top of the x is the x-height, and half of that is where the center goes.

One warning about round. The Light's period has a radius of 33, and one and a half times 33 is 49.5. round(49.5) gives 50, as you'd expect. But round(2.5) gives 2. When a number is exactly halfway, Python rounds to the nearest even number, so that a long column of rounded halves doesn't drift upward. It matters rarely. When a result is off by one and you can't see why, remember it.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is draw_circle.py. It writes out box, KAPPA and circle at the top, so it runs by itself.

# Draws a bullet in every empty master of the current glyph:
# one and a half times the period, centered at half the x-height.
from fly import fl
from fly.pens import FlPen, layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
TIMES_PERIOD = 1.5


def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


KAPPA = 0.5523  # handle length for a quarter circle, as a share of the radius


def circle(pen, cx, cy, radius):
    h = round(radius * KAPPA)
    pen.moveTo((cx - radius, cy))
    pen.curveTo((cx - radius, cy - h), (cx - h, cy - radius), (cx, cy - radius))
    pen.curveTo((cx + h, cy - radius), (cx + radius, cy - h), (cx + radius, cy))
    pen.curveTo((cx + radius, cy + h), (cx + h, cy + radius), (cx, cy + radius))
    pen.curveTo((cx - h, cy + radius), (cx - radius, cy + h), (cx - radius, cy))
    pen.closePath()


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    glyph = pGlyph()
    for master in MASTERS:
        if glyph.contours(master):
            print(f"{master}: already has outlines, skipped")
            continue
        layer = layer_of(glyph.fl, master)
        left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font["period"], master)
        radius = round((right - left) / 2 * TIMES_PERIOD)
        cx = layer.advanceWidth / 2
        cy = box(font, font["x"], master)[3] / 2
        with FlPen(layer, notify="Draw bullet") as pen:
            circle(pen, cx, cy, radius)
        print(f"{master:<9}radius {radius:>4}  center {cx}, {cy}")


main()

With bullet in the Glyph window:

Light    radius   50  center 250.0, 237.0
Regular  radius   90  center 250.0, 239.0
Bold     radius  114  center 250.0, 241.0

Check it with your own tools. anatomy.py should report one closed contour of 12 nodes. The node count from chapter 42 should say 4 on the line and 8 handles, the price of four curves. check_direction.py should find nothing wrong.

Two things about this bullet aren't finished, and I'd rather say so than have you find out at the printer. It sits in the middle of a glyph 500 units wide, which is far too much room for it. The width came from chapter 40's script and has nothing to do with bullets. Spacing is the subject of Part 4. And it has no Unicode value yet, so typing a bullet in a text won't find it. Chapter 23 told you what that number is for, and Part 5 will set it from a script.

Mira looks at the three masters. The bullets grow with the weight, as the periods do. She sends a page to the publisher's designer with a list of ingredients on it.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: curveTo takes two handles and an end point, where a handle's direction is the curve's heading at that node and its length is how long the heading holds. For a quarter of a circle the handles are 0.5523 of the radius, kept in a named constant. Round the numbers you work out before they become nodes, and remember that round sends an exact half to the even neighbor. A measuring pen lets you try a shape and judge it by a number before any font is touched.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Write oval(pen, cx, cy, rx, ry) for a shape with different radii across and up. It needs two handle lengths, one from each radius. Draw the outer contour of Plum's o with it: the box is 38, −10 to 482, 488. Compare your twelve points with the font's, from chapter 41. The font's contour may start at a different node from yours, so match the points by position, not by their place in the list. The four on-curve nodes match. The handles don't: the font's are longer than yours by more than ten units each. Divide one of the font's handle lengths by its radius. What does a share bigger than 0.5523 do to the shape, and why might a type designer want that in an o?
  2. Use AreaPen to find out how much of an o-sized box an oval fills. Draw oval and rect with the same sides into two measuring pens and divide. The answer is the same for every oval. Multiply it by four and you'll know the number.
  3. Change TIMES_PERIOD to 2, undo the bullets and draw again. Then print the three radii without drawing, by swapping FlPen for a pen that only listens. What did you have to change, and what could stay?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Three periods in a row make an ellipsis, and Plum's three masters space them differently. Chapter 49 draws shapes in a loop, and to do it you'll count with range.

docs.title: 49. Shapes from a loop
docs.text:
Thursday. The cookbook's contents page has a row of dots between each recipe and its page number, and the publisher's designer made the rows by typing ellipses one after another. In the Regular it looks fine. The part titles are set in Bold, and there the dots come in clumps of three with almost no room between one clump and the next.

Ines forwards the page with one line: "Is that us or them?"

It's us. Mira opens the Bold ellipsis in the Glyph window and does the sums on paper, with the period's box from chapter 43 beside her. The dots inside an ellipsis are 108 units apart. The ellipsis is 684 wide, but its third dot ends at 746, which is 62 units past the edge of the glyph. The first dot of the next ellipsis starts 74 units in. So between two ellipses the dots are 12 units apart, where inside they're 108. In the Regular the two numbers are 110 and 104, close enough that nobody saw it.

Mira won't touch the ellipsis today, because a text that ends a sentence with one looks right as it is. The contents page needs something else: a glyph made for standing in rows, with every dot the same distance from the next, whether the next dot is in the same glyph or in the one after. She calls it leader.

Three dots are three circles, and you could call circle three times. Today you'll make the loop do it, and to do that the loop has to count.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • box from chapter 43 and circle from chapter 48. You'll write them out again here.
  • A new empty glyph called leader, made with Add Glyphs From List as in the last two chapters.

The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel. The pen numbers come from running the pens in plain Python.

docs.title: Step 1: A loop that counts
docs.text:
Every loop you've written so far walked along something that was already there: the glyphs of a font, the nodes of a contour, the lines of a file. Sometimes there's nothing to walk along. You want to do a thing three times, and that's all. Python has a small tool for it:

for i in range(3):
    print(i)

0
1
2

range(3) hands the loop three numbers, one per round. Two things about them trip up everybody once. The count starts at 0, as positions in a list do. And 3 itself never arrives: the numbers stop before the one you wrote. Three rounds, numbered 0, 1 and 2.

The name i is a habit that programmers share. It stands for "index", and it's one of the few one-letter names I'll use in this book. When the number means something, give it a better name, as you will in a minute.

If you print a range, it doesn't show its numbers:

print(range(5))
print(list(range(5)))

range(0, 5)
[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]

A range is a recipe for numbers, and it makes each one when the loop asks. Wrap it in list when you want to see them all. I do that whenever I'm not sure what a range will give, and I'm unsure more often than I'd like.

docs.title: Step 2: Where to start, where to stop, how far to jump
docs.text:
The first line of that output says range(0, 5). A range has a start, and when you leave it out the start is 0. You can write it yourself:

print(list(range(1, 6)))

[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

It starts at 1 and stops before 6. And there's a third number, the step, which is how far the count jumps each round:

print(list(range(0, 50, 10)))

[0, 10, 20, 30, 40]

Start at 0, add 10 each time, stop before 50. Once more, 50 itself isn't in the list.

That third form is the one a row of dots needs. In Plum's Regular, the dots of the ellipsis are 230 units apart, center to center. If the first center is at 115, the row is:

print(list(range(115, 690, 230)))

[115, 345, 575]

Those are three x coordinates, one for each dot. The loop variable is a position now, and it'll get the name cx.

docs.title: Step 3: Three dots, and a number that isn't whole
docs.text:
Where do 115 and 690 come from? I'd rather work them out than type them. Call the distance from dot to dot the step, and say how many dots you want:

STEP = 230
COUNT = 3

for cx in range(STEP / 2, COUNT * STEP, STEP):
    print(cx)

The first center is half a step in. The row ends after three whole steps. Run it:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 4, in <module>
TypeError: 'float' object cannot be interpreted as an integer

In chapter 11 you met the two kinds of number: whole numbers, and floats with a decimal point. Dividing with / always gives a float, even when the answer comes out even. 230 / 2 is 115.0. And range counts, so it takes whole numbers and nothing else.

You could wrap the division in int(). There's a shorter way, a second division sign that throws the remainder away and keeps the answer whole:

print(230 / 2)
print(230 // 2)
print(7 // 2)

115.0
115
3

Two slashes: floor division. Seven halves is three and a bit, and the bit is dropped. Change the line to range(STEP // 2, COUNT * STEP, STEP) and the loop prints 115, 345 and 575.

Now hand those positions to the pen. The period in the Regular has a radius of 60 and its center is 50 units above the baseline, as chapter 48 found:

Define circle from chapter 48 in this script first, then:

from fly.pens import RecordingPen

pen = RecordingPen()
for cx in range(STEP // 2, COUNT * STEP, STEP):
    circle(pen, cx, 50, 60)
print(len(pen.value))

18

The recording has eighteen orders. A circle is six of them: one moveTo, four curveTo and one closePath. Three circles came from one line that draws.

docs.title: Step 4: Why half a step
docs.text:
The first dot sits half a step from the left edge for a reason, and the reason is the whole point of the leader glyph.

The dot is 120 wide and the step is 230, so the room between two dots is 110. With the first center at half a step, the first dot starts 55 units in, which is half of that room. If the glyph is three steps wide, 690, the last dot ends 55 units before the right edge. Put two leader glyphs side by side and the room between the last dot of one and the first dot of the next is 55 plus 55. That's 110 again, and the row has the same beat all the way across the page.

So the width of the glyph isn't a matter of taste here. It's the count times the step:

width = COUNT * STEP

Plum's own ellipsis is built another way. Its width is meant to be two steps plus the width of a period. In the Regular that's 460 plus 224, which is 684. In the Bold the steps grew to 260, so the width should be 744. It is still 684, the Regular's width, and the third dot hangs over. That's how the rows on the contents page lost their beat.

docs.title: Step 5: Draw it in three masters
docs.text:
The step is different in each master: 160 in the Light, 230 in the Regular, 260 in the Bold. Those are the distances in Plum's ellipsis. I read them in the Glyph window, and chapter 52 will show you how a script reads them. For today they go in a dictionary, with the master names as keys:

STEPS = {"Light": 160, "Regular": 230, "Bold": 260}

The size of the dot and its height come from the period, as they did for the bullet:

font = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph = pGlyph(font, font["leader"])
for master in MASTERS:
    step = STEPS[master]
    left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font["period"], master)
    radius = round((right - left) / 2)
    cy = round((bottom + top) / 2)
    layer = layer_of(glyph.fl, master)
    with FlPen(layer, notify="Draw leader") as pen:
        for cx in range(step // 2, COUNT * step, step):
            circle(pen, cx, cy, radius)

This time the script finds leader by name, so it doesn't matter which glyph you're looking at. The loop over masters has the loop over positions inside it. That's the nesting from chapter 41, and the inner loop runs three times for each master. The with block sits between the two, so each master gets one pen, and all three dots of a master are one step in Edit > Undo.

docs.title: Step 6: Make the width fit
docs.text:
The dots are in, but the glyph is still 500 wide, the width chapter 40's script gave every new glyph. In the Regular the third dot ends at 635, well outside it.

You changed a width once before, in chapter 29, and the pattern was: put the change in a small function, then hand that function to history.commit so that FontLab records one Undo step. You'll set widths often from here on, so make the pattern a function. Define it in this script:

def set_width(glyph, layer, width, title="Set width"):
    def change():
        layer.advanceWidth = width

    package = scripting.current_package()
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    history.commit(title, [layer], [glyph.fl], change, operation="geometry", facts=facts)

There's a function inside a function here, which is new. change is written inside set_width, and it can see the boxes of the function around it: layer and width aren't handed to it, yet it uses them. In chapter 29 widen did the same with boxes at the top of the script. A function looks for a name in its own boxes first and then in the place where it was written.

The script needs the two import lines from safe_edit.py at its top for this:

import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

In the script it's one more line per master, after the with block:

    set_width(glyph, layer, COUNT * step, "Fit leader")

Run the script with a Font window in front. FontLab keeps a separate Undo list for the Glyph window, and how this call behaves there is untested.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is dot_row.py. It writes out box, circle and set_width at the top, so it runs by itself.

# Draws a row of COUNT dots in every empty master of the glyph "leader"
# and fits the width, so that rows of leaders keep an even beat.
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl
from fly.pens import FlPen, layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
STEPS = {"Light": 160, "Regular": 230, "Bold": 260}
COUNT = 3


def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


KAPPA = 0.5523  # handle length for a quarter circle, as a share of the radius


def circle(pen, cx, cy, radius):
    h = round(radius * KAPPA)
    pen.moveTo((cx - radius, cy))
    pen.curveTo((cx - radius, cy - h), (cx - h, cy - radius), (cx, cy - radius))
    pen.curveTo((cx + h, cy - radius), (cx + radius, cy - h), (cx + radius, cy))
    pen.curveTo((cx + radius, cy + h), (cx + h, cy + radius), (cx, cy + radius))
    pen.curveTo((cx - h, cy + radius), (cx - radius, cy + h), (cx - radius, cy))
    pen.closePath()


def set_width(glyph, layer, width, title="Set width"):
    def change():
        layer.advanceWidth = width

    package = scripting.current_package()
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    history.commit(title, [layer], [glyph.fl], change, operation="geometry", facts=facts)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    glyph = pGlyph(font, font["leader"])
    for master in MASTERS:
        if glyph.contours(master):
            print(f"{master}: already has outlines, skipped")
            continue
        step = STEPS[master]
        left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font["period"], master)
        radius = round((right - left) / 2)
        cy = round((bottom + top) / 2)
        layer = layer_of(glyph.fl, master)
        with FlPen(layer, notify="Draw leader") as pen:
            for cx in range(step // 2, COUNT * step, step):
                circle(pen, cx, cy, radius)
        width = COUNT * step
        set_width(glyph, layer, width, "Fit leader")
        print(f"{master:<9}{COUNT} dots  step {step}  radius {radius}  width {width}")


main()

Light    3 dots  step 160  radius 33  width 480
Regular  3 dots  step 230  radius 60  width 690
Bold     3 dots  step 260  radius 76  width 780

Check it with bounds.py. In the Regular the box of leader should run from 55 to 635, in a glyph 690 wide: 55 units of room on each side. In the Light it's 47 on each side, and in the Bold 54. The two sides match in every master, and that's the test. Then type a row of leaders in a text, in the Bold, and look for the clumps.

The script makes six steps in Edit > Undo, a drawing and a width for each master. That's how the two calls are designed. If your copy shows fewer or more, believe your copy.

Mira types a line of leader glyphs under the row of ellipses and sends both to Ines. Ines writes back in a minute: "Second one. Tell the designer how to type it." That's a fair point. A glyph with no Unicode value can't be typed, and Part 5 will deal with it. For now the designer picks it from the Glyphs panel of the layout program.

On Oskar's sheet nothing gets crossed out. Mira adds a line of her own at the bottom, in pencil: "Bold ellipsis: third dot outside the glyph."

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: range makes a loop count when there's nothing to walk along: one number is where to stop, two are start and stop, three add the step, and the stop number itself never arrives. range takes whole numbers only, and // divides without leaving a decimal point. A loop variable can be a coordinate, so one drawing line makes as many shapes as the range has numbers, and the width of a glyph can be worked out from what's in it: here, count times step, so that the rhythm carries from one glyph into the next.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Before you run each of these, write down what you expect: list(range(4)), list(range(2, 9, 3)), list(range(10, 0, -3)), list(range(5, 0)). The third counts down. The fourth gives an empty list and no error, and a loop over it runs zero times. Why is that worth remembering when a script seems to do nothing?
  2. Change COUNT to 5, undo the drawing and run dot_row.py again. The widths should be 800, 1150 and 1300. Which lines of the script did you have to touch? Then work out by hand, for each master, how wide Plum's ellipsis would have to be for rows of it to keep the beat, and compare with the 513, 684 and 684 it has.
  3. Draw a colon without typing a single y coordinate. Make an empty glyph colon.new, and use range with a step to place two dots, one above the other, at the heights of Plum's own colon: the centers in the Regular are at 50 and 428. You'll need a range that goes up the y axis. What are its three numbers?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The part titles are set in capitals, and the art director says the dashes between them hang too low. Chapter 50 makes a raised copy of each dash: shifting, scaling and slanting outlines that are already there.

docs.title: 50. Move, scale, slant
docs.text:
Friday. The cookbook's part titles are set in Bold capitals: SOUPS, then a dash, then STEWS. The art director has circled the dash on the proof and written next to it: "Hangs low. Can it sit in the middle?"

She's right, and it isn't a mistake in Plum. A hyphen is drawn for lowercase text, so it sits near the middle of the x-height. Between capitals it looks as if it slipped. Type families solve this with a second set of dashes that sit higher, and the usual name for one is the old name plus .case.

Mira could draw three rectangles; she knows how since chapter 46. But the dashes exist already, with the right length and the right weight in every master. All a raised dash needs is the old outline, moved up. Today you'll take an outline that's there and put it through a rule that changes every point: up, bigger, mirrored, slanted.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • box from chapter 43 and set_width from chapter 49. You'll write them out again here.
  • Three new empty glyphs: hyphen.case, endash.case and emdash.case. Put the three names in a text file and run Add Glyphs From List.

Steps 1 to 5 use no font at all, so you can see every number. They ran in plain Python. Step 6 and the section after it were not run in FontLab 9.

docs.title: Step 1: A rule for points
docs.text:
Here is Plum's hyphen in the Regular, as a recording. It's a rectangle, 236 units long and 48 thick:

from fly.pens import RecordingPen

hyphen = RecordingPen()
hyphen.moveTo((56, 246))
hyphen.lineTo((292, 246))
hyphen.lineTo((292, 294))
hyphen.lineTo((56, 294))
hyphen.closePath()

Now the rule. The pens call it a transform:

from fly.pens import Transform

up = Transform().translate(0, 74)
print(up)
print(up.transformPoint((56, 246)))

<Transform [1 0 0 1 0 74]>
(56, 320)

Transform() with nothing after it is the rule that changes nothing. .translate(0, 74) makes a new rule from it: add 0 to every x and 74 to every y. "Translate" is the mathematician's word for shift. transformPoint tries the rule on one point, and the point comes back 74 higher.

A transform prints as six numbers. The last two are the shift. You'll see what the first four do in a moment.

docs.title: Step 2: Put the rule between two pens
docs.text:
A recording can do more than show its orders. It can give them again, to any other pen: recording.replay(pen) plays the list back, order by order, as if you were drawing a second time. And a TransformPen is a pen that stands in the middle. It takes each order, applies the rule to the points, and passes the order on to the pen behind it:

from fly.pens import TransformPen

raised = RecordingPen()
hyphen.replay(TransformPen(raised, up))
for order in raised.value:
    print(order)

('moveTo', ((56, 320),))
('lineTo', ((292, 320),))
('lineTo', ((292, 368),))
('lineTo', ((56, 368),))
('closePath', ())

Read the middle line from the inside out. raised is the pen at the end. TransformPen(raised, up) is a pen that shifts and then hands over to raised. And hyphen.replay(...) plays the old orders into that. The x values are untouched and every y is 74 more.

The pen at the end doesn't have to be a recording. Put an FlPen there and the raised hyphen lands in a glyph. That's step 6. Until then I'll use a short function that shows where the four corners go:

def corners(rule):
    out = RecordingPen()
    hyphen.replay(TransformPen(out, rule))
    print([order[1][0] for order in out.value[:-1]])

order[1] is the tuple of points in an order, and [0] takes the first of them. The slice [:-1] leaves out the closePath, which has no points.

docs.title: Step 3: Bigger, flatter, mirrored
docs.text:
scale multiplies:

corners(Transform().scale(2))

[(112, 492), (584, 492), (584, 588), (112, 588)]

The hyphen is twice as long and twice as thick. It has also moved: it began at 56 and now begins at 112. Scaling multiplies every coordinate, so everything moves away from the point 0, 0, the origin of the glyph. A shape that should grow in place needs a shift as well, and step 5 comes back to that.

Give scale two numbers and the two directions get different treatment:

corners(Transform().scale(1, 0.5))

[(56.0, 123.0), (292.0, 123.0), (292.0, 147.0), (56.0, 147.0)]

Same length, half the thickness, and half the height above the baseline too. The numbers have turned into floats, because 0.5 is one.

And a negative number mirrors:

corners(Transform().scale(-1, 1))

[(-56, 246), (-292, 246), (-292, 294), (-56, 294)]

Every x has changed its sign. The hyphen now lies to the left of the origin, outside its glyph. Something else has happened that the corners don't show. Ask the AreaPen from chapter 47:

from fly.pens import AreaPen

before = AreaPen()
hyphen.replay(before)
after = AreaPen()
hyphen.replay(TransformPen(after, Transform().scale(-1, 1)))
print(before.value, after.value)

11328.0 -11328.0

The area has changed its sign. The contour ran counter-clockwise and its mirror image runs clockwise, as the hands of a clock do in a mirror. In chapter 45 direction decided what's black and what's a hole. A mirrored glyph needs every contour reversed afterwards, and a script that forgets this makes glyphs that look fine alone and go wrong where shapes overlap.

docs.title: Step 4: Slant, and a unit that isn't degrees
docs.text:
An oblique is a slanted roman, and twelve degrees is a common slant. skew does it:

corners(Transform().skew(12))

[(-100.42154245074886, 246.0), (135.57845754925114, 246.0), (105.05718097349526, 294.0), (-130.94281902650474, 294.0)]

No error, and nonsense. The hyphen has jumped 156 units to the left, and its top is further left than its bottom, so it leans backwards.

The number was read, but not as degrees. skew and rotate measure angles in radians, the unit mathematicians prefer, in which half a turn is 3.14159 and a bit. Twelve radians is nearly two full turns. Nothing in Python can know that you meant degrees, so there's no complaint. This is the silent kind of mistake again, and the cure is the same as always: look at the numbers that come out.

Python converts for you. The tool lives in a module that comes with Python, called math:

import math

print(math.radians(12))
corners(Transform().skew(math.radians(12)))

0.20943951023931956
[(108.28891417082545, 246.0), (344.2889141708254, 246.0), (354.4916291309865, 294.0), (118.4916291309865, 294.0)]

That's a slant. The bottom edge has moved 52 units to the right and the top edge 62: the higher a point, the further it goes. The y values are untouched.

The long decimals are honest, but a font wants whole numbers. There's a pen for that as well, and it goes in the chain like the other one:

from fly.pens import RoundingPen

out = RecordingPen()
hyphen.replay(TransformPen(RoundingPen(out), Transform().skew(math.radians(12))))
print([order[1][0] for order in out.value[:-1]])

[(108, 246), (344, 246), (354, 294), (118, 294)]

Three pens in a row now: slant, then round, then record.

docs.title: Step 5: Two rules in one, and which goes first
docs.text:
Rules can be chained with dots. The order matters, and it's the opposite of what you'd guess:

print(Transform().translate(100, 0).scale(2))
corners(Transform().translate(100, 0).scale(2))
print(Transform().scale(2).translate(100, 0))
corners(Transform().scale(2).translate(100, 0))

<Transform [2 0 0 2 100 0]>
[(212, 492), (684, 492), (684, 588), (212, 588)]
<Transform [2 0 0 2 200 0]>
[(312, 492), (784, 492), (784, 588), (312, 588)]

In the first chain the corner 56 became 212. That's 56 times 2, plus 100: scaled first, then shifted, though translate is written first. In the second chain 56 became 312, which is 56 plus 100, times 2. The rule written last touches the point first. Read a chain from right to left.

You can see it in the six numbers too. The first four hold the scaling and slanting, the last two the shift, and in the second chain the shift of 100 was itself doubled to 200.

I don't trust myself to remember the direction. I try a chain on one point with transformPoint before I let it near a font.

docs.title: Step 6: Raise the dashes
docs.text:
How far up? The art director said "in the middle", so work it out: the middle of the capitals minus the middle of the dash. box from chapter 43 gives both.

cap_top = box(font, font["H"], master)[3]
left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font["hyphen"], master)
shift = round(cap_top / 2 - (bottom + top) / 2)

In the Regular that's 344 minus 270, which is 74.

The source outline comes out of FontLab with draw, the reader that belongs to the pens. It's the opposite of FlPen: it walks a layer and gives the orders to any pen you hand it. Then the chain is the one from step 2, with an FlPen at the end:

recording = RecordingPen()
draw(layer_of(source.fl, master), recording)
with FlPen(target_layer, notify="Raise dash") as pen:
    recording.replay(TransformPen(pen, Transform().translate(0, shift)))

A pen doesn't carry the advance width, so the script copies that with set_width from chapter 49. Both are written out in the whole script below, so it runs by itself.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Save this as raise_dashes.py.

# Makes raised copies of the dashes for setting between capitals.
# The target glyphs must exist and be empty: hyphen.case and so on.
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl
from fly.pens import FlPen, RecordingPen, Transform, TransformPen, layer_of
from fly.pens.fontlab import draw
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
DASHES = ["hyphen", "endash", "emdash"]
SUFFIX = ".case"


def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


def set_width(glyph, layer, width, title="Set width"):
    def change():
        layer.advanceWidth = width

    package = scripting.current_package()
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    history.commit(title, [layer], [glyph.fl], change, operation="geometry", facts=facts)


def raise_copy(font, name, master):
    source = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    target = pGlyph(font, font[name + SUFFIX])
    if target.contours(master):
        print(f"{target.name} {master}: already has outlines, skipped")
        return
    cap_top = box(font, font["H"], master)[3]
    left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font[name], master)
    shift = round(cap_top / 2 - (bottom + top) / 2)
    source_layer = layer_of(source.fl, master)
    target_layer = layer_of(target.fl, master)
    recording = RecordingPen()
    draw(source_layer, recording)
    with FlPen(target_layer, notify="Raise dash") as pen:
        recording.replay(TransformPen(pen, Transform().translate(0, shift)))
    set_width(target, target_layer, source_layer.advanceWidth, "Fit dash")
    print(f"{target.name:<13}{master:<9}up {shift}")


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    for name in DASHES:
        for master in MASTERS:
            raise_copy(font, name, master)


main()

hyphen.case  Light    up 74
hyphen.case  Regular  up 74
hyphen.case  Bold     up 74
endash.case  Light    up 74
endash.case  Regular  up 74
endash.case  Bold     up 74
emdash.case  Light    up 74
emdash.case  Regular  up 74
emdash.case  Bold     up 74

Nine times 74. I expected three different numbers and went to check. In Plum the dashes get thicker from Light to Bold, 28 units, then 48, then 84, but they thicken around the same middle line, 270, and the capitals are 688 tall in all three masters. So the sum comes out the same each time. The script still works it out per master, because the next family won't be so regular.

Check with bounds.py: hyphen.case in the Regular should have a box from 56, 320 to 292, 368 and a width of 348. Then type H, hyphen.case, H in a text and look.

Run it from a Font window, as in chapter 49, and expect two steps in Edit > Undo for each master of each glyph. That's how the pen is built.

Mira sends the art director a line of capitals with the new dashes. The answer is a thumbs-up and a question: "How do I type those?" It's the same question the leader dots got. A .case glyph has no Unicode value of its own. It's meant to be swapped in by an OpenType feature when text is set in capitals, and features are Part 5. Mira writes "case feature" on a sticky note and puts it next to the screen.

docs.title: Move what's already there
docs.text:
Everything above made a copy. The pens always add: put a shifted hyphen into the hyphen's own layer and you have two hyphens, one on top of the other. Sometimes you want the original to move, and that takes another tool.

The fontlabapp package has one, built for its own panels. It takes the same six numbers a transform prints, as a plain tuple, and it moves the nodes in place as one Undo step. The listing below follows the package's source and was not run, so treat it as a sketch to try on the practice font and nowhere else:

import fly.ap.contours.transform.model as transform_model
import fly.ap.contours.writer as outline_writer

matrix = (1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 12)      # the six numbers: shift up by 12
rows = transform_model.transform_changes(layer, matrix, False, "")
edits = [row.edit for row in rows if row.edit is not None]
outline_writer.apply_work([(glyph.fl, layer, edits)], "Shift up 12", facts,
                          transform_model.TransformEditor())

facts is what history.scan_auto_facts(package) returns, as in set_width. The tool leaves the advance width alone and it skips components, so a glyph built from other glyphs stays where it is. By the package's source it also refuses a glyph that automatic glyphs borrow, unless allow_bases=True is added to the call. Chapter 55 comes back to that keyword.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A transform is a rule that turns one point into another: translate shifts, scale multiplies, skew slants. A TransformPen stands between two pens and applies the rule to everything that passes, so reading an outline with draw and replaying it through a transform makes a changed copy. Scaling works from the origin, a negative scale mirrors and flips the direction, and angles are in radians, which math.radians makes from degrees. In a chain of rules the last one written acts first.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Mirror the hyphen in place. The rule is Transform().translate(348, 0).scale(-1, 1), where 348 is the hyphen's width. Before you run it, read the chain from right to left and work out where the corner 56, 246 goes. Then check with corners. Why does a mirrored hyphen look the same as the hyphen, and what's different about it all the same?
  2. Scale the hyphen to twice its size without letting it move away: the middle of the result should be where the middle of the original was, at 174, 270. You need a scale(2) and one translate. Work out the shift on paper first.
  3. Make a slanted copy. Add an empty glyph hyphen.slant and change raise_dashes.py into a script that replays the hyphen through skew(math.radians(12)) and a RoundingPen. Where does the RoundingPen go in the chain, and what would be lost if you rounded before slanting?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Ines wants the small caps to stop being boxes. Chapter 51 starts each of them as a copy of its capital, and shows the difference between copying a thing and giving it a second name.

docs.title: 51. Copy a glyph
docs.text:
Monday, the tenth week. The small caps have been ten empty glyphs since chapter 40, and one of them holds a placeholder box. The art director's proof page is due on Thursday.

Nobody draws small caps from nothing. You start from the capitals, shrink them to the height of the lowercase, and then spend a week putting back the weight that the shrinking took away. Mira knows the week of drawing is hers. The shrinking is a chore, and chores go to a script.

So today a script copies each capital into its small-cap glyph, scaled down. That part is short, because chapter 50 did nearly the same thing with the dashes. The longer part of this chapter is about the word "copy" itself. Python uses it more strictly than people do, and the difference bites everybody once.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • box from chapter 43 and set_width from chapter 49. You'll write them out again here.
  • The small-cap glyphs from chapters 8 and 40: a.sc to h.sc, zero.sc and one.sc. Leave the box in e.sc where it is. It has a part to play. Every other .sc glyph has to be empty in all three masters. If you drew boxes in f.sc or g.sc, did exercise 2 of chapter 46 without undoing it, or left a practice sketch from chapters 44 and 45, delete those outlines first. If you don't, your run will say already has outlines, skipped where this chapter shows a draft.

The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel. The pen numbers come from running the pens in plain Python.

docs.title: Step 1: Two names, one list
docs.text:
Mira starts with a list of the capitals she wants and makes a second list for the drafts:

caps = ["A", "B", "C"]
drafts = caps
drafts.append("D")
print(drafts)
print(caps)

['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']
['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']

She added D to drafts, and caps has it too. Nothing went wrong and no error came, which is why this one is hard to find when it happens in a long script.

Since chapter 5 I've told you that a variable is a box with a label, and that = puts a thing in the box. That picture has carried you through fifty chapters, and here it gives out. The line drafts = caps didn't build a second list. It tied a second label to the list that was already there. There's one list, and it has two names. Whatever you do to it through one name, you see through the other.

Python can tell you whether two names mean the same thing. You've used the word before, in is None:

print(drafts is caps)

True

docs.title: Step 2: A real copy
docs.text:
To get a second list, you have to ask for one:

caps = ["A", "B", "C"]
drafts = list(caps)
drafts.append("D")
print(drafts)
print(caps)
print(drafts is caps)

['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']
['A', 'B', 'C']
False

list(caps) walks along the old list and builds a new one with the same things in it. Now there are two lists, and they go their own ways. You'll also see caps.copy(), which does the same job. Dictionaries and sets have dict(...), set(...) and their own .copy().

Why did you never run into this with numbers?

a = 5
b = a
b = b + 1
print(a, b)

5 6

Because b + 1 makes a new number, and b = ties the label b to that new number. Nobody changed the 5. You can't change a 5. A number or a piece of text can only be replaced, and replacing moves one label. A list can be changed in place, with append, with reverse, with names[0] = ..., and a change in place is seen through every label the list has.

So the rule is short. = never copies. With numbers and text you can't tell. With lists, dictionaries and sets you can.

docs.title: Step 3: A function gets a label too
docs.text:
The same thing happens when you hand a list to a function. Here's a helper that turns names into small-cap names:

def with_suffix(names):
    for i in range(len(names)):
        names[i] = names[i] + ".sc"
    return names

caps = ["A", "B"]
small = with_suffix(caps)
print(small)
print(caps)

['A.sc', 'B.sc']
['A.sc', 'B.sc']

Inside the function, names is one more label on the caller's list. The function wrote into it, and the caller's list of capitals is gone. A function that changes what it's given, without saying so in its name, is a trap for whoever calls it. The honest version builds a new list and leaves its input alone:

def with_suffix(names):
    return [name + ".sc" for name in names]

A comprehension always makes a new list. That's one more reason I reach for one.

docs.title: Step 4: The same question in a font
docs.text:
Now look at a glyph with the same eyes. When a small cap comes from a capital, there are two ways to get it there.

One is a real copy. The script reads the outline of A, and draws the same shape, smaller, into a.sc. From then on the two have nothing to do with each other. If Mira moves a node in A next month, a.sc stays as it was.

The other is a second label. A glyph can hold a component: a note that says "show the outline of that other glyph here". Plum's eacute has two of them, as you saw in chapter 41, and when the e changes, the eacute changes with it. Chapter 52 is about those.

Which do you want for small caps? A copy, and for a plain reason: the small caps are going to be redrawn. They need their own nodes, because every one of them will be moved. A component can be shifted and scaled, but you can't thicken its stems.

docs.title: Step 5: How much smaller
docs.text:
A small cap stands about as tall as the lowercase x. In the Regular, the top of x is at 478 and the top of H is at 688, as chapter 43 found. The factor is one divided by the other, with box from that chapter:

x_top = box(font, font["x"], master)[3]
cap_top = box(font, font["H"], master)[3]
factor = x_top / cap_top
print(round(factor, 3))

0.695

box gives four numbers, and [3] picks the last one, the top. The factor differs a little by master, because the x-height does: 0.689 in the Light, 0.695 in the Regular and 0.701 in the Bold. So the script works it out for each master and nobody types it.

In chapter 50, scaling was a nuisance, because it's measured from the origin and the hyphen slid away from its place. Here that's what you want. The origin is the left end of the baseline. Scaling from there keeps the letter on the baseline and shrinks its left sidebearing by the same factor as the letter. Scale the width too, and the right sidebearing follows.

The copy itself is the chain from chapter 50, with one pen more:

recording = RecordingPen()
draw(layer_of(source.fl, master), recording)
with FlPen(layer, notify="Small-cap draft") as pen:
    recording.replay(TransformPen(RoundingPen(pen), Transform().scale(factor)))

Read it from the inside out. pen writes into the layer. RoundingPen(pen) rounds each coordinate to a whole number and hands it on. TransformPen(...) scales and hands on to that. The capital's A runs from 13 to 585 and up to 688 in the Regular. Its draft runs from 9 to 406 and up to 478, on the x-height to the unit.

docs.title: Step 6: Which capital for which name
docs.text:
The script gets small-cap names and has to find the capital for each. a.sc comes from A. For a one-letter name that's two string methods you know:

def source_name(name):
    base = name.removesuffix(SUFFIX)
    if len(base) == 1:
        return base.upper()
    return None

zero.sc and one.sc have longer names and get None. That's on purpose. Small-cap figures aren't shrunken figures, and Mira hasn't decided what they'll be.

One more thing, and it comes straight from step 1. The script loops over small-cap names while it draws into the font. I don't loop over font.glyphs for that. I collect the names into a list of my own first, and loop over the list. Today nothing gets added to the font, so it wouldn't matter. In chapter 53 glyphs will be added, and a loop over a list that grows under it is a bad afternoon.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is make_sc_drafts.py. It writes out box and set_width at the top, so it runs by itself:

# Fills every empty one-letter small-cap glyph with a scaled copy of its
# capital and scales the width to match. Drafts only: the stems come out thin.
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl
from fly.pens import FlPen, RecordingPen, RoundingPen, Transform, TransformPen, layer_of
from fly.pens.fontlab import draw
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
SUFFIX = ".sc"


def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


def set_width(glyph, layer, width, title="Set width"):
    def change():
        layer.advanceWidth = width

    package = scripting.current_package()
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    history.commit(title, [layer], [glyph.fl], change, operation="geometry", facts=facts)


def source_name(name):
    base = name.removesuffix(SUFFIX)
    if len(base) == 1:
        return base.upper()
    return None


def factor_for(font, master):
    x_top = box(font, font["x"], master)[3]
    cap_top = box(font, font["H"], master)[3]
    return x_top / cap_top


def draft(font, name, capital, master):
    source = pGlyph(font, font[capital])
    target = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    factor = factor_for(font, master)
    recording = RecordingPen()
    source_layer = layer_of(source.fl, master)
    draw(source_layer, recording)
    layer = layer_of(target.fl, master)
    with FlPen(layer, notify="Small-cap draft") as pen:
        recording.replay(TransformPen(RoundingPen(pen), Transform().scale(factor)))
    width = round(source_layer.advanceWidth * factor)
    set_width(target, layer, width, "Fit small cap")
    return width


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    names = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs if glyph.name.endswith(SUFFIX)]
    for name in names:
        capital = source_name(name)
        if capital is None or font[capital] is None:
            print(f"{name:<9}no capital to copy, skipped")
            continue
        target = pGlyph(font, font[name])
        if any([target.contours(master) for master in MASTERS]):
            print(f"{name:<9}already has outlines, skipped")
            continue
        widths = [draft(font, name, capital, master) for master in MASTERS]
        print(f"{name:<9}from {capital}  widths {widths[0]} {widths[1]} {widths[2]}")


main()

a.sc     from A  widths 382 414 418
b.sc     from B  widths 339 359 362
c.sc     from C  widths 410 431 435
d.sc     from D  widths 445 462 466
e.sc     already has outlines, skipped
f.sc     from F  widths 285 319 322
g.sc     from G  widths 423 454 457
h.sc     from H  widths 422 467 471
zero.sc  no capital to copy, skipped
one.sc   no capital to copy, skipped

The order of your lines follows the order of glyphs in your font, so it may differ from mine.

e.sc was skipped because the box from chapter 46 is still in it. The script won't draw over what's there. A pen adds and never replaces, so drawing again would stack an E on the box. Delete the box by hand in all three masters, run the script again, and you get one new line, e.sc from E widths 305 337 340, with nine lines of "skipped" around it. The guard you wrote for the placeholder script makes this one safe to run twice.

Check a.sc with bounds.py: in the Regular the box should run from 9 to 406 across and from 0 to 478 up, in a glyph 414 wide.

Then look at the drafts next to the lowercase, and you'll see what Mira saw. They're the right height and too light. The stem of the capital I is 82 units wide in the Regular, and so is the stem of the lowercase l. Scaled by 0.695, a capital stem comes out 57 wide. Next to an 82-unit lowercase stem that's a different weight. The overshoot shrank as well: the round capitals go 10 units over the line and the drafts go 7.

That's the week of drawing, and no script in this book will do it. But Mira starts the week with every draft the right height and on the baseline, with matching sidebearings in three masters. And when she touches a node in a.sc, the capital A doesn't move, because the draft is a copy.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: = ties a label to a thing and never copies it, so with a list, a dictionary or a set, two labels mean one thing, and a change through either shows through both. is tells you whether two names mean the same thing, and list(...) or .copy() makes a second one. A function gets a label on what you hand it, so a tidy function builds a new list and leaves its input alone. In a font the same choice has two names: an outline drawn again is a copy, and a component is a second label.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Predict, then run: a = [1, 2], b = a, b = b + [3], print(a, b). Then the same with b += [3] in place of the third line. One of them changes a. Which, and what does that tell you about += on a list?
  2. A dictionary holds lists: groups = {"round": ["O", "C"]}. Write mine = dict(groups), append "G" to mine["round"], and print both dictionaries. The copy is only one level deep. Say in a sentence what dict(...) copied and what it didn't.
  3. Make an empty glyph i.sc, run the script, and read the Regular width of the draft before you look: the capital I is 228 wide. Then measure the draft's stem with bounds.py and work out how many units Mira has to add to bring it to 82.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Oskar's sheet has two lines about glyphs that are built from other glyphs. Chapter 52 opens a component, reads which glyph it points to and how far it's shifted, and crosses one of those lines out.

docs.title: 52. Borrowed shapes
docs.text:
Tuesday. The art director's last note on the Bold was about the lowercase a: the bowl closes up at small sizes. Mira opened the counter a little this morning, eight units, and sent Ines a proof.

Ines calls back. "Good. The German edition is next. You did the ä as well? And the Swedish one with the ring?"

Mira hasn't touched them. She double-clicks adieresis, ready to do the same eight units again, and the bowl is already open. In aring too, and in agrave. She didn't change those glyphs, and they changed.

You know why, roughly. In chapter 41 you found that eacute has two elements and nothing drawn in it, and I said each element points at another glyph. Chapter 51 called that a second label. Today you'll open those pointers and read them: which glyph, and shifted by how much. Then you'll ask the whole font, and the first open line on Oskar's sheet gets crossed out: List the glyphs that are built from other glyphs.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The chapters on loops and dictionaries from Part 2.
  • Nothing in the font changes today. Every script in this chapter reads only.

The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel. So were the names, shifts and counts.

docs.title: Step 1: Ask an element what it borrows
docs.text:
A layer keeps its elements in layer.shapes, as chapter 41 showed. Some of those are drawings and some are components. Fly has a small module that picks out the components and reads them:

import fly.ap.components.writer as parts
from fly import fl
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph = pGlyph(font, font["adieresis"])
layer = layer_of(glyph.fl, "Regular")
for part in parts.components(layer):
    print(parts.base_of(part), parts.offset(part))

a (0.0, 0.0)
dieresis (-12.0, 0.0)

The first line of the script gives a long module name a short one, parts, as you did with history in chapter 29. The module is called writer because most of what's in it changes components. Today you use only the three functions that read.

parts.components(layer) gives a list of the layer's components, in order. parts.base_of(part) gives the name of the glyph a component points at. FontLab calls that glyph the base of the component. parts.offset(part) gives the shift, as a pair of numbers: across and up.

So the ä in the Regular is two notes. One says "show a here, where it is". The other says "show dieresis here, 12 units to the left". There's no outline in the glyph. When Mira opened the bowl of a, there was nothing in adieresis to update. FontLab draws it from the a every time it shows it.

docs.title: Step 2: A pair of numbers
docs.text:
parts.offset gave (-12.0, 0.0): two numbers in parentheses. You've had four numbers that way from box in chapter 43, and you took them apart with four names on the left of the =. A pair comes apart the same way:

dx, dy = parts.offset(part)
print(round(dx), round(dy))

-12 0

The d in dx is a habit from mathematics. It stands for "difference": how far across, compared with where the base glyph has its outline. The numbers are floats, so round tidies them for printing.

The shift belongs to a layer, as everything about an outline does. Ask all three masters:

for master in ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]:
    layer = layer_of(glyph.fl, master)
    for part in parts.components(layer):
        dx, dy = parts.offset(part)
        print(master, parts.base_of(part), round(dx), round(dy))

Light a 0 0
Light dieresis -25 0
Regular a 0 0
Regular dieresis -12 0
Bold a 0 0
Bold dieresis -13 0

The two dots sit in a different place over each weight of a, because each a has a different shape. Whoever built the ä placed them three times.

docs.title: Step 3: Ask the whole font
docs.text:
Now the chore. Go through every glyph, and print the ones that have components:

MASTER = "Regular"

for glyph in font.glyphs:
    layer = layer_of(fl.flGlyph(glyph, font), MASTER)
    texts = []
    for part in parts.components(layer):
        dx, dy = parts.offset(part)
        texts.append(f"{parts.base_of(part)} {round(dx)} {round(dy)}")
    if texts:
        print(f"{glyph.name:<14}{', '.join(texts)}")

Aacute        A 0 0, acute 88 210
Abreve        A 0 0, breve 48 210
Acircumflex   A 0 0, circumflex 48 210
Adieresis     A 0 0, dieresis 50 210
Agrave        A 0 0, grave 18 210
Aring         A 0 0, ring 48 210
...

I've cut the output after six lines. Yours has 85.

Look at the last number in each line: 210. The accents were drawn to sit over lowercase letters. Over a capital, each one is lifted by 210 units, which is the distance from the x-height to the cap height: 688 minus 478. The accents over lowercase letters have a 0 there. Somebody did that sum once and typed it 34 times. In chapter 54 you'll meet a way to let the glyphs carry that information themselves.

Farther down the list there are glyphs you may not have expected:

colon         period 0 0, period 0 378
ellipsis      period 0 0, period 230 0, period 460 0

The colon is two periods, one of them 378 units up. The ellipsis is three, 230 apart. That's where chapter 49's step of 230 came from. I said then that a script could read it, and this is the script.

docs.title: Step 4: Turn the question around
docs.text:
Mira's question this morning ran the other way. She didn't ask "what is adieresis made of?" She asked, without knowing it, "which glyphs change when I change a?"

The list from step 3 has the answer in it, but you'd have to read 85 lines to find it. A dictionary can turn the list around: the key is a base glyph, and the value is a list of the glyphs that borrow it. That's new. Until now the values in your dictionaries were single things, a number or a name. A value can be a list, and then you fill it with append:

users = {}
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    layer = layer_of(fl.flGlyph(glyph, font), MASTER)
    for part in parts.components(layer):
        base = parts.base_of(part)
        users[base].append(glyph.name)

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 6, in <module>
KeyError: 'A'

The first glyph with a component is Aacute, and its first base is A. The script asks the dictionary for the list that belongs to A, to append to it. The dictionary is empty. There's no such list yet, and you can't append to a list that isn't there.

Chapter 22 had the same trouble when it counted, and solved it with get. For a list I'd rather spell it out: if the key is new, give it an empty list first.

        if base not in users:
            users[base] = []
        if glyph.name not in users[base]:
            users[base].append(glyph.name)

The second if is there for glyphs such as the ellipsis, which borrows period three times and should be listed once. Now ask:

print(users["a"])
print(users["period"])

['aacute', 'abreve', 'acircumflex', 'adieresis', 'agrave', 'aring', 'atilde']
['colon', 'ellipsis', 'exclam', 'exclamdown', 'semicolon']

Seven glyphs follow the a. Mira's eight units went into all seven this morning, in the Bold, without a script.

The second line is worth a look too. Five glyphs borrow the period. Make the period heavier, and the colon, the semicolon, the ellipsis and both exclamation marks get heavier dots. That's a comfort when you want it and a surprise when you don't.

docs.title: Step 5: Borrowed and drawn in one glyph
docs.text:
The exclamation mark is on that list. Its dot is a period. Its stem is nobody's, so it's drawn in the glyph. Ask for both:

glyph = pGlyph(font, font["exclam"])
layer = layer_of(glyph.fl, MASTER)
print(len(parts.components(layer)), len(glyph.contours(MASTER)))

1 1

It has one component and one contour of its own. Oskar's sheet has a word for such a glyph: it "mixes its own outlines with borrowed ones". Nothing is wrong with that in FontLab. Some other programs and some font formats don't take it, and I'd guess that's why Oskar wanted them found. Plum has two, exclam and exclamdown.

One more glyph stands out. The line for questiondown reads question 416 688. An upside-down question mark isn't a question mark shifted up and to the right. A component carries a whole transform, the kind you built in chapter 50, and this one turns the base around before it shifts it. The shift alone doesn't tell you that. The module has a test for it:

print(parts.plain_move(part))

plain_move answers True when a component is only shifted, and False when it's also scaled, mirrored, slanted or turned. In Plum, questiondown is the only glyph where the answer is False.

docs.title: Step 6: What follows and what doesn't
docs.text:
Before you rely on components, know where the borrowing stops.

The outline follows. That's the whole idea. And it follows a long way: change the period, and five glyphs change.

The width doesn't follow. A component brings an outline, and the glyph that holds it keeps its own width. adieresis is 471 wide because somebody gave it that number, the same as a. If Mira had made the a eight units wider this morning, the seven accented glyphs would have kept 471, with an a inside that no longer fit. The script from step 4 tells you which glyphs to look at after such a change. That is untested in FontLab 9, so try it on a copy before you trust me. FontLab can also tie one glyph's width to another's, and Part 4 gets to that.

The shift doesn't follow either. The dots of the ä sit 13 units to the left in the Bold because of how the Bold a looked last year. Mira opened the bowl, and the dots stayed where they were. Eight units isn't much. She looks at all seven anyway.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is list_components.py. It prints the list, counts, and then turns the list around.

# Lists every glyph that borrows outlines from other glyphs, with the shift
# of each component, and then the base glyphs that are borrowed most.
# Reads only.
import fly.ap.components.writer as parts
from fly import fl
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTER = "Regular"
TOP = 6


def describe(part):
    dx, dy = parts.offset(part)
    text = f"{parts.base_of(part)} {round(dx)} {round(dy)}"
    if not parts.plain_move(part):
        text = text + " turned"
    return text


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    users = {}
    built = 0
    mixed = 0
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        rich = pGlyph(font, glyph)
        found = parts.components(layer_of(rich.fl, MASTER))
        if not found:
            continue
        kind = "built"
        if rich.contours(MASTER):
            kind = "mixed"
            mixed += 1
        built += 1
        texts = [describe(part) for part in found]
        print(f"{glyph.name:<14}{kind:<7}{', '.join(texts)}")
        for part in found:
            base = parts.base_of(part)
            if base not in users:
                users[base] = []
            if glyph.name not in users[base]:
                users[base].append(glyph.name)

    def how_many(base):
        return len(users[base])

    print()
    print(f"{built} glyphs borrow, {mixed} of them mixed. {len(users)} glyphs are borrowed.")
    for base in sorted(users, key=how_many, reverse=True)[:TOP]:
        print(f"{base:<12}{len(users[base]):>3}  {' '.join(users[base])}")


main()

The end of the output:

exclam        mixed  period 24 4
exclamdown    mixed  period 24 378
questiondown  built  question 416 688 turned
...

85 glyphs borrow, 2 of them mixed. 40 glyphs are borrowed.
acute        14  Aacute Eacute Iacute Oacute Uacute Wacute Yacute aacute eacute iacute oacute uacute wacute yacute
