circumflex   14  Acircumflex Ecircumflex Icircumflex Ocircumflex Ucircumflex Wcircumflex Ycircumflex acircumflex ecircumflex icircumflex ocircumflex ucircumflex wcircumflex ycircumflex
dieresis     14  Adieresis Edieresis Idieresis Odieresis Udieresis Wdieresis Ydieresis adieresis edieresis idieresis odieresis udieresis wdieresis ydieresis
grave        14  Agrave Egrave Igrave Ograve Ugrave Wgrave Ygrave agrave egrave igrave ograve ugrave wgrave ygrave
A             7  Aacute Abreve Acircumflex Adieresis Agrave Aring Atilde
a             7  aacute abreve acircumflex adieresis agrave aring atilde

how_many is a function inside a function, as change was in chapter 49. It sits inside main so that it can see users. Sorting a dictionary sorts its keys, and the key function says by what: the length of each key's list.

Of the 205 glyphs Plum came with, 85 have nothing or nearly nothing drawn in them. The four accents at the top of the table are borrowed 14 times each. Whoever redraws the acute redraws it in 14 letters at once.

None of the small caps is on the list, and neither is leader. You drew those with a pen, so they hold outlines of their own. And no base in Plum is itself built from components. A component can point at a glyph that has components, and fonts with long chains exist. Plum keeps it to one level.

Mira writes the list to a file, as in chapter 26, and pins it over her desk. Then she takes Oskar's sheet and crosses out List the glyphs that are built from other glyphs. The line below it, about the glyphs that mix, she leaves. She knows which two they are. She'd like to ask Oskar what color he had in mind.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A component is an element that shows another glyph's outline, and it knows two things: its base and its transform, which for most components is a plain shift. parts.components(layer) lists them, parts.base_of and parts.offset read them, and parts.plain_move says whether a shift is the whole story. A function can hand back a pair that you take apart with two names, and a dictionary can hold a list for each key, as long as you make the empty list before the first append. The outline of a base carries into every glyph that borrows it, while widths and shifts stay behind.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Change MASTER to "Bold" and run the script again. The counts stay the same and the shifts change. Find the acute over e in all three masters. How far does it travel from the Light to the Bold?
  2. Do the line Mira left. Write mark_mixed.py: for every glyph that has components and contours of its own, set the mark as you did in chapter 14. Pick the color yourself. Run it, look at the Font window, and count the marked cells before you cross anything out.
  3. From users, print every base that's borrowed by one glyph only. There are 16. For each, ask yourself whether borrowing saved anybody any work. Then look at i and j: each is borrowed once, by ij, while the accented i glyphs borrow dotlessi. Why can't iacute be built from i?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The publisher wants the cookbook in Czech and Polish, and Plum has no ě and no ń. Chapter 53 builds one accented letter from a base and an accent, with the shift worked out from numbers you can already read.

docs.title: 53. Build an accented letter
docs.text:
Wednesday. The publisher has sold the cookbook twice more, to Prague and to Warsaw. Ines forwards the email with one line of her own on top: "Can Plum do Czech and Polish by the end of the month?"

Mira types a Polish word from the sample chapter into a Glyph window: koń, a horse. The k and the o come up. Where the ń should be there's a gap.

Chapter 25 saw this coming. Its script compared the characters a language needs with the characters Plum has, and Polish came out short. What's new is that you can now do something about it. You read components yesterday. Today you make a glyph that has them: an n, an acute over it, and a shift that puts the acute in the right place. It'll be one glyph, built slowly, and the chapters after this do the rest of the alphabet.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • box from chapter 43. You'll write it out again here.
  • The Font window in front when you run the last two steps. The tool that adds glyphs refuses to work while a Glyph window is the active one.

The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel. The two refusals you'll read are quoted from the tool's own code.

docs.title: Step 1: What's there and what isn't
docs.text:
A new accented letter needs a base and an accent. Ask the font for both, and for the glyph you're about to make. You know from chapter 6 that a name the font doesn't have gives None:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for name in ["n", "acute", "nacute", "e", "caron", "ecaron"]:
    print(f"{name:<8}{font[name] is not None}")

n       True
acute   True
nacute  False
e       True
caron   False
ecaron  False

The Polish ń can be built today: Plum has the n and the acute. The Czech ě can't. Its accent, the caron, isn't in the font, and no script will draw a caron that suits Plum. Mira puts "caron" on her own list, under the small caps, and you and I get on with Polish.

The new glyph needs a name and a Unicode value. The name follows the pattern of the 85 glyphs you listed yesterday: base name, then accent name, with nothing between them.

BASE = "n"
MARK = "acute"
CHARACTER = "ń"

name = BASE + MARK
print(name, ord(CHARACTER), f"U+{ord(CHARACTER):04X}")

nacute 324 U+0144

If you can't type an ń on your keyboard, write chr(324) in its place. Chapter 23 showed that the two are the same thing.

docs.title: Step 2: A first guess
docs.text:
Where does the acute go? The plain answer is "in the middle, over the letter". You can work that out. box from chapter 43 gives the left and right edge of anything with an outline, and the middle is halfway between them:

from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph


def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


def center(font, name, master):
    left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font[name], master)
    return (left + right) / 2


print(center(font, "n", "Regular"), center(font, "acute", "Regular"))
print(center(font, "n", "Regular") - center(font, "acute", "Regular"))

263.5 250.0
13.5

The middle of the n is at 263.5. The acute, as it's drawn in its own glyph, has its middle at 250. Shift it 13.5 units to the right and the two middles meet.

Before you build anything on that number, test the idea on a letter where you know the right answer. Plum has an oacute, and its designer placed that acute by eye. Do the same sum for o, and then read what the designer did, with yesterday's functions:

import fly.ap.components.writer as parts
from fly.pens import layer_of

print(center(font, "o", "Regular") - center(font, "acute", "Regular"))
layer = layer_of(fl.flGlyph(font["oacute"], font), "Regular")
for part in parts.components(layer):
    print(parts.base_of(part), parts.offset(part))

10.0
o (0.0, 0.0)
acute (50.0, 0.0)

The sum says 10. The designer said 50. That's 40 units apart, and 40 units is a lot for an accent.

The sum is right, and it answers a different question. An acute leans. Its box runs from the bottom-left tip to the top-right end, and the middle of that box is somewhere along the slope. But the eye reads an acute by its lower end, the part that points at the letter. The designer put that end where it looked right. The box knows nothing about it.

A number you can compute is not always the number you want, and the cheap way to find out is to try the sum on a case that's already solved.

docs.title: Step 3: Borrow the designer's eye
docs.text:
You can't compute where an acute looks right. But somebody already decided that for the o, and the n is a similar letter: about as wide, the same height, round on top. So take the decision from the o and correct it for the difference between the two letters.

The n has its middle 3.5 units to the right of the middle of the o: 263.5 against 260. Move the acute by the same 3.5, and it sits over the n as it sits over the o.

Here's that as two functions. The second has five inputs. That's a lot, and each one is a plain name that says what goes in:

def mark_shift(font, composite, mark, master):
    layer = layer_of(fl.flGlyph(font[composite], font), master)
    for part in parts.components(layer):
        if parts.base_of(part) == mark:
            return parts.offset(part)
    return None


def shift_like(font, base, model, mark, master):
    dx, dy = mark_shift(font, model + mark, mark, master)
    nudge = center(font, base, master) - center(font, model, master)
    return round(dx + nudge), round(dy)


for master in ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]:
    print(master, shift_like(font, "n", "o", "acute", master))

Light (42, 0)
Regular (54, 0)
Bold (72, 0)

mark_shift opens a glyph that's already built and finds the shift of one accent in it. shift_like calls it for the model, which is oacute, built from model + mark, the same way you built the new name. Then it adds the nudge.

Read the last line of shift_like again: return round(dx + nudge), round(dy). There are two values after return, with a comma between them. That hands back a pair, a tuple of two, as parts.offset did yesterday. You don't need the parentheses. The comma makes the tuple.

One detail in the numbers. In the Bold, the sum is 70 plus 2.5, and round(72.5) gave 72, where school taught you 73. When a number sits halfway between two whole numbers, Python's round goes to the even one. So 72.5 becomes 72 and 53.5 becomes 54. For half a unit in a font nobody will mind, but now you know why your pocket calculator disagrees.

docs.title: Step 4: Describe the glyph before you make it
docs.text:
In chapter 30 a plan was a list of rows, and the script changed nothing until the plan was complete. Making a glyph works the same way. You write a description, and then you hand the description to a tool that does the work or refuses.

Fly has two small records for the description. Import them with the tool:

import fly.ap.glyphs.creation as creation

part = creation.Part("Regular", "n", 0, 0)
print(part.base, part.x)

n 0

A Part is one component in one master. It has four drawers: master, base, x and y. You fill them in that order. For the ń you need six parts, an n and an acute in each of three masters.

The other record is the glyph:

spec = creation.NewGlyph(
    name="nacute",
    layers=(("Light", 499), ("Regular", 523), ("Bold", 523)),
    unicodes=(324,),
    components=(part,),
)

I've filled these slots by name, as chapter 34 showed, because four unnamed things in a row would be hard to read. layers holds one pair for each master: its name and the advance width the new glyph gets there. Those are the widths of the n. You saw yesterday that a component doesn't bring its width along, so the script has to.

Look at unicodes=(324,). The comma is not a typo. The slot wants a tuple, because a glyph may have several Unicode values. And a tuple with one item needs that comma. Without it, the parentheses are only parentheses:

print((324), (324,))

324 (324,)

The first is the number 324 with brackets around it, as in arithmetic. The second is a tuple that holds one number. It looks odd.

docs.title: Step 5: Make it
docs.text:
Two lines from chapter 29 come back here. The tool wants to know which font file it's working on and what state it's in, and those lines tell it:

import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

package = scripting.current_package()
facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
creation.create_glyphs(package, [spec], "Add nacute", facts)

create_glyphs takes the font, a list of descriptions, a title for the Edit menu, and the facts. The list has one item today. The glyph and its components arrive as one step, so one Edit > Undo should take the whole glyph away again. That is untested, so check it on your copy before you count on it.

The whole script is below. Run it with the Font window in front, and a new cell appears at the end of the font. Open it, type koń in the Glyph window, and look at where the acute sits.

Now run the script a second time, without changing anything:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Refused: nacute exists now. Check the list again.

I've cut the middle of the traceback, because most of it is inside Fly and none of it is yours. The last line is the one to read. The tool looked at the font before it touched anything, found a glyph with that name, and stopped. It changed nothing. A ValueError is how a function says "the thing you gave me is of the right kind, and I still can't use it".

A refusal is better than a second nacute or an overwritten one. A script that greets its user with a traceback could be kinder, though. So the finished script asks first, with the test from step 1, and says in a plain sentence what it found.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is build_one_accent.py:

# Builds one accented letter from a base glyph and an accent. The accent is
# placed as it is in a model glyph the designer made, nudged by the
# difference between the two base letters.
# Run it with the Font window in front.
import fly.ap.components.writer as parts
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.glyphs.creation as creation
from fly import fl
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
BASE = "n"
MARK = "acute"
MODEL = "o"
CHARACTER = "ń"


def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


def center(font, name, master):
    left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font[name], master)
    return (left + right) / 2


def mark_shift(font, composite, mark, master):
    layer = layer_of(fl.flGlyph(font[composite], font), master)
    for part in parts.components(layer):
        if parts.base_of(part) == mark:
            return parts.offset(part)
    return None


def shift_like(font, base, model, mark, master):
    dx, dy = mark_shift(font, model + mark, mark, master)
    nudge = center(font, base, master) - center(font, model, master)
    return round(dx + nudge), round(dy)


def width_of(font, name, master):
    layer = layer_of(fl.flGlyph(font[name], font), master)
    return round(layer.advanceWidth)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    name = BASE + MARK
    if font[name] is not None:
        print(f"{name} is already in the font. Nothing done.")
        return
    for needed in [BASE, MARK, MODEL, MODEL + MARK]:
        if font[needed] is None:
            print(f"There's no {needed} in the font. Nothing done.")
            return

    layers = []
    components = []
    for master in MASTERS:
        dx, dy = shift_like(font, BASE, MODEL, MARK, master)
        layers.append((master, width_of(font, BASE, master)))
        components.append(creation.Part(master, BASE, 0, 0))
        components.append(creation.Part(master, MARK, dx, dy))
        print(f"{master:<9}{BASE} 0 0, {MARK} {dx} {dy}")

    spec = creation.NewGlyph(
        name=name,
        layers=tuple(layers),
        unicodes=(ord(CHARACTER),),
        components=tuple(components),
    )
    package = scripting.current_package()
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    creation.create_glyphs(package, [spec], f"Add {name}", facts)
    print(f"Added {name}, U+{ord(CHARACTER):04X}.")


main()

Light    n 0 0, acute 42 0
Regular  n 0 0, acute 54 0
Bold     n 0 0, acute 72 0
Added nacute, U+0144.

Run it again:

nacute is already in the font. Nothing done.

Three things in main are worth a second look.

A bare return in the middle of a function leaves the function at once and hands back nothing. That's how main stops early without a tower of if and else. Check what could stop you, leave if it does, and the rest of the function can assume that all is well.

The script collects the layers and components in lists, because lists can grow, and turns them into tuples at the end with tuple(...). That's the reverse of list(...) from chapter 51.

And the four capital-letter names at the top are the whole recipe. Change BASE, MODEL and CHARACTER, and the script builds a different letter.

Mira types koń again. The acute sits over the n about where it sits over the o next to it, in all three weights. She nudges nothing. Then she remembers that the Polish word for "horses" starts a sentence in the sample chapter, and that Plum has no capital Ń either.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A new accented letter is a description before it's a glyph: a name, a width for each master, a Unicode value, and one Part for each component in each master. create_glyphs turns the description into a glyph in one step, and refuses with a ValueError when it can't. A sum is worth testing on a case you already know, and where a sum can't see what the eye sees, you can borrow a decision the designer made and adjust it. A function can hand back two values with a comma, a one-item tuple needs its comma, and a bare return leaves a function early.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Build the capital. Set BASE = "N", MODEL = "O" and CHARACTER = "Ń", and predict the last number in each line before you run it. Where does that number come from? You met it yesterday.
  2. Build sacute with o as the model, and look at it in all three weights. The Light gets a shift of −40. Does the acute look right over a letter as narrow as s, or has the model been stretched too far? Write down what you'd change by hand. Chapter 54 comes back to this.
  3. Set MARK = "caron" and run the script. Read the sentence it prints. Then take away the loop over needed, run it again, and read what Python says in its place. Which message would you rather get from a colleague's script?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Typing a shift for every accent over every letter doesn't scale, and borrowing from a model only works while the letters are alike. Chapter 54 looks at anchors: named points that a glyph carries so that accents can find their own place.

docs.title: 54. Anchors
docs.text:
Thursday. Mira prints yesterday's koń large, in all three weights, and pins the sheet next to the window. In the Light and the Regular she'd sign it off. In the Bold the acute over the n sits a little to the right of where the acute over the o sits. It's not much, but once she's seen it she can't look anywhere else.

She opens the Bold n to see whether the letter itself is lopsided, and notices something she has scrolled past for weeks: a few small marks in the glyph that aren't part of the outline. One sits on the x-height line, a little left of the middle. It has a name next to it: acute.

Whoever drew Plum had already written down where the acute goes on an n. Yesterday you and I worked that place out from the o, with some care, and got it nearly right. The answer was in the glyph the whole time.

Those marks are anchors. Today you read them, learn what the names mean, and check the whole font against them.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The nacute from chapter 53. If you skipped it, the last script still runs. It finds one glyph less to complain about.
  • Nothing in the font changes today.

The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel. So was every position and count.

docs.title: Step 1: Ask a layer for its anchors
docs.text:
An anchor is a named point in a layer. It has no outline and doesn't print. Fly reads all the anchors of a layer in one call:

import fly.ap.anchors.writer as anchors
from fly import fl
from fly.pens import layer_of

font = fl.CurrentFont()
layer = layer_of(fl.flGlyph(font["n"], font), "Regular")
points = anchors.anchor_points(layer)
for name in sorted(points):
    print(name, points[name])

acute (242.0, 478.0)
bottom (282.0, 0.0)
top (262.0, 478.0)
topLeft (100.0, 200.0)

anchor_points hands back a dictionary. The keys are the anchor names, and each value is a pair: across and up. You've had dictionaries with numbers in them and, since Tuesday, with lists. A pair as a value is no different. Ask for one anchor by its name, as you'd ask for any key:

print(points["top"])
x, y = points["top"]
print(y)

(262.0, 478.0)
478.0

Read the four anchors as notes the designer left on the letter. top says: an accent that sits centered above goes here, at 262 across, on the x-height. bottom says the same for an accent below, on the baseline. acute is 20 units to the left of top, and it's there for the accent that leans. topLeft you can ignore. It sits at a spot inside the letter where nobody would put anything, and I'd guess it was left over from an experiment.

docs.title: Step 2: The other half is on the accent
docs.text:
An anchor on a letter says where an accent should go. It doesn't say which part of the accent should land there. The accent has to answer that itself:

layer = layer_of(fl.flGlyph(font["acute"], font), "Regular")
marks = anchors.anchor_points(layer)
for name in sorted(marks):
    print(name, marks[name])

_acute (190.0, 478.0)
_acuteHigh (190.0, 478.0)

The names start with an underscore, and that's the whole convention. An anchor with a plain name sits on a letter. The anchor with the same name and an underscore in front sits on an accent. Think of a coat peg on the wall and the loop inside the collar of a coat. acute is the peg. _acute is the loop. Hang the coat, and the two are in the same place.

The acute's loop is at 190 across, which is near the lower tip of the stroke and nowhere near the middle of its box at 250. That's what the eye did yesterday, and what the box couldn't do.

So the shift is a subtraction: where the peg is, minus where the loop is.

def shift_from_anchors(base_points, mark_points, family):
    bx, by = base_points[family]
    mx, my = mark_points["_" + family]
    return bx - mx, by - my


print(shift_from_anchors(points, marks, "acute"))

(52.0, 0.0)

242 minus 190 is 52, and 478 minus 478 is 0. I've called the third input family because a peg and its loop belong together, and I needed one word for the pair. "_" + family builds the loop's name from the peg's name, the same string sum that built nacute yesterday.

Now ask for the wrong pair. The n has a top anchor too:

Run this line on its own, with the function already defined, and the line numbers will be the ones shown:

print(shift_from_anchors(points, marks, "top"))

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
  File "<string>", line 3, in shift_from_anchors
KeyError: '_top'

The n has a peg called top. The acute has no loop called _top, so the dictionary has no such key. The acute hangs on acute pegs only. Other accents use top: the dieresis, the circumflex, the breve, the ring and the tilde all carry _top. A function that's going to be asked about every pair in a font shouldn't fall over at the first pair that doesn't match. Give it a way to say no:

def shift_from_anchors(base_points, mark_points, family):
    if family not in base_points or "_" + family not in mark_points:
        return None
    bx, by = base_points[family]
    mx, my = mark_points["_" + family]
    return bx - mx, by - my

docs.title: Step 3: Test it on a case you know
docs.text:
Yesterday's lesson was to try a sum on a solved case before trusting it. The oacute is solved: its acute is shifted by 50 in the Regular. So ask the anchors of o:

def points_of(font, name, master):
    return anchors.anchor_points(layer_of(fl.flGlyph(font[name], font), master))


print(shift_from_anchors(points_of(font, "o", "Regular"), marks, "acute"))
print(shift_from_anchors(points_of(font, "O", "Regular"), marks, "acute"))

(50.0, 0.0)
(144.0, 210.0)

The first line is 50, to the unit. And look at the second. On Tuesday the accents over capitals all had 210 in their shift, and I said somebody had typed that number 34 times. Nobody did. The capital O has its acute anchor at the cap height, 688. The acute has its loop at 478. Subtract, and 210 comes out. The same accent glyph lands on a lowercase letter and on a capital, and each letter says how high.

A table of shifts would need one number for every pair. With anchors, every letter says once where it takes accents and every accent says once where it's held. A new accent with one _top anchor fits every letter in the font that has a top.

docs.title: Step 4: What the anchors say about yesterday
docs.text:
Now the question that started the morning. Ask the n in all three masters:

for master in ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]:
    shift = shift_from_anchors(
        points_of(font, "n", master), points_of(font, "acute", master), "acute"
    )
    print(master, shift)

Light (40.0, 0.0)
Regular (52.0, 0.0)
Bold (62.0, 0.0)

Yesterday's script gave 42, 54 and 72. Two units off in the Light and the Regular, which nobody will ever see. Ten units off in the Bold, which Mira saw from across the room.

Where did the ten come from? In the Bold, the designer pushed the acute over the o to the right, to suit the heavy round shape under it. That push was a decision about the o. Yesterday's script took the acute's place from the o and carried the push over to the n, which has a straight stem and a shoulder and didn't want it. I said yesterday that borrowing from a model works while the letters are alike. In the Bold, o and n weren't alike enough.

Leave your nacute as it is for now. Chapter 56 builds accented letters from anchors, and it will put this one right along with the rest.

docs.title: Step 5: Ask the whole font
docs.text:
Two questions remain, and both are loops you can write. Which anchor names does Plum use, and how often? And do the 85 built glyphs from Tuesday agree with the anchors, or did the designer shift some accents by hand afterwards?

The first is a tally, as in chapter 22. The second needs one more idea. An accent can have more than one loop, and a letter more than one peg that fits. The acute has _acute and _acuteHigh, and the u has pegs for both. So for one pair of glyphs there can be several shifts that the anchors allow. I collect them all and then ask whether the shift in the glyph is one of them:

def possible_shifts(base_points, mark_points):
    shifts = []
    for family, (bx, by) in base_points.items():
        if "_" + family in mark_points:
            mx, my = mark_points["_" + family]
            shifts.append((bx - mx, by - my))
    return shifts

Look at the for line. items() gives a key and a value on each turn, as in chapter 22, and here the value is a pair. The parentheses around bx, by take that pair apart on the spot. Without them you'd write for family, point in ... and then bx, by = point on the next line. Both are fine.

Then the test is one word you've known since chapter 9:

print((50.0, 0.0) in [(50.0, 0.0), (50.0, 100.0)])

True

in compares a pair with each pair in the list, and two pairs are equal when both their numbers are.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is list_anchors.py:

# Counts the anchor names in the font, then checks every glyph built from a
# base and one accent: does the accent's shift match what the anchors say?
# Reads only.
import fly.ap.anchors.writer as anchors
import fly.ap.components.writer as parts
from fly import fl
from fly.pens import layer_of

MASTER = "Regular"
TOP = 5


def possible_shifts(base_points, mark_points):
    shifts = []
    for family, (bx, by) in base_points.items():
        if "_" + family in mark_points:
            mx, my = mark_points["_" + family]
            shifts.append((bx - mx, by - my))
    return shifts


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    layers = {}
    points = {}
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        layers[glyph.name] = layer_of(fl.flGlyph(glyph, font), MASTER)
        points[glyph.name] = anchors.anchor_points(layers[glyph.name])

    tally = {}
    carriers = 0
    for name in points:
        if points[name]:
            carriers += 1
        for anchor in points[name]:
            tally[anchor] = tally.get(anchor, 0) + 1

    def how_often(anchor):
        return tally[anchor]

    for anchor in sorted(tally, key=how_often, reverse=True)[:TOP]:
        print(f"{anchor:<10}{tally[anchor]:>4}")
    print(f"{carriers} glyphs carry anchors, under {len(tally)} names.")
    print()

    agree = 0
    differ = 0
    no_pair = []
    for name in layers:
        found = parts.components(layers[name])
        if len(found) != 2:
            continue
        base = parts.base_of(found[0])
        mark = parts.base_of(found[1])
        shifts = possible_shifts(points[base], points[mark])
        dx, dy = parts.offset(found[1])
        if not shifts:
            no_pair.append(name)
        elif (dx, dy) in shifts:
            agree += 1
        else:
            differ += 1
            wanted = ", ".join([f"{round(x)} {round(y)}" for x, y in shifts])
            print(f"{name:<12}glyph says {round(dx)} {round(dy)}, anchors say {wanted}")
    print(f"Agree with their anchors: {agree}. Differ: {differ}.")
    print(f"{len(no_pair)} have no matching pair: {' '.join(no_pair)}")


main()

top         99
acute       97
bottom      85
grave       74
ogonek      56
116 glyphs carry anchors, under 18 names.

nacute      glyph says 54 0, anchors say 52 0
Agree with their anchors: 67. Differ: 1.
14 have no matching pair: IJ iacute icircumflex idieresis igrave ij colon quotedbl semicolon guillemotleft guillemotright quotedblbase quotedblleft quotedblright

The order of the 14 names follows your font and may differ from mine.

The script reads every layer and every set of anchors once, at the top, and keeps them in two dictionaries. After that, asking for the anchors of a base or an accent is a lookup by name.

Now read the result, because it says three things about Plum.

Sixty-seven glyphs agree, and none of the designer's glyphs differs. Every accent in the font sits where the anchors put it. Whoever built Plum didn't place accents by hand. They placed anchors, and a tool placed the accents. The one glyph that differs is the one you and I made yesterday without asking.

Fourteen have no matching pair. Ten of those aren't accented letters at all: the colon, the quotation marks and the like are one glyph borrowed two or three times, the IJ and ij are two letters side by side, and nobody hangs a period on a period. The other four are worth a frown. iacute, icircumflex, idieresis and igrave are built on dotlessi, the i without its dot, and dotlessi has no anchors. Those four were placed by hand. If Mira ever changes the dotlessi, their accents will stay where they were.

And look at the fifth line of the tally. Fifty-six glyphs have an anchor called ogonek. The ogonek is the little hook under the Polish ą and ę. Plum has no ogonek glyph. Somebody planned for Polish, set a peg for the hook on 56 letters, and never drew the hook. Mira writes "ogonek" under "caron" on her drawing list, and feels a little less alone with the email from Warsaw.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: An anchor is a named point in a layer, and anchors.anchor_points(layer) gives them as a dictionary from name to position. A plain name is a place on a letter, and the same name with an underscore is the matching place on an accent. The shift for a component is the first minus the second, and it carries the height as well as the sideways position. A dictionary can hold pairs, a for line can take a pair apart in place, and a font's own anchors are a better source than a sum, when the font has them.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Yesterday's first exercise built Nacute with O as the model. Ask the anchors for N and the acute in all three masters. In which master does the model disagree most, and by how many units? Is it the same master as for the lowercase?
  2. The Czech ů is a u with a ring, and Plum has both. Call possible_shifts for u and ring in the Regular, and you get one answer, so the letter can be built. Now call it for u and acute. You get two. Print the anchors of u, find the peg that makes the second one, and say what you think the designer wanted it for.
  3. Change the script so that it also counts built glyphs whose base has anchors while the glyph itself has none. A new glyph such as nacute starts with no anchors of its own. Why might an accented letter want pegs of its own? Think of a letter that carries two accents, one on top of the other.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Four letters stand on a dotlessi that has no anchors, and every new accent Mira draws will need a loop. Chapter 55 writes anchors into glyphs: where to put them, how to work the place out, and how to do it as one step you can undo.

docs.title: 55. Place the anchors
docs.text:
Friday. Yesterday's list ended with four names that bothered Mira all evening: iacute, icircumflex, idieresis and igrave. They stand on dotlessi, and dotlessi has no anchors. Somebody placed those four accents by hand, years ago.

It matters this week because of Prague. The Czech í is there already, but next week's script will build accented letters from anchors, and a letter without pegs will be skipped. Mira wants the dotlessi to carry pegs like its neighbors before she goes home.

She could click three anchors into three masters. That's nine clicks, each one placed by eye, and she'd rather the nine places came from a rule she can read. So today a script writes into the font again: nine anchors, in one step that Edit > Undo can take back.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • box from chapter 43. The scripts below write it out again.
  • list_anchors.py from chapter 54, for the check at the end.

The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel. What the writing tool hands back is read from its code.

docs.title: Step 1: Work out where top goes
docs.text:
Look at a neighbor first. The n has its top at 262 across and 478 up. The outline of the Regular n runs from 70 to 457, so its middle is 263.5. The peg sits near the middle of the letter, on the x-height. That's the rule to copy.

For the sideways position, box from chapter 43 gives you the edges:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph


def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


font = fl.CurrentFont()
for master in ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]:
    left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font["dotlessi"], master)
    print(master, (left + right) / 2, top)

Light 97.0 474.0
Regular 111.0 478.0
Bold 126.0 482.0

The middles are what you'd expect from a stem that gets fatter. Now look at the last column. I printed the top of the box because it seemed the obvious height for the peg: the stem is flat on top, and that's where an accent should hover. But the three numbers differ. The Light stem stops four units short of 478, and the Bold one goes four units over.

Every other lowercase letter in Plum has its top at 478 in all three masters, whatever its outline does. The designer hung the accents from the x-height of the font, and didn't measure each letter. You met that number in chapter 43:

from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.font import pFont

metrics = pFont().fontMetrics()
for master in ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]:
    print(master, metrics.getXHeight(master))

Light 478
Regular 478
Bold 478

As in chapter 43, each of those questions switches the font to the master it names, so the font is on the Bold when the loop ends. Switch back to the Regular in the Font window before you go on. The same holds for the whole script below.

So the place has two sources. Across comes from the letter's own outline, because that's where this letter is. Up comes from the font, because that's a line all the letters share. When you compute a position, ask of each number which of the two it is.

def top_place(font, name, master):
    left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font[name], master)
    return round((left + right) / 2), metrics.getXHeight(master)


print(top_place(font, "dotlessi", "Regular"))

(111, 478)

docs.title: Step 2: Ask the glyphs that are already there
docs.text:
In chapter 53 you tested a sum on a solved case. There are solved cases here too. The four accented i glyphs were placed by hand, and each placement says where its designer thought the peg was.

Yesterday the shift was the peg minus the loop. Turn that around: the peg is the loop plus the shift.

import fly.ap.anchors.writer as anchors
import fly.ap.components.writer as parts
from fly import fl
from fly.pens import layer_of


def layer_for(font, name, master):
    return layer_of(fl.flGlyph(font[name], font), master)


def peg_in(font, composite, family, master):
    accent = parts.components(layer_for(font, composite, master))[1]
    dx, dy = parts.offset(accent)
    loops = anchors.anchor_points(layer_for(font, parts.base_of(accent), master))
    lx, ly = loops["_" + family]
    return round(lx + dx), round(ly + dy)


for master in ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]:
    mine = top_place(font, "dotlessi", master)
    print(master, mine, peg_in(font, "icircumflex", "top", master))

Light (97, 478) (96, 478)
Regular (111, 478) (110, 478)
Bold (126, 478) (110, 478)

peg_in opens a built glyph, takes its second component, which is the accent, reads that accent's loop and adds the shift. I wrote layer_for because the line that fetches a layer by glyph name was about to appear four times.

In the Light and the Regular, the sum and the designer agree to within a unit. In the Bold they're 16 units apart. The Bold stem runs from 60 to 192, so its middle is at 126, and the circumflex sits over 110.

Mira opens the Bold icircumflex and zooms in. The hat sits left of the stem. Nobody had noticed, because nobody sets much Bold î. My guess is that the accent was placed when the Bold stem was thinner, and then the stem grew to the right. A hand-placed accent has no way to follow. That's the argument for anchors, and Plum made it against itself.

So for top, the sum wins. For acute and grave, Mira decides differently. In most of Plum those two pegs sit 20 units left and right of top. On the narrow i the designer spread them much wider, on purpose, so that the leaning accents clear the stem. She wants to keep that. peg_in can read both places out of iacute and igrave, and the script will write them down as they are.

docs.title: Step 3: Describe the edits
docs.text:
As with new glyphs on Wednesday, you describe the work first and hand it to a tool. An edit to an anchor is a tuple of three things: what to do, the anchor's name, and a value.

edit = ("set", "top", (111, 478))

"set" means: put the anchor of this name at this place, and make one if there isn't one. The value is a pair, so this is a tuple with a tuple in it. Count the items: there are three, and the third has two.

Edits belong to a layer, and a layer belongs to a glyph. So one row of work is another tuple of three: the glyph, the layer, and a list of edits for that layer.

rich = pGlyph(font, font["dotlessi"])
layer = layer_of(rich.fl, "Regular")
work = [(rich.fl, layer, [edit])]

Now hand it over. The tool has two doors. require_safe looks at the work and refuses if anything in it can't be undone properly. apply_work does it. Before I show you both working, here's what happens when the edit has the wrong shape. Suppose you'd written the place as two loose numbers:

import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

facts = history.scan_auto_facts(scripting.current_package())
bad = ("set", "top", 111, 478)
anchors.require_safe([(rich.fl, layer, [bad])], facts)

Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 3)

You've written dx, dy = ... often enough. The tool does the same thing with your edit: it takes it apart into three names. Your tuple had four items, and Python won't guess which two belong together. The message doesn't mention anchors, because the tool never got as far as thinking about anchors. When a tool wants tuples of a certain shape, count the commas outside the inner parentheses.

Nothing was written. require_safe runs before anything touches the font, which is the reason to call it first.

docs.title: Step 4: Write them
docs.text:
With the edit in its right shape, go through the first door:

anchors.require_safe(work, facts)

ValueError: FontLab cannot undo edits to these glyphs: dotlessi: base of auto iacute, icircumflex…. Choose other glyphs.

The shape is right now, and the tool still says no. You met the words base of auto in chapter 30's table of reasons. Four glyphs borrow dotlessi: iacute, icircumflex, idieresis and igrave. FontLab builds those four itself, from a recipe, and builds them again whenever a glyph they borrow changes. The refusal names the first two and leaves the rest to the three dots.

Fly's code says why it's wary. When FontLab rebuilds those glyphs, Undo brings back dotlessi, and it may not bring back the anchors and locks of the rebuilt ones. So Fly's rule for a borrowed glyph is "not unless a person agreed". The anchor tool has no way to hear you agree, and on another glyph, one that nothing automatic borrows, its second door apply_work(work, title, facts) would do the whole job. history.commit from chapter 29 can hear you, through the keyword allow_bases=True. Mira agrees: pegs on dotlessi are the point of the afternoon. She saves the font first, and so should you.

The anchor tool lends the two halves of its second door. prepare turns the edits into steps, and write carries them out:

steps = anchors.prepare(layer, [edit])

def change():
    anchors.write(layer, steps)

history.commit("Add top anchor", [layer], [rich.fl], change,
               operation="geometry", facts=facts, allow_bases=True)
print(len(steps))

1

It's the pattern of chapter 29 and of set_width: a small function with the change in it, handed to commit. Open the Regular dotlessi and there should be a top mark over the stem. Then look at iacute. FontLab should have built it again, and it should look as it did. Then choose Edit > Undo: the mark should be gone, and iacute should still look as it did. All of that is untested, which is why it says "should". Try it before you go on.

From here on, the book passes allow_bases=True wherever a script changes a glyph that automatic glyphs borrow, and the rule is the same each time: save first, and look at one borrower afterward. A glyph that FontLab builds itself is another matter. No keyword opens that one, and a script that meets one reports it and leaves it alone.

Now run the lines from steps = ... again, without the Undo. On Wednesday a second run was refused, because a glyph can't be made twice. This time nothing complains and the count is the same:

1

"set" on an anchor that exists moves it to the place you gave. It's already there, so it moves nowhere. A script that you can run twice with the same result as once is a comfortable thing to own. You can run it again after you've fixed a number, and it puts every anchor where the new number says.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is add_top_anchors.py:

# Gives dotlessi the anchors its neighbors have. top is worked out from the
# stem and the x-height. acute and grave are read from the two glyphs where
# the designer placed those accents by hand.
# One Undo step.
import fly.ap.anchors.writer as anchors
import fly.ap.components.writer as parts
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.font import pFont
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
TARGET = "dotlessi"
BY_HAND = {"acute": "iacute", "grave": "igrave"}


def layer_for(font, name, master):
    return layer_of(fl.flGlyph(font[name], font), master)


def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


def top_place(font, name, master, height):
    left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font[name], master)
    return round((left + right) / 2), height


def peg_in(font, composite, family, master):
    accent = parts.components(layer_for(font, composite, master))[1]
    dx, dy = parts.offset(accent)
    loops = anchors.anchor_points(layer_for(font, parts.base_of(accent), master))
    lx, ly = loops["_" + family]
    return round(lx + dx), round(ly + dy)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    metrics = pFont().fontMetrics()
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[TARGET])

    work = []
    for master in MASTERS:
        edits = [("set", "top", top_place(font, TARGET, master, metrics.getXHeight(master)))]
        for family, composite in BY_HAND.items():
            edits.append(("set", family, peg_in(font, composite, family, master)))
        work.append((rich.fl, layer_of(rich.fl, master), edits))
        for operation, name, place in edits:
            print(f"{master:<9}{name:<7}{place[0]:>4}{place[1]:>5}")

    # dotlessi is borrowed by automatic glyphs: see Step 4. Save first.
    planned = [(layer, anchors.prepare(layer, edits)) for glyph, layer, edits in work]

    def change():
        for layer, steps in planned:
            anchors.write(layer, steps)

    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(scripting.current_package())
    layers = [layer for layer, steps in planned]
    history.commit(f"Add anchors to {TARGET}", layers, [rich.fl], change,
                   operation="geometry", facts=facts, allow_bases=True)
    count = sum([len(steps) for layer, steps in planned])
    print(f"{count} anchors on {len(layers)} layers.")


main()

Light    top      97  478
Light    acute    43  478
Light    grave   164  478
Regular  top     111  478
Regular  acute    51  478
Regular  grave   183  478
Bold     top     126  478
Bold     acute    40  478
Bold     grave   180  478
9 anchors on 3 layers.

The comprehension that fills planned prepares every layer's steps before commit is called, because the new anchors have to exist before FontLab starts recording. top_place gets the height handed in now, so that it doesn't reach for a metrics box outside itself. The loop that prints takes each edit apart into three names, as the tool does. And BY_HAND is a small dictionary that says which glyph to ask for which peg. If Mira changes her mind about the acute, that's the line she changes.

Look at the Bold rows. The acute peg is at 40 and the grave at 180, which puts them 70 either side of 110, the old middle. The top is at 126, the new one. The script wrote down what the designer did, and what the designer did was 16 units off. Mira adds a line to her list: "Bold í and ì: look at them." A script can keep a decision, and it can't tell you whether the decision was good.
