grave       75
ogonek      56
117 glyphs carry anchors, under 18 names.

icircumflex glyph says -140 0, anchors say -139 0
idieresis   glyph says -139 0, anchors say -137 0
nacute      glyph says 54 0, anchors say 52 0
Agree with their anchors: 69. Differ: 3.
10 have no matching pair: IJ ij colon quotedbl semicolon guillemotleft guillemotright quotedblbase quotedblleft quotedblright

Three tallies went up by one. The four i glyphs have left the last line. iacute and igrave agree with their anchors, as they must, because the anchors were read from them. icircumflex and idieresis differ by a unit or two, because their peg came from the sum. Those two are automatic glyphs, so no script of ours will move them. Whether FontLab moves them itself when it next builds them, now that dotlessi has a top peg, is something to watch for: in the Bold they are 16 units off.

Ten glyphs remain without a pair, and all ten are punctuation or ligatures. That list is clean.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Anchors are written from a description: rows of glyph, layer and a list of edits, where an edit is ("set", name, (x, y)), checked first by anchors.require_safe, which changes nothing. A glyph that automatic glyphs borrow is refused unless your own history.commit says allow_bases=True around anchors.prepare and anchors.write, after you've saved. A computed position can take one number from the glyph's own outline and the other from a line of the font. A solved case can be read backward to find what its maker assumed, and a tuple can hold a tuple, and a tool that takes it apart will complain about the count if you flatten it.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Change MASTER in list_anchors.py to "Bold" and run it. How far apart are the glyph and the anchors for icircumflex? Open the glyph and look at the gap the number describes.
  2. Which one-letter glyphs have no top anchor? Write a loop over font.glyphs that prints every name of length 1 whose Regular anchors lack top. I get 21. Then look at the Czech and Polish lists from chapter 25. Does either language need an accent above any of the 21?
  3. An edit can take an anchor away: ("remove", "top", None). Write a short script that removes top from the Regular dotlessi, run it, and then run add_top_anchors.py again. Did you end up where you were? Compare that with choosing Edit > Undo twice. Which would you rather explain to a colleague?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Plum's letters have pegs, its accents have loops, and you can make a glyph from a description. Chapter 56 puts the three together: a text file of recipes, one line for each letter, and a script that builds the lot.

docs.title: 56. Build them all
docs.text:
Monday of week eleven. Over the weekend Mira did something that needed no computer. She took the two lists from chapter 25, the Polish letters and the Czech ones that Plum lacks, and wrote next to each letter what it's made of. Ć is a C with an acute. ů is a u with a ring. ě is an e with a caron. It filled a page.

Last Wednesday you built one of those letters with a script that had the base and the accent typed into it as constants. To build Ć you'd change two constants and run it again, and then again for ć. Mira's page has thirty lines. And she already knows the page will grow, because the publisher mentioned Slovak on Friday, in the tone people use for things they haven't decided yet.

So the page shouldn't live inside a script. It should be a text file that Mira can open, read and add to, and the script should do whatever the file says. A line in such a file is usually called a recipe: it names a dish and what goes into it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • tell, ask and choose_text_file from chapter 39. The whole script writes them out again.
  • The anchors on dotlessi from chapter 55, and the nacute from chapter 53. The script copes if either is missing, and your numbers will differ from mine.
  • Bring the Font window to the front before you run the whole script. The tool that makes glyphs refuses while a Glyph window is the active one.

The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel. The writing at the end is read from the code of the tools.

docs.title: Step 1: Write the recipes down
docs.text:
Make a text file called accents.txt in the folder where Plum-practice lives. Every line has four words with spaces between them: the character, the name of the glyph, the base and the accent.

# Accented letters for the Polish and Czech editions.
# character  glyph name  base  accent

# Polish
Ą Aogonek A ogonek
ą aogonek a ogonek
Ć Cacute C acute
ć cacute c acute
Ę Eogonek E ogonek
ę eogonek e ogonek
Ń Nacute N acute
ń nacute n acute
Ś Sacute S acute
ś sacute s acute
Ź Zacute Z acute
ź zacute z acute
Ż Zdotaccent Z dotaccent
ż zdotaccent z dotaccent

# Czech
Č Ccaron C caron
č ccaron c caron
Ď Dcaron D caron
Ě Ecaron E caron
ě ecaron e caron
Ň Ncaron N caron
ň ncaron n caron
Ř Rcaron R caron
ř rcaron r caron
Š Scaron S caron
š scaron s caron
Ť Tcaron T caron
Ů Uring U ring
ů uring u ring
Ž Zcaron Z caron
ž zcaron z caron

# Already in the font, on the dotlessi
í iacute dotlessi acute
î icircumflex dotlessi circumflex
ï idieresis dotlessi dieresis
ì igrave dotlessi grave

That's 34 recipes. Three things about the list before any code.

The character comes first because it carries the Unicode value. In chapter 53 you typed 324 for ń. Here the script can ask ord what the number is, as in chapter 23, and Mira never looks one up.

Four letters from the two lists aren't in the file. The Polish Ł and ł are an L and an l with a stroke through them, and that's drawn, not assembled. The Czech ď and ť carry a caron that looks like an apostrophe, which will need its own accent glyph. Mira leaves all four for the drawing list.

And the last four lines are glyphs Plum has. I put them in on purpose. Two of them have accents that sit off their new anchors, and you made a nacute on Wednesday that's ten units off in the Bold. A script that builds what the recipes say should also notice a glyph that's there and wrong.

Save the file as UTF-8. Most text editors do that without being asked. If the script later reads Ä… where you typed ą, the editor saved it another way.

docs.title: Step 2: Read a line into four names
docs.text:
read_names from chapter 40 reads a file with one name on a line. Here a line has four parts, so the script needs to cut it. You met split in chapter 9, where name.split(".") cut a glyph name at its dots. Call it with nothing in the parentheses and it cuts at spaces:

line = "ń nacute n acute"
print(line.split())
character, name, base, mark = line.split()
print(base, mark)

['ń', 'nacute', 'n', 'acute']
n acute

split() with no argument does two kind things. It treats any run of spaces or tabs as one cut, so you can line the columns up in the file if you like. And it drops the line ending along with them, so there's nothing to strip.

The second line of the sample takes the list of four apart into four names. Now see what a careless line does. Suppose Mira forgot the accent:

character, name, base, mark = "ń nacute n".split()

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 4, got 3)

On Friday a tool complained about too many values, and this is the same complaint from the other side. Four names are waiting and three pieces arrived. The message is honest and useless to Mira, because it doesn't say which line of her file is short. For today the fix is to open the file and look. Tomorrow's chapter makes the script say where.

The function that reads the file is read_names with one more step:

def read_recipes(path):
    recipes = []
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            line = line.strip()
            if not line or line.startswith("#"):
                continue
            character, name, base, mark = line.split()
            recipes.append((character, name, base, mark))
    return recipes

It hands back a list of tuples. A loop can take each one apart in its for line, as you did with pairs last week.

docs.title: Step 3: Find the shift
docs.text:
Thursday's possible_shifts gave every shift the anchors allow, and for u with an acute it gave two. A script that builds glyphs has to pick one. Mine walks through the accent's loops in the order of their names and takes the first one for which the base has a peg:

def shift_for(font, base, mark, master):
    pegs = anchors.anchor_points(layer_for(font, base, master))
    loops = anchors.anchor_points(layer_for(font, mark, master))
    for loop in sorted(loops):
        family = loop[1:]
        if loop.startswith("_") and family in pegs:
            bx, by = pegs[family]
            mx, my = loops[loop]
            return round(bx - mx), round(by - my)
    return None

loop[1:] is a slice from chapter 10, used on a string: everything from the second character on. It turns _acute into acute. Sorted, _acute comes before _acuteHigh, so the plain peg wins when a letter has both. That's a rule I made up. It gives the designer's own result for every built glyph in Plum that has a matching pair, and I checked that before I trusted it.

The function ends in two ways. When a pair fits, return inside the loop hands back the shift and the loop stops there. When no pair fits, the loop runs out and the last line hands back None.

A glyph needs a shift in all three masters, so one more function asks three times and gives up if any answer is missing:

def shifts_for(font, base, mark):
    shifts = {}
    for master in MASTERS:
        shift = shift_for(font, base, mark, master)
        if shift is None:
            return None
        shifts[master] = shift
    return shifts

docs.title: Step 4: Three things can be true of a recipe
docs.text:
Take one recipe whose base and accent are both in the font and whose anchors fit. The glyph it names is in one of four states.

It isn't there. Then the script describes it, as on Wednesday: a width for each master taken from the base, a Unicode value, and two parts in each master.

def new_glyph(font, character, name, base, mark, shifts):
    layers = []
    components = []
    for master in MASTERS:
        dx, dy = shifts[master]
        width = round(layer_for(font, base, master).advanceWidth)
        layers.append((master, width))
        components.append(creation.Part(master, base, 0, 0))
        components.append(creation.Part(master, mark, dx, dy))
    return creation.NewGlyph(
        name=name,
        layers=tuple(layers),
        unicodes=(ord(character),),
        components=tuple(components),
    )

It's there, and its accent sits where the anchors say. Then there's nothing to do.

It's there, and its accent sits somewhere else. Last Wednesday you saw that the tool for new glyphs refuses a name that exists, and it's right to. So this state needs a different tool, one that moves a component that's already in a glyph. It works like Friday's anchor writer. An edit is a pair: which component, and where its shift should be. A row of work is a glyph, a layer and a list of edits.

def moves_for(font, name, shifts):
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    rows = []
    for master in MASTERS:
        layer = layer_of(rich.fl, master)
        accent = parts.components(layer)[1]
        if parts.offset(accent) != shifts[master]:
            rows.append((rich.fl, layer, [(accent.id, shifts[master])]))
    return rows

accent.id is new. Every shape in a layer has an identity that FontLab gives it, and the moving tool wants that and not the shape itself. You don't need to print it or understand it. It's a ticket you hand over.

!= compares two pairs here. parts.offset gives (54.0, 0.0) and the shift is (52, 0). Python treats 54.0 and 54 as equal, so a pair of whole numbers and a pair of numbers with .0 compare as you'd hope.

If all three masters agree, rows stays empty, and an empty list is how this function says "fine as it is".

The fourth state comes from Friday. It's there, and FontLab builds it. Chapter 55 said that no keyword opens such a glyph to a script, and the moving tool would refuse the whole batch over one of them. So the script asks first:

def is_auto(font, name):
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    return any([layer_of(rich.fl, master).autoLayer for master in MASTERS])

autoLayer is true for a layer that FontLab builds from a recipe of its own. An automatic glyph gets a row that says auto, and nothing else happens to it.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is build_accents.py:

#FLM: Build Accented Letters
# Reads recipes from a text file: character, glyph name, base, accent.
# Builds the glyphs that are missing and moves accents that sit off their
# anchors. A recipe it can't follow is skipped without a word.
from pathlib import Path

import fly.ap.anchors.writer as anchors
import fly.ap.components.writer as parts
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.glyphs.creation as creation
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_file_dialog, run_standard_message_box
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def text_files_only(kind, dialog):
    dialog.setNameFilters(["Text files (*.txt)"])


def choose_text_file(caption, folder=""):
    paths = run_file_dialog(qt.QtGui, text_files_only, caption, folder)
    if paths is None:
        return None
    return paths[0]


def read_recipes(path):
    recipes = []
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            line = line.strip()
            if not line or line.startswith("#"):
                continue
            character, name, base, mark = line.split()
            recipes.append((character, name, base, mark))
    return recipes


def layer_for(font, name, master):
    return layer_of(fl.flGlyph(font[name], font), master)


def shift_for(font, base, mark, master):
    pegs = anchors.anchor_points(layer_for(font, base, master))
    loops = anchors.anchor_points(layer_for(font, mark, master))
    for loop in sorted(loops):
        family = loop[1:]
        if loop.startswith("_") and family in pegs:
            bx, by = pegs[family]
            mx, my = loops[loop]
            return round(bx - mx), round(by - my)
    return None


def shifts_for(font, base, mark):
    shifts = {}
    for master in MASTERS:
        shift = shift_for(font, base, mark, master)
        if shift is None:
            return None
        shifts[master] = shift
    return shifts


def new_glyph(font, character, name, base, mark, shifts):
    layers = []
    components = []
    for master in MASTERS:
        dx, dy = shifts[master]
        width = round(layer_for(font, base, master).advanceWidth)
        layers.append((master, width))
        components.append(creation.Part(master, base, 0, 0))
        components.append(creation.Part(master, mark, dx, dy))
    return creation.NewGlyph(
        name=name,
        layers=tuple(layers),
        unicodes=(ord(character),),
        components=tuple(components),
    )


def moves_for(font, name, shifts):
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    rows = []
    for master in MASTERS:
        layer = layer_of(rich.fl, master)
        accent = parts.components(layer)[1]
        if parts.offset(accent) != shifts[master]:
            rows.append((rich.fl, layer, [(accent.id, shifts[master])]))
    return rows


def is_auto(font, name):
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    return any([layer_of(rich.fl, master).autoLayer for master in MASTERS])


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    folder = Path(font.path).parent if font.path else ""
    path = choose_text_file("Choose a recipe file", folder)
    if path is None:
        return

    recipes = read_recipes(path)
    print(f"{len(recipes)} recipes read.")
    have = {glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs}
    specs = []
    work = []
    moved = 0
    fine = 0
    auto = 0
    for character, name, base, mark in recipes:
        if base not in have or mark not in have:
            continue
        shifts = shifts_for(font, base, mark)
        if shifts is None:
            continue
        if name not in have:
            specs.append(new_glyph(font, character, name, base, mark, shifts))
            state = "new"
        elif is_auto(font, name):
            auto += 1
            state = "auto"
        else:
            rows = moves_for(font, name, shifts)
            if rows:
                work = work + rows
                moved += 1
                state = "move"
            else:
                fine += 1
                state = "fine"
        text = ", ".join([f"{shifts[m][0]} {shifts[m][1]}" for m in MASTERS])
        print(f"{name:<13}{state:<6}{base} + {mark}: {text}")
    print(f"{len(specs)} to build, {moved} to move, {fine} fine as they are, {auto} automatic.")

    if not specs and not work:
        return
    if not ask(f"Build {len(specs)} glyphs and move the accents in {moved}?"):
        return

    package = scripting.current_package()
    if work:
        facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
        parts.require_safe(work, facts)
        parts.apply_work(work, "Move accents to their anchors", facts, parts.MoveEditor())
    if specs:
        facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
        creation.create_glyphs(package, specs, "Build accented letters", facts)
    tell(f"Built {len(specs)} glyphs. Moved the accents in {moved}.")


main()

34 recipes read.
Cacute       new   C + acute: 88 210, 101 210, 111 210
cacute       new   c + acute: -4 0, 5 0, 15 0
Nacute       new   N + acute: 92 210, 119 210, 129 210
nacute       move  n + acute: 40 0, 52 0, 62 0
Sacute       new   S + acute: 18 210, 38 210, 48 210
sacute       new   s + acute: -34 0, -25 0, 15 0
Zacute       new   Z + acute: 33 210, 56 210, 66 210
zacute       new   z + acute: -20 0, -12 0, 28 0
Uring        new   U + ring: 57 210, 69 210, 69 210
uring        new   u + ring: 0 0, 12 0, 12 0
iacute       auto  dotlessi + acute: -147 0, -139 0, -140 0
icircumflex  auto  dotlessi + circumflex: -153 0, -139 0, -124 0
idieresis    auto  dotlessi + dieresis: -153 0, -137 0, -123 0
igrave       auto  dotlessi + grave: -116 0, -117 0, -140 0
9 to build, 1 to move, 0 fine as they are, 4 automatic.

The three numbers in each row are the Light, the Regular and the Bold.

main does all its reading and all its sums before it asks, and all its writing after. By the time the question appears, the list in the Output panel says what a yes would do. That order is worth keeping in every script that changes a font.

The facts are scanned twice, once before each kind of writing. The tools want facts that are fresh, and after the accents have moved, the first set describes a font that has changed.

The moves should be one step in the Edit menu, and the new glyphs one step each, as chapter 40 said of empty ones. So undoing everything takes ten trips to Edit > Undo, or one File > Revert if you saved before you ran it. Save before you run it.

docs.title: Read what it did
docs.text:
Nine glyphs are new. The capitals carry 210 in their shifts, and nobody typed it. Eight Polish letters are in the font now, counting the ń from Wednesday, and two Czech ones.

One glyph moved. The nacute went from 42, 54 and 72 to 40, 52 and 62, which settles Thursday's complaint. The script could move it because you made it yourself on Wednesday, as a plain glyph of two parts. The four i letters are FontLab's own, and the script left them alone. The numbers in their rows say where the anchors want the accents. For iacute and igrave that's where they are. The î and ï sit left of it, by 16 units in the Bold, and Mira writes both on her list, to be moved by hand in the Glyph window or left to FontLab's own rebuilding.

Run the script again and every row says fine or auto:

0 to build, 0 to move, 10 fine as they are, 4 automatic.

Then run list_anchors.py from chapter 54 and read its last two lines:

Agree with their anchors: 79. Differ: 2.
10 have no matching pair: IJ ij colon quotedbl semicolon guillemotleft guillemotright quotedblbase quotedblleft quotedblright

Now do a sum that the script didn't do for you. It read 34 recipes. It printed 14 rows. Twenty recipes went in and nothing came out: no row, no warning, no glyph. The comment at the top of the script admits it, "skipped without a word", and the two continue lines are where it happens.

Mira doesn't notice at first. She sets Świętość to admire the new Ś and ć, and gets a box where the ę should be. She checks the file. The line for ę is there, spelled correctly. The script said nothing about it. It costs her ten minutes.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A recipe file keeps the list of what to build outside the script, where the person who knows the letters can edit it. line.split() cuts a line at its spaces, and the pieces can go straight into as many names as there are pieces. A script that builds should check the states of each target: missing, right, there but wrong, and built by FontLab itself, which it reports and leaves alone. Existing components are moved with parts.apply_work(work, title, facts, parts.MoveEditor()), and all the reading comes before the question, all the writing after.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add one print line before each continue in main, so that the script names every recipe it skips and says whether the base, the accent or the anchors were the trouble. How many are skipped for each reason? Which three accents does Mira have to draw?
  2. Slovak needs ŕ and Ŕ, an r and an R with an acute. Add two recipes with the names racute and Racute and run the script. I get shifts of -75, -50 and -40 for the small one. Set the word vŕba and look at it in the Bold.
  3. Slovak also needs ĺ, an l with an acute. Add the recipe, let the script build lacute, and open it. Something is wrong. Print the anchors of l and the box of l, compare the height of the acute peg with the height of the stem, and say what you'd change. The script did what the anchors said. Was the script wrong?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Twenty recipes vanished and the script kept quiet about every one. Chapter 57 makes it collect what went wrong, line by line, and hand Mira a list she can act on.

docs.title: 57. The what-went-wrong list
docs.text:
Tuesday. Yesterday's script read 34 recipes, had a line for 14 and said nothing about the other 20. Mira lost ten minutes over a missing ę.

This morning the recipe file grew. Slovak is no longer a rumor, so Mira added three lines for it, in a hurry, between two phone calls. Ines came by and asked for an ĩ, for a name in a book on Paraguay, and Mira added that as well. She suspects that at least one of the four new lines is wrong, and she'd like the script to tell her which.

Today's change is small. The script will stop treating a recipe it can't follow as nothing. Each one becomes an entry in a list, with the line number in the file and a sentence about what's wrong. The script finishes its work on the recipes that are sound, and then hands the list over.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed, in the state chapter 56 left it. The outputs assume you didn't build racute and Racute in exercise 2 of that chapter. If you did, your row for Racute will say fine.
  • build_accents.py and accents.txt from chapter 56.
  • The Font window in front when you run the whole script.

The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel. The changes of the last four chapters were applied to that file by hand first.

Add Mira's new lines to the end of accents.txt, mistakes and all. Leave an empty line after the last line that's there, so that the line numbers match mine:

# Slovak
Ŕ Racute R acute
ŕ racute rr acute
ľ lcaron l

# For Ines
ĩ itilde i tilde

docs.title: Step 1: What can go wrong with a recipe
docs.text:
Before you write the code, write the list of troubles. I count five.

  1. The line doesn't have four words.
  2. The base isn't in the font.
  3. The accent isn't in the font.
  4. Both are there, and the base has no peg that fits a loop of the accent.
  5. The glyph is in the font already, and it isn't one base with one accent.

Yesterday's script crashed on the first, kept quiet on the next three, and would have crashed on the fifth if a recipe had hit it.

None of the five is a reason to stop. If line 47 is short, lines 1 to 46 are no worse for it. So the rule for today is: when one recipe is in trouble, write the trouble down and go on to the next. Then say everything at the end, in one place. Mira fixes her file once and runs the script again.

A script that stops at the first trouble would need 23 runs for 23 troubles.

docs.title: Step 2: Number the lines
docs.text:
To say "line 47", the reader function has to count lines as it goes. You could keep a counter in a box and add 1 on every turn. Python has a helper that does it for you:

for number, word in enumerate(["ogonek", "caron", "dotaccent"], 1):
    print(number, word)

1 ogonek
2 caron
3 dotaccent

enumerate wraps anything you can loop over and gives a pair on every turn: a count and the item. The 1 says where to start counting. Leave it out and the count starts at 0, which suits Python and doesn't suit a person who's looking at line numbers in a text editor.

In the reader, the count has to include the comment lines and the empty ones, because the editor counts those too. So enumerate goes around the file itself, and the test for lines to skip comes after:

def read_recipes(path):
    recipes = []
    problems = []
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for number, line in enumerate(f, 1):
            words = line.split()
            if not words or words[0].startswith("#"):
                continue
            if len(words) != 4:
                problems.append((number, f"{len(words)} words where 4 are needed: {line.strip()}"))
                continue
            character, name, base, mark = words
            recipes.append((number, character, name, base, mark))
    return recipes, problems

Three things changed from yesterday.

The line is split first and tested afterwards. An empty line splits into an empty list, and not words is true for an empty list, as it is for an empty string.

The count of words is checked before the four names take them. That's the whole cure for yesterday's ValueError. The script looks before it unpacks.

And the function hands back two lists, the recipes and the problems, as a pair. A recipe now carries its line number in front, because trouble can turn up later, when the font is asked, and the script must still know which line to blame.

docs.title: Step 3: A problem is a thing you keep
docs.text:
A problem here is a tuple of two items: a number and a sentence. It's ordinary data. You can put it in a list, sort it, count it and print it, like a width or a name.

In main, every place where yesterday's script said continue and nothing else now leaves a note first:

if base not in have:
    problems.append((number, f"{name}: no glyph named {base} for the base"))
    continue

Write the sentence for the person who'll read it. It names the glyph she wanted, the thing that's missing, and what role that thing played. "KeyError: 'rr'" would be true as well, and Mira would have to work out the rest.

For the fifth kind of trouble, moves_for gets a guard. It used to take the second component of every layer on trust. Now it counts them first and hands back None when a layer holds some other number than two:

found = parts.components(layer)
if len(found) != 2:
    return None

So moves_for has three answers: None for "this glyph isn't what you think", an empty list for "fine", and a list with rows in it for "move these". The caller has to tell None from an empty list, and not rows can't, because it's true for both. Use rows is None.

docs.title: Step 4: Print them in order
docs.text:
The problems come from two places: the reader finds the short lines, and main finds the rest. Put together, they're out of order. sorted puts tuples in order by their first item, so a list of (number, sentence) comes out by line number without your saying how:

print(sorted([(47, "short line"), (5, "no ogonek"), (46, "no rr")]))

[(5, 'no ogonek'), (46, 'no rr'), (47, 'short line')]

That works as long as every entry has the same shape. Suppose that in one of the five places you type the sentence and forget the number:

problems.append(f"{name}: {base} has no peg that fits {mark}")

Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'tuple'

To sort, Python asks of two entries which one is smaller. It can answer that for two tuples and for two strings. For a string and a tuple it has no answer, and says so. The message points at sorted, which is innocent. The fault is thirty lines up, where an entry of the wrong shape went into the list. When a list is filled in several places, check each place for the shape of what goes in.

You'll see that error only when a line in the file reaches that branch.

docs.title: Step 5: One more list, for the drawing table
docs.text:
Twenty of the problems will turn out to be the same three problems. Mira doesn't want to count carons by eye. A tally, as in chapter 22, turns the long list into a short one:

to_draw = {}
...
to_draw[mark] = to_draw.get(mark, 0) + 1

It counts how many recipes are waiting for each missing accent. That's the order in which drawing them pays off.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Here is the new build_accents.py. The three functions that work out shifts and describe a new glyph are as they were.

#FLM: Build Accented Letters
# Reads recipes from a text file: character, glyph name, base, accent.
# Builds the glyphs that are missing and moves accents that sit off their
# anchors. Every recipe it can't follow goes into a list, with its line
# number, and the list is printed at the end.
from pathlib import Path

import fly.ap.anchors.writer as anchors
import fly.ap.components.writer as parts
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.glyphs.creation as creation
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_file_dialog, run_standard_message_box
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def text_files_only(kind, dialog):
    dialog.setNameFilters(["Text files (*.txt)"])


def choose_text_file(caption, folder=""):
    paths = run_file_dialog(qt.QtGui, text_files_only, caption, folder)
    if paths is None:
        return None
    return paths[0]


def read_recipes(path):
    recipes = []
    problems = []
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for number, line in enumerate(f, 1):
            words = line.split()
            if not words or words[0].startswith("#"):
                continue
            if len(words) != 4:
                problems.append((number, f"{len(words)} words where 4 are needed: {line.strip()}"))
                continue
            character, name, base, mark = words
            recipes.append((number, character, name, base, mark))
    return recipes, problems


def layer_for(font, name, master):
    return layer_of(fl.flGlyph(font[name], font), master)


def shift_for(font, base, mark, master):
    pegs = anchors.anchor_points(layer_for(font, base, master))
    loops = anchors.anchor_points(layer_for(font, mark, master))
    for loop in sorted(loops):
        family = loop[1:]
        if loop.startswith("_") and family in pegs:
            bx, by = pegs[family]
            mx, my = loops[loop]
            return round(bx - mx), round(by - my)
    return None


def shifts_for(font, base, mark):
    shifts = {}
    for master in MASTERS:
        shift = shift_for(font, base, mark, master)
        if shift is None:
            return None
        shifts[master] = shift
    return shifts


def new_glyph(font, character, name, base, mark, shifts):
    layers = []
    components = []
    for master in MASTERS:
        dx, dy = shifts[master]
        width = round(layer_for(font, base, master).advanceWidth)
        layers.append((master, width))
        components.append(creation.Part(master, base, 0, 0))
        components.append(creation.Part(master, mark, dx, dy))
    return creation.NewGlyph(
        name=name,
        layers=tuple(layers),
        unicodes=(ord(character),),
        components=tuple(components),
    )


def moves_for(font, name, shifts):
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    rows = []
    for master in MASTERS:
        layer = layer_of(rich.fl, master)
        found = parts.components(layer)
        if len(found) != 2:
            return None
        accent = found[1]
        if parts.offset(accent) != shifts[master]:
            rows.append((rich.fl, layer, [(accent.id, shifts[master])]))
    return rows


def report(problems, to_draw):
    if not problems:
        print("Every recipe could be followed.")
        return
    print()
    print(f"{len(problems)} recipes need a look:")
    for number, text in sorted(problems):
        print(f"  line {number:>2}  {text}")
    if to_draw:
        def how_often(mark):
            return to_draw[mark]

        print()
        print("Accents to draw, and the recipes waiting for each:")
        for mark in sorted(to_draw, key=how_often, reverse=True):
            print(f"  {mark:<11}{to_draw[mark]:>3}")


def is_auto(font, name):
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    return any([layer_of(rich.fl, master).autoLayer for master in MASTERS])


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    folder = Path(font.path).parent if font.path else ""
    path = choose_text_file("Choose a recipe file", folder)
    if path is None:
        return

    recipes, problems = read_recipes(path)
    print(f"{len(recipes)} recipes read.")
    have = {glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs}
    specs = []
    work = []
    to_draw = {}
    moved = 0
    fine = 0
    auto = 0
    for number, character, name, base, mark in recipes:
        if base not in have:
            problems.append((number, f"{name}: no glyph named {base} for the base"))
            continue
        if mark not in have:
            problems.append((number, f"{name}: no glyph named {mark} for the accent"))
            to_draw[mark] = to_draw.get(mark, 0) + 1
            continue
        shifts = shifts_for(font, base, mark)
        if shifts is None:
            problems.append((number, f"{name}: {base} has no peg that fits {mark}"))
            continue
        if name not in have:
            specs.append(new_glyph(font, character, name, base, mark, shifts))
            state = "new"
        elif is_auto(font, name):
            auto += 1
            state = "auto"
        else:
            rows = moves_for(font, name, shifts)
            if rows is None:
                problems.append((number, f"{name}: is in the font, but not as one base and one accent"))
                continue
            if rows:
                work = work + rows
                moved += 1
                state = "move"
            else:
                fine += 1
                state = "fine"
        text = ", ".join([f"{shifts[m][0]} {shifts[m][1]}" for m in MASTERS])
        print(f"{name:<13}{state:<6}{base} + {mark}: {text}")
    print(f"{len(specs)} to build, {moved} to move, {fine} fine as they are, {auto} automatic.")
    report(problems, to_draw)

    if not specs and not work:
        return
    if not ask(f"Build {len(specs)} glyphs and move the accents in {moved}?"):
        return

    package = scripting.current_package()
    if work:
        facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
        parts.require_safe(work, facts)
        parts.apply_work(work, "Move accents to their anchors", facts, parts.MoveEditor())
    if specs:
        facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
        creation.create_glyphs(package, specs, "Build accented letters", facts)
    tell(f"Built {len(specs)} glyphs. Moved the accents in {moved}.")


main()

37 recipes read.
