Add the totals up once by hand. The first line says 37 recipes, 15 rows follow, and 37 minus 15 is 22. The report says 23. The numbers disagree, and they should: the short line on line 47 never became a recipe, so the reader counted 37 sound lines and one problem. Thirty-eight lines were meant as recipes, 15 could be followed and 23 couldn't.

The problems are printed before the question is asked, so Mira can say no, fix her file and come back.

docs.title: Read the report
docs.text:
Twenty lines say the same thing in three flavors, and the short list at the bottom sums them up: draw a caron and 14 letters can be built, an ogonek gives 4, a dot accent gives 2. That's Mira's week, in order.

The last three lines are the ones she typed between phone calls.

Line 46 has rr for the base. Yesterday's script would have skipped it without a sound.

Line 47 has three words. She didn't forget the accent. She stopped, because ľ takes the apostrophe-like caron that Plum doesn't have, and she wasn't sure what to call it. The script can't know that, and reports what it sees.

Line 50 is the interesting one. Both glyphs exist, and the script says that i has no peg that fits tilde. Print the anchors of i and you get bottom and ogonek, nothing above. That's deliberate. An accent above an i replaces the dot, so the letter to build on is dotlessi, which is why the four recipes at the end of yesterday's list are written that way. An absent anchor stopped a wrong glyph from being built, and the report said why.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: When one item in a batch is in trouble, record it as a tuple of a line number and a sentence, and carry on. enumerate(things, 1) counts while you loop, and the size of a list should be checked before you unpack it into names. sorted orders tuples by their first item, and fails with a TypeError when the entries don't share a shape. A function can have three answers, and then is None tells nothing-to-do from can't-be-done.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Fix the three lines. Correct rr. Put a # in front of the ľ line and write after it what's missing. Change the base in the ĩ line to dotlessi. Run the script. If you said yes to the Racute above, I get two glyphs to build, with shifts of -153, -139 and -124 for the itilde, and 20 recipes that need a look.
  2. Add the recipe Ø Oslash O acute, which is nonsense, since the Ø is a drawn letter that Plum has. Which of the five troubles does the script report, and from which function does the answer come? Remove the line afterwards.
  3. Mira wants to mail the list to Oskar. Add a step at the end of report that asks where to save with choose_save_file from chapter 39, and writes the same lines into it, as chapter 26 wrote the glyph list. Keep the printing as well.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The recipes borrow shapes, and a borrowed shape can't drift away from its source. Some of Plum's look-alike glyphs were made the other way, as copied outlines, years ago. Chapter 58 puts two of them side by side and asks whether they are still the same drawing, node for node.

docs.title: 58. Compare two glyphs
docs.text:
Wednesday. Mira is drawing a caron, and while she draws she talks.

"The nine is the six turned upside down. The u is the n turned upside down. The closing bracket is the opening one in a mirror. That's how I made them, seven years ago. Since then I've nudged things. I don't know which pairs are still pairs."

The accented letters of the last few days can't have this trouble. A component borrows a shape, so when the n changes, the ń changes with it. But a nine made by copying the six and turning the copy is a drawing of its own from that moment. Move a node in the six and the nine stays as it was.

So today's question is whether two glyphs are the same drawing. You'll need a way to compare two lists of points, and you'll find out that "the same" needs a number attached to it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The scripts from chapters 42 to 49.

Nothing in this chapter changes the font. The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel.

docs.title: Step 1: A glyph as a list of points
docs.text:
For comparing, a glyph is its points and nothing else. Make each node into a pair of numbers:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()


def points_of(font, name, master):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, font[name]).nodes(master)
    return [(node.x, node.y) for node in nodes]


six = points_of(font, "six", "Regular")
nine = points_of(font, "nine", "Regular")
print(len(six), len(nine))

31 31

The list holds every node, the ones on the outline and the handles alike. Both glyphs have 31, which is a good start. If the counts differed, we could stop here and say no.

docs.title: Step 2: When are two lists equal?
docs.text:
Python compares lists with ==, the same sign it uses for numbers:

print([1, 2, 3] == [1, 2, 3])
print([1, 2, 3] == [3, 2, 1])

True
False

Two lists are equal when they have the same items in the same order. The same items in another order make a different list. Tuples work the same way, and so do lists of tuples: Python goes through both, pair by pair, and says False at the first pair that doesn't match.

print(six == nine)

False

One more thing about == before we go on. FontLab hands out coordinates as numbers with a decimal point, such as 250.0, and you'll often type whole numbers. That makes no difference to a comparison:

print([(1.0, 2)] == [(1, 2.0)])

True

Python compares the values, and 1.0 is the same value as 1. What does make a difference is a coordinate of 250.4 against 250: those are two numbers, however alike the glyphs look on screen. Keep that in mind for step 4.

Nobody expected True for the six and the nine. One is upside down, and they sit in different places between their sidebearings. Before the lists can be compared, both glyphs have to be brought to the same place, and one of them has to be turned.

docs.title: Step 3: Bring both home
docs.text:
The six runs from x 45 to 450, the nine from 40 to 445. Measure every point from the bottom left corner of its own box and that difference is gone:

def at_home(points, how):
    xs = [x for x, y in points]
    ys = [y for x, y in points]
    left, bottom, right, top = min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)
    if how == "turn":
        return [(right - x, top - y) for x, y in points]
    if how == "flip":
        return [(right - x, y - bottom) for x, y in points]
    return [(x - left, y - bottom) for x, y in points]

The last line is the plain case. A point at the left edge gets x 0, a point at the bottom gets y 0.

The "turn" line measures from the opposite corner: how far left of the right edge, how far below the top. Hold a page upside down and that's what happens to every point on it. The "flip" line measures x from the right edge and leaves the heights alone, which is what a mirror does.

Any other word, such as "keep", falls through both ifs to the plain case.

first = at_home(six, "keep")
second = at_home(nine, "turn")
print(first == second)

False

Still False, and for a dull reason. A contour is a loop, and a loop can start anywhere. The six starts at the bottom of its bowl. The turned nine has the same points and starts somewhere else. The order in the list is an accident of where the designer clicked first.

Take the accident away by sorting both lists:

print(sorted(first)[:3])
print(sorted(second)[:3])
print(sorted(first) == sorted(second))

[(0.0, 84.0), (0.0, 260.0), (0.0, 506.0)]
[(0.0, 84.0), (0.0, 260.0), (0.0, 506.0)]
True

The nine is still the six, to the last handle. Try "n" and "u" and you get True again.

docs.title: Step 4: Nearly the same
docs.text:
Now the braces:

left = sorted(at_home(points_of(font, "braceleft", "Regular"), "keep"))
right = sorted(at_home(points_of(font, "braceright", "Regular"), "turn"))
print(left == right)

False

False is all == can say. It doesn't say whether the braces are two different drawings or one drawing with a node a hair out of place, and those call for different things from Mira. We need a distance.

For two points, take the larger of the two differences, across and up:

def gap(p, q):
    return max(abs(p[0] - q[0]), abs(p[1] - q[1]))

Then walk the two sorted lists side by side with zip, from chapter 35, and keep the largest gap:

print(max([gap(p, q) for p, q in zip(left, right)]))

714.0

Seven hundred units. That says the braces have nothing to do with each other, and one look at the Font window says otherwise. The mistake is in the method.

Print the pairs that differ:

print([(p, q) for p, q in zip(left, right) if p != q])

[((105.0, 785.0), (107.0, 71.0)), ((107.0, 71.0), (107.0, 785.0)), ((109.0, 439.0), (110.0, 439.0)), ((112.0, 710.0), (113.0, 146.0)), ((113.0, 146.0), (113.0, 422.0)), ((113.0, 422.0), (113.0, 710.0))]

Look at the first pair. The point at (105, 785) in one brace has a partner at (107, 785) in the other: two units apart. But sorting goes by x first. With x 105 the point comes before (107, 71) in its own list. In the other list its partner has x 107 and comes after. From there the two lists are out of step, and zip pairs each point with a stranger.

Sorting was fine for asking "exactly equal?". It breaks down for "how close?", because a small difference changes the order.

So don't rely on order at all. For each point, look through all the points of the other glyph and take the smallest gap. That's the distance to its nearest neighbor. The largest of those, over the whole glyph, tells how far apart the two drawings are:

def farthest(points, others):
    return max([min([gap(p, q) for q in others]) for p in points])


print(farthest(left, right))

2.0

Read it from the inside. [gap(p, q) for q in others] is the list of gaps from one point p to every point of the other glyph, and min picks the nearest. The outer list does that for every p, and max picks the point that's worst off.

Two units. The braces are one drawing, and somebody has touched one of them since. It's only the Regular, too: in the Light and the Bold the answer is 0.

This looks at 31 times 31 pairs, close to a thousand. Python doesn't mind.

docs.title: Step 5: Say how close is close enough
docs.text:
Now "the same" needs a number. I'll use three verdicts. A gap of 0 is same. Up to 3 units is close, which means: one drawing, with a nudge that Mira should look at. More than 3 is differ.

The 3 is a tolerance, and it's a judgment. I picked it because a nudge of a unit or two is what a slipped hand does, and nobody redraws a letter by three units on purpose. It goes at the top of the script as a constant, where Mira can change it.

docs.title: Step 6: Keep the pairs apart from the code
docs.text:
Which glyphs belong together, and whether a pair is turned or mirrored, is knowledge about Plum. It isn't Python. So it goes into a list at the top, one tuple of three words for each pair:

PAIRS = [
    ("six", "nine", "turn"),
    ("parenleft", "parenright", "flip"),
]

The loop takes a tuple apart into three names, the way chapter 35 took rows apart:

for first, second, how in PAIRS:
    print(first, second, how)

six nine turn
parenleft parenright flip

Mira can add a pair without reading a line of the code below it. She can also get a name wrong, as she did yesterday, so the script checks that both glyphs exist before it measures, and says so when one doesn't. A pair that can't be measured for another reason, because one glyph is built from components and has no nodes of its own, or because the two have different numbers of points, gets None for a distance and its own verdict. The lesson of chapter 57 holds here too: one bad row shouldn't stop the other nine.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Compare Glyph Pairs
# Tells whether pairs of glyphs are still the same drawing, turned upside
# down or mirrored. Changes nothing.
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
TOLERANCE = 3
TITLE = "Halfmoon"
PAIRS = [
    ("six", "nine", "turn"),
    ("n", "u", "turn"),
    ("b", "q", "turn"),
    ("d", "p", "turn"),
    ("parenleft", "parenright", "flip"),
    ("bracketleft", "bracketright", "flip"),
    ("braceleft", "braceright", "turn"),
    ("less", "greater", "flip"),
    ("slash", "backslash", "flip"),
    ("quoteleft", "quoteright", "turn"),
]


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def points_of(font, name, master):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, font[name]).nodes(master)
    return [(node.x, node.y) for node in nodes]


def at_home(points, how):
    xs = [x for x, y in points]
    ys = [y for x, y in points]
    left, bottom, right, top = min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)
    if how == "turn":
        return [(right - x, top - y) for x, y in points]
    if how == "flip":
        return [(right - x, y - bottom) for x, y in points]
    return [(x - left, y - bottom) for x, y in points]


def gap(p, q):
    return max(abs(p[0] - q[0]), abs(p[1] - q[1]))


def farthest(points, others):
    return max([min([gap(p, q) for q in others]) for p in points])


def apart(font, first, second, how, master):
    a = points_of(font, first, master)
    b = points_of(font, second, master)
    if not a or len(a) != len(b):
        return None
    a = at_home(a, "keep")
    b = at_home(b, how)
    return round(max(farthest(a, b), farthest(b, a)))


def verdict(gaps):
    if None in gaps:
        return "not comparable"
    worst = max(gaps)
    if worst == 0:
        return "same"
    if worst <= TOLERANCE:
        return "close"
    return "differ"


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    have = {glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs}
    print(f"{'':<27}{'how':<6}{'L':>4}{'R':>4}{'B':>4}")
    for first, second, how in PAIRS:
        if first not in have or second not in have:
            print(f"{first:<13}{second:<14}one of them is missing")
            continue
        gaps = [apart(font, first, second, how, master) for master in MASTERS]
        numbers = "".join([f"{str(g):>4}" if g is None else f"{g:>4}" for g in gaps])
        print(f"{first:<13}{second:<14}{how:<6}{numbers}  {verdict(gaps)}")


main()

                           how      L   R   B
six          nine          turn     0   0   0  same
n            u             turn     0   0   0  same
b            q             turn    56  52  48  differ
d            p             turn    56  52  48  differ
parenleft    parenright    flip     0   0   0  same
bracketleft  bracketright  flip     0   0   0  same
braceleft    braceright    turn     0   2   0  close
less         greater       flip     2   3   3  close
slash        backslash     flip     0   1   0  close
quoteleft    quoteright    turn     0   0   0  same

apart measures both ways, from the first glyph to the second and back, and keeps the larger number. One way alone could be fooled: if every point of the first has a neighbor in the second, the second might still have a point far from everything. apart also gives None when a glyph has no nodes of its own or when the counts differ, and verdict turns that into words.

docs.title: Read the report
docs.text:
Five pairs are what Mira thought they were.

Two differ by about 50 units in every master, and she laughs when she sees them. The q was never a b turned over. The descender is shorter than the ascender, by design, and the gap is that difference. The script reports a difference. Only a person can say that it's meant.

Three are close. In the Regular, one brace has three nodes off by a unit or two, and the backslash is a unit away from the mirrored slash. Those are slips. Mira writes them on her list.

The less and greater row is odd. It's off in all three masters, by 2, 3 and 3 units. A slip doesn't repeat itself three times. Exercise 1 looks into it.

A report like this doesn't fix anything, and it shouldn't. Which of two braces is the right one isn't something the script knows.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Two lists are equal when they hold the same items in the same order, and sorting takes away an order that doesn't matter. == answers yes or no, and for "how far off?" you need a distance and a tolerance. Sorting and pairing with zip fails when values are nearly equal, and a nearest-neighbor search with min inside max doesn't depend on order. A tolerance is a judgment, and it belongs in a constant with a name.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. In PAIRS, change "flip" to "turn" for less and greater. I get 0, 0, 0. So the greater was made by turning the less upside down, and the less isn't quite the same above and below its middle. Which of the two findings would you report to Mira, and what would you ask her?
  2. Add ("comma", "quoteright", "keep") to the list. I get 20, 20 and 10. Is that a slip or a decision? Look at both glyphs in FontLab before you answer.
  3. Set TOLERANCE to 0 and then to 60, and run the script each time. Which verdicts change? What would a tolerance of 60 hide?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Mira's list has grown since chapter 49: a dot outside its glyph, nudged braces, two accents to look at. Chapter 59 goes through the whole font for the small faults that collect in seven years, and writes them into one report.

docs.title: 59. Clean up
docs.text:
Thursday. The caron is drawn, the ogonek is half drawn, and Mira wants a day off from accents.

"Before we build sixty letters on top of this font," she says, "I'd like to know what's lying around in it."

A font that has been worked on for seven years collects small faults. A node gets dropped on top of another node. A segment three units long is left behind where two shapes were joined. None of it shows at text size. Some of it shows when the font is exported, as a kink, or as a complaint from a program further down the line.

Today's script looks for three such faults and writes them into one list. To find them you'll compare each node with its neighbor, and you'll put more than one condition into a loop. The order of the conditions turns out to matter.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • contours_of from chapter 44. The scripts below write it out again.

The script reads the font. One step at the end marks glyphs, and it asks first. The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel.

docs.title: Step 1: Every node and the one before it
docs.text:
Chapter 42 walked along a contour node by node. A fault of the kind we're after isn't in a node. It's between two nodes, so the loop needs two at a time: each node and the one before it.

A for node in nodes loop gives you one. To reach the neighbor, loop over positions instead. range(len(nodes)) counts 0, 1, 2 and so on up to the last position:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph


def contours_of(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    return pGlyph(font, glyph).contours(master)


font = fl.CurrentFont()
contour = contours_of(font, font["Q"], "Regular")[0]
nodes = contour.nodes()
for i in range(len(nodes)):
    before = nodes[i - 1]
    here = nodes[i]
    print(i, before.x, before.y, "to", here.x, here.y)

0 576.0 -157.0 to 440.0 6.0
1 440.0 6.0 to 440.0 6.0
2 440.0 6.0 to 578.0 43.0
...

I've cut the output after three lines. There are 16.

Look at the first line. When i is 0, i - 1 is -1, and nodes[-1] is the last item of a list, as chapter 10 showed. That's what a closed contour needs. The node before the first is the last one, because the outline is a loop. No special case, and no if.

And look at the second line: 440, 6 to 440, 6. Two nodes sit on one spot.

docs.title: Step 2: Three questions about a pair
docs.text:
How far apart are two nodes? Use the measure from yesterday, the larger of the two differences:

def reach(a, b):
    return max(abs(a.x - b.x), abs(a.y - b.y))

Now the questions. If the reach is 0, the nodes are stacked. If it's small, 3 units or less, and both nodes are on the outline, there's a segment too short to be meant. Otherwise the pair is fine.

My first try:

SHORT = 3

for i in range(len(nodes)):
    a = nodes[i - 1]
    b = nodes[i]
    if reach(a, b) == 0:
        print("two nodes on one spot", a.x, a.y)
    if reach(a, b) <= SHORT and a.isOn() and b.isOn():
        print("short segment", a.x, a.y)

two nodes on one spot 440.0 6.0
short segment 440.0 6.0

One fault, two lines. Zero is less than 3, so the stacked pair passes the second test as well. The two ifs don't know about each other. Python asks each one in turn.

A report that says everything twice looks twice as bad as the font is, and Mira would have to work out which lines are echoes. The cure is elif:

    if reach(a, b) == 0:
        print("two nodes on one spot", a.x, a.y)
    elif reach(a, b) <= SHORT and a.isOn() and b.isOn():
        print("short segment", a.x, a.y)

two nodes on one spot 440.0 6.0

With elif, Python asks the second question only when the answer to the first was no. The two tests now form a ladder, and a pair stops at the first rung that fits. So put the narrowest test at the top. Turn these two around and the stacked nodes would be reported as a short segment, which is true and less useful.

The second test has three parts joined by and. All three must hold. The two isOn() calls are there because a segment runs between two nodes on the outline. A handle that sits close to its node is a different thing, a tight curve, and often it's drawn that way on purpose.

docs.title: Step 3: Open contours don't wrap
docs.text:
The trick with nodes[-1] treats every contour as a loop. An open contour isn't one. Its last node and its first aren't joined, and they may well lie close together: that's what an outline looks like when someone forgot to close it. The pair at position 0 mustn't be tested there.

if i == 0 and not contour.closed:
    continue

Read it aloud: "if this is the first position and the contour is not closed, skip." not turns a yes into a no. and wants both sides.

Plum has no open contours, unless the one you planted in chapter 44 is still there, so this line does nothing today. It's there for the font that has some. A check that's right only for the font on your desk will be wrong for the next one.

docs.title: Step 4: A check that cries wolf
docs.text:
I had a fourth check in mind. In chapter 49, the third dot of the Bold ellipsis sat outside the glyph's width. So why not list every glyph whose outline reaches left of 0 or right of its advance width?

edges = box(font, glyph, master)
if edges is not None and (edges[0] < 0 or edges[2] > width):
    print(glyph.name)

The parentheses matter. Without them, Python would read edges is not None and edges[0] < 0 as one group and edges[2] > width as another, because and binds tighter than or, and a glyph with no box would crash on edges[2].

In the Regular the check names 10 glyphs: J, K, T, Y, f, j, backslash, comma, slash and dieresis. In the Bold it names 44.

Mira looks at the list for a few seconds. "The f hangs over on purpose. So does the j, and the J. The T and the Y have their arms out by design. That's how letters fit together."

The numbers also tell a story of their own: 6 in the Light, 10 in the Regular, 44 in the Bold. The heavier the letter, the less room it has inside its width, and the more of it leans out. That's a property of bold type.

The test is correct and the list is useless. Forty-four names, nearly all of them fine, and somewhere among them perhaps one real fault that nobody will find, because nobody reads a list like that twice. I took the check out. A check earns its place when most of what it reports needs doing. If you can't tell a fault from a decision with a test, leave it to the eye.

docs.title: Step 5: Mixed glyphs
docs.text:
One line on Oskar's sheet has waited since chapter 1: "Mark every glyph that mixes its own outlines with borrowed ones." Chapter 52 found them by reading a list. Here's the test, with the components module from that chapter:

if contours and parts.components(layer):
    ...

A list is true when it has something in it. So this reads: "if there are contours and there are components".

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Each finding is a tuple of glyph name, master and a sentence, kept in a list as in chapter 57.

#FLM: Tidy Report
# Looks for stacked nodes, short segments and glyphs that mix their
# own outlines with components. Prints a list. Marks the glyphs if asked.
import fly.ap.components.writer as parts
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
SHORT = 3
VIOLET = 270
TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def contours_of(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    return pGlyph(font, glyph).contours(master)


def reach(a, b):
    return max(abs(a.x - b.x), abs(a.y - b.y))


def pair_faults(contour):
    faults = []
    nodes = contour.nodes()
    for i in range(len(nodes)):
        if i == 0 and not contour.closed:
            continue
        a = nodes[i - 1]
        b = nodes[i]
        far = reach(a, b)
        if far == 0:
            faults.append(f"two nodes on one spot, {a.x:.0f} {a.y:.0f}")
        elif far <= SHORT and a.isOn() and b.isOn():
            faults.append(f"segment of {far:.0f} units at {a.x:.0f} {a.y:.0f}")
    return faults


def glyph_faults(font, glyph, master):
    found = []
    contours = contours_of(font, glyph, master)
    layer = layer_of(fl.flGlyph(glyph, font), master)
    if contours and parts.components(layer):
        found.append("own outline and a component")
    for number, contour in enumerate(contours, 1):
        for text in pair_faults(contour):
            found.append(f"contour {number}: {text}")
    return found


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    findings = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        for master in MASTERS:
            for text in glyph_faults(font, glyph, master):
                findings.append((glyph.name, master, text))

    for name, master, text in findings:
        print(f"{name:<12}{master:<9}{text}")
    names = []
    for name, master, text in findings:
        if name not in names:
            names.append(name)
    print(f"{len(findings)} findings in {len(names)} glyphs.")

    if not names:
        return
    if not ask(f"Mark these {len(names)} glyphs violet?"):
        return
    for name in names:
        pGlyph(font, font[name]).mark = VIOLET


main()

Q           Light    contour 1: segment of 3 units at 394 -6
Q           Regular  contour 1: two nodes on one spot, 440 6
Q           Bold     contour 1: two nodes on one spot, 495 13
exclam      Light    own outline and a component
exclam      Regular  own outline and a component
exclam      Bold     own outline and a component
exclamdown  Light    own outline and a component
exclamdown  Regular  own outline and a component
exclamdown  Bold     own outline and a component
9 findings in 3 glyphs.

Three functions, each a level deeper: main walks glyphs and masters, glyph_faults walks the contours of one layer, pair_faults walks the nodes of one contour. Each hands a list back to the one above. Written as one piece, this would be a loop in a loop in a loop in a loop, with the tests at the bottom of the stairs.

Two small things in main are worth a look.

enumerate(contours, 1) from chapter 57 numbers the contours, so that a finding can say "contour 2". People count from 1, and the Glyph window won't show Mira a contour number at all, so the position that's printed after it matters more: she can click there.

The loop that fills names collects each glyph name once, in the order of the font. if name not in names asks the list whether it already has the name, and only a new name gets in. A set would drop the repeats too, as chapter 25 did, but a set forgets the order, and here the order is the one in the Font window.

The marking is the only change the script makes, and it comes after a question. As chapter 14 said, don't count on Edit > Undo for marks. Violet is a color Halfmoon hasn't used for anything yet.

docs.title: Read the report
docs.text:
Nine findings sounds like a lot, and it's three things. That's usual. Faults come in families: one slip of the hand shows up in every master, and one old habit shows up in every glyph it touched. Read a report for its families before you count its lines.

The Q has one stray node. It's the same node in all three masters, at the spot where the tail meets the bowl. In the Regular and the Bold it lies on top of its neighbor. In the Light it has drifted 3 units away. Had the script looked for stacked nodes only, the Light would have come out clean, and somebody would have removed the node from two masters and left it in the third. Then the three masters would no longer have the same number of nodes, and FontLab couldn't blend between them. Mira removes the node by hand, in all three masters, in the Glyph window. It takes her a minute.

That's why this script reports and doesn't repair. Deleting a node takes one line. Knowing that it must go from every master at once, and checking that the curve keeps its shape, is the work, and for one node the hand is faster and safer.

The exclam and the exclamdown are the two mixed glyphs. They're marked now. Mira crosses out the line on Oskar's sheet. Six of the eleven lines are done.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: range(len(things)) loops over positions, and things[i - 1] reaches the neighbor. At position 0 it wraps around to the last item, which suits a closed loop and has to be guarded for an open one. Two ifs are two separate questions, if and elif are one ladder with the narrowest test on top, and and binds tighter than or, so use parentheses when you mix them. A check that reports mostly decisions and few faults does harm, because it teaches people to stop reading.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Set SHORT to 10 and run the report without marking. Do you get more findings? Open one in the Glyph window and decide whether it's a fault.
  2. Swap the if and the elif test in pair_faults, so that the short-segment test comes first. What does the report say about the Q now, and what has been lost?
  3. Add a count by kind at the end, with a dictionary as in chapter 22: how many findings are stacked nodes, how many short segments, how many mixed glyphs? You can tell the kind from a word in the sentence, with in.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The font is tidy, the caron and the ogonek are drawn, and the recipe file is waiting. Chapter 60 puts the pieces of this part into one script and builds the Czech and Polish letters in an afternoon.

docs.title: 60. The Latin extension, delivered
docs.text:
Friday afternoon of week eleven, nine days after the publisher's letter. In Mira's own Plum the caron and the ogonek are drawn, in all three masters. She'd like to send the Czech and Polish letters off before she goes home.

Your Plum-practice doesn't have her drawings. So this chapter does what a studio does when a drawing is late: it makes stand-ins. A caron is close to a circumflex turned over. A dot accent is one dot of the dieresis, set in the middle. Neither is as good as what Mira drew, and both are good enough to build with and to replace later. The ogonek can't be made from anything in the font. It stays on the list, and you'll see the report say so.

There's no new font work in this chapter and very little new Python. You'll take pieces from the last twenty chapters and put them in a row.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed, and the Font window in front.
  • box, box_of, contours_of and circle from chapters 43 to 48. The scripts below write them out again.
  • build_accents.py from chapter 57 and your accents.txt, with the three bad lines put right as in exercise 1 of that chapter: rr corrected to r, a # in front of the ľ line, and dotlessi as the base for ĩ. Run build_accents.py once more before you start, and say yes, so that it has nothing left to build.

This chapter adds glyphs. Work on the practice copy. The outputs below were computed from Plum's source file, not copied from FontLab's Output panel. The pen results come from running the pens in plain Python.

docs.title: Step 1: Turn the builder into a module
docs.text:
Today's script needs the builder from chapter 57 as its last stage. Copying 150 lines into a second file would give you two builders to keep in step, and chapter 33 showed the way out: put the functions in a module.

Save build_accents.py under a second name, accentkit.py, in the same folder. In accentkit.py, delete the last line, the one that says main(). Now the file defines everything and does nothing, which is what a module should do when it's imported.

Then replace the whole content of build_accents.py with this:

#FLM: Build Accented Letters
import accentkit

accentkit.main()

Run it. It should behave as it did this morning: it asks for the recipe file, prints its rows and finds nothing to build. The script is three lines long now, and the work lives in one place.

docs.title: Step 2: A caron from a circumflex
docs.text:
Chapter 50 flipped a hyphen left to right with Transform().scale(-1, 1). To flip top to bottom, the minus goes to the second number. A bare scale(1, -1) would throw the accent below the baseline, since it turns every height into its negative. To flip the accent in place, add its bottom and its top and move up by that much:

from fly import fl
from fly.pens import RecordingPen, Transform, TransformPen, layer_of
from fly.pens.fontlab import draw
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph


def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


font = fl.CurrentFont()
left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font["circumflex"], "Regular")
flip = Transform().translate(0, bottom + top).scale(1, -1)
print(bottom, top, flip.transformPoint((250, 614)))

539.0 655.0 (250.0, 580.0)

The circumflex in the Regular stands between 539 and 655. Its inner point, at 614, lands at 580: as far above the bottom as it used to be below the top.

Record the circumflex and replay it through the flip, as chapter 51 did with the small caps:

source = layer_of(fl.flGlyph(font["circumflex"], font), "Regular")
recording = RecordingPen()
draw(source, recording)
flipped = RecordingPen()
recording.replay(TransformPen(flipped, flip))
print(flipped.value[:3])

[('moveTo', ((134.0, 655.0),)), ('lineTo', ((197.0, 655.0),)), ('lineTo', ((250.0, 580.0),))]

It looks right. It isn't. Chapter 50 said it in one sentence that slips the mind: a mirror image runs the other way round. The circumflex ran counter-clockwise, so this caron runs clockwise. Drawn into a glyph it would look fine on its own. On top of a c it could punch a white hole where the two overlap, and check_direction.py from chapter 45 would name it.

The pens have a filter for this. ReverseContourPen passes on every contour it gets with the direction turned around:

from fly.pens import ReverseContourPen

flipped = RecordingPen()
recording.replay(TransformPen(ReverseContourPen(flipped), flip))
print(flipped.value[:3])

[('moveTo', ((134.0, 655.0),)), ('lineTo', ((221.0, 539.0),)), ('lineTo', ((280.0, 539.0),))]

The same points, walked the other way. Read the pens from the outside in: the drawing is flipped first, then reversed, then recorded. Whenever you mirror an outline once, reverse it once.

docs.title: Step 3: A dot from the dieresis
docs.text:
The dot accent, as on the ż, needs a dot of the right size at the right height. The dieresis has two. Take the box of one of them, with box_of from chapter 45:

def contours_of(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    return pGlyph(font, glyph).contours(master)


def box_of(nodes):
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


dot = contours_of(font, font["dieresis"], "Regular")[0]
left, bottom, right, top = box_of(dot.nodes())
radius = round((right - left) / 2)
height = round((bottom + top) / 2)
print(radius, height)

46 581

A radius of 46, with its center 581 units up. circle from chapter 48 draws it, and the center goes to x 250, the middle of an accent glyph 500 units wide. In the Light the numbers are 27 and 592, in the Bold 63 and 592.

docs.title: Step 4: Loops for the new accents
docs.text: An accent without a loop can't be hung on anything, as chapter 54 showed. The circumflex has its _top loop at 250, 478 in every master. The caron is the same shape turned over, and the dot sits on the same middle line, so both get a copy of that loop. The edit is the kind chapter 55 wrote: ("set", "_top", (250, 478)).

docs.title: Step 5: The stages in a row
docs.text:
Here is the plan for the afternoon, as a list:

  1. Make two empty glyphs, caron and dotaccent, 500 wide, with their Unicode values.
  2. Draw the flipped circumflex into one and the dot into the other.
  3. Give each a _top loop.
  4. Hand over to the builder.

Each line is a function you could write from an earlier chapter, and main calls them in that order. Each stage also has to cope with a second run. If caron is in the font already, stage 1 leaves it off its list, and stages 2 and 3 work only on that list. Stage 2 also skips a layer that has an outline, for the day a run is interrupted halfway. Mira will run this on her own Plum, where her drawn caron is waiting, and the script mustn't draw a stand-in on top of it.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Extend Latin
# Makes stand-in caron and dotaccent glyphs if the font has none, gives
# them _top anchors, then builds the accented letters from the recipe file.
import accentkit
import fly.ap.anchors.writer as anchors
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.glyphs.creation as creation
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from fly.pens import FlPen, RecordingPen, ReverseContourPen, Transform, TransformPen
from fly.pens.fontlab import draw
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
WIDTH = 500
MIDDLE = 250
MODEL = "circumflex"
STAND_INS = {"caron": 0x02C7, "dotaccent": 0x02D9}
TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


def box_of(nodes):
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


def contours_of(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    return pGlyph(font, glyph).contours(master)


KAPPA = 0.5523  # handle length for a quarter circle, as a share of the radius


def circle(pen, cx, cy, radius):
    h = round(radius * KAPPA)
    pen.moveTo((cx - radius, cy))
    pen.curveTo((cx - radius, cy - h), (cx - h, cy - radius), (cx, cy - radius))
    pen.curveTo((cx + h, cy - radius), (cx + radius, cy - h), (cx + radius, cy))
    pen.curveTo((cx + radius, cy + h), (cx + h, cy + radius), (cx, cy + radius))
    pen.curveTo((cx - h, cy + radius), (cx - radius, cy + h), (cx - radius, cy))
    pen.closePath()


def draw_caron(font, master):
    left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font[MODEL], master)
    flip = Transform().translate(0, bottom + top).scale(1, -1)
    recording = RecordingPen()
    draw(accentkit.layer_for(font, MODEL, master), recording)
    layer = accentkit.layer_for(font, "caron", master)
    with FlPen(layer, notify="Draw stand-in caron") as pen:
        recording.replay(TransformPen(ReverseContourPen(pen), flip))


def draw_dot(font, master):
    dot = contours_of(font, font["dieresis"], master)[0]
    left, bottom, right, top = box_of(dot.nodes())
    radius = round((right - left) / 2)
    height = round((bottom + top) / 2)
    layer = accentkit.layer_for(font, "dotaccent", master)
    with FlPen(layer, notify="Draw stand-in dot") as pen:
        circle(pen, MIDDLE, height, radius)


def loop_rows(font, names):
    rows = []
    for name in names:
        rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
        for master in MASTERS:
            model = accentkit.layer_for(font, MODEL, master)
            place = anchors.anchor_points(model)["_top"]
            layer = accentkit.layer_for(font, name, master)
            rows.append((rich.fl, layer, [("set", "_top", place)]))
    return rows


def make_stand_ins(font, package):
    have = {glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs}
    missing = [name for name in STAND_INS if name not in have]
    if not missing:
        print("caron and dotaccent are in the font. No stand-ins made.")
        return
    specs = []
    for name in missing:
        layers = tuple([(master, WIDTH) for master in MASTERS])
        specs.append(creation.NewGlyph(name=name, layers=layers, unicodes=(STAND_INS[name],)))
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    creation.create_glyphs(package, specs, "Add stand-in accents", facts)

    for name in missing:
        for master in MASTERS:
            if contours_of(font, font[name], master):
                continue
            if name == "caron":
                draw_caron(font, master)
            else:
                draw_dot(font, master)

    work = loop_rows(font, missing)
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    anchors.require_safe(work, facts)
    anchors.apply_work(work, "Add loops to stand-in accents", facts)
    print(f"Stand-ins made: {', '.join(missing)}.")


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    if font[MODEL] is None or font["dieresis"] is None:
        tell("This font has no circumflex or no dieresis to copy from.")
        return
    make_stand_ins(font, scripting.current_package())
    accentkit.main()


main()

0x02C7 is a number written in base 16, the way Unicode charts print it. It's the same number as 711. Python takes either. With the 0x form you can copy a value from a chart without doing sums.

Run it, choose accents.txt, and the Output panel shows this. I've left out the 17 rows that say fine or auto.

docs.title: What the afternoon produced
docs.text:
The Edit menu has a good many new Undo steps: one for the two empty accents, one for each of the six layers drawn, one for the loops and one for the sixteen letters. To take the afternoon back you'd undo them all, newest first. It's simpler to close the practice font without saving.

Count what this part has put into the practice font from recipes and accents: nacute in chapter 53, nine letters in chapter 56, three in chapter 57, two stand-in accents and sixteen letters today. Thirty-one glyphs. The last sixteen took about as long as reading this page.

Run inventory.py from chapter 20 as well. Its glyph count is up by 18 since this morning, and none of the new glyphs is empty.

Czech is complete, apart from the ď and the ť, whose caron has a different form that Mira has to draw. Polish lacks four letters with an ogonek and the Ł and ł, which are drawn letters. The report names the four, and Mira knows about the others. In her own Plum, with her ogonek in place, the same script and the same file report nothing to look at.

She sends the fonts to the publisher at ten to five.

Before she goes, Mira crosses out one more line on Oskar's sheet: Rebuild the accented letters from the base letters and the accents. That makes seven of eleven. The next one down reads Make the left sidebearing of the d, q and g match the o, and nobody in the studio has wanted to touch the spacing since Oskar left.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A script that has grown useful becomes a module: move its functions to a file that does nothing on import, and keep a three-line script that calls it. A long job is a row of stages, each a function that copes with being run again. Flipping an outline reverses its direction, and ReverseContourPen turns it back. A stand-in built with anchors can be replaced by a better drawing later without touching the letters that use it, and a number can be written in base 16 with 0x in front.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Run check_direction.py from chapter 45. It should have nothing to say about caron or ccaron. Then take ReverseContourPen out of draw_caron, delete the caron glyph and the fourteen letters that use it by hand, run extend_latin.py again, and run the check once more. What does it report? Put the pen back afterwards.
  2. Open ccaron and ecircumflex side by side in the Bold. The stand-in caron is as wide as the circumflex. A drawn caron is usually a little narrower and steeper. Write down two things you'd tell Mira to change, and notice that she can change them in one glyph.
  3. Add "macron": 0x00AF to STAND_INS and write draw_macron: a rectangle with rect from chapter 46, copied in, as wide as the circumflex's box and as thick as the hyphen. Add Ā Amacron A macron and ā amacron a macron to the recipe file. You'll have to change the if and else in make_stand_ins into a ladder with elif.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Part 3 ends here. The font has its letters, and each one has a width that somebody chose by eye, years ago. Chapter 61 opens Part 4 with the question Oskar's sheet has been asking all along: how much white is there on each side of a letter, and how do you read it with a script?

docs.title: Part 4: Space
docs.text:
Every letter brings its own white with it.

The proofs look uneven.

The Czech and Polish fonts went out, and the publisher's typesetter wrote back within days. The new letters are fine. The Bold "looks gappy", mostly in chapter headings, and she can't say where. A script can't judge how a line looks. It can measure the white between every two letters, and that is where this part starts.

The first eight chapters are about sidebearings, the white that belongs to each glyph. You measure it, set it, copy it from one letter to its relatives, link it with a rule, give the figures one width, and find the glyph that doesn't fit its group. Then you open up the whole Bold.

The next eleven are about kerning, the corrections for single pairs. You read the pairs and the classes, build classes from a list, set a pair, find the largest and the smallest, look for pairs that point at glyphs that are gone, make a proof to read, send the table out to a reviewer as a spreadsheet, and turn the Bold's kerning down.

The last chapter gathers the checks of the part into one audit that you can run again after every change.

Oskar's sheet has four lines open when the part begins. This part crosses out two of them, in chapters 63 and 74:

  • Make the left sidebearing of the d, q and g match the o.
  • Find kerning pairs that are larger than they should be.

You need the small helpers from Part 2, which each chapter writes out again where it uses them, the practice copy of Plum with the letters Part 3 added, and Fly installed in FontLab 9.

docs.title: 61. The space around a letter
docs.text:
Monday of week twelve. The Czech and Polish fonts went out on Friday, and the publisher's typesetter has written back already. The new letters are fine. The Bold isn't. "It looks gappy," she writes. "Chapter headings mostly. I can't tell you where, it's the whole line."

Mira sets a line of Bold and looks at it for a while. She agrees, and she can't say where either. Ines asks the question that starts this part of the book: "Can the script see it?"

It can. A script can't judge how a line looks, but it can measure the white between every two letters, and a line looks gappy when those whites aren't alike. Part 3 was about the black shapes. Part 4 is about the space between them, and this chapter measures it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The helpers box, tell and ask_text from chapters 39 and 43. The scripts below write them out again, so each one runs by itself.

Nothing in this chapter changes the font. I couldn't run it in FontLab 9. The numbers come from Plum's source file.

docs.title: Step 1: Three numbers, in every master
docs.text:
You met the three numbers in chapter 35. A glyph stands in a box as wide as its advance width. The gap from the left edge of the box to the leftmost point of the shape is the left sidebearing, LSB for short. The gap on the other side is the right sidebearing, RSB.

In chapter 35 you asked for them like this, and got the numbers of whichever master was showing:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()
rich = pGlyph(font, font["n"])
print(rich.getLSB(), rich.getAdvance(), rich.getRSB())

70 523 66

The typesetter's complaint is about the Bold, so you need to choose the master. Each of the three questions takes a master's name between its parentheses:

for master in ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]:
    print(master, rich.getLSB(master), rich.getAdvance(master), rich.getRSB(master))

Light 84 499 80
Regular 70 523 66
Bold 56 523 32

Read the three rows before going on, since the whole chapter is in them. In the Light and the Regular, the n has a little more room on the left than on the right: 84 and 80, 70 and 66. That's usual. The left side of an n is a straight stem and the right side is the foot of an arch, and designers give them nearly the same space.

In the Bold the numbers are 56 and 32. The right side has little more than half of what the left has. And look at the middle column. The Bold n is 523 wide, the same as the Regular.

docs.title: Step 2: Check the sum
docs.text:
Three numbers that describe one box ought to add up. The width is the left sidebearing, plus the black part, plus the right sidebearing. box from chapter 43 gives the black part. Here it is again, so these lines run by themselves:

def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


left, bottom, right, top = box(font, font["n"], "Bold")
black = right - left
print(left, black, rich.getLSB("Bold") + black + rich.getRSB("Bold"))

56.0 435.0 523.0

It adds up, and it tells you something else. The left sidebearing is the same number as the left edge of the box, 56. It has to be: a glyph's box starts at 0, so the distance from 0 to the shape is where the shape starts. The right sidebearing is what's left over on the other side.

The black part of the Bold n is 435 units wide. In the Regular it's 387. So the letter grew by 48 units and its box grew by nothing. The stems had to get fatter somewhere, and they got fatter into the sidebearings, more on the right than on the left.

Mira nods at this. The Bold was made in a hurry, years ago, for one book jacket. Somebody thickened the Regular and never went back to the widths.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Here's a line that looks as if it does the same job with less typing. Chapter 11 used glyph.width, so:

glyph = font["n"]
for master in ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]:
    black = glyph.width - rich.getLSB(master) - rich.getRSB(master)
    print(master, black)

Light 359.0
Regular 387.0
Bold 435.0

No error, and two right answers out of three. The Light n is 335 units of black, and this says 359.

glyph.width has no place for a master's name. It answers for the master that's showing in the Font window, which is the Regular here: 523. The loop took the Regular's width and subtracted the Light's sidebearings from it. For the Regular that's right. For the Bold it's right by luck, since the two widths happen to be equal. For the Light it's 24 units off, and nothing in the output says so.

The rule for the rest of this part: when a line names a master, every number on that line must come from that master. Use rich.getAdvance(master), and keep glyph.width for quick looks at the master on screen.

docs.title: Step 4: The white between two letters
docs.text:
A reader never sees a sidebearing. What the eye sees between an n and an i is one white strip: the right sidebearing of the n and the left sidebearing of the i, side by side. So the gap between two letters is a sum of two numbers that belong to two different glyphs.

def gap(font, first, second, master):
    return pGlyph(font, font[first]).getRSB(master) + pGlyph(font, font[second]).getLSB(master)


print(gap(font, "n", "i", "Regular"), gap(font, "n", "i", "Bold"))

126 78

That's 66 and 60 in the Regular, 32 and 46 in the Bold.

Now a whole word. The classic one for testing spacing is minimum: seven letters, all upright strokes, so the gaps should come out nearly equal. To get every pair of neighbors, use zip from chapter 35 and a slice from chapter 10. word[1:] is the word without its first letter, and zipping a word with that pairs each letter with the next one:

word = "minimum"
print(list(zip(word, word[1:])))

[('m', 'i'), ('i', 'n'), ('n', 'i'), ('i', 'm'), ('m', 'u'), ('u', 'm')]

Seven letters, six gaps. zip stops when the shorter of its two lists runs out, so the last m has no partner and nothing goes wrong. Now measure each pair:

for master in ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]:
    gaps = [gap(font, a, b, master) for a, b in zip(word, word[1:])]
    print(master, gaps)

Light [154, 158, 154, 158, 160, 168]
Regular [126, 130, 126, 130, 132, 140]
Bold [60, 80, 78, 80, 66, 92]

There it is. In the Light the six gaps run from 154 to 168. In the Regular, from 126 to 140. In both, the widest gap is 14 units more than the narrowest, on gaps of well over a hundred. No eye will catch that.

In the Bold they run from 60 to 92. The widest gap is half as big again as the narrowest, and the two sit a few letters apart in the same word. That's what "gappy" means, and now it has numbers.

docs.title: Step 5: One number for unevenness
docs.text:
Reading six numbers per master works for one word. To compare words you want one number, and the simplest is the difference between the widest and the narrowest gap. I'll call it the spread. max and min from chapter 36 give it:

def spread(gaps):
    return max(gaps) - min(gaps)


print(spread([60, 80, 78, 80, 66, 92]))

32

A spread of 14 on gaps of 130 is about a tenth. A spread of 32 on gaps of 76 is over four tenths. The spread on its own doesn't say that, so the script below prints the smallest gap next to it.

One caution about what the number means. A spread of 0 is not the goal. Round letters need less room than straight ones, since a curve pulls away from its neighbor at the top and the bottom, so a well-spaced noon has a narrower gap in the middle than at its ends. The spread is useful for words made of one kind of stroke, like minimum, and for comparing one master with another. Exercise 2 looks at this.

docs.title: Step 6: Which letters to blame
docs.text:
The gaps say where the line is uneven. To find out why, print the sidebearings of the letters in the word, each letter once. A set from chapter 25 drops the repeats, and sorted puts what's left in order:

print(sorted(set("minimum")))

['i', 'm', 'n', 'u']

For the Bold, the table for these four comes out like this:

i     46   222    24
m     56   788    14
n     56   523    32
u     52   523    36

The left sidebearings are close: 46 for the i, which is a little tight, and 52 to 56 for the rest. The right sidebearings are 24, 14, 32 and 36. The m has 14 units on its right and 56 on its left. Every gap after an m is narrow, and every gap after a u is wide.

So the trouble is on the right sides, and the m is the worst of them. Mira writes it on her list. Chapter 62 starts to do something about it.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
The script asks for a word and prints the gaps in each master, then the letters. It works for words in small letters whose glyphs are named like the letter itself, which is true of a to z. For anything else it says so and stops. Chapter 77 does better with names.

#FLM: Sidebearing Report
# Asks for a word, prints the white between its letters in each master,
# then the sidebearings of each letter. Changes nothing.
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box, run_text_dialog
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

TITLE = "Halfmoon"
MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask_text(label, start=""):
    return run_text_dialog(qt.QtGui, label, start, TITLE)


def gap(font, first, second, master):
    return pGlyph(font, font[first]).getRSB(master) + pGlyph(font, font[second]).getLSB(master)


def spread(gaps):
    return max(gaps) - min(gaps)


def gap_line(font, word, master):
    gaps = [gap(font, a, b, master) for a, b in zip(word, word[1:])]
    numbers = " ".join([f"{g:>4}" for g in gaps])
    return f"{master:<9}{numbers}   smallest {min(gaps)}, spread {spread(gaps)}"


def letter_lines(font, word, master):
    lines = []
    for letter in sorted(set(word)):
        rich = pGlyph(font, font[letter])
        lines.append(f"{letter:<4}{rich.getLSB(master):>5}{rich.getAdvance(master):>6}{rich.getRSB(master):>6}")
    return lines


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    word = ask_text("Word to measure, in small letters:")
    if not word or len(word) < 2:
        return
    missing = [letter for letter in sorted(set(word)) if font[letter] is None]
    if missing:
        tell(f"No glyph named: {' '.join(missing)}")
        return

    print(word)
    for master in MASTERS:
        print(gap_line(font, word, master))
    for master in MASTERS:
        print()
        print(f"{master}: left, width, right")
        for line in letter_lines(font, word, master):
            print(line)


main()

Run it and type minimum. The top of the output:

minimum
Light     154  158  154  158  160  168   smallest 154, spread 14
Regular   126  130  126  130  132  140   smallest 126, spread 14
Bold       60   80   78   80   66   92   smallest 60, spread 32

Below it come three small tables, one for each master. The Bold one is the table from step 6.

" ".join(...) over a list of formatted numbers is a trick worth keeping. f"{g:>4}" makes each number four characters wide, pushed to the right, and join from chapter 25 puts one space between them. The columns line up whatever the numbers are.

Mira prints the three lines and pins them over her desk. Ines reads them and asks whether every word is that bad. Mira types hobnob.

hobnob
Light     130  134  137  130  134   smallest 130, spread 7
Regular   104  108  108  104  108   smallest 104, spread 4
Bold       62   64   59   62   64   smallest 59, spread 5

The Bold is as even here as the other two. So the Bold isn't wrong everywhere. It's wrong in some letters, and a script can find out which.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Every glyph has an advance width and two sidebearings in each master, and getLSB, getAdvance and getRSB take the master's name. glyph.width belongs to the master on screen, so don't mix it with numbers from another master. The white between two letters is the right sidebearing of the first plus the left sidebearing of the second, and zip(word, word[1:]) gives the neighbors in a word. The spread of the gaps is a rough measure of evenness, good for comparing masters and poor as a target.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Run the script on nun and on mum. Before you look, work out the Bold gaps for mum by hand from the table in step 6. Which of the two words is more even in the Bold, and which letter makes the difference?
  2. Run it on noon. In the Regular the gaps are 104, 76 and 108. Is the middle gap a fault? Set the word in the Regular, look at it, and decide. Then write one sentence on why a script that tried to make all gaps equal would spoil the font.
  3. Add a column to letter_lines: the width of the black part, which is the advance width minus both sidebearings. For the Bold m it should be 718. Then compare with the Regular m. How many units did the black grow by, and how much of that came out of the right sidebearing?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The Bold m has 14 units on its right and should have about as much as the n. Chapter 62 sets a sidebearing from a script, looks at what moves when you do that, and checks the result afterwards.

docs.title: 62. Set a sidebearing
docs.text:
Tuesday of week twelve. Yesterday's printout is still pinned over Mira's desk, and she has circled two numbers on it in pencil. The Bold m has 14 units of white on its right, where the n has 32. The Bold i has 46 on its left, where the other stems have 56.

"Give the m 32 on the right and the i 56 on the left," she says. "Those two first. Then we look again."

Two numbers to set. The first takes one line you already know. The second takes a line that looks the same and does the wrong thing, and the reason is worth the whole chapter: a right sidebearing and a left sidebearing are not changed the same way.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed. Keep the Font window in front, as in chapter 53.
  • The helpers box, ask and tell from chapters 39 and 43, and set_width from chapter 49. The scripts below write them out again, so each one runs by itself.
  • sb_report.py from chapter 61, to look at the result.

This chapter changes the font. Every change is one Undo step. I couldn't run it in FontLab 9, so the outputs are worked out from Plum's source file and from the code of the tools.

docs.title: Step 1: The right side is the width
docs.text:
Chapter 61 said it in passing: the right sidebearing is what's left of the width after the shape ends. So to get more white on the right you make the box wider, and nothing else has to happen.

Start with the numbers as they are:

from fly import fl
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()
rich = pGlyph(font, font["m"])
print(rich.getLSB("Bold"), rich.getAdvance("Bold"), rich.getRSB("Bold"))

56 788 14

Mira wants 32 where there's 14. That's 18 more, so the width goes from 788 to 806. Do the sum in the script, not in your head, since the script will have to do it for other glyphs later:

want = 32
width = rich.getAdvance("Bold") + want - rich.getRSB("Bold")
print(width)

806

Now set it. set_width from chapter 49 takes the rich glyph, the layer, the new width and a name for the Undo step. Here it is again, so this runs by itself:

import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting


def set_width(glyph, layer, width, title="Set width"):
    def change():
        layer.advanceWidth = width

    package = scripting.current_package()
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    history.commit(title, [layer], [glyph.fl], change, operation="geometry", facts=facts)


layer = layer_of(rich.fl, "Bold")
set_width(rich, layer, width, "Set right sidebearing")
print(rich.getLSB("Bold"), rich.getAdvance("Bold"), rich.getRSB("Bold"))

56 806 32

The left sidebearing stayed at 56. The shape didn't move. Only the right edge of the box went 18 units further out.

That last print isn't decoration. Chapter 29 had you print before and after a change, and here it earns its place: you asked for a right sidebearing, you set a width, and the only proof that the one led to the other is to ask for the sidebearing again.

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
Now the i. It has 46 on the left and should have 56. Ten more. The same recipe, then, with one thing to settle first. The i is borrowed by ij, which FontLab builds itself, and chapter 55 showed what follows: the change is refused with Refused. i: base of auto ij. unless history.commit hears allow_bases=True. So set_width gets a fifth parameter and passes it on:

def set_width(glyph, layer, width, title="Set width", allow_bases=False):
    def change():
        layer.advanceWidth = width

    package = scripting.current_package()
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    history.commit(title, [layer], [glyph.fl], change, operation="geometry",
                   facts=facts, allow_bases=allow_bases)

The default is False, so every call you've written so far behaves as before. Save the font, as chapter 55 asked, and then:

rich = pGlyph(font, font["i"])
layer = layer_of(rich.fl, "Bold")
print(rich.getLSB("Bold"), rich.getAdvance("Bold"), rich.getRSB("Bold"))

set_width(rich, layer, rich.getAdvance("Bold") + 10, "Set left sidebearing",
                   allow_bases=True)
print(rich.getLSB("Bold"), rich.getAdvance("Bold"), rich.getRSB("Bold"))

46 222 24
46 232 34

No error. The width grew by 10, as told. But the left sidebearing is still 46, and the ten units of white turned up on the right, where nobody wanted them.

Think of the box again. Its left edge is at 0, always. You can't move that edge to the left to make room, because there is no "left of 0" for a box to start at. A wider box is wider on the right. The white on the left is the distance from 0 to the shape, and the only way to make it bigger is to move the shape.

Choose Edit > Undo once, and the i should be 222 wide again. That's what the one Undo step is for. I haven't seen it in FontLab 9.

docs.title: Step 3: Move the shape, then widen the box
docs.text:
So a left sidebearing needs two things done together. The shape moves right by 10. And the box gets 10 wider, or the right sidebearing would shrink from 24 to 14, since the shape has moved towards the right edge.

You know one way to move a shape: chapter 50 drew it again through a TransformPen. That would do for the outline, but an i isn't only an outline. It has anchors, and they must move with it, or every accent built on the i would sit 10 units to the left of the stem afterwards. The tools behind FontLab's own metrics panel have a function that does the whole job on a layer:

import fly.ap.metrics.panel.model as metrics

metrics.shift_and_set(layer, 10, 232)

Don't run that line yet. shift_and_set takes a layer, the distance to move everything on it to the right, and the new width. It moves the outline, the components and the anchors, and then it sets the width. A distance of 0 is allowed, and then it only sets the width.

It doesn't make an Undo step by itself. For that it goes inside the pattern from chapter 29, a small function handed to history.commit:

import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

def change():
    metrics.shift_and_set(layer, 10, 232)

package = scripting.current_package()
facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
history.commit("Set left sidebearing", [layer], [rich.fl], change, operation="geometry",
               facts=facts, allow_bases=True)
print(rich.getLSB("Bold"), rich.getAdvance("Bold"), rich.getRSB("Bold"))

56 232 24

Left 56, right 24, as it was. One Undo step should take all of it back.

docs.title: Step 4: What moved and what stayed
docs.text:
Look at what else is on that layer. Chapter 54 showed how to read the anchors:

import fly.ap.anchors.writer as anchors

print(anchors.anchor_points(layer))

{'bottom': (141.0, 0.0), 'ogonek': (162.0, 0.0)}

Before the change they stood at 131 and 152. They went along with the stem, 10 units each, so a mark hung on the bottom peg still hangs under the same part of the letter.

Here's the full account for a change to the left sidebearing:

Thing What happens The outline moves right by the difference Anchors on the layer move with it Components on the layer move with it The advance width grows by the difference The right sidebearing stays The other masters stay; you changed one layer

And for the right sidebearing: the width changes, and nothing else at all.

docs.title: Step 5: Who borrows this glyph?
docs.text:
There's one more thing that moved, and it isn't on the i's layer. Chapter 52 ended with a warning: the outline of a base carries into every glyph that borrows it, while widths and shifts stay behind. You have moved the outline of the i. Who borrows the i?

import fly.ap.components.writer as parts

for glyph in font.glyphs:
    found = parts.components(layer_of(pGlyph(font, glyph).fl, "Bold"))
    if "i" in [parts.base_of(part) for part in found]:
        print(glyph.name, [(parts.base_of(part), parts.offset(part)) for part in found])

ij [('i', (0.0, 0.0)), ('j', (222.0, 0.0))]

One glyph, the Dutch ij. It's an i with no shift and a j shifted 222 to the right, which was the width of the i when FontLab built it. Now the i inside it stands 10 units further right. If the j stands where it stood, the two have come 10 units closer in a glyph that is still 460 wide, and nobody asked for that. If FontLab built the ij again when its base changed, the j may be at 232 and the width 470. I can't tell you which. Run the loop and read the line.

The m has no such trouble. Nothing in Plum borrows it. And for a right sidebearing the question doesn't come up in this form at all, since no outline moves. It comes up in another form: a glyph that borrows the n, like ntilde, keeps its own width, so widening the n leaves the ntilde as tight as before. Chapter 63 deals with that.

So the rule before any change to a left sidebearing: list the borrowers first, and look at each one afterward. The ij is an automatic glyph, so a script can't mend it, as chapter 56 found with the î. If it's still 460 wide, the cure is by hand, in the Glyph window. Mira writes "ij, Bold" on her list.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
The script sets one or both sidebearings of one glyph in one master. None for a side means "leave it". It prints the plan, names the borrowers, asks, makes the change and prints the result.

#FLM: Set Sidebearings
# Sets the left and right sidebearing of one glyph in one master.
# None for a side leaves it alone. One Undo step.
import fly.ap.components.writer as parts
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.metrics.panel.model as metrics
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

TITLE = "Halfmoon"
GLYPH = "i"
MASTER = "Bold"
LEFT = 56
RIGHT = None


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def box(font, glyph, master="Regular"):
    nodes = pGlyph(font, glyph).nodes(master)
    if not nodes:
        return None
    xs = [node.x for node in nodes]
    ys = [node.y for node in nodes]
    return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)


def plan(rich, master, left, right):
    dx = 0
    width = rich.getAdvance(master)
    if left is not None:
        dx = left - rich.getLSB(master)
        width += dx
    if right is not None:
        width += right - rich.getRSB(master)
    return dx, width


def borrowers(font, name, master):
    found = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        layer = layer_of(pGlyph(font, glyph).fl, master)
        if name in [parts.base_of(part) for part in parts.components(layer)]:
            found.append(glyph.name)
    return found


def numbers(rich, master):
    return f"left {rich.getLSB(master)}, width {rich.getAdvance(master)}, right {rich.getRSB(master)}"


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None or font[GLYPH] is None:
        tell(f"Open a font that has a glyph named {GLYPH}.")
        return
    if box(font, font[GLYPH], MASTER) is None:
        tell(f"{GLYPH} has no outline in {MASTER}, so it has no sidebearings to set.")
        return
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[GLYPH])
    layer = layer_of(rich.fl, MASTER)
    dx, width = plan(rich, MASTER, LEFT, RIGHT)
    if dx == 0 and width == rich.getAdvance(MASTER):
        print(f"{GLYPH} {MASTER}: {numbers(rich, MASTER)}. Nothing to do.")
        return

    print(f"{GLYPH} {MASTER} now: {numbers(rich, MASTER)}")
    print(f"Plan: move the shape by {dx}, set the width to {width}.")
    users = borrowers(font, GLYPH, MASTER)
    if users and dx != 0:
        print(f"The shape also moves inside: {' '.join(users)}")
    elif users:
        print(f"Borrowed by: {' '.join(users)}")
    if not ask(f"Change {GLYPH} in {MASTER}?"):
        return

    def change():
        metrics.shift_and_set(layer, dx, width)

    package = scripting.current_package()
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    # The question above is the agreement that allow_bases stands for.
    history.commit("Set sidebearings", [layer], [rich.fl], change, operation="geometry",
                   facts=facts, allow_bases=True)
    print(f"{GLYPH} {MASTER} after: {numbers(rich, MASTER)}")


main()

Choose Edit > Undo until the i is back at 46 and 222, then run the script as it stands:

i Bold now: left 46, width 222, right 24
Plan: move the shape by 10, set the width to 232.
The shape also moves inside: ij
i Bold after: left 56, width 232, right 24

Run it a second time and it has nothing to do:

i Bold: left 56, width 232, right 24. Nothing to do.

A few things in it are worth a second look.

plan works out both numbers before anything is touched. The width starts as it is, grows by the move on the left, and grows again by whatever the right side needs. Either if can be skipped, so one function serves for the left side, the right side or both. It returns a pair, as mark_shift did in chapter 53.

change is written inside main, after the question. It's the function-in-a-function from chapter 49, and it sees layer, dx and width because it was written where those boxes live.

The guard with box keeps the script away from glyphs with no outline of their own. A space has a width and no shape, so "left sidebearing" means nothing for it. A glyph made only of components is a different case, and chapter 63 takes it up.

Mira runs the script for the i and, with three constants changed, for the m. Then she runs sb_report.py on minimum again:

Bold       88   80   88   80   84   92   smallest 80, spread 12

Yesterday that line read 60, 80, 78, 80, 66, 92, with a spread of 32. The spread is now 12, a little under the 14 of the other two masters. She sets the word, looks, and says it's better and still not right. The whole Bold is tight, she thinks, not only uneven. That's a job for chapter 68. First there are the other glyphs with the m's problem, and nobody has counted them yet.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: The right sidebearing changes when the width changes, and nothing moves. The left sidebearing changes only when the shape moves, and the width has to change by the same amount to keep the right side as it was. metrics.shift_and_set(layer, dx, width) moves the outline, the components and the anchors of a layer and sets its width, and it belongs inside history.commit. A moved outline shows up in every glyph that borrows it, so list the borrowers before you move anything and print the numbers again afterwards.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Oskar once left a note that said "Give the H 60 on each side." Do it in the Bold: set GLYPH = "H", LEFT = 60 and RIGHT = 60. The Bold H starts at left 56, width 672, right 40. Work out the plan on paper before you run the script. You should get a move of 4 and a width of 696.
  2. Set the right sidebearing of the Bold n to 40, with LEFT = None. Then print the three numbers of the Bold ntilde. Its width is still 523. In one sentence: why does the script not warn you about ntilde, and should it?
  3. Set GLYPH = "ij" and run the script. It stops at the guard and says the glyph has no outline, since ij is two borrowed shapes. Now try the width alone, in the Scripting panel: set_width(rich, layer, 470, allow_bases=True) for the Bold layer of ij. By Fly's code that should stop with a refusal that begins Refused: auto layer. Why does allow_bases=True not help here? Chapter 55 has the answer.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The d, the q and the g begin with the same round stroke as the o, and Oskar's sheet says their left sides should match it. Chapter 63 copies sidebearings from one glyph to others, with a dictionary that says who follows whom.

docs.title: 63. Copy the spacing
docs.text:
Wednesday of week twelve. Ines has Oskar's sheet out again. Seven of its eleven lines are crossed out, and the next one reads: Make the left sidebearing of the d, q and g match the o.

It's a sensible line. The d, the q and the g all begin with the same round stroke as the o. If the bowl is the same, the white in front of it should be the same. A designer sets the o with care and wants the others to follow it.

"Follow" is the word for this chapter. Yesterday you gave a glyph a number. Today you give it a model: this glyph takes its left side from that one. Written down for several glyphs, that's a dictionary, and the dictionary turns out to be the most useful part of the script.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed, and the Font window in front.
  • The helpers ask and tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write them out again, so each one runs by itself.
  • The font as chapter 62 left it. The exercises there are optional, and this chapter says where they'd show.

This chapter changes the font, in two Undo steps. I couldn't run it in FontLab 9. The numbers come from Plum's source file.

docs.title: Step 1: Look first
docs.text:
Before you copy anything, see how far apart the four glyphs are:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for master in ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]:
    lefts = [pGlyph(font, font[name]).getLSB(master) for name in ["o", "d", "q", "g"]]
    print(master, lefts)

Light [50, 53, 53, 53]
Regular [38, 38, 38, 38]
Bold [30, 30, 30, 30]

In the Regular and the Bold, the job is done already. Somebody matched them by hand, and my guess is Oskar, before he wrote the line. In the Light, the three followers stand 3 units further in than the o.

Three units in a Light, on three glyphs. It's the smallest job on the sheet so far, and that's a good reason to do it with a script: the script will say "nothing to do" for six of the nine layers, and you'll believe it, where by hand you'd have opened all nine to check.

docs.title: Step 2: A dictionary that says who follows whom
