docs.text:
Chapter 21 used a dictionary to look things up: a name goes in, a width comes out. The same thing can hold a rule. The key is the glyph that follows. The value is its model.

LEFT_LIKE = {"d": "o", "q": "o", "g": "o"}

print(LEFT_LIKE["g"])

o

Read LEFT_LIKE["g"] as a question: whose left side does the g take? The answer is o.

With that, the difference for one glyph in one master is two lookups and a subtraction:

name = "d"
model = LEFT_LIKE[name]
dx = pGlyph(font, font[model]).getLSB("Light") - pGlyph(font, font[name]).getLSB("Light")
print(name, "follows", model, "and must move by", dx)

d follows o and must move by -3

Minus 3: the shape goes 3 units to the left. Chapter 62 showed what goes with that. The width shrinks by 3 as well, so that the right side stays as it is.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
The first way that comes to mind is the way the sentence on Oskar's sheet runs. The o is the boss, so the o came first:

LEFT_LIKE = {"o": "d", "o": "q", "o": "g"}
print(LEFT_LIKE)
print(len(LEFT_LIKE))

{'o': 'g'}
1

Three pairs went in and one came out. Chapter 21's third exercise showed this: a dictionary holds each key once, and when the same key turns up again the later value takes its place, with no error. Here the key o turned up three times.

What makes it worse is that the script would have run. It would have found one rule, "the o follows the g", and moved the o, the one glyph that was supposed to stay put.

So the direction matters, and there's a way to remember it. Each follower has one model, but a model can have many followers. A dictionary allows a value to repeat and doesn't allow a key to repeat. The thing there's one of per entry goes on the left: the follower is the key.

docs.title: Step 4: A plan for every layer
docs.text:
Now walk through the font and collect what has to change. Each row of the plan holds the rich glyph, the master, the distance to move and the new width, the same two numbers as in chapter 62:

rows = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.name not in LEFT_LIKE:
        continue
    rich = pGlyph(font, glyph)
    model = pGlyph(font, font[LEFT_LIKE[glyph.name]])
    for master in ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]:
        dx = model.getLSB(master) - rich.getLSB(master)
        if dx != 0:
            rows.append((rich, master, dx, rich.getAdvance(master) + dx))

for rich, master, dx, width in rows:
    print(rich.name, master, dx, width)

d Light -3 520
g Light -3 520
q Light -3 520

glyph.name not in LEFT_LIKE asks whether the name is one of the dictionary's keys. For a dictionary, in looks at the keys only.

Three rows out of nine layers. The other six had a difference of 0 and were left out.

docs.title: Step 5: One Undo step for all of it
docs.text:
In chapter 62 every change was its own Undo step. For three layers that belong to one decision, one step is better: if Mira doesn't like the result, she undoes once.

history.commit has taken a list of layers and a list of glyphs all along. You've been handing it lists with one thing in each. Hand it longer lists, and do all the work inside the one small function:

import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.metrics.panel.model as metrics
from fly.pens import layer_of

layers = [layer_of(rich.fl, master) for rich, master, dx, width in rows]
owners = {}
for rich, master, dx, width in rows:
    owners[rich.name] = rich.fl


def change():
    for (rich, master, dx, width), layer in zip(rows, layers):
        metrics.shift_and_set(layer, dx, width)


package = scripting.current_package()
facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
history.commit("Copy left sidebearings", layers, list(owners.values()), change,
               operation="geometry", facts=facts, allow_bases=True)

allow_bases=True is there for the g. FontLab builds gbreve from it, so the g is a borrowed glyph, and chapter 55 explained what that keyword agrees to. Save the font before you run this.

Two things here are new.

owners is a dictionary used for its bad habit. The tool wants each glyph once, and a glyph with changes in two masters would turn up twice in the rows. Storing it under its name twice keeps one copy, which is the very thing that went wrong in step 3 and is wanted here. owners.values() gives the values without the keys, and list makes a list of them.

The for line inside change takes two things apart at once. zip pairs each row with its layer, so each turn of the loop gets a pair: a row, which is itself four things, and a layer. The parentheses around the four names say where the row ends. You saw the same shape in chapter 54 with for family, (bx, by) in ....

Run the loop from step 1 again:

Light [50, 50, 50, 50]
Regular [38, 38, 38, 38]
Bold [30, 30, 30, 30]

docs.title: Step 6: The ones who follow without being told
docs.text:
Chapter 62 ended with a loose thread. When a base glyph changes, the glyphs that borrow it get the new outline and keep their old width. The g has one borrower in Plum, gbreve, the Turkish ğ. Its g has now moved 3 units left with the Light g, and its box is still 523 wide where the g is 520.

Nobody would write gbreve into a dictionary by hand, along with seventy others. But the font already knows who follows whom here: an accented letter follows its first component. So this second map can be read out of the font. The rule I'll use has three parts. The glyph has no outline of its own and at least two components. The first component isn't shifted. And every other component is an accent, which means its glyph carries a loop anchor, one whose name starts with _, as chapter 54 showed.

The third part matters. Without it the rule would catch ij, which begins with an unshifted i and is rightly wider than an i. A j carries no loop, so ij is left alone.

In the script below that's the function follow_rows. It makes rows of the same shape as before, with a move of 0, since only the width has to follow.

There's a catch, and chapter 56 met it first. gbreve is a glyph FontLab builds itself, and no script of ours may write into it. So follow_rows hands back two things: the rows it can change, and the names of the automatic letters it had to leave. On the font as it stands now the first list is empty and the second holds one name, gbreve, whose Light is 523 wide over a g of 520. That's what Plum's file says. FontLab may have made it 520 by itself when the g changed, and then the second list is empty too. I haven't seen which.

If you did exercise 2 of chapter 62 and widened the Bold n, the first list isn't empty. nacute and ncaron are yours, built in chapters 53 and 60, and they get rows. ntilde came with Plum and is automatic, so it joins gbreve. That exercise asked whether the script should have warned you. This is the answer: better than a warning is a second pass that puts right what it may and names the rest.

One thing this pass doesn't do: it doesn't move the breve. The g under it went 3 units left, and so did the top peg on the g, from 262 to 259. The breve sat at a shift of 12 where 9 is now right. Chapter 57's builder would say auto for it and leave it. So gbreve goes on Mira's list beside the î: look at it, and see what FontLab did.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Copy Sidebearings
# Gives glyphs the left or right sidebearing of a model glyph,
# then makes accented letters as wide as their base letter.
import fly.ap.anchors.writer as anchors
import fly.ap.components.writer as parts
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.metrics.panel.model as metrics
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
LEFT_LIKE = {"d": "o", "q": "o", "g": "o"}
RIGHT_LIKE = {}


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def side_rows(font):
    rows = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        name = glyph.name
        if name not in LEFT_LIKE and name not in RIGHT_LIKE:
            continue
        rich = pGlyph(font, glyph)
        for master in MASTERS:
            dx = 0
            width = rich.getAdvance(master)
            if name in LEFT_LIKE:
                model = pGlyph(font, font[LEFT_LIKE[name]])
                dx = model.getLSB(master) - rich.getLSB(master)
                width += dx
            if name in RIGHT_LIKE:
                model = pGlyph(font, font[RIGHT_LIKE[name]])
                width += model.getRSB(master) - rich.getRSB(master)
            if dx != 0 or width != rich.getAdvance(master):
                rows.append((rich, master, dx, width))
    return rows


def is_accent(font, name, master):
    layer = layer_of(pGlyph(font, font[name]).fl, master)
    return any([family.startswith("_") for family in anchors.anchor_points(layer)])


def follow_rows(font):
    rows = []
    left = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        rich = pGlyph(font, glyph)
        for master in MASTERS:
            layer = layer_of(rich.fl, master)
            found = parts.components(layer)
            if len(found) < 2 or rich.contours(master):
                continue
            if parts.offset(found[0]) != (0, 0):
                continue
            if not all([is_accent(font, parts.base_of(part), master) for part in found[1:]]):
                continue
            base = pGlyph(font, font[parts.base_of(found[0])])
            if base.getAdvance(master) == rich.getAdvance(master):
                continue
            if layer.autoLayer:
                left.append(f"{rich.name} {master}")
            else:
                rows.append((rich, master, 0, base.getAdvance(master)))
    return rows, left


def show(rows):
    for rich, master, dx, width in rows:
        print(f"{rich.name:<10}{master:<9}move {dx}, width {rich.getAdvance(master)} to {width}")


def apply(rows, title):
    layers = [layer_of(rich.fl, master) for rich, master, dx, width in rows]
    owners = {}
    for rich, master, dx, width in rows:
        owners[rich.name] = rich.fl

    def change():
        for (rich, master, dx, width), layer in zip(rows, layers):
            metrics.shift_and_set(layer, dx, width)

    package = scripting.current_package()
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    history.commit(title, layers, list(owners.values()), change,
                   operation="geometry", facts=facts, allow_bases=True)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    models = list(LEFT_LIKE.values()) + list(RIGHT_LIKE.values())
    missing = [name for name in models if font[name] is None]
    if missing:
        tell(f"No glyph named: {' '.join(missing)}")
        return

    rows = side_rows(font)
    show(rows)
    print(f"{len(rows)} layers to change.")
    if rows and ask(f"Copy sidebearings on {len(rows)} layers?"):
        apply(rows, "Copy sidebearings")

    rows, left = follow_rows(font)
    show(rows)
    print(f"{len(rows)} accented letters differ from their base in width.")
    if left:
        print(f"Automatic, left to FontLab: {', '.join(left)}")
    if rows and ask(f"Make {len(rows)} accented letters as wide as their base?"):
        apply(rows, "Follow base widths")


main()

Choose Edit > Undo to take back what you did in step 5, then run it and answer Yes:

d         Light    move -3, width 523 to 520
g         Light    move -3, width 523 to 520
q         Light    move -3, width 523 to 520
3 layers to change.
0 accented letters differ from their base in width.
Automatic, left to FontLab: gbreve Light

Run it again and both counts are 0. The last line stays for as long as gbreve is 523 wide.

main uses the name rows twice, first for the side rows and then for the follower rows. That's allowed. The second assignment throws out the first list, which has done its work by then. The follower rows must be made after the first change and not before, since they compare with widths that the first change sets.

if rows and ask(...) leans on something chapter 35 used as if not rows:. An empty list counts as false. With no rows, Python doesn't go on to the second half, and nobody is asked a question about 0 layers.

The rows of the two passes have the same shape, four things each, so show and apply serve both. That wasn't luck. I gave the follower rows a move of 0 so that they'd fit.

Ines crosses out the line: eight of eleven. Mira looks at the sheet and then at the dictionary on the screen. "Three letters," she says. "It should be thirty. Half the alphabet follows the n or the o." She's right, and thirty entries typed one by one is a poor way to say something that simple.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A dictionary can hold a rule: the follower is the key, its model is the value, and many followers may share a model. Written the other way round, the entries overwrite each other with no error. in on a dictionary looks at the keys, and .values() gives the values. One history.commit can take many layers, with the work done in a loop inside the small function, and an accented letter's width follows its base.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. The b and the p end with the round stroke the o ends with. Set LEFT_LIKE = {} and RIGHT_LIKE = {"b": "o", "p": "o"} and run the script. You should see four rows: Light widths from 523 to 520, Bold widths from 543 to 548. Before you answer Yes for the Bold, look at the Bold o itself: 30 on the left, 8 on the right. Is it a good model there? Say what copying from a bad model does.
  2. Open accents.txt from chapter 56, add the line ğ gbreve g breve, and run the builder from chapter 57. It should say auto for gbreve and show shifts of 9, 22 and 22. Open the Light gbreve and read the breve's shift there. Did FontLab follow the g?
  3. Add "c": "o" and "e": "o" to LEFT_LIKE. The Light c moves by -3 and the Light e by 2. Which accented letters does the second pass then bring into line, and which does it name as automatic? Only the ones you built yourself can get a row: cacute, ccaron and ecaron, if you made them in chapters 56 and 60.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Mira's thirty letters fall into a few families: those that start like an n, those that start like an o, those that end like one or the other. Chapter 64 writes the families down as a dictionary of lists and builds the follower map from them.

docs.title: 64. Letters that space alike
docs.text:
Thursday of week twelve. Mira has drawn two columns on the back of a proof. Over one she's written starts like n, and under it b h k l m p r. Over the other, starts like o, and under it c d e g q. It took her under a minute.

"That's how I think about it," she says. "Not thirty rules. A few families."

Yesterday's dictionary had one entry for each follower: d follows o, q follows o, g follows o. Mira's paper has it the other way up, one entry for each model, with a list of followers. Her way is shorter to write and easier to check by eye. Yesterday's way is what a script needs for looking things up. This chapter keeps both: you write the families, and four lines of Python turn them into the follower map.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The helper tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write it out again, so each one runs by itself.
  • The font as chapters 62 and 63 left it: the Bold m with 32 on the right, the Bold i with 56 on the left, and the Light d, g and q with 50 on the left.

This chapter reads and prints. It changes nothing in the font. I couldn't run it in FontLab 9, and the numbers come from Plum's source file with those three changes applied.

docs.title: Step 1: Let the font show its families
docs.text:
Before you write Mira's columns down, see whether the font agrees with her. Go through the lowercase and put each letter into a list with the others that have the same left sidebearing. That's the dictionary of lists from chapter 52, where the key was a base glyph. Here the key is a number:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()
groups = {}
for name in "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz":
    left = pGlyph(font, font[name]).getLSB("Regular")
    if left not in groups:
        groups[left] = []
    groups[left].append(name)

for left in sorted(groups):
    print(left, " ".join(groups[left]))

-61 j
1 x
8 v w y
25 t
26 f z
33 s
38 c d e g o q
47 a
60 i
66 u
70 b h k l m n p r

sorted(groups) gives the keys in order. Asked to sort a dictionary, Python sorts what in looks at: the keys.

There they are. The last line is Mira's first column plus the n itself. The line for 38 is her second column plus the o. She didn't look anything up; the Regular was spaced by somebody who thought the same way.

Now look at the line for 26: f z. Those two don't begin alike at all. The f starts with a thin crossbar and the z with a flat stroke. They happen to have the same number. So a script can find letters that share a value, but it can't tell a family from a coincidence. That knowledge is Mira's, and it has to be written down by a person.

docs.title: Step 2: Write the families down
docs.text:
A dictionary again, with the model as the key and the list of followers as the value:

LEFT = {
    "n": ["b", "h", "k", "l", "m", "p", "r"],
    "o": ["c", "d", "e", "g", "q"],
}

print(LEFT["o"])
print(len(LEFT), len(LEFT["n"]))

['c', 'd', 'e', 'g', 'q']
2 7

Two families, and seven followers in the first. Spread over several lines like this, with a comma after the last entry too, the dictionary reads much as Mira's paper does. Python doesn't mind the line breaks inside the braces, and it doesn't mind the last comma.

The i and the u aren't in it. In the Regular the i has 60 and the u has 66, where the n has 70. Mira says that's on purpose: a single stem needs a touch less white than a stem with an arch behind it. So they stay out. A family is a decision, and leaving a letter out is a decision too.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Chapter 63's script wants the map the other way round: follower first, model second. So turn it. My first try went through the families and stored each model under its followers:

like = {}
for model, members in LEFT.items():
    like[members] = model

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 3, in <module>
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'

"Unhashable" is one of Python's less helpful words. What it means here: a list can't be a key. A dictionary finds its keys fast because it trusts them never to change, and a list can change, with append for one. Text, numbers and tuples can be keys. Lists can't.

But the message, odd as it is, points at the real slip. I didn't want the whole list ["b", "h", "k", ...] to be one key. I wanted seven keys, one for each letter in it. members is a list, and I used it as if it were a name.

docs.title: Step 4: Turn it round
docs.text:
Seven keys from one list means a loop inside the loop:

like = {}
for model, members in LEFT.items():
    for name in members:
        like[name] = model

print(like)

{'b': 'n', 'h': 'n', 'k': 'n', 'l': 'n', 'm': 'n', 'p': 'n', 'r': 'n', 'c': 'o', 'd': 'o', 'e': 'o', 'g': 'o', 'q': 'o'}

Twelve entries from two. That's the follower map in the form chapter 63 used, and nobody typed it.

There's a trap left in those four lines, and you know it from yesterday. Suppose Mira, on a tired afternoon, writes the u into two families of the same side. The second like["u"] = ... would overwrite the first with no error, and which family won would depend on the order of the lines. So check before you store:

like = {}
doubles = []
for model, members in LEFT.items():
    for name in members:
        if name in like:
            doubles.append(name)
        like[name] = model

If doubles isn't empty at the end, the script should say so and stop. A letter can follow one model on each side, not two.

docs.title: Step 5: Who is out of line?
docs.text:
With families written down, one question can be asked of the whole font: which followers don't have their model's value? For one follower and one model, in all three masters:

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
model = pGlyph(font, font["o"])
rich = pGlyph(font, font["c"])

offs = [rich.getLSB(master) - model.getLSB(master) for master in MASTERS]
print(offs)
print(", ".join([f"{off:+}" for off in offs]))

[3, 0, 0]
+3, +0, +0

The c stands 3 units further in than the o in the Light, and matches it in the other two.

{off:+} is a small new thing for f-strings. The + after the colon asks for the sign to be shown always, so 3 prints as +3. For a list of differences that's what you want: you see at once which way each one goes.

And any(offs) tells you whether there's anything to report. Chapter 44 used any on a list of True and False. On numbers it works the same way, since 0 counts as false and every other number as true.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Spacing Groups
# Checks families of letters that should share a sidebearing,
# and prints the follower maps for copy_sb.py.
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
LEFT = {
    "n": ["b", "h", "k", "l", "m", "p", "r"],
    "o": ["c", "d", "e", "g", "q"],
}
RIGHT = {
    "n": ["a", "h", "m"],
    "o": ["b", "p"],
    "l": ["d", "g", "q", "u"],
}


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def follower_map(families):
    like = {}
    doubles = []
    for model, members in families.items():
        for name in members:
            if name in like:
                doubles.append(name)
            like[name] = model
    return like, doubles


def side_values(font, name, side):
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    if side == "left":
        return [rich.getLSB(master) for master in MASTERS]
    return [rich.getRSB(master) for master in MASTERS]


def report(font, families, side):
    differ = 0
    for model, members in families.items():
        wanted = side_values(font, model, side)
        print(f"{side} like {model}: " + ", ".join([str(value) for value in wanted]))
        for name in members:
            values = side_values(font, name, side)
            offs = [value - want for value, want in zip(values, wanted)]
            if any(offs):
                differ += 1
                cells = "".join([f"{value:>5}" for value in values])
                print(f"  {name:<3}{cells}   off by " + ", ".join([f"{off:+}" for off in offs]))
    return differ


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    left_like, left_doubles = follower_map(LEFT)
    right_like, right_doubles = follower_map(RIGHT)
    if left_doubles or right_doubles:
        print("In two families of one side:", " ".join(left_doubles + right_doubles))
        return
    names = list(LEFT) + list(RIGHT) + list(left_like) + list(right_like)
    missing = sorted(set([name for name in names if font[name] is None]))
    if missing:
        print("No glyph named:", " ".join(missing))
        return

    differ = report(font, LEFT, "left") + report(font, RIGHT, "right")
    print(f"{differ} of {len(left_like) + len(right_like)} followers differ from their model.")
    print()
    print(f"LEFT_LIKE = {left_like}")
    print(f"RIGHT_LIKE = {right_like}")


main()

left like n: 84, 70, 56
left like o: 50, 38, 30
  c     53   38   30   off by +3, +0, +0
  e     48   38   30   off by -2, +0, +0
right like n: 80, 66, 32
  a     80   66   41   off by +0, +0, +9
right like o: 50, 38, 8
  b     53   38    3   off by +3, +0, -5
  p     53   38    3   off by +3, +0, -5
right like l: 84, 70, 34
  d     84   70   29   off by +0, +0, -5
  g     85   70   29   off by +1, +0, -5
  q     84   70   29   off by +0, +0, -5
  u     84   70   36   off by +0, +0, +2
9 of 21 followers differ from their model.

LEFT_LIKE = {'b': 'n', 'h': 'n', 'k': 'n', 'l': 'n', 'm': 'n', 'p': 'n', 'r': 'n', 'c': 'o', 'd': 'o', 'e': 'o', 'g': 'o', 'q': 'o'}
RIGHT_LIKE = {'a': 'n', 'h': 'n', 'm': 'n', 'b': 'o', 'p': 'o', 'd': 'l', 'g': 'l', 'q': 'l', 'u': 'l'}

Some notes on the listing.

follower_map returns two things, the map and the list of doubles, and main takes them apart on one line. The function doesn't print or stop. It hands back what it found and leaves the decision to main, as the builder did with its problems in chapter 57.

list(LEFT) makes a list of a dictionary's keys, for the same reason sorted(groups) sorted them. The line after it collects every name the script is going to look up, models and followers alike, and set from chapter 25 drops the repeats before the missing ones are printed.

report is called twice, and its two results are added. Each call prints as it goes and returns how many followers were out of line.

The last two lines print a dictionary inside an f-string. Python writes a dictionary out in a form that Python can read back in. So those two lines of output are two lines of a script: you can copy them from the Output panel and paste them over the two constants at the top of copy_sb.py. A script has written part of another script. The first exercise does it.

Now read the report the way Mira does, by columns.

The middle column, the Regular, is clean. Every follower sits on its model, on both sides. That's the master Oskar and Mira looked at most.

The Light has small drifts: 3 units, 2 units, 1. They're slips of the hand, and nobody would defend them.

The Bold column is where the numbers get large, and Mira stops there. "Look at the models," she says. The Bold o has 30 on its left and 8 on its right. A round letter should be the same on both sides, or near it. The Bold n has 56 and 32. The Bold was made by fattening the Regular inside widths that were never looked at again, and the weight grew into the right sidebearings.

So the families can't mend the Bold yet. If you copy from a model that's wrong, you spread the mistake neatly over thirty glyphs. Her decision: use the left families now, where the models are sound in all three masters. Leave the right side of the Bold until its models have been put right. Chapter 67 finds them and chapter 68 changes them.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A dictionary of lists says "these belong to that" in the fewest words, and a loop inside a loop turns it into a dictionary that answers "whom does this one follow?". A list can't be a key, and TypeError: unhashable type: 'list' usually means you used a whole list where you meant each thing in it. Grouping by a measured value finds letters that share a number, and it can't tell a family from a coincidence. A copied sidebearing is only as good as its model.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Copy the LEFT_LIKE line from the Output panel into copy_sb.py from chapter 63, set RIGHT_LIKE = {} there, and run it. You should be offered two layers, the Light c (move -3, width 412 to 409) and the Light e (move 2, width 451 to 453), and then five accented letters whose widths follow: ccedilla, eacute, ecircumflex, edieresis and egrave, plus any you built on c and e in chapter 60. Run spacing_groups.py again. The count should be 7 of 21. Later chapters print their numbers for a font without this change, so undo it when you've looked.
  2. Put "u" into the "n" list of RIGHT as well as the "l" list, and run the script. Then take the check out of follower_map and print right_like["u"]. Which family won, and why that one?
  3. Change step 1 to group by the right sidebearing in the Bold. How many groups have more than one letter? Compare with the Regular, where d g l q u share 70. What does the difference tell you about the Bold?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Copying a sidebearing puts a number in a glyph, and the number goes stale the day the model changes. FontLab can hold the rule itself, as a short piece of text like =n, and do the sum whenever it's needed. Chapter 65 writes those rules by script.

docs.title: 65. Rules that FontLab keeps
docs.text:
Friday of week twelve. Mira has been looking at the Light o all morning and wants 2 more units of white on its left. That's a small change to one glyph. It's also the end of Wednesday's work: the d, the g and the q were given the number 50 because the o had 50, and when the o has 52 they'll still have 50.

You could run copy_sb.py again, and it would put them right. But somebody has to remember to run it, every time a model changes, for as long as the font lives. Oskar remembered. Then Oskar left.

FontLab has a way to store the rule in place of the number. Each layer has three small text fields, one for the left side, one for the right, one for the width. Leave a field empty and the number is yours to set. Write =o into the left one and you've told FontLab that this glyph's left side is whatever the o's is. FontLab calls these linked metrics, and what you write in the field is a metrics expression.

For Python, the expression is a string. Python doesn't know what =o means and doesn't need to. Your script builds a piece of text, hands it over, and FontLab reads it. So this chapter is about building strings with care, for a reader that isn't a person.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed, and the Font window in front.
  • The helpers ask and tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write them out again, so each one runs by itself.
  • The LEFT_LIKE line that spacing_groups.py printed in chapter 64.

This chapter changes the font, in one Undo step. I couldn't run it in FontLab 9. I can show you what the script stores. What FontLab then does with it, and when, I've read about and not seen. Step 5 is a check for that, and you should trust the check over my description.

docs.title: Step 1: Read the three fields
docs.text:
The fields are called metricsLeft, metricsRight and metricsWidth, and they belong to the layer:

from fly import fl
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()
layer = layer_of(pGlyph(font, font["g"]).fl, "Light")
print([str(layer.metricsLeft), str(layer.metricsRight), str(layer.metricsWidth)])

['', '', '']

Three empty strings. Plum has no linked metrics anywhere; I checked its source file.

Two small habits in that line. str(...) around each field makes sure you have ordinary Python text, whatever kind of text FontLab hands back. And the three values are printed inside a list. Printed on its own, an empty string shows as nothing at all, and you can't tell it from a line that didn't print. Inside a list it shows with its quotes.

An empty string counts as false, as an empty list does. So "has this layer any rule?" is a short question:

print(any([str(layer.metricsLeft), str(layer.metricsRight), str(layer.metricsWidth)]))

False

docs.title: Step 2: Write one rule
docs.text:
Chapter 64's report had one odd line in the Light: the g has 85 on its right where the l, its model, has 84. One unit. Give the g a rule for it:

import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

rich = pGlyph(font, font["g"])


def change():
    layer.metricsRight = "=l"


package = scripting.current_package()
facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
history.commit("Link metrics", [layer], [rich.fl], change,
               operation="geometry", facts=facts, allow_bases=True)

print([str(layer.metricsLeft), str(layer.metricsRight), str(layer.metricsWidth)])
print(rich.getLSB("Light"), rich.getAdvance("Light"), rich.getRSB("Light"))

The commit carries allow_bases=True because gbreve borrows the g, as chapter 55 explained. Save the font first. The first print will show the rule in its place:

['', '=l', '']

The second is the one I can't show you. If FontLab has worked the rule out at once, you'll see 50 519 84: the right side has come down from 85 to 84 and the width with it. If you see 50 520 85, the rule is stored and the sum hasn't been done yet. Open the g in a Glyph window, look at the Metrics table, and run the last line again.

A word on what =l means in that field. The expression is in the right field and names a glyph, and as far as I've been able to read, that means the same side of the named glyph: the right sidebearing of the l. In the left field =l would mean its left sidebearing. In the width field it would mean its advance width.

The equals sign is part of the text. The scripts I've read all write it, and I'd write it always.

The Light g now carries this rule, and nothing later in the part needs it. Take it off again: put "" in place of "=l" in change and run the lines once more.

To take a rule away, store the empty string: layer.metricsRight = "". The number that's there stays.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
The u was left out of the n family in chapter 64, on purpose. Its left side isn't the n's. But look at the two in all three masters: 80 and 84 in the Light, 66 and 70 in the Regular, 52 and 56 in the Bold. The u stands 4 units closer than the n every time. That's a rule too, and an expression can say it: =n-4.

To build that text from a model's name and a number, I tried the obvious thing:

model = "n"
extra = -4
text = "=" + model + extra

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 3, in <module>
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

Python won't glue a number onto text. It's the refusal you met in Part 1, and an f-string cures it: it turns the number into text for you.

print(f"={model}{extra}")

=n-4

That looks right, and it's right by luck. The minus sign came with the number. Try it with 10:

extra = 10
print(f"={model}{extra}")

=n10

No error this time, and that's worse. =n10 is a perfectly good string. To FontLab it would be a rule about a glyph called n10, which Plum doesn't have. A person reading n10 might guess what you meant. A program reads what's there.

docs.title: Step 4: Build the text properly
docs.text:
Chapter 64 had the tool for this: {extra:+} prints a number with its sign, always.

for extra in [10, -4, 0]:
    print(f"={model}{extra:+}")

=n+10
=n-4
=n+0

The first two are what you want. The third works as a sum but reads badly, and Mira will be reading these in the Metrics table for years. So make the plain case plain, in a function of its own:

def rule(model, extra):
    if extra == 0:
        return f"={model}"
    return f"={model}{extra:+}"


print(rule("n", 10), rule("n", -4), rule("o", 0))

=n+10 =n-4 =o

There's a habit worth taking from this. When a script writes text for another program to read, put the writing in one small function and try it on the awkward cases before you use it: a positive number, a negative one, zero. A slip in a sentence for a person costs a frown. A slip here goes into thirty-nine layers without a sound.

docs.title: Step 5: Ask the font whether the rules hold
docs.text:
You can't see into FontLab's arithmetic, but you can do the same sum yourself and compare. For each follower, the number its rule should give is the model's left sidebearing plus the extra:

LEFT_LIKE = {"c": "o", "e": "o", "u": "n"}
LEFT_EXTRA = {"u": -4}

for name, model in LEFT_LIKE.items():
    want = pGlyph(font, font[model]).getLSB("Light") + LEFT_EXTRA.get(name, 0)
    have = pGlyph(font, font[name]).getLSB("Light")
    print(name, have, want, f"{have - want:+}")

c 53 50 +3
e 48 50 -2
u 80 80 +0

LEFT_EXTRA.get(name, 0) is the get from chapter 22: the extra if there is one, and 0 for everybody else. Only the exceptions need writing down.

If you did the first exercise of chapter 64, the c and the e are at 50 already and all three lines end in +0.

Run this before you write the rules and again after. Before, it tells you which glyphs will move. After, it tells you whether they did.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Link Metrics
# Stores a left-sidebearing rule such as =n or =n-4 in each follower,
# in every master, and checks whether the numbers agree with the rules.
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
LEFT_LIKE = {'b': 'n', 'h': 'n', 'k': 'n', 'l': 'n', 'm': 'n', 'p': 'n', 'r': 'n', 'c': 'o', 'd': 'o', 'e': 'o', 'g': 'o', 'q': 'o', 'u': 'n'}
LEFT_EXTRA = {"u": -4}
CLEAR = False


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def rule(model, extra):
    if extra == 0:
        return f"={model}"
    return f"={model}{extra:+}"


def link_rows(font):
    rows = []
    for name, model in LEFT_LIKE.items():
        text = "" if CLEAR else rule(model, LEFT_EXTRA.get(name, 0))
        rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
        for master in MASTERS:
            layer = layer_of(rich.fl, master)
            if str(layer.metricsLeft) != text:
                rows.append((rich, layer, text))
    return rows


def off_rule(font):
    lines = []
    for name, model in LEFT_LIKE.items():
        rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
        base = pGlyph(font, font[model])
        for master in MASTERS:
            off = rich.getLSB(master) - base.getLSB(master) - LEFT_EXTRA.get(name, 0)
            if off != 0:
                lines.append(f"  {name:<4}{master:<9}{off:+}")
    return lines


def show_off(font):
    lines = off_rule(font)
    print(f"{len(lines)} of {len(LEFT_LIKE) * len(MASTERS)} layers are off their rule.")
    for line in lines:
        print(line)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    names = list(LEFT_LIKE) + list(LEFT_LIKE.values())
    missing = sorted(set([name for name in names if font[name] is None]))
    if missing:
        tell(f"No glyph named: {' '.join(missing)}")
        return

    rows = link_rows(font)
    texts = {}
    owners = {}
    for rich, layer, text in rows:
        texts[rich.name] = text
        owners[rich.name] = rich.fl
    for name, text in texts.items():
        print(f"{name:<4}left  {text}")
    print(f"{len(rows)} layers to change.")
    show_off(font)
    if not rows or not ask(f"Store rules in {len(rows)} layers?"):
        return

    def change():
        for rich, layer, text in rows:
            layer.metricsLeft = text

    package = scripting.current_package()
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    layers = [layer for rich, layer, text in rows]
    history.commit("Link metrics", layers, list(owners.values()), change,
                   operation="geometry", facts=facts, allow_bases=True)
    show_off(font)


main()

The first part of what it prints I'm sure of:

b   left  =n
h   left  =n
k   left  =n
l   left  =n
m   left  =n
p   left  =n
r   left  =n
c   left  =o
d   left  =o
e   left  =o
g   left  =o
q   left  =o
u   left  =n-4
39 layers to change.
2 of 39 layers are off their rule.
  c   Light    +3
  e   Light    -2

Thirteen followers in three masters make 39 layers. Answer Yes, and the script stores the rules and asks the font again. If FontLab has done its sums by then, the last line is:

0 of 39 layers are off their rule.

If it still says 2, the rules are in and the numbers haven't caught up. Open the Light c in a Glyph window, look at its left field in the Metrics table, where =o should stand, and run the script again. It will find nothing to store, print 0 layers to change. and report the count once more. Tell me which of the two you saw; it's one of the things in this book I most want to know.

Some notes on the listing.

LEFT_LIKE is the line chapter 64 printed, pasted in, with the u added by hand at the end. LEFT_EXTRA holds the one exception.

link_rows skips a layer whose field already holds the right text. That's what makes a second run harmless, and it's the same idea as the builder in chapter 56 that left good glyphs alone.

texts and owners are both dictionaries used to keep one of each: three rows for the b, one line in the list, one glyph for the Undo step.

CLEAR = True turns the script into its own opposite. Every rule becomes the empty string, and the layers that hold a rule get it taken away. When you write a script that sets something up, it's worth a line or two to let it take the same thing down.

The rules are for the left side only. Mira's decision from yesterday stands: the right-hand models in the Bold aren't fit to follow yet.

Now the thing Mira wanted this morning. She gives the Light o 2 more units on the left, with set_sb.py from chapter 62. If the rules work as they should, the c, the d, the e, the g and the q go with it, and nobody has to remember anything. She runs the script afterwards to see. 0 of 39 layers are off their rule. is the line she'll look for from now on, and any other count names the layers to look at.

One warning to carry forward. A layer with a rule doesn't take orders about numbers. If you run set_sb.py on the Light d now and ask for 60 on the left, the number and the rule disagree, and I can't tell you which wins. The careful tools in fly.ap step around linked layers for that reason, and chapter 68 will meet them. Change the model, or change the rule.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A layer has three text fields, metricsLeft, metricsRight and metricsWidth: empty means no rule, and =n or =n-4 is a rule FontLab works out from another glyph. Your script only builds the text, so {extra:+} keeps the sign, and a small function tried on a positive number, a negative one and zero catches =n10 before it reaches the font. A dictionary with .get(name, 0) holds only the exceptions. When you can't see how another program does its sum, do the sum yourself and compare.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Before you run the script, guess what rule("H", 0), rule("H", 12) and rule("H", -12) give. Then print them.
  2. The i isn't in a family either. Compare its left side with the n's in all three masters. After chapter 62 you should find 74 and 84, 60 and 70, 56 and 56. Can one rule of the form =n-10 serve all three? What would it do to the Bold, and is that what Mira asked for on Tuesday?
  3. Set CLEAR = True, run the script, and read the three fields of the Light c as in step 1. Then set it back to False and run again. How many Undo steps did the two runs make?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The publisher's price list is set in Plum, and its columns of figures look uneven, though all ten figures have the same width. Chapter 66 finds out why and centers each figure in its box.

docs.title: 66. Figures that line up
docs.text:
Monday of week thirteen. The publisher's spring price list came back from the typesetter with a note in the margin: "Columns wobble. Pounds worst." Ines pins it to the board. Thirty titles, thirty prices, set in Plum, with the figures stacked in columns so that a reader can run an eye down the pence.

Figures made for columns are called tabular figures: every one of them has the same advance width, so the fourth figure of one price stands under the fourth figure of the next. Figures made for running text are proportional: the 1 is narrow and the 0 is wide, as letters are. Plum has one set of figures, and Mira is sure they were drawn as tabular.

"Then why do they wobble?" Ines asks.

That's a question with numbers in it, so it's a question for a script.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed, and the Font window in front.
  • The helpers ask and tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write them out again, so each one runs by itself.

The script at the end changes the font, in one Undo step. I couldn't run it in FontLab 9. The measurements come from Plum's source file.

docs.title: Step 1: Are they tabular?
docs.text:
The figures have names, not digits: the glyph for 0 is called zero. Write the ten names down once and ask each for its width:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

FIGURES = ["zero", "one", "two", "three", "four",
           "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine"]
font = fl.CurrentFont()
widths = [pGlyph(font, font[name]).getAdvance("Regular") for name in FIGURES]
print(widths)
print(set(widths), len(set(widths)))

[490, 490, 490, 490, 490, 490, 490, 490, 490, 490]
{490} 1

Ten times 490. A set keeps one of each, as chapter 25 showed, so a set of the widths with one thing in it means "all the same". len(set(widths)) == 1 is a tidy test for it, and you'll use it again.

The Light gives 456 ten times, and the Bold 490. Mira was right. The figures are tabular, in all three masters. So the wobble isn't in the widths.

docs.title: Step 2: The signs that go with them
docs.text:
"Pounds worst," the note said. A price isn't only figures. Ask the currency signs too:

SIGNS = ["dollar", "Euro", "sterling", "yen"]

for master in ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]:
    print(master, [pGlyph(font, font[name]).getAdvance(master) for name in SIGNS])

Light [456, 456, 489, 480]
Regular [490, 490, 480, 490]
Bold [490, 490, 480, 490]

There's the first fault. The dollar and the euro sign have the figures' width. The pound sign doesn't, in any master: it's 33 units too wide in the Light and 10 too narrow in the other two. The yen is off in the Light. In a column of prices in pounds, every line begins with a sign of the wrong width, and everything after it stands 10 units to the side of where the column above expects it.

(Euro has a capital letter. It's the name the glyph has carried since the 1990s, and names must match letter for letter.)

docs.title: Step 3: Same width isn't the whole story
docs.text:
Mira looks at the Bold column of the price list longer than at the others. "They're all leaning," she says. Print the three numbers of chapter 61 for a few Bold figures:

for name in ["zero", "four", "eight"]:
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    print(name, rich.getLSB("Bold"), rich.getAdvance("Bold"), rich.getRSB("Bold"))

zero 28 490 -4
four 24 490 -19
eight 37 490 5

The Bold zero has 28 units of white on its left and less than nothing on its right: the black pokes 4 units out of its own box. It's the Bold's old trouble again. The figures were fattened inside widths nobody changed, and they grew to the right.

In running text that only looks tight. In a table it does something else. A tabular figure is a black shape in a fixed box, and a column looks straight when each shape sits in the middle of its box. The Regular zero does: 36 and 36. The Regular seven doesn't quite: 53 and 29.

So there are two things to do. Give the signs the figures' width. And put every shape in the middle of its box.

docs.title: Step 4: The centering sum
docs.text:
Take the Regular seven: 53 on the left, 490 wide, 29 on the right.

The black is what's left when you take both sidebearings from the width. I'll call it the ink, to keep it apart from the Bold's kind of black:

left, width, right = 53, 490, 29
ink = width - left - right
print(ink)

408

The box is 490 and the ink is 408, so there are 82 units of white to share. Half on each side:

target = 490
print((target - ink) / 2)

41.0

The seven should have 41 on its left. It has 53, so it moves by 41 minus 53: 12 units to the left. Its width stays 490, and the right side comes out as 41 too.

Now the same sum for the Regular two, which has 41, 490 and 50:

left, width, right = 41, 490, 50
ink = width - left - right
print(ink, (target - ink) / 2)

399 45.5

That's the mistake of the chapter, and Python didn't complain about it. 91 units of white don't halve evenly. If you hand 45.5 on, the script moves the outline by 4.5 units, and every node of the two lands on a half. Plum's nodes all sit on whole units, and as far as I know a font with nodes on halves gets them rounded at export, each on its own. I haven't checked that in FontLab 9. You've met the cure: // from chapter 49, the division that keeps whole numbers whole.

print((target - ink) // 2)

45

45 on the left, and the odd unit goes to the right: 46. You could round instead. But chapter 53 showed that round sends a half to the nearest even number, so 45.5 would become 46 and 44.5 would become 44, and the spare unit would land left for one figure and right for the next. With // it always lands on the right. In a column, always is better than nearly.

docs.title: Step 5: One function for the sum
docs.text:
def centered(left, width, right, target):
    ink = width - left - right
    new_left = (target - ink) // 2
    return new_left - left


print(centered(53, 490, 29, 490))
print(centered(41, 490, 50, 490))
print(centered(59, 480, 28, 490))

-12
4
-11

The function takes four plain numbers and returns the distance to move. It knows nothing about fonts, so you can try it on numbers you've worked out on paper before any glyph is touched. The third line is the Regular pound sign: 59, 480 and 28 going into a box of 490. Its ink is 393, the white is 97, the left share is 48, and it moves 11 to the left while its box grows by 10.

Moving and setting the width in one go is what metrics.shift_and_set did in chapter 62. Nothing new is needed for the writing.

Where does target come from? From the figures themselves: max of their ten widths. Today the ten are equal and max has nothing to decide. If one of them ever differs, the widest wins, and that's the safe direction: a shape can always be given more room, and it can't always be squeezed.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Make Tabular
# Gives figures and currency signs one width in each master
# and centers each shape in it.
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.metrics.panel.model as metrics
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
FIGURES = ["zero", "one", "two", "three", "four",
           "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine"]
SIGNS = ["dollar", "Euro", "sterling", "yen"]


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def centered(left, width, right, target):
    ink = width - left - right
    new_left = (target - ink) // 2
    return new_left - left


def plan_rows(font):
    rows = []
    for master in MASTERS:
        widths = [pGlyph(font, font[name]).getAdvance(master) for name in FIGURES]
        target = max(widths)
        if len(set(widths)) > 1:
            print(f"{master}: the figures have {len(set(widths))} widths. Using {target}.")
        for name in FIGURES + SIGNS:
            rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
            left = rich.getLSB(master)
            width = rich.getAdvance(master)
            right = rich.getRSB(master)
            dx = centered(left, width, right, target)
            if dx != 0 or width != target:
                rows.append((rich, master, dx, width, target))
    return rows


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    missing = [name for name in FIGURES + SIGNS if font[name] is None]
    if missing:
        tell(f"No glyph named: {' '.join(missing)}")
        return

    rows = plan_rows(font)
    for rich, master, dx, width, target in rows:
        print(f"{rich.name:<10}{master:<9}move {dx:+}, width {width} to {target}")
    print(f"{len(rows)} layers to change.")
    if not rows or not ask(f"Center {len(rows)} layers?"):
        return

    layers = [layer_of(rich.fl, master) for rich, master, dx, width, target in rows]
    owners = {}
    for rich, master, dx, width, target in rows:
        owners[rich.name] = rich.fl

    def change():
        for row, layer in zip(rows, layers):
            metrics.shift_and_set(layer, row[2], row[4])

    package = scripting.current_package()
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    history.commit("Make tabular", layers, list(owners.values()), change, operation="geometry", facts=facts)
    print(f"Done. {len(plan_rows(font))} layers still off.")


main()

The Regular part of what it prints:

one       Regular  move +15, width 490 to 490
two       Regular  move +4, width 490 to 490
three     Regular  move +10, width 490 to 490
four      Regular  move -7, width 490 to 490
five      Regular  move -1, width 490 to 490
six       Regular  move -3, width 490 to 490
seven     Regular  move -12, width 490 to 490
nine      Regular  move +2, width 490 to 490
dollar    Regular  move +3, width 490 to 490
Euro      Regular  move -16, width 490 to 490
sterling  Regular  move -11, width 480 to 490
yen       Regular  move -1, width 490 to 490

Twelve lines there. The zero and the eight are missing from it because they were in the middle already. The Light has twelve lines as well, and the Bold fourteen: every Bold figure moves left, by between 6 and 22 units. The list ends:

38 layers to change.

And after you answer Yes, if the font reads back at once what was written into it:

Done. 0 layers still off.

That last line plans the whole job a second time and counts what's left. It's the check-after habit of chapter 62 in one line: the script that knows how to find the fault is the best judge of whether the fault has gone. If it prints anything other than 0, run the script again and read its list.

The structure is copy_sb.py from chapter 63 again. Rows are planned first, as tuples. They're shown. You're asked. Then one change function does all of them inside one history.commit, so that one Edit > Undo should take all 38 back. I haven't seen it in FontLab 9. When a pattern has worked three times, it's worth recognizing as yours.

One line in change is lazier than I'd like: row[2] and row[4]. They're the move and the target, by position in the tuple. It works, and a week from now you won't remember what the 2 and the 4 were. The second exercise mends it.

Nothing borrows the figures in Plum, so no composite is left behind today. If your own font has fractions or superior figures built from components of these, run the borrowers check from chapter 62 first.

docs.title: What Mira does with it
docs.text:
She runs it, prints the price list again, and pins the new sheet beside the old one. The pounds column is straight. The Bold column no longer leans.

Then she takes the one back out. Centered by arithmetic, the Regular 1 moved 15 units to the right, and to her eye it now stands too far from the figure before it. A 1 is a stem with a flag on its left; its black isn't spread evenly over its ink, and its middle for the eye isn't its middle for the ruler. She moves it back 6 by hand.

That isn't the script failing. The sum gives every figure the same fair start in an afternoon's worth of clicks, and the eye spends its time on the one that needs it. She adds a line to her list: "Figures: Bold zero has 12 a side. Whole Bold tight."

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Tabular figures share one advance width, and len(set(widths)) == 1 tests that. Equal widths aren't enough for straight columns: each shape also has to sit in the middle of its box, and the signs that stand with the figures need the same box. The white to share is the box less the ink, and // halves it in whole numbers, with the spare unit always on the same side. A function that takes plain numbers can be tried on paper sums before it meets a glyph.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Work out on paper what centered(28, 490, -4, 490) gives, and what the Bold zero's two sidebearings are afterwards. Then run the line. A negative sidebearing goes through the sum like any other number: why does the ink come out larger than the box less 28?
  2. Change plan_rows so that each row carries the layer too, and change so that it unpacks every row into names, as the for lines in main do. The zip and the positions row[2] and row[4] should both disappear.
  3. Add "percent" to SIGNS and run the script, and answer No. What does it offer to do with the percent sign, which is 798 wide in the Regular? Take the name out again.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The figures showed a fault that the eye had missed for years and a script found in a second: one glyph whose number didn't match its neighbors'. Chapter 67 looks for that kind of fault everywhere, by comparing each glyph with the usual value of its group.

docs.title: 67. Find the odd one out
docs.text:
Tuesday of week thirteen. Yesterday's price list had a fault nobody had seen in years: one sign whose width didn't match its neighbors'. Mira wonders aloud how many more of those Plum is carrying. On Thursday she left herself a note, "Bold right side: wait", because the Bold's models were themselves in doubt. If the n is wrong, there's no use copying it.

So today's question is put differently. It isn't "does this letter match its model?" It's "which letter in this group doesn't look like the rest of the group?" Nobody has to be the model. The group votes.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The helper tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write it out again, so each one runs by itself.

Today's script reads and prints. It changes nothing. I couldn't run it in FontLab 9; the numbers come from Plum's source file, with the changes of chapters 62 and 63 worked in. If you did the exercises of those chapters, a few of your lines will differ, and I'll say where.

docs.title: Step 1: A group and its numbers
docs.text:
Start with six capitals whose right side is a straight stem. Read their right sidebearings in the Bold:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()
names = ["H", "I", "J", "M", "N", "U"]
values = [pGlyph(font, font[name]).getRSB("Bold") for name in names]
print(values)

[40, 40, -24, 52, 42, 36]

You can see the odd one. Five numbers live near 40 and one is far below zero. (If you gave the Bold H 60 a side in chapter 62, your first number is 60, and you have two odd ones.)

You can see it at a glance with six numbers on one line. The script has to see it in nine groups and three masters without you, so it needs a rule. The rule has two parts: what's usual for the group, and how far from usual is too far.

docs.title: Step 2: The average, and why it lets you down
docs.text:
The first idea everyone has for "usual" is the average: add them up and divide by how many there are.

usual = sum(values) / len(values)
print(usual)

31.0

sum adds up a list, as it did in chapter 37. Now say that a letter is odd when it's more than 8 units from the usual value, in either direction. abs from chapter 36 takes the direction away:

for name, value in zip(names, values):
    if abs(value - usual) > 8:
        print(name, value)

H 40
I 40
J -24
M 52
N 42

Five odd ones out of six. That's this chapter's mistake, and there's no error message to announce it. The script ran, and what it says is nonsense: when nearly everybody is odd, the yardstick is.

Look at what happened. The J is so far off that it dragged the average down to 31, a value no letter in the group has or is near. Measured from there, the honest letters look wrong. The average asks every number for its opinion and weighs the loudest one most. For finding a fault, that's the wrong way round: the faulty number is the one you least want to have a say.

docs.title: Step 3: The one in the middle
docs.text:
There's a steadier kind of usual. Put the numbers in order and take the one in the middle:

ordered = sorted(values)
print(ordered)
print(ordered[len(ordered) // 2])

[-24, 36, 40, 40, 42, 52]
40

sorted you've had since chapter 10, and // halves the length without leaving the whole numbers. Six things halve to 3, and position 3, counting from 0, holds 40.

The J is still in the list. But it sits at the far end, and the far end has no say about the middle. It could be −24 or −2,400 and the middle would still be 40. Statisticians call this value the median. I'll call it the middle one.

With an even count there are two numbers in the middle, here both 40, and the line takes the upper of the two. A statistician would take the point halfway between them. For this job a value that some letter really has is the better answer, so the line stays as it is.

Wrap it up and try again:

def middle(values):
    ordered = sorted(values)
    return ordered[len(ordered) // 2]


usual = middle(values)
for name, value in zip(names, values):
    if abs(value - usual) > 8:
        print(name, value, f"{value - usual:+}")

J -24 -64
M 52 +12

Two, and both deserve a look. The J is 64 units short. The M has 12 more than its neighbors, which may be a decision and may be a leftover. The script can't tell you which. It can tell you where to look.

docs.title: Step 4: How far is too far
docs.text:
The 8 in that test is a choice, and it's yours to make. Call it the tolerance and try three values on the whole font, all groups and masters:

Tolerance Letters reported 4 19 6 11 8 6

At 4 you get 19 lines, and most of them are things a designer did on purpose: the Light N, 6 units less than the H, because its diagonal lets light in. At 8 you get six, and you can look at six before lunch. There's no right value. Start high, deal with what you find, and lower it when the list is empty and you still have appetite.

Since it's a choice, it goes at the top of the script, in capitals, with the other things you might change.

docs.title: Step 5: Groups as data
docs.text:
Each group needs three things: a label for the report, a side, and the names. That's a tuple, and the groups together are a list of tuples, as the rows of chapter 35 were:

GROUPS = [
    ("cap stems", "left", "BDEFHIKLMNPRU"),
    ("cap rounds", "left", "CGOQ"),
    ("cap stems", "right", "HIJMNU"),
]

for label, side, names in GROUPS:
    print(label, side, list(names))

cap stems left ['B', 'D', 'E', 'F', 'H', 'I', 'K', 'L', 'M', 'N', 'P', 'R', 'U']
cap rounds left ['C', 'G', 'O', 'Q']
cap stems right ['H', 'I', 'J', 'M', 'N', 'U']

A small saving is at work here. The names are single letters, so I wrote each group as one string, and list cut it into its characters. A string is a row of characters, and a for loop walks along it one at a time, as it did with a word in chapter 11; list collects what such a walk would meet. It works only while every glyph name is one character long. The day you want germandbls in a group, that group becomes a proper list with quotes and commas, and the rest of the script won't notice the difference.

The families of chapter 64 said "these follow that one". These groups say less: "these belong together". That's why a dictionary with a model as its key was right there and a plain list is right here.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Sidebearing Outliers
# Reports letters whose sidebearing is far from the middle value of their group.
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
TOLERANCE = 8
GROUPS = [
    ("cap stems", "left", "BDEFHIKLMNPRU"),
    ("cap rounds", "left", "CGOQ"),
    ("cap stems", "right", "HIJMNU"),
    ("cap rounds", "right", "DOQ"),
    ("small stems", "left", "bhklmnpr"),
    ("small rounds", "left", "cdegoq"),
    ("small stems", "right", "ahmn"),
    ("small l", "right", "dglqu"),
    ("small rounds", "right", "bop"),
]


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def middle(values):
    ordered = sorted(values)
    return ordered[len(ordered) // 2]


def side_value(font, name, side, master):
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    return rich.getLSB(master) if side == "left" else rich.getRSB(master)


def odd_ones(font, master, side, names):
    values = [side_value(font, name, side, master) for name in names]
    usual = middle(values)
    found = []
    for name, value in zip(names, values):
        if abs(value - usual) > TOLERANCE:
            found.append((name, value, usual))
    return found


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    count = 0
    for master in MASTERS:
        for label, side, names in GROUPS:
            names = [name for name in names if font[name] is not None]
            if len(names) < 3:
                print(f"{label} {side}: too few letters to compare.")
                continue
            for name, value, usual in odd_ones(font, master, side, names):
                count += 1
                print(f"{master:<9}{label:<13}{side:<6}{name:<3}{value:>4}   usual {usual:>3}  ({value - usual:+})")
    print(f"{count} to look at, tolerance {TOLERANCE}.")


main()

Save it as sb_outliers.py. On the practice font it prints:

Light    cap stems    left  U    78   usual  88  (-10)
Bold     cap stems    left  L    66   usual  56  (+10)
Bold     cap stems    right J   -24   usual  40  (-64)
Bold     cap stems    right M    52   usual  40  (+12)
Bold     cap rounds   right D    17   usual   0  (+17)
Bold     small stems  right a    41   usual  32  (+9)
6 to look at, tolerance 8.

Three things in the script are worth a second look.

side_value picks the getter with the short if of chapter 37: one value if the side is "left", the other if it isn't. Anything that isn't "left" counts as right, including a typing slip like "rihgt". In a list of nine groups that you can read at a glance I've let that stand.

The line that filters names keeps the script alive in a font that lacks a letter, and the test under it refuses to judge a group of fewer than three. Two numbers have no middle worth the name: whichever of the two is the larger gets called usual, and the other one gets the blame.

continue is the word from chapter 44. It ends this turn of the inner loop and goes on to the next group.

docs.title: Reading the report
docs.text:
Six lines, and the report has done what a report can do. The rest is looking.

Bold J, −24. A fault. The Regular J has 68 on its right and the Light has 80. In the Bold the stem grew fat and the width stayed at 239, so the black hangs 24 units out of its own box and into the next letter. This is the odd one of the chapter's title.

Bold D, +17. Read this one twice, because the report has it backwards. The usual value for the Bold round capitals is 0: the O has −6 and the Q has 0. A round letter with nothing on its right is the Bold's trouble again. The D with its 17 is the nearest of the three to healthy. The group voted, and the group was wrong.

That's the limit of the method and you should know it by heart. The middle one protects you from one bad number among good ones. It can't protect you when most of a group has gone the same wrong way, because then the wrong way is the usual way. A check like this finds letters that differ. Whether the different one is the sick one or the only well one takes a person.

Bold a, +9, M, +12 and L, +10, Light U, −10. Mira opens each in the Glyph window. The a and the M she leaves: the Bold a has a tail that wants the room. The L she can't explain, and the U neither. Both go on her list with a question mark.

Then she mends the J with a tool she already has. In set_sb.py from chapter 62 she sets:

GLYPH = "J"
MASTER = "Bold"
LEFT = None
RIGHT = 40

The width goes from 239 to 303 and nothing moves, since the right side is the width's business alone. The script's Borrowed by: line names IJ, which borrows the J as ij borrowed the j. Its width will want the same 64 units. She writes "IJ, Bold" under "ij, Bold" on the list.

One fault found and mended, two questions, and one whole group, the Bold rounds, shown to be wrong together. That last one isn't a job for a tolerance. It's a job for tomorrow.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: To find the odd one in a group you need a usual value and a tolerance, and abs measures the distance between them without direction. The average is a poor usual value, because one wild number drags it away; the middle of the sorted list stays put, and sorted(values)[len(values) // 2] finds it. A script can run without any error and still report nonsense, and "nearly everything is flagged" is the sign. The method finds what differs from the group, so it says nothing when a whole group is wrong.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Set TOLERANCE = 6 and run the script. You should get 11 lines. Two of the new ones are the Regular O and Q on the left, both 36 against a usual 44. Print the four values of that group and say why "usual 44" is an accident of where the middle fell. What would you change in the group, and not in middle, to make the report fair?
  2. Python has the statisticians' median ready-made: import statistics, then statistics.median(values). Put it into middle and run the script at tolerance 8 again. The Bold round capitals have three members, so nothing changes there. For an even count it returns the point halfway between the two middle values, as a float, so 61 can come back as 61.0 or as a number ending in .5. Which groups have an even count, and does any line of the report change?
  3. Add a group for the diagonals, ("diagonals", "right", "AVWXYvwxy"), and run it. The list gets long. Diagonals don't share a sidebearing the way stems do. Take the group out again, and write one sentence in a comment above GROUPS saying what a letter must have in common with the others before it may join one.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Every count this week has ended with the same note on Mira's list: the whole Bold is tight on the right. Chapter 68 stops mending it letter by letter and opens up all of it at once, by adding to every right sidebearing with one script.

docs.title: 68. Open it up a little
docs.text:
Wednesday of week thirteen. Mira's list has said the same thing in four different hands since last Monday. "Whole Bold tight." "Bold o: 30 and 8." "Bold zero has 12 a side." "Bold rounds wrong together." Yesterday's script couldn't help with it, because a fault that every letter shares isn't an odd one.

The cause has been plain since chapter 61. When the Bold was made, the black grew and the widths stayed. The left sides were set by hand to sensible values. The right sides got whatever was left over.

Ines has a second reason to care. The catalog sets its captions in the Bold at a small size, and small type wants more air between its letters, not less.

So today every Bold right side in the alphabet gets a new value, in one go. The question is which value.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed, and the Font window in front.
  • The helpers ask, ask_text and tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write them out again, so each one runs by itself.
  • copy_sb.py from chapter 63, for the accented letters at the end.

The script changes the font, in one Undo step. I couldn't run it in FontLab 9. Its numbers come from Plum's source file with the changes of chapters 62, 63 and 67 worked in.

docs.title: Step 1: The obvious cure, and what's wrong with it
docs.text:
Too tight means too little, so add some. Say 20 units on the right of every letter. Before you write anything into the font, work out what that would give for four letters:

from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box, run_text_dialog
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask_text(label, start=""):
    return run_text_dialog(qt.QtGui, label, start, TITLE)


font = fl.CurrentFont()
for name in ["n", "o", "H", "D"]:
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    print(name, rich.getLSB("Bold"), rich.getRSB("Bold") + 20)

n 56 52
o 30 28
H 56 60
D 56 37

Left side, then the right side as it would be. The n and the o come out close to even, which looks promising. The H would have more on its right than on its left, and the D has 37 where the round o has 28.

Adding the same number to everything is called tracking, and it's what a layout program does when you ask it to letterspace a line. It moves every letter apart by the same amount. It can't make an uneven font even: whatever was 16 units out before is 16 units out after. For Ines's captions tracking would be fine, if the Bold were sound to begin with. It isn't, so the mending comes first.

There's a second thing wrong with it, and it's about scripts and not about type. Run an "add 20" script twice and you've added 40. Nothing in the font remembers that you've been there already. A script like that is safe only in the hands of somebody who never loses count.

docs.title: Step 2: A better source
docs.text:
There's one master where the right sides are known to be good. Last Thursday's report found the Regular clean: every follower matched its model. So take the Bold's right sides from the Regular's, made smaller by the amount the Bold is tighter.

How much tighter is it meant to be? The left sides say. They were set by hand:

print(56 / 70)
print(30 / 38)

0.8
0.7894736842105263

The Bold n has 56 on its left where the Regular has 70, and the o has 30 against 38. Both come to about 0.8, four fifths. Somebody chose that, on purpose, for the left sides. Give the right sides the same treatment:

print(66 * 0.8)
print(38 * 0.8)
print(70 * 0.8)

52.800000000000004
30.400000000000002
56.0

Those are the Regular right sides of n, o and H at four fifths. Two things to notice.

The stray 4 and 2 at the far end aren't yours. A computer stores 0.8 in a form that can't hold it whole, as you can't write a third in full in decimal figures, and the tiny error shows up after the multiplying. It's about a hundred million millionth of a unit. You'll never see it in a font, and you shouldn't try to remove it. You remove the whole tail:

print(round(66 * 0.8), round(38 * 0.8), round(70 * 0.8))

53 30 56

And look at what came out. The Bold o gets 30 on the right, and it has 30 on the left. The H gets 56 and has 56. Nobody told the script that round letters and straight letters ought to be even on both sides. The Regular knew, and the sum carried it over.

This sum also has a property that "add 20" lacks. It reads the Regular and writes the Bold. Run it twice and the second run finds everything already in place. Run it with 0.85 next week and you get 0.85 of the Regular, not 0.85 on top of 0.8. A script that works out its answer from a source it doesn't change can be run as often as you like.

docs.title: Step 3: Ask for the factor
docs.text:
0.8 is a guess from two letters, and Ines will want to try others. So the script asks, with ask_text from chapter 39 and a starting value in the field:

text = ask_text("Right sides, as a share of the Regular's:", "0.8")
print(round(66 * text))

Click OK, and:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 2, in <module>
TypeError: type str doesn't define __round__ method

That's today's mistake. The message says round was handed a str, a piece of text. But you multiplied 66 by something first. What did that give? Take the round away and look:

print(66 * text)

0.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80.80

Sixty-six times the text 0.8, end to end. Whatever comes out of a text field is text, even when every character in it is a figure. And a number times a text isn't an error in Python. It means "repeat": 3 * "ab" is "ababab". So the wrong line ran without complaint, and the complaint came one step later, from round, which didn't know what to do with a string 198 characters long.

The cure is to say what you mean. float turns a text into a number with a decimal point:

factor = float(text)
print(factor, round(66 * factor))

0.8 53

float is short for "floating point", the name of that inexact way of storing numbers you met a minute ago. Its sister int makes whole numbers and refuses "0.8".

docs.title: Step 4: When the text isn't a number
docs.text:
Mira types the factor the way she writes it on paper, with a comma: 0,8.

ValueError: could not convert string to float: '0,8'

Python wants a point. And somebody will type four fifths one day, or nothing. A person who mistypes into a field shouldn't get a traceback for it. Chapter 19 had the tool: try the conversion, and if it raises ValueError, say so kindly and stop.

def ask_factor(start):
    text = ask_text("Right sides, as a share of the Regular's:", start)
    if text is None:
        return None
    try:
        return float(text.strip())
    except ValueError:
        tell(f"{text} isn't a number I can read. Use a point, as in 0.8.")
        return None

The function has three ways out. Cancel gives None. A good number gives the number. Bad text gives a message and then None. Whoever calls it has one thing to check: None means stop.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Open Up Bold
# Sets the Bold's right sidebearings to a share of the Regular's.
import string

import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.metrics.panel.model as metrics
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box, run_text_dialog
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

SOURCE = "Regular"
TARGET = "Bold"
LETTERS = string.ascii_uppercase + string.ascii_lowercase


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def ask_text(label, start=""):
    return run_text_dialog(qt.QtGui, label, start, TITLE)


def ask_factor(start):
    text = ask_text(f"Right sides, as a share of the {SOURCE}'s:", start)
    if text is None:
        return None
    try:
        return float(text.strip())
    except ValueError:
        tell(f"{text} isn't a number I can read. Use a point, as in 0.8.")
        return None


def plan_rows(font, factor):
    rows = []
    for name in LETTERS:
        if font[name] is None:
            continue
        rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
        layer = layer_of(rich.fl, TARGET)
        if str(layer.metricsRight) or str(layer.metricsWidth):
            print(f"{name}: has a rule for its right side or width. Left alone.")
            continue
        old = rich.getRSB(TARGET)
        new = round(rich.getRSB(SOURCE) * factor)
