        if new != old:
            rows.append((rich, layer, old, new, rich.getAdvance(TARGET) + new - old))
    return rows


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    factor = ask_factor("0.8")
    if factor is None:
        return

    rows = plan_rows(font, factor)
    for rich, layer, old, new, width in rows:
        print(f"{rich.name:<4}{old:>5} to {new:>3}   width {rich.getAdvance(TARGET)} to {width}")
    print(f"{len(rows)} layers to change, factor {factor}.")
    if not rows or not ask(f"Set {len(rows)} right sidebearings in the {TARGET}?"):
        return

    def change():
        for rich, layer, old, new, width in rows:
            metrics.shift_and_set(layer, 0, width)

    package = scripting.current_package()
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    layers = [layer for rich, layer, old, new, width in rows]
    owners = [rich.fl for rich, layer, old, new, width in rows]
    history.commit("Open up", layers, owners, change,
                   operation="geometry", facts=facts, allow_bases=True)
    print(f"Done. {len(plan_rows(font, factor))} layers still off.")


main()

Save it as open_up.py. With 0.8 in the field it prints 52 lines, one for every letter of the alphabet in both cases. Here are the first five and three from the middle:

A     -33 to   9   width 596 to 638
B      15 to  35   width 517 to 537
C      26 to  23   width 621 to 618
D      17 to  33   width 665 to 681
E       9 to  31   width 485 to 507
m      32 to  53   width 806 to 827
n      32 to  53   width 523 to 544
o       8 to  30   width 520 to 542
52 layers to change, factor 0.8.

Your m line may read differently if you skipped chapter 62, where its width went to 806. What comes after "to" won't: 53, whatever it was before.

Notes on the listing.

import string brings in a small module from the library that came with Python. string.ascii_uppercase is the text "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ" and string.ascii_lowercase is the same in small letters. Typing the alphabet yourself is a fine way to lose a letter, and yesterday's trick of looping over a string does the rest.

The commit passes allow_bases=True. Most letters of the alphabet are borrowed by automatic accented letters, and without the keyword the script would stop at A with a refusal. Chapter 55 said what the keyword agrees to, so save the font before you answer Yes.

Each row carries its layer, which is what exercise 2 of chapter 66 asked you to do. The script fetches every layer once, while planning, and change has nothing to look up.

shift_and_set(layer, 0, width) moves the drawing by nothing and sets the width. A right side is the width's business alone, as chapter 62 found.

The metricsRight test does what chapter 65 said it would. A layer whose right side follows a rule gets its value from the rule, and a script that wrote a number over it would be arguing with the font. On Plum no Bold layer has such a rule, and nothing is skipped.

And C goes down, from 26 to 23. The script doesn't only give. It sets each right side to its share of the Regular's, and two letters, C and G, had more than their share. All 52 changes together add 1,511 units to the alphabet. The W gains most, 85.

docs.title: Did it work?
docs.text:
Answer Yes, and run sb_report.py from chapter 61 on the word that started all this, in the Bold:

minimum
   109  104  109  104  105  112   smallest 104, spread 8

Last Monday that line read 60, 80, 78, 80, 66 and 92. After chapter 62's two repairs the smallest gap was 80 and the spread was 12. The Regular has 126 to 140 in the same places. The Bold's six gaps now rise and fall in step with the Regular's, at a little over four fifths of their size. That was the intention when somebody set its left sides.

Then the letters that follow. The accented letters still have their old widths, and the rule from chapter 63 says a composite is as wide as its base. In copy_sb.py, set both dictionaries to {} and run it. The first pass finds nothing to do. The second offers the Bold layers of the accented letters you built yourself in chapters 53, 56 and 60, where the base under them got wider, and makes them as wide as their bases. Plum's own accented letters are automatic, so the script names them on its last line and leaves them to FontLab. There are more than sixty of those layers. Look at one, the Bold aacute say, to see whether FontLab has made it as wide as the a. IJ and ij aren't accented letters and stay as they were. They've been on Mira's list since chapter 62, and they stay on it.

Two things today's script didn't touch, on purpose. The figures keep the width chapter 66 gave them. And the drawn letters outside the plain alphabet, germandbls, ae, oslash and their kind, aren't in LETTERS. The third exercise brings them in.

docs.title: What Ines thinks
docs.text:
She sets a caption in the new Bold at the catalog's size and holds it at arm's length. Better. For the smallest size she'd like a touch more, so Mira runs the script again with 0.85: 45 layers change, the n goes from 53 to 56 and the o from 30 to 32. She lets copy_sb.py bring the accents along and prints. They pin both proofs up. After a while Mira chooses Edit > Undo twice, once for the accents and once for the letters, and the font is back at 0.8. "The font is right at 0.8," she says. "Captions can be tracked in the layout. That's what tracking is for."

She crosses four lines off her own list.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Adding one amount to every sidebearing keeps every unevenness, and a script that adds can't be run twice safely. A script that reads one master and writes another gives the same result however often you run it. Multiplying by a decimal factor leaves a long tail, and round cuts it off and gives a whole number. Text from a field is text: float turns it into a number, and try with except ValueError catches what float can't read.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Make ask_factor accept 0,8. Chapter 30's replace can turn the comma into a point before float sees the text. Then type 0,8,5 and check that the person still gets the kind message.
  2. A factor of 8 is surely a slip for 0.8, and it would set the n to 528. Make ask_factor refuse anything below 0.5 or above 1.5, with a message that says what the limits are. Where does the test go: inside the try, or after it? Try both and say which reads better.
  3. Add "germandbls", "ae" and "oslash" to the letters. LETTERS is a string and can't hold a ten-letter name as one thing, so turn it into a list first: list(string.ascii_uppercase + string.ascii_lowercase) + ["germandbls", "ae", "oslash"]. Run the script and answer No. Which of the three would change most?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The sidebearings are in order: every letter has a left and a right that make sense on their own. Some pairs of letters still don't sit well together, and no sidebearing can mend that, because what suits A beside H is wrong for A beside V. Chapter 69 opens the list of exceptions the font keeps for such pairs: its kerning.

docs.title: 69. What kerning is
docs.text:
Thursday of week thirteen. The sidebearings are in order, and Mira wants to see what they can do on their own. She sets a headline from the catalog, AVOCADO TOAST, and switches the kerning off in the layout program.

She winces. Between the A and the V there's a hole you could park a bicycle in. Between the T and the O there's another. The letters C, A, D sit together like strangers on a bench.

Nothing is wrong with the sidebearings. A sidebearing is one number for one side of one letter, and it has to serve next to every neighbor the letter will ever have. The A leans away from the letter on its right. Next to an H, that's fine: the H stands straight and the space between them is an honest wedge. Next to a V, which leans the same way, the two slopes run side by side and the wedge becomes a channel.

No value for the A's right side can be right for both. So a font keeps a second list, of exceptions: for this letter followed by that one, move them this much closer, or this much further apart. That list is the font's kerning, and one line of it is a kerning pair.

Today you read the list. You change nothing.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The helper tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write it out again, so each one runs by itself.

I couldn't run today's code in FontLab 9. The pairs and values come from Plum's source file, and your font should print the same. The practice font's kerning hasn't been touched by any chapter so far.

docs.title: Step 1: What the sidebearings give
docs.text:
Start with the hole. The gap between two letters is the right side of the first plus the left side of the second, as in chapter 61:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

def gap(font, first, second, master):
    one = pGlyph(font, font[first])
    two = pGlyph(font, font[second])
    return one.getRSB(master) + two.getLSB(master)


font = fl.CurrentFont()
print(gap(font, "H", "H", "Regular"))
print(gap(font, "A", "V", "Regular"))

146
21

Read those two with care, because they seem to say the opposite of what Mira saw. Two Hs have 146 units between them, and A and V have 21, a seventh of that. And the AV is the pair that looks too open.

The number measures the wrong thing. A sidebearing runs from the edge of the letter's box to the outermost point of the drawing. For an H the outermost point is a stem, top to bottom, and 146 units is what you see. For an A the outermost point is the tip of a foot, down on the baseline. The V's is the tip of an arm, up at the cap height. Those two tips are 21 units apart, sideways. But one is at the bottom and the other at the top, and between them runs a white stripe as wide as the letters lean.

The eye judges the white area between two letters. It doesn't measure the nearest points. Stems make the two agree, which is why chapters 61 to 68 could work with plain numbers. Diagonals, overhangs and round shapes pull them apart, and those are the letters a kerning list is full of.

docs.title: Step 2: Read the list
docs.text:
The font keeps one kerning list for each master. kerning_pairs reads one of them:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

package = scripting.current_package()
pairs = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, "Regular")
print(len(pairs))

106

scripting.current_package() you've used since chapter 29, each time as the first half of an Undo step. Here it's the way in. Kerning belongs to the font as a whole and not to any glyph, so you ask the font's package for it.

106 pairs. That's a small list. A text face from a big foundry may carry several thousand. Plum is a display face with a short alphabet, and somebody kerned it by hand, pair by pair.

docs.title: Step 3: Ask for a pair
docs.text:
pairs is a dictionary. The value is a number of units. The key has to name two glyphs at once, and you know from chapter 64 what can and can't be a key: a list can't, and a tuple can. So the key is a tuple of two names:

print(pairs[("A", "V")])

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
KeyError: ('A', 'V')

That's today's mistake, and it's an instructive one. KeyError is chapter 21's complaint: no such key. Yet Mira saw with her own eyes that the font tightens AV when the kerning is on. The pair has to be there.

When a dictionary says a key is missing and you're sure it isn't, look at the keys it does have:

for pair in sorted(pairs)[:6]:
    print(pair)

('@L_A', '@R_C')
('@L_A', '@R_O2')
('@L_A', '@R_U2')
('@L_A', '@R_W2')
('@L_A', '@R_Y2')
('@L_A', '@R_wacute')

Tuples of two, as I said. sorted puts tuples in order by their first item and, among equals, by their second, and @ comes before the letters. But these aren't glyph names. Plum has no glyph called @L_A.

A name that starts with @ stands for a group of glyphs that kern alike. The font's makers called this one L_A, and from the name you can guess what's in it: the A, as the left-hand letter of a pair, and probably its accented forms. Such a group is a kerning class. One pair with a class in it does the work of many plain pairs. Chapter 71 opens the classes up. For today, treat @L_A as "the A and its relatives, standing first".

Now you can find the pair. Ask for every key whose second half is V:

print(sorted([pair for pair in pairs if pair[1] == "V"]))

[('@L_A', 'V'), ('L', 'V'), ('R', 'V')]

Three pairs end in V: one for the A family, one for L and one for R. pair[1] is the second item of the tuple, since a tuple is indexed like a list.

print(pairs[("@L_A", "V")])

-55.0

There it is. Negative means closer: when a V follows an A, the font moves the V 55 units to the left. The value is a decimal number, like a width, and for the same reason. FontLab stores its measurements that way.

So the real distance between the tips is 21 minus 55, which is −34. The foot of the A reaches 34 units under the arm of the V. On the page that looks right. The boxes overlap and the drawings don't touch.

docs.title: Step 4: Walk the whole list
docs.text:
A dictionary hands you key and value together through .items(), as in chapter 22. Here each key is itself a pair, and you can unpack it in the same line by putting it in parentheses:

for (first, second), value in sorted(pairs.items())[:4]:
    print(f"{first:<14}{second:<12}{value:>5.0f}")

@L_A          @R_C          -13
@L_A          @R_O2          -7
@L_A          @R_U2         -20
@L_A          @R_W2         -41

(first, second), value mirrors the shape of what comes out: a tuple of two, then a number. Leave the parentheses off and Python expects three things, finds two, and complains.

Alphabetical order is fine for looking something up, and it tells you little about the font. Order by value says more. Chapter 36's key function does that. Each item is a (pair, value) couple, so the value is item 1:

def by_value(item):
    return item[1]


for (first, second), value in sorted(pairs.items(), key=by_value)[:3]:
    print(first, second, value)

L T -113.0
quoteright @R_eacute -112.0
quoteright @R_oacute -112.0

The tightest pair in the Regular is LT, at 113 units. Think of the shapes: the L has an empty corner at top right and the T an empty corner at bottom left, and the two fit like a hand in a glove. Then come the apostrophe pairs, quoteright before a small round letter, as in l'eau.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: List Kerning
# Reports the kerning pairs of one master: how many, the tightest, the loosened.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTER = "Regular"
HOW_MANY = 8


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def by_value(item):
    return item[1]


def show(title, items):
    print(title)
    for (first, second), value in items:
        print(f"  {first:<14}{second:<12}{value:>5.0f}")


def busiest(pairs):
    tally = {}
    for first, second in pairs:
        tally[first] = tally.get(first, 0) + 1
    return sorted(tally.items(), key=by_value, reverse=True)


def main():
    package = scripting.current_package()
    if package is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    pairs = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, MASTER)
    if not pairs:
        print(f"No kerning in {MASTER}.")
        return

    ordered = sorted(pairs.items(), key=by_value)
    looser = [item for item in ordered if item[1] > 0]
    print(f"{len(pairs)} pairs in {MASTER}: {len(pairs) - len(looser)} tighten, {len(looser)} loosen.")
    show(f"The {HOW_MANY} tightest:", ordered[:HOW_MANY])
    show("Loosened:", looser)
    print("Most pairs begin with:")
    for first, count in busiest(pairs)[:3]:
        print(f"  {first:<14}{count:>3}")


main()

Save it as list_kerning.py. On Plum it prints:

106 pairs in Regular: 102 tighten, 4 loosen.
The 8 tightest:
  L             T            -113
  quoteright    @R_eacute    -112
  quoteright    @R_oacute    -112
  quoteright    c            -112
  quoteright    ccedilla     -112
  quoteright    d            -112
  quoteright    e            -112
  quoteright    g            -112
Loosened:
  questiondown  exclamdown     11
  r             @R_yacute      14
  r             y              14
  t             quoteright     14
Most pairs begin with:
  quoteright     25
  T              14
  @L_A           11

The order among the seven pairs at −112 may not be this one. sorted keeps equal items in the order it met them, and I can't tell you from here in which order FontLab hands the pairs over. If yours come out shuffled, the font is the same.

A few notes on the listing.

for first, second in pairs: loops over the dictionary itself, which gives the keys. Each key is a tuple of two, and the loop unpacks it. No parentheses are needed this time, because there's no value alongside.

by_value serves twice. An item from pairs.items() is (pair, value) and an item from tally.items() is (name, count). In both, item 1 is the number to sort by. The function doesn't care what item 0 is.

if not pairs: is the empty test of chapter 35. An empty dictionary counts as false, as an empty list does.

docs.title: Reading the report
docs.text:
102 tighten, 4 loosen. Kerning is nearly always a matter of closing holes. The four that open something up are worth knowing. r before y: the arm of the r and the arm of the y would touch. t before an apostrophe, as in don't: the same. And the two Spanish opening marks, ¿¡, which would otherwise sit too close.

Most pairs begin with quoteright. A quarter of the list is about the apostrophe. It's a small mark hung high in a wide box, with empty space under it, and every low letter that follows needs pulling in.

Then T and the A family. An overhang and a diagonal: the two kinds of shape from step 1.

Mira reads down the report with the headline in front of her. AV: there, −55. TO? She runs the search from step 3 with pair[0] == "T" and finds fourteen pairs, with a, e, o, u, w, y and some classes, and none with a capital O. She tries the classes: nothing named @R_O2 after T either. So the hole she saw between T and O isn't a pair that got switched off. It was never kerned.

"How do I know that for sure?" she asks. "I looked for ('A', 'V') and that wasn't there either, and it was kerned all along."

It's a fair question, and today's tools can't answer it. To say what the font does for a given pair of letters, you have to know which classes each letter belongs to and try every combination. FontLab has a call that does that, and it's tomorrow's first line.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A sidebearing has to serve every neighbor, and kerning is the list of exceptions for particular pairs. scripting.kerning_pairs(package, master) gives one master's pairs as a dictionary whose keys are tuples of two names and whose values are units, negative for closer. A tuple can be a key where a list can't, and for (first, second), value in pairs.items(): unpacks key and value in one line. A name starting with @ is a kerning class, a group that stands in for its members.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Change MASTER to "Light" and then to "Bold". You should get 100 pairs and 102. Then print the pairs that begin with @L_A in each of the two, side by side. Ten of the eleven values are the same. A Bold and a Light don't want the same kerning. What does that suggest about how the Bold's list was made?
  2. Write a loop that prints every pair whose first half is T, with its value, tightest first. There are fourteen. Which is tighter in the Regular: T before a, or T before @R_aacute? Keep your answer for chapter 71.
  3. Yesterday you gave the Bold A a right side of 9 where it had −33. Every Bold pair that begins with the A family was made for the old value. Print them. How many are there, and what would you have to do to each value to put the letters back where they stood on Tuesday? Don't do it. Chapter 79 comes back to this.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Mira's question stands: what does the font do for T and O, or for T and ó, when the pair you look up isn't in the list under that name? Chapter 70 asks FontLab for the value that applies, and puts it next to the value that's written down.

docs.title: 70. Look up a pair
docs.text:
Friday of week thirteen. Ines is laying out the drinks page of the catalog and calls across the room: "What's T o at the moment?"

It's the kind of question a studio asks ten times a day, and it deserves an answer in ten seconds. Yesterday's report can't give one. It reports on a hundred pairs and leaves the looking to you. And Mira's own question from yesterday is still open: she looked for A and V, got a KeyError, and the pair was kerned all along, under another name.

Today's script takes two glyph names and says what the font does with them, in every master, and where the value comes from.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The helpers ask_text and tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write them out again, so each one runs by itself.

Nothing is changed today. I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The values come from Plum's source file, with the classes worked out by hand, so today's outputs lean on one assumption: that FontLab looks a pair up the way step 2 describes: the two glyphs first, then their classes.

docs.title: Step 1: A quiet wrong answer
docs.text:
Yesterday's KeyError was at least honest. Chapter 22 showed a way around it: get, with a value to hand back when the key is missing.

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

package = scripting.current_package()
pairs = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, "Regular")
print(pairs.get(("T", "o"), 0))
print(pairs.get(("A", "V"), 0))

-84.0
0

That's today's mistake, and there's no traceback to warn you. The first answer is right. The second is wrong: AV is kerned by 55 units, as you found yesterday. The dictionary holds that pair under ("@L_A", "V"), so the lookup under ("A", "V") misses, and get covers the miss with a polite 0.

A script built on that line would tell Ines that AV isn't kerned. She'd believe it, because 0 looks like an answer.

The default in get is a fine tool when a missing key truly means nothing, as in chapter 22's tally: a letter you haven't counted yet has a count of 0. Here a missing key means "not written under these two names", which is a different thing from "no kerning". When a miss and a zero mean different things, don't let get paint one over the other. Leave the default off:

print(pairs.get(("A", "V")))

None

get with no second value hands back None for a miss. Now the miss is visible, and it can't be mistaken for a number.

docs.title: Step 2: Ask the font what applies
docs.text:
The dictionary from kerning_pairs is a copy of what's written down. FontLab itself keeps the list in its own form, and that one knows about the classes. You reach it through the package:

kerning = package.kerning("Regular")
print(scripting.kerning_pair_value(kerning, "A", "V"))
print(scripting.kerning_pair_value(kerning, "Aacute", "V"))
print(scripting.kerning_pair_value(kerning, "T", "O"))

-55.0
-55.0
0

package.kerning("Regular") is the Regular's kerning as FontLab holds it. kerning_pair_value asks it one question: when this glyph is followed by that one, how far does the second move? FontLab looks for a pair written for the two glyphs themselves. If there's none, it tries the classes they belong to. If nothing fits, the answer is 0.

So A before V gives −55, through the class @L_A. Aacute before V gives the same, because Á is in that class too. Nobody ever wrote a pair for Á and V, and the font has one anyway. That's what classes are for.

And T before O gives 0. This time the zero can be trusted. It doesn't come from a missing key. It comes from FontLab, after it tried every way of reading the pair. Mira's hole between T and O was never kerned, and now she knows it for sure.

You now have two answers for every pair, and they're both worth having:

  • what's written, from pairs.get((first, second)): a number, or None;
  • what applies, from kerning_pair_value: always a number.

docs.title: Step 3: Put the two together
docs.text:
Three cases can come out, and each one tells you where to go if you want to change the value:

def source(written, applies):
    if written is not None:
        return "its own pair"
    if applies != 0:
        return "through a class"
    return "not kerned"


for first, second in [("T", "o"), ("A", "V"), ("T", "O")]:
    written = pairs.get((first, second))
    applies = scripting.kerning_pair_value(kerning, first, second)
    print(first, second, applies, source(written, applies))

T o -84.0 its own pair
A V -55.0 through a class
T O 0 not kerned

The order of the two tests matters. A pair that's written gets the first answer, even if its value is 0, because somebody can write a zero on purpose: "this pair gets nothing, whatever its class says". The test is is not None, and not if written:, for that very reason. An if treats the number 0 as false, the way it treats None. A written zero would slip through if written: and be reported as not written.

One honest gap: if a class pair itself has the value 0, source calls it "not kerned". On Plum there is no such pair, and the next chapter gives you the means to tell the two apart.

docs.title: Step 4: Names from a text field
docs.text:
The script should ask which glyphs you mean. ask_text gives back one piece of text, and you need two names, or more. Chapter 9 split a name at its dots with split("."). With nothing in the parentheses, split cuts at every run of spaces:

print("T o".split())
print("  T   oacute n i c a ".split())

['T', 'o']
['T', 'oacute', 'n', 'i', 'c', 'a']

Extra spaces at the ends or in the middle do no harm. That's a kindness to whoever types.

These are glyph names, not letters. Mira types T ó the first time, and the script has to say something better than a traceback, because the font has no glyph called ó. Its name is oacute. So check every name before asking the font anything:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
names = "T ó".split()
unknown = [name for name in names if font[name] is None]
print(unknown)

['ó']

With more than two names you get a chain: each glyph with the one after it. Chapter 61 did that with zip(word, word[1:]), and it works the same on a list of names.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Pair Value
# Says what kerning applies between the glyphs you name, in every master.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box, run_text_dialog

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask_text(label, start=""):
    return run_text_dialog(qt.QtGui, label, start, TITLE)


def source(written, applies):
    if written is not None:
        return "its own pair"
    if applies != 0:
        return "through a class"
    return "not kerned"


def look(package, master, first, second):
    pairs = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, master)
    kerning = package.kerning(master)
    written = pairs.get((first, second))
    applies = scripting.kerning_pair_value(kerning, first, second)
    return applies, source(written, applies)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    text = ask_text("Glyph names, with spaces between:", "T o")
    if text is None:
        return
    names = text.split()
    unknown = [name for name in names if font[name] is None]
    if unknown:
        tell(f"No glyph named {', '.join(unknown)}. Use glyph names, as in oacute.")
        return
    if len(names) < 2:
        tell("I need at least two glyph names.")
        return

    package = scripting.current_package()
    for first, second in zip(names, names[1:]):
        print(first, second)
        for master in MASTERS:
            applies, where = look(package, master, first, second)
            print(f"  {master:<9}{applies:>5.0f}   {where}")


main()

Save it as pair_value.py. Run it and click OK on the T o that's already in the field:

T o
  Light      -55   its own pair
  Regular    -84   its own pair
  Bold      -108   its own pair

"Minus 84 in the Regular," Mira calls back. Ten seconds.

Two notes on the listing.

look returns two things, as plan did in chapter 62, and the loop unpacks them into applies and where. It reads the pairs afresh for every pair and master. For a handful of names that costs nothing you'd notice, and it keeps the function whole: give it a master and two names, and it needs nothing else.

{applies:>5.0f} prints the value without its .0. It also takes the plain 0 that comes back when nothing applies, so "not kerned" lines up with the rest.

docs.title: What Ines was really asking
docs.text:
Ines's headline isn't To. It's the name of a drink, Tónica. Mira runs the script again and types T oacute:

T oacute
  Light      -56   through a class
  Regular    -45   through a class
  Bold       -43   through a class

Look at the Regular. Before a plain o the T pulls in by 84. Before ó it pulls in by 45, hardly more than half. Mira's first thought is that it's a slip. Then she looks at the shapes. The bar of the T hangs over the o, and that's why the pair can be so tight. An acute accent stands where the bar wants to be. Pull the ó in by 84 and the accent runs into the bar. Somebody saw that and wrote a looser value for the whole accented family: one class pair, T before @R_oacute, and every accented o is covered.

So o and ó kern differently after T, on purpose, and the names in yesterday's list say how. ("T", "o") is a pair for the plain letter. ("T", "@R_oacute") is a pair for the class. The plain o isn't in that class at all.

The Light tells another story: −55 for o and −56 for ó, as good as equal. Maybe the Light's thin accent clears the bar. Maybe nobody got round to it. The list can't say which, and neither can I. Mira adds a line to her notes: "Light: T before accents, same as plain. Meant?" It's a question for Oskar.

There's a second route to the same glyph, worth knowing if you'd rather type letters than names: chapter 24 found a glyph by its character. I've kept today's script to names, because half of what gets kerned, the small capitals and the alternates, has no character of its own.

Then she types the whole word, T oacute n i c a, and gets five pairs. Only the first is kerned. The other four say "not kerned" in all three masters, and they need nothing: n, i, c and a have stems and bowls, and the sidebearings of chapters 61 to 68 look after those.

docs.title: Why three masters disagree
docs.text:
One more thing shows in both outputs, and it'll matter for the rest of this part. Each master has its own list. The Regular's T o is −84 and the Bold's is −108, and no rule ties them together. When FontLab makes a weight between two masters, it blends their values for the pair, as it blends their outlines. As far as I know, a pair that's written in one master and absent from the next counts as 0 there, and the blend runs from the value to nothing. I haven't tested that in FontLab 9. That's why a kerning script always says which master it means, and why today's prints all three.

It also means yesterday's count of 106 was one master's truth. The Light has 100 pairs and the Bold 102. Six pairs are in the Regular and not in the Light, and four of them are missing from the Bold too.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: get with a default hides a missing key, and get without one hands back None, which can't be mistaken for a value. A font has two answers for a pair: what's written under those two names, and what applies once the classes are counted. scripting.kerning_pair_value(kerning, first, second) asks package.kerning(master) what applies, with 0 for nothing. Test with is not None when 0 is a real value.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Run the script on T a and on T aacute. In which master is the difference between the plain and the accented letter biggest? Then try V a and V aacute. Why might the V need no such difference? Look at where its overhang is.
  2. Add a fourth case to source. When a pair is written and a class pair would give a different value, the written one wins. You can't see the class value yet, so settle for less: when written is not None and differs from applies, return "written, but something else applies". On a sound font that line never prints. Run T o and make sure it doesn't.
  3. Make the script print one more line at the end: how many units the kerning takes out of the whole run in the Regular. Add up applies over all the pairs, with a total that starts at 0, as in chapter 11. For T oacute n i c a you should get −45, and for A V O C A D O, −55.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: "Through a class" is as much as today's script can say. Which class? Who's in it? Why is o outside @R_oacute when ó is in? Chapter 71 opens the font's kerning classes and prints every one with its members.

docs.title: 71. Kerning classes
docs.text:
Monday of week fourteen. The publisher has sent a title from the Czech edition: Těšín, the name of a town. Mira sets it in the practice font, with the ě that chapter 60 built, and something is off at the very start. The ě stands away from the T as if it belonged to the next word.

She runs Friday's pair_value.py twice, once on T eacute and once on T ecaron:

T eacute
  Light      -61   through a class
  Regular    -52   through a class
  Bold       -36   through a class
T ecaron
  Light        0   not kerned
  Regular      0   not kerned
  Bold         0   not kerned

The é is pulled in under the bar of the T. The ě isn't. They're the same letter with different hats. "Through a class" is all Friday's script could say, so today you open the classes and read who's in them.

docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The helper tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write it out again, so each one runs by itself.
  • The Uring and uring from chapter 56 and the ecaron from chapter 60. If you skipped those chapters, the last part of today's report will be empty, and the rest holds.

Nothing is changed today. I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The classes and their members come from Plum's source file.

docs.title: Step 1: Read the classes
docs.text:
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

package = scripting.current_package()
classes = scripting.kerning_classes(package, "Regular")
print(len(classes))
print(sorted(classes))

17
['L_A', 'L_O', 'L_U', 'L_W', 'L_Y', 'R_A2', 'R_C', 'R_O2', 'R_U2', 'R_W2', 'R_Y2', 'R_aacute', 'R_eacute', 'R_oacute', 'R_uacute', 'R_wacute', 'R_yacute']

Seventeen classes, in a dictionary with their names as keys. sorted on a dictionary gives its keys in order, as it did with the pairs. The names carry no @ here. The @ is a mark the pair list puts in front, to tell a class from a glyph of the same name.

Like the pairs, the classes are kept for each master, which is why the call wants a master's name. In Plum the three masters hold the same seventeen. The first exercise checks that.

Now look at one:

print(classes["L_A"])

(['A', 'Aacute', 'Abreve', 'Acircumflex', 'Adieresis', 'Agrave', 'Aring', 'Atilde'], 'left')

Round brackets outside, square brackets inside. The value is a tuple of two things: a list of glyph names, and a word. The list is the membership. The word says in which place of a pair the class may stand.

docs.title: Step 2: A wrong answer with no complaint
docs.text:
Is Aacute in the class? You can see that it is. Ask Python:

print("Aacute" in classes["L_A"])

False

That's today's mistake. No error, and an answer that contradicts the line above it.

in asks whether something is one of the items of a collection. classes["L_A"] is the tuple, and the tuple has two items: a list and the word 'left'. Is "Aacute" one of those two? No. It's inside the first of them, and in doesn't look inside. It compares with each item as a whole.

Take the tuple apart first, and ask the list:

members, side = classes["L_A"]
print("Aacute" in members, side)

True left

When a value is a tuple, unpack it into names as soon as you get it. members and side say what they are. classes["L_A"][0] would work too, and a month from now it would tell you nothing.

docs.title: Step 3: Which side is which
docs.text:
'left' is a word to be careful with. It doesn't mean the left side of the letter. It means the letter stands on the left in the pair, which is to say first. A class marked left gathers glyphs that look alike on their right-hand edge, the edge that meets the next letter. L_A holds the A and its accented forms because all eight end with the same diagonal.

A class marked right is for the second place in a pair, and its members look alike on their left-hand edge. There's a third word, both, for a class that may stand in either place. Plum has none of those.

To keep my own head straight, I'll say first and second from here on, and the script will too.

Walk through all seventeen. Each value is a tuple, so the loop can unpack it in parentheses, as chapter 69 did with the keys:

for name, (members, side) in sorted(classes.items()):
    print(name, side, len(members))

L_A left 8
L_O left 7
L_U left 5
L_W left 5
L_Y left 5
R_A2 right 8
R_C right 2
R_O2 right 7
R_U2 right 5
R_W2 right 5
R_Y2 right 5
R_aacute right 7
R_eacute right 4
R_oacute right 6
R_uacute right 4
R_wacute right 4
R_yacute right 4

Whoever made Plum named the classes for their side, L_ and R_. That was a courtesy. Nothing in FontLab requires it, and you shouldn't rely on the name: the word in the tuple is what counts.

Five classes for the first place and twelve for the second. All five of the first kind are capitals with their accents. The lowercase letters have classes for the second place only, because that's where Plum's kerning needs them: after T, V, W, Y and the apostrophe, among others.

docs.title: Step 4: Turn it round
docs.text:
The dictionary answers "who's in this class?" Mira's question runs the other way: "which class is this glyph in?" Chapter 64 turned a dictionary of lists round with a loop inside a loop, and the same works here:

def class_of(classes, wanted):
    found = {}
    for name, (members, side) in classes.items():
        if side in [wanted, "both"]:
            for glyph in members:
                found[glyph] = name
    return found


second = class_of(classes, "right")
print(second.get("eacute"), second.get("ecaron"), second.get("e"))

R_eacute None None

get without a default, as on Friday, so that a glyph in no class shows as None.

There's the answer to this morning's puzzle. eacute is in R_eacute, and the pair T before @R_eacute covers it. ecaron is in no class. It didn't exist when the classes were made. Chapter 60 built it and never told the kerning.

The plain e is in no class either, and that one is on purpose. Friday showed why: after a T, the plain letter takes a tighter value than the accented ones, so it has a pair of its own and stays out of the family.

Two glyphs outside the class, then, one by design and one by oversight, and None for both. The dictionary can't tell them apart. For that you need to know something about the glyphs themselves.

docs.title: Step 5: Who ought to be in
docs.text:
Here's a rule that separates the two cases. The members of R_eacute are all built the same way: an e with an accent on top, as components. A glyph that's built on that base letter with an accent, and isn't a member, was probably forgotten. The plain e isn't built on anything, so the rule leaves it alone.

Chapter 52 read a glyph's components, and chapter 63 used them to find accented letters. The base is the first component:

from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph


def base_letter(font, name):
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    found = parts.components(layer_of(rich.fl, MASTER))
    if len(found) < 2 or rich.contours(MASTER):
        return None
    return parts.base_of(found[0])

A glyph with fewer than two components, or with a drawing of its own, has no base letter in this sense, and the function says None.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: List Kerning Classes
# Prints the kerning classes of one master and the accented letters
# that were left out of the class their relatives are in.
import fly.ap.components.writer as parts
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTER = "Regular"
PLACE = {"left": "first", "right": "second", "both": "either"}


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def base_letter(font, name):
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    found = parts.components(layer_of(rich.fl, MASTER))
    if len(found) < 2 or rich.contours(MASTER):
        return None
    return parts.base_of(found[0])


def show(classes, wanted):
    print(f"{PLACE[wanted].capitalize()} in a pair:")
    for name, (members, side) in sorted(classes.items()):
        if side == wanted:
            print(f"  {name:<10}{len(members):>2}  {' '.join(sorted(members))}")


def left_out(font, classes):
    bases = {}
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        base = base_letter(font, glyph.name)
        if base is not None:
            bases[glyph.name] = base
    rows = []
    for name, (members, side) in sorted(classes.items()):
        family = set([bases[member] for member in members if member in bases])
        for glyph_name in sorted(bases):
            if bases[glyph_name] in family and glyph_name not in members:
                rows.append((glyph_name, name, PLACE[side]))
    return rows


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    classes = scripting.kerning_classes(package, MASTER)
    if not classes:
        print(f"No kerning classes in {MASTER}.")
        return

    print(f"{len(classes)} classes in {MASTER}.")
    for wanted in ["left", "right", "both"]:
        show(classes, wanted)
    rows = left_out(font, classes)
    print(f"{len(rows)} left out:")
    for glyph_name, name, place in rows:
        print(f"  {glyph_name:<12}is built like the members of {name} ({place})")


main()

Save it as list_kern_classes.py. On the practice font it prints:

First in a pair:

  L_O        7  O Oacute Ocircumflex Odieresis Ograve Oslash Otilde
  L_U        5  U Uacute Ucircumflex Udieresis Ugrave
  L_W        5  W Wacute Wcircumflex Wdieresis Wgrave
  L_Y        5  Y Yacute Ycircumflex Ydieresis Ygrave
Second in a pair:
  R_A2       8  A Aacute Abreve Acircumflex Adieresis Agrave Aring Atilde
  R_C        2  C Ccedilla
  R_O2       7  O Oacute Ocircumflex Odieresis Ograve Oslash Otilde
  R_U2       5  U Uacute Ucircumflex Udieresis Ugrave
  R_W2       5  W Wacute Wcircumflex Wdieresis Wgrave
  R_Y2       5  Y Yacute Ycircumflex Ydieresis Ygrave
  R_aacute   7  aacute abreve acircumflex adieresis agrave aring atilde
  R_eacute   4  eacute ecircumflex edieresis egrave
  R_oacute   6  oacute ocircumflex odieresis ograve oslash otilde
  R_uacute   4  uacute ucircumflex udieresis ugrave
  R_wacute   4  wacute wcircumflex wdieresis wgrave
  R_yacute   4  yacute ycircumflex ydieresis ygrave
Either in a pair:
0 left out:

Wait for the last line. I've printed what the shipped font gives, and yours should end differently if you built the letters of chapters 56 and 60:

Either in a pair:
4 left out:
  Uring       is built like the members of L_U (first)
  Uring       is built like the members of R_U2 (second)
  ecaron      is built like the members of R_eacute (second)
  uring       is built like the members of R_uacute (second)

Uring is there twice because the capital U has a class for each place.

Notes on the listing.

PLACE is a small dictionary that translates FontLab's three words into mine. It's used twice, once for the headings and once for the last column, and if you'd rather keep left and right, it's one line to change.

capitalize is new. It gives back a text with its first letter made a capital, so "first".capitalize() is First. It saves writing the three headings out.

left_out first builds a dictionary, bases, from every accented composite to its base letter: eacute to e, ecaron to e, Aring to A. Then, for each class, it collects the base letters of the members into a set, the class's family. For R_eacute that set is {"e"}. Any composite whose base is in the family and whose name isn't among the members goes on the list.

The [... if member in bases] part skips members that aren't composites, such as the plain A in L_A and the Oslash, which is a drawing of its own. They belong to their class and say nothing about its family.

docs.title: Reading the report
docs.text:
Three things stand out.

The capitals have the plain letter in the class, and the lowercase don't. R_A2 starts with A, and R_aacute has no a. A capital's accent sits above the cap height, clear of every neighbor, so Á kerns like A. A lowercase accent sits right where the bar of a T or the arm of a V wants to go. That's Friday's finding, written into the structure of the classes.

Thirty glyphs are in two classes. The A and its seven relatives are in L_A and in R_A2. That isn't a conflict. One class speaks for them when they come first and the other when they come second. What a glyph can't be is in two classes for the same place, because then FontLab would have two answers to one question.

Three glyphs were left out, as far as this rule can see. They are the ecaron of chapter 60 and the Uring and uring of chapter 56. The other letters from those chapters are built on D, E, N, R, S, T, Z and small letters that have no class in Plum, so there's nothing for them to be left out of. The rule has a blind spot, though. R_C holds C and Ccedilla, and in Plum the Ç is drawn in one piece. Neither member is a composite, so the class has no family the rule can read, and your Cacute and Ccaron pass unnoticed. They very likely belong there. A check that reads how glyphs are built can only find what was built that way.

Mira reads the ecaron line twice. "So I add ecaron to that list and Těšín is mended?"

Yes. One name added to one class, and every pair that has @R_eacute in it covers the new letter: after T, V and P, after the W and Y classes, after the apostrophe. That's six pairs in each master that nobody has to write. It's also a change to the font, and the first one this part makes to the kerning. It gets its own chapter, tomorrow.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A kerning class is a named list of glyphs that kern alike in one place of a pair. scripting.kerning_classes(package, master) gives them as a dictionary: the class name is the key, and the value is a tuple of the member list and a word, left for first in a pair, right for second, both for either. in looks at the items of a collection and not inside them, so unpack the tuple first, as for name, (members, side) in classes.items(): does. A glyph made after the classes were set up belongs to none until somebody adds it.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Read the classes of the Light and the Bold into two more dictionaries and compare each with the Regular's using ==. Two dictionaries are equal when they have the same keys with equal values. You should get True twice. What would it mean for an interpolated weight if one master's R_eacute had five members and another's four?
  2. Use class_of(classes, "left") and class_of(classes, "right") to print, for one glyph name you type into the script, its class when first and its class when second. Try Oslash, oslash, T and ecaron.
  3. class_of writes found[glyph] = name without looking. If a glyph were in two classes for the same place, the later one would win and you'd never know. Add a test that prints a warning when glyph is already in found. On Plum it stays silent. Why is this the mistake of chapter 63 again?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The report found three letters outside their families. Chapter 72 puts them in, and then turns the idea round: a script that proposes classes from the way the glyphs are built, the capital C and its relatives among them.

docs.title: 72. Make a class
docs.text:
Tuesday of week fourteen. Yesterday's report ended with three names: ecaron, built like the members of R_eacute and not among them, and Uring and uring, missing from the classes of the U and the u. Mira could open the Classes panel and drag the glyphs in. For one glyph in one class that's the right tool.

But it's three glyphs in three masters, and yesterday also turned up Cacute and Ccaron, which the report couldn't see. And the Polish edition is waiting for four letters with an ogonek that aren't drawn yet. Each time letters arrive, somebody has to remember the classes. So today's script holds the rule and applies it: every accented letter built on this base belongs in that class.

It's the first script of this part that changes the kerning.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The helpers ask and tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write them out again, so each one runs by itself.
  • The accented letters of chapters 56 and 60. Without them the script finds nothing to add.
  • A saved copy of the font from before today.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The way the classes are written is copied from one of Fly's own tools, which does the same job, and I haven't seen it work from a script of mine. Read the note before the listing.

docs.title: Step 1: A rule that catches too much
docs.text:
Which glyphs belong with the e? A first idea: the ones whose names start with e. Chapter 9 gave you startswith:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
print(sorted([glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs if glyph.name.startswith("e")]))

['e', 'eacute', 'ecaron', 'ecircumflex', 'edieresis', 'egrave', 'eight', 'ellipsis', 'emdash', 'endash', 'equal', 'exclam', 'exclamdown']

Your list may differ by a name or two, depending on which exercises you did. The trouble is the same: eight, ellipsis, two dashes, the equals sign and two exclamation marks. Put that list into a kerning class and an em dash after a T would be pulled in by 52 units, like an é.

That's today's mistake. A name is a label somebody chose, and a rule that reads labels finds whatever the labels happen to share. You could patch it: names that start with e and end with an accent's name. Then eogonek arrives, with its accent underneath, and the patch needs a patch.

Yesterday's rule read the glyph and not its label: a glyph belongs with the e when it's built from an e and an accent, as components. Take base_letter from yesterday, with the master as a third parameter this time, and build the list with it:

def built_on(font, base, master):
    return sorted([glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs if base_letter(font, glyph.name, master) == base])


print(built_on(font, "e", "Regular"))
print(built_on(font, "C", "Regular"))
print(built_on(font, "T", "Regular"))

['eacute', 'ecaron', 'ecircumflex', 'edieresis', 'egrave']
['Cacute', 'Ccaron']
['Tcaron']

No figures, no dashes. The rule is a comprehension with a condition, as in chapter 37, and the condition is a question put to each glyph.

docs.title: Step 2: A new list, and the old one kept
docs.text:
The class has four members. The rule gives five names. The plan is the old members, in their old order, with the newcomers after them:

old = ["eacute", "ecircumflex", "edieresis", "egrave"]
added = [name for name in built_on(font, "e", "Regular") if name not in old]
new = old + added
print(added)
print(new)
print(old)

['ecaron']
['eacute', 'ecircumflex', 'edieresis', 'egrave', 'ecaron']
['eacute', 'ecircumflex', 'edieresis', 'egrave']

+ between two lists makes a third list, with the items of the first and then the items of the second. Neither of the two is touched, and the last line shows it: old still has four names.

I'm making a point of that because append behaves differently. old.append("ecaron") would change old itself. Then there'd be no "before" left to compare with, and the script couldn't say what it's about to do. A script that changes a font should always be able to show the old state beside the new one.

Why keep the old order? Because FontLab keeps no separate "main glyph" for a class. By custom the first member stands for the whole class, in panels and in other people's scripts. Sort these lists and the first member stays first, by luck. A class led by n that also held h and m would come out of a sort with h in front.

docs.title: Step 3: A class that isn't there yet
docs.text:
Tcaron has no class to join. The T has fourteen pairs in each master, all written for the glyph T itself, and the Ť shares none of them. The cure is a class for the first place in a pair, with T and Ť in it. Call it L_T, after Plum's own habit.

For the plan, a class that doesn't exist is a class with no members. On Friday I warned you off get with a default, because there a missing key and a zero meant different things. Here they mean the same, and the default is the right tool:

classes = scripting.kerning_classes(package, "Regular")
old, old_side = classes.get("L_T", ([], "left"))
print(old, old_side)

[] left

The default has to have the shape of a real value: a tuple of a list and a word, so that it unpacks like one. A new class starts from the base letter itself, and then the rule adds the rest:

start = old if old else ["T"]

An empty list counts as false, so start is the old members when there are any and ["T"] when there are none.

docs.title: Step 4: The rules as data
docs.text:
Each class has a place in the pair and a base letter. That's a dictionary, and with yesterday's three classes for the U and the u it has six entries:

RULES = {
    "R_eacute": ("right", "e"),
    "R_C": ("right", "C"),
    "L_T": ("left", "T"),
    "L_U": ("left", "U"),
    "R_U2": ("right", "U"),
    "R_uacute": ("right", "u"),
}

When the ogonek letters come, eogonek is built on e and the first rule picks it up. Whether it should be picked up is a fair question: its accent hangs below and never meets the bar of a T, so it might kern better with the plain e. The script prints its plan and asks before it writes. The script lists what the rule would add, and you read the list before it writes.

docs.title: How the writing works
docs.text:
The reading went through scripting.kerning_classes. For the writing there's no ready-made function, so the script does what Fly's own tool for building accented letters does when it adds its new glyphs to their classes.

The classes of one master live at package.kerning(master).groups. That object takes a class name in square brackets, like a dictionary, and you assign a tuple to it:

package.kerning("Regular").groups["R_eacute"] = (new, "KernRight")

The list is the membership. The word is FontLab's own name for the place: KernLeft for first, KernRight for second, KernBothSide for either. Yesterday's left and right were Fly's shorter spellings of the same three. Assigning to a name that exists replaces the class, and assigning to a new name creates it.

That line alone would leave no step in the Edit menu. So it goes inside history.commit, as every change since chapter 62 has, with three differences. The operation is "metadata", because no outline moves. Two lines at the start of the change tell the package and its kerning to note their state, so that Undo has something to go back to. And retain hands commit the three objects that hold kerning. I'm passing those on as I found them. If your FontLab refuses the commit, nothing has been written, and the Classes panel will do the job by hand.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Build Kerning Classes
# Adds accented letters to the kerning class their base letter stands for,
# in every master, and makes the class if the font has none.
import fly.ap.components.writer as parts
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
NATIVE = {"left": "KernLeft", "right": "KernRight"}
PLACE = {"left": "first", "right": "second"}
# class name: (place in the pair, base letter whose accented forms belong)
RULES = {
    "R_eacute": ("right", "e"),
    "R_C": ("right", "C"),
    "L_T": ("left", "T"),
    "L_U": ("left", "U"),
    "R_U2": ("right", "U"),
    "R_uacute": ("right", "u"),
}


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def base_letter(font, name, master):
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    found = parts.components(layer_of(rich.fl, master))
    if len(found) < 2 or rich.contours(master):
        return None
    return parts.base_of(found[0])


def built_on(font, base, master):
    return sorted([glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs if base_letter(font, glyph.name, master) == base])


def plan(font, package, master):
    classes = scripting.kerning_classes(package, master)
    rows = []
    for name, (side, base) in RULES.items():
        old, old_side = classes.get(name, ([], side))
        if old_side != side:
            print(f"{master} {name}: is a class for the {old_side}, not the {side}. Left alone.")
            continue
        start = old if old else [base]
        new = start + [found for found in built_on(font, base, master) if found not in start]
        if new != old:
            rows.append((master, name, side, old, new))
    return rows


def write(font, package, rows):
    layers = []
    owners = {}
    for master, name, side, old, new in rows:
        for glyph_name in new:
            if glyph_name not in old:
                rich = pGlyph(font, font[glyph_name])
                layers.append(layer_of(rich.fl, master))
                owners[glyph_name] = rich.fl
    container = package.kerningContainer()

    def change():
        package.checkInitHistoryState(0)
        container.checkInitHistoryState(0)
        for master, name, side, old, new in rows:
            package.kerning(master).groups[name] = (new, NATIVE[side])

    history.commit(
        "Build kerning classes",
        layers,
        list(owners.values()),
        change,
        operation="metadata",
        facts=history.scan_auto_facts(package),
        retain=[package, package.mastersContainer(), container],
    )


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    rows = []
    for master in MASTERS:
        rows = rows + plan(font, package, master)
    for master, name, side, old, new in rows:
        added = " ".join([glyph_name for glyph_name in new if glyph_name not in old])
        print(f"{master:<9}{name:<10}{PLACE[side]:<8}{len(old)} to {len(new)}   + {added}")
    print(f"{len(rows)} classes to write.")
    if not rows or not ask(f"Write {len(rows)} kerning classes?"):
        return
    write(font, package, rows)
    still = []
    for master in MASTERS:
        still = still + plan(font, package, master)
    print(f"Done. {len(still)} classes still to write.")


main()

Save it as build_kern_classes.py. On the practice font, with the letters of chapters 56 and 60 in it, the plan reads:

Light    R_eacute  second  4 to 5   + ecaron
Light    R_C       second  2 to 4   + Cacute Ccaron
Light    L_T       first   0 to 2   + T Tcaron
Light    L_U       first   5 to 6   + Uring
Light    R_U2      second  5 to 6   + Uring
Light    R_uacute  second  4 to 5   + uring
Regular  R_eacute  second  4 to 5   + ecaron
Regular  R_C       second  2 to 4   + Cacute Ccaron
Regular  L_T       first   0 to 2   + T Tcaron
Regular  L_U       first   5 to 6   + Uring
Regular  R_U2      second  5 to 6   + Uring
Regular  R_uacute  second  4 to 5   + uring
Bold     R_eacute  second  4 to 5   + ecaron
Bold     R_C       second  2 to 4   + Cacute Ccaron
Bold     L_T       first   0 to 2   + T Tcaron
Bold     L_U       first   5 to 6   + Uring
Bold     R_U2      second  5 to 6   + Uring
Bold     R_uacute  second  4 to 5   + uring
18 classes to write.

Then it asks. Click Yes, and it should end with:

Done. 0 classes still to write.

Notes on the listing.

plan works on one master and main adds the three plans together with +, the same joining of lists as in step 2. Classes are kept for each master, and a class that's in one master and missing from the next is trouble for every weight in between. So the script never writes to one master alone.

The old_side != side test guards against a rule that names an existing class for the wrong place. Writing "R_eacute": ("left", "e") by a slip would otherwise turn a second-place class into a first-place one, and every pair that names it would stop making sense.

write gathers the layers of the glyphs that join a class, and their glyphs, because commit wants to know what the change touches. owners is a dictionary so that a glyph that joins in three masters is listed once, as in chapter 65.

The last three lines of main plan again after writing. If the change went in, there's nothing left to plan. It's the same check as "0 layers still off" in chapter 68, and it's the only sign the script has that the font took the change.

docs.title: Did it work?
docs.text:
Don't take the script's word. Ask the font, with the tools of the last two days.

Run list_kern_classes.py. It should count 18 classes where it counted 17, show L_T under "First in a pair", and end with 0 left out:.

Then run pair_value.py on T ecaron:

T ecaron
  Light      -61   through a class
  Regular    -52   through a class
  Bold       -36   through a class

The same three numbers as T eacute yesterday morning. Nobody wrote a pair. The pair for T before @R_eacute was there all along, and the letter has joined the family it speaks for. A Cacute should now give −32, −13 and −32, from the one pair that names @R_C.

Mira sets Těšín again and the ě sits under the bar. Then she tries Ťo, with the script's Tcaron o, and gets "not kerned" three times.

That's as it should be, and it's worth a minute. L_T is a class with no pairs. All fourteen pairs of the T are still written for the glyph T, and a class without pairs changes nothing in the font. It's a name waiting to be used. Today's whole change, the new class included, should be one step in Edit > Undo. I haven't seen it in FontLab 9.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A rule that reads how a glyph is built is safer than one that reads its name. old + added makes a new list and leaves both of its parts alone, where append changes the list it's called on. The classes of a master are at package.kerning(master).groups, and assigning (members, "KernLeft") or (members, "KernRight") to a name replaces or creates a class. Write classes in every master at once, keep the first member first, and remember that a class does nothing until a pair names it.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a rule for a class L_S, first in a pair, on the base S. Run the script and read the plan before you click. Which glyphs does it propose? One of them wasn't built by you. Click No if you'd rather not keep it.
  2. The plan prints eighteen lines for six classes, because the masters agree. Change the printing so that a class whose plan is the same in all three masters gets one line that starts with all. A dictionary from (name, tuple(new)) to a list of masters will do it. Why tuple(new) and not new? Chapter 64 has the answer.
  3. Add the rule "R_aacute": ("left", "a") by way of a deliberate slip, run the script, and read the line it prints. Then take the rule out again.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: L_T needs pairs, and Mira's TO from Thursday has needed one for a week. Chapter 73 writes to the kerning list: adding a pair, changing one, and taking one away.

docs.title: 73. Set a pair
docs.text:
Wednesday of week fourteen. Two things have waited for this chapter.

The first is the TO of TOAST. Chapter 69 found that Plum never kerned it, and since yesterday there's a class, L_T, with no pairs to its name.

The second is new. Mira sets AVOCADO in the Bold and the A and the V have run into each other. Chapter 68 gave the Bold A 42 more units on its right, and it didn't help enough. Run pair_value.py on A V:

A V
  Light      -69   through a class
  Regular    -55   through a class
  Bold       -69   through a class

The Bold has the Light's number, to the unit. Somebody copied the Light's kerning into the Bold years ago and never went through it. In the Regular the tips of the two letters end up 34 units into each other, which is what a diagonal next to a diagonal wants. In the Bold, the space between them is −2 before any kerning, and the pair takes away 69 more. Mira tries values in the Kerning panel until the Bold pair looks like the Regular one, and settles on −27.

She could leave it at that, with the number typed in the panel. Today you write it from a script, because by Friday there'll be many such numbers.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The helpers ask and tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write them out again, so each one runs by itself.
  • The class L_T from chapter 72. Step 3 shows what happens without it.
  • pair_value.py from chapter 70, to check the result.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The values that come back are worked out from Plum's source file, and the two refusals in step 3 are copied from the source of the function that makes them.

docs.title: Step 1: The shape of an order
docs.text:
The function that writes kerning is write_kerning, in Fly's kerning toolkit. It takes the package, a set of edits, and a name for the Undo step:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.kerning.batch as kerning_batch

package = scripting.current_package()
edits = {"Bold": {("A", "V"): -27}}
kerning_batch.write_kerning(package, edits, "Set kerning pairs")

Look at edits before you run anything. It's a dictionary with one key, a master's name. The value under that key is another dictionary, and that inner one has the shape you know from chapter 69: a pair as the key, a number as the value.

A dictionary inside a dictionary is new, and it reads the way it's written. edits["Bold"] is the inner dictionary, the orders for one master. edits["Bold"][("A", "V")] is one number. The outer level says where, and the inner level says what.

The whole batch goes in as one piece. write_kerning checks every order in it before it changes anything, makes all the changes as one Undo step, and gives back True if the font changed and False if every pair already had its value.

Now run it, and check with pair_value.py, this time on A V Aacute V:

A V
  Light      -69   through a class
  Regular    -55   through a class
  Bold       -27   its own pair
Aacute V
  Light      -69   through a class
  Regular    -55   through a class
  Bold       -69   through a class

docs.title: Step 2: The pair that was too narrow
docs.text:
That's today's mistake, and the report shows it in two places.

"Its own pair", says the Bold line for A V. The script didn't change the pair that was there. It wrote a second one beside it, for the glyph A alone, and chapter 70 told you what happens then: a pair for the glyph wins over a pair for its class. So AV is mended.

ÁV isn't. Nor are ÄV, ÅV and the other four. They still go through the class pair, and the class pair still says −69. I asked for ("A", "V") because that's what I saw on the page. The font keeps this kerning as ("@L_A", "V").

The mended A now hides the fault. Anyone who checks AV will see a good pair and move on. Before you write a pair, ask where the value comes from at present, and write to that place. Friday's script tells you: "through a class" means the order must name the class.

So the repair has two parts: take the narrow pair out again, and change the right one. An order with None for its value removes a pair:

edits = {"Bold": {("A", "V"): None, ("@L_A", "V"): -27}}
kerning_batch.write_kerning(package, edits, "Set kerning pairs")

None and 0 are different orders. A pair with the value 0 is still a pair, and for a glyph it still overrides the class, with nothing. None means the pair is gone and the class speaks again.

Check once more, and both A V and Aacute V should read −27 in the Bold, through a class.

docs.title: Step 3: Two refusals
docs.text:
write_kerning won't write everything you hand it. Try a value with a half in it:

edits = {"Bold": {("@L_A", "V"): -27.5}}
kerning_batch.write_kerning(package, edits, "Set kerning pairs")

The last line of the traceback should begin:

ValueError: Kerning on Bold: @L_A V = -27.5 is not a whole number

and go on to say that no changes were applied. Kerning in this toolkit is whole units. If a value comes out of a sum, round it first, as chapter 68 did.

Then try a class the font doesn't have. If you skipped chapter 72, this is what the pair for TO gets you:

ValueError: Unknown or wrong-side kerning class: L_T on Light

The same line appears when the class exists and stands in the wrong place, for instance ("@R_O2", "T"): R_O2 is a class for the second place, and the order puts it first. A glyph name the font doesn't have is refused as well, with Unknown glyph.

Both refusals come before anything is written. That's the use of handing over the batch in one piece: one bad order among many, and the font stays as it was.

docs.title: Step 4: Before and after
docs.text:
A script that changes many pairs should show a line for each first, with the old value beside the new. The old value is whatever chapter 69's dictionary has under the same key, or None:

def text(value):
    return "none" if value is None else f"{value:.0f}"


pairs = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, "Bold")
old = pairs.get(("@L_A", "V"))
print(text(old), "to", text(-27))

-69 to -27

text turns a value into something printable, with the word none for a pair that isn't there. It's needed twice in every line, for the old value and for the new, since a removal has None on the new side.

An order whose old and new values are equal isn't an order, and the plan leaves it out. That makes the script safe to run twice.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Set Pairs
# Adds, changes or removes the kerning pairs listed in EDITS,
# in one Undo step, after showing old and new values.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.kerning.batch as kerning_batch
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
# master: {(first, second): value}. A class has @ in front. None removes a pair.
EDITS = {
    "Light": {("@L_T", "@R_O2"): -30},
    "Regular": {("@L_T", "@R_O2"): -20},
    "Bold": {("@L_T", "@R_O2"): -20, ("@L_A", "V"): -27},
}


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def text(value):
    return "none" if value is None else f"{value:.0f}"


def plan(package):
    rows = []
    for master in MASTERS:
        pairs = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, master)
        for (first, second), new in EDITS.get(master, {}).items():
            old = pairs.get((first, second))
            if old != new:
                rows.append((master, first, second, old, new))
    return rows


def main():
    if fl.CurrentFont() is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    rows = plan(package)
    for master, first, second, old, new in rows:
        print(f"{master:<9}{first:<8}{second:<8}{text(old):>6} to {text(new):>5}")
    print(f"{len(rows)} pairs to write.")
    if not rows or not ask(f"Write {len(rows)} kerning pairs?"):
        return

    edits = {}
    for master, first, second, old, new in rows:
        if master not in edits:
            edits[master] = {}
        edits[master][(first, second)] = new
    try:
        kerning_batch.write_kerning(package, edits, "Set kerning pairs")
    except ValueError as problem:
        print(f"Refused, nothing written: {problem}")
        return
    print(f"Done. {len(plan(package))} pairs still to write.")


main()

Save it as set_pair.py. With step 2's repair already made, it prints:

Light    @L_T    @R_O2     none to   -30
Regular  @L_T    @R_O2     none to   -20
Bold     @L_T    @R_O2     none to   -20
3 pairs to write.

The order for @L_A V is in EDITS and not in the plan, because the font already has −27 there. If you undid step 2, you'd see four lines, the fourth reading -69 to -27.

Click Yes:

Done. 0 pairs still to write.

Notes on the listing.

EDITS.get(master, {}) is get with a default that fits: a master with no orders is a master with an empty set of orders, and the loop over an empty dictionary does nothing. It lets you leave a master out of EDITS altogether.

The plan compares old != new with a float on one side and a whole number on the other. Python counts -27.0 and -27 as equal, so a pair that already has its value drops out. None is equal only to None, so "no pair, and none wanted" drops out too.

The middle of main builds the dictionary of dictionaries from the rows. if master not in edits: makes the inner dictionary the first time a master turns up, which is the pattern chapter 64 used for a dictionary of lists. Sending only the rows of the plan, and not EDITS as it stands, means the font is asked to change what the reader was shown and nothing else.

The try and except ValueError are from chapter 19. as problem gives the error a name, so the next line can print its text. A refusal here is a message for the person at the desk, not a crash, so the script prints the reason in one line and stops.

docs.title: The value for TO
docs.text:
Where do −30, −20 and −20 come from? From looking. The space between T and O before kerning is 70 units in the Light, 34 in the Regular and 36 in the Bold. Mira set HOTOH and took space out until the O after the T sat as it does after the H. A script can carry a number into three masters and sixty glyphs. It can't tell you what the number should be.

The pair is written from class to class. @L_T holds T and Ť, and @R_O2 holds O and its six relatives, so one line in each master covers fourteen combinations. Check two of them with pair_value.py, on T O Tcaron Odieresis. Both should say "through a class", with the same three values.

The T's fourteen older pairs are still written for the glyph T, and Ť has no share in them. Moving them to the class is the second exercise.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: kerning_batch.write_kerning(package, edits, name) takes a dictionary of dictionaries: a master's name, then pairs with their values. A number adds or changes a pair, and None removes it, which is different from setting it to 0. Find out where a value comes from before you change it: if it comes through a class, the order must name the class. Values are whole numbers, a class must exist and stand in the right place, and one bad order stops the whole batch before anything is written.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. The Regular has a pair ("questiondown", "exclamdown") with the value 11, the Bold has it at 28, and the Light doesn't have it. A pair in one master only is a hazard for every weight in between. Decide whether to give it to all three or to none, and write the order. Check with pair_value.py, then undo: later chapters count the pairs as they are.
  2. Move the pair T before o to the class: for each master, remove ("T", "o") and add ("@L_T", "o") with the value the old pair had. Chapter 70 printed the three values. Write the six orders, read the plan, and run it. Then check T o and Tcaron o, and undo when you've seen them.
  3. Put ("@L_A", "V"): -27.5 into EDITS beside a good order and run the script. Which line does it print, and how many pairs were written?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: One pair is mended. How many others in the Bold are as deep as AV was, and which pairs carry the most weight in this font? Chapter 74 sorts the kerning list by the size of each value, whichever way it points, and sets the pairs against the space they act on.

docs.title: 74. The biggest pairs
docs.text:
Thursday of week fourteen. Yesterday Mira mended one pair in the Bold, AV, which had the Light's value and pulled the letters into each other. She doesn't believe it was the only one.

"Which pairs do the most work?" she asks. "Show me the big ones, and I'll look at those first."

It's a fair way to check a hundred pairs when you have time for ten. This chapter builds that list, finds that it's the wrong list, and builds a better one. Nothing in the font changes today.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The helper tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write it out again, so each one runs by itself.
  • The font as chapters 68, 72 and 73 left it. If you skipped one of them, your numbers will differ from mine, and the method won't. The Bold table in step 3 also assumes you ran copy_sb.py on the Bold's accented letters, as chapter 68 suggested.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The tables below are worked out from Plum's source file, with the changes of the earlier chapters applied by hand.

docs.title: Step 1: Sort by size
docs.text:
Chapter 69 sorted the kerning list by value, most negative first. That puts the four pairs that add space at the far end, as if they mattered least. "Big" should mean far from zero in either direction, and chapter 36 had the function for that: abs.

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

package = scripting.current_package()
pairs = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, "Regular")


def by_size(item):
    return abs(item[1])


big = sorted(pairs.items(), key=by_size, reverse=True)
for (first, second), value in big[:8]:
    print(f"{first:<14}{second:<12}{value:>6.0f}")

big[:8] is a slice, as in chapter 10: the first eight of a list. Since the list is sorted, they're the eight biggest. Sort, then slice: that's how you take the top of anything.

L             T             -113
quoteright    c             -112
quoteright    @R_oacute     -112
quoteright    g             -112
...

I've cut the output short, because below the first line I can't tell you what order you'll see. Nine pairs share the value −112. sorted keeps things that are equal in the order they came in, and they came in the order the font happens to hold them. Run it tomorrow on another machine and the eight may be a different eight of the nine.
