A list that can change between two runs is a poor thing to hand to somebody. The cure is to give the sort a second thing to go by when the first is equal, and a key function does that by returning a tuple:

def by_size(item):
    (first, second), value = item
    return (-abs(value), first, second)


big = sorted(pairs.items(), key=by_size)

Python compares tuples the way you'd compare words in a dictionary: by the first part, then, if those are equal, by the second, and so on. So this sorts by size, then by the first name, then by the second.

The minus sign replaces reverse=True. I want the biggest size first and the names from A to Z, and reverse would turn both around. Negating the number turns only the number around.

L             T             -113
quoteright    @R_eacute     -112
quoteright    @R_oacute     -112
quoteright    c             -112
quoteright    ccedilla      -112
quoteright    d             -112
quoteright    e             -112
quoteright    g             -112

docs.title: Step 2: The wrong list
docs.text:
Mira reads it and shrugs. Seven of the eight lines are the apostrophe before a round letter. She sets l'eau and d'où, and they're fine.

In the Bold it's the same picture, with −124 in place of −112 and ten such pairs at the top. The pair she mended yesterday stood at −69, far down the list, and it was the one that collided.

That's today's mistake, and it was in the question. The size of a pair says how far the second glyph moves. It doesn't say where the glyph ends up. The apostrophe has a lot of white beside it and the pair takes most of it away, which is the pair doing its job. The A and the V in the Bold had no white to give, and a middling pair pushed them together.

So measure each pair against the space it acts on. Chapter 61 gave you that: the right side of the first glyph plus the left side of the second. Add the pair's value, and you have what's left:

from fly import fl
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

font = fl.CurrentFont()
a = pGlyph(font, font["quoteright"])
b = pGlyph(font, font["e"])
space = a.getRSB("Regular") + b.getLSB("Regular")
print(space, space + pairs[("quoteright", "e")])

54 -58.0

54 units of white before kerning and −58 after. A negative number here means the boxes around the two shapes overlap. Whether the shapes touch is another matter, and I'll come back to it.

docs.title: Step 3: A stand-in for a class
docs.text:
Half the pairs name a class, and a class has no sidebearings. Which glyph should stand for @L_A?

Chapter 72 kept the first member in front for this moment: by custom, the first member of a class stands for the rest. Since the members were grouped because their sides are alike, any of them would give nearly the same number.

def stand_in(side, classes):
    if side.startswith("@"):
        members, place = classes[side[1:]]
        return members[0]
    return side


classes = scripting.kerning_classes(package, "Regular")
print(stand_in("@L_A", classes), stand_in("V", classes))

A V

side[1:] is a slice of a string: everything from the second character on, which takes off the @. The kerning list writes class names with the sign and the dictionary of classes has them without.

docs.title: Step 4: Sort by what's left
docs.text:
Now each pair becomes a row of five: two names, the value, the space, and what's left. Sort by the last, smallest first, with the names to settle ties:

def by_left(row):
    first, second, value, space, left = row
    return (left, first, second)

In the Bold, the top of that list is the apostrophe again: nine pairs with −105 left. Mira looks at l'eau in the Bold. The apostrophe sits above the e, and the two never meet. The measurement is of boxes, and these two shapes are at different heights.

She says to leave the apostrophe out. A script can't see that for itself, so it gets a list, and you decide what goes on it:

HIGH = ["quoteright"]

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Top Pairs
# For each master, lists the kerning pairs that leave the least room
# between the two glyphs, and counts the ones that go deeper than DEEP.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
HOW_MANY = 8
DEEP = -70
# Glyphs that sit above the lowercase and pass over it.
HIGH = ["quoteright"]


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def stand_in(side, classes):
    if side.startswith("@"):
        members, place = classes[side[1:]]
        return members[0]
    return side


def by_left(row):
    first, second, value, space, left = row
    return (left, first, second)


def pair_rows(font, package, master):
    pairs = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, master)
    classes = scripting.kerning_classes(package, master)
    rows = []
    for (first, second), value in pairs.items():
        a = stand_in(first, classes)
        b = stand_in(second, classes)
        if a in HIGH or b in HIGH:
            continue
        space = pGlyph(font, font[a]).getRSB(master) + pGlyph(font, font[b]).getLSB(master)
        rows.append((first, second, value, space, space + value))
    return sorted(rows, key=by_left)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    for master in MASTERS:
        rows = pair_rows(font, package, master)
        deep = [row for row in rows if row[4] < DEEP]
        print(f"{master}: {len(rows)} pairs measured, {len(deep)} leave less than {DEEP}.")
        for first, second, value, space, left in rows[:HOW_MANY]:
            print(f"  {first:<14}{second:<12}{value:>6.0f}{space:>7}{left:>7.0f}")


main()

Save it as top_pairs.py. On the practice font it should print:

Light: 75 pairs measured, 1 leave less than -70.
  @L_Y          @R_A2          -90     18    -72
  @L_Y          e             -103     44    -59
  @L_A          @R_Y2          -90     40    -50
  @L_Y          o              -96     46    -50
  @L_Y          z              -62     23    -39
  V             @R_A2          -69     34    -35
  @L_A          T              -63     33    -30
  @L_A          V              -69     42    -27
Regular: 81 pairs measured, 1 leave less than -70.
  L             T             -113     20    -93
  @L_Y          @R_A2          -65     -1    -66
  @L_A          @R_Y2          -71     19    -52
  @L_A          T              -61     12    -49
  T             y              -55      6    -49
  @L_Y          e              -72     24    -48
  @L_Y          o              -72     24    -48
  T             e              -84     36    -48
Bold: 77 pairs measured, 17 leave less than -70.
  T             w             -105      1   -104
  @L_Y          @R_A2          -90     -8    -98
  T             @R_wacute      -94      1    -93
  L             V              -90      4    -86
  @L_A          @R_Y2          -90      5    -85
  @L_Y          e             -103     19    -84
  T             e             -108     28    -80
  T             o             -108     28    -80

The three columns of numbers are the pair's value, the space before kerning, and what's left.

Notes on the listing.

pair_rows returns its rows already sorted, so main can slice them and count in them without thinking about order.

deep is a comprehension with a condition, as in chapter 37, and only its length is used. Counting the things that pass a test is a list of them and len.

The count comes before the slice in the output, and it's the more useful of the two. A top eight always has eight lines, whatever the state of the font. The count tells you whether those eight are the whole problem or the visible part of it.

DEEP is −70 because below it the Light and the Regular have one pair each. It's a line drawn from this font, and another design would need another number.

docs.title: What the list says
docs.text:
Read the three headings together. One pair goes deeper than −70 in the Light, one in the Regular, and seventeen in the Bold.

The Bold's kerning is too strong throughout, as AV suggested. Chapter 69's first exercise showed why: most of its values are the Light's, copied over. The Light has wide sidebearings and can afford a pair of −90. In the Bold the same −90 lands on 5 units of white.

Mira won't mend seventeen pairs one at a time, and the seventeen are only the ones past the line. The whole Bold wants its kerning turned down in proportion. That's chapter 79.

Two lines get a mark in pencil. L T in the Regular leaves −93, where the Light leaves −10 and the Bold −66. A master in the middle shouldn't be the extreme one. And T w in the Bold leaves −104: the arm of the T would reach halfway across the w. She sets both in a Glyph window, and both are wrong.

The script found them, and it was Mira who judged them. L T with −93 could have been right, since the bar of a T does go over the foot of an L. A measurement of boxes can't say what two shapes do inside their boxes, and that's why the apostrophe had to be left out by hand.

Ines gets out Oskar's sheet. The next open line reads: Find kerning pairs that are larger than they should be. The list on the screen is that line done, so she crosses it out: nine of eleven. Finding was the chore. The mending takes the rest of this part.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: To take the top of a list, sort it and slice it: rows[:8]. A key function that returns a tuple settles ties, and a minus sign in the key turns one part around where reverse=True would turn all of them. The size of a kerning value says how far a glyph moves, and the space plus the value says where it ends up. A list like this one points at pairs, and you still have to look at them.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Print the three pairs in the Regular that are farthest from the top of the size list, with big[-3:]. Chapter 10 had that slice too. Are they pairs you'd miss if they were gone? Chapter 75 asks the same question of the whole font.
  2. Add "quotedbl" and "asterisk" to HIGH and run the script. Does any count change? Why not? Look at which glyphs Plum's pairs name.
  3. Sort the Bold's rows by space, smallest first, and print the top eight. These are the pairs where the letters were already close before kerning. Which of them does the left list also show?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The far end of the size list holds pairs of 7 and 8 units. Does anyone see them? Chapter 75 finds the pairs too small to matter and removes them, after a dry run that shows what would go.

docs.title: 75. Pairs too small to matter
docs.text:
Friday of week fourteen. Yesterday's list had a far end, and the first exercise looked at it: pairs of 7 and 8 units.

Plum is drawn on 1,000 units to the em. Set at 10 points, a pair of 7 units moves a letter by seven hundredths of a point. Nobody sees that. Each such pair still costs a line in the kerning list, a moment of somebody's attention at every review, and a few bytes in every exported font.

Fonts that have been kerned by eye, or by an automatic tool, can carry hundreds of these. Plum has ten, which is enough to learn on and few enough to check by hand. Today you find them, decide which may go, and remove those. It's the first script in this part that deletes, so it starts as a dry run.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The helpers ask and tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write them out again, so each one runs by itself.
  • The kerning as chapter 73 left it. Chapter 74 changed nothing.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The lists below are worked out from Plum's source file.

docs.title: Step 1: Find them
docs.text:
Fly's kerning toolkit has a function for this search. Give it the package, a list of masters and a threshold, and it gives back the pairs whose value is closer to zero than the threshold:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.kerning.edit.model as kerning_edit

package = scripting.current_package()
found = kerning_edit.small_pairs(package, ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"], 10)
for master in found:
    for first, second, value in found[master]:
        print(f"{master:<9}{first:<8}{second:<12}{value:>4.0f}")

found is a dictionary with a master's name as the key and a list of rows under it. Each row is two names and a value. The rows come sorted by size, smallest first, with the names to settle ties, which is the tuple key you wrote yesterday.

Light    X       @R_O2          7
Light    t       quoteright     8
Regular  @L_A    @R_O2         -7
Regular  @L_A    Q             -7
Regular  @L_O    @R_A2         -7
Regular  @L_W    @R_uacute     -7
Regular  @L_W    u             -7
Regular  Q       @R_A2         -7
Regular  R       V             -8
Bold     R       V             -9

"Closer to zero" is strict: a pair of 10 or −10 is not on the list. The Regular has two of those, P before a and before the á family, and they stay.

This is a dry run in the plainest sense. The function reads and reports, and the font is as it was.

docs.title: Step 2: The list is not the plan
docs.text:
The same toolkit has remove_run, which would take these ten pairs out in what should be one Undo step. I'm not going to call it, and here's why.

Mira reads the first line and stops. X before the O family has 7 units in the Light. She looks the pair up with pair_value.py:

X O
  Light        7   through a class
  Regular    -23   through a class
  Bold       -41   through a class

It runs from +7 through −23 to −41. The Light's 7 is one end of a pair that does real work in the other two weights. Take it out of the Light and the pair exists in two masters and is missing from the third. Chapter 73's first exercise called that a hazard, and it is one: a weight between the Light and the Regular is made by mixing the two, and a missing pair counts as 0 in the mixing. For this pair the result would hardly differ. But the kerning lists of the three masters would no longer hold the same pairs, and the next person to compare them would have to work out why.

So today's mistake is to take the search for the decision. small_pairs answers "which values are small in this master?" The question for the font is "which pairs are small in every master where they exist?" Only those are too small to matter.

Asking that takes a look sideways, at the same pair in the other masters:

tables = {master: scripting.kerning_pairs(package, master) for master in ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]}
values = [tables[master].get(("X", "@R_O2")) for master in tables]
print(values)

[7.0, -23.0, -41.0]

The first line is a dictionary comprehension, as in chapter 37: it reads each master's kerning once and keeps the three dictionaries under their names. The second collects one pair's three values, with None where a master doesn't have it.

Now the test. A value is harmless if it's missing or small:

def is_small(value):
    return value is None or abs(value) < 10


print(all([is_small(value) for value in values]))

False

all is from chapter 44: true when every item in the list is true. For X before O only the first is, so the pair stays. For R before V the three values are None, −8 and −9, and all three pass.

The order inside is_small matters. abs(None) is a TypeError. Because or stops at the first true part, a missing value never reaches abs.

docs.title: Step 3: Remove with None
docs.text:
Chapter 73 showed how a pair is removed: an order with None for its value. The plan gives rows, and the rows become orders the same way as on Wednesday, a dictionary for each master:

edits = {}
for master, first, second, value in drop:
    if master not in edits:
        edits[master] = {}
    edits[master][(first, second)] = None

All of them go to write_kerning in one batch, and so they make one Undo step.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Drop Tiny Pairs
# Lists kerning pairs smaller than THRESHOLD. A pair is removed only if it is
# small or missing in every master. With DRY_RUN = True it only prints.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.kerning.batch as kerning_batch
import fly.ap.kerning.edit.model as kerning_edit
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
THRESHOLD = 10
DRY_RUN = True


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def is_small(value):
    return value is None or abs(value) < THRESHOLD


def elsewhere(tables, master, first, second):
    parts = []
    for other in MASTERS:
        value = tables[other].get((first, second))
        if other != master and value is not None:
            parts.append(f"{other} {value:.0f}")
    return ", ".join(parts)


def plan(package):
    tables = {master: scripting.kerning_pairs(package, master) for master in MASTERS}
    found = kerning_edit.small_pairs(package, MASTERS, THRESHOLD)
    drop = []
    keep = []
    for master in MASTERS:
        for first, second, value in found[master]:
            values = [tables[other].get((first, second)) for other in MASTERS]
            row = (master, first, second, value)
            if all([is_small(other) for other in values]):
                drop.append(row)
            else:
                keep.append(row + (elsewhere(tables, master, first, second),))
    return drop, keep


def main():
    if fl.CurrentFont() is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    drop, keep = plan(package)
    for master, first, second, value, why in keep:
        print(f"keep  {master:<9}{first:<8}{second:<12}{value:>4.0f}   {why}")
    for master, first, second, value in drop:
        print(f"drop  {master:<9}{first:<8}{second:<12}{value:>4.0f}")
    print(f"{len(keep) + len(drop)} small pairs found, {len(drop)} to remove.")
    if DRY_RUN or not drop:
        return
    if not ask(f"Remove {len(drop)} kerning pairs?"):
        return

    edits = {}
    for master, first, second, value in drop:
        if master not in edits:
            edits[master] = {}
        edits[master][(first, second)] = None
    kerning_batch.write_kerning(package, edits, "Drop tiny pairs")
    drop, keep = plan(package)
    print(f"Done. {len(drop)} to remove.")


main()

Save it as drop_tiny_pairs.py and run it as it stands:

keep  Light    X       @R_O2          7   Regular -23, Bold -41
keep  Light    t       quoteright     8   Regular 14, Bold 15
keep  Regular  @L_A    @R_O2         -7   Light -32, Bold -32
keep  Regular  @L_A    Q             -7   Light -24, Bold -32
keep  Regular  @L_O    @R_A2         -7   Light -26, Bold -26
keep  Regular  Q       @R_A2         -7   Light -24, Bold -32
drop  Regular  @L_W    @R_uacute     -7
drop  Regular  @L_W    u             -7
drop  Regular  R       V             -8
drop  Bold     R       V             -9
10 small pairs found, 4 to remove.

Ten were found, and six of them have a bigger relative in another master. Four lines may go: three pairs, one of which lives in two masters.

Read the four before you go on. W before u at −7 in the Regular only, and the same from the class of W to the class of ú. R before V at −8 and −9. Mira sets Wu and RV with kerning on and off and can't tell which is which.

Then change DRY_RUN to False, run again, and click Yes:

Done. 0 to remove.

The Regular now has 104 pairs and the Bold 102. One Undo should bring the four back. I haven't seen it in FontLab 9.

Notes on the listing.

DRY_RUN is the switch from chapter 31. A script that deletes should ship with the switch on. The person who turns it off has read the list at least once.

elsewhere builds the reason for a kept line: the values in the other masters. It's there for the reader of the report. A line that says only "keep" makes you look the pair up, and with the other values printed you don't have to.

row + (elsewhere(...),) joins two tuples. The comma inside the second pair of brackets is what makes it a tuple of one. Without it, the brackets would be ordinary brackets around a string, and adding a string to a tuple is a TypeError.

plan returns two lists, as plan did in chapter 62. The last lines of main run it again after the write and count what's left, so "Done" is followed by a number that was measured after the change.

docs.title: Two cautions
docs.text:
The rule "small in every master" is safe for Plum. It isn't the whole of the matter in every font.

First, a small pair can be an exception. Suppose a class pair says −60, and one member of the class has its own pair of −5 because for that glyph the −60 was far too much. The −5 is small. Remove it and that glyph gets the class's −60, which nobody wanted. None of today's four is such a pair: R belongs to no class, and the two W pairs are class pairs themselves. In a font with more exceptions, look each dropped pair up with pair_value.py before and after. A value that went from small to large is one of these.

Second, the threshold is a judgement. Ten units is 1 per cent of the em. For a text face used at 9 to 12 points that's below what the eye resolves. For a display face set at 200 points, ten units is 2 points, and somebody put them there on purpose. Change THRESHOLD to suit the design.

docs.title: What the kept lines say
docs.text:
The six kept lines are worth a second look, and Mira gives them one.

Four of them are the same story. The A family before the O family, the A family before Q, and both the other way round: −7 in the Regular, and between −24 and −32 in the Light and the Bold. A middle weight with a quarter of the kerning of its neighbors isn't a design. Someone stopped halfway. She writes "AO, OA, AQ, QA: Regular, finish" on her list, under L T and T w from yesterday.

The script was looking for pairs to delete and found four that want to be bigger.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: kerning_edit.small_pairs(package, masters, threshold) lists, for each master, the pairs whose value is closer to zero than the threshold. A pair that's small in one master may be large in the next, so collect its values across the masters with get, test for None before calling abs, and test them together with all. A script that deletes starts with DRY_RUN = True and prints what it would keep, and why, beside what it would drop. Before removing a small pair that belongs to a single glyph, check that a class pair doesn't take its place.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Set DRY_RUN = True again and THRESHOLD = 12. The plan should find sixteen small pairs. How many may go now, and which two are new on the drop list? Don't remove them: put the threshold back to 10 when you've looked.
  2. Change is_small so that a missing value doesn't count as small. Which of the four pairs would still be dropped? Is that a better rule or a worse one for a font with three masters?
  3. Write the four orders for Mira's note, with −20 as a first guess for each, and put them into EDITS in set_pair.py. Read the plan, and don't click Yes: the values want her eye first.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 72 added glyphs to classes. What about the other direction: a class that lists a glyph the font no longer has, or a pair that names a class nobody made? Chapter 76 looks for kerning that points at nothing.

docs.title: 76. Pairs for glyphs that are gone
docs.text:
Monday of week fifteen. Ines wants the kerning in a spreadsheet by Wednesday, for a reviewer outside the studio. Before it goes, she asks a question she has learned to ask of every font that has been renamed, trimmed and extended for three months.

"Does the kerning mention anything that isn't there?"

Kerning is kept by name. A pair says A and V, and a class lists A, Aacute, Aring. Rename a glyph or delete it, and whatever still carries the old name points at nothing. Such a pair is called an orphan. It does no harm on screen. It may stop an export, which I haven't tried, or travel into a spreadsheet and come back as a question nobody can answer.

Today's script looks for three kinds of loose end and changes nothing.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The helper tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write it out again, so each one runs by itself.
  • The kerning as chapter 75 left it: 101, 104 and 102 pairs.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The outputs below are worked out from Plum's source file. I also haven't seen what FontLab 9 does to kerning when you rename or delete a glyph in the Font window. It may tidy up after you. A check like this one is how you'd find out.

docs.title: Step 1: Two sets and a minus sign
docs.text:
You need two collections of names: the ones the kerning uses and the ones the font has. Chapter 25 introduced the set, a collection that holds each thing once, and chapter 40 built the second of these two:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
package = scripting.current_package()
have = {glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs}
pairs = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, "Regular")

used = set()
for first, second in pairs:
    used.add(first)
    used.add(second)
print(len(used))

54

The 104 pairs of the Regular use 54 different names between them.

Now the question. Sets can be subtracted. used - have is a new set with everything that's in used and not in have:

gone = sorted(used - have)
print(len(gone), gone[:4])

18 ['@L_A', '@L_O', '@L_T', '@L_U']

That's called the difference of two sets. It replaces a loop with an if and a not in inside it, and it reads the way you'd say it: the used names, less the ones we have.

docs.title: Step 2: Eighteen false alarms
docs.text:
Eighteen names that aren't in the font would be bad news. Look at the four you can see. Each begins with @.

They're classes. A pair can name a class on either side, a class isn't a glyph, and so no class name will ever be in have. The check compared two lists that weren't lists of the same kind of thing.

It's the mistake to expect whenever you subtract one set from another. Before the minus sign, ask whether both sides hold the same kind of name. Here the fix is to split used in two, and check each half against its own list:

glyph_names = {name for name in used if not name.startswith("@")}
class_names = {name[1:] for name in used if name.startswith("@")}
classes = scripting.kerning_classes(package, "Regular")

print(sorted(glyph_names - have))
print(sorted(class_names - set(classes)))

[]
[]

Both are set comprehensions with a condition. The second takes the @ off with name[1:], as chapter 74 did, because the dictionary of classes has the names without it. set(classes) makes a set of a dictionary's keys.

Two empty lists. Every glyph a pair names is in the font, and so is every class.

docs.title: Step 3: Can the check find anything?
docs.text:
An empty result has two explanations. Either the font is clean, or the check can't see dirt. You've met the second kind already: a check that compared classes with glyphs would have cried wolf on every font, and one with the test the wrong way round would stay silent on every font.

So give the check something to find. Put the work into functions that take plain dictionaries and a set, and feed them a small kerning table you made up, with faults whose number you know:

def orphans(pairs, classes, have):
    used = set()
    for first, second in pairs:
        used.add(first)
        used.add(second)
    glyph_names = {name for name in used if not name.startswith("@")}
    class_names = {name[1:] for name in used if name.startswith("@")}
    return sorted(glyph_names - have), sorted(class_names - set(classes))


def lost_members(classes, have):
    rows = []
    for name in sorted(classes):
        members, place = classes[name]
        gone = sorted(set(members) - have)
        if gone:
            rows.append((name, gone))
    return rows


test_have = {"A", "Aacute", "V"}
test_pairs = {("A", "V"): -60, ("A", "V.old"): -60, ("@L_A", "@R_gone"): -40}
test_classes = {"L_A": (["A", "Aacute", "Aring.old"], None)}

print(orphans(test_pairs, test_classes, test_have))
print(lost_members(test_classes, test_have))

(['V.old'], ['R_gone'])
[('L_A', ['Aring.old'])]

Three faults went in and three came out: a pair for a glyph that isn't there, a pair for a class nobody made, and a class with a member that's gone. The second function is the third kind of loose end. It turns each class's member list into a set and subtracts the font from it.

Neither function touches FontLab. They take dictionaries and a set and give back lists, which is why a made-up table could stand in for a font. Whenever a check comes back empty, this is the way to learn whether to believe it.

docs.title: Step 4: Pairs that some masters lack
docs.text:
There's a fourth loose end, and chapter 75 circled it: a pair that exists in one master and not in the others. It's another difference of sets. The keys of the kerning dictionaries are the pairs, so collect all of them, then ask of each master which ones it lacks:

tables = {master: scripting.kerning_pairs(package, master) for master in MASTERS}
everything = set()
for master in tables:
    everything = everything | set(tables[master])

The first line makes a dictionary with one kerning table for each master, under the master's name. It's a dictionary comprehension, the kind chapter 75 used: a list comprehension with a key and a colon in front. It needs MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"] above it.

The upright bar joins two sets into one that holds everything from both. That's called the union. After the loop, everything holds each pair that any master has, once.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Orphan Pairs
# Reports kerning that points at nothing: pairs for missing glyphs or classes,
# class members that are gone, and pairs that some masters lack.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def orphans(pairs, classes, have):
    used = set()
    for first, second in pairs:
        used.add(first)
        used.add(second)
    glyph_names = {name for name in used if not name.startswith("@")}
    class_names = {name[1:] for name in used if name.startswith("@")}
    return sorted(glyph_names - have), sorted(class_names - set(classes))


def lost_members(classes, have):
    rows = []
    for name in sorted(classes):
        members, place = classes[name]
        gone = sorted(set(members) - have)
        if gone:
            rows.append((name, gone))
    return rows


def uneven(tables):
    everything = set()
    for master in MASTERS:
        everything = everything | set(tables[master])
    rows = []
    for pair in sorted(everything):
        missing = [master for master in MASTERS if pair not in tables[master]]
        if missing:
            rows.append((pair, missing))
    return len(everything), rows


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    have = {glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs}
    tables = {}
    for master in MASTERS:
        pairs = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, master)
        classes = scripting.kerning_classes(package, master)
        tables[master] = pairs
        glyphs, groups = orphans(pairs, classes, have)
        members = lost_members(classes, have)
        print(f"{master}: {len(pairs)} pairs, {len(glyphs)} missing glyphs, "
              f"{len(groups)} missing classes, {len(members)} classes with lost members.")
        for name in glyphs:
            print(f"  no glyph {name}")
        for name in groups:
            print(f"  no class @{name}")
        for name, gone in members:
            print(f"  @{name} lists {', '.join(gone)}")

    total, rows = uneven(tables)
    print(f"{total} different pairs, {len(rows)} not in every master.")
    for (first, second), missing in rows:
        print(f"  {first:<14}{second:<12}not in {', '.join(missing)}")


main()

Save it as orphan_pairs.py. On the practice font it should print:

Light: 101 pairs, 0 missing glyphs, 0 missing classes, 0 classes with lost members.
Regular: 104 pairs, 0 missing glyphs, 0 missing classes, 0 classes with lost members.
Bold: 102 pairs, 0 missing glyphs, 0 missing classes, 0 classes with lost members.
104 different pairs, 3 not in every master.
  P             @R_aacute   not in Light, Bold
  P             a           not in Light, Bold
  questiondown  exclamdown  not in Light

Notes on the listing.

The long print is split over two lines inside its brackets. Two f-strings that stand next to each other with nothing between them are joined into one, so this is a single string. It's a way to keep a long line readable.

uneven returns a count and a list, and main unpacks them. The pairs come out in the order of sorted, which compares tuples part by part, as in chapter 74. @ sorts before the small letters, so the class pair comes first.

missing is a comprehension over the masters that keeps the names of those without the pair. An empty list means the pair is everywhere, and if missing: skips it.

docs.title: What the report says
docs.text:
Plum has no orphans. Three months of renaming and nothing points at a missing glyph. Ines says that's the first font this year she could say that of, and takes the three lines at the bottom to Mira.

P before a, and before the á family, is −10 in the Regular and absent from the other two. Chapter 75 kept those two because −10 is not less than 10. They're small, they're in one master, and nobody remembers making them. questiondown before exclamdown is 11 in the Regular and 28 in the Bold, and the Light has none.

Mira's answer is that all three are hers to settle, and that a script shouldn't. A pair missing from a master is either an oversight, to be filled in with set_pair.py, or a leftover, to be removed from the masters that have it. The report can't tell which. It goes on her list.

docs.title: If you do find an orphan
docs.text:
Suppose the report had named one. You'd want to remove the pair, and chapter 73's tool for that is an order with None.

As far as I can read Fly's source, that won't work here. write_kerning checks every pair in its orders before it writes, and one of the checks is that each glyph exists. A pair that names a missing glyph fails it, even when the order is to remove the pair. The whole batch is refused with a message that begins Unknown glyph.

That refusal is sensible for writing and unhelpful for cleaning. I haven't tried it in FontLab 9, and I haven't found another route in Fly. Until I have, remove an orphan by hand: open the Kerning panel, find the pair and delete it there. If it's a class member that's gone, open the Classes panel and take the name out of the class. Then run the report again.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Kerning is kept by name, and a name can outlive its glyph. a - b gives the things in set a that aren't in set b, a | b gives everything in either, and set(d) makes a set of a dictionary's keys. Before you subtract, check that both sets hold the same kind of thing: class names begin with @ and are never glyph names. An empty result needs a test, so write the check as a function of plain dictionaries and sets and run it on made-up data with known faults.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a fourth fault to the made-up table: a class "R_V" with the members ["V", "W.old"]. Predict the output of lost_members and run it.
  2. Sets have a third sign, &, for the things that are in both. Use it to count the pairs that all three masters share. You should get 101, which is 104 less the three in the report.
  3. Print the names that have kerning in the Regular and none in the Light: the difference of the two masters' used sets. You should get two names. Which pairs brought them in?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The kerning is consistent enough to show. Before the spreadsheet, the reviewer needs something to look at: lines of text where every pair sits between letters that are known to be spaced right. Chapter 77 builds that proof text out of the kerning list.

docs.title: 77. A kerning proof
docs.text:
Tuesday of week fifteen. The reviewer is called Tobias, he works two towns away, and he judges kerning the way everyone does: by looking at letters. A table of 104 pairs with numbers beside them tells him nothing until he has seen each pair set.

A pair on its own is hard to judge too. AV in the middle of a white page could be right or wrong by twenty units and you wouldn't know. Type designers set the pair between letters whose spacing is already trusted: HHAVHH for capitals, nnaynn for small letters. The eye compares the gap in the middle with the even gaps on either side.

Chapter 61 tested sidebearings with one such word, minimum, typed by hand. Today a script makes one for every pair in the kerning list and opens them in a Glyph window. The font doesn't change.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The helper tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write it out again, so each one runs by itself.
  • The kerning as chapter 75 left it. The Regular has 104 pairs.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The strings below were built in plain Python from Plum's source file. I haven't seen the tab that the last step opens.

docs.title: Step 1: Glue four strings together
docs.text:
Start with one pair and a plus sign. Between two strings, + joins them end to end:

first = "A"
second = "V"
print("HH" + first + second + "HH")

HHAVHH

That's a proof word. Now the frame has to suit the letters. A capital wants H beside it and a small letter wants n. Chapter 13 had the question to ask of a name:

def frame(name):
    if name[0].isupper():
        return "HH"
    return "nn"


def word(first, second):
    return frame(first) + first + second + frame(second)


print(word("A", "V"), word("T", "o"), word("r", "y"))

HHAVHH HHTonn nnrynn

name[0] is the first character of the name. Each side gets the frame that suits it, so To has capitals before it and small letters after, as it would in a word.

docs.title: Step 2: Names are not letters
docs.text:
Try it on two more pairs from the Regular's list:

print(word("A", "wacute"), word("quoteright", "c"))

HHAwacutenn nnquoterightcnn

Put those in a Glyph window and you'd see the words "wacute" and "quoteright" spelled out in Plum. The kerning list holds glyph names. A text field takes characters. For A and V the name and the character are the same thing, which is why the first try looked fine. A name was taken for the thing it names, and for the plain letters the two happen to look alike, so nothing warned you.

There are two ways out. One is to turn each name into its character through the glyph's Unicode value, and that fails for a glyph without one, as a small cap called a.sc would be. The other is FontLab's own way of writing a glyph by name in text: a slash, then the name. /wacute means the glyph called wacute. It works for every glyph, with or without a Unicode value, so the script uses it for all of them:

def frame(name):
    if name[0].isupper():
        return "/H/H"
    return "/n/n"


def word(first, second):
    return frame(first) + "/" + first + "/" + second + frame(second)


print(word("A", "wacute"), word("quoteright", "c"))

/H/H/A/wacute/n/n /n/n/quoteright/c/n/n

It's harder for you to read and FontLab reads it without guessing. Each slash ends the name before it, so there's never a doubt where wacute stops.

docs.title: Step 3: A class sends its first member
docs.text:
Most of the list names classes, and a class can't be set as text. Chapter 74 solved this: the first member stands for the class. Bring stand_in over as it is:

def stand_in(side, classes):
    if side.startswith("@"):
        members, place = classes[side[1:]]
        return members[0]
    return side

So the pair @L_A before @R_Y2 becomes /H/H/A/Y/H/H. Tobias sees AY, and what he decides holds for ÁÝ, ÄŸ and the rest of both families. If he doubts that, chapter 70's pair_value.py will tell him the value for any two glyphs he names.

docs.title: Step 4: Many words, one string
docs.text:
You have a word for each pair. A Glyph window wants one text. Chapter 25 gave you join: a separator, a dot, and a list of strings.

words = [word("A", "V"), word("T", "o"), word("r", "y")]
print(" ".join(words))

/H/H/A/V/H/H /H/H/T/o/n/n /n/n/r/y/n/n

A space between the words makes them words: FontLab can break the line there.

Could two pairs give the same word? If a class's first member also had a pair of its own, yes: @L_A before V and A before V would both come out as /H/H/A/V/H/H. The script keeps a word only the first time it appears. A set would do that, but a set forgets the order, and the order is how Tobias will find his way. So it's a list and a not in:

words = []
for first, second in sorted(pairs):
    text = word(stand_in(first, classes), stand_in(second, classes))
    if text not in words:
        words.append(text)

docs.title: Step 5: Open the tab
docs.text:
Fly has a function that opens a Glyph window tab with a text in it:

import fly.ap.proof.tabs.text as proof_tab

proof_tab.open_text_tab("/H/H/A/V/H/H", expected_id=package.id)

expected_id is a safety catch. package.id is the number that identifies the font you read the kerning from, the one chapter 30 passed along as facts.package_id. If somebody has switched to another font between the reading and the opening, the function refuses with The source font changed or closed; run the proof again. A proof of one font's pairs set in another font's letters would be worse than no proof.

The tab shows whichever master is current in FontLab. The pairs differ a little from master to master, so the script builds its text from the master you name in MASTER, and you should have that master showing when you run it.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Kerning Proof Text
# Builds one proof word for each kerning pair of MASTER, with HH or nn
# on either side, and opens them in a Glyph window tab.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.proof.tabs.text as proof_tab
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTER = "Regular"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def frame(name):
    if name[0].isupper():
        return "/H/H"
    return "/n/n"


def word(first, second):
    return frame(first) + "/" + first + "/" + second + frame(second)


def stand_in(side, classes):
    if side.startswith("@"):
        members, place = classes[side[1:]]
        return members[0]
    return side


def proof_words(pairs, classes):
    words = []
    for first, second in sorted(pairs):
        text = word(stand_in(first, classes), stand_in(second, classes))
        if text not in words:
            words.append(text)
    return words


def main():
    if fl.CurrentFont() is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    pairs = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, MASTER)
    classes = scripting.kerning_classes(package, MASTER)
    words = proof_words(pairs, classes)
    print(f"{MASTER}: {len(pairs)} pairs, {len(words)} proof words.")
    for text in words[:3]:
        print(" ", text)
    proof_tab.open_text_tab(" ".join(words), expected_id=package.id)


main()

Save it as kern_proof_text.py. It should print:

Regular: 104 pairs, 104 proof words.
  /H/H/A/C/H/H
  /H/H/A/O/H/H
  /H/H/A/U/H/H

and open a tab with 104 words in it, beginning HHACHH HHAOHH HHAUHH. That's the design. I haven't seen the tab, and three things about it are open: whether a text of some 1,800 characters is accepted in one go, whether FontLab wraps it into lines, and whether the tab opens with kerning switched on. If the pairs look unkerned, look for the kerning switch in the tab's own controls.

Notes on the listing.

proof_words takes two dictionaries and returns a list. It never touches FontLab, so, as with yesterday's checks, you can try it on a made-up table.

The pairs are sorted by name, so the class pairs come first and the proof walks through A, then O, then T. That suits a first reading, because pairs that share a first letter sit side by side and can be compared with each other as well as with their frames. A reviewer who has an hour might prefer the deepest pairs first, and exercise 2 gives him that.

The script prints the first three words before it opens the tab. When a script hands a long text to a window, print the start of it. If the window shows something odd, you can tell whether the text was wrong or the window. I haven't seen the tab in FontLab 9, so that print is also the only part of the result this chapter can vouch for.

In Plum's Regular no word repeats: 104 pairs, 104 words. The not in is there for the font where one does.

docs.title: What Tobias does with it
docs.text:
Mira runs the script, looks at the tab for a minute, and marks two words herself before anything leaves the studio. HHLTHH is the pair chapter 74 flagged, and set between capitals it is as bad as the number said: the T sits on the foot of the L. And HHAOHH, one of the four pairs from Friday's note, shows almost no kerning at all next to its neighbors.

Then she prints the tab to a PDF and sends it. Tobias will write on a printout. What comes back are corrections by pair, and the script for taking those in is tomorrow's.

Fly also ships ready-made kerning proofs, long texts that type designers have used for years. fly.ap.kerning.proofs.run("kernking") opens one. They test a font against the pairs that matter in general. Today's proof tests the pairs this font has, which is a different question: the first finds what's missing, the second checks what's there.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A proof word puts a pair between letters whose spacing is trusted: HH beside capitals, nn beside small letters, chosen with name[0].isupper(). A glyph name is not a character, and in FontLab text you write a glyph by name as a slash and the name. " ".join(words) makes one text of many words, and a list with not in drops repeats and keeps the order. open_text_tab(text, expected_id=package.id) opens the text in a Glyph window, and refuses if the font has changed meanwhile.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Change frame so that figures get /zero/zero around them. A glyph is a figure if its name is one of zero, one, and so on up to nine: write the ten names in a list and use in. Plum has no figure pairs yet, so test word("seven", "one") by hand.
  2. Sort the pairs by value before making words, deepest first. You'll need sorted(pairs.items(), key=...) with a tuple key, as in chapter 74, and a loop that unpacks (first, second), value. Which word leads now?
  3. Make a second list of words with the pair turned round: for A before V, the word for V before A. Print only those whose turned pair is not in the kerning. It's a quick way to find pairs kerned in one direction only.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Tobias's corrections will come as a table: pair, master, new value. Chapter 78 writes the kerning out to a file a spreadsheet can open, and reads his edited copy back in.

docs.title: 78. Kerning in a spreadsheet
docs.text:
Wednesday of week fifteen. Tobias has the proof and a pencil. What he doesn't have is FontLab, and he isn't going to get it for one job. He's asked for the kerning as a table he can open in a spreadsheet, one row for each pair and one column for each weight. He'll change the cells he disagrees with and send the file back.

Review often happens outside the font editor. Chapter 28 sent a metrics table out as a CSV file and read one back. Today kerning makes the same round trip, and the way back is the harder half: the script has to find the handful of cells that changed among three hundred, and write only those.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The helpers ask and tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write them out again, so each one runs by itself.
  • The reports folder next to your font, from chapter 26.
  • A spreadsheet program, or a text editor and some patience.
  • The kerning as chapter 75 left it: 101, 104 and 102 pairs.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The file contents and counts below were produced in plain Python from Plum's source file.

docs.title: Step 1: One row for each pair
docs.text:
Monday's report collected every pair that any master has, with a union of sets. That collection is the table's rows. Each row has the two names and then three values, with an empty cell where a master lacks the pair:

def cell(value):
    if value is None:
        return ""
    return f"{value:.0f}"


print([cell(-69.0), cell(None), cell(11.0)])

['-69', '', '11']

The values come from FontLab as floats, and :.0f writes them without the .0 that would make Tobias wonder whether halves are allowed.

A row is a list, as chapter 28 said, and lists can be joined with a plus sign:

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
print(["First", "Second"] + MASTERS)

['First', 'Second', 'Light', 'Regular', 'Bold']

That's the heading row. The rows under it are built the same way: two names, plus a comprehension that asks each master for the pair with get. The whole of the writing is in the script below, in write_table. Run it with MODE = "out" and it should say:

104 rows written to plum-kerning.csv

Open the file in a text editor before you open it in a spreadsheet. The first lines should be:

First,Second,Light,Regular,Bold
@L_A,@R_C,-32,-13,-32
@L_A,@R_O2,-32,-7,-32
@L_A,@R_U2,-18,-20,-18

docs.title: Step 2: Be Tobias
docs.text:
You have no Tobias, so you'll have to do his part. Open plum-kerning.csv in a spreadsheet and make these ten changes. They're the loose ends that the last four chapters collected on Mira's list, with the values he chose from the proof:

First Second Column Was Becomes @L_A @R_O2 Regular −7 −24 @L_A Q Regular −7 −20 @L_O @R_A2 Regular −7 −20 L T Regular −113 −70 P @R_aacute Regular −10 empty P a Regular −10 empty Q @R_A2 Regular −7 −20 T @R_wacute Bold −94 −60 T w Bold −105 −60 questiondown exclamdown Light empty 8

Save the result as CSV under a new name, plum-kerning-tobias.csv, in the same folder. Keep the file you sent. When a correction looks odd next week, you'll want to see what the cell said before.

A warning about spreadsheets. Some of them see a cell that begins with @ and take it for a formula. If yours complains about the first column, import the file with that column set to text.

docs.title: Step 3: Read it back, and count
docs.text:
Reading a CSV is chapter 28's csv.reader, which gives each row as a list of strings. Compare each cell with the font, and collect the ones that differ:

changes = []
for row in rows[1:]:
    if not row:
        continue
    first, second = row[0], row[1]
    for master, text in zip(MASTERS, row[2:]):
        if text != tables[master].get((first, second)):
            changes.append((master, first, second, text))
print(len(changes))

rows[1:] skips the heading. zip is from chapter 35: it walks two lists side by side, here the three master names and the three cells after the names.

312

Three hundred and twelve changes, where Tobias made ten. 104 rows of three cells is 312: every cell in the file differs from the font.

You've been here before. A file holds text. The cell says "-32", a string, and the font says -32.0, a number, and a string is never equal to a number, whatever they look like when printed. The empty cell is "" and the font's answer for a missing pair is None, and those aren't equal either.

Had the script gone on to write its "changes", it would have handed 312 strings to write_kerning. As far as I can read its source, that function refuses anything that isn't a whole number, so the font would have been safe. The count is still what told you, before any write: when a plan is thirty times bigger than you expected, stop and find out why.

docs.title: Step 4: Turn a cell into a value
docs.text:
Each cell has to become what the font would hold: a whole number, or None for an empty cell. Fly has a function made for this cell:

import fly.ap.kerning.edit.model as kerning_edit

print([kerning_edit.parse_cell("-32"), kerning_edit.parse_cell(""), kerning_edit.parse_cell(" 8 ")])
print(kerning_edit.parse_cell("−70"))

[-32, None, 8]
-70

It strips spaces, reads the number, and returns None for an empty cell. The second line shows a courtesy you'd not have thought of until it bit you. Some spreadsheets and some careful typists write a true minus sign, −, where a keyboard gives a hyphen, -. To a person they're the same. To Python's float the first is not a number at all. parse_cell accepts both.

And -32 == -32.0 is true: a whole number and a float with the same value are equal. So the parsed cell can be compared with the font's value directly.

What if a cell holds ? or ask Mira? parse_cell raises a ValueError, as float did in chapter 68. Tobias is a person with a pencil, so the script should expect it: catch the error with chapter 19's try, note the row and the text, and go on to the next cell. One bad cell shouldn't hide the nine good ones, and it shouldn't be written either.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Kerning CSV
# MODE "out" writes every kerning pair to a CSV table, one column per master.
# MODE "in" reads an edited copy and writes only the cells that changed.
import csv
from pathlib import Path

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.kerning.batch as kerning_batch
import fly.ap.kerning.edit.model as kerning_edit
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
MODE = "out"
OUT_NAME = "plum-kerning.csv"
IN_NAME = "plum-kerning-tobias.csv"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def cell(value):
    if value is None:
        return ""
    return f"{value:.0f}"


def write_table(tables, address):
    everything = set()
    for master in MASTERS:
        everything = everything | set(tables[master])
    with open(address, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
        writer = csv.writer(f)
        writer.writerow(["First", "Second"] + MASTERS)
        for first, second in sorted(everything):
            values = [cell(tables[master].get((first, second))) for master in MASTERS]
            writer.writerow([first, second] + values)
    return len(everything)


def read_changes(tables, address):
    with open(address, encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
        rows = list(csv.reader(f))
    changes = []
    problems = []
    for number, row in enumerate(rows[1:], 2):
        if not row:
            continue
        first, second = row[0], row[1]
        for master, text in zip(MASTERS, row[2:]):
            try:
                new = kerning_edit.parse_cell(text)
            except ValueError:
                problems.append((number, master, text))
                continue
            old = tables[master].get((first, second))
            if new != old:
                changes.append((master, first, second, old, new))
    return changes, problems


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    tables = {master: scripting.kerning_pairs(package, master) for master in MASTERS}
    folder = Path(font.path).parent / "reports"

    if MODE == "out":
        count = write_table(tables, folder / OUT_NAME)
        print(f"{count} rows written to {OUT_NAME}")
        return

    changes, problems = read_changes(tables, folder / IN_NAME)
    for master, first, second, old, new in changes:
        print(f"{master:<9}{first:<14}{second:<12}{cell(old):>5} ->{cell(new):>5}")
    print(f"{len(changes)} cells differ from the font.")
    for number, master, text in problems:
        print(f"row {number}, {master}: can't read {text!r}")
    if problems or not changes:
        return
    if not ask(f"Write {len(changes)} kerning values?"):
        return

    edits = {}
    for master, first, second, old, new in changes:
        if master not in edits:
            edits[master] = {}
        edits[master][(first, second)] = new
    kerning_batch.write_kerning(package, edits, "Kerning from CSV")
    tables = {master: scripting.kerning_pairs(package, master) for master in MASTERS}
    changes, problems = read_changes(tables, folder / IN_NAME)
    print(f"Done. {len(changes)} cells differ from the font.")


main()

Save it as kerning_csv.py. Change MODE to "in" and run it:

Regular  @L_A          @R_O2          -7 ->  -24
Regular  @L_A          Q              -7 ->  -20
Regular  @L_O          @R_A2          -7 ->  -20
Regular  L             T            -113 ->  -70
Regular  P             @R_aacute     -10 ->
Regular  P             a             -10 ->
Regular  Q             @R_A2          -7 ->  -20
Bold     T             @R_wacute     -94 ->  -60
Bold     T             w            -105 ->  -60
Light    questiondown  exclamdown        ->    8
10 cells differ from the font.

Ten, and they're the ten in the table above. Click Yes:

Done. 0 cells differ from the font.

All three masters now have 102 pairs, and the same 102. Run Monday's orphan_pairs.py and its last line should read 102 different pairs, 0 not in every master. One Undo should take all ten back. I haven't seen it in FontLab 9.

Notes on the listing.

enumerate(rows[1:], 2) numbers the rows from 2, because that's the number the spreadsheet shows beside the first row under the heading. A message that says "row 37" should mean the row 37 Tobias sees.

{text!r} in an f-string prints the text with its quotes, as repr would. For a cell with a stray space or nothing in it, the quotes are what let you see the problem.

if problems or not changes: return stops in two cases. If any cell couldn't be read, nothing is written until a person has looked at it. A half-applied review is hard to reason about afterwards.

cell serves both directions. It formats values for the file and for the report, so an empty old or new value prints as a gap.

An empty cell under a pair that exists means "remove this pair", through the None order of chapter 73. That's the right meaning for a kerning table and a dangerous one for a careless reviewer, which is one more reason the script prints every change and asks.

The same check as on Friday closes the run: read the font again, compare again, and print the count.

docs.title: What the round trip settled
docs.text:
Mira's list from the last four chapters is empty. The L T of the Regular no longer sits apart from its neighbors. The four A and O pairs of the Regular are in line with the other weights. The two P pairs are gone, and the Spanish question mark has its pair in the Light.

Two of Tobias's values are in the Bold, and both pull its kerning back. He wrote one more line at the bottom of the printout, in pencil: "Bold: all of it feels a notch too strong. Not pair by pair." That was Mira's own note of last Thursday, and it's tomorrow's chapter.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A kerning table for review has one row for each pair that any master holds, and an empty cell where a master lacks it. What comes back from a file is text: "-32" is not -32.0, and "" is not None. kerning_edit.parse_cell turns a cell into a whole number or None, and you collect only the cells that differ from the font. If the count of changes is far from what you expect, or a cell can't be read, stop before writing.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. In your copy of Tobias's file, put ? in one cell and run the script with MODE = "in". Read the message. Then put the old value back.
  2. Add a column Note at the end of the table when writing, empty for every row. Does read_changes still work on a file with that column? Work out why from what zip does when one list is longer than the other.
  3. Write the table with the rows sorted by the Regular's value, deepest first, and pairs the Regular lacks at the end. You'll need a key function that returns a tuple, and a decision about what a missing value sorts as.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: "All of it a notch too strong." Chapter 79 turns the whole of the Bold's kerning down by a percentage, in one step, and looks hard at what rounding does to small pairs on the way.

docs.title: 79. Scale the kerning
docs.text:
Thursday of week fifteen. Tobias's pencil note says the Bold's kerning is "a notch too strong. Not pair by pair." Mira agrees, and she knows why. Most of the Bold's values were carried over from the Light, as chapter 74 found, and they were too strong from the start. Chapter 68 then opened up every right side, and a pair that pulled two letters together by 90 units is now pulling across a wider gap than it was drawn for.

Nobody wants to retype 102 values. The relations between the pairs are sound: AV should stay deeper than AO. What's wrong is the strength of all of them together. So every value gets multiplied by the same number, a little less than one. The arithmetic is one line. Most of the chapter is about what happens to the fractions.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The helpers ask and tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write them out again, so each one runs by itself.
  • The kerning as chapter 78 left it: 102 pairs in each master.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The numbers below were computed in plain Python from Plum's source file with the changes of chapters 72 to 78 applied.

docs.title: Step 1: How strong is a master's kerning?
docs.text:
"Too strong" needs a number before you change it. A fair one is the sum of all the values, each taken without its sign, so that a pair which pushes apart counts as much as one which pulls together. Chapter 36 had abs for that:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

package = scripting.current_package()
for master in ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]:
    pairs = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, master)
    print(master, sum([abs(value) for value in pairs.values()]))

Light 5232.0
Regular 4924.0
Bold 5988.0

The same 102 pairs in each, and the Bold spends a fifth more than the Regular on them. That agrees with what two people saw on paper.

Mira's first thought is 80 per cent. That would bring the Bold to about 4,790, under the Regular, and a bold face usually wants a little more kerning than its regular, since its letters are heavier and its gaps show more. She settles on 85 per cent, which gives about 5,090.

docs.title: Step 2: Multiply one value
docs.text:
value = -90.0
print(value * 85 / 100)

-76.5

Kerning values are whole units, so that has to become −76 or −77. You know round from chapter 11:

print(round(-76.5), round(-59.5), round(-8.5))

-76 -60 -8

Look at those three. −76.5 went toward zero. −59.5 went away from zero. −8.5 went toward zero again. Python's round sends a half to the nearest even number. That's a sound rule for statistics, because the halves don't all lean the same way. For kerning it means that two pairs which were equal steps apart can end up at uneven steps, and which way a half goes depends on whether its neighbor is odd or even.

Fly's kerning tools use the rule from school: a half goes away from zero, always.

import fly.ap.kerning.edit.model as kerning_edit

print(kerning_edit.scaled(-90, 85), kerning_edit.scaled(-70, 85), kerning_edit.scaled(-10, 85))

-77 -60 -9

scaled(value, percent) multiplies, divides by a hundred and rounds that way. In the Bold, 6 of the 102 products land on a half at 85 per cent, and for 4 of them the two rules disagree. One unit, in four pairs: nobody will see it. The reason to use scaled is that Fly's kerning tools round the same way, so your script's result will match what a colleague gets from them.

docs.title: Step 3: The plan
docs.text:
A plan is a dictionary from pair to new value, holding only the pairs that change. A value that would become 0 gets None, the removal order of chapter 73, because a pair of 0 does nothing and still takes up room:

def scale_plan(pairs, percent):
    plan = {}
    for pair, value in pairs.items():
        new = kerning_edit.scaled(value, percent)
        if new == value:
            continue
        if new == 0:
            new = None
        plan[pair] = new
    return plan

It takes a dictionary and a number and never touches FontLab, so try it on a made-up table first:

print(scale_plan({("A", "V"): -90.0, ("r", "y"): 2.0, ("o", "o"): 0.4}, 85))

{('A', 'V'): -77, ('o', 'o'): None}

Three pairs in, two orders out. r y at 2 would be 1.7, which rounds back to 2, so it's left alone. The 0.4 becomes nothing and is removed.

docs.title: Step 4: Eighty-five of what?
docs.text:
Now the real table. Chapter 68 scaled the sidebearings with a factor, 0.8, and the hand remembers:

PERCENT = 0.85

pairs = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, "Bold")
plan = scale_plan(pairs, PERCENT)
gone = [pair for pair in plan if plan[pair] is None]
print(len(plan), "pairs change,", len(gone), "would be removed.")

102 pairs change, 58 would be removed.

The function wanted a percentage and got a factor. It did what it was told: it scaled every value to 0.85 per cent of itself. −90 became −0.765, which rounds to −1. Anything under 59 became less than a half and was marked for removal. One click on Yes and the Bold would have had 44 pairs left, each of them −1.

Two things stood between that and the font. The function is called with a number whose unit is in the parameter's name, percent, and the constant is named PERCENT, so the mistake is visible in the script to anyone who reads it. And the plan was counted before it was written. "58 would be removed" is not what turning something down by a notch looks like.

The script gets a guard as well. A percentage under 10 or over 300 is almost certainly a slip, so it refuses and says why. Set PERCENT = 85:

102 pairs change, 0 would be removed.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Scale Kerning
# Multiplies every kerning value of MASTER by PERCENT / 100.
# Halves round away from zero. A pair that becomes 0 is removed.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.kerning.batch as kerning_batch
import fly.ap.kerning.edit.model as kerning_edit
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTER = "Bold"
PERCENT = 85
SHOW = 7


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


def strength(pairs):
    return sum([abs(value) for value in pairs.values()])


def scale_plan(pairs, percent):
    plan = {}
    for pair, value in pairs.items():
        new = kerning_edit.scaled(value, percent)
        if new == value:
            continue
        if new == 0:
            new = None
        plan[pair] = new
    return plan


def size_then_name(item):
    pair, value = item
    return (abs(value), pair)


def main():
    if fl.CurrentFont() is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    if PERCENT < 10 or PERCENT > 300:
        tell(f"PERCENT is {PERCENT}. Write 85 for 85 per cent.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    pairs = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, MASTER)
    plan = scale_plan(pairs, PERCENT)
    gone = [pair for pair in plan if plan[pair] is None]

    print(f"{MASTER} at {PERCENT} per cent. The {SHOW} smallest pairs:")
    for (first, second), value in sorted(pairs.items(), key=size_then_name)[:SHOW]:
        new = plan.get((first, second), value)
        print(f"  {first:<12}{second:<12}{value:>5.0f} -> {new}")
    print(f"{len(plan)} pairs change, {len(gone)} would be removed.")
    if not plan:
        return
    if not ask(f"Scale {len(plan)} pairs of the {MASTER} to {PERCENT} per cent?"):
        return

    before = strength(pairs)
    kerning_batch.write_kerning(package, {MASTER: plan}, "Scale kerning")
    pairs = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, MASTER)
    print(f"Done. Strength {before:.0f} -> {strength(pairs):.0f}, {len(pairs)} pairs.")


main()

Save it as scale_kerning.py. It should print:

Bold at 85 per cent. The 7 smallest pairs:
  @L_W        @R_aacute     -10 -> -9
  @L_W        @R_oacute     -12 -> -10
  V           @R_uacute     -14 -> -12
  V           u             -14 -> -12
  r           @R_yacute      14 -> 12
  r           y              14 -> 12
  t           quoteright     15 -> 13
102 pairs change, 0 would be removed.

and, after Yes:

Done. Strength 5988 -> 5090, 102 pairs.

One Undo step should take it back. I haven't seen it in FontLab 9.

Notes on the listing.

The script shows the smallest pairs because that's where scaling does its damage. A big pair loses 15 per cent of itself, give or take a hair. A small one can't. −10 should become −8.5 and becomes −9, which is 90 per cent. −12 becomes −10, which is 83. Had there been a pair of 3, it would have become 2.55 and rounded back to 3: not scaled at all. The smaller the value, the coarser the steps it can take. That's worth seeing before you agree, and it's why chapter 75 removed the tiny pairs first.

size_then_name returns a tuple, as the sort keys of chapter 74 did: smallest size first, and the pair's names to settle ties, so the list comes out in the same order every time.

plan.get((first, second), value) uses the second argument of get from chapter 22's tally: if the pair isn't in the plan, it stays as it is, and the line shows its present value.

{MASTER: plan} is the whole of the edit that write_kerning wants: a dictionary from master name to that master's orders.

The last line reads the font again and measures again, as every writing script in this part has done.

docs.title: Don't run it twice
docs.text:
Run the script a second time and it will scale the scaled values: 85 per cent of 85 per cent is about 72. Nothing in the font says "this has been scaled", so the script can't know. The Undo step is your way back, and the strength it prints is your way of knowing where you are: the Bold should read 5,090 after one run. If it reads about 4,320, it has been run twice.

Scaling isn't its own undo either. You might think 118 per cent would take the 85 back. Try the smallest pair: −10 became −9, and −9 at 118 per cent is −10.62, which rounds to −11. Every rounding loses what was after the decimal point, and no later multiplication can find it again. To go back, use Undo, or keep the CSV from yesterday, which holds every value as it was.

docs.title: What Mira sees
docs.text:
She runs Tuesday's proof script again. The Bold's HHAYHH has let go a little, from −90 to −77, and the quoteright pairs no longer look as if the apostrophe were falling into the letter after it. L T is at −72, in step with its neighbors.

She writes "Bold kerning: 85%" in the project notebook, with the date. A number like that is soon forgotten and can't be recovered from the font.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: To change how strong a whole master's kerning is, multiply every value by one percentage, and measure the strength before and after with the sum of abs(value). Python's round sends a half to the even neighbor, and kerning_edit.scaled(value, percent) sends it away from zero, as Fly's kerning tools do. Name a quantity by its unit, and refuse values that can only be slips: 0.85 is not 85. Scaling twice compounds, and scaling back doesn't restore what rounding dropped, so write down the percentage you used.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Without writing anything, find out how many pairs of the Bold would be removed at 3 per cent. Change PERCENT, and change the guard for the moment so that it lets you. Put both back afterwards.
  2. Add a constant ONLY_NEGATIVE = True. When it's on, scale_plan should leave the positive pairs alone. You'll need one more if with continue. How many pairs change now?
  3. kerning_edit.round_to(value, step) snaps a value to a multiple of step, with the same rule for halves. Write a plan that rounds every Bold pair to a multiple of 5 and print how many would change. Don't write it. Some designers keep all kerning on a grid like that, and some think it throws away good work.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The spacing is set and the kerning is reviewed. Chapter 80 gathers the checks of this part into one audit that Mira can run on a Friday, and holds it against the proof that started it all.

docs.title: 80. The proof comes back clean
docs.text:
Friday of week fifteen. Nearly four weeks ago the publisher's typesetter wrote that the Bold looked gappy and she couldn't say where. Since then the Bold has had its right sides opened, its J mended, its figures lined up, its kerning sorted into classes, reviewed and turned down. A new set of fonts goes to her this afternoon.

Before it does, Mira wants one page that says the spacing is in order, and she wants to be able to make that page again in a month, after the next round of changes, without remembering what was on it. Each check on it exists already, somewhere in the last nineteen chapters. Today's script gathers them. It changes nothing in the font.

The new idea: a function can be put in a list like any other value.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The helper tell from chapter 39. The scripts below write it out again, so each one runs by itself.
  • The font as chapter 79 left it.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The counts below were computed in plain Python from Plum's source file with this part's changes applied.

docs.title: Step 1: One check, one function
docs.text:
Every check in this part asked a question and collected the answers that were wrong. Give them all the same form: a function that takes the font and the kerning, and returns a list of problems as plain sentences. An empty list means the check passed.

Here is chapter 73's rule that kerning values are whole numbers, in that form:

def check_whole(font, tables, classes):
    problems = []
    for master in tables:
        for (first, second), value in tables[master].items():
            if value != int(value):
                problems.append(f"{master}: {first} {second} is {value}")
    return problems

tables is the dictionary from chapter 76: master name to that master's pairs. classes is the same for the classes. This check doesn't use font or classes at all. It takes them anyway, so that every check can be called the same way, and you'll see in a moment why that's worth an unused parameter or two.

And here is chapter 61's word test:

WORD = "minimum"
SPREAD_LIMIT = 16


def check_word(font, tables, classes):
    problems = []
    for master in MASTERS:
        gaps = [gap(font, a, b, master) for a, b in zip(WORD, WORD[1:])]
        if max(gaps) - min(gaps) > SPREAD_LIMIT:
            problems.append(f"{master}: gaps in {WORD} run from {min(gaps)} to {max(gaps)}")
    return problems

gap is the function from chapter 61: the right sidebearing of one letter plus the left sidebearing of the next.

docs.title: Step 2: A list of functions
docs.text:
You've passed a function to another function since chapter 36: sorted(rows, key=by_width) hands over by_width without brackets, and sorted calls it when it wants to. A function's name without brackets is the function itself, a value like a number or a string. So it can go in a list:

CHECKS = [check_word, check_whole]

for check in CHECKS:
    problems = check(font, tables, classes)
    for line in problems:
        print(line)

Each time round the loop, check is a different function, and check(font, tables, classes) calls whichever one it is. That's why they all take the same three things. Adding a check to the audit is now one line in the list, and the loop never changes.

Run that with the two checks, and with the tables read as in chapter 76. It prints nothing at all. The Output panel stays empty.

docs.title: Step 3: What does silence mean?
docs.text:
Ines looks at the empty Output panel. "Is that good, or did it not run?"

It's a fair question and the script can't answer it. An audit that prints nothing when all is well prints the same nothing when MASTERS is empty, when the kerning failed to load, or when a check has a slip in it that makes it skip everything. This is the mistake to avoid in any checking script: silence that might mean "clean" and might mean "didn't look".

There are two cures and the audit needs both.

The first is to make each check say how much it looked at. A line that reads whole values: 306 looked at, ok can be believed. A line that reads 0 looked at, ok tells you at once that something upstream is empty. So each check returns two things: a count and the list of problems. The full script below has every check in that form, with a looked counter beside the list.

The second is to see every check fail once. You did this in chapters 75 and 76 with made-up tables, and it's the same here, with the counting version of check_whole:

fake = {"Light": {("A", "V"): -66.5, ("T", "o"): -40.0}}
print(check_whole(None, fake, None))

(2, ['Light: A V is -66.5'])

Two values looked at, one problem, and it's the one you planted. The function never touches its first and third arguments, so None will do for them.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Spacing Audit
# Runs the spacing and kerning checks of Part 4 and prints one line for each.
# Changes nothing.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

TITLE = "Halfmoon"

MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
WORD = "minimum"
SPREAD_LIMIT = 16
SAME_WIDTH = ["zero", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven",
              "eight", "nine", "dollar", "Euro", "sterling", "yen"]
DEEPEST = -120


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def gap(font, first, second, master):
    return pGlyph(font, font[first]).getRSB(master) + pGlyph(font, font[second]).getLSB(master)


def check_word(font, tables, classes):
    problems = []
    looked = 0
    for master in MASTERS:
        gaps = [gap(font, a, b, master) for a, b in zip(WORD, WORD[1:])]
        looked = looked + len(gaps)
        if max(gaps) - min(gaps) > SPREAD_LIMIT:
