            problems.append(f"{master}: gaps in {WORD} run from {min(gaps)} to {max(gaps)}")
    return looked, problems


def check_same_width(font, tables, classes):
    problems = []
    looked = 0
    for master in MASTERS:
        widths = [pGlyph(font, font[name]).getAdvance(master) for name in SAME_WIDTH]
        looked = looked + len(widths)
        if len(set(widths)) != 1:
            problems.append(f"{master}: figure widths are {sorted(set(widths))}")
    return looked, problems


def check_whole(font, tables, classes):
    problems = []
    looked = 0
    for master in tables:
        for (first, second), value in tables[master].items():
            looked = looked + 1
            if value != int(value):
                problems.append(f"{master}: {first} {second} is {value}")
    return looked, problems


def check_deep(font, tables, classes):
    problems = []
    looked = 0
    for master in tables:
        for (first, second), value in tables[master].items():
            looked = looked + 1
            if value < DEEPEST:
                problems.append(f"{master}: {first} {second} is {value:.0f}")
    return looked, problems


def check_names(font, tables, classes):
    have = {glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs}
    problems = []
    looked = 0
    for master in tables:
        for pair in tables[master]:
            looked = looked + 1
            for side in pair:
                if side.startswith("@"):
                    if side[1:] not in classes[master]:
                        problems.append(f"{master}: no class {side}")
                elif side not in have:
                    problems.append(f"{master}: no glyph {side}")
    return looked, problems


def check_same_pairs(font, tables, classes):
    everything = set()
    for master in tables:
        everything = everything | set(tables[master])
    problems = []
    for first, second in sorted(everything):
        missing = [master for master in tables if (first, second) not in tables[master]]
        if missing:
            problems.append(f"{first} {second} is not in {', '.join(missing)}")
    return len(everything), problems


CHECKS = [
    ("word spacing", check_word),
    ("figure widths", check_same_width),
    ("whole values", check_whole),
    ("deepest pair", check_deep),
    ("names in pairs", check_names),
    ("same pairs", check_same_pairs),
]


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    tables = {master: scripting.kerning_pairs(package, master) for master in MASTERS}
    classes = {master: scripting.kerning_classes(package, master) for master in MASTERS}

    total = 0
    for label, check in CHECKS:
        looked, problems = check(font, tables, classes)
        total = total + len(problems)
        verdict = "ok"
        if problems:
            verdict = f"{len(problems)} problems"
        print(f"{label:<16}{looked:>4} looked at   {verdict}")
        for line in problems:
            print("   ", line)
    print(f"{len(CHECKS)} checks, {total} problems.")


main()

Save it as spacing_audit.py. On the font as chapter 79 left it, it should print:

word spacing      18 looked at   ok
figure widths     42 looked at   ok
whole values     306 looked at   ok
deepest pair     306 looked at   ok
names in pairs   306 looked at   ok
same pairs       102 looked at   ok
6 checks, 0 problems.

Seven lines, and every one says how much stood behind its "ok": 18 gaps, 42 widths, 306 kerning values, 102 different pairs.

Notes on the listing.

CHECKS is a list of tuples, a label and a function, and the loop unpacks each as for label, check in CHECKS. The label is what a person reads. The function is what the script calls.

CHECKS stands after the functions it names. Python reads a file from the top, and a name must exist before a line can use it. Inside a function's body that doesn't matter until the function is called, which is why main can sit anywhere. In a line at the left margin it matters at once.

Every check loops over tables or MASTERS and counts as it goes. The count costs one line and it's what makes the "ok" worth reading.

check_names is chapter 76's orphan check, written to give sentences. for side in pair walks the two names of a pair, since a tuple can be looped over like a list.

check_same_pairs counts different pairs, not values, so its number is 102 where the others say 306.

The limits at the top are opinions, and they're Mira's. A spread of 16 in minimum is what she accepts: the Light and the Regular both come to 14, and the Bold to 8. −120 is deeper than any pair Plum has now. A limit belongs in a constant with a name, where the next person can find it and disagree.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
You've seen one check fail on a made-up table. See the audit fail on the font. Change DEEPEST to −110 and run it again:

deepest pair     306 looked at   18 problems
    Light: quoteright @R_eacute is -112
    Light: quoteright @R_oacute is -112

and sixteen more lines like them, nine in the Light and nine in the Regular, then 6 checks, 18 problems. All eighteen are the apostrophe before a round letter, at −112. The Bold has none, since yesterday took its deepest pairs to −105. Mira knows these pairs and wants them as they are, so the limit goes back to −120. That's an honest way to deal with a known exception: the limit is moved in plain sight, and the next pair that goes deeper will still be caught.

docs.title: What the audit doesn't say
docs.text:
Read the seven lines again and notice what they claim. The gaps in one word are even. Fourteen glyphs share a width. The kerning is tidy, consistent and within a limit. None of that says the font is well spaced. A font could pass every line and look dreadful, if the limits were met by values that are wrong together.

The audit says something narrower and still worth having: nothing has slipped since a person last looked. The looking was done by Mira over four weeks and by Tobias with a pencil. The script holds what they decided, so that a careless edit in week twenty shows up as a line that isn't "ok".

Mira pastes the seven lines into the mail that goes with the fonts.

The typesetter's answer comes on Monday. "Headings are fine now. The whole thing sits better, I can't say why." Ines reads it twice. She can say why, to the unit: the Bold's right sides are four fifths of the Regular's, and its kerning is 85 per cent of what it was.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A function's name without brackets is the function, and it can be stored in a list or a tuple and called later. Give a family of checks the same parameters and the same kind of result, and one loop can run them all. A check that reports nothing when it passes can't be told from a check that didn't run, so return how much was looked at and see every check fail once before you trust its "ok". An audit shows that nothing has slipped since a person judged the font, and it doesn't do the judging.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a check check_strength that reports a master whose kerning strength, as chapter 79 measured it, is more than 1.05 times the Regular's. It should look at three numbers. It should report the Light, at about 1.06. Is that a problem, or a limit to discuss with Mira?
  2. Plant a fault in the font: give the Bold sterling ten more units of width with set_sb.py or by hand. Run the audit, read the line, then undo.
  3. Chapter 64's follower report is missing from the audit. Write check_followers using the LEFT families: a problem is a follower whose left sidebearing differs from its model's by more than 3. Decide what "looked at" should count.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The letters are drawn and the space between them is set. Part 5 is about words: the names of glyphs, the names of fonts, and the text that scripts read and write. It starts with an export that complains about a glyph called uni0041.alt2 copy.

docs.title: Part 5: Words
docs.text:
Every drawer needs a label somebody else can read.

The font must work in real text.

The spacing is settled and the publisher is about to set whole books in Plum. A typesetter doesn't pick glyphs out of a grid. She types, and the font has to turn her typing into the right shapes: the letter she pressed, the small cap she asked for, the fraction in a recipe. When that fails, the cause is almost never a drawing. It's a name, a code or a line of feature text.

The first six chapters are about names and Unicode, the two labels every glyph carries. You check the names against the rules, derive each label from the other, find glyphs with two characters, ask which languages the font covers, and propose a better order for the Font window.

The next eight are about OpenType features. You read the feature text, write a small-caps feature by script, build features from glyph suffixes, make ligatures, keep classes up to date, write fractions, check the text before you compile it, and measure how much of the alphabet each feature covers. No call compiles features from Python, so the Compile button stays in your hand throughout.

Then five chapters on Font Info: the names, the vertical numbers, the version, the copyright line, and one settings file for a family delivered as several fonts.

The last chapter gathers the checks into one pre-flight, and lists the tests a person still does by hand.

Oskar comes back from his leave in the middle of this part, in chapter 93, three days a week. From then on he's in the room, with stories about what went wrong before anybody checked. His sheet has two lines open when the part begins. This part crosses out one of them, in chapter 100:

  • Put the family name and the version in every weight.

You need the practice copy of Plum as Part 4 left it, and Fly installed in FontLab 9. Each script defines the small helpers it uses, such as tell and ask from chapter 39, so you can start at any chapter. That copy has 251 glyphs: Plum's 205, the fifteen with a suffix from Part 2, and the thirty-one accented letters and accents Part 3 built. The counts in this part are for that font. If you closed it without saving at the end of chapter 60, your counts are lower by thirty-one wherever glyphs or characters are counted, and chapter 91 will find four capitals missing from a class where I find nineteen. Nothing in this part was run in FontLab 9 by me. Each chapter says how its outputs were computed.

docs.title: 81. Good names
docs.text:
Monday of week sixteen. The typesetter's mail about the headings is an hour old when a second one arrives, from the same publisher and a different desk. Their production system has turned back Friday's test fonts. It quotes one glyph name, uni0041.alt2 copy, and says nothing else.

Ines knows where the name came from. Somebody duplicated an alternate A in the real Plum to try an idea, FontLab called the duplicate "copy", and nobody tidied up. She sends Mira a short list of other names she doesn't trust and asks for something that checks all of them, and the font's own, before the next export.

A glyph name is a string. This chapter is about asking a string what it is made of.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The tell function from chapter 39. The script below defines it again, so it runs by itself.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The outputs below were computed in plain Python. I haven't seen which names FontLab itself refuses when you type them into the Font window, or what an export says about a bad one, so this chapter claims nothing about either.

docs.title: Step 1: What a name may contain
docs.text:
The rules for glyph names are older than FontLab and most font tools agree on them. A name is made of the letters A to Z and a to z, the digits, the period and the underscore. It doesn't start with a digit. It is at most 63 characters long. .notdef is the one name that starts with a period.

The period and the underscore each have a job. A period separates a glyph's base name from a suffix that says which variant it is: a.sc, zero.alt. An underscore joins the parts of a ligature: f_i. Chapters 89 and 90 build features from these two marks and no others, which is one reason to keep them clean now.

A space breaks the rules, and so does a hyphen. So does ñ as a name, though it looks harmless: the letter is called ntilde.

Fly's own rename tool allows the hyphen. Fonts that go to print shops and web servers shouldn't have it, so Mira's rule leaves it out.

docs.title: Step 2: Ask the whole string
docs.text:
In chapter 13 you asked a string isupper(). Strings answer other questions of that kind. One of them sounds like what you need: isalnum() is true when every character is a letter or a digit.

for name in ["Aacute", "a.sc", "3quarters", "ñ"]:
    print(name, name.isalnum())

Aacute True
a.sc False
3quarters True
ñ True

Three of the four answers are wrong for our purpose. a.sc is a good name and gets False, because a period is neither letter nor digit. 3quarters is a bad name and gets True. And ñ gets True, because to Python it is a letter. Python knows the alphabets of the world. Glyph names know one.

A ready-made question answers what its author meant by it. Before you lean on one, try it on the cases you care about, good and bad.

docs.title: Step 3: Ask each character
docs.text:
So write the alphabet down yourself. A string can serve as a set of allowed characters, since in works on strings character by character:

LOWER = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"
DIGITS = "0123456789"
ALLOWED = LOWER + LOWER.upper() + DIGITS + "._"

print(len(ALLOWED))
print("a" in ALLOWED, " " in ALLOWED, "ñ" in ALLOWED)

64
True False False

Twenty-six small letters, twenty-six capitals, ten digits, two marks. Now collect the characters of a name that aren't in it. This is a comprehension with a condition, as in chapter 37, looping over a string as chapter 9 did:

def strays(text, allowed):
    return [ch for ch in text if ch not in allowed]


print(strays("a.sc", ALLOWED))
print(strays("uni0041.alt2 copy", ALLOWED))
print(strays("germandbls-old", ALLOWED))

[]
[' ']
['-']

The function returns the offenders, not True or False. An empty list means the name is clean, and a list with something in it tells you what to look for. That matters with a space. [' '] shows it between quotes, where you can see it. Printed bare, a space at the end of a name is invisible.

strays takes the allowed characters as a parameter, so it can serve again with a different alphabet. It will, in step 5.

docs.title: Step 4: The rules about position
docs.text:
The alphabet isn't the whole rule. Three more checks look at where a character stands, and each is one line with tools you have:

name = "3quarters"
print(name[0] in DIGITS)

name = "a.sc."
print(name[-1] == ".")

name = "e..sc"
print(".." in name)

True
True
True

name[0] is the first character and name[-1] the last. The square brackets you used on lists in chapter 10 work the same way on strings. ".." in name asks whether two periods stand side by side anywhere: in on strings finds a run of characters, not only a single one. Neither a.sc. nor e..sc has a stray character. Both are typing slips that leave an empty piece where a suffix should be.

Put together, with the same shape as the checks in chapter 80: one name in, a list of plain sentences out.

def name_problems(name):
    if name in SPECIAL:
        return []
    problems = []
    if len(name) > LONGEST:
        problems.append(f"is {len(name)} characters long, the limit is {LONGEST}")
    if name[0] in DIGITS:
        problems.append("starts with a digit")
    if name[0] == "." or name[-1] == ".":
        problems.append("starts or ends with a period")
    if ".." in name:
        problems.append("has two periods in a row")
    bad = strays(name, ALLOWED)
    if bad:
        problems.append(f"has characters that aren't allowed: {bad}")
    return problems

SPECIAL holds .notdef, which is let through before any rule can object to its period. Every if stands alone, with no elif, because one name can break several rules and the report should list them all.

docs.title: Step 5: Two kinds of good name
docs.text:
uni0041.alt2 copy has a second oddity, apart from its space. Its base says uni0041 where you'd expect A.

Both are legal. A and Aacute are friendly names, the ones people read. uni0041 and uni00C1 say the same thing by code point: uni and then four hex digits, in capitals. You met hex in chapter 6. Programs can work out the character from such a name without a table, which is why exported fonts often carry them, and they are called production names. FontLab can show you friendly names while you work and write production names on export. I haven't found a call in Fly that translates one into the other, so this book doesn't use one.

In a working file a uni name is usually a glyph that came in from somewhere else and hasn't been given its friendly name. That's worth a note in the report, not a complaint. Recognising one takes split from chapter 9 to cut the suffix off, and strays again with a different alphabet:

HEX = DIGITS + "ABCDEF"


def is_uni_name(name):
    base = name.split(".")[0]
    if not base.startswith("uni") or len(base) != 7:
        return False
    return not strays(base[3:], HEX)


for name in ["uni00C1", "uni00C1.sc", "unicorn", "uni00c1"]:
    print(name, is_uni_name(name))

uni00C1 True
uni00C1.sc True
unicorn False
uni00c1 False

base[3:] is a slice, as on a list: everything after the first three characters. not strays(...) is true when the list is empty. unicorn has the right length and the wrong digits. uni00c1 has small letters where the rule wants capitals, and tools that read production names won't recognise it. Chapter 82 turns names like these into friendly ones.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Name Check
# Checks every glyph name in the font, and any names pasted into EXTRA,
# against the naming rules. Changes nothing.
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


EXTRA = [
    "uni0041.alt2 copy", "3quarters", "e..sc", "ñ",
    "germandbls-old", "a.sc.", "uni00C1", "A.alt2",
]

LOWER = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"
DIGITS = "0123456789"
ALLOWED = LOWER + LOWER.upper() + DIGITS + "._"
HEX = DIGITS + "ABCDEF"
LONGEST = 63
SPECIAL = [".notdef"]


def strays(text, allowed):
    return [ch for ch in text if ch not in allowed]


def is_uni_name(name):
    base = name.split(".")[0]
    if not base.startswith("uni") or len(base) != 7:
        return False
    return not strays(base[3:], HEX)


def name_problems(name):
    if name in SPECIAL:
        return []
    problems = []
    if len(name) > LONGEST:
        problems.append(f"is {len(name)} characters long, the limit is {LONGEST}")
    if name[0] in DIGITS:
        problems.append("starts with a digit")
    if name[0] == "." or name[-1] == ".":
        problems.append("starts or ends with a period")
    if ".." in name:
        problems.append("has two periods in a row")
    bad = strays(name, ALLOWED)
    if bad:
        problems.append(f"has characters that aren't allowed: {bad}")
    return problems


def report(label, names):
    count = 0
    for name in names:
        for problem in name_problems(name):
            count = count + 1
            print(f"  {name!r} {problem}")
    print(f"{label}: {len(names)} names, {count} problems")
    coded = [name for name in names if is_uni_name(name)]
    if coded:
        print(f"  named by code point: {coded}")


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    report("font", [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs])
    if EXTRA:
        report("pasted list", EXTRA)


main()

Save it as name_check.py. With Ines's eight names in EXTRA, it should print:

font: 251 names, 0 problems
  'uni0041.alt2 copy' has characters that aren't allowed: [' ']
  '3quarters' starts with a digit
  'e..sc' has two periods in a row
  'ñ' has characters that aren't allowed: ['ñ']
  'germandbls-old' has characters that aren't allowed: ['-']
  'a.sc.' starts or ends with a period
pasted list: 8 names, 6 problems
  named by code point: ['uni0041.alt2 copy', 'uni00C1']

The 251 is Plum's 205 glyphs, the fifteen you added in Part 2 and the thirty-one from Part 3. Your count depends on the exercises you did and saved. The zero is the part that should match: every glyph in the practice font was named by Plum's designer or by a script of yours that added a clean suffix.

Notes on the listing.

{name!r} is chapter 78's way of printing a text with its quotes. For a name that might end in a space, the quotes show where it stops.

report is called twice with a label and a list, once for the font and once for the pasted names. It neither knows nor cares where a list came from.

The font line prints even when there's nothing to report. Chapter 80 gave the reason: a check that stays silent when it passes can't be told from a check that never ran.

Empty EXTRA when you've dealt with its names. if EXTRA: then skips the second report.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text: Take SPECIAL out of name_problems by making it an empty list, and run again. The font line should now say 1 problems, with '.notdef' starts or ends with a period above it. The rule was written by people who also wrote its one exception, and a checker has to carry both. Put .notdef back.

docs.title: What the check doesn't say
docs.text:
A name can pass every rule here and still be wrong. Aacute on a glyph that draws a B is a good name. So is a.sc in a font where the other small caps end in .smcp. The script checks spelling. Whether a name is true, and whether the names agree with each other, takes the chapters that follow.

Mira runs it on the real Plum. Six lines, and she renames those glyphs by hand in the Font window, which for six is quicker than writing anything. Ines's reply is one line: "And the three hundred from the Greek import?"

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A ready-made string question such as isalnum answers its author's idea of a letter, so test it on your own cases first. A string of allowed characters with in gives you an alphabet you control, and returning the offending characters is more use than returning False. name[0], name[-1] and ".." in name check position. Glyph names come in two kinds, friendly and production, and both are legal.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a rule: a name that contains copy gets the sentence looks like a leftover duplicate. Which of Ines's eight names should now have two problems?
  2. Make a name of 64 characters with "a" * 64 and pass it to name_problems. Then try 63.
  3. is_uni_name rejects uni00c1. Write is_sloppy_uni(name) that is true for a uni name whose hex digits include small letters. You'll need a third alphabet.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Three hundred glyphs came in from another file with names like glyph123, each with its Unicode value intact. Chapter 82 gives them names from a lookup table, and a script renames glyphs again, which it last did in Part 2.

docs.title: 82. Names from Unicode
docs.text:
Tuesday of week sixteen. The Greek for the real Plum was drawn two years ago by a freelancer, in another program, and it came into Ines's file last night as three hundred glyphs called glyph201, glyph202 and so on. The drawings are fine. Every glyph kept its Unicode value. Only the names were lost on the way.

"Three hundred," Ines says. "I am not typing three hundred names."

She doesn't have to. A glyph that knows its code point can be given a name by looking the code point up in a table, and a table is a dictionary.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The tell function from chapter 39. The script below defines it again, so it runs by itself.
  • rename_suffix.py from chapter 31, to remind you of its shape. You'll build this chapter's script on it.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The outputs below were computed in plain Python from Plum's source file and from the name table in Fly's source. The renaming itself goes the way chapter 31's did, and I haven't seen either of them rename a glyph.

Your practice font has no Greek and no glyph called glyph201. Step 5 plants three such names so that the script has something to find.

docs.title: Step 1: A table by hand
docs.text:
You met the dictionary in chapter 21 with names on the left. The left side can be a number as well:

NAMES = {0x5E: "asciicircum", 0x7C: "bar", 0x23: "numbersign"}

print(NAMES[0x5E])
print(NAMES)

asciicircum
{94: 'asciicircum', 124: 'bar', 35: 'numbersign'}

0x5E is the sixteen-digit way of writing 94, as chapter 6 said, and Python stores the plain number whichever way you write it. Writing the keys in hex keeps them looking like the Unicode charts, where the circumflex sign sits at U+005E.

Ask the table for a code point it doesn't hold and you get an error you know from chapter 21:

print(NAMES[0x3A9])

KeyError: 937

get asks the same question politely and takes a second argument, the answer to give when the key is missing:

print(NAMES.get(0x3A9))
print(NAMES.get(0x3A9, "?"))

None
?

That second argument does most of the work in this chapter.

docs.title: Step 2: Borrow a bigger table
docs.text:
Three entries won't name a font. Somebody has typed the long table already, and it ships inside Fly:

from fly.ap.glyphs.identity_tools.glyph_identity.unicode_from_names import AGL

print(len(AGL))
print(AGL["eacute"], AGL["A"])

376
233 65

The import line is long because the table lives deep inside a tool that does the opposite job from ours: it finds a code point for a glyph that has a name. AGL stands for Adobe Glyph List, the published list most Latin glyph names come from. Fly's copy holds 376 of its names.

It runs the wrong way for us. Its keys are names and its values are code points, and you can only look a dictionary up by its keys. So turn it round. items() hands you each key with its value, and you file them the other way about:

BY_CODE = {}
for name, code in AGL.items():
    BY_CODE[code] = name

print(len(BY_CODE))
print(BY_CODE[233])

376
eacute

Look at the first number. A dictionary can't hold the same key twice, so if two names in AGL shared a code point, the second would overwrite the first and BY_CODE would come out shorter. It has 376 entries, the same as AGL. Nothing was lost. Chapter 63 showed what an overwritten key looks like. Compare the two lengths every time you turn a dictionary round.

The three-line loop has a one-line form, in the manner of chapter 37's comprehensions, with braces and a colon:

BY_CODE = {code: name for name, code in AGL.items()}

Both build the same dictionary. The script below uses the short one.

docs.title: Step 3: When the table has no answer
docs.text:
The table has no Greek. BY_CODE.get(0x3A9) gives None for the capital omega, and it will for most of Ines's three hundred.

There is a rule for this case, and you saw its result in chapter 81: a glyph with no better name is called uni and its code point as four hex digits. Mira's first try:

def name_for(code):
    return BY_CODE.get(code, f"uni{code:x}")

print(name_for(0x5E))
print(name_for(0x3A9))

asciicircum
uni3a9

The first answer is right. The second looks right and isn't. uni3a9 has three digits where the rule wants four, and small letters where it wants capitals. Chapter 81's is_uni_name says False to it. A program reading the exported font would take uni3a9 for a word somebody made up, and wouldn't know the glyph is an omega.

The format from chapter 23 mends both faults. 04 pads to four digits with zeros and a capital X asks for capital letters:

def name_for(code):
    return BY_CODE.get(code, f"uni{code:04X}")

print(name_for(0x3A9))
print(name_for(0x5E))

uni03A9
asciicircum

uni03A9 isn't pretty, and it is correct: every font tool reads it as "the glyph for U+03A9". Friendlier Greek names such as Omega need a bigger table than this one. Fly has none, and FontLab's own was out of my reach while I wrote this, so the script settles for names that are right.

docs.title: Step 4: Test the table on names you trust
docs.text:
Before a table renames three hundred glyphs, find out whether it agrees with the names the font already has. Every glyph in Plum that has a code point also has a name somebody chose with care. Ask the table about each and compare:

from fly import fl
from fly.ap.glyphs.identity_tools.glyph_identity.unicode_from_names import AGL

BY_CODE = {code: name for name, code in AGL.items()}
font = fl.CurrentFont()

agree = 0
differ = 0
unknown = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.unicode is None:
        continue
    listed = BY_CODE.get(glyph.unicode)
    if listed is None:
        unknown.append(glyph.name)
    elif listed == glyph.name:
        agree += 1
    else:
        differ += 1
        print(f"{glyph.name} is {listed} in the table")
print(f"{agree} agree, {differ} differ, {len(unknown)} not in the table")
print(unknown)

On Plum as it shipped this should print:

196 agree, 0 differ, 8 not in the table
['Wacute', 'Wdieresis', 'Wgrave', 'Ygrave', 'wacute', 'wdieresis', 'wgrave', 'ygrave']

Your font has more glyphs than that by now, so your first and last numbers will be larger and your list longer. The middle number is the one to watch, and it should be 0. If it isn't, each line above the total names a glyph where your font and the table disagree, and a person has to decide which of them is right.

The eight are the Welsh letters. The table is partial, and for those eight name_for would answer uni1E82 and its neighbors. That is worth knowing before you trust it with a font: where the table is silent, a good name can be replaced by a merely correct one. The script in this chapter only touches glyphs whose names are placeholders, so it can't do that harm.

docs.title: Step 5: Plant three, then name them
docs.text:
To have something to rename, take three glyphs nobody kerns and no feature mentions, and spoil their names. Put this in the Scripting panel and run it once:

from fly import qt
import fly.ap.glyphs.names.model as names
from fly.ap.glyphs.identity_tools.glyph_identity.batch_rename import apply_renames

PLANT = [["numbersign", "glyph201"], ["asciicircum", "glyph202"], ["bar", "glyph203"]]
facts = names.scan()
print(apply_renames(None, qt.QtCore, facts.package_id, PLANT))

It should print the three pairs back. They're listed in the order the three glyphs have in the font, because the script below walks the font and will meet them in that order. One Undo step takes them away again if you change your mind.

Now the script needs to know a placeholder when it sees one. glyph followed by nothing but digits is a placeholder. glyphs isn't, and neither is glyph12a:

PREFIX = "glyph"
DIGITS = "0123456789"

def is_placeholder(name):
    number = name.removeprefix(PREFIX)
    if number == name or number == "":
        return False
    return not [ch for ch in number if ch not in DIGITS]

for name in ["glyph201", "glyph", "glyphs", "glyph12a", "Glyph1"]:
    print(name, is_placeholder(name))

glyph201 True
glyph False
glyphs False
glyph12a False
Glyph1 False

removeprefix is the twin of removesuffix from chapter 31. It cuts the given start off a string and returns the rest, and when the string doesn't start that way it returns the string unchanged. That gives the first test: if nothing was cut off, the name didn't begin with glyph. The last line is chapter 81's strays, written in place: collect every character that isn't a digit, and say True only if the list is empty.

The rest is chapter 31's shape: collect, plan, show, apply.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Fix Names
# Gives every glyph called glyph1, glyph2 and so on a name from its code point.
# Prints a plan first. With DRY_RUN = True it stops there.
# Afterward, by hand: fix the old names in Features and in kerning classes.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.glyphs.names.model as names
from fly.ap.glyphs.identity_tools.glyph_identity.batch_rename import (
    apply_renames,
    plan_renames,
)
from fly.ap.glyphs.identity_tools.glyph_identity.unicode_from_names import AGL
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


DRY_RUN = True
PREFIX = "glyph"
DIGITS = "0123456789"
BY_CODE = {code: name for name, code in AGL.items()}


def is_placeholder(name):
    number = name.removeprefix(PREFIX)
    if number == name or number == "":
        return False
    return not [ch for ch in number if ch not in DIGITS]


def name_for(code):
    return BY_CODE.get(code, f"uni{code:04X}")


def collect(font):
    pairs = []
    skipped = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if not is_placeholder(glyph.name):
            continue
        if glyph.unicode is None:
            skipped.append(glyph.name)
        else:
            pairs.append([glyph.name, name_for(glyph.unicode)])
    return pairs, skipped


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    pairs, skipped = collect(font)
    for name in skipped:
        print(f"{name:<12}has no code point, skipped")
    if not pairs:
        print("No placeholder names with a code point.")
        return

    facts = names.scan()
    plan = plan_renames(facts, pairs)
    problems = 0
    for old, new, status in plan:
        print(f"{old:<12}{new:<16}{status}")
        if status != "ok":
            problems += 1
    print(f"{len(plan)} to rename, {problems} with problems")

    if DRY_RUN:
        print("Dry run. Nothing changed. Set DRY_RUN = False to rename.")
    elif problems > 0:
        print("Nothing changed. Fix the problems first.")
    else:
        renamed = apply_renames(None, qt.QtCore, facts.package_id, pairs)
        print(len(renamed), "renamed")


main()

Save it as fix_names.py. With the three planted names in the font, it should print:

glyph201    numbersign      ok
glyph202    asciicircum     ok
glyph203    bar             ok
3 to rename, 0 with problems
Dry run. Nothing changed. Set DRY_RUN = False to rename.

Read the plan. Three placeholders, three names you recognize, three times ok. Set DRY_RUN = False, run it again, and the last line should say 3 renamed. Set the switch back to True before you close the file.

Notes on the listing.

collect returns two lists, the pairs to rename and the names it had to leave. A placeholder with no code point can't be looked up in any table. The script says so by name and goes on, and a person has to open that glyph and see what it is.

plan_renames is the judge here, as it was in chapter 31. It knows things name_for doesn't: whether the new name is already taken in the font, and whether two glyphs are about to be given the same name.

The comment about features and kerning classes came along from chapter 31, and it still holds. A rename changes the glyph's name and nothing that mentions it. The three glyphs you planted were chosen because nothing mentions them.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Spoil the table. Under the BY_CODE line, add:

BY_CODE[0x7C] = "numbersign"

Now the table claims that the bar and the number sign share a name. Plant the three names again if you've already mended them, leave DRY_RUN = True, and run:

glyph201    numbersign      duplicate target
glyph202    asciicircum     ok
glyph203    numbersign      duplicate target
3 to rename, 2 with problems
Dry run. Nothing changed. Set DRY_RUN = False to rename.

Two glyphs can't have one name, and the plan says so for both, since it can't tell which of them you meant. With the switch off the script would stop at "Nothing changed. Fix the problems first." and rename none of the three, the good one in the middle included. That is deliberate. A half-done rename is harder to check than one that didn't happen.

Take the line out again.

docs.title: What the table can't tell you
docs.text:
A code point says which character a glyph stands for. It doesn't say which drawing it is. A small-cap omega and a swash omega carry no code point at all, so in Ines's import they arrive as placeholders the script reports and skips. Somebody who can see them has to name those, with the suffixes from chapter 81.

And a wrong code point gives a wrong name with full confidence. If the freelancer's file had the omega at the code point of the ohm sign, this script would name it for the ohm sign and print ok. Chapter 83 looks at that from the other side.

Ines runs the script on the real Plum. Two hundred and sixty-one glyphs get uni names in one Undo step. Thirty-nine are skipped, and she prints their list and takes it to her desk with a pencil.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A dictionary can be a lookup table with numbers for keys, and get with a second argument gives you a fallback for everything the table doesn't hold. Turning a dictionary round takes one line, and comparing the lengths before and after tells you whether anything was overwritten. Test a borrowed table against names you already trust before you let it rename anything. The format {code:04X} writes a code point the way a uni name needs it.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add your own names on top of the borrowed table. Write MINE = {0x1E82: "Wacute", 0x1E84: "Wdieresis"} and make name_for ask MINE first, then BY_CODE, then fall back to the uni name. Run Step 4's test with it. How many are "not in the table" now?
  2. Make the dry run say where each new name came from. Add a fourth column that reads table or uni. You can tell which it is without changing name_for: ask BY_CODE whether it has the code.
  3. Code points above U+FFFF don't fit in four hex digits, and the rule for them is a single u followed by five or six digits, as in u1F600. Change name_for so that it writes those names for codes of 0x10000 and more. Test it in the Scripting panel on 0x1F600 and on 0x3A9 without touching a font.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Naming a glyph from its code point works when the code point is there and right. Chapter 83 goes the other way: it finds the glyphs that have a good name and no code point, or the wrong one, and proposes what it should be.

docs.title: 83. Unicode from names
docs.text:
Wednesday of week sixteen. Yesterday's script named 261 Greek glyphs from their code points. This morning Ines finds the opposite trouble in the same file. A dozen glyphs carry good names, numbersign among them, and type nothing: somewhere in the import their code points fell off. One more has the code point of its neighbor.

A glyph with no code point can't be typed. The keyboard sends a number, the font looks the number up, and a glyph nobody listed under that number stays in the drawer.

Yesterday the number was trusted and the name was made from it. Today the name is trusted and the number is made from it. It's the same table, read from the other side.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed. Chapter 82's three planted names should be mended, so that the font has asciicircum, bar and numbersign again.
  • The tell function from chapter 39. The script below defines it again, so it runs by itself.
  • The Font window in front, and no Glyph window or glyph tab open. Fly refuses to write code points while a glyph is open for editing.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The plans and counts below were computed in plain Python from Plum's source file and from Fly's own planning code. I haven't seen the write happen, and I haven't seen what Fly says when a glyph tab is open.

Your practice font has no glyph that lost its code point. Step 4 spoils three.

docs.title: Step 1: The number inside a name
docs.text:
Some names carry their code point in plain sight. uni03A9 is the Greek capital omega, U+03A9. Getting the number out is a slice and a conversion:

def code_from_uni(name):
    return int(name[3:])

print(code_from_uni("uni0041"))

41

It ran, it printed a number, and the number is wrong. U+0041 is the capital A, and A is number 65. What you got is 41, which is the closing parenthesis. int read 0041 as an everyday number and threw away the zeros.

Try a name with a letter among its digits and Python complains:

print(code_from_uni("uni00C1"))

ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '00C1'

"Base 10" is the giveaway. Chapter 23 warned about this trap: a hex number with no letters in it looks like an everyday number and isn't one. The error for 00C1 is the kind one. The silence for 0041 would have put a parenthesis on the A key.

Tell int which way of counting the text uses:

def code_from_uni(name):
    return int(name[3:], 16)

print(code_from_uni("uni0041"))
print(code_from_uni("uni00C1"))

65
193

docs.title: Step 2: The table, the right way round
docs.text:
Most names don't carry a number. eacute doesn't. For those you need the table from chapter 82, and this time you need it the way it was made, with names on the left:

from fly.ap.glyphs.identity_tools.glyph_identity.unicode_from_names import AGL

print(AGL["eacute"])
print("eacute" in AGL)
print("a.sc" in AGL)

233
True
False

Yesterday you turned this dictionary round to get BY_CODE. Looking up by name needs no turning. A dictionary answers one kind of question fast: "what stands next to this key?" If you want to ask from the other side, you build a second dictionary. Mira keeps both, and she names each after its left side.

docs.title: Step 3: Let Fly read the name
docs.text:
Between uni names and the table there's a third kind. Wacute isn't in the table, as chapter 82 found. Yet its name says what it is: a W with an acute. Fly has a function that tries all three routes in order. Run it on a handful of names:

from fly.ap.glyphs.identity_tools.glyph_identity.unicode_from_names import code_for_name

for name in ["uni03A9", "eacute", "Wacute", "a.sc", "f_i", "uni03a9"]:
    code, source = code_for_name(name)
    print(f"{name:<10}{code}  {source!r}")

uni03A9   937  'uni'
eacute    233  'AGL'
Wacute    7810  'derived'
a.sc      None  ''
f_i       None  ''
uni03a9   None  ''

The function hands back two things, and code, source = ... puts them in two boxes, as plan did in chapter 62. The second says how the first was found: from a uni name, from the table, or derived from a letter and an accent word.

Three names got None, and each for a reason.

a.sc has a suffix. A small-cap a is a second drawing of a letter that already has its code point on the plain a. It gets none of its own, and a feature brings it in, which chapter 88 writes.

f_i is a ligature, two letters in one glyph. It gets none either.

uni03a9 has a lowercase a in its hex digits. Chapter 81's is_uni_name turned such names down, and Fly does too.

So "no code point" isn't always a fault. The fault is a name that implies a code point which the glyph doesn't have.

docs.title: Step 4: Spoil three glyphs
docs.text:
Take the same three glyphs as yesterday. Two lose their code point and bar gets the one that belongs to asciicircum. Put this in the Scripting panel and run it once, with the Font window in front:

import fly.ap.glyphs.names.model as names

PLANT = {"asciicircum": [], "numbersign": [], "bar": [0x5E]}

facts = names.scan()


def spoil():
    for name, codes in PLANT.items():
        facts.entries[name].record.unicodes = codes


names.commit("Spoil three code points", [facts.entries[name] for name in PLANT],
             spoil, operation="unicode", facts=facts, window=facts.package_id)

This is the write itself, with nothing wrapped round it. A glyph's code points are a list, unicodes, because a glyph may have more than one, which is chapter 84's subject. An empty list means none. The assignment sits inside a function, and names.commit runs that function as one Undo step, the same arrangement as history.commit in chapter 29. window= asks Fly to check the Font window rule before anything is written.

You won't write this by hand again in this chapter. Fly has a planner and a writer for the job, and they're built like the rename pair from chapter 31.

docs.title: Step 5: The plan
docs.text:
plan_unicodes takes the facts, a list of names and a switch. It returns one row for every name that implies a code point: the name, the codes the glyph has now, the code the name implies, the source and a status.

from fly.ap.glyphs.identity_tools.glyph_identity.unicode_from_names import plan_unicodes

facts = names.scan()
plan = plan_unicodes(facts, list(facts.entries), False)
for name, current, code, source, status in plan:
    if status != "same":
        print(f"{name:<14}{current}  {code}  {status}")

numbersign    []  35  assign
asciicircum   []  94  used by bar
bar           [94]  124  encoded differently

list(facts.entries) is every glyph name in font order: looping over a dictionary gives its keys, and list collects them.

Four statuses can turn up. same means the glyph already has the code its name implies, and on Plum that's nearly all of them. assign means the glyph has none and the code is free. used by bar means another glyph holds that code, and Fly won't give one code point to two glyphs. encoded differently means the glyph has a code, it isn't the implied one, and the switch says not to replace.

The switch is the third argument. False fills gaps only. True also replaces a code that disagrees with the name.

docs.title: Step 6: Apply, and apply again
docs.text:
The whole script is below. Run it as it stands and you get the plan with codes written the Unicode way:

numbersign    none      U+0023  AGL      assign
asciicircum   none      U+005E  AGL      used by bar
bar           U+005E    U+007C  AGL      encoded differently
232 already right, 1 to assign, 2 stuck, 16 with names that imply nothing
Dry run. Nothing changed. Set DRY_RUN = False to assign.

These counts are for the practice font as the book has left it: Plum's 205 glyphs, the fifteen suffixed glyphs from Part 2 and the thirty-one glyphs Part 3 built, 251 in all. The sixteen names that imply nothing are .notdef and the fifteen with a suffix. If you skipped a chapter or did an exercise that added glyphs, your first and last numbers differ and the three rows don't.

Two rows are stuck and they're stuck on each other. bar sits on the circumflex's code, so asciicircum can't have it. With OVERWRITE = False the script won't move bar.

Mira reads the two rows, agrees that bar is the one in the wrong, and sets OVERWRITE = True and DRY_RUN = False:

numbersign    none      U+0023  AGL      assign
asciicircum   none      U+005E  AGL      used by bar
bar           U+005E    U+007C  AGL      assign
232 already right, 2 to assign, 1 stuck, 16 with names that imply nothing
2 assigned

One row is still stuck. The plan is made before anything changes, and when it was made bar still held U+005E. Now it doesn't. Run the script a second time:

asciicircum   none      U+005E  AGL      assign
234 already right, 1 to assign, 0 stuck, 16 with names that imply nothing
1 assigned

A third run prints one line, which begins 235 already right, 0 to assign, 0 stuck, and that line is how you know you're done. A script you can run until it has nothing left to say is a comfortable script to own.

Then set both switches back.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Fix Unicodes
# Finds glyphs whose name implies a code point they don't have.
# Prints a plan. With DRY_RUN = True it stops there.
# OVERWRITE = True also replaces a code point that disagrees with the name.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.glyphs.names.model as names
from fly.ap.glyphs.identity_tools.glyph_identity.unicode_from_names import (
    apply_unicodes,
    plan_unicodes,
)
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


DRY_RUN = True
OVERWRITE = False


def show_codes(codes):
    if not codes:
        return "none"
    return " ".join(f"U+{code:04X}" for code in codes)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    facts = names.scan()
    everyone = list(facts.entries)
    plan = plan_unicodes(facts, everyone, OVERWRITE)

    same = 0
    stuck = 0
    todo = []
    for name, current, code, source, status in plan:
        if status == "same":
            same += 1
            continue
        print(f"{name:<14}{show_codes(current):<10}U+{code:04X}  {source:<9}{status}")
        if status == "assign":
            todo.append(name)
        else:
            stuck += 1
    silent = len(everyone) - len(plan)
    print(f"{same} already right, {len(todo)} to assign, {stuck} stuck, "
          f"{silent} with names that imply nothing")

    if DRY_RUN:
        print("Dry run. Nothing changed. Set DRY_RUN = False to assign.")
    elif todo:
        changed = apply_unicodes(None, qt.QtCore, facts.package_id, todo, OVERWRITE)
        print(len(changed), "assigned")


main()

Save it as fix_unicodes.py.

Notes on the listing.

Chapter 31's script refused to rename anything while one row had a problem. This one assigns the clean rows and leaves the stuck ones, because a stuck row here often comes loose once its neighbor is mended, as you saw. apply_unicodes makes its own plan again before it writes and touches only rows that say assign, so a font that changed since the printout can't be written from stale news.

continue skips the rest of the loop body for this row and goes on to the next. You met it in chapter 44.

silent is a subtraction. The plan holds only names that imply something, so whatever is missing from it implied nothing.

The two strings in the last print stand side by side with nothing between them. Python joins neighbors like that into one string, which is a way to keep a long line inside the page.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Fly's table has a few surprises, and one of them matters to Ines today:

print(code_for_name("Delta"))

(8710, 'AGL')

8710 is U+2206, the increment sign from mathematics. The Greek capital delta is U+0394. The old name list that this table comes from gave the name Delta to the maths sign, long before anyone drew Greek for it. A Greek glyph called Delta with U+0394 would show up in the plan as encoded differently, and with OVERWRITE = True the script would move it to the maths sign and report success.

That's the reason OVERWRITE is off unless somebody has read the rows. It's also the reason yesterday's script called Greek glyphs uni0394 and didn't guess.

docs.title: Which side do you trust?
docs.text:
Chapter 82 trusts the number and writes the name. This chapter trusts the name and writes the number. Run both on one glyph and the second undoes nothing: it agrees with whatever the first left. Run either on a glyph where both sides are wrong and you get a wrong answer with a tidy status.

So decide for each batch which side is good. Ines's Greek import had good numbers and junk names. The dozen glyphs from this morning had good names and no numbers. No script can make that decision for her, though a dry run puts the rows in front of her.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A lookup table answers from its left side, so a question asked from the other side needs a second table or the first one turned round. int(text, 16) reads hex, and leaving out the 16 gives either an error or a silently wrong number. A function can return a value and a note on where the value came from, and a status word on every row lets a script act on the clean rows and leave the rest. A plan describes the font before the write, so a second run can find work that the first run made possible.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Write show_char(code) that returns the character for a code point with chr from chapter 23, and add it as a last column to the plan rows. Which of the three planted rows shows a character you can't tell from its neighbor at a glance?
  2. Count the sources. Loop over the whole plan, not only the rows that changed, and build a dictionary from source to count with .get(source, 0) + 1. On Plum as it ships you should see 196 from the table and 8 derived. Which eight? Chapter 82 printed their count for another reason.
  3. Spoil the font differently: give numbersign the code 0x7C and leave bar alone. Before you run the dry run, write down what status each of the two glyphs will get with OVERWRITE = False, and then with True. Run both and compare. Undo the spoiling afterward.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Some glyphs are meant to have two code points: one drawing that serves the space and the no-break space. Chapter 84 finds the glyphs that carry more than one, and gives a second code point to two that should.

docs.title: 84. One glyph, two characters
docs.text:
Thursday of week sixteen. Tobias sends a screenshot of a web page set in Plum. One line reads "page 12" and the gap between the word and the number is wider than every other gap on the page, and a different gray.

Ines knows the cause before she opens the file. The author typed a no-break space there, so that "page" and "12" never part at a line end. A no-break space is a character of its own, U+00A0. Plum has no glyph for it, so the browser borrowed a space from another font.

Plum doesn't need a new drawing. The no-break space should look like the space, to the unit. What the font needs is a second number on the glyph it already has.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed, and the three code points from chapter 83 mended.
  • The tell function from chapter 39. The script below defines it again, so it runs by itself.
  • The Font window in front and no glyph open for editing, as in chapter 83.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The list behavior in Steps 1 to 3 is plain Python and I ran it. The report and plan were computed from Plum's source file. I haven't seen FontLab accept a list of two code points from a script: Fly's own tools shorten such lists and never lengthen them, so the write in this chapter is one step past what I could read in source. Keep the dry run on until you've looked at the plan, and check the glyph afterward.

docs.title: Step 1: A list in a drawer
docs.text:
In chapter 83 you wrote record.unicodes = [] and I said the code points of a glyph are a list. Look at one:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
space = font["space"]
print(space.unicodes)
print(space.unicode)
print(len(space.unicodes))

[32]
32
1

A glyph is a wardrobe with drawers, as it has been since chapter 6. Most drawers hold one thing: a name, a width. This drawer holds a list, and a list can hold none, one or several. unicode without the s is a shortcut to the first item, or None when the list is empty.

Every glyph in Plum has one code point, except .notdef, which has none. So every list you can print today is one item long. You're about to make two that are longer.

docs.title: Step 2: Two names for one list
docs.text:
Before you touch a glyph, try the idea on a plain list. This needs no font:

codes = [32]
longer = codes
longer.append(160)
print(longer)
print(codes)

[32, 160]
[32, 160]

You appended to longer and codes grew too. Nothing went wrong inside Python. longer = codes doesn't copy a list. It ties a second label to the same box. There's one list here with two names, and whatever you do through one name you see through the other.

With numbers and strings you never noticed, because you can't change a number in place. append changes a list in place, and so the sharing shows.

Now make a new list on purpose:

codes = [32]
longer = codes + [160]
print(longer)
print(codes)

[32, 160]
[32]

+ between two lists builds a third and leaves both alone. Now you have the old list and the new one, and you can compare them, print them side by side or throw the new one away.

That second form is the one to use on a glyph. Fly's own code always builds a new list and assigns it to the drawer in one statement, and I follow it. What space.unicodes.append(160) does to the font, I can't tell you. It may change the glyph behind Undo's back and it may change nothing at all, and neither is what you want.

docs.title: Step 3: Order counts
docs.text:
Put the new code in front and see what the shortcut says:

codes = [32]
wrong = [160] + codes
print(wrong)
print(wrong[0])

[160, 32]
160

The first item is the glyph's main code point. It's what unicode returns and what chapter 82's name_for reads. With 160 in front, fix_names.py would look at your space, find nbspace in the table and offer to rename it. Every script in this book that asks a glyph for its one code point would get the newcomer.

So the old code stays first and the extra goes on the end.

docs.title: Step 4: Who has what
docs.text:
A report first. Two questions: which glyphs have more than one code point, and is any code point on two glyphs? The first is a loop with len. The second needs the table turned round again, from code to names, and this time the right side is a list because the whole point is to catch a code with two owners:

def owners(all_codes):
    found = {}
    for name, codes in all_codes.items():
        for code in codes:
            if code not in found:
                found[code] = []
            found[code].append(name)
    return found

It's the dictionary of lists from chapter 64, with a loop inside a loop because each glyph may bring several codes. In chapter 82 you turned a table round with one line and checked the lengths to see whether anything had been overwritten. Here nothing can be overwritten: a second owner joins the list.

all_codes is a plain dictionary, name to list of code points, read from the font once at the top of the script:

all_codes = {glyph.name: list(glyph.unicodes) for glyph in font.glyphs}

list(...) makes a copy of each glyph's list. After Step 2 you know why: the script should hold its own lists and not labels tied to the font's.

docs.title: Step 5: The plan
docs.text:
What should be added goes in a dictionary at the top:

WANTED = {"space": 0xA0, "hyphen": 0xAD}

U+00AD is the soft hyphen, the character a writer puts inside a long word to say "you may break here". Fonts give it the hyphen's drawing.

Each wanted pair gets a status, the way chapter 83's rows did. The glyph may be missing. It may have the code already. Another glyph may hold the code. Otherwise the code can be added:

def plan_extras(all_codes, wanted):
    taken = owners(all_codes)
    rows = []
    for name, code in wanted.items():
        if name not in all_codes:
            rows.append((name, code, "no such glyph"))
        elif code in all_codes[name]:
            rows.append((name, code, "has it"))
        elif code in taken:
            rows.append((name, code, f"used by {taken[code][0]}"))
        else:
            rows.append((name, code, "add"))
    return rows

The order of the tests matters. "Has it" is asked before "used by", because a glyph that already has the code is itself in the owners list and would be reported as its own rival.

Run the whole script as a dry run:

More than one code point:
  0 found
One code point on two glyphs:
  0 found
space       U+0020          U+00A0  add
hyphen      U+002D          U+00AD  add
Dry run. Nothing changed. Set DRY_RUN = False to add.

Set DRY_RUN = False and run again. It ends with 2 added. Set it back and run a third time:

More than one code point:
  hyphen      U+002D U+00AD
  space       U+0020 U+00A0
  2 found
One code point on two glyphs:
  0 found
space       U+0020 U+00A0   U+00A0  has it
hyphen      U+002D U+00AD   U+00AD  has it
Dry run. Nothing changed. Set DRY_RUN = False to add.

hyphen comes first in the report because it comes first in the font. The plan follows WANTED.

Then look with your own eyes. Select space in the Font window and open the Glyph panel: the Unicode field should show both code points. If it shows one, the write didn't take, and I'd like to hear about it.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Double Encoded
# Reports glyphs with more than one code point and code points on two glyphs.
# Then adds the extra code points in WANTED, each as a second code point.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.glyphs.names.model as names
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


DRY_RUN = True
WANTED = {"space": 0xA0, "hyphen": 0xAD}


def show_codes(codes):
    if not codes:
        return "none"
    return " ".join(f"U+{code:04X}" for code in codes)


def owners(all_codes):
    found = {}
    for name, codes in all_codes.items():
        for code in codes:
            if code not in found:
                found[code] = []
            found[code].append(name)
    return found


def plan_extras(all_codes, wanted):
    taken = owners(all_codes)
    rows = []
    for name, code in wanted.items():
        if name not in all_codes:
            rows.append((name, code, "no such glyph"))
        elif code in all_codes[name]:
            rows.append((name, code, "has it"))
        elif code in taken:
            rows.append((name, code, f"used by {taken[code][0]}"))
        else:
            rows.append((name, code, "add"))
    return rows


def report(all_codes):
    print("More than one code point:")
    count = 0
    for name, codes in all_codes.items():
        if len(codes) > 1:
            print(f"  {name:<12}{show_codes(codes)}")
            count += 1
    print(f"  {count} found")
    print("One code point on two glyphs:")
    count = 0
    for code, glyph_names in owners(all_codes).items():
        if len(glyph_names) > 1:
            print(f"  U+{code:04X}  {' '.join(glyph_names)}")
            count += 1
    print(f"  {count} found")


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    all_codes = {glyph.name: list(glyph.unicodes) for glyph in font.glyphs}
    report(all_codes)

    rows = plan_extras(all_codes, WANTED)
    todo = {}
    for name, code, status in rows:
        print(f"{name:<12}{show_codes(all_codes.get(name, [])):<16}U+{code:04X}  {status}")
        if status == "add":
            todo[name] = all_codes[name] + [code]

    if DRY_RUN:
        print("Dry run. Nothing changed. Set DRY_RUN = False to add.")
        return
    if not todo:
        return

    facts = names.scan()
    allowed, refused = names.editable(facts, list(todo), "unicode")
    for name, reason in refused.items():
        print(f"{name}: left alone, {reason}")

    def add():
        for name in allowed:
            facts.entries[name].record.unicodes = todo[name]

    names.commit("Add extra code points", [facts.entries[name] for name in allowed],
                 add, operation="unicode", facts=facts, window=facts.package_id)
    print(len(allowed), "added")


main()

Save it as double_encoded.py.

Notes on the listing.

todo maps each name to the complete new list, built with + in the loop that prints the plan. By the time add runs there's nothing left to work out: it puts each finished list in its drawer.

names.editable sorts the names into those Fly will let you change and those it won't, with a reason for each refusal. Chapter 83's apply_unicodes did this for you out of sight. Here you call the write yourself, so you ask yourself.

def add() sits inside main. A function defined inside another can see the outer one's boxes, facts, todo and allowed, with no need to pass them. It's the arrangement from chapter 49, where commit wants a function it can call with no arguments.

glyph_names in report is called that and not names, because names is already the label on Fly's module at the top of the file. Reuse the label inside the function and the module is out of reach there.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Step 5 gave space and hyphen their second codes, so first take that back: choose Edit > Undo once, and check that the step it names is "Add extra code points". Now give the no-break space to the wrong glyph. In the Glyph panel, select period and type 002E,00A0 into the Unicode field. Then run the dry run:

More than one code point:
  period      U+002E U+00A0
  1 found
One code point on two glyphs:
  0 found
space       U+0020          U+00A0  used by period
hyphen      U+002D          U+00AD  add
Dry run. Nothing changed. Set DRY_RUN = False to add.

The script won't give U+00A0 to space while period holds it. It also won't take it off period: taking a code away is a decision, and this script only adds. Clear it by hand in the Glyph panel, or undo, and the plan says add again. Then set DRY_RUN = False, run the script once more so that space and hyphen have their second codes back, and set the switch to True. Later chapters count on those two codes.

Had the script added it anyway, the second report would have had its first line: one code point, two glyphs. Which of the two a program shows when you type that character isn't something I'd want to guess.

docs.title: How this sits with chapter 83
docs.text:
Run fix_unicodes.py after this chapter. It should still say everything is right. Its test for same asks whether the code a name implies is somewhere in the glyph's list, and space still has 32. The second code point is nobody's business but yours.

Run fix_names.py and it's content too, as long as the old code is first. That's Step 3 again.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: An object's drawer can hold a list, and a list has a length and an order that both mean something. Giving a list a second name doesn't copy it, so build a new list with + when you want to keep the old one. A script that changes a font should compute the complete new value first and assign it in one statement inside an Undo step. A dictionary of lists catches the case a plain dictionary hides: two owners for one key.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a third pair to WANTED that gives U+2010, the typographer's hyphen, to hyphen. A dictionary can't hold two entries for "hyphen". Change WANTED so each name maps to a list of codes, and change plan_extras and the todo loop to match. What does the report print for hyphen afterward?
  2. Write remove_code(codes, code) that returns a new list without one code, using a comprehension from chapter 37. Check on a plain list that the one you passed in is unchanged. Then say what should happen if the code to remove is the first one, and make the function refuse that case by returning the list untouched.
  3. len(codes) != len(set(codes)) is true when a list holds the same item twice. Chapter 25 introduced sets. Try it on [32, 160, 160]. FontLab is said to drop such repeats when a list is assigned, so a font should never show one. Add the test to report anyway and see that it finds nothing.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: "Does it do Turkish?" asks the client, and nobody in the room is sure. Chapter 85 keeps the characters each language needs in a file and holds the font against it.

docs.title: 85. Which languages can it write?
docs.text:
Friday of week sixteen. The publisher has sold the cookbook to a house in Istanbul, and an email arrives with one line in it: "Does Plum do Turkish?"

Ines thinks so. Mira thinks so too, and then remembers that Turkish has two letters i, one with a dot and one without, in both cases, and can't say from memory whether Plum has all four.

In chapter 25 you answered this question for German with two sets and a minus sign. The letters were typed into the script. That was fine for one language on one afternoon. Halfmoon gets this email every month, each time about another language, and the person who knows what Czech needs isn't the person who edits scripts. The letters belong in a file that anybody can open, and the script should read whatever the file holds.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed. The font must be saved, because the script looks for its data file in the folder where the font lives.
  • The tell function from chapter 39. The script below defines it again, so it runs by itself.
  • A plain text editor to make the data file.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. Reading the file, the sets and the report are plain Python, and I ran them against the code points in Plum's source file. The only FontLab parts are font.path and glyph.unicodes, which earlier chapters use the same way.

docs.title: Step 1: The file
docs.text:
Make a text file called languages.txt in the folder that holds Plum-practice, the folder where smallcaps.txt went in chapter 27. Save it as UTF-8, which is what a plain text editor does unless you tell it otherwise.

# Letters each language needs beyond A to Z and a to z.
# One language to a line: name, colon, letters. Both cases written out.
French: ÀÂÆÇÉÈÊËÎÏÔŒÙÛÜŸ àâæçéèêëîïôœùûüÿ
German: ÄÖÜẞ äöüß
Spanish: ÁÉÍÑÓÚÜ áéíñóúü ¿¡
Turkish: ÇĞİÖŞÜ çğıöşü
Polish: ĄĆĘŁŃÓŚŹŻ ąćęłńóśźż
Czech: ÁČĎÉĚÍŇÓŘŠŤÚŮÝŽ áčďéěíňóřšťúůýž

You can copy the lines from this page. The format is my invention and it's small on purpose: a person can read it, fix it and add a line without knowing any Python. Lines that start with # are notes, as in the art director's file.

These six lines are a working list and not a ruling. Each holds the letters a language's own alphabet adds to the basic twenty-six. Borrowed words, quotation marks and currency signs aren't in it. If your client's Polish editor says a letter is missing from my line, the editor is right and you add it.

docs.title: Step 2: One line into two parts
docs.text:
Each line has a name, a colon and letters. split from chapter 9 cuts a string wherever it finds a separator:

line = "Turkish: ÇĞİÖŞÜ çğıöşü"
name, letters = line.split(":", 1)
print(name)
print(letters)

Turkish
 ÇĞİÖŞÜ çğıöşü

The 1 says "cut once". A line with a second colon further along would still give two parts, and the two boxes on the left would still fit.

Leave the colon out of a line in the file and the two boxes can't be filled:

name, letters = "Welsh ŴŶ ŵŷ".split(":", 1)

ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 2, got 1)

Python found one part and you asked for two. When somebody else edits the file, this is the message you'll get on the telephone, so it's worth knowing by sight. The fix is in the file, not in the script.

The letters still have spaces in them: one in front and one between the cases. A set makes short work of that. Turn the text into a set of characters and take the space out:

extra = set(letters) - {" "}
print(len(extra))

12

Twelve letters, six in each case.

docs.title: Step 3: The whole file into a dictionary
docs.text:
One language is a name and a set. Six languages are a dictionary from name to set. The reading loop is chapter 27's with the split added:

def read_languages(path):
    languages = {}
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            line = line.strip()
            if line == "" or line.startswith("#"):
                continue
            name, letters = line.split(":", 1)
            languages[name.strip()] = set(letters) - {" "}
    return languages

Blank lines and notes are skipped. Each other line becomes one entry.

Until now your dictionaries held numbers, strings and lists on the right. A set goes there as well. The right side of a dictionary takes anything.

docs.title: Step 4: What the font can type
docs.text:
The other half is the set of characters the font has. In chapter 25 you built it with a loop and add, one code point for each glyph. Since yesterday a glyph can have two, so read the whole list:

have = {chr(code) for glyph in font.glyphs for code in glyph.unicodes}
print(len(have))

237

That's a comprehension from chapter 37 in curly braces, which makes a set where square brackets make a list. It has two for parts, read left to right like two loops, one inside the other: for every glyph, for every code of that glyph, the character.

237 is Plum's 204, plus the 31 glyphs Part 3 built, each with a character of its own, plus the no-break space and the soft hyphen from chapter 84. If you closed the practice font without saving at the end of chapter 60, you have 206, and the last two lines of the report below will be longer than mine.

docs.title: Step 5: The report
docs.text:
For each language, the need is the basic alphabet joined with the extras. The gap is need minus have:

def report(languages, have):
    for name, extra in languages.items():
        need = set(BASIC) | extra
        missing = sorted(need - have)
        if missing:
            print(f"{name:<9}lacks {len(missing):>2}: {' '.join(missing)}")
        else:
            print(f"{name:<9}complete ({len(need)} characters)")

Run the whole script, which is below:

French   complete (84 characters)
German   lacks  1: ẞ
Spanish  complete (68 characters)
Turkish  complete (64 characters)
Polish   lacks  6: Ą ą Ę ę Ł ł
Czech    lacks  2: ď ť

Mira writes back to the publisher before lunch: yes, Plum does Turkish, all four i letters included.

The German line is worth a second look. ẞ is the capital sharp s, a letter German spelling admitted in 2017. Plenty of fonts lack it and German has been set without it for centuries. Whether "lacks 1" means "can't write German" is a judgment, and the script doesn't make it. It reports what's missing from the list it was given.

Polish and Czech are nearly there, which is Part 3's work showing. Polish lacks the four letters with an ogonek, which Mira hasn't drawn for the practice font, and the Ł and ł, whose stroke isn't an accent at all. Czech lacks ď and ť. They take the apostrophe-like caron that stopped Mira at the ľ in chapter 57. Without Part 3's glyphs the two lines would read lacks 16 and lacks 18.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Language Report
# Reads languages.txt from the font's folder and says, for each language,
# which of its characters the current font can't type.
from pathlib import Path

from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


BASIC = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"
FILE_NAME = "languages.txt"


def read_languages(path):
    languages = {}
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            line = line.strip()
            if line == "" or line.startswith("#"):
                continue
            name, letters = line.split(":", 1)
            languages[name.strip()] = set(letters) - {" "}
    return languages


def report(languages, have):
    for name, extra in languages.items():
        need = set(BASIC) | extra
        missing = sorted(need - have)
        if missing:
            print(f"{name:<9}lacks {len(missing):>2}: {' '.join(missing)}")
        else:
            print(f"{name:<9}complete ({len(need)} characters)")


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    path = Path(font.path).parent / FILE_NAME
    if not path.exists():
        tell(f"I can't find {FILE_NAME} next to the font.")
        return
    languages = read_languages(path)
    have = {chr(code) for glyph in font.glyphs for code in glyph.unicodes}
    report(languages, have)


main()

Save it as language_report.py.

Notes on the listing.

The script changes nothing in the font, so it has no dry run and no Undo step. You can run it on any font at any time.

path.exists() asks whether the file is there before open tries it. Without the test, a missing file gives FileNotFoundError and a traceback, which is accurate and no help to Ines. The message box tells her what to do.

sorted(need - have) turns the set into a list in a fixed order. A set has no order of its own, and a report that shuffles its letters from run to run is hard to compare with last month's.

BASIC is a string, not a set, and set(BASIC) converts it where it's used. It could be built once at the top. Fifty-two characters, six times: nobody will notice.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
The file writes both cases out. That looks like wasted typing. Chapter 25 got the capitals for free with upper(). Try it on Turkish:

small = "çğıöşü"
print(small.upper())

ÇĞIÖŞÜ

Look at the third letter. The small dotless ı became a plain capital I, which is right: in Turkish the dotless pair is I and ı. The trouble is the letter that isn't there. Turkish also has a dotted capital, İ, whose small partner is the plain i. Python's upper() follows the rule that fits most languages and turns i into I, so no amount of uppercasing a Turkish alphabet will ever produce İ.

A need built that way never asks for İ. Hold it against a font that lacks the letter:

need = set(small) | set(small.upper())
pretend = have - {"İ"}
print(sorted(need - pretend))

[]

Nothing missing, says the script, about a font that can't set the word İstanbul. A wrong "complete" is worse than a wrong "lacks", because nobody checks good news.

German has the same trap from the other side: "ß".upper() gives SS, two letters, and never ẞ.

So the file spells out every letter, and the script doesn't derive one case from the other.

docs.title: What the report can't tell you
docs.text:
Having a glyph for every letter is where language support starts. The glyphs also have to be drawn right, spaced, and kerned against their neighbors. A font can pass this report with an ğ whose breve crashes into the line above.

The file is short. Fly has a similar set of lists built in, eight of them, and there's no larger collection in any of the packages I could read. For a serious answer about a language you don't speak, ask somebody who reads it, and put what they tell you in the file.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Data that changes, or that other people look after, belongs in a file and not in the script. A line of text becomes structured data with a split, a strip and one conversion, here to a set. A dictionary can hold sets, and a comprehension in curly braces builds one. Letter case isn't the same in every language, so a script shouldn't work out one case from the other when a person can write both down.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a line for Welsh: ÂÊÎÔÛŴŶ âêîôûŵŷ. Run the report. Then add the grave and dieresis letters you can find in Plum from chapter 82's "eight not in the table" and see whether the count of characters goes up while the font stays complete.
  2. Give the report a second kind of line: a font that lacks more than four letters of a language probably never meant to support it. Print not attempted for those, and the full list only for the near misses. Which of the six languages change their line?
  3. Turn the question round. For one language, print what the font has that neither BASIC nor that language's extras need, as chapter 25 did with have - need. Most of it will be figures and punctuation. Use c.isalpha() in a comprehension to keep only the letters. It's a method every string has, and it answers True when the string is made of letters and nothing else. What's left tells you which other languages Sora Sagano had in mind.

docs.title: Next
