docs.text: The Font window shows the Greek import in the order it arrived, which is no order at all. Chapter 86 sorts glyphs by more than one thing at a time: kind first, then name.

docs.title: 86. Put the font in order
docs.text:
Monday of week seventeen. Ines scrolls through her Plum in the Font window and stops. The three hundred Greek glyphs sit at the end in the order the import delivered them, and the import had no order. Further up, AE comes after Atilde, the two ligatures sit between z and the figures, and the accents trail in at the bottom behind the euro sign.

"Capitals, then small letters, then figures, then the rest," she says. "And alphabetical inside each."

That's two rules, one inside the other. In chapter 36 you sorted a table by one thing: width, or name. Today's sort has several parts to its key.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed. The font must be saved, because the script writes a text file next to it.
  • The tell function from chapter 39. The script below defines it again, so it runs by itself.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The sorting is plain Python, and I ran it on the glyph names and code points in Plum's source file. The numbers below are for Plum as it ships, 205 glyphs. Yours will be higher: by the small caps and alternates from Part 2, which have no code points, and by the letters Part 3 built, which have. Part 3's two stand-in accents land in odd places too, as the notes below say.

One limit, stated early. This chapter's script works out an order, prints it and saves it. It doesn't move a single glyph. I found no way to reorder a font from Python that I could vouch for, and Fly's own ordering tool says the same about itself. The end of the chapter shows what to do with the list.

docs.title: Step 1: What plain sorting does
docs.text:
Take the names in font order and sort them:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
names = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs]
by_name = sorted(names)
print(" ".join(by_name[:8]))
print(" ".join(by_name[66:72]))

.notdef A AE Aacute Abreve Acircumflex Adieresis Agrave
Ydieresis Ygrave Z a aacute abreve

Two things happen that Ines didn't ask for. AE jumps ahead of Aacute, and every capital comes before every small letter, so Z is followed by a.

Python compares strings one character at a time, by code point. Capital E is 69 and small a is 97, so AE beats Aa. You met the cure in chapter 36: sort on the name in lowercase.

def lowered(name):
    return name.lower()

print(" ".join(sorted(names, key=lowered)[:10]))

.notdef A a Aacute aacute Abreve abreve Acircumflex acircumflex acute

Now it's a dictionary, in the bookshop sense. Capitals and small letters are shuffled together, and the accent acute has wandered in among the letters because its name starts with a. Neither sort knows what a glyph is. Both look only at spelling.

docs.title: Step 2: A key with two parts
docs.text:
Tuples compare too, and the way they do it is the whole lesson of this chapter:

print((1, "zeta") < (2, "alpha"))
print((1, "b") < (1, "a"))

True
False

Python looks at the first items. If they differ, that settles it, and the rest is never read. Only when the first items are equal does it move on to the second. So a tuple key means "sort by this, and among equals by that". A league table works this way: points first, goal difference when points are level.

Try it on four small rows:

rows = [("small", "b"), ("cap", "B"), ("small", "a"), ("cap", "A")]
print(sorted(rows))

[('cap', 'A'), ('cap', 'B'), ('small', 'a'), ('small', 'b')]

Grouped, then ordered inside each group. cap came before small only because c comes before s in the alphabet, which is luck. The first part of the key should be a number that you choose.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
A first idea for the number: the code point. Capitals have low code points, small letters higher ones. Build the keys and sort:

keys = [(65, "A"), (None, ".notdef"), (97, "a")]
print(sorted(keys))

TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'int'

.notdef has no code point, so its unicode is None, and Python won't say whether None is less than 65. It's a fair refusal. Nothing is neither small nor large.

Every part of a sort key has to be comparable with the same part of every other key. A key function must never hand back None in one row and a number in the next. Your small caps have no code points either, so this would have hit a.sc as well.

And code points would have been a poor first part even without the error. Aacute is 193, far beyond z at 122. Sorting by code point puts the accented capitals after the whole basic alphabet.

docs.title: Step 4: What kind of glyph is it?
docs.text:
What Ines named were kinds: capitals, small letters, figures. Python knows the kind of every character in Unicode. The knowledge is in a module that comes with Python, unicodedata:

import unicodedata

for char in "Aa5,+":
    print(char, unicodedata.category(char))

A Lu
a Ll
5 Nd
, Po
+ Sm

Each answer is two letters. The first is the broad kind: L letter, N number, P punctuation, S symbol, Z separator. The second narrows it: Lu is an uppercase letter, Ll a lowercase one.

This works for Aacute and for a Greek alpha as well as for A. It's the standard's own classification, so you don't need a list of capitals.

Two small tables turn the codes into Ines's words, and a list gives the order she wants them in:

KINDS = ["special", "capitals", "small letters", "other letters", "figures",
         "punctuation", "symbols", "spaces", "unknown"]
BY_CATEGORY = {"Lu": "capitals", "Ll": "small letters"}
BY_LETTER = {"L": "other letters", "N": "figures", "P": "punctuation",
             "S": "symbols", "Z": "spaces"}

The function looks in the exact table first and falls back to the broad one:

def kind_of(name, codes):
    if name == ".notdef":
        return "special"
    base = name.split(".")[0]
    code = codes.get(name)
    if code is None:
        code = codes.get(base)
    if code is None:
        return "unknown"
    category = unicodedata.category(chr(code))
    if category in BY_CATEGORY:
        return BY_CATEGORY[category]
    return BY_LETTER.get(category[0], "unknown")

codes is a dictionary from glyph name to first code point, or None. A glyph without a code borrows its base's: a.sc splits at the dot into a and sc, and a is a small letter. So small caps and alternates sort next to the letters they belong to. A glyph with no code and no base to borrow from is unknown, and those go last where you can find them.

The function always returns one of the nine words. It never returns None. That's Step 3's rule kept.

docs.title: Step 5: The key and the suggested order
docs.text:
The first part of the key is the position of the kind in KINDS, a number you chose by ordering that list. The second is the name in lowercase. The third is the name as spelled:

def order_key(name, codes):
    return (KINDS.index(kind_of(name, codes)), name.lower(), name)

print(order_key("Aacute", codes))
print(order_key("five", codes))

(1, 'aacute', 'Aacute')
(4, 'five', 'five')

The third part looks like a repeat. It's there for the day two names differ only in case inside one kind. Without it their keys would be equal and their order would depend on where they stood before. With it, the same font always gives the same list.

Run the whole script. It counts the kinds, then says how far the font is from the suggested order:

   1  special
  67  capitals
  70  small letters
   1  other letters
  10  figures
  37  punctuation
  18  symbols
   1  spaces
136 of 205 glyphs would change place
   6  Agrave        AE
   7  Aring         Agrave
   8  Atilde        Aring
   9  AE            Atilde
  24  IJ            Iacute
Saved glyph-order.txt

The lines under the count are the first five places where the two orders part: position, the glyph there now, the glyph the suggested order puts there. AE moves up three places and pushes three glyphs down. 136 sounds dramatic. Most of those glyphs shift by a place or two because one neighbor moved.

One line in the count is odd: one "other letter" in a font of plain Latin. It's circumflex. The standard files that accent under modifier letters, while acute, grave and the others are symbols. So the suggested order puts circumflex between the small letters and the figures, away from its family. The classification is the standard's and it's consistent, but it isn't always what a type designer would choose. Exercise 2 mends this. In your font the stand-in caron from chapter 60 is a second "other letter" for the same reason, and dotaccent is one more symbol.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Sort Glyphs
# Proposes a glyph order: by kind, then by name. Prints how the font differs
# and saves the suggested order as glyph-order.txt. Does not reorder the font.
import unicodedata
from pathlib import Path

from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


KINDS = ["special", "capitals", "small letters", "other letters", "figures",
         "punctuation", "symbols", "spaces", "unknown"]
BY_CATEGORY = {"Lu": "capitals", "Ll": "small letters"}
BY_LETTER = {"L": "other letters", "N": "figures", "P": "punctuation",
             "S": "symbols", "Z": "spaces"}
FILE_NAME = "glyph-order.txt"
SHOW = 5


def kind_of(name, codes):
    if name == ".notdef":
        return "special"
    base = name.split(".")[0]
    code = codes.get(name)
    if code is None:
        code = codes.get(base)
    if code is None:
        return "unknown"
    category = unicodedata.category(chr(code))
    if category in BY_CATEGORY:
        return BY_CATEGORY[category]
    return BY_LETTER.get(category[0], "unknown")


def order_key(name, codes):
    return (KINDS.index(kind_of(name, codes)), name.lower(), name)


def propose(codes):
    def key(name):
        return order_key(name, codes)

    return sorted(codes, key=key)


def count_kinds(codes):
    counts = {}
    for name in codes:
        kind = kind_of(name, codes)
        counts[kind] = counts.get(kind, 0) + 1
    for kind in KINDS:
        if kind in counts:
            print(f"{counts[kind]:>4}  {kind}")


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    codes = {glyph.name: glyph.unicode for glyph in font.glyphs}
    now = list(codes)
    new = propose(codes)
    count_kinds(codes)

    moved = [(place, old, name)
             for place, (old, name) in enumerate(zip(now, new)) if old != name]
    print(f"{len(moved)} of {len(now)} glyphs would change place")
    for place, old, name in moved[:SHOW]:
        print(f"{place:>4}  {old:<14}{name}")

    order_file = Path(font.path).parent / FILE_NAME
    with open(order_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for name in new:
            f.write(name + "\n")
    print("Saved", FILE_NAME)


main()

Save it as sort_glyphs.py.

Notes on the listing.

codes does two jobs. It maps names to code points, and because a dictionary keeps the order things went in, list(codes) is the font's present order. sorted(codes, ...) sorts the names, since looping over a dictionary gives its keys.

propose defines key inside itself, as chapter 84's main defined add. sorted calls the key function with one argument, the item. order_key wants two. The inner function takes the one and supplies the other from the box it can see.

zip(now, new) pairs the two lists place by place, and enumerate numbers the pairs. You've used both before, most recently in chapter 78. The round brackets in for place, (old, name) unpack the pair inside the numbered item.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Take "unknown" off the end of KINDS and run the script on a font that has a glyph with no code point and no base, such as a glyph201 left over from chapter 82. If you have none, test the line by itself:

KINDS.index("unknown")

ValueError: 'unknown' is not in list

index raises an error when the item isn't there. That's the right behavior here. A kind missing from the order list is a mistake in the script, and a sort that quietly put such glyphs somewhere would hide it. Put the word back.

docs.title: Using the list
docs.text:
The file has one glyph name to a line, in the proposed order. What then?

FontLab can reorder a font by hand. Per the User Guide for FontLab 8, the Font window in its Index mode lets you drag glyphs into place, and Font > Sort Glyphs reorders the font by the rules it offers. I haven't checked that menu in FontLab 9, and I don't know of a rule there that matches Ines's two-part one. For a few misplaced glyphs, dragging with the list open beside you is quick. For three hundred, the list is what you hand to whoever builds the fonts, since export tools commonly accept a glyph order as a text file.

So the script's product is a decision written down. That has worth by itself: next month the same script will tell Ines in one line whether the font has drifted.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Tuples compare item by item, so a tuple key sorts by its first part and settles ties with the next. Every part of a key must be comparable across all rows, which rules out None. The order of a list can itself be data: KINDS.index(...) turns a word into a rank you chose. unicodedata.category tells you what kind of character a code point is, for every script in Unicode.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Ines changes her mind: figures before letters. Change one line and run again. How many glyphs would change place now?
  2. Bring circumflex home. Add a dictionary OVERRIDES = {"circumflex": "symbols"} and have kind_of look there before anything else, with .get. The count should then read 19 symbols and no "other letters" line.
  3. Add a part to the key so that inside each kind a base glyph is followed at once by its suffixed forms, and only then by the next base: a, a.alt, a.sc, aacute. Print the keys for those four names with and without your change. Hint: name.split(".")[0].lower() as the second part, and think about why a.sc sorts before aacute already but A.sc and Aacute might not agree.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Plum has features, and nobody at Halfmoon has read them since Oskar left. Chapter 87 opens the feature text and lists what's in it.

docs.title: 87. What features does this font have?
docs.text:
Tuesday of week seventeen. The cookbook's typesetter wants small caps in the chapter openings and asks which OpenType features Plum has. Ines says "ligatures, I think" and looks at Mira. Mira looks at Oskar's chair.

A font's features are a text. Somebody wrote it, or a program did, and FontLab keeps it with the font. You can read it in the Features panel. Today a script reads it, because a script can count what it reads and Ines wants a summary she can paste into an email.

It's also the first step toward writing features, which starts tomorrow. Nobody should write into a text they haven't read.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The tell function from chapter 39. The script below defines it again, so it runs by itself.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the text handling in plain Python on the feature text stored in Plum's source file, and the output below comes from that. I'm assuming Fly's reader hands back that same text, wrapper lines included. If your first printout looks different from mine, trust yours and adjust the tests in Step 4.

This chapter changes nothing in the font.

docs.title: Step 1: Get the text
docs.text:
Fly reads the features in one call:

from fly import fl
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

package = scripting.current_package()
blocks = scripting.read_feature_blocks(package)
print(list(blocks))
print(len(blocks["prefix"]))
print(len(blocks["features"]))

['prefix', 'features']
916
2

scripting.current_package() is the way in that you used for kerning in chapter 69. blocks is a dictionary with two keys. prefix is one string of 916 characters: the part of the feature text that comes before any feature and serves them all. features has two items.

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
Plum has a liga feature. blocks["features"] sounds like a dictionary from tag to text, so ask for it by tag:

print(blocks["features"]["liga"])

TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str

Read the complaint from the left. "List indices": Python is telling you that blocks["features"] is a list. A list wants a position, a whole number, and you handed it a word.

Look at what the list holds:

for tag, code in blocks["features"]:
    print(tag, len(code))

liga 106
cpsp 93

It's a list of pairs, tag and text. There's a reason it's a list. Features apply in the order they're written, so the order is part of the data, and a list is the type whose business is order.

When you want to look one up by tag, turn the pairs into a dictionary. dict takes a list of pairs and makes each pair an entry:

by_tag = dict(blocks["features"])
code = by_tag["liga"]

Chapter 82 turned a dictionary round. This turns a list of pairs into one. Keep the list for walking through in order and the dictionary for asking by name.

docs.title: Step 3: One string, many lines
docs.text:
Print the liga text:

print(code)

feature liga {
# GSUB feature: Standard Ligatures
# Lookups: 1

  sub f i by fi;
  sub f l by fl;
} liga;

Seven lines on screen. To Python it's still one string, 106 characters long. The line breaks are characters in it, the \n you met at the end of every line in chapter 26. Loop over the string and you'd get f, e, a, one character at a time.

To work line by line, cut the string at its line breaks:

lines = code.splitlines()
print(len(lines))
print(lines[4])

7
  sub f i by fi;

splitlines returns a list of strings, one for each line, with the breaks removed. A file gave you its lines one at a time in a loop. A string in memory gives them all at once with this method. After that the work is the same.

docs.title: Step 4: Which lines are rules?
docs.text:
Of the seven lines, two do something. sub f i by fi; says: where f is followed by i, substitute the glyph fi. The rest is packaging. The first and last lines open and close the feature. Lines that start with # are comments, and one line is empty.

Comments in feature text start with #, the same sign Python uses, and can also follow code on a line. The prefix has one of those:

languagesystem DFLT dflt; # Default default

One cut handles both cases. Split the line at # and keep the first piece:

print("languagesystem DFLT dflt; # Default default".split("#")[0].strip())
print([" # Lookups: 1".split("#")[0].strip()])

languagesystem DFLT dflt;
['']

A line with a trailing comment keeps its code. A line that's nothing but a comment becomes an empty string, and you already skip those. So:

def rule_lines(code):
    rules = []
    for line in code.splitlines():
        line = line.split("#")[0].strip()
        if line == "" or line.startswith("feature") or line.startswith("}"):
            continue
        rules.append(line)
    return rules


print(rule_lines(code))

['sub f i by fi;', 'sub f l by fl;']

This is a filter made of four plain tests, and it will be wrong about feature text more elaborate than Plum's. A glyph name can't contain #, so that cut is safe. But a feature may hold named groups of rules called lookups, with their own opening and closing lines, and this function would count the opening line as a rule. For a first look at a small font it does the job. I'll say more under "What the summary leaves out".

docs.title: Step 5: What kind of rules?
docs.text:
The first word of a rule says what it does. sub substitutes one glyph or several for others. pos moves glyphs or changes their spacing. Count the first words with the tally from chapter 22:

def tally_words(rules):
    tally = {}
    for rule in rules:
        word = rule.split()[0]
        tally[word] = tally.get(word, 0) + 1
    return tally

split() with nothing in the parentheses cuts at any run of spaces, so [0] is the first word.

The prefix needs a different look. It holds two kinds of code line. A line that starts with @ defines a class, a named list of glyphs in square brackets. The others are declarations such as languagesystem. For a class, the summary should give the name and the size, not sixty-three glyph names:

rule = "@cpsp = [A B C];"
name = rule.split("=")[0].strip()
members = rule.split("[")[1].split("]")[0].split()
print(name, len(members))

@cpsp 3

The middle line is three splits in a row. Cut at [ and take what follows. Cut that at ] and take what precedes. Cut the result at spaces. Each split works on what the one before handed over, left to right.

Run the whole script:

Prefix: 37 lines, 3 of them code
  class @cpsp: 63 glyphs
  languagesystem DFLT dflt;
  languagesystem latn dflt;
liga  7 lines, 2 rules: 2 replace
      sub f i by fi;
      sub f l by fl;
cpsp  6 lines, 1 rules: 1 move
      pos @cpsp <5 0 10 0>;

That's all of it. Plum has two features. liga swaps in the two ligatures. cpsp, capital spacing, adds a little room around each of 63 capitals when a typesetter asks for it: that's what the four numbers in angle brackets do to the class @cpsp. There are no small caps. Mira writes the typesetter one line, and Ines adds "yet".

docs.title: Step 6: Comments can be wrong
docs.text:
Thirty-four of the prefix's 37 lines aren't code. Print them and read:

for line in blocks["prefix"].splitlines():
    if line.startswith("# G") or line.startswith("# Font"):
        print(line)

# Generated on: 2021-6-16 4:23
# Generated by: FontLab 7.1.5
# Font PostScript name: Vegur-Regular
# GSUB lookups: 1
# GSUB features: 1 (liga)
# GPOS lookups: 2
# GPOS features: 2 (cpsp, kern)

A program wrote this header in 2021, and the name in it is Vegur-Regular, which isn't this font's name. It lists three features. The text below it has two: there's no kern block. As far as I know FontLab builds that one from the kerning table at export, so it needn't be written here.

The header was true once. Nothing kept it true. Your script counted what's there, and the comment reports what a program saw in 2021. When the two disagree, believe the count. The same goes for comments in your own scripts, which is a reason to keep them few.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: List Features
# Prints a summary of the font's feature text: classes and declarations
# in the prefix, then each feature with its rules. Changes nothing.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


MEANING = {"sub": "replace", "pos": "move"}
SHOW_RULES = True


def rule_lines(code):
    rules = []
    for line in code.splitlines():
        line = line.split("#")[0].strip()
        if line == "" or line.startswith("feature") or line.startswith("}"):
            continue
        rules.append(line)
    return rules


def tally_words(rules):
    tally = {}
    for rule in rules:
        word = rule.split()[0]
        tally[word] = tally.get(word, 0) + 1
    return tally


def show_prefix(prefix):
    rules = rule_lines(prefix)
    print(f"Prefix: {len(prefix.splitlines())} lines, {len(rules)} of them code")
    for rule in rules:
        if rule.startswith("@"):
            name = rule.split("=")[0].strip()
            members = rule.split("[")[1].split("]")[0].split()
            print(f"  class {name}: {len(members)} glyphs")
        else:
            print(f"  {rule}")


def show_feature(tag, code):
    rules = rule_lines(code)
    parts = []
    for word, count in tally_words(rules).items():
        parts.append(f"{count} {MEANING.get(word, word)}")
    print(f"{tag}  {len(code.splitlines())} lines, {len(rules)} rules: {', '.join(parts)}")
    if SHOW_RULES:
        for rule in rules:
            print(f"      {rule}")


def main():
    if fl.CurrentFont() is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    blocks = scripting.read_feature_blocks(package)
    show_prefix(blocks["prefix"])
    for tag, code in blocks["features"]:
        show_feature(tag, code)
    if not blocks["features"]:
        print("No features.")


main()

Save it as list_features.py.

Notes on the listing.

MEANING.get(word, word) looks a word up and, when it isn't in the table, gives the word back unchanged. An unknown first word then prints as itself, and the summary still makes sense.

SHOW_RULES is for bigger fonts. A feature with four hundred substitutions shouldn't print four hundred lines into a summary. Set it to False and you get one line for each feature.

rule_lines serves both the prefix and the features. The prefix has no feature or } lines, so those two tests never fire there and do no harm.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
A class definition may run over several lines. People write them that way when the list is long. Try the function on one, with no font involved:

text = "@caps = [A B C\n  D E F];\n"
print(rule_lines(text))

['@caps = [A B C', 'D E F];']

Two "rules" from one definition. show_prefix would then report a class of three glyphs and print D E F]; as a declaration. The function assumes one statement to a line, and feature text doesn't have to keep to that. What ends a statement is the semicolon.

A sturdier reader would join the whole text and cut at ;. Exercise 3 asks for it.

docs.title: What the summary leaves out
docs.text:
The script reads feature text as lines of words. It doesn't understand the language. It can't tell you whether a rule is valid, whether the glyphs it names exist, or what the font does when a feature is switched on. Lookups, language-specific sections and contextual rules, the ones with a ' after a glyph name, pass through as lines beginning with whatever word they begin with.

Chapter 91 checks glyph names in classes against the font. Chapter 93 looks at what can be checked short of compiling. For anything past that there's the Features panel, where FontLab reads the text with a real parser and tells you what it thinks.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A long text is one string with line-break characters in it, and splitlines turns it into a list you can loop over. A list of pairs keeps order and dict turns it into a lookup when you need one. Chained splits take a line apart from the outside in. A comment says what its author believed when they wrote it, and code that counts says what's there now.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add "languagesystem" handling to show_prefix: collect the script tags, the second word of each such line, into a list and print one line, scripts: DFLT latn, in place of the two declarations.
  2. The grammar of the summary is off: 1 rules. Write plural(count, word) that returns 1 rule or 2 rules and use it in both places. Then decide what it should do with 0.
  3. Write statements(code) that removes comments line by line as rule_lines does, joins what's left with spaces, and cuts at ;. Drop empty pieces. Test it on the two-line class above: you should get one statement. What happens to the feature liga { line now, and how would you take it out?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The typesetter wants small caps and Plum has no feature for them. Chapter 88 writes one, from the list of .sc glyphs you already have.

docs.title: 88. Write a feature
docs.text:
Wednesday of week seventeen. The typesetter's answer came overnight: no small caps feature, no small caps in the cookbook. The glyphs exist. Ines has drawn sixty of them in her Plum since March. But a layout program doesn't go looking for glyphs called a.sc. It switches on a feature called smcp, and the feature has to say, glyph by glyph, what replaces what.

Sixty lines that differ only in a name. You know what that sentence means by now.

Yesterday you read feature text. Today a script writes some, and for the first time in this book the thing your script produces is itself a program, in another language, that another piece of software will read.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The ten .sc glyphs your practice font has by now: a.sc, b.sc and c.sc from chapter 8, and d.sc to h.sc, zero.sc and one.sc from chapter 40. With fewer or more, your lists differ from mine in length and in nothing else.
  • list_features.py from chapter 87. The script below defines tell and ask from chapter 39 again, so it runs by itself.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The text building is plain Python and I ran all of it. The step that writes the text into the font follows Fly's source, and I haven't seen it work.

docs.title: Step 1: One rule
docs.text:
The rule you need for one glyph is short:

sub a by a.sc;

Substitute a by a.sc. The words sub and by are fixed, the semicolon ends the rule, and the two names change. That's an f-string with two holes:

base = "a"
alternate = "a.sc"
print(f"sub {base} by {alternate};")

sub a by a.sc;

docs.title: Step 2: Which glyphs?
docs.text:
You want every glyph whose name ends in .sc, paired with the glyph it stands in for. The base name is the name with the last three characters cut off:

from fly import fl

SUFFIX = ".sc"

font = fl.CurrentFont()
names = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs]
pairs = []
for name in names:
    if name.endswith(SUFFIX):
        base = name[:-len(SUFFIX)]
        if base in names:
            pairs.append((base, name))
pairs.sort()
print(len(pairs))
print(pairs[:3])
print(pairs[-2:])

10
[('a', 'a.sc'), ('b', 'b.sc'), ('c', 'c.sc')]
[('one', 'one.sc'), ('zero', 'zero.sc')]

name[:-len(SUFFIX)] is the slice from chapter 10 with a computed end: everything except the last three characters, and still right if you change SUFFIX to .ss01 tomorrow.

pairs.sort() puts the pairs in alphabetical order, so the feature comes out the same whatever order the glyphs were made in. Tuples sort by their first item, as chapter 86 showed.

The inner if matters. A rule that names a glyph the font doesn't have won't compile, and one bad rule takes the whole feature text down with it. If someone has made Q.sc and deleted Q, the script must leave that pair out. Note the dot in SUFFIX, too. Without it, a glyph called disc would count as a small cap of di.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Now the text. You have a list, you want its items on separate lines, and chapter 25 gave you join for gluing a list into a string. Glue with a line break:

print("\n".join(pairs))

TypeError: sequence item 0: expected str instance, tuple found

join glues strings. Item 0 of pairs is ('a', 'a.sc'), a tuple, and Python won't guess how you'd like a tuple written out. In chapter 25 the list held glyph names, which were strings already, so the question never came up.

The pairs are data. The lines are text made from the data. Make the text first, one string for each pair, and then join:

lines = []
for base, alternate in pairs:
    lines.append(f"    sub {base} by {alternate};")
body = "\n".join(lines)
print(body)

    sub a by a.sc;
    sub b by b.sc;
    sub c by c.sc;
    sub d by d.sc;
    sub e by e.sc;
    sub f by f.sc;
    sub g by g.sc;
    sub h by h.sc;
    sub one by one.sc;
    sub zero by zero.sc;

The four spaces at the start of each f-string are indentation for the human who reads the feature later. The feature language doesn't care about them.

Look at what join does and doesn't do. It puts the glue between items: nine line breaks for ten lines. Nothing goes before the first or after the last. That's why the list approach beats adding "\n" to a growing string in a loop, where you always end up with one break too many or too few.

docs.title: Step 4: The wrapper
docs.text:
A feature needs an opening line and a closing line around its rules. You saw both yesterday:

TAG = "smcp"
text = "feature " + TAG + " {\n" + body + "\n} " + TAG + ";"
print(text)

feature smcp {
    sub a by a.sc;
    sub b by b.sc;
    sub c by c.sc;
    sub d by d.sc;
    sub e by e.sc;
    sub f by f.sc;
    sub g by g.sc;
    sub h by h.sc;
    sub one by one.sc;
    sub zero by zero.sc;
} smcp;

That's a complete feature. I used + here where an f-string would have done, for one reason: curly braces. Inside an f-string a { opens a hole, and the feature language wants a real one. You can write a real brace in an f-string by doubling it, {{, and it gets hard to read fast.

The tag appears twice and must match. Keeping it in one constant means it can't disagree with itself.

docs.title: Step 5: Fly has this already
docs.text:
Collecting suffix pairs and wrapping them is common enough that Fly carries both as functions:

import fly.ap.features.code as fea_code

pairs = fea_code.suffix_pairs(names, "sc")
print(fea_code.feature_text("smcp", pairs) == text)

True

The same text, character for character. You built it by hand so that you know what's inside. From here on the script uses Fly's two functions, for what they add. suffix_pairs leaves out pairs whose base is missing, as yours did, and also names that would be unsafe in feature text. It returns the pairs sorted by name, so the feature comes out in the same order every time. feature_text checks the tag and refuses a list in which the same glyph is replaced twice.

It doesn't refuse an empty list. With no .sc glyphs you'd get a feature with nothing in it:

print(fea_code.feature_text("smcp", []))

feature smcp {

} smcp;

The script has to catch that case itself, before it writes.

docs.title: Step 6: Into the font
docs.text:
Writing follows the shape you know: read, build the new state, show it, ask, write.

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

package = scripting.current_package()
blocks = scripting.read_feature_blocks(package)
others = [(tag, code) for tag, code in blocks["features"] if tag != TAG]
updated = {"prefix": blocks["prefix"],
           "features": others + [(TAG, text)]}

blocks is what the font has now. updated is what you want it to have: the same prefix, every feature except an old smcp, and the new smcp at the end. Leaving the old one out first means the script can run a second time, after Ines draws ten more small caps, and replace its own work. A feature tag may appear only once, so appending twice would be refused.

blocks itself stays untouched. The comprehension and the + each make a new list, which is the lesson of chapter 84 put to use.

Then the write:

used = [name for pair in pairs for name in pair]
result = scripting.write_feature_blocks(
    package, blocks, updated,
    references=used, undo_name="Write smcp feature")
print(result)

{'changed': 1}

The call takes both states. It compares blocks with the font as it is at that moment, and refuses if someone edited the features after you read them. references is the list of glyph names your new text mentions, flattened from the pairs by a comprehension with two for parts, the kind you met in chapter 85. Fly checks that each one is still in the font. undo_name is what the change should be called under Edit > Undo, if it lands there as the source says.

Run list_features.py afterward:

smcp  12 lines, 10 rules: 10 replace
      sub a by a.sc;
      sub b by b.sc;
      sub c by c.sc;
      sub d by d.sc;
      sub e by e.sc;
      sub f by f.sc;
      sub g by g.sc;
      sub h by h.sc;
      sub one by one.sc;
      sub zero by zero.sc;

docs.title: Text isn't a working feature
docs.text:
The font now holds the text. It doesn't yet act on it. Feature text has to be compiled, turned into the tables a layout program reads, and Fly's feature code says in its own words that it never does that. I know of no call that compiles from Python.

Open Window > Panels > Features. You should see smcp in the list with your ten rules. Click the panel's Compile button, look in the Output panel for complaints, then type abc in a Glyph window's text and switch the feature on. If the three letters change to your small caps, the feature works. If the panel reports an error, it will name a line. Read the line. Your script wrote it.

I'm describing this from the User Guide for FontLab 8, and haven't pressed that button in FontLab 9.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Make Small Caps Feature
# Writes or replaces the smcp feature from the font's .sc glyphs.
# Does not compile: do that in the Features panel afterward.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.features.code as fea_code
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


TAG = "smcp"
SUFFIX = "sc"
DRY_RUN = True


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    names = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs]
    pairs = fea_code.suffix_pairs(names, SUFFIX)
    if not pairs:
        print(f"No .{SUFFIX} glyphs with a base. Nothing to write.")
        return
    text = fea_code.feature_text(TAG, pairs)

    package = scripting.current_package()
    blocks = scripting.read_feature_blocks(package)
    others = [(tag, code) for tag, code in blocks["features"] if tag != TAG]
    verb = "Add"
    if len(others) < len(blocks["features"]):
        verb = "Replace"
    print(text)
    print(f"{verb} {TAG}: {len(pairs)} rules")

    if DRY_RUN:
        print("Dry run. Nothing written.")
        return
    if not ask(f"{verb} the {TAG} feature with {len(pairs)} rules?"):
        return
    updated = {"prefix": blocks["prefix"],
               "features": others + [(TAG, text)]}
    used = [name for pair in pairs for name in pair]
    result = scripting.write_feature_blocks(
        package, blocks, updated,
        references=used, undo_name=f"Write {TAG} feature")
    print(result)
    print("Now compile in the Features panel.")


main()

Save it as make_smcp.py. First run, with DRY_RUN = True:

feature smcp {
    sub a by a.sc;
    sub b by b.sc;
    sub c by c.sc;
    sub d by d.sc;
    sub e by e.sc;
    sub f by f.sc;
    sub g by g.sc;
    sub h by h.sc;
    sub one by one.sc;
    sub zero by zero.sc;
} smcp;
Add smcp: 10 rules
Dry run. Nothing written.

Notes on the listing.

SUFFIX has no dot here. suffix_pairs accepts it with or without one and adds its own, so disc is safe either way.

verb is worked out by comparing two lengths. If filtering by tag made the list shorter, there was an old smcp and this run replaces it. The reader of the dry run should know which.

The script has no try. If the write is refused, Fly raises an error with a sentence such as "Feature source changed; refresh the preview before applying." That sentence in the Output panel tells you more than anything I'd wrap around it. Run the script again and it will read the features afresh.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Change TAG to "smallcaps" and run with DRY_RUN = True:

ValueError: Feature tag must contain four ASCII letters or digits.

The error comes from feature_text, before anything touches the font. Feature tags are four characters, always, and layout programs know the registered ones by heart. smcp means small capitals from lowercase. A tag you invent is a feature no program will offer its user. Put smcp back.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Text for another program is built in two stages: one string for each item, then join to put the separators between them. join takes strings only, so data has to be formatted before it's glued. A write that replaces its own earlier output can be run again without harm, and that's worth arranging on purpose. A feature written into the font is text until FontLab compiles it.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Make A.sc in the Font window and run the dry run. The script proposes sub A by A.sc; under smcp. That's wrong: capitals to small caps is a different feature, c2sc. Split the pairs into two lists with base[0].isupper() and print two features. Don't write them yet.
  2. Build the text for smcp yourself again, as in Steps 3 and 4, but with each rule followed by a comment that gives the base glyph's code point: sub a by a.sc; # U+0061. You have the format from chapter 23.
  3. After a real run, undo with Edit > Undo and run list_features.py. Is smcp gone? Write down what you saw. I couldn't check it, and chapter 100 will want to know.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Small caps are one suffix. Ines's Plum has six: .sc, .alt, .ss01, .tf, .onum, .case. Chapter 89 makes a feature for each from one table.

docs.title: 89. Features from suffixes
docs.text:
Thursday of week seventeen. The small caps work in the typesetter's test file, and she has already asked what else there is. There's plenty. Ines's Plum has glyphs ending in .sc, .alt, .ss01, .tf, .onum and .case, and each suffix wants a feature of its own.

Mira starts the obvious way. She opens make_smcp.py, changes TAG and SUFFIX, runs it, changes them again. On the third round she types onum in one constant and forgets the other, and writes old-style figures into the tnum feature.

A pair of constants you edit six times is a table that hasn't been written down yet. Today you write it down.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • Your suffixed glyphs from Part 2: ten ending in .sc, four in .ss01 (a, g, y, ampersand), and zero.alt.
  • rename_suffix.py from chapter 31. The script below defines tell and ask from chapter 39 again, so it runs by itself.
  • The smcp feature from chapter 88. If you skipped the write there, today's script adds it.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the counting and the text building in plain Python on Plum's glyph names plus those fifteen. The write is the one from chapter 88, and I haven't seen it work.

docs.title: Step 1: Which suffixes are there?
docs.text:
Before a table of suffixes, a list of the ones the font has. The suffix is what follows the first period in a name. split(".", 1) cuts at the first period only, as it cut at the first colon in chapter 85, and the tally is the one from chapter 22:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
names = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs]
tally = {}
for name in names:
    if "." in name:
        suffix = name.split(".", 1)[1]
        tally[suffix] = tally.get(suffix, 0) + 1
print(tally)

{'notdef': 1, 'sc': 10, 'ss01': 4, 'alt': 1}

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
Three of those are suffixes. The first isn't. .notdef is a whole name that happens to start with a period, and the split did what you asked:

print(".notdef".split(".", 1))

['', 'notdef']

An empty base and a "suffix" of notdef. There was no error and nothing looked broken. If the next step had been a feature, the script would have gone looking for a tag for notdef.

This kind of mistake is the reason to print a tally before you build on it. Four entries are few enough to read, and you know your font well enough to see which one doesn't belong. The mend is a second condition:

def suffixes(names):
    tally = {}
    for name in names:
        if "." in name and not name.startswith("."):
            suffix = name.split(".", 1)[1]
            tally[suffix] = tally.get(suffix, 0) + 1
    return tally


print(suffixes(names))

{'sc': 10, 'ss01': 4, 'alt': 1}

docs.title: Step 3: The table
docs.text:
A dictionary from suffix to feature tag:

TAGS = {"sc": "smcp", "ss01": "ss01"}

The suffix is the studio's habit. The tag is fixed by the OpenType specification. ss01 happens to be both, which is why the alternates were renamed in chapter 31. For sc the two differ, and only the table knows that they belong together.

Walk the tally and look each suffix up:

for suffix in suffixes(names):
    print(suffix, TAGS[suffix])

sc smcp
ss01 ss01
KeyError: 'alt'

The font has a suffix the table doesn't. You met KeyError in chapter 21. Here it would be a poor way to stop, because a font will always have a stray suffix or two, and the script should say so and carry on with the rest:

for suffix, count in suffixes(names).items():
    if suffix not in TAGS:
        print(f".{suffix:<6}{count:>3}  no tag in the table, skipped")
        continue
    print(f".{suffix:<6}{count:>3}  {TAGS[suffix]}")

.sc     10  smcp
.ss01    4  ss01
.alt     1  no tag in the table, skipped

A skipped line in a report is a question for a person. Here the person is you.

docs.title: Step 4: What is zero.alt?
docs.text:
Fly has an opinion on the question. It carries a table like yours, a much longer one:

from fly.ap.features.identity_tools.feature_explorer.suffix_report import suggested_tag

for suffix in suffixes(names):
    print(suffix, suggested_tag(suffix))

sc smcp
ss01 ss01
alt salt

It agrees with you twice and suggests salt, stylistic alternates, for alt. That's a fair guess from the name. It's what the function answers for any suffix it doesn't know, too, so it is a guess and no more.

You know something the function doesn't. Chapter 31 left zero.alt out of the renaming because it's the slashed zero, and OpenType has a feature for that glyph alone, called zero. The suffix says "alternate". The glyph is something more particular.

You could add "alt": "zero" to the table. That would be true today and false the day someone draws q.alt. The better mend is in the font: give the glyph a name that says what it is. Open rename_suffix.py, set NEW_SUFFIX = ".zero", empty the SKIP set, do the dry run, read the one line, and then do it for real. Put NEW_SUFFIX and SKIP back afterward. Then add the entry the name has earned:

TAGS = {"sc": "smcp", "ss01": "ss01", "zero": "zero"}

So the table is yours, and Fly's function is a second opinion to ask when you meet a suffix you didn't invent. The script uses your table because your table holds what the studio decided.

docs.title: Step 5: One write for all of them
docs.text:
For each suffix in the table you make the pairs and the text as in chapter 88. All the new features then go into the font in a single write. One write is one step to undo, and the font is never left with half the set.

The new features replace old ones with the same tags and leave the others alone:

new_tags = [tag for tag, text in made]
kept = [(tag, code) for tag, code in blocks["features"] if tag not in new_tags]
updated = {"prefix": blocks["prefix"], "features": kept + made}

Chapter 88 filtered on one tag with !=. With a list of tags the test becomes not in. Nothing else changes.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Features From Suffixes
# Writes or replaces one feature for each suffix in TAGS.
# Does not compile: do that in the Features panel afterward.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.features.code as fea_code
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


TAGS = {"sc": "smcp", "ss01": "ss01", "zero": "zero"}
DRY_RUN = True


def suffixes(names):
    tally = {}
    for name in names:
        if "." in name and not name.startswith("."):
            suffix = name.split(".", 1)[1]
            tally[suffix] = tally.get(suffix, 0) + 1
    return tally


def plan(names, tags):
    made = []
    used = []
    for suffix, count in suffixes(names).items():
        if suffix not in tags:
            print(f".{suffix:<6}{count:>3}  no tag in the table, skipped")
            continue
        tag = tags[suffix]
        if tag in [done for done, text in made]:
            print(f".{suffix:<6}{count:>3}  {tag} is already made, skipped")
            continue
        pairs = fea_code.suffix_pairs(names, suffix)
        print(f".{suffix:<6}{count:>3}  {tag}  {len(pairs)} paired")
        if pairs:
            made.append((tag, fea_code.feature_text(tag, pairs)))
            used = used + [name for pair in pairs for name in pair]
    return made, used


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    names = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs]
    made, used = plan(names, TAGS)
    if not made:
        print("Nothing to write.")
        return

    package = scripting.current_package()
    blocks = scripting.read_feature_blocks(package)
    new_tags = [tag for tag, text in made]
    kept = [(tag, code) for tag, code in blocks["features"] if tag not in new_tags]
    print(f"{len(made)} features to write: {' '.join(new_tags)}")
    print(f"{len(kept)} features kept: {' '.join(tag for tag, code in kept)}")

    if DRY_RUN:
        print("Dry run. Nothing written.")
        return
    if not ask(f"Write {len(made)} features?"):
        return
    updated = {"prefix": blocks["prefix"], "features": kept + made}
    result = scripting.write_feature_blocks(
        package, blocks, updated,
        references=used, undo_name="Write features from suffixes")
    print(result)
    print("Now compile in the Features panel.")


main()

Save it as features_from_suffixes.py. The dry run:

.sc     10  smcp  10 paired
.ss01    4  ss01  4 paired
.zero    1  zero  1 paired
3 features to write: smcp ss01 zero
2 features kept: liga cpsp
Dry run. Nothing written.

After the real run, list_features.py shows the two new ones behind smcp:

ss01  6 lines, 4 rules: 4 replace
      sub a by a.ss01;
      sub ampersand by ampersand.ss01;
      sub g by g.ss01;
      sub y by y.ss01;
zero  3 lines, 1 rules: 1 replace
      sub zero by zero.zero;

Notes on the listing.

plan prints as it goes and returns two things, the features and the glyph names they mention. Printing inside the function that decides keeps each reason next to its decision.

The two numbers on a line can differ. The first counts glyphs with the suffix, the second counts those whose base glyph exists. .sc 11 smcp 10 paired means one small cap has nothing to replace, and you'd go and find out which.

' '.join(tag for tag, code in kept) has a comprehension without its square brackets. Inside the parentheses of a call you may leave them off.

smcp moved. It's written again from the glyphs, as it would have to be the day Ines adds i.sc, and it now sits after cpsp with the other new ones.

Mira's run on the real Plum is longer. Her table has six entries, with "tf": "tnum" and "onum": "onum" for the two extra sets of figures and "case": "case" for the punctuation that sits higher between capitals. The dry run prints six lines and one surprise: .sc 60 smcp 59 paired. Somebody drew germandbls.sc, and the base glyph in that file is still called uni00DF. Chapter 82's script mends the base name, and the second dry run says 60.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Change the table so that two suffixes claim one tag: "zero": "ss01". Dry run:

.sc     10  smcp  10 paired
.ss01    4  ss01  4 paired
.zero    1  ss01 is already made, skipped
2 features to write: smcp ss01

A tag may appear once in a font's features. Without the check in plan, the script would hand Fly two ss01 blocks and Fly would refuse the lot, small caps included. With it, one line tells you which table entry to look at. Put "zero": "zero" back.

If you want two suffixes in one feature, say .alt and .ss01 both under ss01, the rules have to be merged into one block. Exercise 3.

docs.title: What the table can't know
docs.text:
Order. Features apply in the order they're written, and two of yours touch the same letters. With ss01 and small caps both on, a meets smcp first and becomes a.sc. The ss01 rule looks for a, finds a.sc, and does nothing. Turn the order round and you'd get a.ss01, which smcp has no rule for. Neither result is the small cap of the alternate a. That glyph, a.ss01.sc or whatever you'd call it, doesn't exist. I'm reasoning from how features are documented to work, and haven't tested the two together.

The script takes suffixes in the order it finds them in the font. For Plum that's good enough. In a family where it matters, the table becomes a list of pairs in the order you choose, for the reason chapter 87 gave.

Meaning. The table says .sc glyphs go under smcp. It can't check that a.sc is a small cap. A glyph with the wrong suffix gets the wrong feature without complaint, as zero.alt nearly did.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A dictionary used as a table turns a choice you'd make by editing constants into data the script loops over. A split can succeed on a name it was never meant for, so print what you collected before you build on it. When a table lacks an entry, report the gap and carry on. When a name misleads the script, mending the name usually serves better than teaching the script an exception.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a line to the dry run for every table entry the font has no glyphs for. Put "case": "case" in the table to test it. You'll need the keys of TAGS and the keys of the tally, and chapter 25's set subtraction.
  2. Make A.sc and B.sc. They belong under c2sc, capitals to small caps, and smcp should keep only lowercase bases and figures. Filter the pairs for sc into two lists with base[0].isupper(), and build two features from one suffix.
  3. Let the table map a tag to a list of suffixes: {"ss01": ["ss01", "alt"]}. Collect the pairs for every suffix in the list into one list, then call feature_text once. What does feature_text say when a.alt and a.ss01 both exist? It's the error chapter 88 met: Duplicate substitution source glyphs.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Plum's liga feature has two ligatures, fi and fl. Ines's has eleven, with names like f_f_i. Chapter 90 reads a rule out of each name.

docs.title: 90. Ligatures
docs.text:
Friday of week seventeen. The typesetter sends a scan of a proof with one word circled: office. In the middle of it sit an ff ligature and then a plain i with its dot crowding the hook of the second f. Ines drew an ffi ligature years ago for this very collision. The font has the glyph. The feature never reaches it.

Ines's Plum has eleven ligatures, and the liga feature that lists them was typed by hand, one rule at a time, in the order in which the glyphs were drawn. The order turns out to matter.

A ligature's name already says what it's made of. Today a script reads the rule out of each name and puts the rules in the right order.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • Two new, empty glyphs called f_f and f_f_i. Make them as you made the small caps in chapter 8, with Font > New Glyph…. They don't need drawings today.
  • list_features.py from chapter 87. The script below defines tell and ask from chapter 39 again, so it runs by itself.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the name reading and the sorting in plain Python on Plum's glyph names plus those two. The write is the one from chapter 88, and I haven't seen it work.

docs.title: Step 1: A name that is a recipe
docs.text:
The convention is old and simple. A ligature is named after its parts, joined with underscores: f_f_i replaces f, f, i. You have cut names at periods since chapter 9. This cut is at another character:

print("f_f_i".split("_"))

['f', 'f', 'i']

That list is the left side of the rule. Join it with spaces, which is join from chapter 88 with a different glue:

name = "f_f_i"
parts = name.split("_")
print(f"sub {' '.join(parts)} by {name};")

sub f f i by f_f_i;

Don't confuse this with list(name), which cuts a string into its characters and would give you ['f', '_', 'f', '_', 'i'], underscores included.

docs.title: Step 2: The two that don't follow the rule
docs.text:
Plum has two ligatures already, and neither has an underscore:

print("fi".split("_"))

['fi']

One part. A string without the separator comes back whole, in a list of one. fi and fl got their names decades before the underscore convention, and nearly every font still uses them. No rule will read f and i out of fi, because the same rule would read m and u out of mu.

When a pattern covers most cases and a short list covers the rest, write the short list down:

LEGACY = {"fi": ["f", "i"], "fl": ["f", "l"]}


def recipe(name):
    if name in LEGACY:
        return LEGACY[name]
    if "_" in name and not name.startswith("."):
        return name.split("_")
    return []

Table first, pattern second, and an empty list for every glyph that isn't a ligature. The glyph called underscore, by the way, is safe. Its name has no underscore character in it.

docs.title: Step 3: Collect the rules
docs.text:
Walk the font and keep each glyph that has a recipe. As in chapter 88, a rule may only name glyphs the font has:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
names = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs]
known = set(names)
rules = []
for name in names:
    parts = recipe(name)
    if not parts:
        continue
    missing = [part for part in parts if part not in known]
    if missing:
        print(f"{name}: no glyph {' '.join(missing)}, left out")
        continue
    rules.append((parts, name))
print(rules)

[(['f', 'i'], 'fi'), (['f', 'l'], 'fl'), (['f', 'f'], 'f_f'), (['f', 'f', 'i'], 'f_f_i')]

Four rules, in font order: the two old ones, then the two you made this morning. known is a set, as in chapter 25, because all the script ever asks of it is whether a name is in the font.

docs.title: Step 4: Why the order matters
docs.text:
Write those four rules into a feature in that order and set the word office. A layout program walks along the text. At each glyph it tries the rules it has for that spot and takes the first that fits. It arrives at the first f. f i? No, the next glyph is another f. f l? No. f f? Yes. It swaps in f_f and moves on, and the next glyph is i, alone. The rule for f f i was fourth in line and never got its turn.

That's the proof on Ines's desk. Nothing is wrong with any single rule. The short rule stands in front of the long one that starts the same way.

The cure is to put longer rules first. Then f f i is tried before f f, and the short rule only catches what the long one leaves.

A caution about how sure I am. The specification for the feature language says a compiler should sort ligature rules this way by itself. Some do. I haven't seen what FontLab 9 does, and the hand-typed feature in Ines's font suggests that somewhere along the way nobody did. Sorting costs one line, and sorted text is right under either behavior.

docs.title: Step 5: The mistake
docs.text:
Longest first. sorted takes a key, and len measures length:

by_len = sorted(rules, key=len)
print(by_len == rules)

True

Nothing moved. The list came back as it went in, and there was no error to say why.

Ask what len measured:

print([len(rule) for rule in rules])

[2, 2, 2, 2]

Every rule is a pair, parts and name, and the length of a pair is two. You wanted the length of the first item in the pair. sorted did its job on four equal keys, and when keys are equal it keeps the old order.

Chapter 36 said that sorted hands the key function a whole row. len is a function like any other, and it measured what it was handed. Reaching inside the row is up to you, so write a key that does:

def longest_first(rule):
    parts, name = rule
    return (-len(parts), name)


for parts, name in sorted(rules, key=longest_first):
    print(f"sub {' '.join(parts)} by {name};")

sub f f i by f_f_i;
sub f f by f_f;
sub f i by fi;
sub f l by fl;

The key is a tuple, as in chapter 86. Its first part is the number of parts with a minus sign, so that 3 becomes -3 and sorts ahead of -2. That's a way to get largest first for one part of a key while the rest stays in the usual order. The second part is the name, which settles ties and makes the output the same on every run.

docs.title: Step 6: Replace in place
docs.text:
Chapter 88 took the old feature out and put the new one at the end. For liga that would be a change nobody asked for: it's the font's first feature, and chapter 87 said features apply in the order they're written. So this time the new text goes where the old text was:

features = []
found = False
for tag, code in blocks["features"]:
    if tag == TAG:
        code = text
        found = True
    features.append((tag, code))
if not found:
    features.append((TAG, text))

A loop that copies every item and changes one on the way through. found is a flag: it starts as False, and the loop sets it if it meets the tag. After the loop, the flag tells you whether there was anything to replace. If there wasn't, the feature goes at the end after all.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Make Ligature Feature
# Writes or replaces the liga feature from ligature glyph names.
# Does not compile: do that in the Features panel afterward.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


TAG = "liga"
LEGACY = {"fi": ["f", "i"], "fl": ["f", "l"]}
DRY_RUN = True


def recipe(name):
    if name in LEGACY:
        return LEGACY[name]
    if "_" in name and not name.startswith("."):
        return name.split("_")
    return []


def collect(names):
    known = set(names)
    rules = []
    for name in names:
        parts = recipe(name)
        if not parts:
            continue
        missing = [part for part in parts if part not in known]
        if missing:
            print(f"{name}: no glyph {' '.join(missing)}, left out")
            continue
        rules.append((parts, name))
    return rules


def longest_first(rule):
    parts, name = rule
    return (-len(parts), name)


def feature_text(tag, rules):
    lines = []
    for parts, name in sorted(rules, key=longest_first):
        lines.append(f"    sub {' '.join(parts)} by {name};")
    return "feature " + tag + " {\n" + "\n".join(lines) + "\n} " + tag + ";"


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    names = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs]
    rules = collect(names)
    if not rules:
        print("No ligature glyphs. Nothing to write.")
        return
    text = feature_text(TAG, rules)
    print(text)

    package = scripting.current_package()
    blocks = scripting.read_feature_blocks(package)
    features = []
    found = False
    for tag, code in blocks["features"]:
        if tag == TAG:
            code = text
            found = True
        features.append((tag, code))
    if not found:
        features.append((TAG, text))
    verb = "Replace" if found else "Add"
    print(f"{verb} {TAG}: {len(rules)} rules")

    if DRY_RUN:
        print("Dry run. Nothing written.")
        return
    if not ask(f"{verb} the {TAG} feature with {len(rules)} rules?"):
        return
    used = []
    for parts, name in rules:
        used = used + parts + [name]
    updated = {"prefix": blocks["prefix"], "features": features}
    result = scripting.write_feature_blocks(
        package, blocks, updated,
        references=used, undo_name=f"Write {TAG} feature")
    print(result)
    print("Now compile in the Features panel.")


main()

Save it as make_liga.py. The dry run:

feature liga {
    sub f f i by f_f_i;
    sub f f by f_f;
    sub f i by fi;
    sub f l by fl;
} liga;
Replace liga: 4 rules
Dry run. Nothing written.

After a real run, list_features.py shows liga still in first place:

liga  6 lines, 4 rules: 4 replace

Notes on the listing.

"Replace" if found else "Add" is the if with an else that chooses between two values, which you met inside a comprehension in chapter 37. It works anywhere a value can stand. Chapter 88 did the same job in three lines. Use the short form when both outcomes are plain values and the line stays readable. Otherwise write it out.

feature_text is your own this time. Fly's function of that name, which chapters 88 and 89 used, makes rules with one glyph on the left, and a ligature has several.

The comment lines that Plum's old liga text carried are gone, because the script writes the whole feature anew. A script that owns a feature owns all of it. If you want a comment in there, the script has to write it. Exercise 2.

used may name a glyph more than once, f six times here. I read Fly's source to see whether that's a problem. It only checks that every name is in the font.

docs.title: A second opinion
docs.text:
Fly has a ligature finder of its own:

from fly.ap.features.identity_tools.feature_explorer.ligature_finder import run

for row in run(names):
    print(row)

By its source this should print two rows:

('f_f', 'f f', 'Ready')
('f_f_i', 'f f i', 'Ready')

It reads underscore names and reports those whose parts are missing with a status that says so. It knows nothing of fi and fl, and it lists rules by name, short before long. That's why this chapter built its own. Fly's finder does one thing yours doesn't: for a name such as f_i.ss01 it carries the suffix to every part and looks for f.ss01 and i.ss01. Whether that's right depends on your font. In some, f_i.ss01 is an alternate ligature of the plain f and i.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Make a glyph called c_t and run the dry run. You get a fifth rule, sub c t by c_t;, under liga. Now ask Ines. The ct ligature with its looping bridge is ornament, and she'd never want it switched on in running text. It belongs to dlig, discretionary ligatures, which the user turns on by choice.

The name gave you the parts. It couldn't tell you the feature. That decision belongs to the designer, and the script needs a place to record it: a set of names, say, that go to dlig. Exercise 3. Delete c_t when you're done.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: split works with any separator, and a string without the separator comes back whole in a list of one. A short table of exceptions in front of a pattern handles names that are older than the pattern. A key function receives the whole row, so a len that should measure one item needs a function that picks the item out. A minus sign in a tuple key sorts that part largest first and leaves the other parts alone.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add "ffi": ["f", "f", "i"] and "ff": ["f", "f"] to LEGACY, without making glyphs of those names. Does the output change? Then say why a table entry for a glyph the font lacks costs nothing here.
  2. Have feature_text write a first line inside the braces: # written by make_liga.py, 4 rules. Run list_features.py and check that it still counts four rules. Chapter 87's comment handling is what makes that work.
  3. Add DISCRETIONARY = {"c_t", "s_t"} and split the collected rules into two lists by name in DISCRETIONARY. Print two features, liga and dlig, in the dry run. Don't write them.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 87 found a class in the prefix, @cpsp, with 63 capitals in it. Nobody has checked since whether those 63 names are all still in the font. Chapter 91 reads classes, checks them and writes one.

docs.title: 91. Classes in features
docs.text:
Monday of week eighteen. The Istanbul publisher sends a cover proof. The title is set in Plum's capitals with capital spacing turned on, and one word looks wrong: in İSTANBUL the first letter sits closer to the S than any other letter sits to its neighbor.

Mira knows where to look. Chapter 87 found a class called @cpsp in the features prefix, with 63 capitals in it, and the cpsp feature gives a little room to every glyph in that class. Sixty-three was the number of capitals Plum had when somebody typed the list. The font has more now.

A class in feature code is a list of glyph names with a name of its own. Nothing ties it to the font. Glyphs can be added, renamed and deleted, and the list stays as it was typed. Today you read the list, compare it with the font and write it again.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • list_features.py from chapter 87. The script below defines tell and ask from chapter 39 again, so it runs by itself.
  • The accented capitals you built in Part 3. If you built fewer than I did, your counts will be smaller than mine.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the reading, the comparing and the text building in plain Python on Plum's own prefix and glyph names, plus the fifteen capitals from Part 3. The write is the one from chapter 88, and I haven't seen it work.

docs.title: Step 1: Keep the names this time
docs.text:
Chapter 87 cut a class line apart to count its members. Today you keep them. The function takes one line of the prefix and answers with a name and a list, or with None if the line doesn't define a class:

def class_line(line):
    code = line.split("#")[0].strip()
    if not code.startswith("@") or "=" not in code:
        return None
    name = code.split("=")[0].strip()
    members = code.split("[")[1].split("]")[0].split()
    return name, members


print(class_line("@cpsp = [A B C];  # capitals"))
print(class_line("languagesystem DFLT dflt;"))

('@cpsp', ['A', 'B', 'C'])
None

The first line of the function drops a comment, as rule_lines did. The three splits in a row are chapter 87's. A function with two kinds of answer, a pair or None, is the shape recipe almost had on Friday. The caller has to ask which one came back before using it.

Now the real prefix:

from fly import fl
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

font = fl.CurrentFont()
package = scripting.current_package()
blocks = scripting.read_feature_blocks(package)
for line in blocks["prefix"].splitlines():
    found = class_line(line)
    if found is not None:
        name, members = found
        print(name, len(members), members[:3], members[-2:])

@cpsp 63 ['A', 'B', 'C'] ['Ydieresis', 'Ygrave']

One class, 63 names, from A to Ygrave.

docs.title: Step 2: Is every member still in the font?
docs.text:
This is the check chapter 87 said was coming. A class that names a glyph the font no longer has should stop the features from compiling. I haven't seen the message FontLab gives, but it would arrive at export time, on a Friday.

known = {glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs}
gone = [name for name in members if name not in known]
print(len(gone), gone)

0 []

Nothing is missing. All 63 are in the font. That was the worry, and it turns out to be unfounded. The proof on the desk is still wrong, though.

docs.title: Step 3: Ask it the other way round
docs.text:
"Is every member in the font?" has a twin: "is every glyph that belongs in the class a member?" The first question needs only the two lists. The second needs a rule that says what belongs.

For capital spacing the rule is simple to state: every capital letter. Chapter 86 showed how Python knows a capital. unicodedata.category gives Lu, letter uppercase, for each one:

import unicodedata


def by_category(font, category):
    names = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        code = glyph.unicode
        if code is not None and unicodedata.category(chr(code)) == category:
            names.append(glyph.name)
    return names


capitals = by_category(font, "Lu")
missing = [name for name in capitals if name not in members]
print(len(capitals), len(missing))
print(" ".join(missing))

82 19
Abreve Gbreve Idotaccent Scedilla Cacute Nacute Sacute Zacute Uring Racute Zdotaccent Ccaron Dcaron Ecaron Ncaron Rcaron Scaron Tcaron Zcaron

There it is: Idotaccent, the İ of İSTANBUL. Nineteen capitals get no capital spacing. Fifteen are the ones you built in Part 3, and they come in the order you built them, because by_category walks the font and new glyphs sit at its end. The first four were in Plum when it came to you, which means the class was already out of date before anyone at Halfmoon touched the font. Three of those four are Turkish.

So the first check found nothing and the second found nineteen. A list can be wrong in two directions, and a check that covers one of them says nothing about the other.

docs.title: Step 4: The mistake
docs.text:
Write the class line again with all 82 names. Mira's first try glues the pieces together the quick way:

members = ["A", "B", "C"]
line = "@cpsp = " + str(members) + ";"
print(line)

@cpsp = ['A', 'B', 'C'];

Python is content. str of a list is how Python writes a list: quotes around each item, commas between. Feature code writes a list its own way, with spaces and nothing else. A compiler would stop at the first quote.

You can see this one because you printed the line before writing it into the font. With 82 names on one long line you might not look closely, so look at a short one first. The cure is join, as in chapter 88:

line = "@cpsp = [" + " ".join(members) + "];"
print(line)

@cpsp = [A B C];

Whenever a program writes text for another program to read, the other program's grammar decides, and str knows only Python's.

docs.title: Step 5: Keep the old order, add at the end
docs.text:
The new list could be the 82 capitals in font order. But someone chose the order of the old list, the alphabet first and the accented letters after, and a person comparing the old line with the new one will want to see what changed. So keep the old members in their order and put the new ones behind them:

def rebuilt(members, known, should):
    kept = [name for name in members if name in known]
    added = [name for name in should if name not in members]
    return kept + added

kept drops a member only when the font has lost the glyph. added holds whatever the rule asks for and the list lacks. A name a person once put in by hand stays in, whether the rule knows it or not.

The line then goes back where it was. The prefix is 37 lines of text, one of which you change. That's Friday's loop again, which copies every item and replaces one on the way through:

lines = []
for line in blocks["prefix"].splitlines():
    found = class_line(line)
    if found is not None and found[0] == "@cpsp":
        line = "@cpsp = [" + " ".join(fresh) + "];"
    lines.append(line)
prefix = "\n".join(lines)

Every other line, comments included, passes through untouched.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Feature Classes
# Checks the classes in the features prefix against the font
# and rebuilds the ones named in WANTED.
# Does not compile: do that in the Features panel afterward.
import unicodedata

from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


WANTED = {"@cpsp": "Lu"}
DRY_RUN = True


def class_line(line):
    code = line.split("#")[0].strip()
    if not code.startswith("@") or "=" not in code:
        return None
    name = code.split("=")[0].strip()
    members = code.split("[")[1].split("]")[0].split()
    return name, members


def by_category(font, category):
    names = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        code = glyph.unicode
        if code is not None and unicodedata.category(chr(code)) == category:
            names.append(glyph.name)
    return names


def rebuilt(members, known, should):
    kept = [name for name in members if name in known]
    added = [name for name in should if name not in members]
    return kept + added


def new_prefix(prefix, font):
    known = {glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs}
    lines = []
    used = []
    changed = 0
    for line in prefix.splitlines():
        found = class_line(line)
        if found is not None:
            name, members = found
            gone = [member for member in members if member not in known]
            print(f"{name}: {len(members)} glyphs, {len(gone)} not in the font")
            if name in WANTED:
                should = by_category(font, WANTED[name])
                fresh = rebuilt(members, known, should)
                extra = [member for member in fresh if member not in members]
                print(f"  rebuilt: {len(fresh)} glyphs, added {' '.join(extra) or 'none'}")
                if fresh != members:
                    line = name + " = [" + " ".join(fresh) + "];"
                    used = used + fresh
                    changed += 1
        lines.append(line)
    return "\n".join(lines), used, changed


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    blocks = scripting.read_feature_blocks(package)
    prefix, used, changed = new_prefix(blocks["prefix"], font)
    print(f"{changed} class lines to rewrite.")
    if changed == 0:
        return
    if DRY_RUN:
        print("Dry run. Nothing written.")
        return
    if not ask(f"Rewrite {changed} class lines in the prefix?"):
        return
    updated = {"prefix": prefix, "features": list(blocks["features"])}
    result = scripting.write_feature_blocks(
        package, blocks, updated,
        references=used, undo_name="Rebuild feature classes")
    print(result)
    print("Now compile in the Features panel.")


main()

Save it as feature_classes.py. The dry run:

@cpsp: 63 glyphs, 0 not in the font
  rebuilt: 82 glyphs, added Abreve Gbreve Idotaccent Scedilla Cacute Nacute Sacute Zacute Uring Racute Zdotaccent Ccaron Dcaron Ecaron Ncaron Rcaron Scaron Tcaron Zcaron
1 class lines to rewrite.
Dry run. Nothing written.

After a real run, list_features.py should say class @cpsp: 82 glyphs. Run the script a second time and it reports 0 class lines to rewrite. and stops, because the list it would build is the list that's there.

Notes on the listing.

WANTED maps a class name to a Unicode category. It's a small table with one row, built for more.

' '.join(extra) or 'none' uses or between two values. An empty string counts as false, so when nothing was added the or hands over its second value. Use it for a default in a printed line, and write an if for anything more important.

new_prefix returns three things, and main unpacks three. The function reports every class it meets, including classes that aren't in WANTED. The first check, for members the font has lost, costs nothing and applies to any class.

The cpsp feature itself isn't touched. It says pos @cpsp <5 0 10 0>;, and it will find the longer list under the same name.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Change the table to {"@cpsp": "Ll"}, as if you'd mistyped the category, and do the dry run:

@cpsp: 63 glyphs, 0 not in the font
  rebuilt: 147 glyphs, added a aacute abreve acircumflex adieresis agrave aring …
