I've cut the line short. It goes on for eighty-four names, Plum's seventy lowercase letters and the fourteen from Part 3. The script kept the 63 capitals, since it never removes a name a person put in, and added every lowercase letter. Nothing in the code could tell it that capital spacing on lowercase letters is nonsense. What stops you is the dry run and the number in it: 147 where you expected about 80. Put "Lu" back.

docs.title: What the rule can't know
docs.text:
Unicode's idea of a capital and the designer's may differ. Your ten small caps have no code points, so by_category never sees them, and for capital spacing that's correct. For a class of "everything as tall as a capital" it would be wrong, and you'd add a second source of names: a suffix, say, as in chapter 89.

A feature class isn't a kerning class. Chapter 71's kerning classes say which glyphs kern alike on one side, and each glyph may be in one class per side. A feature class is a list and nothing more. A glyph may be in ten of them. FontLab keeps the two kinds in the same place inside the font, as far as I can tell from the source, and I haven't seen how its Classes panel shows a class that the prefix text defines. This script reads and writes the prefix text only, because that's the route with an Undo step behind it.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A feature class is a named list of glyph names in the feature text, and it doesn't follow the font when glyphs come and go. A list can be wrong by holding what it shouldn't or by lacking what it should, and each direction needs its own check. Text written for another program has to follow that program's grammar, so build it with join and never with str of a list. When you rebuild a list a person made, keep their order and add to the end, so the change can be read.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a count of names that appear twice in a class. Test it on class_line("@x = [A B A];"). Chapter 22's tally will do it.
  2. The figures get no class in Plum. Extend the script so that a class in WANTED that the prefix lacks is added as a new line at the end of the prefix: "@figures": "Nd". Print the line in the dry run. You should get ten names.
  3. Before the ask, print the old line and the new line of each rewritten class, one under the other, cut to 70 characters with a slice. Which end of the line would you rather see?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Plum has one set of figures. The typesetter's recipes want fractions from them, for the half cups and the sixteenths of an inch. Chapter 92 writes the figure features.

docs.title: 92. Fractions and figures
docs.text:
Tuesday of week eighteen. The cookbook is full of quantities: 1/2 cup of sugar, 3/16 of an inch of pastry. The typesetter sets them with full-size figures and a slash, and asks whether Plum can do proper fractions, with a small figure up, a slanted bar and a small figure down.

Ines says the font needs three things for that. It needs small figures that sit high, called numerators. It needs small figures that sit on the baseline, called denominators. And it needs a frac feature that knows which is which. She'll draw the figures. The feature is Mira's.

Until now each feature you wrote did one thing to one glyph at a time. frac has to do two things in order, and the second depends on what stands before the glyph. Today you write three features, and one of them has two stages.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • Add Glyphs From List.py from chapter 40 and list_features.py from chapter 87. The script below defines tell and ask from chapter 39 again, so it runs by itself.
  • The five features the font has after chapter 91.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the name building and the text building in plain Python on Plum's glyph names. I also played the typesetting program by hand, with a few lines of Python that apply the rules as I understand them, to get the glyph sequences this chapter quotes. No real layout program has seen this feature. Treat the frac text as a careful draft until chapter 93 and a compile have looked at it.

docs.title: Step 1: The mistake
docs.text:
Twenty-one glyphs are missing: ten numerators, ten denominators and the bar. Mira types the names of the first set the fast way:

names = [figure + ".numr" for figure in "0123456789"]
print(names)

['0.numr', '1.numr', '2.numr', '3.numr', '4.numr', '5.numr', '6.numr', '7.numr', '8.numr', '9.numr']

Ten names, all wrong. A loop over a string gives characters, and the figure glyphs aren't named after their characters. The glyph for 0 is called zero. Chapter 81 said what a glyph name may start with, and a digit wasn't on the list.

Had she made glyphs from those names, nothing would have stopped her until a feature tried to pair 0.numr with a glyph called 0. The names of the figures are in the font, so ask the font. Chapter 91's by_category does it, with the category for decimal digits:

import unicodedata

from fly import fl


def by_category(font, category):
    names = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        code = glyph.unicode
        if code is not None and unicodedata.category(chr(code)) == category:
            names.append(glyph.name)
    return names


font = fl.CurrentFont()
figures = by_category(font, "Nd")
print(figures)

['zero', 'one', 'two', 'three', 'four', 'five', 'six', 'seven', 'eight', 'nine']

docs.title: Step 2: Twenty-one glyphs from a file
docs.text:
Build the full list of names and write it where chapter 40's script can find it:

from pathlib import Path

needed = ["fraction"]
for suffix in [".numr", ".dnom"]:
    needed = needed + [name + suffix for name in figures]
print(len(needed), needed[:3], needed[-1])

path = Path(font.path).parent / "fraction-glyphs.txt"
with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("\n".join(needed) + "\n")

21 ['fraction', 'zero.numr', 'one.numr'] nine.dnom

fraction is the standard name of the slanted bar, a character of its own at U+2044 and a different glyph from slash. The suffixes .numr and .dnom are the ones Fly's suggested_tag knows, which chapter 89 showed you how to ask.

Now run Add Glyphs From List from the Scripts menu, choose fraction-glyphs.txt, and say yes. You have 21 empty glyphs. Ines will fill them. A feature only needs the names.

docs.title: Step 3: The two simple features
docs.text:
numr turns every figure into its numerator, and dnom into its denominator. These are chapter 88's small caps under another name, and Fly's two functions build them. suffix_pairs takes the suffix without its period:

import fly.ap.features.code as fea_code

names = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs]
pairs = fea_code.suffix_pairs(names, "numr")
print(len(pairs), pairs[:2])

10 [('eight', 'eight.numr'), ('five', 'five.numr')]

A typesetter who wants a superior-looking 2 on its own can switch on numr for that one character. These two features are also where frac gets its vocabulary.

docs.title: Step 4: What a fraction needs
docs.text:
Think about 3/16 as a row of glyphs: three slash one six. The result should be three.numr fraction one.dnom six.dnom.

No single rule of the kind you've written can do it. "Replace one by one.numr" and "replace one by one.dnom" can't both hold. Which one is right depends on the side of the bar the figure stands on. Feature code can say that, in two stages.

Stage one makes everything a numerator and turns the slash into the bar:

three.numr fraction one.numr six.numr

Stage two walks along the row and changes a numerator into a denominator when the glyph before it is the bar or a denominator:

three.numr fraction one.dnom six.numr
three.numr fraction one.dnom six.dnom

The six changes because the one before it has already changed. The rule feeds itself along the row, which is why one rule handles a denominator of any length.

A stage is called a lookup. A feature may hold several, and they run in the order they're written, each over the whole row before the next begins. The order matters here in the way it mattered for ligatures. Swap the two stages and the second finds no numerators to change, because the first hasn't made any yet.

docs.title: Step 5: Say it in feature code
docs.text:
Here's the text the script will produce. Three pieces of grammar are new:

feature frac {
    @frac_plain = [zero one two three four five six seven eight nine];
    @frac_up = [zero.numr one.numr two.numr ... nine.numr];
    @frac_down = [zero.dnom one.dnom two.dnom ... nine.dnom];
    lookup frac_all_up {
        sub @frac_plain by @frac_up;
        sub slash by fraction;
    } frac_all_up;
    lookup frac_after_bar {
        sub [fraction @frac_down] @frac_up' by @frac_down;
    } frac_after_bar;
} frac;

I've shortened two lines with dots. The script writes them out in full.

The classes are defined inside the feature. Chapter 91's class sat in the prefix because any feature might want it. These three serve one feature and live with it.

sub @frac_plain by @frac_up; replaces a class by a class. It means ten rules at once: the first name by the first name, the second by the second. Both lists must have the same length and the same order. The script builds all three from one list of figures, so they can't drift apart.

lookup name { ... } name; wraps a stage and gives it a name.

The last rule has a mark, the ' after @frac_up. The mark says which glyph is replaced. What stands before it is context: it must be there for the rule to fire, and it's left alone. Read it aloud as "after the bar or a denominator, a numerator becomes a denominator".

Building the text is string work. A small function writes a list of names in the feature language's brackets, which is the lesson of chapter 91's mistake put where it can't be forgotten:

def group(names):
    return "[" + " ".join(names) + "]"


print(group(["zero", "one"]))

[zero one]

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Figure Features
# Writes or replaces numr, dnom and frac from the figure glyphs.
# Does not compile: do that in the Features panel afterward.
import unicodedata

from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.features.code as fea_code
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(
        qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No
    )
    return answer == box.Yes


DRY_RUN = True


def by_category(font, category):
    names = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        code = glyph.unicode
        if code is not None and unicodedata.category(chr(code)) == category:
            names.append(glyph.name)
    return names


def group(names):
    return "[" + " ".join(names) + "]"


def frac_text(figures):
    up = [name + ".numr" for name in figures]
    down = [name + ".dnom" for name in figures]
    lines = [
        "feature frac {",
        f"    @frac_plain = {group(figures)};",
        f"    @frac_up = {group(up)};",
        f"    @frac_down = {group(down)};",
        "    lookup frac_all_up {",
        "        sub @frac_plain by @frac_up;",
        "        sub slash by fraction;",
        "    } frac_all_up;",
        "    lookup frac_after_bar {",
        "        sub [fraction @frac_down] @frac_up' by @frac_down;",
        "    } frac_after_bar;",
        "} frac;",
    ]
    return "\n".join(lines)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    names = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs]
    figures = by_category(font, "Nd")
    needed = ["slash", "fraction"]
    for suffix in [".numr", ".dnom"]:
        needed = needed + [name + suffix for name in figures]
    missing = [name for name in needed if name not in names]
    if missing:
        print(f"{len(missing)} glyphs missing: {' '.join(missing)}")
        print("Nothing to write.")
        return

    made = []
    for tag in ["numr", "dnom"]:
        pairs = [pair for pair in fea_code.suffix_pairs(names, tag) if pair[0] in figures]
        made.append((tag, fea_code.feature_text(tag, pairs)))
    made.append(("frac", frac_text(figures)))
    for tag, text in made:
        print(f"{tag}: {len(text.splitlines())} lines")

    package = scripting.current_package()
    blocks = scripting.read_feature_blocks(package)
    new_tags = [tag for tag, text in made]
    kept = [(tag, code) for tag, code in blocks["features"] if tag not in new_tags]
    print(f"{len(kept)} features kept: {' '.join(tag for tag, code in kept)}")
    if DRY_RUN:
        print(made[2][1])
        print("Dry run. Nothing written.")
        return
    if not ask(f"Write {len(made)} features?"):
        return
    updated = {"prefix": blocks["prefix"], "features": kept + made}
    result = scripting.write_feature_blocks(
        package, blocks, updated,
        references=figures + needed, undo_name="Write figure features")
    print(result)
    print("Now compile in the Features panel.")


main()

Save it as figure_features.py. The dry run begins:

numr: 12 lines
dnom: 12 lines
frac: 12 lines
5 features kept: liga cpsp smcp ss01 zero
feature frac {
    @frac_plain = [zero one two three four five six seven eight nine];

and goes on with the text you saw in step 5.

Notes on the listing.

The script refuses to write anything unless all 22 glyphs it will name are in the font. Delete eight.dnom and nine.dnom and it says 2 glyphs missing: eight.dnom nine.dnom and stops. Chapter 88's script left out a pair that lacked a glyph and wrote the rest. That was right for small caps, where nine are better than none. A fraction feature with eight denominators would set 3/16 correctly and 3/18 wrongly, and the reader of the cookbook would be the one to find out. So this script stops and names the missing glyphs.

if pair[0] in figures keeps numr and dnom to the figures. If someone later draws a.numr for an ordinal, it won't slip into a feature that frac leans on.

frac comes last of the three, and all three come after the features you had. The order among different features matters less here than the order of the stages inside frac.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
After a real run, look at the result with list_features.py:

frac  12 lines, 8 rules: 1 @frac_plain, 1 @frac_up, 1 @frac_down, 2 lookup, 3 replace

Eight rules, it says, and five of them aren't rules. Chapter 87 warned you that rule_lines was a filter made of four plain tests and would be wrong about feature text more complicated than Plum's. Now Plum has such text, and you wrote it. The lister counts a class definition as a rule whose first word is @frac_plain, and a lookup line as a rule whose first word is lookup.

It printed no error, and the three real rules are in the count. The number is wrong all the same, and anyone who reads "8 rules" in a report will believe it. A tool that reads text line by line stays honest only while the text stays as plain as the tool expects. Chapter 93 starts from this line.

docs.title: What the feature can't know
docs.text:
Stage one turns every figure in reach into a numerator. Switch frac on for a whole recipe and "2 cups" becomes a small raised 2 followed by "cups". For "1 1/2" the whole number goes up with the rest: one.numr space one.numr fraction two.dnom. So the typesetter applies frac to the fraction and nothing else, which is how this plain form of the feature is meant to be used. There are longer versions that look for the slash first and leave other figures alone. They need more context rules than a first fraction feature should carry.

You might expect figure sets here too. Plum has one set of figures, and chapter 66 found them tabular already, so there's nothing to switch between. In a font with .tf or .onum figures, chapter 89's table handles them.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A feature can hold several lookups, which run in order, each over the whole row of glyphs. A rule can replace a class by a class when both lists have the same length and order, and building them from one source list keeps them matched. A mark after a name says which glyph a rule replaces, and what stands before it is context. A loop over a string gives characters, and glyph names for figures have to come from the font.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. The typesetter might type the real fraction bar, U+2044, in place of a slash. Does stage one need a rule for it? Give the fraction glyph its code point first (fix_unicodes.py from chapter 83 may propose it), then say which glyph the row already holds.
  2. Write shape(text), a function that plays the two stages on a list of glyph names: stage one with a comprehension, stage two with range(1, len(row)) and a test on row[i - 1]. Try it on ["three", "slash", "one", "six"]. Then swap the stages and see what comes out.
  3. The cookbook also uses ½ as a single character in a few headings. Does the font have onehalf? If it does, would you add sub one slash two by onehalf; to frac, and in which stage?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The lister has now been wrong once in public, and none of the features you wrote since chapter 88 has been compiled by a script. Chapter 93 writes the checks that can be made without a compiler, and says where the Compile button comes in.

docs.title: 93. Does it compile?
docs.text:
Wednesday of week eighteen. Oskar's leave ended on Monday. He's back three days a week, the sheet he left is on the wall with nine lines through it, and he hasn't said a word about it. At the coffee machine he tells a story. Two years ago a Friday export stopped with a message about features. Someone had tidied a feature by hand on Thursday evening and lost a semicolon. Nobody found it until Monday, and the fonts went out three days late.

Plum had two features when it came to you. It has eight now, six added by scripts of yours and one rewritten, and none has been through a compiler since you wrote it. Compiling turns feature text into the tables a layout program reads, and the compiler is the only judge of whether the text is valid.

I know of no call that compiles from Python. You do it with the Compile button in the Features panel. A script can still do something useful first: it can read the text and catch the cheap mistakes, a missing semicolon, a brace left open, a glyph that isn't in the font. Today you write that script and learn how far to trust it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The tell function from chapter 39. The script below defines it again, so it runs by itself.
  • The eight features the font has after chapter 92: liga, cpsp, smcp, ss01, zero, numr, dnom, frac.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the checker in plain Python on Plum's two features plus the text that chapters 88 to 92 produce, and on the broken strings below. I haven't seen FontLab's compiler accept or refuse any of it.

docs.title: Step 1: Words
docs.text:
Most of what can be checked comes down to one question: is every word in a rule something the font or the feature language knows? So cut a line into words. Feature code glues punctuation to names, as in [zero one]; so turn each punctuation mark into a space first. replace from chapter 30 does one mark at a time:

PUNCTUATION = "[];<>"


def words_of(code):
    for mark in PUNCTUATION:
        code = code.replace(mark, " ")
    return code.split()


print(words_of("sub f i by fi;"))
print(words_of("pos @cpsp <5 0 10 0>;"))

['sub', 'f', 'i', 'by', 'fi']
['pos', '@cpsp', '5', '0', '10', '0']

Each word is then one of four things: a word of the language, a number, a class, or a glyph name. The numbers need a test. isdigit says whether a string is all digits, and it trips on a minus sign:

print("35".isdigit(), "-35".isdigit())

True False

Kerning taught you that font numbers are often negative. lstrip("-") returns the string without any minus signs at its left end, and then isdigit can answer:

def is_number(word):
    return word.lstrip("-").isdigit()

docs.title: Step 2: Check a line
docs.text:
The checker never stops at the first problem. It collects every problem as a sentence in a list and hands the list back, so one run shows everything that's wrong:

WORDS = {"sub", "by", "from", "pos", "="}


def check_line(code, known, classes):
    problems = []
    words = words_of(code)
    if "=" in words and words[0].startswith("@"):
        classes.add(words[0])
        words = words[1:]
    for word in words:
        if word in WORDS or is_number(word):
            continue
        if word.startswith("@"):
            if word not in classes:
                problems.append(f"class {word} is not defined")
        elif word not in known:
            problems.append(f"no glyph {word}")
    return problems

known is the set of glyph names in the font. classes is the set of class names defined so far. A line that defines a class, such as @frac_up = [...], adds its name to that set before its members are checked. A class has to be defined above the line that uses it, and reading from the top down gets that right without extra work.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Mira wraps a loop around check_line, runs it over the font, and gets this:

frac line 10: class @frac_up' is not defined
8 features checked, 1 problems.

Line 10 of frac is the rule with the mark: sub [fraction @frac_down] @frac_up' by @frac_down;. The class @frac_up is defined, seven lines higher. The checker is looking for a class called @frac_up', with the mark stuck to it, because nobody told words_of that ' is punctuation.

The feature is fine and the checker is wrong. This is worse than it looks. A checker that raises a false alarm gets ignored, and it will be ignored on the day the alarm is real. Add the mark:

PUNCTUATION = "[];'<>"

Before you believe a report from a tool you wrote, read the line it complains about.

docs.title: Step 4: The shape of a feature
docs.text:
Three more checks look at a feature as a whole. It should open with feature TAG { and close with } TAG;. Every line of code should end with a semicolon or an opening brace. And the braces should balance, which is counting. A string's count method says how many times a piece occurs in it:

opened = 0
for code in ["feature frac {", "lookup a {", "} a;"]:
    opened = opened + code.count("{") - code.count("}")
print(opened)

1

One brace is still open at the end, so something is missing.

docs.title: Step 5: Test the checker
docs.text:
How do you know a checker catches what it should? The font's features are all sound, so running it over the font proves only that it stays quiet. Feed it bad text on purpose. Take the smallest feature and break it four ways. The snippet calls check_feature, which is in the whole script below, and known is the set of the font's glyph names, as in step 2:

good = "feature zero {\n    sub zero by zero.zero;\n} zero;"
tests = [
    good.replace("zero.zero", "zero.zreo"),
    good.replace("zero.zero;", "zero.zero"),
    good.replace("} zero;", "} zreo;"),
    good.replace("\n} zero;", ""),
]
for text in tests:
    print(check_feature("zero", text, known, set()))

[('zero', 2, 'no glyph zero.zreo')]
[('zero', 2, 'no semicolon at the end')]
[('zero', 3, 'should close with: } zero;')]
[('zero', 2, 'should close with: } zero;'), ('zero', 0, "braces don't balance: 1 left open")]

Each broken text gets the complaint it deserves, with the line number. replace made the breaks, so each test differs from the good text in one place and you can see which. The last one gets two, both true. Keep these four lines in a file of their own. When you change the checker next month, run them again.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Check Features
# Reads the feature text and reports what a compiler would trip over.
# Changes nothing. It does not compile: the Features panel does that.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


WORDS = {"sub", "by", "from", "pos", "="}
PUNCTUATION = "[];'<>"


def words_of(code):
    for mark in PUNCTUATION:
        code = code.replace(mark, " ")
    return code.split()


def is_number(word):
    return word.lstrip("-").isdigit()


def check_line(code, known, classes):
    problems = []
    words = words_of(code)
    if "=" in words and words[0].startswith("@"):
        classes.add(words[0])
        words = words[1:]
    for word in words:
        if word in WORDS or is_number(word):
            continue
        if word.startswith("@"):
            if word not in classes:
                problems.append(f"class {word} is not defined")
        elif word not in known:
            problems.append(f"no glyph {word}")
    return problems


def check_feature(tag, text, known, classes):
    classes = set(classes)
    problems = []
    rows = []
    for number, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), 1):
        code = line.split("#")[0].strip()
        if code:
            rows.append((number, code))
    if not rows:
        return [(tag, 0, "empty")]
    number, code = rows[0]
    if code != "feature " + tag + " {":
        problems.append((tag, number, f"should open with: feature {tag} {{"))
    number, code = rows[-1]
    if code != "} " + tag + ";":
        problems.append((tag, number, f"should close with: }} {tag};"))
    opened = 0
    for number, code in rows:
        opened = opened + code.count("{") - code.count("}")
        if not code.endswith(";") and not code.endswith("{"):
            problems.append((tag, number, "no semicolon at the end"))
        first = code.split()[0]
        if first in ["feature", "lookup"] or first.startswith("}"):
            continue
        for sentence in check_line(code, known, classes):
            problems.append((tag, number, sentence))
    if opened != 0:
        problems.append((tag, 0, f"braces don't balance: {opened} left open"))
    return problems


def prefix_classes(prefix):
    classes = set()
    for line in prefix.splitlines():
        code = line.split("#")[0].strip()
        if code.startswith("@") and "=" in code:
            classes.add(code.split("=")[0].strip())
    return classes


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    known = {glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs}
    package = scripting.current_package()
    blocks = scripting.read_feature_blocks(package)
    classes = prefix_classes(blocks["prefix"])
    problems = []
    seen = []
    for tag, text in blocks["features"]:
        if tag in seen:
            problems.append((tag, 0, "this tag appears twice"))
        seen.append(tag)
        problems = problems + check_feature(tag, text, known, classes)
    for tag, number, sentence in problems:
        print(f"{tag} line {number}: {sentence}")
    print(f"{len(blocks['features'])} features checked, {len(problems)} problems.")
    if not problems:
        print("Now compile in the Features panel. That is the real test.")


main()

Save it as check_features.py. On the font as it stands:

8 features checked, 0 problems.
Now compile in the Features panel. That is the real test.

Notes on the listing.

A problem is a tuple of three: the tag, the line number, the sentence. The functions that find problems only build the list, and main does all the printing. Chapter 100 will want problems from several checkers at once, in a simpler shape, and it can have them because nothing down here prints.

classes = set(classes) at the top of check_feature makes a copy. The classes from the prefix are visible to every feature. A class defined inside frac belongs to frac, and the copy keeps check_line from adding it to the shared set.

enumerate(text.splitlines(), 1) counts from 1. Chapter 78 started its count at 2 to match a spreadsheet, and here 1 matches the first line of a feature as the Features panel shows it. Comment lines and empty lines are skipped but still counted.

A brace in an f-string opens a slot, so to print a brace you write it twice: {{ and }} print one each. Chapter 88 stepped round this with +. The line f"should close with: }} {tag};" looks odd and is correct.

Line number 0 means "the feature as a whole". It reads a little strangely in the report. Exercise 3 is about that.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Now do Oskar's Thursday evening. Open Window > Panels > Features, find zero, and delete the semicolon after zero.zero. Run the script:

zero line 2: no semicolon at the end
8 features checked, 1 problems.

Don't repair it yet. Click the panel's Compile button and read what FontLab says in the Output panel. I can't tell you the words, because I haven't seen them. Write them down next to the checker's sentence. Does the compiler name the feature? The line? Is its line number counted within the feature or from the top of all the feature text?

Put the semicolon back, run the script, compile again. You now know what both judges say about the same mistake, and you'll recognize the compiler's message when it comes on a Friday.

docs.title: What the checker can't know
docs.text:
The checker knows five words of a language that has dozens. Feature code also has ignore, lookupflag, script, language, include and more. Put script latn; into a feature and this script will say no glyph script and no glyph latn, two false alarms of the kind step 3 warned about. When you start using a new word, add it to WORDS before you run the check, and add a test string to step 5's list.

It's also blind in the other direction. sub a b by c d; passes every check here, with all its glyphs present and a semicolon at the end, and I'd expect a compiler to refuse it, since a rule can't replace two glyphs by two. The checker reads words and doesn't know the grammar.

So a clean report means that none of the cheap mistakes are there. It doesn't mean the features compile, which is why the last line the script prints sends you to the button.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A check that collects every problem in a list, as data, can report them all at once and can be reused by another script. To test a checker, feed it text you broke on purpose and see that each break gets its own complaint. A false alarm is a bug in the checker, and it costs trust, so read the line before you believe the report. replace in a loop turns punctuation into spaces, count counts pieces of a string, and lstrip("-") lets isdigit cope with negative numbers.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a fifth broken text to step 5: a rule that uses @figs, which nobody defined. What does the checker say, and on which line?
  2. liga needs its long rules before its short ones, as chapter 90 explained. Write check_order(text) that returns a problem when a sub rule with fewer glyphs before by stands above one with more. Test it on a string with the two rules in the wrong order.
  3. Change the printing in main so that a problem with line number 0 prints as zero: empty, without the words "line 0". One if will do it.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The features are written and checked. Which glyphs do they reach? The font has ten small caps and eighty-four lowercase letters, and a reader who switches small caps on will see the difference. Chapter 94 counts what each feature covers and what it leaves out.

docs.title: 94. Test words
docs.text:
Thursday of week eighteen. Tobias, who proofed the kerning in chapter 77, sets a chapter heading from the cookbook in small caps: "Plum jam, baked figs". He sends back a screenshot. Some letters have turned into small capitals and the rest are still lowercase, so the line looks like a ransom note.

Nothing is broken. The smcp feature replaces the ten glyphs that have a small cap, and Ines has drawn ten. Yesterday's checker passed the feature, and it was right to: every rule in it is valid. The checker was never asked whether the rules are enough.

That's a question about two sets, the glyphs a feature replaces and the glyphs it ought to replace. You compared two sets in chapter 25, when a list of wanted glyphs met the font. Today you do it again, and the script also hands Tobias something to type.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The tell function from chapter 39. The script below defines it again, so it runs by itself.
  • The eight features the font has after chapter 92.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran it in plain Python on Plum's glyph names and code points and on the feature text that chapters 88 to 92 produce. The counts are for the practice font with Part 3's glyphs in it. Without them you have 70 lowercase letters where I have 84, and 62 not covered where I have 76.

docs.title: Step 1: What does a feature replace?
docs.text:
Read the rules back out of the text. A one-for-one rule has four words, sub a by a.sc, once the semicolon is gone:

def replacements(text):
    pairs = []
    for line in text.splitlines():
        words = line.split("#")[0].replace(";", " ").split()
        if len(words) == 4 and words[0] == "sub" and words[2] == "by":
            pairs.append((words[1], words[3]))
    return pairs

Any line that isn't such a rule is skipped: the opening line, the closing line, a ligature rule with five words, a class. This function reads one kind of rule and ignores the rest without complaint, which is the right manners for a reader and would be the wrong manners for yesterday's checker.

Now get at one feature's text. blocks["features"] is a list of pairs, tag and text. dict turns a list of pairs into a dictionary, as in chapter 87, so you can ask for a feature by its tag:

from fly import fl
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

font = fl.CurrentFont()
package = scripting.current_package()
blocks = scripting.read_feature_blocks(package)
texts = dict(blocks["features"])
pairs = replacements(texts["smcp"])
sources = {source for source, target in pairs}
print(len(pairs), sorted(sources))

10 ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f', 'g', 'h', 'one', 'zero']

docs.title: Step 2: What should it replace?
docs.text:
Small caps are for lowercase letters. Unicode's category for those is Ll, letter lowercase, and chapter 91's function collects glyphs by category. This time keep the character with each name, in a dictionary, because Tobias will want characters to type:

import unicodedata


def by_categories(font, categories):
    found = {}
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        code = glyph.unicode
        if code is not None and unicodedata.category(chr(code)) in categories:
            found[glyph.name] = chr(code)
    return found


characters = by_categories(font, ["Ll"])
should = set(characters)
print(len(should), characters["a"], characters["germandbls"])

84 a ß

set(characters) makes a set of the dictionary's keys. The practice font has 84 lowercase letters, Plum's 70 and the fourteen Part 3 built. The count takes in the accented letters and a few you might not think of as letters at first, such as germandbls and dotlessi.

docs.title: Step 3: Three questions, three operators
docs.text:
Chapter 25 gave you the operators. & keeps what's in both sets. - keeps what's in the first and not in the second.

covered = should & sources
missing = should - sources
extra = sources - should
print(len(covered), len(missing), sorted(extra))

8 76 ['one', 'zero']

Eight lowercase letters have a small cap and 76 don't. Two glyphs are replaced that aren't lowercase letters: the figures one and zero, whose small-cap glyphs you made in chapter 40. extra isn't a fault here. It's the rest of what the feature does, and the report should say so.

docs.title: Step 4: The mistake
docs.text:
Mira writes the subtraction from memory, the wrong way round:

missing = sources - should
text = "".join(sorted(characters[name] for name in missing))

KeyError: 'zero'

Your message may say 'one'. A set has no order, so either can come first.

a - b and b - a are different sets. Python has no way to know which you meant, and both are legal. She was lucky. The wrong set held a name the characters dictionary doesn't have, and the lookup failed loudly. Had the line printed names, it would have said "missing: one zero" with a straight face, and the report would have blamed the two figures that are covered and kept silent about 62 letters that aren't.

Say the subtraction aloud when you write it: "what should be there, minus what is there, leaves what's missing".

docs.title: Step 5: Words to type
docs.text:
A list of 76 glyph names is hard to act on. A row of characters can be pasted into a Glyph window, with the feature switched on, and looked at:

WIDTH = 60


def as_text(names, characters):
    text = "".join(sorted(characters[name] for name in names))
    return text[:WIDTH] + ("..." if len(text) > WIDTH else "")


print(as_text(covered, characters))
print(as_text(missing, characters))

abcdefgh
ijklmnopqrstuvwxyzßàáâãäåæçèéêëìíîïñòóôõöøùúûüýÿăćčěğĩıĳńňœŕ...

sorted puts the characters in code point order, plain letters first. The slice cuts a long row at 60 characters and the dots admit the cut. The value-with-a-choice from chapter 37 adds them only when something was cut.

The first row is what Tobias can set in small caps today: "a bad head", "a faded badge", and little more. The second row is Ines's list of what's still to draw.

The two rows do different jobs. Paste the first into a Glyph window, switch the feature on, and every character should change. If one doesn't, the feature text and the compiled feature disagree, and it's time for the Compile button. Paste the second and nothing should change. I haven't watched either happen, and the place where a Glyph window lets you switch features on is something to find in FontLab's own manual.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Feature Coverage
# For each feature in WANTED, compares the glyphs its rules replace
# with the glyphs that ought to be replaced. Changes nothing.
import unicodedata

from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


WANTED = {"smcp": ["Ll"], "numr": ["Nd"], "dnom": ["Nd"]}
WIDTH = 60


def replacements(text):
    pairs = []
    for line in text.splitlines():
        words = line.split("#")[0].replace(";", " ").split()
        if len(words) == 4 and words[0] == "sub" and words[2] == "by":
            pairs.append((words[1], words[3]))
    return pairs


def by_categories(font, categories):
    found = {}
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        code = glyph.unicode
        if code is not None and unicodedata.category(chr(code)) in categories:
            found[glyph.name] = chr(code)
    return found


def as_text(names, characters):
    text = "".join(sorted(characters[name] for name in names))
    return text[:WIDTH] + ("..." if len(text) > WIDTH else "")


def report(tag, text, font):
    pairs = replacements(text)
    sources = {source for source, target in pairs}
    characters = by_categories(font, WANTED[tag])
    should = set(characters)
    covered = should & sources
    missing = should - sources
    extra = sources - should
    print(f"{tag}: {len(pairs)} rules, {len(covered)} of {len(should)} covered")
    print(f"  try:     {as_text(covered, characters)}")
    print(f"  missing: {as_text(missing, characters)}")
    if extra:
        print(f"  also:    {' '.join(sorted(extra))}")
    return len(missing)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    blocks = scripting.read_feature_blocks(package)
    texts = dict(blocks["features"])
    total = 0
    for tag in WANTED:
        if tag not in texts:
            print(f"{tag}: no such feature")
            continue
        total += report(tag, texts[tag], font)
    print(f"{total} glyphs not covered.")


main()

Save it as feature_coverage.py. It prints:

smcp: 10 rules, 8 of 84 covered
  try:     abcdefgh
  missing: ijklmnopqrstuvwxyzßàáâãäåæçèéêëìíîïñòóôõöøùúûüýÿăćčěğĩıĳńňœŕ...
  also:    one zero
numr: 10 rules, 10 of 10 covered
  try:     0123456789
  missing: 
dnom: 10 rules, 10 of 10 covered
  try:     0123456789
  missing: 
76 glyphs not covered.

Notes on the listing.

WANTED maps a tag to a list of categories, where chapter 91's table held one category per row. A feature for capitals and lowercase together could say ["Lu", "Ll"].

frac isn't in the table. Its rules replace classes, and replacements would find two four-word rules in it, one of them between classes, sub @frac_plain by @frac_up. A coverage figure built on that would be nonsense, so the script doesn't offer one. liga is left out for a similar reason: nobody can say which letter sequences ought to have a ligature.

report prints and also returns a number, the count of missing glyphs, which main adds up. Chapter 93 kept finding and printing apart. This script is small enough to get away with mixing them, and chapter 100 will ask it to stop.

The try row for numr is the test string for the fraction figures. Type it with the feature on once Ines has drawn them, and ten small raised figures should appear.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Make a new glyph called i.sc. A copy of I will do, or an empty glyph from chapter 40's script. Run the coverage script:

smcp: 10 rules, 8 of 84 covered

Still 8. The glyph is in the font and the report doesn't see it, because the report reads the feature's rules and the feature was written before i.sc existed. This is chapter 91's lesson from another side. Feature text is a list somebody wrote on a certain day, and the font moves on without it.

Run make_smcp.py from chapter 88 again, so the feature is rebuilt from the suffixes, and then the coverage script: 11 rules, 9 of 84. Whenever glyphs are added, the order of work is to rebuild the feature, check it, measure its coverage and compile it. Chapter 100 puts the middle two into one run.

docs.title: What the rule can't know
docs.text:
Look at the end of the missing list. The script cut it at 60 characters, and the last two of the 76 are fi and fl. Unicode files the two ligature characters under lowercase letters, so the script wants small caps for them. No designer draws those. In a sound font, small caps are applied before ligatures or the ligature rules leave small caps alone, and "fi" in small caps is an F and an I.

The same goes for germandbls, the ß. Its small cap is often two glyphs, SS, which a one-for-one rule can't express.

So the 76 is an upper limit, and the true to-do list is a few shorter. A category is a fair first guess at "what should be covered". Ines's judgment is the second. Exercise 2 gives the script a way to hear it.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Whether a feature is valid and whether it's complete are separate questions, and the second is a comparison of two sets. & gives what two sets share, and - gives what the first has and the second lacks, so the order of a subtraction decides the answer. dict turns a list of pairs into a dictionary you can look things up in. A report that prints characters to type is more use to a proofreader than a list of glyph names.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add "zero": ["Nd"] to WANTED and run the script. The answer is 1 of 10 covered. Is that a fault in the feature? Say why a slashed-zero feature and this table don't fit together.
  2. Add a set NO_SMALL_CAP = {"fi", "fl", "germandbls"} at the top and subtract it from should when the tag is smcp. What does the last line of the report say now?
  3. Tobias wants words, not rows of letters. Take a list of ten words from the cookbook and print the ones that use only covered characters: a word passes when set(word) - set(as_text(covered, characters)) is empty. Mind the dots that as_text may add.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Eight features are written, checked and measured. The words the font can set are in order. There are other words inside a font: its own name, which a menu shows before anyone sees a glyph. Chapter 95 reads the family name and its relatives out of Font Info.

docs.title: 95. The font has a name
docs.text:
Friday of week eighteen. The typesetter in Istanbul installs the three weights and writes back within the hour. Light and Bold sit in the font menu where she expects them. The Regular is listed apart from the other two, and her layout program calls it by a slightly different name.

Oskar takes the sheet from chapter 1 off the wall. Two lines are still open. He taps the first: family name and version in every weight. "Names," he says. "A font has about six of them, and they have to agree."

The names live in Font Info. Some belong to the whole font and some to each master. Today you read them all, in every master, and check them against a few rules. You change nothing yet. The tool of the day is a dictionary that lists the fields you care about, so that one loop can read them all.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The tell function from chapter 39. The script below defines it again, so it runs by itself.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The field names come from the stub that describes FontLab's objects, and the values I print are the ones in Plum's source file. I ran the script in plain Python against a stand-in that holds those values. Reading a master's own names by switching to that master is how Fly's tools do it for the style name. For the full name and the PostScript name I'm assuming the same holds, and I haven't seen it.

docs.title: Step 1: One field, then many
docs.text:
You've read from font.info since chapter 11. The package has the same drawer:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

package = scripting.current_package()
info = package.info
print(info.familyName)
print(info.openTypeNameDesigner)

GG Plum
Sora Sagano

Two fields take two lines. Six fields would take six, and the report would need a label for each. Put the fields in a dictionary, with the attribute name as the key and the label as the value:

FONT_WIDE = {
    "familyName": "Family",
    "openTypeNameDesigner": "Designer",
    "openTypeNameVersion": "Version name",
}

The keys are strings now, and info."familyName" isn't Python. The function that fetches an attribute by its name in a string is getattr:

for key, label in FONT_WIDE.items():
    print(f"{label:<16}{getattr(info, key)}")

Family          GG Plum
Designer        Sora Sagano
Version name    Version 1.000

getattr(info, "familyName") and info.familyName are the same question. The first form lets a table decide what to ask. Add a row to the table and the report grows by a line, with no new code.

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
The rules for a name are string rules: not empty, no space at either end, no two spaces in a row. Mira adds a fourth row to the table, "copyright": "Copyright", and a first check:

for key, label in FONT_WIDE.items():
    value = getattr(info, key)
    if value != value.strip():
        print(label, "has a space at an end")

AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'strip'

Plum has no copyright line. A text field that nobody has filled in reads as None, and None has no strip. Three fields worked, so the loop looked finished. The fourth was the first empty one.

Fly's own tools write getattr(package.info, key) or "". You met or between two values in chapter 91: when the left side is empty or None, the right side is used. After that every value is a string, and "empty" is one more thing for the check to report:

def read_fields(info, table):
    return {key: getattr(info, key) or "" for key in table}

This is a dictionary built in one line, the way chapter 37 built lists, with braces and a colon in place of the brackets: for each key in the table, the key and its value from the font.

docs.title: Step 3: Names that belong to a master
docs.text:
Family, designer and version are the same for the whole font. The style name isn't: Light, Regular and Bold each have their own. So do the full name and the PostScript name, which is the one programs use behind the scenes.

To read a master's names, make that master the current one, then ask:

package.setMaster("Bold")
print(package.info.styleName)

That changes what the user sees. The font was showing Regular, and now it shows Bold. A report that leaves the font on another master than it found is rude, and it's confusing when a tool does that behind your back. Remember where you were and go back:

original = package.master
for master in package.masters:
    package.setMaster(master)
    print(master, package.info.styleName)
package.setMaster(original)

There's a hole in this. If any line inside the loop raises an error, Python stops there, and the last line never runs. The font stays on whichever master the loop had reached. Python has a form for "do this afterward, no matter what":

original = package.master
try:
    for master in package.masters:
        package.setMaster(master)
        print(master, package.info.styleName)
finally:
    package.setMaster(original)

You know try from chapter 19, where except caught an error. finally catches nothing. The error still stops the script and still prints its traceback. But on the way out, Python runs the finally lines first. Use it whenever a script borrows something it must hand back.

docs.title: Step 4: The house rules
docs.text:
How should the other names follow from family and style? Oskar's rules for Halfmoon:

  • The full name is the family, a space, the style: GG Plum Bold.
  • The PostScript name is the family without spaces, a hyphen, the style without spaces: GGPlum-Bold.
def house_names(family, style):
    return {
        "postscriptFullName": f"{family} {style}",
        "postscriptFontName": family.replace(" ", "") + "-" + style.replace(" ", ""),
    }


print(house_names("GG Plum", "Bold"))

{'postscriptFullName': 'GG Plum Bold', 'postscriptFontName': 'GGPlum-Bold'}

These are one foundry's rules. Other foundries leave "Regular" out of the full name, and a font made that way isn't broken. What matters is that the three weights of one family follow the same rule.

A PostScript name also has rules that aren't a matter of taste. It may hold only plain ASCII characters, no spaces, none of the ten bracket-like characters, and at most 63 characters in all. isascii asks a string whether all of it is ASCII:

PS_LIMIT = 63
PS_FORBIDDEN = "[](){}<>/% "


def ps_problems(name):
    problems = []
    if len(name) > PS_LIMIT:
        problems.append(f"{len(name)} characters, limit {PS_LIMIT}")
    bad = [c for c in name if c in PS_FORBIDDEN or not c.isascii()]
    if bad:
        problems.append("not allowed: " + " ".join(repr(c) for c in bad))
    return problems


print(ps_problems("GGPlum-Bold"))
print(ps_problems("GG Plum-Café"))

[]
["not allowed: ' ' 'é'"]

repr from chapter 19 puts quotes around each character, which is the only way to make a space visible in a report.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Font Names
# Prints the names in Font Info, font-wide and for each master,
# and checks them against the house rules. Changes nothing.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


FONT_WIDE = {
    "familyName": "Family",
    "openTypeNameDesigner": "Designer",
    "openTypeNameVersion": "Version name",
    "copyright": "Copyright",
}
PER_MASTER = {
    "styleName": "Style",
    "postscriptFullName": "Full name",
    "postscriptFontName": "PostScript name",
}
PS_LIMIT = 63
PS_FORBIDDEN = "[](){}<>/% "


def read_fields(info, table):
    return {key: getattr(info, key) or "" for key in table}


def house_names(family, style):
    return {
        "postscriptFullName": f"{family} {style}",
        "postscriptFontName": family.replace(" ", "") + "-" + style.replace(" ", ""),
    }


def text_problems(value):
    problems = []
    if value == "":
        problems.append("empty")
    if value != value.strip():
        problems.append("space at an end")
    if "  " in value:
        problems.append("two spaces in a row")
    return problems


def ps_problems(name):
    problems = []
    if len(name) > PS_LIMIT:
        problems.append(f"{len(name)} characters, limit {PS_LIMIT}")
    bad = [c for c in name if c in PS_FORBIDDEN or not c.isascii()]
    if bad:
        problems.append("not allowed: " + " ".join(repr(c) for c in bad))
    return problems


def show(label, value, problems):
    note = "   <-- " + ", ".join(problems) if problems else ""
    print(f"  {label:<16}{value}{note}")
    return len(problems)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    count = 0
    print("Whole font")
    wide = read_fields(package.info, FONT_WIDE)
    for key, label in FONT_WIDE.items():
        count += show(label, wide[key], text_problems(wide[key]))

    original = package.master
    try:
        for master in package.masters:
            package.setMaster(master)
            names = read_fields(package.info, PER_MASTER)
            house = house_names(wide["familyName"], names["styleName"])
            print(master)
            for key, label in PER_MASTER.items():
                problems = text_problems(names[key])
                if key == "postscriptFontName":
                    problems = problems + ps_problems(names[key])
                if key in house and names[key] != house[key]:
                    problems.append(f"house rule says {house[key]}")
                count += show(label, names[key], problems)
    finally:
        package.setMaster(original)
    print(f"{count} things to look at.")


main()

Save it as font_names.py. If Plum's names reach the script the way they stand in the source file, it prints:

Whole font
  Family          GG Plum
  Designer        Sora Sagano
  Version name    Version 1.000
  Copyright          <-- empty
Light
  Style           Light
  Full name       GG Plum Light
  PostScript name GGPlum-Light
Regular
  Style           Regular
  Full name       GG Plum   <-- house rule says GG Plum Regular
  PostScript name GGPlum   <-- house rule says GGPlum-Regular
Bold
  Style           Bold
  Full name       GG Plum Bold
  PostScript name GGPlum-Bold
3 things to look at.

There's the typesetter's Regular. Light and Bold carry their style in both names. The Regular carries it in neither, so a program that sorts by PostScript name files GGPlum away from GGPlum-Bold. The family name is the same in every weight, as it must be, since the font keeps only one. The weights disagree in the names built from it.

Notes on the listing.

The two tables are the script's memory of what to read. FONT_WIDE and PER_MASTER are kept apart because the two kinds are read differently, once or once per master.

show prints one line and returns the number of problems on it, so main can keep a count.

The script says "things to look at" and doesn't say "errors". An empty copyright line is a gap that chapter 98 fills. The Regular's names follow an older habit. A person decides what to change.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Misspell a key in PER_MASTER: "styleNmae". Put the font on Regular and run the script. The whole-font part prints, then:

AttributeError: 'fgFontInfo' object has no attribute 'styleNmae'

The wording of the object's name may differ on your screen. Now look at the font. It should still be on Regular, though the script had switched to Light when it fell over. The finally lines ran on the way out.

To see what they saved you from, turn the two finally lines into comments, replace them with except ZeroDivisionError: and pass so the try stays legal, and run again. Same error, and the font is left on Light. Put the finally back and correct the key.

docs.title: What the script can't do
docs.text:
It doesn't write. Fly's guarded writer, write_font_info, accepts the family name, the style name, the designer, the copyright and the version name. It refuses the full name and the PostScript name with Unsupported Font Info field. I found no proven way to set those two from a script, so the Regular's names are a job for the Font Info window: open File > Font Info, find the names of the Regular master, and type what the report says. Then run the report again and expect one thing to look at, the copyright.

FontLab can also build these names from family and style on its own. Where that button is, and what it makes of "Regular", is a question for FontLab's manual and five minutes of trying.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A dictionary of field names and labels lets one loop read as many fields as the table has rows, and getattr fetches an attribute whose name is in a string. An unfilled text field reads as None, and or "" turns it into a string before any string method touches it. try with finally runs its last lines whether or not an error happens, which is how a script hands back what it borrowed. Some of a font's names belong to the whole font and some to each master, and a report has to visit each master to see them.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add "openTypeNameDesignerURL": "Designer URL" to FONT_WIDE. What does Plum have there?
  2. Some programs still cut PostScript names at 29 characters. Add a second, softer check to ps_problems that says longer than 29 without calling it forbidden. Test it with a made-up name.
  3. Write same_everywhere(package, key), which visits every master, collects getattr(package.info, key) or "" in a set, and returns True when the set has one member. Use try and finally. Try it with "familyName" and with "styleName".

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The names are read and one of them is on its way to being repaired. Font Info also holds numbers, and three of them decide whether the top of an Å gets cut off on a web page. Chapter 96 reads the vertical metrics and sets one.

docs.title: 96. The numbers in Font Info
docs.text:
Monday of week nineteen. The publisher's web designer has a question before she builds the cookbook's site: will the ring on the Å in "Ångström's rye" be cut off in a tight heading? She has been bitten by another foundry's font, where every accented capital lost its top in one browser.

Oskar draws a box on the whiteboard, with a glyph in it. "A program doesn't look at your outlines to decide how tall a line is. It reads a few numbers from Font Info and believes them. If a glyph is taller than the numbers say, some programs cut it off at the edge of the box."

Today you read those numbers in every master, measure the tallest and lowest glyph, and compare. Then you set one number wrong on purpose, to see that the report notices.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The tell function from chapter 39. The script below defines it again, so it runs by itself.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The Font Info values are the ones in Plum's source file. The glyph heights I computed from the same file, adding each component's shift to the outline it borrows. If you built accented capitals in Part 3, one of yours may tie with Aring for the tallest. The way the script asks a layer for its box is the way Fly's metrics panel asks.

docs.title: Step 1: Eight numbers, three systems
docs.text:
A font file carries the height of a line three times, for three families of programs. The names are historical and you don't need to love them:

  • typo: ascender, descender and line gap. These are the ascender, descender and line gap you see in FontLab's Font Info.
  • hhea: ascender, descender and line gap again, read by Apple's systems.
  • win: an ascent and a descent, read by Windows. Many programs treat these two as the edges of the box and clip there.

That's eight fields. You know from chapter 95 what to do with a list of fields: put them in a table and let getattr read them. They belong to each master, so the reading visits every master and goes back, with try and finally:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

FIELDS = {
    "openTypeOS2TypoAscender": "typo ascender",
    "openTypeOS2TypoDescender": "typo descender",
    "openTypeOS2TypoLineGap": "typo line gap",
    "openTypeHheaAscender": "hhea ascender",
    "openTypeHheaDescender": "hhea descender",
    "openTypeHheaLineGap": "hhea line gap",
    "openTypeOS2WinAscent": "win ascent",
    "openTypeOS2WinDescent": "win descent",
}


def read_numbers(package):
    numbers = {}
    original = package.master
    try:
        for master in package.masters:
            package.setMaster(master)
            numbers[master] = {key: getattr(package.info, key) for key in FIELDS}
    finally:
        package.setMaster(original)
    return numbers


package = scripting.current_package()
numbers = read_numbers(package)
for key, label in FIELDS.items():
    print(f"{label:<16}{numbers['Regular'][key]:>6.0f}")

typo ascender      765
typo descender    -235
typo line gap      200
hhea ascender      965
hhea descender    -235
hhea line gap        0
win ascent         965
win descent        235

numbers is a dictionary of dictionaries: a master's name leads to that master's eight values. There's no or "" this time. These are numbers, and a number field that nobody set reads as 0, which is a value the report should show.

Look at the last line. The two descenders are −235 and the win descent is 235. Windows counts its descent downward, as a positive number. Keep that in mind for Step 3.

docs.title: Step 2: The tallest and the lowest glyph
docs.text:
In chapter 43 you found a glyph's box from its nodes, and a glyph built from components had none. The package's layers answer for the whole glyph, components included:

from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
layer = package.findName("Aring").findLayer("Regular")
box = layer.boundingBox
print(box.y(), box.y() + box.height())

0.0 885.0

box.y() is the bottom edge and the height is added to get the top. The Å stands on the baseline and its ring ends at 885.

Now every glyph. Keep the height together with the name in a tuple, so the report can say which glyph it was:

def extremes(package, font, master):
    low = None
    high = None
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        layer = package.findName(glyph.name).findLayer(master)
        if layer is None or layer.isNull:
            continue
        box = layer.boundingBox
        if box.width() == 0 and box.height() == 0:
            continue
        bottom = box.y()
        top = box.y() + box.height()
        if low is None or bottom < low[0]:
            low = (bottom, glyph.name)
        if high is None or top > high[0]:
            high = (top, glyph.name)
    return low, high


print(extremes(package, font, "Regular"))

((-235.0, 'bar'), (885.0, 'Aring'))

low and high start as None, because before the first glyph there's no lowest anything. if low is None or bottom < low[0] reads: take this glyph if it's the first, or if it's lower than the lowest so far. Empty glyphs, like the space and the fraction figures nobody has drawn yet, are skipped. Their box has no size and would pull both answers toward zero.

The lowest glyph is the vertical bar, at −235. The tallest is the Å.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Room above is the win ascent minus the tallest top. Mira writes the room below the same way round:

n = numbers["Regular"]
low, high = extremes(package, font, "Regular")
print("above", n["openTypeOS2WinAscent"] - high[0])
print("below", low[0] - n["openTypeOS2WinDescent"])

above 80.0
below -470.0

Minus 470: the bar sticks out of the box by nearly half the font's height, in a font that has been sold for years. That can't be true, and the number is too large to be a drawing fault. When a result is absurd, suspect the sum before the font.

The bottom of the box is at −235. The field says 235, because Windows counts downward. The room below is the distance from −235 up to the glyph's bottom, which is low[0] + n["openTypeOS2WinDescent"]: −235 plus 235, zero. The bar touches the edge and doesn't cross it.

Signs are the classic trap of vertical metrics, and no error message will ever warn you. A descender is negative, a win descent is positive, and a script that mixes them prints a confident wrong number.

docs.title: Step 4: Do the three systems agree?
docs.text:
A line's height is ascender minus descender plus line gap. Work it out for the two systems that have all three numbers:

typo = n["openTypeOS2TypoAscender"] - n["openTypeOS2TypoDescender"] + n["openTypeOS2TypoLineGap"]
hhea = n["openTypeHheaAscender"] - n["openTypeHheaDescender"] + n["openTypeHheaLineGap"]
print(typo, hhea)

1200.0 1200.0

765 + 235 + 200 and 965 + 235 + 0. The two systems split the line differently and arrive at the same 1,200 units. If they didn't, the same text would have different line spacing on a Mac and in Windows, and somebody would spend a day blaming the layout.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Vertical Metrics
# For each master: the tallest and lowest glyph against the clip lines,
# and the line height by two systems. Changes nothing.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


FIELDS = {
    "openTypeOS2TypoAscender": "typo ascender",
    "openTypeOS2TypoDescender": "typo descender",
    "openTypeOS2TypoLineGap": "typo line gap",
    "openTypeHheaAscender": "hhea ascender",
    "openTypeHheaDescender": "hhea descender",
    "openTypeHheaLineGap": "hhea line gap",
    "openTypeOS2WinAscent": "win ascent",
    "openTypeOS2WinDescent": "win descent",
}


def extremes(package, font, master):
    low = None
    high = None
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        layer = package.findName(glyph.name).findLayer(master)
        if layer is None or layer.isNull:
            continue
        box = layer.boundingBox
        if box.width() == 0 and box.height() == 0:
            continue
        bottom = box.y()
        top = box.y() + box.height()
        if low is None or bottom < low[0]:
            low = (bottom, glyph.name)
        if high is None or top > high[0]:
            high = (top, glyph.name)
    return low, high


def read_numbers(package):
    numbers = {}
    original = package.master
    try:
        for master in package.masters:
            package.setMaster(master)
            numbers[master] = {key: getattr(package.info, key) for key in FIELDS}
    finally:
        package.setMaster(original)
    return numbers


def report(master, n, low, high):
    problems = 0
    print(master)
    top_room = n["openTypeOS2WinAscent"] - high[0]
    bottom_room = low[0] + n["openTypeOS2WinDescent"]
    for label, found, room in [("tallest", high, top_room), ("lowest", low, bottom_room)]:
        note = f"room {room:.0f}" if room >= 0 else f"STICKS OUT by {-room:.0f}"
        print(f"  {label:<8}{found[1]:<12}{found[0]:>6.0f}   {note}")
        if room < 0:
            problems += 1
    typo = (n["openTypeOS2TypoAscender"] - n["openTypeOS2TypoDescender"]
            + n["openTypeOS2TypoLineGap"])
    hhea = (n["openTypeHheaAscender"] - n["openTypeHheaDescender"]
            + n["openTypeHheaLineGap"])
    note = "" if typo == hhea else "   <-- they differ"
    print(f"  line    typo {typo:.0f}, hhea {hhea:.0f}{note}")
    if typo != hhea:
        problems += 1
    return problems


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    numbers = read_numbers(package)
    problems = 0
    for master in package.masters:
        low, high = extremes(package, font, master)
        if high is None:
            print(f"{master}: no outlines")
            continue
        problems += report(master, numbers[master], low, high)
    for key, label in FIELDS.items():
        values = {numbers[master][key] for master in package.masters}
        if len(values) > 1:
            found = ", ".join(f"{m} {numbers[m][key]:.0f}" for m in package.masters)
            print(f"{label} is not the same in every master: {found}")
            problems += 1
    print(f"{problems} things to look at.")


main()

Save it as vertical_metrics.py. On Plum as shipped it should print:

Light
  tallest Aring          875   room 90
  lowest  bar           -235   room 0
  line    typo 1200, hhea 1200
Regular
  tallest Aring          885   room 80
  lowest  bar           -235   room 0
  line    typo 1200, hhea 1200
Bold
  tallest Aring          896   room 69
  lowest  bar           -235   room 0
  line    typo 1200, hhea 1200
0 things to look at.

Mira sends the web designer one line: the ring has 69 units of room in the tightest weight, and nothing in the family sticks out.

Notes on the listing.

The last loop in main collects one field's values from all masters in a set. A set keeps each value once, so a set with more than one member means the masters disagree. That's exercise 3 of chapter 95, put to work. The weights of a family should share these eight numbers. If they don't, a line's spacing changes when a word in it goes bold.

The typo ascender is 765, and the Å is 885. That's no fault. The typo ascender describes where the lowercase ascenders end and helps set the line spacing. The win ascent is the number that has to clear the accents.

The room shrinks from 90 to 69 as the weight grows, because a bolder ring is a taller ring. The Bold is the master to watch.

docs.title: Set a number, and take it back
docs.text:
The report says zero. A check that has never found anything hasn't been tested, as chapter 93 argued about its checker. So give it something to find. Lower the Bold's win ascent to 880, below the ring:

old = numbers["Bold"]["openTypeOS2WinAscent"]
changes = [("Bold", "openTypeOS2WinAscent", old, 880)]
result = scripting.write_font_info(package, changes, undo_name="Lower Bold win ascent")
print(result)

{'changed': 1}

A change is a tuple of four things: the master, the field, the value you believe is there now, and the value you want. The writer compares the third with the font before it touches anything. If the font has moved on since you read it, the writer refuses with changed since preview; refresh the tool. and writes nothing. It also wants a name for the Undo step, as the feature writer did in chapter 88.

Run vertical_metrics.py again. The Bold now reads:

Bold
  tallest Aring          896   STICKS OUT by 16
  lowest  bar           -235   room 0
  line    typo 1200, hhea 1200
win ascent is not the same in every master: Light 965, Regular 965, Bold 880
2 things to look at.

Both checks fired. Now choose Edit > Undo, once, and run the report a third time. It should say zero again. If it doesn't, write the number back the way you changed it, with 880 as the old value and 965 as the new.

docs.title: What the script can't tell you
docs.text:
Which programs clip, and where, differs from one to the next and changes over the years. Some use the win pair, some the hhea pair, and some use the typo set when a certain switch in the font is on. In Plum that switch is off. The report measures against the win pair because it's the oldest and strictest habit. In Plum the hhea ascender is the same 965, so the answer holds for both.

The script also can't say what the numbers should be. Raising the win ascent to make room for a taller accent moves every line of text that's ever set in the font. That's a decision for Oskar and Ines, made once, before the first release.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Font Info holds the height of a line three times, as the typo, hhea and win numbers, and programs believe those numbers and never look at the outlines. A layer's bounding box gives the top and bottom of a whole glyph, components included, and a loop that starts from None finds the tallest and lowest. The win descent is counted downward as a positive number, so the room below is an addition, and a sign mistake there raises no error. write_font_info takes changes as tuples of master, field, old value and new value, and refuses when the old value no longer matches the font.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Print the eight numbers for all three masters as a table, one row per field and one column per master.
  2. Change extremes so it also returns the second-tallest glyph. Which is it in the Bold, and how far below the Å?
  3. Ines is thinking about Vietnamese, where a capital can carry two accents and reach 1,050 units. Without changing the font, work out what win ascent, hhea ascender and typo line gap would give 30 units of room and keep the two line heights equal.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The font's names and numbers have been read. One number changes every time a file leaves the building: the version. Chapter 97 raises it, writes it in the form the name wants, and notes the day.

docs.title: 97. Version and date
docs.text:
Tuesday of week nineteen. The typesetter in Istanbul writes again: the capital spacing in her headline still misses the Turkish İ. Mira fixed that in chapter 91, eight days ago. Which file is the typesetter using?

Nobody can say. The file she got on the Friday before the fix says Version 1.000. The file on Mira's disk, with the fix, the fractions and the repaired names, also says Version 1.000. Two different fonts carry the same label, and the only way to tell them apart is to open both and count glyphs.

"Every file that leaves the building gets a new number," Oskar says. "And we write down the day." He has a paper notebook for this, with gaps in it.

Today's script raises the version by one step, writes the version name to match, and adds a dated line to the font's note. The Python is small: whole numbers that roll over, and a format that pads a number with zeros.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The tell function from chapter 39. The script below defines it again, so it runs by itself.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the script in plain Python against a stand-in that holds Plum's version fields and empty notes. The plan it builds has the same shape as the plan Fly's own version tool builds. I read that tool's source to see what the writer accepts. The dates below are from my run. Yours will be today's.

docs.title: Step 1: A version is two numbers and a name
docs.text:
Font Info keeps the version three times:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

package = scripting.current_package()
info = package.info
print(info.versionMajor, info.versionMinor)
print(info.openTypeNameVersion)

1 0
Version 1.000

The major number is the 1 before the point. The minor number is the part after it, a whole number from 0 to 999. The version name is what people see in a font menu or a file's properties. A script changes the two numbers, and then it has to rebuild the name, or the three will tell different stories.

docs.title: Step 2: The next number
docs.text:
Most releases raise the minor number by one. A big release raises the major number and starts the minor again at zero. And minor 999 has nowhere to go, so the step after 1.999 is 2.000:

def next_version(major, minor, step):
    if step == "major":
        return major + 1, 0
    if minor == 999:
        return major + 1, 0
    return major, minor + 1


print(next_version(1, 0, "minor"))
print(next_version(1, 999, "minor"))
print(next_version(1, 37, "major"))

(1, 1)
(2, 0)
(2, 0)

The function returns two numbers at once, as a tuple, the way extremes did yesterday. Three return lines, and Python leaves at the first one whose condition holds. You'll never reach 999 at Halfmoon's pace. The line is there because a function that takes any minor number should have an answer for every one.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Mira builds the name with an f-string:

major, minor = next_version(1, 0, "minor")
print(f"Version {major}.{minor}")

Version 1.1

It looks right, and it's wrong by a factor of a hundred. Read as a decimal number, 1.1 is 1.100: minor 100, not minor 1. The next release would print 1.2, then 1.3, and the tenth would print 1.10, which sorts before 1.2 in every file list. The convention is three digits after the point, with zeros in front.

You've used the part after the colon in an f-string to set a width, since chapter 12. A zero in front of the width pads with zeros where spaces would go, and d says the value is a whole number:

def version_name(major, minor):
    return f"Version {major}.{minor:03d}"


print(version_name(1, 1))
print(version_name(1, 42))
print(version_name(2, 0))

Version 1.001
Version 1.042
Version 2.000

Now the name has a fixed shape, and that pays twice. Names sort in release order. And the script can test whether a font's name and numbers agree before it touches anything: build the name from the numbers, and compare.

docs.title: Step 4: The day
docs.text:
You met date.today() in chapter 18. It prints as year, month, day, and isoformat() gives that same text as a string you can glue to others:

from datetime import date

line = f"{date.today().isoformat()}: {version_name(1, 1)}"
print(line)

2026-11-17: Version 1.001

Year first is on purpose. Dates written this way sort correctly as plain text, and nobody has to wonder whether 11/12 is in November or December.

Where does the line go? Font Info has a field for the date a font was made, and I found no proven way to write it from a script. Fly's own version tool leaves it alone and adds a line to the font's note instead, a free text field for the people who work on the font. The note is kept per master, so the line goes into every master's note, after whatever is already there:

def note_changes(package, line):
    changes = []
    original = package.master
    try:
        for master in package.masters:
            package.setMaster(master)
            old = package.info.note or ""
            new = old + "\n" + line if old else line
            changes.append((master, "note", old, new))
    finally:
        package.setMaster(original)
    return changes

"\n" is the line break from chapter 26. An empty note gets the line alone. A note with text in it gets a line break first, so each release sits on its own line. The function writes nothing. It builds the list of changes, four-part tuples as in chapter 96, and hands them back.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Bump Version
# Raises the font's version by one step, writes the version name to match,
# and adds a dated line to each master's note.
from datetime import date

from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


DRY_RUN = True
STEP = "minor"


def next_version(major, minor, step):
    if step == "major":
        return major + 1, 0
