    if minor == 999:
        return major + 1, 0
    return major, minor + 1


def version_name(major, minor):
    return f"Version {major}.{minor:03d}"


def note_changes(package, line):
    changes = []
    original = package.master
    try:
        for master in package.masters:
            package.setMaster(master)
            old = package.info.note or ""
            new = old + "\n" + line if old else line
            changes.append((master, "note", old, new))
    finally:
        package.setMaster(original)
    return changes


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    info = package.info
    major = int(info.versionMajor)
    minor = int(info.versionMinor)
    old_name = info.openTypeNameVersion or ""
    if old_name != version_name(major, minor):
        print(f"The numbers say {version_name(major, minor)}, the name says {repr(old_name)}.")
        print("Make them agree in Font Info first. Nothing was changed.")
        return
    new_major, new_minor = next_version(major, minor, STEP)
    new_name = version_name(new_major, new_minor)
    line = f"{date.today().isoformat()}: {new_name}"
    changes = [
        (None, "versionMajor", info.versionMajor, new_major),
        (None, "versionMinor", info.versionMinor, new_minor),
        (None, "openTypeNameVersion", old_name, new_name),
    ] + note_changes(package, line)
    print(f"{old_name} -> {new_name}")
    print(f"Note line for {len(package.masters)} masters: {line}")
    if DRY_RUN:
        print("Dry run. Nothing was changed.")
        return
    result = scripting.write_font_info(package, changes, undo_name="Bump version")
    print(f"{result['changed']} fields changed.")


main()

Save it as bump_version.py. The dry run prints:

Version 1.000 -> Version 1.001
Note line for 3 masters: 2026-11-17: Version 1.001
Dry run. Nothing was changed.

Set DRY_RUN = False and run it once:

Version 1.000 -> Version 1.001
Note line for 3 masters: 2026-11-17: Version 1.001
6 fields changed.

Notes on the listing.

The three version fields have None where a master's name would go. They belong to the whole font. The three note changes name their master. All six go to the writer in one call, so they succeed or fail together and make one step in Edit > Undo. A font with a new number and the old name would be worse than a font nobody touched.

int(...) is around the two numbers because a number field may come back as 1.0, and :03d refuses anything that isn't a whole number. The changes still carry the values as the font gave them, since the writer compares them with what it reads itself.

The check before the work is the fixed shape paying off. If someone typed Version 1.0 into Font Info by hand, the script says so and stops. It could overwrite the name. It doesn't, because a name that disagrees with the numbers means a person did something the script doesn't understand.

Run it a second time on another day, and the Bold's note holds two lines:

2026-11-17: Version 1.001
2026-11-20: Version 1.002

That's Oskar's notebook, kept inside the font, and nobody can forget to fill it in. To read it without a script, open File > Font Info and look for the note field of a master. When the typesetter next asks which file she has, the answer is in the file: she reads the version name in her font menu, and Mira reads the note to see what day that was and looks up what changed since.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Set DRY_RUN = True again, so nothing is written. Change STEP to "Minor", with a capital, and run. The script reports 1.002, or whatever comes next for you, and no error. "Minor" isn't "major", so the first if is skipped, and everything that isn't "major" counts as a minor step. A typing slip passed for a valid choice.

Now try STEP = "mayor". Same thing: a minor step, where you meant a major one. That's the dangerous direction. Make the function strict, with two new lines at its top:

def next_version(major, minor, step):
    if step not in ("major", "minor"):
        raise ValueError(f"STEP must be 'major' or 'minor', not {repr(step)}")
    if step == "major":
        return major + 1, 0
    if minor == 999:
        return major + 1, 0
    return major, minor + 1

You've read ValueError at the bottom of Fly's refusals since chapter 88. Lines like this one raised them, and this is the first time you write one yourself. raise stops the script the way Python's own errors do, with your sentence at the bottom of the traceback. Use it when going on would mean guessing. Run again with "mayor", read your own error message, and set STEP back to "minor".

docs.title: What the script can't do
docs.text:
It can't know that a file left the building. It raises the number when you run it, and running it is still a decision. Part 6 builds the Friday export as one script, and that script is the right place to call this one, so the number and the export can't drift apart.

It doesn't touch the creation date in Font Info, for the reason given in step 4.

And one thing I haven't seen: whether undoing the six changes takes one Edit > Undo or several. Try it on the practice copy and write down what you find. If the note and the numbers come apart, run font_names.py from chapter 95 and correct the version by hand.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A font's version lives in two whole numbers and a name, and a script that changes one has to change all three in the same call. {minor:03d} pads a whole number with zeros to three digits, which keeps version names in a fixed shape that sorts and can be checked. date.today().isoformat() gives the day as year, month and day, and a dated line in each master's note is a release log that travels with the font. raise ValueError(...) lets your own function refuse a value that it would otherwise have to guess about.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Call next_version with minor 998, 999 and 0, for both steps, and check the six answers against what you expect before you run them.
  2. Write parse_version(name), which takes "Version 1.042" and returns (1, 42). Use split. What should it do with "1.042", without the word?
  3. Print the Regular's note as a numbered list of releases, newest first. splitlines from chapter 87 gives the lines, and reversed(lines) hands a list over back to front.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The font says which release it is. It still doesn't say whose it is: Plum has no copyright line, as chapter 95's report keeps pointing out. Chapter 98 writes one that spans several lines, and looks at the legal fields a script can only read.

docs.title: 98. Copyright and license
docs.text:
Wednesday of week nineteen. Ines forwards a paragraph from the publisher's contract. The delivered fonts must carry a copyright notice and a license statement "in the font data". She has the wording from the studio's lawyer, three sentences in an email, and she wants those three sentences in the fonts, letter for letter, in every release from now on.

Chapter 95's report has been saying Copyright <-- empty since Friday. Today that line goes away.

Legal text is the one kind of text in a font that nobody at the studio is allowed to improve. So the script shouldn't hold it as a short string squeezed between quotation marks, where a person has to scroll sideways to proofread it. It should hold it the way the lawyer wrote it, line under line. Python has a string for that.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The tell function from chapter 39. The script below defines it again, so it runs by itself.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the script in plain Python against a stand-in with Plum's legal fields, which are all empty except the designer's web address. The copyright field is one that Fly's guarded writer accepts. I haven't seen FontLab store the line.

One thing about the wording. In the story, Plum belongs to Halfmoon and the notice says so. Your practice font is GG Plum by Sora Sagano, released under CC0, which means its designer gave up the rights. A notice that claimed otherwise would be false, even in a practice copy, and false notices have a way of surviving into files that get passed on. The text in this chapter says what is true of the file on your disk.

docs.title: Step 1: A string with lines in it
docs.text:
Three quotation marks open a string that may run over several lines. Three more close it:

COPYRIGHT = """
GG Plum by Sora Sagano.
Released under CC0 1.0 Universal: no rights reserved.
Practice copy for the Halfmoon book.
"""

print(COPYRIGHT)

GG Plum by Sora Sagano.
Released under CC0 1.0 Universal: no rights reserved.
Practice copy for the Halfmoon book.

The text sits at the left edge of the script, as in the email. Ines can read it there without knowing any Python, and that's the reason to write it this way.

Look at the output, though. There's an empty line above the text and one below it.

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
Mira hands the string to the writer as it is, in a dry run of her own, and looks at what she'd be storing:

print(repr(COPYRIGHT))
print(len(COPYRIGHT))

'
GG Plum by Sora Sagano.
Released under CC0 1.0 Universal: no rights reserved.
Practice copy for the Halfmoon book.
'
116

repr shows the string as Python holds it, as it did in chapter 19. There are four in it. A triple-quoted string keeps every line break you typed, including the one straight after the opening quotes and the one before the closing quotes. What looked like three tidy lines is a string that starts and ends with a line break.

A copyright field is one line. Some programs show only the first line of it, and the first line here is empty. Chapter 95's check would also object: a line break counts as a space for strip, so text_problems would report space at an end.

The string is right for a person to read and wrong for a font to hold. Keep it, and convert it.

docs.title: Step 3: From lines to one line
docs.text:
splitlines, from chapter 87, cuts the text at its line breaks:

print(COPYRIGHT.splitlines())

['', 'GG Plum by Sora Sagano.', 'Released under CC0 1.0 Universal: no rights reserved.', 'Practice copy for the Halfmoon book.']

Four pieces, the first one empty. Strip each piece, drop the empty ones, and join the rest with single spaces:

def one_line(text):
    lines = [line.strip() for line in text.splitlines()]
    return " ".join(line for line in lines if line)


print(repr(one_line(COPYRIGHT)))
print(len(one_line(COPYRIGHT)))

'GG Plum by Sora Sagano. Released under CC0 1.0 Universal: no rights reserved. Practice copy for the Halfmoon book.'
114

if line is true for any string with something in it and false for the empty string, the same shortcut as or "" in chapter 95. The strip is there for the day the text moves. If you ever move the text into a function, your editor will indent it, and those spaces become part of every line. one_line removes them.

Why not COPYRIGHT.replace("\n", " ")? Try it. You get a space at each end and, if a line was indented, a run of spaces in the middle. Splitting and joining is the dependable way to tidy text. You'll use it again.

docs.title: Step 4: The fields a script can only read
docs.text:
Font Info has more legal fields than the copyright line: a trademark, a license text, a web address for the license, the designer's address, the manufacturer, and a four-letter vendor code. Fly's guarded writer accepts none of them. Ask it, and it answers Unsupported Font Info field, as it did for the PostScript name in chapter 95.

So the script reads them and tells you which are empty, and you fill those in by hand. A table again, and getattr:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

READ_ONLY = {
    "trademark": "Trademark",
    "openTypeNameLicense": "License",
    "openTypeNameLicenseURL": "License URL",
    "openTypeNameDesignerURL": "Designer URL",
    "openTypeNameManufacturer": "Manufacturer",
    "openTypeOS2VendorID": "Vendor",
}

info = scripting.current_package().info
for key, label in READ_ONLY.items():
    value = getattr(info, key) or ""
    print(f"{label:<14}{value or '<-- empty'}")

Trademark     <-- empty
License       <-- empty
License URL   <-- empty
Designer URL  http://www.dotcolon.net/
Manufacturer  <-- empty
Vendor        <-- empty

value or '<-- empty' prints the value if there is one and the marker if there isn't. You used the same turn with or 'none' in chapter 91.

These fields belong to the whole font, so there's no master to visit and no finally.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Legal Fields
# Reports the legal fields of Font Info and writes the copyright line
# from the text at the top of this script.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


DRY_RUN = True

COPYRIGHT = """
GG Plum by Sora Sagano.
Released under CC0 1.0 Universal: no rights reserved.
Practice copy for the Halfmoon book.
"""

READ_ONLY = {
    "trademark": "Trademark",
    "openTypeNameLicense": "License",
    "openTypeNameLicenseURL": "License URL",
    "openTypeNameDesignerURL": "Designer URL",
    "openTypeNameManufacturer": "Manufacturer",
    "openTypeOS2VendorID": "Vendor",
}


def one_line(text):
    lines = [line.strip() for line in text.splitlines()]
    return " ".join(line for line in lines if line)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    info = package.info
    empty = 0
    for key, label in READ_ONLY.items():
        value = getattr(info, key) or ""
        if value == "":
            empty += 1
        print(f"{label:<14}{value or '<-- empty'}")
    print(f"{empty} of {len(READ_ONLY)} fields are empty. Fill them in File > Font Info.")
    old = info.copyright or ""
    new = one_line(COPYRIGHT)
    if old == new:
        print("Copyright is already what this script says.")
        return
    print(f"Copyright now: {repr(old)}")
    print(f"Copyright new: {repr(new)}")
    print(f"{len(new)} characters.")
    if DRY_RUN:
        print("Dry run. Nothing was changed.")
        return
    result = scripting.write_font_info(package, [(None, "copyright", old, new)],
                                       undo_name="Set copyright")
    print(f"{result['changed']} field changed.")


main()

Save it as legal_fields.py. The dry run prints:

Trademark     <-- empty
License       <-- empty
License URL   <-- empty
Designer URL  http://www.dotcolon.net/
Manufacturer  <-- empty
Vendor        <-- empty
5 of 6 fields are empty. Fill them in File > Font Info.
Copyright now: ''
Copyright new: 'GG Plum by Sora Sagano. Released under CC0 1.0 Universal: no rights reserved. Practice copy for the Halfmoon book.'
114 characters.
Dry run. Nothing was changed.

Read the new line against the three lines at the top of the script, word by word. This is the proofreading step, and no check can do it for you. Then set DRY_RUN = False and run. The last line becomes 1 field changed. Run it once more:

The first line and the last now read:

5 of 6 fields are empty. Fill them in File > Font Info.
Copyright is already what this script says.

Notes on the listing.

The script compares before it writes. If the font already holds the line, it says so and stops, which makes it safe to run before every release. You can't write the notice twice, and you find out when somebody has changed it.

The old and new values are printed with repr, quotation marks and all. For text that has to be right to the letter, that's the honest way to print: a space at the end or a stray line break would show.

The change has None for its master, as the version fields did yesterday. The copyright belongs to the whole font.

The text has no © sign. The sign is legal in a font, but I haven't seen what this field does with characters outside plain ASCII, so the sample stays inside it. If your studio's wording needs the sign, run chapter 95's font_names.py afterwards and look at what came back.

docs.title: Fill in the rest by hand
docs.text:
For the five empty fields, open File > Font Info and find the legal and credits pages. For the practice font, the truthful entries are short. The license is the CC0 statement, and its address is https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/. There's no trademark and no vendor code, and leaving those empty is correct. An empty field is only a fault when something belongs in it.

That's why the script prints <-- empty and doesn't count errors. It can see that a field is blank. It can't know whether blank is right.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Indent the three lines of text inside the triple quotes by four spaces, as if an editor had done it, and run the dry run. The new line should be the same 114 characters, because one_line strips each piece.

Now replace the body of one_line with return text.replace("\n", " ").strip() and run again. Count the characters and look at the spaces between the sentences. Put the function back.

docs.title: What the script can't do
docs.text:
It can't write the license, the trademark or the vendor code. The pattern for writing fields beyond the six text fields the guarded writer takes exists, and nobody has proved for these fields that it stores, undoes and saves correctly. Legal text is the last place to be the first to find out.

It doesn't know the law. It copies a text from the top of a file into a field. Whether the text is the right one is a question for Ines and the lawyer.

And it holds the wording inside the script, which means each font family would need its own copy of the script. Tomorrow's chapter moves settings like this one out of the code and into a file.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A triple-quoted string keeps text on several lines as you typed it, including the line breaks after the opening quotes and before the closing ones. splitlines, strip and " ".join turn such a block into one clean line, where replace would leave stray spaces. repr and len show text as it is stored, which is how you proofread a string that has to be right to the letter. Fly's writer accepts the copyright line and refuses the other legal fields, so the script reports those and a person fills them in.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Print the copyright line wrapped to the Output panel: put a line break after every full stop that ends a sentence. replace is enough here. What keeps the full stop in 1.0 from being cut?
  2. Add a check to the report: a web address should start with https://. You met startswith in chapter 9. Which of Plum's fields fails, and is that yours to change?
  3. The year in a real notice goes stale. Build the line Copyright 2026 Halfmoon Type. with the year taken from date.today().year, print it, and don't write it to the practice font.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Three masters share one copyright line because they live in one font. A family delivered as several files has no such luck. Chapter 99 keeps the shared values in one settings file and checks every open font against it.

docs.title: 99. The same info in every font
docs.text:
Thursday of week nineteen. Oskar opens the studio's oldest family, Quince, which was delivered years ago as six separate font files. He reads the six copyright lines aloud. Two say 2019 and four say 2020. One spells the studio "Half Moon". One has a full stop at the end and five don't. The designer is "O. Lindqvist" in three files and "Oskar Lindqvist" in the others.

"Nobody decided any of that," he says. "Somebody typed it six times."

Plum's three weights live in one font, so they share one family name and one copyright line. As soon as a family is several files, each file has its own Font Info, and typing a thing six times produces six spellings. The cure is to type it once, in a file that belongs to no font, and have a script compare every open font with it.

That file is today's new thing. Until now a script's settings sat at its top, in capitals, and changing them meant editing the script. A settings file keeps the values outside the code.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The tell function from chapter 39. The script below defines it again, so it runs by itself.
  • A second font to compare. Close FontLab's font, copy Plum-practice.vfj in your file manager, name the copy Plum-practice-copy.vfj, and open both. In the copy, open File > Font Info, change the designer to S. Sagano and empty the copyright line. Now you have a family of two that disagrees.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the script in plain Python with two stand-in fonts and a real settings file, including the broken files below. The way it lists the open fonts is copied from Fly's own tools. One limit shapes the whole chapter: Fly's writer refuses to write into any font except the current one, so the script reports on all open fonts and changes one.

docs.title: Step 1: Write the settings file
docs.text:
JSON is a text format for the kind of data you keep in dictionaries and lists. Python reads and writes it with the json module. Let the script write the first file from the good font, so you don't have to type it. Click the window of Plum-practice, the font with the right values, and run:

import json
from pathlib import Path

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

package = scripting.current_package()
info = package.info
settings = {
    "familyName": info.familyName,
    "openTypeNameDesigner": info.openTypeNameDesigner,
    "copyright": info.copyright,
}
path = Path(package.path).parent / "family-info.json"
with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(settings, f, indent=4, ensure_ascii=False)
print(path)

json.dump takes the data and an open file. indent=4 puts each entry on its own line, and ensure_ascii=False keeps a letter like é as itself. Open family-info.json in a text editor:

{
    "familyName": "GG Plum",
    "openTypeNameDesigner": "Sora Sagano",
    "copyright": "GG Plum by Sora Sagano. Released under CC0 1.0 Universal: no rights reserved. Practice copy for the Halfmoon book."
}

It looks like a Python dictionary, and that resemblance is a trap you'll walk into in step 3. Ines can open this file and correct a name without ever seeing a line of code.

docs.title: Step 2: Read it back
docs.text:
with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
    settings = json.load(f)
print(settings["openTypeNameDesigner"])
print(len(settings))

Sora Sagano
3

json.load gives back a dictionary, the same one you dumped. The keys are the attribute names from chapter 95, so getattr(package.info, key) can read the matching field for each. The settings file has become the table.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Mira adds a line to the file by hand, for the version name, changes her mind and deletes it. She leaves the comma on the line above, after the copyright text. In a Python dictionary a comma after the last entry is allowed. She runs the reading code:

json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 5 column 1 (char 209)

JSON is stricter than Python. No comma after the last entry. Double quotation marks only, never single ones. No comments. The message is the reader's view of the mistake: after a comma it expected another name in quotes, and at line 5 it found the closing brace. Your Python may word it differently, and the line number will be there either way. Look at that line and the one before it.

A settings file is edited by people, in a hurry, without a traceback to guide them. So the script must expect the file to be wrong and say so in a sentence. JSONDecodeError is a kind of ValueError, which you've caught since chapter 19.

docs.title: Step 4: Trust nothing from outside
docs.text:
Even a file that parses can be wrong. Somebody could misspell a key, or add "versionMajor": 2 because it seemed handy, and a script that passes every key to the writer would do what the file says. Decide what the file may contain, and check at the door:

ALLOWED = {"familyName", "openTypeNameDesigner", "copyright"}


def read_settings(path):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        settings = json.load(f)
    for key, value in settings.items():
        if key not in ALLOWED:
            raise ValueError(f"{key} is not a field this script may set")
        if not isinstance(value, str):
            raise ValueError(f"{key} must be text in quotation marks")
    return settings

isinstance(value, str) asks whether a value is a string. In JSON, 2026 without quotes is a number, and a number in the family name would be refused later by the writer with a message about some other tool. Better to refuse here, with the key's name. The raise lines are yours, as in chapter 97.

After read_settings returns, the rest of the script can believe the dictionary. Every check of the file happens in one function, at the moment the file comes in.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Sync Font Info
# Compares every open font with family-info.json, which sits beside the
# current font, and writes the differences into the current font only.
import json
from pathlib import Path

from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


DRY_RUN = True
FILE_NAME = "family-info.json"
ALLOWED = {"familyName", "openTypeNameDesigner", "copyright"}


def read_settings(path):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        settings = json.load(f)
    for key, value in settings.items():
        if key not in ALLOWED:
            raise ValueError(f"{key} is not a field this script may set")
        if not isinstance(value, str):
            raise ValueError(f"{key} must be text in quotation marks")
    return settings


def differences(package, settings):
    found = []
    for key, wanted in settings.items():
        actual = getattr(package.info, key) or ""
        if actual != wanted:
            found.append((None, key, actual, wanted))
    return found


def main():
    current = scripting.current_package()
    if current is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    path = Path(current.path).parent / FILE_NAME
    try:
        settings = read_settings(path)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        tell(f"I can't find {FILE_NAME} beside the font.")
        return
    except ValueError as problem:
        tell(f"{FILE_NAME} can't be used: {problem}")
        return
    packages = [fl.flPackage(item) for item in fl.flWorkspace.instance().packages()]
    todo = []
    waiting = 0
    for package in packages:
        found = differences(package, settings)
        mine = package.id == current.id
        print(f"{Path(package.path).name}{'  (current)' if mine else ''}")
        for master, key, actual, wanted in found:
            print(f"  {key}: {repr(actual)} should be {repr(wanted)}")
        if not found:
            print("  agrees")
        elif mine:
            todo = found
        else:
            waiting += 1
    if waiting:
        print(f"{waiting} other fonts differ. Click each one and run again.")
    if not todo:
        print("Nothing to change in the current font.")
        return
    if DRY_RUN:
        print(f"Dry run. {len(todo)} fields would change in the current font.")
        return
    result = scripting.write_font_info(current, todo, undo_name="Sync Font Info")
    print(f"{result['changed']} fields changed in the current font.")


main()

Save it as sync_font_info.py. With Plum-practice in front, the dry run prints:

Plum-practice.vfj  (current)
  agrees
Plum-practice-copy.vfj
  openTypeNameDesigner: 'S. Sagano' should be 'Sora Sagano'
  copyright: '' should be 'GG Plum by Sora Sagano. Released under CC0 1.0 Universal: no rights reserved. Practice copy for the Halfmoon book.'
1 other fonts differ. Click each one and run again.
Nothing to change in the current font.

Click the copy's window and run again. The (current) label moves, and the last line becomes Dry run. 2 fields would change in the current font. Set DRY_RUN = False, run, and run once more:

Plum-practice.vfj
  agrees
Plum-practice-copy.vfj  (current)
  agrees
Nothing to change in the current font.

Notes on the listing.

fl.flWorkspace.instance().packages() is FontLab's list of open fonts, and fl.flPackage(item) turns each entry into a package like the one current_package() gives you. Each package has an id, a number that's different for every open font. Comparing ids is how the script knows which of them is in front.

differences builds the writer's four-part tuples straight away, with the value it found as the old value. The report prints from the same list that the writer gets, so what you read in the dry run is what will be written.

The script takes no family name or designer from its own top. FILE_NAME and ALLOWED say where to look and what is permitted, and the values themselves come from the file. The same script serves Plum and Quince without an edit, which the copyright script of chapter 98 couldn't.

There are two except lines after one try. Python takes the first that fits. A missing file and a broken file need different sentences, because the reader has to do different things about them.

The script reads other fonts and writes only the one in front. I'd have liked one run to repair them all. Fly's writer answers a font that isn't current with The preview font is no longer current; reopen the tool., and I found no proven way to bring another font to the front from a script. For Quince, that's six clicks and six runs, and every run prints how many fonts still differ. Six runs of a script that can't misspell is still better than typing six lines.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Each of these breaks the settings file, and the script should answer each with one sentence and change nothing. Repair the file after each.

  1. Put a comma after the last entry. You should see the message from step 3, after family-info.json can't be used:.
  2. Misspell a key as copyrihgt: copyrihgt is not a field this script may set.
  3. Replace "GG Plum" with 2026, without quotes: familyName must be text in quotation marks.
  4. Rename the file: I can't find family-info.json beside the font.

Four ways to be wrong, four sentences, and no traceback. A person who has never seen Python can fix each one.

docs.title: What the script can't do
docs.text:
It compares only fonts that are open. A font left closed on the disk isn't checked, and the script can't know that it exists.

It looks for the settings beside the current font. If the six files of a family live in six folders, each run reads a different file, or none.

It sets three text fields. The version is deliberately not among them. A version changes with every release, by a rule, and chapter 97 owns that rule.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A settings file keeps values outside the code, so a person can change them without editing a script, and JSON is the usual format: json.dump writes a dictionary and json.load reads it back. JSON is stricter than Python, with double quotes only and no comma after the last entry. Whatever comes from a file gets checked in one place, as it comes in, and refused with a sentence that names the key. fl.flWorkspace.instance().packages() lists the open fonts, which a script can read freely, though Fly's writer changes only the current one.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add "styleName" to ALLOWED and to the file. Why is that a bad idea for a family, and what does the report say about the three masters?
  2. Make the report end with a count: 2 of 2 fonts agree. or 1 of 2 fonts agree.
  3. Write the opposite script: for every open font, save its three values to <file name>-info.json beside it. Compare two of the files in a text editor.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Names, Unicode, features and Font Info each have their own checking script now, and nobody will remember to run them all before a delivery. Chapter 100 calls them all from one.

docs.title: 100. It sets real text
docs.text:
Friday of week nineteen. This afternoon the publisher's typesetter installs Plum in her layout program and pours a real chapter into it: a cover line in capitals, a recipe with ½ cup of flour, a heading in small caps. Nobody at Halfmoon will be in the room.

Four weeks ago Mira couldn't have said whether the font was fit to go. Now she has a folder of scripts that each answer one question: are the names good, does every character have one glyph, do the features mention glyphs that exist, does Font Info say the same thing everywhere. Oskar's worry is a different one. "There are nineteen of them," he says. "On a Friday, you'll run nine."

So the last script of Part 5 adds nothing new to the font. It asks the old questions in one run and gives one answer.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The tell function from chapter 39. The script below defines it again, so it runs by itself.
  • The work of chapters 81 to 99 done. If you skipped some, the pre-flight will tell you which.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the script in plain Python against a stand-in built from Plum's source file plus the glyphs and features this part added, and then against the same font with five faults put in. Your counts will differ from mine wherever your font does.

docs.title: Step 1: Every check has the same shape
docs.text:
Chapter 80 collected the spacing checks in a list and ran them in a loop. That works when every check takes the same things and gives back the same things. Here each one takes the font and its package, and returns how many things it looked at and a list of sentences:

def check_unicodes(font, package):
    owners = {}
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if glyph.unicode is None:
            continue
        if glyph.unicode not in owners:
            owners[glyph.unicode] = []
        owners[glyph.unicode].append(glyph.name)
    problems = []
    for code, names in owners.items():
        if len(names) > 1:
            problems.append(f"U+{code:04X} belongs to {' and '.join(names)}")
    return len(owners), problems

This is chapter 84's question asked backwards. That chapter looked for a glyph with two characters. This one looks for a character with two glyphs, which a typesetter meets as the wrong letter appearing when she types.

The function prints nothing. Chapter 93 kept finding and printing apart, and chapter 94 mixed them and said it would have to stop. Here's why. A check that prints can only be used where its printing is wanted. A check that returns a list can be counted, sorted, saved to a file, or shown in a window in Part 7.

docs.title: Step 2: Short versions, and why
docs.text:
The pre-flight doesn't call name_check.py or check_features.py. Each of those files ends with the line main(), so importing one would run it, as you saw in chapter 33. The pre-flight carries its own short version of each question instead. Chapter 81 has six rules about names, and the pre-flight has two. The long scripts are still the ones to run when a short check complains.

The features check is the newest idea in the listing. It collects every word in the feature text and asks which suffixed glyphs aren't among them:

def check_features(font, package):
    blocks = scripting.read_feature_blocks(package)
    text = blocks["prefix"] + " ".join(code for tag, code in blocks["features"])
    for ch in "[];'<>{}":
        text = text.replace(ch, " ")
    words = set(text.split())
    suffixed = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs if "." in glyph.name[1:]]
    problems = [f"{name}: no feature mentions it" for name in suffixed if name not in words]
    return len(suffixed), problems

A glyph called i.sc that no feature mentions can't be reached by anybody who types. That was chapter 94's lesson, when a new small cap sat in the font and the feature didn't know. glyph.name[1:] skips the first character, so .notdef isn't taken for a suffixed glyph.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
One check that crashes shouldn't stop the other four. Mira knows try and except, so her loop reads:

for label, check in CHECKS:
    try:
        looked, problems = check(font, package)
    except Exception:
        continue

Exception is the family that nearly every error belongs to, ValueError and KeyError and AttributeError among them. Catching it catches them all.

Then she mistypes a field name in the Font Info check, copyrihgt, and runs:

Glyph names   274 looked at   ok
Unicode       235 looked at   ok
Features       35 looked at   ok
Metrics         8 looked at   ok
5 checks, 0 problems.
Version 1.001: ready for the hand tests.

Four lines for five checks, and the word "ready". The Font Info check crashed part way, the loop moved on in silence, and the total stayed at zero. She only notices because she counts the lines.

This is the worst thing a checking script can do. A check that didn't run has told you nothing, and the script reported it as a pass. Chapter 80 asked what silence means. Here it meant a crash.

The repair is to say so, count it in a broken total that starts at zero, and refuse to call the font ready:

for label, check in CHECKS:
    try:
        looked, problems = check(font, package)
    except Exception as problem:
        broken += 1
        print(f"{label:<13}DID NOT RUN: {type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")
        continue

type(problem).__name__ is the error's kind as a word, the same word that starts the last line of a traceback. With the typo still in place:

Font Info    DID NOT RUN: AttributeError: 'Info' object has no attribute 'copyrihgt'
Metrics         8 looked at   ok
5 checks, 0 problems, 1 did not run.
Not ready.

FontLab's wording after AttributeError: will differ from my stand-in's. The first three words of the line won't.

Catching Exception is right in this one place, a loop whose job is to keep going and report. Everywhere else, catch the narrow error you expect, as you have since chapter 19. A wide except with nothing printed hides your own typos from you.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Preflight
# Five read-only checks before a font leaves the building:
# names, Unicode, features, Font Info, metrics. Changes nothing.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


ALLOWED = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789._"
TEXT_FIELDS = ["familyName", "openTypeNameDesigner", "copyright", "openTypeNameVersion"]
METRICS = [
    "openTypeOS2TypoAscender", "openTypeOS2TypoDescender", "openTypeOS2TypoLineGap",
    "openTypeHheaAscender", "openTypeHheaDescender", "openTypeHheaLineGap",
    "openTypeOS2WinAscent", "openTypeOS2WinDescent",
]


def check_names(font, package):
    problems = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        name = glyph.name
        if name == ".notdef":
            continue
        bad = [ch for ch in name if ch not in ALLOWED]
        if bad or name[0] in "0123456789.":
            problems.append(f"{name}: not a good glyph name")
    return len(font.glyphs), problems


def check_unicodes(font, package):
    owners = {}
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if glyph.unicode is None:
            continue
        if glyph.unicode not in owners:
            owners[glyph.unicode] = []
        owners[glyph.unicode].append(glyph.name)
    problems = []
    for code, names in owners.items():
        if len(names) > 1:
            problems.append(f"U+{code:04X} belongs to {' and '.join(names)}")
    return len(owners), problems


def check_features(font, package):
    blocks = scripting.read_feature_blocks(package)
    text = blocks["prefix"] + " ".join(code for tag, code in blocks["features"])
    for ch in "[];'<>{}":
        text = text.replace(ch, " ")
    words = set(text.split())
    suffixed = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs if "." in glyph.name[1:]]
    problems = [f"{name}: no feature mentions it" for name in suffixed if name not in words]
    tags = [tag for tag, code in blocks["features"]]
    for tag in sorted(set(tags)):
        if tags.count(tag) > 1:
            problems.append(f"{tag}: this tag appears {tags.count(tag)} times")
    return len(suffixed), problems


def check_info(font, package):
    info = package.info
    problems = []
    for key in TEXT_FIELDS:
        if not getattr(info, key):
            problems.append(f"{key} is empty")
    wanted = f"Version {int(info.versionMajor)}.{int(info.versionMinor):03d}"
    if info.openTypeNameVersion != wanted:
        problems.append(f"the numbers say {wanted}, the name says {info.openTypeNameVersion}")
    return len(TEXT_FIELDS) + 1, problems


def check_metrics(font, package):
    seen = {key: set() for key in METRICS}
    original = package.master
    try:
        for master in package.masters:
            package.setMaster(master)
            for key in METRICS:
                seen[key].add(getattr(package.info, key))
    finally:
        package.setMaster(original)
    problems = [f"{key} differs between masters" for key in METRICS if len(seen[key]) > 1]
    return len(METRICS), problems


CHECKS = [
    ("Glyph names", check_names),
    ("Unicode", check_unicodes),
    ("Features", check_features),
    ("Font Info", check_info),
    ("Metrics", check_metrics),
]


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    total = 0
    broken = 0
    for label, check in CHECKS:
        try:
            looked, problems = check(font, package)
        except Exception as problem:
            broken += 1
            print(f"{label:<13}DID NOT RUN: {type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")
            continue
        total += len(problems)
        verdict = f"{len(problems)} problems" if problems else "ok"
        print(f"{label:<13}{looked:>4} looked at   {verdict}")
        for line in problems:
            print("   ", line)
    print(f"{len(CHECKS)} checks, {total} problems, {broken} did not run.")
    if total == 0 and broken == 0:
        print(f"{package.info.openTypeNameVersion}: ready for the hand tests.")
    else:
        print("Not ready.")


main()

Save it as preflight.py. On a font that has been through the whole part:

Glyph names   274 looked at   ok
Unicode       235 looked at   ok
Features       35 looked at   ok
Font Info       5 looked at   ok
Metrics         8 looked at   ok
5 checks, 0 problems, 0 did not run.
Version 1.001: ready for the hand tests.

The 274 are Plum's 205 glyphs, the fifteen suffixed ones from Part 2, the thirty-one Part 3 built, and this part's two ligatures, fraction and twenty small figures. The 235 are the glyphs with a character: Plum's 204 and Part 3's thirty-one. The check counts glyphs, so the two extra characters on space and hyphen don't show. If you closed the practice font without saving at the end of chapter 60, yours says 243 and 204. The 35 are the suffixed glyphs: ten small caps, four alternates, the slashed zero, ten numerators and ten denominators. If you kept i.sc from chapter 94, yours says 36.

And on a font with five faults put in, which is the run that shows the script earns its place:

Glyph names   277 looked at   1 problems
    a.sc-old: not a good glyph name
Unicode       236 looked at   ok
Features       38 looked at   3 problems
    a.sc-old: no feature mentions it
    i.sc: no feature mentions it
    mu.alt: no feature mentions it
Font Info       5 looked at   1 problems
    copyright is empty
Metrics         8 looked at   1 problems
    openTypeOS2WinAscent differs between masters
5 checks, 6 problems, 0 did not run.
Not ready.

The Unicode line went up by one and stayed ok. The planted mu.alt carries U+00B5, a character no other glyph in Plum has, so nothing is shared and that check has no complaint. Each line names a chapter's script to reach for: 81 for the name, 89 or 94 for the features, 98 for the copyright, 96 for the metrics.

Notes on the listing.

The Font Info check counts five: four text fields and the version. It compares the version name with the name built from the two numbers, the same :03d as chapter 97.

The metrics check puts each master's value into a set per field. A set with more than one member means the masters disagree. The finally puts the font back on the master you were looking at, as in chapter 95.

The last line prints the version name. When the typesetter writes back in a month, "ready" will mean something only if you know which file was ready.

docs.title: The hand tests
docs.text:
The script says "ready for the hand tests", and it chose those words with care. Python in FontLab can't press Compile and can't set a line of text. A person does these, every time:

  1. Open Window > Panels > Features and click Compile. Read the Output panel.
  2. In a Glyph window, type İSTANBUL with capital spacing on. The capitals of chapter 91 should stand apart evenly.
  3. Type 1/2 and 3/16 with fractions on. Chapter 92's feature text has never been compiled by me, so this is the test I trust least.
  4. Type abcdefgh with small caps on, then fi ff ffi.
  5. If you did exercise 3 of chapter 88, look at what you wrote down about Undo.

Then export the font, install it, and set a paragraph in a program that isn't FontLab. Part 6 turns the export into a script. The looking stays with you.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Make a new glyph called j.sc, the way you made i.sc in chapter 94, and run the pre-flight. You should get j.sc: no feature mentions it and Not ready. Delete the glyph.

Then change "copyright" in TEXT_FIELDS to "copyrihgt". You should get the DID NOT RUN line. Replace the three lines under except with a bare continue, run again, and count the lines. Put everything back.

docs.title: What the pre-flight doesn't say
docs.text:
It doesn't say the features work. It says they mention the glyphs they should. It doesn't say the names are right, only that they're made of allowed characters. A pass means that nothing a script can see is wrong, which is narrower than "the font is good" and still worth having at four o'clock on a Friday.

Oskar takes the sheet from the first morning off the wall. The family name and the version in every weight gets its line through it. Ten of eleven are crossed out. The one left is the Friday export.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Checks that take the same arguments and return the same pair, a count and a list of sentences, can sit in a list and run in one loop. A check that returns its findings can be reused anywhere, and one that prints can't. Catching Exception keeps a loop of checks going, but a check that crashed must be printed and counted as "did not run", never passed over as a success. A script can check what's written in a font, and a person still has to compile the features and set real text.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a sixth check: every glyph with a Unicode value has a name that chapter 82's rule would give it. Start with the letters only.
  2. Guard the last line of check_features.py with if __name__ == "__main__": from chapter 33. Now import check_features is safe. Call its check_feature from the pre-flight for each feature.
  3. Write the report to reports/preflight-<version>.txt as well as printing it, with chapter 26's file writing. Collect the lines in a list first.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The font sets real text. It's still a FontLab file on one desk, and the last open line on the sheet says the whole family goes to a dated folder every Friday. Part 6 builds the script that does it.

docs.title: Part 6: Families
docs.text:
One drawing, five weights.

One font becomes five, and the five leave the building.

It's week twenty. The art director has seen the Regular and the Bold and wants what lies between them, and a good deal that doesn't: nine weights, for the rest of the cookbook series. Plum has three drawings, a Light, a Regular and a Bold. Everything in this part follows from that sum.

The first four chapters look at what "three drawings of one font" means to a script. You list the masters, check that every glyph is built the same way in each, find the contours that start at different points, and lay the widths side by side.

The next six work between the masters. You copy anchors and kerning from the one you trust to the others, do the arithmetic of a weight halfway between two drawings, read the axis, plan the instances, and blend one new drawing of the figures.

Then three chapters get files out of FontLab: one style, then the family, then a folder of Oskar's old fonts opened and closed again without a mark.

Five chapters distrust the result. A check before anything ships, two proof pages, a list of what changed since last week, and a second opinion from fontTools, which reads the exported file and knows nothing of FontLab.

The last two put it together. One script runs the Friday, and one says whether the release is finished.

Oskar's sheet had one line left when this part began:

  • Export the whole family to a dated folder every Friday

It's crossed out in chapter 119.

Three things in this part a script doesn't do, and each chapter says so where it matters. The export itself is done by hand in File > Export Font As, with scripts on both sides of it. The instances are typed into Font Info from a line a script prepares. And five weights ship, not nine: the other four need drawings nobody has made.

You need the practice copy of Plum as Part 5 left it, and Fly installed in FontLab 9. Nothing in this part was run in FontLab 9 by me. Each chapter says how its outputs were computed.

docs.title: 101. More than one drawing
docs.text:
Monday of week twenty. The publisher's art director has seen the cookbook set in Plum and writes two lines to Ines. The Regular is a little light for the ingredient lists, and the Bold is too heavy for them. Could there be something in between? And while Halfmoon is at it, a full range of weights for the rest of the series?

Ines says yes on the telephone and then asks Oskar how long it takes. Oskar looks at Mira.

Plum has three drawings of every glyph: a Light, a Regular and a Bold. FontLab calls them masters. Everything between them can be worked out from them, and that's what this part of the book is for. Before any of it, Mira notices something about her own scripts. Since chapter 40 they have begun with a line she typed by hand, MASTERS = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]. The scripts know about three masters because she told them. If a fourth arrives, every one of those lines is wrong, and nothing will say so.

Today's script asks the font instead.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the script in plain Python against a stand-in with the glyphs this book has added. The layer order in step 3 is read from Plum's source file, where it's plain to see. What FontLab hands a script may be ordered differently, and step 3 is written so that it doesn't matter.

docs.title: Step 1: Ask the font for its masters
docs.text:
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.masters.inspect.model as masters_model

package = scripting.current_package()
print(package.masters)
print(package.master)
masters = masters_model.master_order(package)
for master in masters:
    print(master, masters_model.location_text(package, master))

['Light', 'Regular', 'Bold']
Regular
Light wght 300
Regular wght 400
Bold wght 700

package.masters is the list of master names, and package.master, without the s, is the one you're looking at now. Chapter 95 moved that marker about with setMaster and put it back.

master_order gives the same names sorted by weight, lightest first. For Plum the two lists agree. In a font where somebody added the Light last, they wouldn't, and a report in the order of creation is hard to read. location_text says where each master sits: wght is the weight axis and the number is the master's place on it. Chapter 107 is about those numbers. For today they're labels.

docs.title: Step 2: A master is a layer in every glyph
docs.text:
A master isn't a thing stored in one place. It's a name, and every glyph is expected to have a layer with that name. Chapter 96 asked a glyph for one:

glyph = package.findName("a")
layer = glyph.findLayer("Bold")
print(layer.name, layer.advanceWidth)

findLayer gives the layer, or it gives nothing, and "nothing" comes in two forms: Python's None, or a hollow object whose isNull is true. Test for both, every time. A small function keeps the test in one place:

def has_layer(glyph, master):
    layer = glyph.findLayer(master)
    return layer is not None and not layer.isNull

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
A glyph also has a list of all its layers, glyph.layers. Mira has a list of three masters and a list of three layers, so she walks them side by side with zip from chapter 35:

for master, layer in zip(package.masters, glyph.layers):
    print(master, layer.name)

Light Bold
Regular Regular
Bold Light

The master called Light is paired with the layer called Bold. Had she printed widths, the table would have looked fine and been upside down, with the Bold's numbers under "Light".

print([layer.name for layer in glyph.layers])

['Bold', 'Regular', 'Light']

A glyph keeps its layers in the order they were stored, and nothing says this is the order of the masters. In Plum's file every glyph has them backwards. Two lists of the same length aren't two lists in the same order.

So the rule for this whole part: never take a layer by its position. Take the master's name and ask the glyph for the layer with that name.

The same goes for the masters themselves. package.masters[0] is whichever master was made first, and in another font that could be the Bold. When a script means the Light, it should say "Light", or take the first name from master_order, which at least puts the lightest first.

docs.title: Step 4: A loop inside a loop
docs.text:
The question "does every glyph have a layer for every master?" has two "every" in it, and each one is a loop. Put the second inside the first, as chapter 71 did for the glyphs of every kerning class:

from fly import fl

found = {master: 0 for master in masters}
for glyph in fl.CurrentFont().glyphs:
    fl_glyph = package.findName(glyph.name)
    for master in masters:
        if has_layer(fl_glyph, master):
            found[master] += 1

The outer loop takes a glyph. For that one glyph, the inner loop runs through all the masters. Then the outer loop takes the next glyph and the inner one starts again from the first master. With 274 glyphs and three masters, the line under the if is reached 822 times.

found is a dictionary with one counter per master, built with the comprehension from chapter 95. The inner loop adds to the counter that belongs to its master.

The indentation says which loop a line belongs to. fl_glyph = ... is done once per glyph. The if is done once per glyph and master. If you indent a line one level too deep, it runs three times as often, and Python won't complain.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Masters Report
# Lists the font's masters, then looks in every glyph for a layer
# for every master. Changes nothing.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.masters.inspect.model as masters_model
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)



def has_layer(glyph, master):
    layer = glyph.findLayer(master)
    return layer is not None and not layer.isNull


def main():
    package = scripting.current_package()
    if package is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    masters = masters_model.master_order(package)
    for master in masters:
        mark = "*" if master == package.master else " "
        print(f"{mark} {master:<9}{masters_model.location_text(package, master)}")

    found = {master: 0 for master in masters}
    strangers = []
    reordered = 0
    count = 0
    for glyph in fl.CurrentFont().glyphs:
        count += 1
        fl_glyph = package.findName(glyph.name)
        for master in masters:
            if has_layer(fl_glyph, master):
                found[master] += 1
        names = [layer.name for layer in fl_glyph.layers]
        for name in names:
            if name not in masters:
                strangers.append(f"{glyph.name}: {name}")
        if [name for name in names if name in masters] != masters:
            reordered += 1

    print(f"{count} glyphs x {len(masters)} masters = {count * len(masters)} layers to find")
    for master in masters:
        print(f"{master:<9}{found[master]:>4} found, {count - found[master]} missing")
    print(f"{len(strangers)} layers that belong to no master")
    for line in strangers:
        print("   ", line)
    print(f"{reordered} glyphs keep their layers in another order")


main()

Save it as masters_report.py. On my stand-in it prints:

  Light    wght 300
* Regular  wght 400
  Bold     wght 700
274 glyphs x 3 masters = 822 layers to find
Light     274 found, 0 missing
Regular   274 found, 0 missing
Bold      274 found, 0 missing
0 layers that belong to no master
205 glyphs keep their layers in another order

My count is for the font as Part 5 left it: Plum's 205 glyphs and the 69 the book has added. Yours depends on how many exercises you did. The three "missing" numbers should be 0 whatever it is. If one isn't, a glyph lacks a drawing in that weight, and nothing in this part will work for it until it has one.

Notes on the listing.

The star marks the master you're looking at. The script reads package.master and never changes it, so there's nothing to put back and no finally.

There are two inner loops under one outer loop. The first asks about masters, the second walks the glyph's own layers. A glyph can hold layers that aren't masters: a mask you traced from, a backup FontLab made. The script lists those as strangers. They do no harm, and you want to know they're there before a later script copies "every layer".

The last line compares two lists with !=. Two lists are equal when they hold the same things in the same order. The comprehension keeps only the layer names that are masters, so a stranger in the middle doesn't count as disorder.

My 205 is the number of glyphs that came with Plum. I've assumed that the glyphs you made with chapter 40's script keep the order in which that script made their layers. I haven't seen it. Whatever your number is, it does no damage: it only tells you how many glyphs would have fooled Mira's zip.

The script uses the font for the list of glyphs and the package for their layers, as chapter 96 did.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
After the loop that prints the masters, add the line masters = masters + ["Medium"], and run.

274 glyphs x 4 masters = 1096 layers to find
Light     274 found, 0 missing
Regular   274 found, 0 missing
Bold      274 found, 0 missing
Medium      0 found, 274 missing

That's what a typed list does when it disagrees with the font: the script looks for layers that don't exist. Here it says so, because has_layer tests what findLayer gave back. A script that went straight on to layer.advanceWidth would have stopped with an error on the first glyph, or worse, read a width from the hollow object. Take the line out.

docs.title: What the report doesn't say
docs.text:
It says each glyph has a layer for each master. It doesn't say the three drawings in those layers belong together. A Light a with two contours and a Bold a with three would both be "found". Whether the drawings match is tomorrow's question.

It also doesn't say that three masters are enough for the art director's range. They're the corners. What lies between them is worked out, and the working out starts in chapter 106.

And it reads one font. Oskar's old families were six files with one master each, and for those the question "does every weight have this glyph?" is asked across files, not across layers. Chapter 99 walked over open fonts, and chapter 113 will do it for a folder. Plum keeps its weights in one file, which is why a loop inside a loop is enough today.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A font's masters are names, read from package.masters or in weight order from master_order, and a script should ask for them and never type them. Each master is a layer of that name in every glyph, fetched with findLayer and tested for both None and isNull. A glyph's own list of layers follows no order you can count on, so layers are taken by name and never by position. A loop inside a loop asks a question about every pair, here every glyph with every master, and the indentation decides how often each line runs.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Print a table of advance widths: one row for each of a, n, H, zero, one column per master. Use masters_model.widths(fl_glyph, masters), which returns pairs of master and width.
  2. Go back to one script from Part 3 that starts with MASTERS = [...] and replace the typed list with the font's. What has to come first?
  3. Add a third inner question: in how many glyphs is one master's layer empty while another's isn't? Chapter 96's bounding box is one way to tell.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Every glyph has its three layers. Chapter 102 asks whether the three drawings in them have the same skeleton, which they must before anything can be worked out between them.

docs.title: 102. The same skeleton
docs.text:
Tuesday of week twenty. Oskar tells a story from his second year at Halfmoon. A client asked for a Medium of a family that had a Regular and a Bold. The program worked it out in a second, and every glyph was there except the g, which wasn't a letter any more. One loop was folded through the other. It took him an afternoon to find out why. In the Bold, somebody had tidied the ear of the g and removed one node.

"Halfway between twenty nodes and nineteen," he says, "there's nothing."

A weight between two masters is made node by node: the first node of the Light with the first node of the Bold, the second with the second. That only works when both drawings have the same contours, each contour has the same number of nodes, and a node that's a handle in one is a handle in the other. Type designers call such drawings compatible. Yesterday's report said every glyph has three layers. Today's asks whether the three drawings in them share a skeleton.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I worked out the outputs in plain Python from Plum's source file, for the 205 glyphs Plum came with. I can't know what you drew in the glyphs you added in Part 3, so for those your run is the first one anybody has made.

docs.title: Step 1: One glyph's skeleton
docs.text:
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.masters.inspect.model as masters_model

package = scripting.current_package()
masters = masters_model.master_order(package)
glyph = package.findName("a")
signatures, ok, problems = masters_model.check_glyph(glyph, masters)
print(ok, problems)
print(signatures["Regular"])

True []
(('ooohhohhoohhohhoohhohhohhohho', 'ohhohhoohhoo'), ('acute', 'bottom', 'grave', 'ogonek', 'top'), ())

check_glyph returns three things, and you unpack them as in chapter 42. ok is True or False. problems is a list of words, empty when all is well. signatures is a dictionary with one entry per master.

Look at the entry for the Regular. It's a tuple of three tuples: the contours, the names of the anchors, and the names of the components. The a has two contours, the outside and the bowl, and each is written as a string. An o is a node on the outline and an h is a handle, the two kinds you counted in chapter 42. The outside has 29 letters and the bowl has 12.

Nothing in the signature says where a node is. Coordinates are what differs between a Light and a Bold, so they're left out, and what remains is the skeleton. Two masters are compatible when their signatures are equal, and Python compares tuples with ==: the same things in the same order, all the way down.

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
Before Mira found check_glyph, she'd have used what she had. Chapter 42's node_counts gives the number of nodes in a layer, and two layers with the same count look like a match. Try that idea on two made-up skeletons:

light = ("oooo", "oohhohho")
bold = ("oooooo", "oohhoh")
print(sum([len(contour) for contour in light]))
print(sum([len(contour) for contour in bold]))
print(light == bold)

12
12
False

Both have twelve nodes. In the Light they're shared out four and eight, in the Bold six and six. A check on totals passes these two, and nothing can be made between them. Somebody who removes a node in one place and adds one in another, on a tired afternoon, produces this pair.

A total throws away the structure, and the structure is what you wanted to compare. Compare the whole thing.

docs.title: Step 3: Say where
docs.text:
check_glyph says contours when the contours differ. That sends you to the right glyph and leaves you counting nodes on screen. A small function can find the first place where two skeletons part:

def first_difference(a, b):
    if len(a) != len(b):
        return f"{len(a)} contours and {len(b)}"
    for number, (one, other) in enumerate(zip(a, b), 1):
        if one == other:
            continue
        if len(one) != len(other):
            return f"contour {number}: {len(one)} nodes and {len(other)}"
        for place, (x, y) in enumerate(zip(one, other), 1):
            if x != y:
                return f"contour {number}: node {place} is {x} and {y}"
    return ""

It asks three questions, from coarse to fine, and returns at the first one that finds something. Are there as many contours? If so, take them in pairs. Is this pair the same length? If so, take the letters in pairs.

zip pairs the contours of one master with those of the other, and enumerate(..., 1) from chapter 57 numbers the pairs from one. The loop line unpacks both at once: number gets the count and (one, other) gets the pair. The parentheses are needed, because each turn hands over a number and a pair, and the pair is opened inside.

Yesterday zip was the mistake, and today it's the tool. The difference is what you know about the two lists. Yesterday nothing said the two lists were in the same order. Here the order is the very thing being tested: the first contour of one master is supposed to be the first contour of the other.

print(first_difference(light, bold))

contour 1: 4 nodes and 6

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Compatibility Check
# Compares the structure of every glyph across the masters.
# Changes nothing.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.masters.inspect.model as masters_model
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)



def first_difference(a, b):
    if len(a) != len(b):
        return f"{len(a)} contours and {len(b)}"
    for number, (one, other) in enumerate(zip(a, b), 1):
        if one == other:
            continue
        if len(one) != len(other):
            return f"contour {number}: {len(one)} nodes and {len(other)}"
        for place, (x, y) in enumerate(zip(one, other), 1):
            if x != y:
                return f"contour {number}: node {place} is {x} and {y}"
    return ""


def explain(signatures, masters):
    lines = []
    real = [m for m in masters if signatures.get(m) is not None]
    for master in real[1:]:
        text = first_difference(signatures[real[0]][0], signatures[master][0])
        if text:
            lines.append(f"{real[0]} and {master}: {text}")
    if len({signatures[m][1] for m in real}) > 1:
        for master in real:
            names = " ".join(signatures[master][1]) or "none"
            lines.append(f"{master} anchors: {names}")
    return lines


def main():
    package = scripting.current_package()
    if package is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    masters = masters_model.master_order(package)
    checked = 0
    automatic = 0
    bad = 0
    for glyph in fl.CurrentFont().glyphs:
        fl_glyph = package.findName(glyph.name)
        signatures, ok, problems = masters_model.check_glyph(fl_glyph, masters)
        if signatures and all([signatures[m] is None for m in signatures]):
            automatic += 1
            continue
        checked += 1
        if ok:
            continue
        bad += 1
        print(f"{glyph.name}: {', '.join(problems)}")
        for line in explain(signatures, masters):
            print("   ", line)
    print(f"{checked} glyphs compared in {len(masters)} masters, {bad} don't match.")
    print(f"{automatic} glyphs are built automatically and were left out.")


main()

Save it as compat_check.py. On Plum as it came:

132 glyphs compared in 3 masters, 0 don't match.
73 glyphs are built automatically and were left out.

Plum is clean. Your font has more glyphs, and I'd expect the ones you drew with a script to match as well, because one loop drew the same shape in every master. A glyph you drew by hand in one master only is the likely place for a line of complaint.

Notes on the listing.

Seventy-three of Plum's accented letters are assembled by FontLab from their parts, and for those check_glyph puts None where a signature would be. There's nothing to compare, since FontLab rebuilds them whenever the parts change. The script counts them and says so, in keeping with chapter 80: a glyph that wasn't checked isn't a glyph that passed. all from chapter 44 asks whether every entry is None. It also answers True for an empty list, so signatures and comes first: a glyph with no master layer at all has an empty dictionary, and it should be compared and reported, not counted as automatic.

explain compares each master with the first one that has a signature. It doesn't compare every pair, and it doesn't have to. If the Light matches the Regular and the Light matches the Bold, the Regular matches the Bold.

For anchors the script prints the names in each master, since a missing anchor is found faster by reading three short lines than by any arithmetic. The set in len({...}) > 1 holds the different anchor tuples, and more than one of them means the masters disagree. That's the trick check_glyph uses itself.

Twelve of Plum's glyphs are put together from other glyphs by hand and not by FontLab. For those the first part of the signature is empty and the third part holds the names of the pieces, in order. An aacute that is a plus acute in two masters and a plus grave in the third would come back with the word components. The pieces themselves are checked under their own names, so a fault in the a is reported once, at the a, and not again for every letter built on it.

A string is compared the way a tuple is, one place after another, which is why the inner loop can zip two strings and walk their letters as chapter 7 walked a name.

signatures.get(master) is the careful way to ask a dictionary, from chapter 22. If a glyph lacks a layer, the master isn't in the dictionary at all, and get answers None where square brackets would stop the script.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Open n in the Glyph window, switch to the Bold, click one node on a straight part of the stem and press Delete. Then open A, switch to the Light, and delete its anchors. Run the script.

A: anchors
    Light anchors: none
    Regular anchors: acute bottom grave ogonek top
    Bold anchors: acute bottom grave ogonek top
n: contours
    Light and Bold: contour 1: 20 nodes and 19
132 glyphs compared in 3 masters, 2 don't match.
73 glyphs are built automatically and were left out.

If you deleted a node on a curve, its handles went with it and your second number is smaller. Now undo both changes with Edit > Undo in each glyph, and run again until the count is back to 0. Don't go on with a damaged n. Tomorrow needs it whole.

docs.title: What the check doesn't see
docs.text:
Two skeletons can be equal and the glyph can still come out wrong. The signature of a square is oooo wherever its first node is. If the Light starts at the bottom left and the Bold starts at the top right, the check passes, and the shape between them turns inside out on the way. The same goes for two contours of equal build stored in a different order, such as the two dots of a dieresis.

Fly's own note on its comparison says as much: it isn't a certificate for export, and coordinates are outside it. FontLab also has a test of its own, isCompatible, on layers. It takes a second argument called strong, and I couldn't find out what that adds, so this book doesn't use it.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Masters can be mixed only when their drawings are compatible: the same contours, the same number of nodes in each, the same kinds of node in the same places. check_glyph reduces each master's layer to a signature, a tuple of tuples and strings, and comparing two signatures with == compares their whole structure in one step. A total can agree where the structure doesn't, so compare the structure and then report the first place it differs. An equal skeleton is necessary and not sufficient, because the check ignores where each contour starts.

  3. Write the two made-up skeletons that first_difference can't tell apart although the drawings would twist. What would the function need to be given to see it?
