docs.text: Chapter 103 looks at where each contour starts, which today's check passes over, and moves a start point with a little arithmetic on positions.

docs.title: 103. Where the contour starts
docs.text:
Wednesday of week twenty. Yesterday's check came back clean, and Oskar isn't satisfied.

"Draw me a square," he says, and Mira draws one on the back of the proof. "Number the corners from the bottom left, going round. Now draw a fatter square next to it and number that one from the top right." She does. "Join the ones, join the twos."

The four lines cross in the middle. A shape halfway between the two squares, made by joining node 1 to node 1 and node 2 to node 2, isn't a square. It's a knot. Both squares have four nodes on one contour, and yesterday's script would call them a match.

A contour is a ring, and a ring has no beginning. A list has one. So FontLab picks one node of the ring to be number 0, and that choice is the start point. For masters to mix, the choice has to fall on the same corner in every master. Today's script finds the contours where it doesn't and turns the ring until it does.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9 with the Regular showing, and Fly installed.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I computed the outputs in plain Python from the outlines in Plum's source file, for the 205 glyphs Plum came with, and I moved the start points in a stand-in, not in FontLab.

docs.title: Step 1: Turn a ring
docs.text:
Forget the font for a minute. Here is a ring of six letters:

ring = list("abcdef")
turned = ring[2:] + ring[:2]
print(turned)

['c', 'd', 'e', 'f', 'a', 'b']

ring[2:] is the slice from position 2 to the end and ring[:2] is the slice before position 2. Chapter 10 took slices of a list of widths, and these are the same slices. Glue the two together the other way round and the ring has turned: what was at position 2 is now at 0. Nothing was added or lost, and every letter still has the same neighbours.

That's what a new start point does to a contour. The outline on screen doesn't move. Only the numbering does.

docs.title: Step 2: Arithmetic that goes round
docs.text:
After the turn, where is e? It was at position 4, the ring turned by 2, so it's at 2. Where is a? It was at 0, and 0 minus 2 is −2, which isn't a position you'd want to say out loud. It's at 4.

Python has an operator for arithmetic that goes round. % gives the remainder of a division:

print(7 % 6, 6 % 6, (0 - 2) % 6)

1 0 4

Seven steps round a ring of six land on position 1. Six steps land where you began. Two steps back from 0 land on 4. A clock does this with twelve, and you've done it all your life.

So when a ring of count nodes turns to start at start, the node that was at old moves to (old - start) % count.

Now turn the question round, because the script needs it the other way. Some node sits at position here. You want it at position there. Which start does that?

def new_start(here, there, count):
    return (here - there) % count

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Mira's first version had the subtraction the other way round, (there - here) % count. It looks as reasonable as the right one. So test it on the ring before it touches a font. Put e, which is at 4, at position 1:

start = (1 - 4) % 6
turned = ring[start:] + ring[:start]
print(start, turned, turned.index("e"))

3 ['d', 'e', 'f', 'a', 'b', 'c'] 1

The last number comes from index, which chapter 86 used to ask a list where a value sits. That one happens to work. Try to put e at position 0, with the wrong formula and then with the right one:

for start in [(0 - 4) % 6, (4 - 0) % 6]:
    turned = ring[start:] + ring[:start]
    print(start, turned.index("e"))

2 2
4 0

The wrong formula leaves e at 2. It passed the first test by luck: on a ring of six, a turn of three is the same in both directions. One test that passes isn't a proof, and a test with a number that sits in the middle of the ring is a poor test. index, by the way, gives the position of the first thing in a list that equals what you ask for.

A wrong sign in a font would have turned every faulty contour further from where it should be, and the report would still have said "1 contour moved".

docs.title: Step 4: Which node should be the same?
docs.text:
The script needs a node it can recognise in every master. Positions differ between masters, so "the node at 255, −10" is no use. Fly's choice is the lowest node on the outline, and the leftmost of them if there are several:

import fly.ap.contours.writer as outline
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.fontui.outline_order as order
import fly.ap.masters.inspect.model as masters_model

package = scripting.current_package()
layer = package.findName("e").findLayer("Regular")
contour = masters_model.own_contours(layer)[0]
points = outline.node_points(contour)
print(len(points), order.bottom_left(points), points[12])

23 12 (255.0, -10.0, True)

own_contours gives the contours drawn in this layer, without those borrowed from other glyphs. node_points gives each node as a tuple of x, y and whether it's on the outline. bottom_left gives the position, in that list, of the lowest node. In the Regular e it's number 12 of 23, the bottom of the bowl.

If the Bold's lowest node is also number 12, the two rings start at the same corner. If it's number 6, the Bold's ring was turned, and new_start(6, 12, 23) says where it has to start to put things right.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Start Points
# Finds contours that start at a different node than in the master
# you're looking at, and moves the start to match.
from fly import fl, qt
import fly.ap.contours.writer as outline
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.fontui.outline_order as order
import fly.ap.masters.inspect.model as masters_model
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


DRY_RUN = True
SKIP = ["Oslash"]


def new_start(here, there, count):
    return (here - there) % count


def plan(glyph, trusted, master):
    steps = []
    model = masters_model.own_contours(glyph.findLayer(trusted))
    contours = masters_model.own_contours(glyph.findLayer(master))
    for number, (good, contour) in enumerate(zip(model, contours), 1):
        points = outline.node_points(contour)
        there = order.bottom_left(outline.node_points(good))
        here = order.bottom_left(points)
        if here is None or here == there or not contour.closed:
            continue
        start = new_start(here, there, len(points))
        if not points[start][2]:
            print(f"{glyph.name} {master} contour {number}: by hand, node {start} is a handle")
            continue
        steps.append((number, contour, start))
    return steps


def main():
    package = scripting.current_package()
    if package is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    trusted = package.master
    others = [m for m in masters_model.master_order(package) if m != trusted]
    moves = []
    for font_glyph in fl.CurrentFont().glyphs:
        if font_glyph.name in SKIP:
            continue
        glyph = package.findName(font_glyph.name)
        signatures, ok, problems = masters_model.check_glyph(glyph, [trusted] + others)
        if not ok or signatures[trusted] is None:
            continue
        for master in others:
            layer = glyph.findLayer(master)
            for number, contour, start in plan(glyph, trusted, master):
                print(f"{glyph.name} {master} contour {number}: start at node {start}")
                moves.append((glyph, layer, contour, start))
    print(f"{len(moves)} contours start somewhere else than in {trusted}.")
    if DRY_RUN:
        print("Dry run. Nothing was changed.")
        return
    if not moves:
        return

    def change():
        for glyph, layer, contour, start in moves:
            if contour.setStartPoint(start) is False:
                raise RuntimeError(f"FontLab refused the start node in {glyph.name}.")

    glyphs = []
    layers = []
    for glyph, layer, contour, start in moves:
        if glyph not in glyphs:
            glyphs.append(glyph)
        if layer not in layers:
            layers.append(layer)
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    history.commit("Match start points", layers, glyphs, change,
                   operation="geometry", facts=facts, allow_bases=True)

main()

Save it as start_points.py. On Plum as it came, with the Regular showing:

0 contours start somewhere else than in Regular.
Dry run. Nothing was changed.

Notes on the listing.

The master you're looking at is the one the script trusts. The others are brought into line with it. Look at the right master before you run.

Glyphs that failed yesterday's check are passed over, and so are the automatic ones. Moving a start point in a contour whose masters have different node counts would repair nothing.

A start point has to be a node on the outline. If the arithmetic lands on a handle, the lowest node isn't the same node in both masters after all, and the script says by hand and leaves it.

The change itself is contour.setStartPoint(start). The loop only collects the moves, as chapter 68 collected its rows, and one change makes them all, so a run is one Undo step however many contours it turns. The call answers False when FontLab won't do it, and the script turns that into an error, which takes every move of the run back with it. glyphs and layers are built with not in because one glyph can have a move in two masters, and each belongs in the list once.

Run it with the Font window in front. Fly refuses a change to many glyphs from a Glyph window, with a message that begins Switch to the Font window first, because Undo there only reaches the glyphs that window shows.

The commit carries allow_bases=True. Without it Fly refuses any glyph that other glyphs are built from automatically, with a message that begins Refused. and says base of auto, and the e is such a glyph: eacute and three more borrow it. The refusal has a reason. When a base changes, FontLab rebuilds the glyphs that borrow it, and Fly's own notes say Undo may not put their anchors back as they were. A turned start point doesn't change the outline, so the rebuilt glyphs should look as before. I haven't watched it happen. Save the font before a real run, and afterward look at one borrower of each glyph the script names.

SKIP has one name in it. Empty the list and run, and you get:

Oslash Bold contour 1: start at node 20

Nothing is wrong with the Oslash. Its slash pokes out below the bowl at the left, and at the bottom the bowl itself dips under the baseline. In the Regular the bowl is lower by a few units, in the Bold the tip of the slash is. The lowest node is a different node, the script takes that for a turned ring, and its cure would cause the twist it was written to prevent. "The lowest node" is a guess about which node is which, and it was right for 170 of Plum's 171 contours. Read the dry run, look at each glyph it names, and put the false alarms in SKIP.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Go to the Bold of e, select a node on the outline a few nodes away from the start, and choose Contour > Set Start Point. I believe that's where the command is. If it isn't, right-click the node. Switch back to the Regular, bring the Font window to the front, and run:

e Bold contour 1: start at node 17
1 contours start somewhere else than in Regular.
Dry run. Nothing was changed.

Your node number depends on the node you picked. Set DRY_RUN = False, run, set it back to True, and run once more. The second run should print 0. That second run is the test: the script found its own repair in order.

docs.title: What the script doesn't do
docs.text:
It doesn't look at the order of the contours. If the Light keeps the bowl of the e first and the Bold keeps the bar first, and both have as many nodes, nothing here notices. I found no call that reorders contours and is known to work, so that repair stays in the Glyph window.

It doesn't look at direction either. Chapter 45 measured that for one master. A contour that runs clockwise in one master and the other way in the next twists as surely as a turned ring.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A contour is a ring stored as a list, the start point is the node at position 0, and masters mix properly only when that node is the same corner in each. A ring turns by gluing two slices together in the other order, and % does the arithmetic of positions that go round. A formula should be tested on a small made-up ring with more than one case, since one passing test can be luck. The lowest node is a useful guess at "the same node" and it is sometimes wrong, so the script proposes and you read before you let it write.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. A contour has 23 nodes and should start at the node now at 20. Where will the node now at 3 end up? Work it out, then check with a list made by list(range(23)).
  2. Write turned_back(ring, start) that undoes a turn. Test it on the ring of letters.
  3. Change the script so that it trusts the master named in a constant at the top, and not the one on screen. Which is safer, and for whom?

docs.text: Chapter 104 puts the widths of every glyph in every master into one table, a dictionary whose values are dictionaries.

docs.title: 104. Widths across masters
docs.text:
Thursday of week twenty. The cookbook has a nutrition table at the back of every chapter: energy, fat, sugar, salt, and a row of totals in Bold. The typesetter asks one question before she builds it. If she sets the totals in Bold under figures in Regular, will the columns still line up?

In chapter 66 Mira made sure the figures of each weight share one width. That answers a narrower question, the one about a column set in a single weight. The typesetter is asking about two weights in one column, and nobody has looked at that.

Looking at it needs a table with two directions: glyphs down the side, masters across the top. You've built tables as lists of rows. Today's is a dictionary whose values are dictionaries, and most of the chapter is about reading one of those without getting lost.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The figures as chapter 66 left them.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The widths below are read from Plum's source file, with the four currency signs at the widths chapter 66 gave them. The widths of period and hyphen in step 3 are the shipped ones. If you've changed those, your numbers differ and the lesson doesn't.

docs.title: Step 1: One glyph in every master
docs.text:
Chapter 101's exercise used masters_model.widths. It takes a glyph and the list of masters and gives back pairs:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.masters.inspect.model as masters_model

package = scripting.current_package()
masters = masters_model.master_order(package)
pairs = masters_model.widths(package.findName("zero"), masters)
print(pairs)
row = dict(pairs)
print(row["Bold"])

[('Light', 456.0), ('Regular', 490.0), ('Bold', 490.0)]
490.0

A list of pairs becomes a dictionary with dict, as in chapter 94. Now the width can be asked for by the master's name, which is the rule from chapter 101: by name, never by position.

The widths come back as numbers with a decimal point. They're whole numbers in Plum, and :.0f in an f-string prints them without the tail.

docs.title: Step 2: A dictionary of those
docs.text:
One such row per glyph, kept under the glyph's name:

table = {}
for name in ["zero", "one", "two"]:
    table[name] = dict(masters_model.widths(package.findName(name), masters))

print(table["zero"])
print(table["zero"]["Light"])

{'Light': 456.0, 'Regular': 490.0, 'Bold': 490.0}
456.0

Chapter 73 had a dictionary inside a dictionary, the orders for each master. The reading rule is the same. table["zero"] is the inner dictionary, one glyph's row. table["zero"]["Light"] goes into that row and takes one number out. Read the brackets from left to right, as you'd run a finger down the side of a table and then across.

Which key goes outside is your choice, and it decides what's cheap to ask. With the glyph outside, "all the widths of zero" is one lookup. "All the widths in Bold" isn't stored anywhere. You collect it with a loop:

bold = [table[name]["Bold"] for name in table]

Had you built it the other way, master outside, the second question would be one lookup and the first a loop. Neither is wrong. Pick the one that matches the question you ask more often, and write a function for the other.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Mira's first version filled the inner dictionary by hand, and to save a line she made the empty row once, before the loop:

row = {}
table = {}
for name in ["zero", "period", "hyphen"]:
    for master, width in masters_model.widths(package.findName(name), masters):
        row[master] = width
    table[name] = row

for name in table:
    print(name, table[name])

zero {'Light': 348.0, 'Regular': 348.0, 'Bold': 348.0}
period {'Light': 348.0, 'Regular': 348.0, 'Bold': 348.0}
hyphen {'Light': 348.0, 'Regular': 348.0, 'Bold': 348.0}

Three glyphs, all 348 wide in every weight. That's the hyphen's row, three times.

There's one row. table[name] = row doesn't copy it. It puts the same dictionary under a second name, and a third. Each turn of the loop then writes over the numbers in that one dictionary, and at the end all three names lead to whatever the last glyph left there.

print(table["zero"] is table["hyphen"])

True

is asks whether two names lead to the same object, which is a harder test than ==. You've used it with None since chapter 8, where there's only one None to lead to.

The repair is to make a new dictionary on every turn. Move row = {} inside the outer loop, or do what step 2 did: dict(...) builds a fresh one each time it's called. It's a quiet fault, because every row looks like a proper row. On the figures alone Mira wouldn't have seen it at all, since their rows really are alike. She saw it because she'd put a period in the test.

docs.title: Step 4: Turn the table round
docs.text:
Step 3 left you with a table of three hyphens. Build step 2's table again before you go on, and then, to ask "does this master keep its figures on one width?", collect the names under each width:

table = {}
for name in ["zero", "one", "two"]:
    table[name] = dict(masters_model.widths(package.findName(name), masters))


def by_width(table, master):
    found = {}
    for name in table:
        width = table[name][master]
        if width not in found:
            found[width] = []
        found[width].append(name)
    return found


print(by_width(table, "Regular"))

{490.0: ['zero', 'one', 'two']}

It's the grouping from chapter 100: a dictionary of lists, with a new empty list made when a key is first seen, inside the loop, where it belongs. If the result has one key, the master is tabular. If it has two, the shorter list holds the culprits.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Master Widths
# Prints the widths of the tabular glyphs in every master and says
# whether each master keeps them on one width. Changes nothing.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.masters.inspect.model as masters_model
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


TABULAR = ["zero", "one", "two", "three", "four",
           "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine",
           "dollar", "Euro", "sterling", "yen"]


def width_table(package, names, masters):
    table = {}
    for name in names:
        glyph = package.findName(name)
        if glyph is None:
            continue
        table[name] = dict(masters_model.widths(glyph, masters))
    return table


def by_width(table, master):
    found = {}
    for name in table:
        width = table[name][master]
        if width not in found:
            found[width] = []
        found[width].append(name)
    return found


def usual_width(found):
    best = None
    for width in found:
        if best is None or len(found[width]) > len(found[best]):
            best = width
    return best


def main():
    package = scripting.current_package()
    if package is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    masters = masters_model.master_order(package)
    table = width_table(package, TABULAR, masters)

    print(f"{'':<10}" + "".join([f"{master:>9}" for master in masters]))
    for name in table:
        print(f"{name:<10}" + "".join([f"{table[name][m]:>9.0f}" for m in masters]))

    problems = 0
    usual = {}
    for master in masters:
        found = by_width(table, master)
        usual[master] = usual_width(found)
        if len(found) == 1:
            print(f"{master}: one width, {usual[master]:.0f}")
            continue
        for width in found:
            if width != usual[master]:
                problems += len(found[width])
                print(f"{master}: {' '.join(found[width])} at {width:.0f}, the rest at {usual[master]:.0f}")

    sharing = {}
    for master in masters:
        if usual[master] not in sharing:
            sharing[usual[master]] = []
        sharing[usual[master]].append(master)
    for width in sharing:
        print(f"{width:.0f}: {' and '.join(sharing[width])}")
    print(f"{len(table)} glyphs in {len(masters)} masters, {problems} off the column.")


main()

Save it as master_widths.py. It prints:

              Light  Regular     Bold
zero            456      490      490
one             456      490      490
two             456      490      490
three           456      490      490
four            456      490      490
five            456      490      490
six             456      490      490
seven           456      490      490
eight           456      490      490
nine            456      490      490
dollar          456      490      490
Euro            456      490      490
sterling        456      490      490
yen             456      490      490
Light: one width, 456
Regular: one width, 490
Bold: one width, 490
456: Light
490: Regular and Bold
14 glyphs in 3 masters, 0 off the column.

Notes on the listing.

width_table skips a name the font doesn't have. findName gives None for those, and a missing yen shouldn't stop a report about figures.

usual_width finds the width that most glyphs have. It's the widest-glyph loop from chapter 18, which keeps the best one seen so far, with the length of a list as the thing compared. The script needs it so that, when a master has two widths, it can name the few glyphs that left the column and not the many that stayed.

The header line starts with f"{'':<10}", an empty string padded to ten places. It's there so the master names stand over their columns. Inside an f-string written with double quotes, the empty string has to use single ones.

The last block turns the result round once more: masters collected under their usual width. That's the line the typesetter wanted.

The script trusts chapter 101. masters_model.widths gives None for a master whose layer is missing, and :>9.0f can't format None: the script would stop with a TypeError in the middle of the table. I left it that way on purpose. Run masters_report.py first, and if it says a layer is missing, that's the thing to repair before you ask about widths.

The dictionaries keep the order in which things went in, so the rows come out in the order of TABULAR and the columns in the order of masters. Nothing is sorted, because the order you typed is the order a person expects to read figures in.

docs.title: What the answer is
docs.text:
Regular and Bold share 490. A Bold total sits under Regular figures digit for digit, and the table holds. The Light is narrower, 456, so a column that mixes Light with either of the others will drift by 34 units a digit. Oskar's answer to the typesetter is two sentences: totals in Bold are safe, and don't mix Light into a column of figures.

Whether the Light ought to be 490 as well is a design question. Its figures are thinner and would look lost in so much room, which is likely why Sora Sagano drew them narrower. The script lays the numbers out, and a person reads them and decides. Nobody changes anything today.

There's a second thing in that output, for the art director's in-between weight. Whatever lies between Regular and Bold lies between 490 and 490. A weight worked out from those two will have figures 490 wide without anybody arranging it. Chapter 106 shows why.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
In the Glyph window, switch to the Bold master, open seven and type 480 into its width field. Run the script. Under the table it prints:

Light: one width, 456
Regular: one width, 490
Bold: seven at 480, the rest at 490
456: Light
490: Regular and Bold
14 glyphs in 3 masters, 1 off the column.

The table above those lines shows 480 in the Bold column too, and in fourteen rows of near-identical numbers you'd likely read past it. The sentence under the table is why the script doesn't stop at printing. Undo the change and run again until the last line says 0.

docs.title: What the report doesn't say
docs.text: It compares advance widths. A figure can have the right width and sit off-center in it, which was chapter 66's subject. It also covers only the glyphs in TABULAR. Your fraction figures from chapter 92 aren't in the list, and neither is the space a typesetter uses to pad a column.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A dictionary of dictionaries holds a table with two directions, and table[glyph][master] reads it one bracket at a time from the left. The key you put outside decides which question is a single lookup, and a short function turns the table round for the other question. Assigning a dictionary doesn't copy it, so a row made once outside the loop becomes one row under many names, which is will confirm. Each master of Plum keeps its figures on one width, Regular and Bold share theirs, and the Light doesn't.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add the ten .numr and ten .dnom glyphs from chapter 92 as a second group and report it separately. What do you expect of glyphs made empty by chapter 40's script?
  2. Write by_master(table) that returns the same numbers with the master as the outer key. Check one number both ways.
  3. For every glyph in the font, count how many have the same width in Regular and Bold. On shipped Plum it was all 205. Chapter 68 changed that in your font: by how many?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The masters agree where they should. Chapter 105 copies things from one master to the others: anchors that were placed in the Regular and are wanted in all three.

docs.title: 105. Copy between masters
docs.text:
Friday of week twenty. A publisher of Latin dictionaries has asked whether Plum can set ǣ, the ae with a macron that marks a long vowel. It can't yet. The ae and the AE have an acute anchor and no top, so there's nowhere to hang the macron.

Mira placed a top on both glyphs before lunch. She did it in the Regular, because that's the master she had on screen, and went to eat.

So two glyphs now have an anchor in one master out of three. Chapter 102's check would call that a mismatch, and it would be right. Today's script finds anchors that exist in one master and are missing in another, and puts them there. The question is where "there" is, since the three drawings aren't the same width.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • Chapter 55 fresh in your mind: an edit is ("set", name, (x, y)), and a row of work is a glyph, a layer and a list of edits.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the arithmetic on the anchors and widths in Plum's source file, and the numbers below come from there.

docs.title: Step 1: Do what Mira did
docs.text:
Put the two anchors in. This is chapter 55's route, on two glyphs and one master. First the tools and the two places, which Mira read off the Glyph window:

import fly.ap.anchors.writer as anchors
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly.pens import layer_of

PLACES = {"ae": (377, 478), "AE": (426, 688)}

Then the work, one entry for each glyph, checked and written in one go:

package = scripting.current_package()
facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
work = []
for name in PLACES:
    glyph = package.findName(name)
    layer = layer_of(glyph, "Regular")
    work.append((glyph, layer, [("set", "top", PLACES[name])]))
anchors.require_safe(work, facts)
done = anchors.apply_work(work, "Add top to ae and AE", facts)
print(done["anchors"], "anchors on", done["layers"], "layers.")

2 anchors on 2 layers.

The x values are each glyph's acute plus 20, which is how Plum's other letters keep their top and acute apart. The heights are the x-height and the cap height.

require_safe lets these two through. Nothing in Plum is built from ae or AE, so chapter 55's refusal doesn't come up. I picked the story for that reason, and it comes back in Step 5.

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
The plain idea: read the anchor in the Regular, write the same numbers in the Light.

Before trying it on Mira's anchors, try it on an anchor whose right answer you can look up. The H has a top in all three masters. Ask what the plain idea would have written:

glyph = package.findName("H")
regular = layer_of(glyph, "Regular")
light = layer_of(glyph, "Light")
print(regular.advanceWidth, anchors.anchor_points(regular)["top"])
print(light.advanceWidth, anchors.anchor_points(light)["top"])

672.0 (336.0, 688.0)
612.0 (306.0, 688.0)

The Regular keeps the anchor at 336. The Light keeps it at 306. Copy the 336 across and the macron sits 30 units to the right of where Plum's designer put it, on every H with an accent.

Nothing would have complained. The script would have printed a tidy count, the check from chapter 102 would have passed, and the fault would have turned up in a proof weeks later as accents that lean right in the Light.

Look at the four numbers again. 336 is half of 672. 306 is half of 612. The anchor is in the middle of the glyph in both masters. An x position has no meaning without the width it was measured in.

docs.title: Step 3: Scale it
docs.text:
Keep the anchor at the same share of the width. If it sits 336 units into 672, that's a share of 336/672. In a glyph 612 wide, the same share is:

def scaled(x, source_width, target_width):
    return round(x * target_width / source_width)

print(scaled(336, 672, 612))

306

Multiply first, divide last. x / source_width * target_width is the same sum on paper, and on a computer the early division leaves a long tail that the multiplication then stretches. You saw such a tail in chapter 68.

The y stays as it is. Plum's three masters share their x-height and cap height, so an anchor at 688 in one is at 688 in all.

One formula checked against one anchor is a hunch. Plum has plenty of anchors that exist in all masters, so the rule can be tested on the lot. I took the seventeen glyphs with anchors that are drawn by hand and aren't borrowed by anything, 43 anchors in all, and predicted each Light position from the Regular one:

Rule Right to the unit Within 3 units Same x 3 3 Scaled x 14 36

Scaling is much better and it isn't perfect. The seven it misses are of two kinds. cedilla sits at x 100 in every master, whatever the width: it's a parking place and no one moved it. topRight hangs at the right edge of a stem, and stems get thinner in the Light by more than the glyph gets narrower.

So the script's output is a first guess. For an anchor in the middle of a letter the numbers will be right or a unit off. For one that hangs on an edge, look.

docs.title: Step 4: Find what's missing
docs.text:
For one glyph and one pair of layers, the missing anchors are the names in the first that aren't in the second:

def missing_edits(source, target):
    have = anchors.anchor_points(target)
    edits = []
    if source.advanceWidth == 0:
        return edits
    for name, (x, y) in anchors.anchor_points(source).items():
        if name not in have:
            new_x = scaled(x, source.advanceWidth, target.advanceWidth)
            edits.append(("set", name, (new_x, round(y))))
    return edits

anchor_points gives a dictionary from anchor name to a pair, and for name, (x, y) in ... .items() unpacks the pair on the way, as chapter 86 did with numbered pairs. The test on the width is there because scaled divides by it. A glyph of no width has no shares.

The function returns edits in chapter 55's form and touches nothing. It only ever adds. An anchor that's already in the target stays where its designer put it, even if the rule would put it elsewhere.

docs.title: Step 5: The glyphs it must leave alone
docs.text:
Chapter 55 met two kinds of glyph that Fly's anchor writer won't touch. A glyph that FontLab builds itself can't be edited at all. A glyph that such glyphs borrow can be edited only through your own commit with allow_bases=True.

A script that walks the whole font will meet both. If it hands one to require_safe, the whole batch is refused and nothing is written, the good rows included. So ask first, glyph by glyph:

print(repr(history.refusal(facts, "ae", "geometry")))
print(repr(history.refusal(facts, "o", "geometry")))
print(repr(history.refusal(facts, "aacute", "geometry")))

''
'base of auto oacute, ocircumflex…'
'has auto layers'

refusal answers with the reason as a string, and with an empty string when there's none. An empty string counts as false in an if, so if history.refusal(...) reads as "if there's a reason not to". The second line is my reading of Fly's code, which names the first two borrowers and then stops. Which two it names in your font I can't tell you.

The script sets such glyphs aside and names them at the end. For a borrowed glyph you then have a choice: place the anchor by hand in each master, or use chapter 55's commit. I left that out of today's script on purpose. Adding an anchor to o makes FontLab rebuild at least five glyphs, oacute to otilde, and that's a decision for a person with the glyph on screen.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Sync Masters
# Copies anchors that exist in the trusted master but are missing in
# another master. The x is scaled by the widths. Dry run by default.
import fly.ap.anchors.writer as anchors
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.masters.inspect.model as masters_model
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


TRUSTED = "Regular"
DRY_RUN = True


def scaled(x, source_width, target_width):
    return round(x * target_width / source_width)


def missing_edits(source, target):
    have = anchors.anchor_points(target)
    edits = []
    if source.advanceWidth == 0:
        return edits
    for name, (x, y) in anchors.anchor_points(source).items():
        if name not in have:
            new_x = scaled(x, source.advanceWidth, target.advanceWidth)
            edits.append(("set", name, (new_x, round(y))))
    return edits


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    others = [m for m in masters_model.master_order(package) if m != TRUSTED]
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    work = []
    left_alone = []
    count = 0
    for font_glyph in font.glyphs:
        glyph = package.findName(font_glyph.name)
        source = layer_of(glyph, TRUSTED)
        for master in others:
            target = layer_of(glyph, master)
            edits = missing_edits(source, target)
            if not edits:
                continue
            if history.refusal(facts, glyph.name, "geometry"):
                if glyph.name not in left_alone:
                    left_alone.append(glyph.name)
                continue
            for kind, name, (x, y) in edits:
                print(f"{glyph.name} {master}: {name} at {x}, {y}")
            work.append((glyph, target, edits))
            count += len(edits)
    print(f"{count} anchors missing in {len(work)} layers.")
    if left_alone:
        print("Left alone, FontLab builds glyphs with them:")
        print(" ".join(left_alone))
    if DRY_RUN:
        print("Dry run. Nothing was changed.")
        return
    if not work:
        return
    anchors.require_safe(work, facts)
    done = anchors.apply_work(work, f"Copy anchors from {TRUSTED}", facts)
    print(f"{done['anchors']} anchors on {done['layers']} layers.")


main()

Save it as sync_masters.py and run it:

AE Light: top at 414, 688
AE Bold: top at 426, 688
ae Light: top at 372, 478
ae Bold: top at 377, 478
4 anchors missing in 4 layers.
Dry run. Nothing was changed.

In the Bold the numbers equal the Regular's, because those two glyphs are as wide in the Bold as in the Regular. In the Light, AE is 829 wide against 852, and 426 × 829 / 852 is 414.5. round gives 414: a half goes to the even neighbor, as chapter 53 found.

Read the list, then set DRY_RUN = False and run. The last line becomes 4 anchors on 4 layers., and Edit > Undo should take all four back in one step, named Copy anchors from Regular. Set DRY_RUN back to True and run again:

0 anchors missing in 0 layers.
Dry run. Nothing was changed.

Notes on the listing.

TRUSTED is a name you type, where chapter 103 took the master on screen. Mira's habit decided it: she places anchors in the Regular. A constant at the top says so to whoever reads the script next.

All the work goes to apply_work in one list, so the whole run is one Undo step. Chapter 103 made one step for each contour. Either is defensible. Here the edits are small and alike, and one step is easier to take back.

require_safe is still called, though the loop has already set the refused glyphs aside. It also checks things refusal doesn't, such as two anchors with one name. And if my loop has a hole, I'd like to hear about it before anything is written.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Go to the Light of o, select the top anchor and delete it. Run the dry run:

0 anchors missing in 0 layers.
Left alone, FontLab builds glyphs with them:
o
Dry run. Nothing was changed.

The script saw the gap and declined to fill it. Now undo your deletion with Edit > Undo, and run once more to see the last two lines go.

If you'd like to see what the script was avoiding, take the if history.refusal block out, delete the anchor again and run with DRY_RUN = False. By Fly's code you get a ValueError that begins FontLab cannot undo edits to these glyphs and nothing is written. Put the block back, and the anchor.

docs.title: What about guides and metrics?
docs.text:
Oskar's notes list three things that drift between masters: anchors, guides and the font's own measurements.

Plum's glyphs carry no guides, so there's nothing to copy, and I found no way to write the font's guides from Python with Undo. The font's measurements, ascender and the rest, have their own route, the one chapter 96 used, and they don't scale by a glyph's width. The script stays with anchors.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A position copied between masters has to be scaled by the two widths, and you multiply before you divide. A rule can be tested on the data you already trust before it writes anything new. A function that returns a reason as a string, empty for none, can be used as a yes or no. A script that walks a whole font should set aside what it may not touch and say so, since one refused glyph stops the batch.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Run the dry run with TRUSTED = "Light". With Mira's anchors copied, it should find nothing. Delete the top from the Regular of AE, run again, and compare the number it offers with 426, where the anchor was. It says 425. Where did the unit go?
  2. In the Bold, the acute of ae sits at 376, which is 19 to the right of the Regular's 357, though the widths are equal. The scaling rule can't know that. Write beside(layer, source, name, model) that places a missing anchor as far from the target's model anchor as it is in the source: for top with acute as model, 20 to the right. It should give 372, 396 and 415 for the Light ae, the Bold ae and the Light AE.
  3. Make the script report anchors that exist in both masters and sit more than 10 units from where the rule would put them. Change nothing. On Plum as shipped, which anchor names fill the list?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The art director's weight between Regular and Bold is still waiting. Chapter 106 works out by hand what "halfway between" two drawings means, one number at a time.

docs.title: 106. Halfway between
docs.text:
Monday of week twenty-one. The art director's note from last Monday is still pinned over Mira's desk: "The Regular is a little light for the ingredient lists, and the Bold is too heavy for them. Could there be something in between?"

"A Medium", Mira says. "Halfway between Regular and Bold. FontLab can do that, I've seen Oskar do it."

It can, and chapter 110 will ask it to. But first I'd like you to do it yourself, with a pencil's worth of arithmetic, on the plainest glyph in the font. When a weight comes out wrong three weeks from now, you'll want to know what sum was done, and it's a small one.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • Chapter 102's result: every glyph you compare has the same skeleton in all three masters.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The sums are plain Python and I ran those. The glyph's coordinates come from Plum's source file.

docs.title: Step 1: One number
docs.text:
Plum's hyphen is a rectangle, as chapter 50 found. In the Regular its bottom edge is at y 246. In the Bold it's at 228. Where is it halfway?

You don't need a computer for that: 237. Say how you got it, though. You took the distance from one to the other, which is 228 minus 246, or −18. You took half of it, −9. You added that to where you started.

def lerp(a, b, t):
    return a + (b - a) * t

print(lerp(246, 228, 0.5))

237.0

That's the whole of interpolation. a is where you start, b is where you'd end, and t says how much of the way you go: 0 for none of it, 1 for all of it, 0.5 for half. The name lerp is what programmers call it, short for "linear interpolation", and you'll meet it in other people's code.

Try the ends, to be sure the function does what the sentence says:

print(lerp(246, 228, 0), lerp(246, 228, 1))

246 228

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
Now the Medium. In Plum the weights have numbers: Light is 300, Regular is 400, Bold is 700. Chapter 101 printed them. A Medium is 500 by long custom. So:

print(lerp(246, 228, 500))

-8754

The bottom of the hyphen is nearly nine thousand units below the baseline. Nothing stopped the sum. lerp did what it was told: it went 500 times the distance from Regular to Bold.

The 500 is a place on the weight scale. t is a share of the way from one master to the other. They're different kinds of number, and the function can't tell, since both are numbers.

docs.title: Step 3: From a weight to a share
docs.text:
How much of the way from 400 to 700 is 500? It's 100 along a road of 300. A third.

def share(value, low, high):
    return (value - low) / (high - low)

print(share(500, 400, 700))

0.3333333333333333

share is lerp run backward. lerp takes a share and gives a place. share takes a place and gives the share. Put one inside the other:

t = share(500, 400, 700)
print(lerp(246, 228, t), lerp(294, 312, t))

240.0 300.0

The Medium's hyphen runs from 240 to 300, so it's 60 thick. The Regular's is 48 and the Bold's is 84.

And here's what the arithmetic tells Mira that her eye hadn't. She said "halfway", and 500 is a third of the way. Halfway between 400 and 700 is 550, and its hyphen would be 66 thick. Whether the chapter titles want 60 or 66 is hers to judge. But she now knows that the word and the number meant two different fonts.

docs.title: Step 4: A whole outline
docs.text:
A glyph is a lot of numbers, and each one gets the same sum with the same t. Fly reads a layer's outline as a list of contours, each a list of (x, y, on) tuples, the form chapter 103 used:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.masters.interpolation.model as interpolation
from fly.pens import layer_of

package = scripting.current_package()
glyph = package.findName("hyphen")
regular = interpolation.outline(layer_of(glyph, "Regular"))
bold = interpolation.outline(layer_of(glyph, "Bold"))
print(regular)
print(bold)

[[(56.0, 246.0, True), (292.0, 246.0, True), (292.0, 294.0, True), (56.0, 294.0, True)]]
[[(56.0, 228.0, True), (292.0, 228.0, True), (292.0, 312.0, True), (56.0, 312.0, True)]]

One contour, four nodes, in both. Node 1 of the Regular goes with node 1 of the Bold, node 2 with node 2. That's zip, twice: once to pair the contours, once to pair the nodes inside each pair.

def between(first, second, t):
    result = []
    for one, other in zip(first, second):
        contour = []
        for (x1, y1, on), (x2, y2, also_on) in zip(one, other):
            contour.append((round(lerp(x1, x2, t)), round(lerp(y1, y2, t)), on))
        result.append(contour)
    return result

Now you can see why chapters 102 and 103 mattered. zip pairs by position and asks no questions. If the Bold had five nodes, zip would stop at four and the fifth would vanish. If the Bold's contour started at another corner, each node would travel toward the wrong partner, and the rectangle would fold on its way. The sum is innocent. The pairing is where glyphs go wrong.

So the script asks before it pairs. interpolation.problem(a, b) gives None when two outlines can be paired, and a sentence when they can't.

Handles get the same treatment as nodes. A handle is a pair of numbers, and it moves a third of the way toward its partner like everything else. That's why a curve between two masters stays a curve.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Lerp
# Works out one glyph between two masters, by hand. Changes nothing.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.masters.interpolation.model as interpolation
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


GLYPH = "hyphen"
LOW = "Regular"
HIGH = "Bold"
WEIGHT = 500


def lerp(a, b, t):
    return a + (b - a) * t


def share(value, low, high):
    return (value - low) / (high - low)


def weight_of(package, master):
    axis = package.axes[0]
    return float(package.location(master)[axis.shortName])


def between(first, second, t):
    result = []
    for one, other in zip(first, second):
        contour = []
        for (x1, y1, on), (x2, y2, also_on) in zip(one, other):
            contour.append((round(lerp(x1, x2, t)), round(lerp(y1, y2, t)), on))
        result.append(contour)
    return result


def main():
    if fl.CurrentFont() is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    glyph = package.findName(GLYPH)
    if glyph is None:
        tell(f"There is no glyph named {GLYPH}.")
        return
    low_layer = layer_of(glyph, LOW)
    high_layer = layer_of(glyph, HIGH)
    low = interpolation.outline(low_layer)
    high = interpolation.outline(high_layer)
    reason = interpolation.problem(low, high)
    if reason:
        print(f"{GLYPH}: {LOW} and {HIGH} don't match, {reason}")
        return
    t = share(WEIGHT, weight_of(package, LOW), weight_of(package, HIGH))
    print(f"{GLYPH} at {WEIGHT}: t is {t:.3f}, from {LOW} to {HIGH}")
    for number, contour in enumerate(between(low, high, t), 1):
        for x, y, on in contour:
            kind = "node" if on else "handle"
            print(f"  contour {number}: {x:>5} {y:>5}  {kind}")
    width = round(lerp(low_layer.advanceWidth, high_layer.advanceWidth, t))
    print(f"  width {width}")


main()

Save it as lerp.py and run it:

hyphen at 500: t is 0.333, from Regular to Bold
  contour 1:    56   240  node
  contour 1:   292   240  node
  contour 1:   292   300  node
  contour 1:    56   300  node
  width 348

Notes on the listing.

weight_of asks the font where a master sits on its first axis. Plum has one axis, so the first is the only one. I read this route in Fly's own code, which uses it to put the masters in order. I haven't seen the numbers come back in FontLab 9, and if yours aren't 400 and 700, the first line of output will show it.

The width is one more number, and it gets the same lerp. Kerning does too, and anchors. A master is a long list of numbers, and the font between two masters is the same sum done on every one of them.

between rounds, because a font's coordinates are whole units. The sum itself gives 240.0 here, since a third of 18 is 6. With other numbers it gives a long tail, and what the rounding does to two nodes that should stay level is a thing to look at in a proof.

LOW and HIGH are two masters, and Plum has three. Which two? The pair on either side of the weight you want. 500 lies between 400 and 700, so it's Regular and Bold. A 350 lies between 300 and 400, so it would be Light and Regular. The Light has no say in the Medium at all. A family with three masters is two roads that meet at the Regular, and each weight is on one of them. The script trusts you to pick the right pair, and the Break it section shows what the wrong pair does.

It also explains a thing you may have wondered about in chapter 104. The figures were 490 wide in the Regular and in the Bold, and 456 in the Light. On the road from Regular to Bold a figure's width doesn't move, whatever t is. On the other road it does.

The script changes nothing. It prints what an in-between glyph would be. Drawing it into the font is chapter 110's work.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
The scale has room below the Light. A Thin is 100 by custom. Set LOW = "Light", HIGH = "Regular" and WEIGHT = 100, and run:

hyphen at 100: t is -2.000, from Light to Regular
  contour 1:    56   276  node
  contour 1:   292   276  node
  contour 1:   292   264  node
  contour 1:    56   264  node
  width 348

Read the y values. The first two nodes were the bottom edge and they're at 276. The last two were the top and they're at 264. The bottom is above the top. The hyphen has turned inside out.

t is −2: go twice the distance, the other way. From Regular to Light the bar loses 20 units of thickness, 48 down to 28. Go that far twice more and it loses another 40, which is 12 more than it had.

Nothing raised an error, and the outline still has four nodes in the right order, so chapter 102's check would pass it. Going beyond the masters is called extrapolation, and the sum allows it without complaint. A share between 0 and 1 stays between drawings somebody made. Outside that range you get a guess, and on thin strokes the guess goes wrong fast.

Put the three constants back.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Interpolation is one sum, a + (b - a) * t, done on every coordinate, width and kerning value with the same t. A weight like 500 has to be turned into a share of the way between two masters before it can be used, and "halfway" and "Medium" turned out to be different shares. The sum pairs numbers by position, so it's only as good as the matching skeletons of chapters 102 and 103. A share below 0 or above 1 still gives an answer, and nothing warns you when the answer is a glyph turned inside out.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Fly has its own blend: interpolation.blend(low, high, t). In main, print its result next to yours. It doesn't round. For the hyphen at 500 the two should agree but for the .0. Then try WEIGHT = 475. The sum gives 241.5 and 298.5, and round sends both halves to the even neighbor, 242 and 298. How thick is the bar before the rounding, and after?
  2. Set GLYPH = "period". The dot has curves, so the output has handles. Check one handle with a calculator: read its position in the Regular and in the Bold from two runs with WEIGHT = 400 and WEIGHT = 700, and go a third of the way.
  3. Set LOW = "Light", HIGH = "Bold" and WEIGHT = 400. That asks for a Regular made from the two outer masters. The sum gives a hyphen from 249 to 291, 42 thick. The Regular that was drawn is 48 thick. What does that tell you about why Plum has a third master at all?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Chapter 107 reads what the font itself knows about its weight scale: the axis, where each master sits on it, and the list of weights it has been told to produce.

docs.title: 107. Axes and instances
docs.text:
Tuesday of week twenty-one. The art director liked the idea of a Medium so much that she talked to the publisher, and the publisher talked to somebody else. This morning's email has a list:

Thin, ExtraLight, Light, Regular, Medium, SemiBold, Bold, ExtraBold, Black. Nine weights, please, for the rest of the series.

Mira reads it twice. "We have three."

She has three drawings. How many weights the font can make from them is another question, and the font holds part of the answer. Yesterday you typed 400 and 700 into a script because chapter 101 had printed them. Today you ask the font where its masters sit, what it calls the scale they sit on, and which weights it has already been told to produce. Then you hold the client's list against it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • Yesterday's share, which turned a weight into a part of the way between two masters.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran it against a stand-in built from Plum's source file, and the output below comes from there.

docs.title: Step 1: The axis
docs.text:
A scale that a font's drawings vary along is an axis. Plum has one:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting

package = scripting.current_package()
axis = list(package.axes)[0]
print(axis.name, axis.tag, axis.shortName)
print(axis.minimal, axis.default, axis.maximum)

weight wght wt
300.0 400.0 700.0

A font can have several axes, so package.axes is a collection, and list makes a plain list of it that the whole script can count. Chapter 106 took the first one straight off with package.axes[0], which works as well.

Three names for one thing, and each has its user. weight is for people. wght is the tag that goes into the exported font, four characters like a feature tag, and it's the one a browser or a layout program asks for. wt is FontLab's own short name, the one its Python objects use as a key.

The lowest value is spelled minimal. You'd guess minimum, since its partner is maximum. I did, and the code I checked it against says otherwise.

docs.title: Step 2: Where a master sits
docs.text:
Each master has a location, its place on every axis the font has. With one axis that's one number:

def on_axis(axis, location):
    return float(axis.valueWeight(location, 0.0))

for name in package.masters:
    print(name, on_axis(axis, package.location(name)))

Light 300.0
Regular 400.0
Bold 700.0

valueWeight is an odd name for "the value of this location on this axis". The word weight in it has nothing to do with bold or light. It would be called the same on a width axis. The 0.0 is what to answer if the location says nothing about this axis.

Yesterday's weight_of got the same numbers by indexing the location with the short name. Both routes are in code I trust. I've moved to this one because it reads a location wherever it comes from, and in a minute one will come from somewhere else.

docs.title: Step 3: Small records
docs.text:
A master is now two facts that belong together: a name and a value. You've kept such pairs as tuples. Today there will be three facts for some rows, and row[2] says nothing to a reader. A small dictionary with the same keys in every row says what each thing is:

def by_value(record):
    return record["value"]


def master_records(package, axis):
    records = []
    for name in package.masters:
        value = on_axis(axis, package.location(name))
        records.append({"name": name, "value": value})
    return sorted(records, key=by_value)

Chapter 104 kept a dictionary of dictionaries, a table you look things up in. This is the other common shape, a list of dictionaries: rows you walk through in order. Programmers call such a row a record.

The list is sorted by value, with a key function as in chapter 36. Chapter 101 said why: package.masters comes in the order the masters were made, and nothing says that's light to bold.

docs.title: Step 4: Instances
docs.text:
A master is a drawing. An instance is a weight the font is told to produce: a name and a location, and no drawing of its own. FontLab makes its outlines by yesterday's sum when you export. An instance can sit on a master, and then there's nothing to work out.

def instance_records(package, axis):
    records = []
    for instance in package.instances:
        value = on_axis(axis, instance.location)
        records.append({"name": instance.name, "value": value,
                        "export": instance.exportable})
    return sorted(records, key=by_value)

print(instance_records(package, axis))

Here's where I have to be plain about what I don't know. Plum's source file doesn't list instances the way it lists masters. It has a note on the axis that names three places, Light, Regular and Bold, at 300, 400 and 700. Whether FontLab 9 hands those to Python as three instances, or as none, I can't tell from the file. So the script counts what it gets, and both answers are fine:

[]

or three records. What you won't see either way is a Medium. Nobody has asked this font for one before.

docs.title: Step 5: Hold the list against it
docs.text:
The client's nine weights, with the numbers custom gives them:

WANTED = [
    ("Thin", 100),
    ("ExtraLight", 200),
    ("Light", 300),
    ("Regular", 400),
    ("Medium", 500),
    ("SemiBold", 600),
    ("Bold", 700),
    ("ExtraBold", 800),
    ("Black", 900),
]

For each, find the two masters it lies between and say how far along. zip(masters, masters[1:]) pairs each master with the next one, the trick from chapter 61:

def place(value, masters):
    if value < masters[0]["value"]:
        return f"below {masters[0]['name']}, no drawing to lean on"
    if value > masters[-1]["value"]:
        return f"above {masters[-1]['name']}, no drawing to lean on"
    for low, high in zip(masters, masters[1:]):
        if low["value"] < value < high["value"]:
            t = (value - low["value"]) / (high["value"] - low["value"])
            return f"{low['name']} to {high['name']}, t {t:.3f}"

masters = master_records(package, axis)
for name, value in WANTED:
    print(f"{name:<12}{value:>5}  {place(value, masters)}")

Thin          100  below Light, no drawing to lean on
ExtraLight    200  below Light, no drawing to lean on
Light         300  None
Regular       400  None
Medium        500  Regular to Bold, t 0.333
SemiBold      600  Regular to Bold, t 0.667
Bold          700  None
ExtraBold     800  above Bold, no drawing to lean on
Black         900  above Bold, no drawing to lean on

Three lines say None, and they're the three weights the font is surest of.

low < value < high is true for a value strictly between the two. 400 is not strictly between 300 and 400, nor between 400 and 700. It's on the fence, and the test leaves the fence out on both sides. So the loop ends without a return, the function runs off its end, and a function that does that hands back None, as chapter 16 found.

You could change one < to <=. Then 400 would be "Light to Regular, t 1.000", which is true and unhelpful. The better answer is to say what it is, first. These lines go at the top of place, before the others:

def place(value, masters):
    for master in masters:
        if master["value"] == value:
            return f"is the {master['name']} master"

When a function sorts things into cases, write down what happens at the borders before you write the middle. The middle is rarely where it goes wrong.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: List Instances
# Reads the weight axis, the masters on it and the font's instances,
# and says where each wanted weight falls. Changes nothing.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


WANTED = [
    ("Thin", 100),
    ("ExtraLight", 200),
    ("Light", 300),
    ("Regular", 400),
    ("Medium", 500),
    ("SemiBold", 600),
    ("Bold", 700),
    ("ExtraBold", 800),
    ("Black", 900),
]


def by_value(record):
    return record["value"]


def on_axis(axis, location):
    return float(axis.valueWeight(location, 0.0))


def master_records(package, axis):
    records = []
    for name in package.masters:
        value = on_axis(axis, package.location(name))
        records.append({"name": name, "value": value})
    return sorted(records, key=by_value)


def instance_records(package, axis):
    records = []
    for instance in package.instances:
        value = on_axis(axis, instance.location)
        records.append({"name": instance.name, "value": value,
                        "export": instance.exportable})
    return sorted(records, key=by_value)


def place(value, masters):
    for master in masters:
        if master["value"] == value:
            return f"is the {master['name']} master"
    if value < masters[0]["value"]:
        return f"below {masters[0]['name']}, no drawing to lean on"
    if value > masters[-1]["value"]:
        return f"above {masters[-1]['name']}, no drawing to lean on"
    for low, high in zip(masters, masters[1:]):
        if low["value"] < value < high["value"]:
            t = (value - low["value"]) / (high["value"] - low["value"])
            return f"{low['name']} to {high['name']}, t {t:.3f}"


def main():
    if fl.CurrentFont() is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    axes = list(package.axes)
    if not axes:
        print("This font has no axis. It is one drawing.")
        return
    axis = axes[0]
    print(f"Axis {axis.name} ({axis.tag}, short name {axis.shortName}): "
          f"{axis.minimal:g} to {axis.maximum:g}, default {axis.default:g}")
    masters = master_records(package, axis)
    print(f"{len(masters)} masters:")
    for record in masters:
        print(f"  {record['name']:<12}{record['value']:>5g}")
    instances = instance_records(package, axis)
    print(f"{len(instances)} instances:")
    for record in instances:
        mark = "" if record["export"] else "  (not exported)"
        print(f"  {record['name']:<12}{record['value']:>5g}{mark}")
    have = [record["value"] for record in instances]
    print(f"{len(WANTED)} weights wanted:")
    for name, value in WANTED:
        listed = "listed" if value in have else "not listed"
        print(f"  {name:<12}{value:>5}  {listed:<11} {place(value, masters)}")


main()

Save it as list_instances.py and run it:

Axis weight (wght, short name wt): 300 to 700, default 400
3 masters:
  Light         300
  Regular       400
  Bold          700
0 instances:
9 weights wanted:
  Thin          100  not listed  below Light, no drawing to lean on
  ExtraLight    200  not listed  below Light, no drawing to lean on
  Light         300  not listed  is the Light master
  Regular       400  not listed  is the Regular master
  Medium        500  not listed  Regular to Bold, t 0.333
  SemiBold      600  not listed  Regular to Bold, t 0.667
  Bold          700  not listed  is the Bold master
  ExtraBold     800  not listed  above Bold, no drawing to lean on
  Black         900  not listed  above Bold, no drawing to lean on

If your FontLab lists three instances, three lines in the last block say listed.

Notes on the listing.

:g in a format prints a number the short way: 300.0 as 300, and 412.5 as 412.5. The values arrive as floats and none of them needs its .0.

"" if record["export"] else " (not exported)" is the one-line if from chapter 40. An instance can be switched off for export and kept in the list, and the report should say so.

The script looks at the first axis and no further. A font with weight and width would need place to think in two directions at once, and Plum doesn't ask that of us.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Take the sorted out of master_records, so it ends return records. Run it. On Plum you may see no change at all: if package.masters happens to come light to bold, the unsorted list is the sorted one.

Then make it fail on purpose. Put records.reverse() before the return and run again. The first lines are:

  Thin          100  not listed  below Bold, no drawing to lean on
  ExtraLight    200  not listed  below Bold, no drawing to lean on
  Light         300  not listed  is the Light master
  Regular       400  not listed  is the Regular master
  Medium        500  not listed  below Bold, no drawing to lean on

Medium is "below Bold" and has lost its neighbors. place reads masters[0] as the lightest and trusts the list to be in order. It never checks. The sorted in master_records is the only thing that puts the list in order, and it looked like a nicety.

Put the sorted back and take the reverse out.

docs.title: What Mira writes back
docs.text:
The report answers the email better than a yes would.

Five of the nine are safe. Three are drawings, and Medium and SemiBold lie between two drawings, a third and two thirds of the way from Regular to Bold.

Four are outside. Thin and ExtraLight are lighter than anything Mira has drawn, ExtraBold and Black are heavier, and yesterday's hyphen showed what the sum does out there. A Thin at 100 is twice as far below the Light as the Light is below the Regular.

So she writes: five weights now. The other four need a new drawing at each end, a Thin and a Black, and those are weeks of work, not a script.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: An axis has a name for people, a tag for the exported font and a short name for FontLab's objects, and a master's location says where it sits on that axis. An instance is a named place on the axis with no drawing of its own. A list of small dictionaries with the same keys keeps facts that belong together in rows you can sort and walk. A function that sorts values into cases needs its borders decided first, because a value that sits on a border falls through tests written for the middle.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a "share" key to each wanted weight's row: build a list of records from WANTED with name, value and the t from yesterday's share, or None when the weight is a master or outside. Print only the rows where it isn't None.
  2. The client's second thought: "and a Book, a little heavier than Regular". Add ("Book", 450) to WANTED, keep the list in order of weight with sorted and a key function for tuples, and read where it falls. It should say Regular to Bold, t 0.167.
  3. Print axis.designMin and axis.designMax next to minimal and maximum. In Plum I expect the same numbers. A font can show its users one scale and draw on another, and you should know the two exist before you meet a font where they differ.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Five weights are within reach and the font lists none of them, or three. Chapter 108 turns the table of wanted weights into a plan for instances, and looks hard at the last step, the one that writes them into the font.

docs.title: 108. Make the instances
docs.text:
Wednesday of week twenty-one. The client has answered Mira's email. Five weights now, the four outer ones when there are drawings for them, and could the list please be in the font by Friday.

"In the font" means instances. A master is a drawing. An instance is an order: make me a font at this place on the axis, and call it this. Yesterday's report said Plum has none of its own.

Five instances could be typed by hand in two minutes. Oskar's old families had nine weights in four widths, and he typed all thirty-six, twice, because the first time he put the SemiBold of the Condensed at 500. So today the list comes out of a table, and the table is the one you already have.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed, and saved.
  • list_instances.py from chapter 107.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The planning is plain Python and I ran it. What FontLab does with the result I describe from the User Guide, and I say where I'm guessing.

docs.title: Where this chapter stops, and why
docs.text:
I'll say this before the steps, since it shapes them.

FontLab has a call that adds an instance to a font from Python. I found it in the list of everything FontLab offers to scripts. I didn't find one script, in Fly or in any of the tools around it, that uses the call. Nobody I can read has tried it and written down what happened. I don't know whether Edit > Undo takes it back.

A book that told you to run that on a font you care about would be doing you no favor. So the script in this chapter plans, and a person does the last step in Font Info, where FontLab's own buttons do the writing. The call itself is at the end, marked for what it is.

A script that does nine tenths of a job and hands the last tenth to a person, with the text ready to paste, is a respectable script. The typing was where Oskar's mistake happened, and the typing is what you take away.

docs.title: Step 1: A plan is a table with one more column
docs.text:
You have the client's table as WANTED, a list of pairs. A plan says, for each row, what's to be done about it. That's a third value, so each row becomes a record, as yesterday's masters did:

def plan(wanted, low, high, taken):
    rows = []
    for name, value in wanted:
        if value < low or value > high:
            status = "outside the masters"
        elif value in taken:
            status = "already there"
        else:
            status = "new"
        rows.append({"name": name, "value": value, "status": status})
    return rows

low and high are the outermost masters, and taken is a list of the places where the font already has an instance. Three outcomes, tested in an order that matters: a weight outside the masters is refused first, whatever else is true of it.

Try it without FontLab, with numbers you make up:

rows = plan([("Thin", 100), ("Regular", 400), ("Medium", 500)], 300, 700, [400.0])
for row in rows:
    print(row)

{'name': 'Thin', 'value': 100, 'status': 'outside the masters'}
{'name': 'Regular', 'value': 400, 'status': 'already there'}
{'name': 'Medium', 'value': 500, 'status': 'new'}

A function that takes plain lists and numbers can be tested at your desk with no font open. That's worth arranging whenever you can.

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
My first plan didn't take places. It took names:

names = ["Light", "(Regular)", "Bold"]
wanted = [("Light", 300), ("Regular", 400), ("Medium", 500)]
print([name for name, value in wanted if name not in names])

['Regular', 'Medium']

It wants to make a Regular, in a font that has one. The font's list says (Regular), with parentheses, and "Regular" isn't "(Regular)". To Python they're two strings with nothing in common but most of their letters.

The parentheses are FontLab's way of marking a word that's left out when names are joined: the style is "Bold", and "Bold Italic", and the plain one is "Regular" only when there's nothing else to say. Plum's source file writes its middle weight that way.

I could strip the parentheses before comparing. Then the next font would say "Semi Bold" with a space, or "Demi", and I'd be patching names forever. The name is a label for people. What makes an instance the same instance is where it sits. So compare places:

taken = [300.0, 400.0, 700.0]
print([name for name, value in wanted if value not in taken])

['Medium']

The font gives 400.0 and the table says 400, and in finds it all the same, since Python counts a whole number and its float as equal.

docs.title: Step 3: One line for Font Info
docs.text:
FontLab keeps a short list for each axis, which the User Guide calls the axis instances. It lives in Font Info > Axes, in a text field, and it reads like this:

Light=300, (Regular)=400, Bold=700

A name, an equals sign, a place, and commas between. A name with a space goes in double quotes. That's a format a script can write:

DEFAULT_STYLE = "Regular"


def axis_line(rows):
    parts = []
    for row in rows:
        if row["status"] == "outside the masters":
            continue
        name = row["name"]
        if name == DEFAULT_STYLE:
            name = f"({name})"
        if " " in name:
            name = f'"{name}"'
        parts.append(f"{name}={row['value']:g}")
    return ", ".join(parts)

The line holds every weight that's inside the masters, the ones already there too. You'll replace the field's contents, so the old entries have to be in the new text or they're gone.

f'"{name}"' is an f-string in single quotes so that it can hold double ones. You've seen the two kinds of quote take turns since chapter 2.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Make Instances
# Plans the instances the client asked for and writes the plan to a file.
# The font is not changed: you paste one line into Font Info yourself.
from pathlib import Path

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


WANTED = [
    ("Thin", 100),
    ("ExtraLight", 200),
    ("Light", 300),
    ("Regular", 400),
    ("Medium", 500),
    ("SemiBold", 600),
    ("Bold", 700),
    ("ExtraBold", 800),
    ("Black", 900),
]
DEFAULT_STYLE = "Regular"


def on_axis(axis, location):
    return float(axis.valueWeight(location, 0.0))


def plan(wanted, low, high, taken):
    rows = []
    for name, value in wanted:
        if value < low or value > high:
            status = "outside the masters"
        elif value in taken:
            status = "already there"
        else:
            status = "new"
        rows.append({"name": name, "value": value, "status": status})
    return rows


def axis_line(rows):
    parts = []
    for row in rows:
        if row["status"] == "outside the masters":
            continue
        name = row["name"]
        if name == DEFAULT_STYLE:
            name = f"({name})"
        if " " in name:
            name = f'"{name}"'
        parts.append(f"{name}={row['value']:g}")
    return ", ".join(parts)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    axis = list(package.axes)[0]
    spots = [on_axis(axis, package.location(m)) for m in package.masters]
    taken = [on_axis(axis, i.location) for i in package.instances]
    rows = plan(WANTED, min(spots), max(spots), taken)
    for row in rows:
        print(f"{row['name']:<12}{row['value']:>5g}  {row['status']}")
    new = [row for row in rows if row["status"] == "new"]
    line = axis_line(rows)
    print(f"{len(new)} new instances. Axis instances for {axis.name}:")
    print(line)
    path = Path(font.path).parent / "instances-plan.txt"
    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(line + "\n")
    print(f"Saved as {path.name}.")


main()

Save it as make_instances.py and run it:

Thin          100  outside the masters
ExtraLight    200  outside the masters
Light         300  new
Regular       400  new
Medium        500  new
SemiBold      600  new
Bold          700  new
ExtraBold     800  outside the masters
Black         900  outside the masters
5 new instances. Axis instances for weight:
Light=300, (Regular)=400, Medium=500, SemiBold=600, Bold=700
Saved as instances-plan.txt.

If yesterday's report listed three instances in your font, the rows for Light, Regular and Bold say already there and the count is 2. The line is the same either way.

Notes on the listing.

on_axis is yesterday's function, copied. You wrote it in chapter 107; here it is again so this script runs by itself. Two copies of one small function is a fair price for a script you can open, read and run without hunting for anything else.

min(spots) and max(spots) find the outer masters without sorting anything. Yesterday needed the order, to find neighbors. Today only the two ends matter.

The file is written the way chapter 26 wrote one, next to the font. A plan on paper outlives the Output panel, and Mira can attach it to her reply.

docs.title: The last step, by hand
docs.text:
Save the font first. Then:

  1. Open Font Info and go to Axes. Select the weight axis.
  2. Find the field for axis instances. Replace what's in it with the line from instances-plan.txt.
  3. Go to Instances and click From Axes. By the User Guide, that replaces the list of instances with one for each axis instance.
  4. Click OK.

I've read those pages and haven't clicked those buttons in FontLab 9. If a label differs on your screen, trust the screen.

Now run list_instances.py. It should say 5 instances: and name them, and then run make_instances.py once more: five rows of already there, and 0 new instances. The same script is the plan before the work and the check after it.

docs.title: The call I didn't use
docs.text:
For the record, this is what the list of FontLab's calls says would add one instance:

instance = fl.flInstance("Medium", "Medium", fl.flLocation({"wt": 500}))
package.addInstance(instance)

The second "Medium" is the style name. fl.flLocation with a dictionary from the axis's short name to a place is proved: Fly uses it elsewhere. The other two calls are names in a list, and no more than that to me. If you try them, do it on a copy of the font, saved, and expect no Undo. Then run list_instances.py and see what the font says.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Ines calls the 600 weight "Demi", and adds it to the table without looking for a 600 that's already there. Put ("Demi", 600), after the SemiBold row and run:

SemiBold      600  new
Demi          600  new

6 new instances. Axis instances for weight:
Light=300, (Regular)=400, Medium=500, SemiBold=600, Demi=600, Bold=700
