Two names for one place, and the plan passed them both. plan checks each row against the font. It never checks the rows against each other. Paste that line and you'd export two files that hold the same font under different names, and the client would ask which one is real.

Take the row out. Exercise 2 closes the hole.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A plan is the wanted table with a column added that says what to do about each row, and a function that builds it from plain lists can be tested with no font open. Things that have both a name and a place should be matched by the place, since names are spelled for people. A script can stop short of the write, hand a person the text to paste, and then serve as the check that the work was done. When a call exists and nobody has written down what it does, say so and keep it away from the font you care about.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add ("Extra Light", 350) to the table, with the space. Where does it land in the line, and is that where you'd want it? Sort the rows by value inside axis_line, using a key function as chapter 36 did.
  2. Make plan notice two rows with one value. Keep a list of the values seen so far, and give the second row the status same place as an earlier row. axis_line should leave such rows out.
  3. The client's names have no spaces and Ines would like "Semi Bold" on the menu. Write spaced(name) that puts a space before each capital letter but the first, using isupper() on each character. Then axis_line has to quote the result.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: A new weight needs kerning as much as it needs outlines. Chapter 109 looks at the pairs in each master and finds the ones that exist in one master and are missing in the next.

docs.title: 109. Kerning in every master
docs.text:
Thursday of week twenty-one. The Latin dictionary sent a page of test words, and ae turns up after capitals more than anyone expected: Tae, Vae, Kae. Mira kerned T ae and V ae on Tuesday, in the Regular. Ines, checking the bold headwords on Wednesday, kerned K ae, in the Bold.

Neither told the other. So the font now has two pairs that exist in one master, and a third that exists in another, and chapter 80's audit, which was clean in week fifteen, isn't any more.

A pair that's missing in a master isn't an error to FontLab. It's a pair with no kerning. In a font between two masters, it's worse: chapter 106's sum has a number at one end and nothing at the other.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • Chapter 73's way of writing pairs, and chapter 76's sets.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the script on the kerning this book has built up since chapter 69, with Fly's own planning function doing the planning, and the output below comes from there.

docs.title: Step 1: Do what they did
docs.text:
Three pairs, two masters, one order, in chapter 73's form:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.kerning.batch as kerning_batch

package = scripting.current_package()
edits = {
    "Regular": {("T", "ae"): -48, ("V", "ae"): -36},
    "Bold": {("K", "ae"): -20},
}
kerning_batch.write_kerning(package, edits, "Kern ae after capitals")

ae is in no kerning class, so these are plain pairs between two glyphs.

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
Which pairs does the Bold lack? Chapter 76 gave you the tool. A dictionary's keys make a set, and one set minus another is what the first has and the second hasn't:

regular = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, "Regular")
bold = scripting.kerning_pairs(package, "Bold")
print(sorted(set(regular) - set(bold)))

[('T', 'ae'), ('V', 'ae')]

Two pairs. Copy them to the Bold and the job looks finished.

It isn't, and the line can't tell you so. a - b answers one question: what does a have that b lacks? Ines's K ae is in the Bold and not in the Regular. Seen from the Regular it doesn't exist. Subtraction has a direction.

print(sorted(set(bold) - set(regular)))

[('K', 'ae')]

With two masters you could remember to ask both ways. With three you'd ask six times, and with the nine weights the client wants, seventy-two. Ask one question instead: which pairs exist anywhere, and for each, where is it missing?

docs.title: Step 3: Every pair, every master
docs.text:
Chapter 76 built the set of all pairs with |, which joins two sets. Do that, then walk it:

def gaps(tables):
    everywhere = set()
    for master in tables:
        everywhere = everywhere | set(tables[master])
    rows = []
    for pair in sorted(everywhere):
        absent = [master for master in tables if pair not in tables[master]]
        if absent:
            rows.append((pair, absent))
    return rows

tables is a dictionary from master name to that master's pairs, as in chapter 75. Each row is a pair and the list of masters that lack it. A pair that's everywhere gets an empty list and isn't a row.

masters = ["Light", "Regular", "Bold"]
tables = {m: scripting.kerning_pairs(package, m) for m in masters}
for pair, absent in gaps(tables):
    print(pair, absent)

('K', 'ae') ['Light', 'Regular']
('T', 'ae') ['Light', 'Bold']
('V', 'ae') ['Light', 'Bold']

All three, and each says where it's missing. The direction is gone, because no master was the one doing the asking.

docs.title: Step 4: What value goes in?
docs.text:
Finding a gap is counting. Filling it means inventing a number, and that needs more care.

The plain answer: take the Regular's value. But chapter 79 turned every pair in the Bold down to 85 percent, because the Bold's letters sit closer. A new pair copied at full strength would be the one pair in the Bold that missed that decision.

Fly's copying function takes a percentage for that reason. copy_plan works out the edits without making them:

import fly.ap.kerning.edit.model as kerning_edit

plan = kerning_edit.copy_plan(tables["Regular"], tables["Bold"], "missing", 85)
print(plan)

{('T', 'ae'): -41, ('V', 'ae'): -31}

The word "missing" is the mode: add what the target lacks and leave everything else alone. There are two more. "matching" overwrites pairs both masters have and adds none. "replace" makes the target a copy of the source, and that deletes pairs the source doesn't have. Under "replace", Ines's K ae would be gone from the Bold. Today's script never says that word.

85 percent of −48 is −40.8, and the plan says −41. Fly rounds to whole units, as it did in chapter 79.

Now the caution. I checked how well one master predicts another, on the 102 pairs that all three already have. The Light's value is within 5 units of the Regular's for 41 of them, and more than 20 units away for 12. The Bold, against 85 percent of the Regular, does no better: 34 close, 19 far. Kerning doesn't scale the way an anchor's position did in chapter 105. T a is −86 in the Light and −87 in the Bold, with −80 between them.

Why not? An anchor sits on the drawing, so when the drawing stretches, the anchor goes with it. A kerning value answers the white shapes that two letters make together, and those change with weight in their own way. A bolder T has a thicker bar and a thicker stem, and the gap under the bar doesn't shrink by any fixed share. Whoever kerned the three masters looked at each one.

So a copied value is a place to start. It beats a missing pair, since the font between masters now has two ends to work from. Somebody still has to look at "Tae" in the Bold.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Kerning Masters
# Finds kerning pairs that are in some masters and not in others, and
# copies the ones missing from the trusted master. Dry run by default.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.kerning.edit.model as kerning_edit
import fly.ap.masters.inspect.model as masters_model
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


TRUSTED = "Regular"
PERCENT = {"Light": 100, "Bold": 85}
DRY_RUN = True


def gaps(tables):
    everywhere = set()
    for master in tables:
        everywhere = everywhere | set(tables[master])
    rows = []
    for pair in sorted(everywhere):
        absent = [master for master in tables if pair not in tables[master]]
        if absent:
            rows.append((pair, absent))
    return rows


def show(pair, tables):
    cells = []
    for master in tables:
        value = tables[master].get(pair)
        cells.append("-" if value is None else f"{value:g}")
    first, second = pair
    return f"{first:<14}{second:<14}" + "".join([f"{c:>9}" for c in cells])


def main():
    if fl.CurrentFont() is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    masters = masters_model.master_order(package)
    tables = {m: scripting.kerning_pairs(package, m) for m in masters}
    rows = gaps(tables)
    print(f"{'':<28}" + "".join([f"{m:>9}" for m in masters]))
    for pair, absent in rows:
        print(show(pair, tables))
    print(f"Pairs not in every master: {len(rows)}.")
    orphans = [pair for pair, absent in rows if TRUSTED in absent]
    if orphans:
        print(f"Not in {TRUSTED}, and yours to settle: {len(orphans)}.")
    source = tables[TRUSTED]
    for master in masters:
        if master == TRUSTED:
            continue
        percent = PERCENT.get(master, 100)
        edits = kerning_edit.copy_plan(source, tables[master], "missing", percent)
        for pair in sorted(edits):
            print(f"{master}: {pair[0]} {pair[1]} would get {edits[pair]}")
        if DRY_RUN or not edits:
            continue
        counts = kerning_edit.copy_run(
            package, TRUSTED, [master], "missing", percent,
            undo_name=f"Copy missing kerning to {master}")
        print(f"{master}: added {counts[master][0]}.")
    if DRY_RUN:
        print("Dry run. Nothing was changed.")


main()

Save it as kerning_masters.py and run it:

                                Light  Regular     Bold
K             ae                    -        -      -20
T             ae                    -      -48        -
V             ae                    -      -36        -
Pairs not in every master: 3.
Not in Regular, and yours to settle: 1.
Light: T ae would get -48
Light: V ae would get -36
Bold: T ae would get -41
Bold: V ae would get -31
Dry run. Nothing was changed.

Notes on the listing.

show prints a dash where a master has no pair. tables[master].get(pair) gives None for a missing key, and the test is is None, since a pair kerned at 0 would count as false and print as a dash too.

PERCENT records the house's decisions, one per master. PERCENT.get(master, 100) means a master nobody has an opinion about gets the value unchanged. When the Medium becomes a master of its own one day, the script still runs.

copy_run does the work copy_plan described, and gives back a dictionary from master to three counts: added, changed, removed. Under "missing" the last two are always 0, so the script prints the first. The script calls it once for each master because each has its own percentage. That's one Undo step per master, named for it.

The script reads the tables once, at the top, and never again. After a real run, tables is out of date: it still shows the gaps that were filled a moment ago. That's harmless here, since the script ends. It's the reason the check is a second run and not a line at the bottom. A script that reported on its own work from numbers it read beforehand would be telling you what it meant to do.

K ae is counted and left. It isn't in the trusted master, so the script has nothing to copy from, and it won't guess which way the truth runs. Mira might agree with Ines and kern it in the Regular. She might decide the Bold doesn't need it. The line yours to settle puts it in front of her.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Set DRY_RUN = False and run. Two lines join the output:

Light: added 2.
Bold: added 2.

Set it back and run again:

                                Light  Regular     Bold
K             ae                    -        -      -20
Pairs not in every master: 1.
Not in Regular, and yours to settle: 1.
Dry run. Nothing was changed.

Now the breaking. Change "missing" to "replace" in the copy_plan line only, and leave the dry run on. The Scripting panel fills up. Here are the first lines, and one from the middle:

Light: @L_A @R_C would get -13
Light: @L_A @R_O2 would get -24
Light: @L_A @R_U2 would get -20

Bold: K ae would get None

I count 156 lines where a moment ago there were none: 72 in the Light and 84 in the Bold. "replace" makes the target a copy of the source, so every pair whose value differs is rewritten. The Light's @L_A @R_C is −32, a number somebody chose by looking at the Light, and the plan would flatten it to the Regular's −13. Chapter 79's work on the Bold would go the same way, turned to 85 percent of the Regular whatever it was before.

And one line among the 156 says None. That's how the plan says "delete". Ines's pair, the one the script said it would leave for Mira, would be removed by a script whose comment says it copies.

One word did all of that. The dry run is the reason you read about it in a panel and didn't find it in a proof a week later. Put "missing" back and run once more, to see the short output return.

A typing slip in the mode is caught sooner. By Fly's code, "mising" raises ValueError: Unknown copy mode: mising, and nothing is planned at all.

docs.title: Settle the last one
docs.text:
Mira sets KAE in the Bold and looks at it with and without Ines's pair. Ines was right. The arm of the K and the bowl of the a leave a hole, and it's there in the Regular too. So the pair belongs in the trusted master, and this is chapter 73's call once more:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.kerning.batch as kerning_batch

package = scripting.current_package()
edits = {"Regular": {("K", "ae"): -24}}
kerning_batch.write_kerning(package, edits, "Kern K ae")

Now the script has something to copy from. Run it, still as a dry run:

                                Light  Regular     Bold
K             ae                    -      -24      -20
Pairs not in every master: 1.
Light: K ae would get -24
Dry run. Nothing was changed.

The yours to settle line has gone, because the pair is in the Regular now. The Bold isn't mentioned: it has a value, Ines's −20, and "missing" leaves a value alone. Set DRY_RUN = False and run, then set it back and run again:

Light: added 1.

                                Light  Regular     Bold
Pairs not in every master: 0.
Dry run. Nothing was changed.

An empty table under the header is what a finished job looks like here. Each master now holds 105 pairs, the same 105, and later chapters count on that number. If you skip this section, your Light and your Regular hold 104 and chapter 114 will say so.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Set subtraction has a direction, so to compare several masters you build the set of everything and ask of each item where it's missing. Finding a gap is certain and filling it is a guess, which is why the script reports every gap and fills only from the master you named. A copied kerning value should follow the decisions already made for its master, here 85 percent in the Bold, and it still needs an eye. A plan you can print before it runs will show you a wrong mode while it's still harmless.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Undo the last section's three steps with Edit > Undo until K ae is only in the Bold again. Then settle it the other way: take the pair out of the Bold, with None as the value in chapter 73's write_kerning. Run the script and count the pairs. Redo your way back to 105 before you go on.
  2. Add a third column to each gap row: the master with the value of the largest size, the one furthest from 0. max with a key function does it, and chapter 36 has the pattern.
  3. gaps tells you a pair is missing. Write far_apart(tables, limit) for pairs that every master has, where the largest and smallest values differ by more than limit. With a limit of 40, how many of your 105 pairs does it list, and would you call them faults?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The font can say where a Medium sits and has kerning at both ends of the road. Chapter 110 draws one: a new layer made from two masters, glyph by glyph.

docs.title: 110. A new master from two
docs.text:
Friday of week twenty-one. The art director wants to see the chapter numbers in the weight between Regular and Bold before she decides anything. She doesn't want a font. She wants eleven glyphs, the ten figures and the hyphen, drawn the way a Medium would draw them, so that "12" and "3-4" can go on a title page by Monday.

On Monday you did that sum yourself for one rectangle. Today FontLab does it for whole glyphs, curves and all, and puts the result where Mira can see it and change it: in a new layer of each glyph.

One limit before you start. The chapter's title says a master, and what you'll make is smaller. A master belongs to the whole font. I found the calls that add one, and I found nobody who uses them, so I won't hand them to you. What Fly's own tools do, and what this chapter does, is add an in-between layer to the glyphs you name. For eleven glyphs on a title page that's the right size anyway.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, saved, with Fly installed.
  • Chapter 106's sum and chapter 55's rule about borrowed glyphs.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The two calls that make and attach the layer are the ones Fly's Layer Manager uses, and I've followed its order. The output is from a stand-in.

docs.title: Step 1: Ask FontLab for the glyph in between
docs.text:
A glyph can be asked what it would look like at a place on the axis. The place is a location, built from the axis's short name and a number. Chapter 107 printed the short name: wt.

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl

package = scripting.current_package()
glyph = package.findName("hyphen")
layer = glyph.interpolateInstance(fl.flLocation({"wt": 500}), False)
print(layer.advanceWidth)

348.0

The False says "don't round the coordinates". The layer that comes back has an outline and a width, like any other.

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
So the hyphen has a Medium now. Count its layers:

print([layer.name for layer in glyph.layers])

['Bold', 'Regular', 'Light']

Three, as before. Run the two lines ten times and there are still three.

interpolateInstance makes a layer and gives it to you. It doesn't put it in the glyph. The layer is loose: your variable holds it, and nothing else in FontLab knows it exists. When the script ends, the variable goes and the layer goes with it.

You've met something like it in chapter 46. The RecordingPen there took every order and changed nothing in FontLab, because nothing connected it to a glyph. Making a thing and attaching it are two steps, and the second is the one that changes the font.

docs.title: Step 3: Give it a name FontLab can read
docs.text:
Before the layer is attached it needs a name, and the name matters more than usual.

Call it Medium and FontLab has a fourth layer that it treats as a loose sketch. Nothing says where on the axis it belongs. Call it :wt=500 and FontLab reads the name as a place: this layer is the glyph at weight 500. That's an intermediate layer. When FontLab makes a weight between 400 and 700 it will pass through this drawing on the way, so if Mira thickens the hyphen here, every weight near 500 follows.

You could type the name yourself. Fly builds it, and checks the number while it does:

import fly.ap.studios.layer_manager.intermediate as intermediate

values, name = intermediate.location_values(package, {"wt": 500})
print(values, name)

{'wt': 500.0} :wt=500

Two answers come back, and you unpack them as in chapter 76. values is the location, cleaned up. name is the layer name that says the same thing.

docs.title: Step 4: Which glyphs can take one?
docs.text:
Not every glyph can. Fly's tool asks each glyph a list of questions before it writes, and gives the first reason that stops it, or an empty string:

import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history

facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
for glyph_name in ["hyphen", "e", "eacute"]:
    glyph = package.findName(glyph_name)
    print(glyph_name, repr(intermediate.keep_reason(package, glyph, name, values, facts)))

hyphen ''
e 'base of auto eacute, ecircumflex…'
eacute 'has auto layers'

The second and third lines are chapter 55's rule again. e is borrowed by glyphs that FontLab builds, and eacute is one of those glyphs. Chapter 55 said the book would pass allow_bases=True for a borrowed glyph. Not today. Fly's own tool doesn't offer that choice for new layers, and I won't go where it didn't. So the letters most words need can't be done by this script, which is one more reason the art director is getting figures.

The other reasons you may meet: layer already exists, master outlines are incompatible (chapter 102's subject), and location already exists on followed by a layer's name.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Blend Master
# Adds an in-between layer to a list of glyphs, at one place on the
# weight axis. FontLab does the sum. Dry run by default.
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.studios.layer_manager.intermediate as intermediate
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


GLYPHS = ["zero", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven",
          "eight", "nine", "hyphen"]
WEIGHT = 500
DRY_RUN = True


def has_layer(glyph, name):
    layer = glyph.findLayer(name)
    return layer is not None and not layer.isNull


def interpolated(glyph, values, name):
    layer = glyph.interpolateInstance(fl.flLocation(values), False)
    if layer is None or layer.isNull or layer.autoLayer:
        return None
    layer.name = name
    return layer


def main():
    if fl.CurrentFont() is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    axis = package.axes[0]
    values, name = intermediate.location_values(package, {axis.shortName: WEIGHT})
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    ready = []
    for glyph_name in GLYPHS:
        glyph = package.findName(glyph_name)
        if glyph is None:
            print(f"{glyph_name}: no such glyph")
            continue
        why = intermediate.keep_reason(package, glyph, name, values, facts)
        if why:
            print(f"{glyph_name}: left alone, {why}")
            continue
        ready.append(glyph)
    print(f"Ready for a layer named {name}: {len(ready)} of {len(GLYPHS)}.")
    if DRY_RUN:
        print("Dry run. Nothing was changed.")
        return
    prepared = []
    for glyph in ready:
        layer = interpolated(glyph, values, name)
        if layer is None:
            print(f"{glyph.name}: FontLab could not interpolate it")
            continue
        prepared.append((glyph, layer))
    if not prepared:
        return

    def change():
        for glyph, layer in prepared:
            glyph.addLayer(layer)

    glyphs = [glyph for glyph, layer in prepared]
    history.commit(f"Add {name} layers", [], glyphs, change,
                   operation="geometry", facts=facts)
    added = [glyph for glyph in glyphs if has_layer(glyph, name)]
    print(f"Layers added: {len(added)}.")


main()

Save it as blend_master.py and run it:

Ready for a layer named :wt=500: 11 of 11.
Dry run. Nothing was changed.

Save the font, set DRY_RUN = False and run again:

Ready for a layer named :wt=500: 11 of 11.
Layers added: 11.

Edit > Undo should offer Add :wt=500 layers, one step for all eleven.

Notes on the listing.

The script works in two passes. The first makes all the loose layers and attaches nothing. The second, inside change, attaches them. If FontLab can't interpolate the seventh glyph, you learn it before the font has been touched, and the other ten still go in as one step.

interpolated returns None in three cases: FontLab gave nothing, gave an empty layer, or gave an automatic one. A function that returns either a thing or None is the pattern of chapter 16, and the caller tests for it.

The commit's second slot, the list of layers, is empty. That slot is for layers that already exist and are about to change, and here none of them does. The new ones are named by the glyphs that receive them.

has_layer is chapter 101's function, with the layer's name in place of a master's. The last line counts what's in the font after the write. It doesn't count what the script meant to add.

docs.title: After the run: did FontLab do Monday's sum?
docs.text:
Chapter 106 said the hyphen at 500 runs from 240 to 300. Ask the new layer:

import fly.ap.masters.interpolation.model as interpolation

glyph = package.findName("hyphen")
print(interpolation.outline(glyph.findLayer(":wt=500")))

If FontLab's sum is the one you did by hand, you'll see this:

[[(56.0, 240.0, True), (292.0, 240.0, True), (292.0, 300.0, True), (56.0, 300.0, True)]]

That's a prediction. I haven't seen the line, and if yours differs I'd like to know by how much. A difference of a fraction would be the rounding you switched off. A difference of whole units would mean FontLab's road from Regular to Bold isn't the straight one of chapter 106, and that would be worth a letter to the people who make it.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Leave DRY_RUN = False and run the script a second time:

zero: left alone, layer already exists
one: left alone, layer already exists
two: left alone, layer already exists

and so on down to the hyphen, ending with

Ready for a layer named :wt=500: 0 of 11.

Nothing was added twice, because the question was asked again and the font's answer had changed.

Now ask for a weight nobody drew toward. Set WEIGHT = 800:

ValueError: weight: choose a finite coordinate inside the design range.

The script stops at location_values, before any glyph is looked at. The design range is the axis's own, 300 to 700 in Plum. Chapter 106 turned a hyphen inside out by going outside it, and Fly won't build a layer there.

Set WEIGHT back to 500 and DRY_RUN back to True.

docs.title: What Mira does with it
docs.text:
She opens two in the Glyph window, picks the layer :wt=500 in the Layers & Masters panel, and looks. The interpolation is a fair first drawing. The place where the curve of the 2 meets its foot is heavier than she'd like, and she pulls two nodes. That's the use of an in-between layer: the arithmetic does most of it, and a person corrects where the arithmetic is dull.

She should keep one thing in mind, and so should you. The eleven glyphs now have a say at 500 that the font's other glyphs don't. A whole font exported at Medium would mix corrected figures with letters that are pure arithmetic. For a title page that's fine. For a released Medium, it's the start of a job that somebody has to finish or undo.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: interpolateInstance makes a loose layer at a location, and addLayer inside a commit is what puts it in the glyph. A layer named in the form :wt=500 is an intermediate layer, a drawing FontLab passes through between masters, while any other name is a sketch. Fly's keep_reason gives the first reason a glyph can't take such a layer, and borrowed and automatic glyphs are among those it keeps. Asking the questions again on every run is what makes a second run harmless.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add "e", "eacute" and "Zero" to GLYPHS and do a dry run. You should get three lines of explanation and 11 of 14. Which of the three is a typing mistake, and how does the script tell it from the other two?
  2. Make the script count the reasons. Collect each why in a dictionary from reason to number, as in chapter 22, and print it at the end.
  3. Print, for each ready glyph, the width FontLab's loose layer has and the width chapter 106's lerp gives from the Regular and Bold widths. For the figures both should be 490. Try WEIGHT = 350 and see whether they still agree.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The figures can go on the title page once there's a font file to set them with. Chapter 111 is about getting one font out of FontLab and into a folder, and about how much of that a script can do.

docs.title: 111. Export one font
docs.text:
Monday of week twenty-two, ten past two. The typesetter writes: "Send me an OTF of the Regular by five. I want to try the new fractions in the index."

Everything this book has done so far stayed inside FontLab. The file on Mira's disk is a source: it holds three masters, layers nobody will ship, notes, and an Undo history. The typesetter can't install that. She needs a font file, and making one from the source is called exporting.

This chapter exports one font. It's also the chapter where I have to tell you the most plainly what a script can't yet do for you.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9 and saved, with Fly installed.
  • Chapter 26's Path, and chapter 97's version number.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The script's file handling is plain Python, and I ran it on a folder of stand-in files. The steps in FontLab's export window come from the FontLab User Guide, and I haven't clicked them in version 9.

docs.title: Where this chapter stops, and why
docs.text:
FontLab has a Python call for exporting. Its documentation says so, and the call is in the list of names FontLab offers. But I've read every script in the collections this book draws on, and none of them uses it. I can't tell you the names of its settings with confidence, or whether it waits until the file is written, or what it does when a file is already there.

I'm not going to print a call I can't vouch for in the one chapter where a wrong file goes to a client. So the export is done by hand, in File > Export Font As, and it takes six clicks. The script does the two jobs around it: beforehand it decides where the file goes, and afterward it checks that a real file arrived. People skip both of those when they're in a hurry, and five o'clock is a deadline.

docs.title: Step 1: What you can export
docs.text:
The export window offers profiles, and a profile is a named set of settings for one format. Four matter to this part of the book:

  • OpenType PS (.otf): one style in one file, with the outlines kept as the curves you drew. It's what the typesetter asked for.
  • OpenType TT (.ttf): one style in one file, with the curves converted to the kind that screens prefer.
  • OpenType Variations (.ttf): every master and the weight axis in a single file. The program that uses the font does chapter 106's sum itself.
  • DesignSpace + UFO: the source, in an open format that other font tools read. It isn't installable.

The first two are single-style formats, so FontLab asks which content you mean: the current layer, the instances, or the masters. For one Regular, it's the current layer, and the current layer had better be the Regular.

docs.title: Step 2: Where it goes
docs.text:
A font file sent to a client should be findable in six months. Give every export its own folder, named for the day and the version:

from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
package = scripting.current_package()
info = package.info
version = f"{info.versionMajor}.{info.versionMinor:03d}"
folder = Path(font.path).parent / "exports" / f"{date.today()}-v{version}"
print(folder)

/Users/mira/Halfmoon/exports/2026-12-07-v1.001

Your path and date will differ. The version is chapter 97's, with its :03d. date.today() prints with the year first, so a folder list sorted by name is also sorted by time.

The folder doesn't exist yet. Chapter 26 made one with mkdir(exist_ok=True). Here two are missing, exports and the dated one inside it, and mkdir refuses to make a folder whose parent isn't there. parents=True tells it to make whatever is missing on the way:

folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Now the check. After the export, is the font there?

if folder.exists():
    print("Exported.")

Exported.

Run that before you've exported anything. It says Exported.

The folder exists because the line above it made the folder. The test asked about the folder and the message spoke about the font. A script that reports success by looking at its own preparations will always report success.

Ask about the thing itself. What files are in the folder?

for path in sorted(folder.iterdir()):
    print(path.name, path.suffix, path.stat().st_size)

Before the export that loop prints nothing, which is the truth. iterdir() gives each item in a folder as a Path. path.suffix is the end of the name from the last dot, such as .otf. path.stat().st_size is the file's size in bytes: stat asks the disk for the facts it keeps about a file, and the size is one of them.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Export Current
# Makes a dated folder for an export, says what to choose in FontLab,
# and on the next run reports what arrived. Exports nothing itself.
from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


WANTED = [".otf"]


def export_folder(font, package):
    info = package.info
    version = f"{info.versionMajor}.{info.versionMinor:03d}"
    return Path(font.path).parent / "exports" / f"{date.today()}-v{version}"


def arrived(folder):
    rows = []
    for path in sorted(folder.iterdir()):
        if path.is_file() and not path.name.startswith("."):
            rows.append((path.name, path.suffix.lower(), path.stat().st_size))
    return rows


def instructions(folder, package):
    print("Nothing there yet. In FontLab:")
    print(f"  1. Pick the master to send. Now: {package.master}.")
    print("  2. File > Export Font As.")
    print("  3. Profile: OpenType PS (.otf). Content: Current layer.")
    print(f"  4. Destination: Folder, {folder}")
    print("  5. Family and Profile subfolders off. Existing files: Skip.")
    print("Then run this script again.")


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    if not font.path:
        tell("Save the font first, so the export has a home.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    folder = export_folder(font, package)
    folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    print(f"Export folder: {folder.parent.name}/{folder.name}")
    rows = arrived(folder)
    if not rows:
        instructions(folder, package)
        return
    for name, suffix, size in rows:
        note = "  EMPTY" if size == 0 else ""
        print(f"  {name:<28}{size / 1024:>8.1f} KB{note}")
    for suffix in WANTED:
        good = [row for row in rows if row[1] == suffix and row[2] > 0]
        print(f"{suffix}: {len(good)} good.")


main()

Save it as export_current.py. Save the font too, with File > Save, since an export is made from what FontLab holds and you want the source on disk to match it. Then run the script:

Export folder: exports/2026-12-07-v1.001
Nothing there yet. In FontLab:
  1. Pick the master to send. Now: Regular.
  2. File > Export Font As.
  3. Profile: OpenType PS (.otf). Content: Current layer.
  4. Destination: Folder, /Users/mira/Halfmoon/exports/2026-12-07-v1.001
  5. Family and Profile subfolders off. Existing files: Skip.
Then run this script again.

Do what it says. Then run it again:

Export folder: exports/2026-12-07-v1.001
  GGPlum-Regular.otf              60.0 KB
.otf: 1 good.

I made up that file name and that size. FontLab names the file from the font's names, and I haven't seen what it calls this one. The script doesn't care: it reports whatever is there.

Notes on the listing.

The script is run twice, and the folder tells it which run this is. Empty means "tell me what to do", and anything else means "tell me what I've got". Nothing has to be remembered between the runs, so nothing can be remembered wrong.

package.master is the name of the master FontLab is showing. Line 1 of the instructions prints it because "Current layer" exports the layer you're looking at, and if Mira was last working on the Bold, the typesetter gets a Bold in a file she'll take for the Regular.

arrived leaves out names that begin with a dot. Your computer keeps small files of its own in folders, and they aren't fonts. It lowers the suffix, because .OTF and .otf are the same format to everyone but Python.

size / 1024 turns bytes into kilobytes. A kilobyte here is 1,024 bytes, and :>8.1f is chapter 12's right-hand column with one decimal.

The fifth instruction says Skip for existing files. FontLab offers four choices there, and the User Guide lists them: Rename, Overwrite, Move to Trash, Skip. A dated folder that already holds a file has been sent to somebody. With Skip, a second export on the same day does nothing to it, and you find out because the file's size doesn't change. If the font changed, chapter 97's script gives it a new version, and the new version gets a new folder.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
The check counts a file as good when its size is above 0. See why that's there. In Finder or Explorer, make an empty text file in the export folder and name it Test.otf. Run the script:

Export folder: exports/2026-12-07-v1.001
  GGPlum-Regular.otf              60.0 KB
  Test.otf                         0.0 KB  EMPTY
.otf: 1 good.

Two files end in .otf and one is good. A suffix is a claim a file makes about itself, and anything can make it. An export that was interrupted, or a disk that filled up, can leave a name with nothing behind it. The typesetter's computer would refuse it at one minute to five.

A size above 0 is a low bar too. It proves there are bytes, and it doesn't prove they're a font. Chapter 118 opens the file and reads what's inside. Delete Test.otf.

docs.title: The call I didn't use
docs.text:
For the record, here are the names. FontLab's list of Python names has an ExportControl with settings called profileName, destinationFolder, conflictMode and contentMode, and the workspace has exportFont(package, control). The User Guide says that's the scripted route.

What those settings accept, I don't know. conflictMode and contentMode take numbers, and no list says which number means Skip or Current layer. If you try the call, try it on a copy of the font and into an empty folder, and write down what each number did. Then chapters 112 and 119 can use it, and you'll know something I don't.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Exporting makes a font file from the source, through a profile that fixes the format, and for single-style formats you also say which master or instance you mean. mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) makes a folder and any missing folders above it, and a folder named by date and version keeps each export apart. A check has to look at the result and not at the preparations: iterdir, suffix and stat().st_size say what files exist, what they claim to be and whether anything is in them. The export itself is done by hand in this book, because the scripted call exists and nobody I could read has shown how it behaves.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. The typesetter also wants a TTF. Set WANTED = [".otf", ".ttf"], run the script, and read the last two lines. Then export with OpenType TT (.ttf) into the same folder and run it again.
  2. Add a line after the good count that prints MISSING in capitals when the count is 0, so that a missing format can't be read past.
  3. Write newest(exports), which takes the exports folder and returns the dated folder that sorts last. Why does sorting by name work here, and what name would break it?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: One font went out. The client's list has five weights that Plum can make and two formats for each. Chapter 112 works out all ten file names before any of them exists.

docs.title: 112. Export them all
docs.text:
Tuesday of week twenty-two. The typesetter liked the fractions. Now the publisher wants the family: five weights, each as OTF for the printer and TTF for the office. That's ten files.

Mira exports them before lunch and sends a folder. At four the publisher's production desk writes back: "Where's the SemiBold for Word?"

Nine files had arrived, and nobody had counted them, because nine files in a folder look like a lot of files.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • Chapter 111's dated folder, and chapter 108's five instances if you want to do the export for real.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. The script reads a folder and never asks FontLab to export, so I ran it in plain Python on stand-in files with names I made up. What FontLab calls its exported files, I haven't seen.

docs.title: Step 1: Say what should be there
docs.text:
Chapter 111 looked at a folder and reported what it found. That works for one file. For ten it's the wrong way round, since a list of what's there can't show you what isn't. You have to say first what you expect.

Five styles and two formats. A loop inside a loop visits every combination:

STYLES = ["Light", "Regular", "Medium", "SemiBold", "Bold"]
FORMATS = [".otf", ".ttf"]

for suffix in FORMATS:
    for style in STYLES:
        print(f"GG Plum {style} {suffix}")

GG Plum Light .otf
GG Plum Regular .otf
GG Plum Medium .otf
GG Plum SemiBold .otf
GG Plum Bold .otf
GG Plum Light .ttf
GG Plum Regular .ttf
GG Plum Medium .ttf
GG Plum SemiBold .ttf
GG Plum Bold .ttf

You've put a loop inside a loop before: in chapter 71, to walk every glyph of every kerning class, and in chapter 101, to look for every master in every glyph. There the inner list changed with each class. Here both lists stay as they are, and the inner loop runs through all its items for each single item of the outer one, so the count is one length times the other: 2 times 5. When the client adds WOFF2 next month, you add one string to FORMATS and the list grows to 15 by itself.

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
Now match the list against the folder. The quick way is to ask whether the style's name is in the file's name:

from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("/Users/mira/Halfmoon/exports/2026-12-08-v1.001")
names = [path.name for path in folder.rglob("*.otf")]
print(sorted([name for name in names if "Bold" in name]))

['GGPlum-Bold.otf', 'GGPlum-SemiBold.otf']

Two files answer to "Bold". in asks whether one string appears anywhere inside another, and Bold appears inside SemiBold. A check built on that line would see the SemiBold's file, tick the box for the Bold, and stay quiet if the real Bold were missing. Font style names nest like this all the time: Light sits in ExtraLight, and Italic in every italic.

The cure is to compare whole names and not parts. That has its own snag, because I can't tell you how FontLab spells the file. It might be GGPlum-SemiBold.otf, or GG Plum SemiBold.otf, or something with an underscore.

So compare what all those spellings share. Take the letters and digits, lower them, and drop everything else:

def key(text):
    return "".join([c for c in text.lower() if c.isalnum()])

print(key("GGPlum-SemiBold"))
print(key("GG Plum SemiBold"))
print(key("GG Plum" + "Bold"))

ggplumsemibold
ggplumsemibold
ggplumbold

isalnum() is chapter 81's question, asked of one character at a time. "".join glues the survivors back together with nothing between them. Two spellings of the same file give the same key, and the Bold's key isn't the SemiBold's, because the comparison is now == on the whole thing.

Why not compare the file names as they are, with ==? Because then the script would hold my guess about FontLab's spelling, and the first time the guess was wrong, all ten files would be MISSING while sitting in the folder. A check that cries wolf gets ignored within a week. The squeezed key asks less: the family, then the style, in that order, with whatever punctuation the exporter likes.

It can still be fooled. If two families were named GG Plum and GGP Lum, their keys would be the same. No font office names its families that way, and you now know where the weak spot is, which is more than the in test offered.

docs.title: Step 3: Look in every folder
docs.text:
rglob appeared in that snippet without a word. folder.iterdir() lists what's directly in a folder. folder.rglob("*") lists everything in it and in every folder below, however deep. The * means "any name".

That matters because the export window can sort its output into subfolders by family or by profile, and I don't know which switches you left on. With rglob, the script finds the files either way. path.relative_to(folder) then prints the path from the export folder down, such as otf/GGPlum-Bold.otf, so you see where each one landed.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Export Family
# Lists every font file a full export should leave in today's folder,
# then says which are there, which are missing and which are strangers.
from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


STYLES = ["Light", "Regular", "Medium", "SemiBold", "Bold"]
FORMATS = [".otf", ".ttf"]


def export_folder(font, package):
    info = package.info
    version = f"{info.versionMajor}.{info.versionMinor:03d}"
    return Path(font.path).parent / "exports" / f"{date.today()}-v{version}"


def key(text):
    return "".join([c for c in text.lower() if c.isalnum()])


def expected(family):
    table = {}
    for suffix in FORMATS:
        for style in STYLES:
            table[(key(family + style), suffix)] = f"{family} {style} {suffix}"
    return table


def found(folder):
    table = {}
    for path in sorted(folder.rglob("*")):
        if path.is_file() and not path.name.startswith("."):
            table[(key(path.stem), path.suffix.lower())] = path
    return table


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    folder = export_folder(font, package)
    if not folder.exists():
        tell(f"No folder {folder.name} yet. Run export_current.py.")
        return
    want = expected(package.info.familyName)
    have = found(folder)
    missing = 0
    for item in want:
        if item in have and have[item].stat().st_size > 0:
            print(f"  ok       {have[item].relative_to(folder)}")
        else:
            print(f"  MISSING  {want[item]}")
            missing += 1
    for item in have:
        if item not in want:
            print(f"  extra    {have[item].relative_to(folder)}")
    print(f"{len(want)} wanted, {len(want) - missing} there, {missing} missing.")


main()

Save it as export_family.py. Before it can find anything, do the export. Run export_current.py for today's folder and its path. Then, in File > Export Font As, choose OpenType PS (.otf), set the content to Instances, set the destination to that folder, and export. Do the same with OpenType TT (.ttf). Those are the User Guide's words for the steps, and chapter 111 said how far I trust them.

On the afternoon in the story, the script would have said this:

  ok       otf/GGPlum-Light.otf
  ok       otf/GGPlum-Regular.otf
  ok       otf/GGPlum-Medium.otf
  ok       otf/GGPlum-SemiBold.otf
  ok       otf/GGPlum-Bold.otf
  ok       ttf/GGPlum-Light.ttf
  ok       ttf/GGPlum-Regular.ttf
  ok       ttf/GGPlum-Medium.ttf
  MISSING  GG Plum SemiBold .ttf
  ok       ttf/GGPlum-Bold.ttf
  extra    otf/GGPlum-Regular.fea
10 wanted, 9 there, 1 missing.

The file names are my stand-ins. Yours come from FontLab.

Mira exports the SemiBold again as TTF, drags the .fea file out of the folder, and runs the script once more. It ends:

10 wanted, 10 there, 0 missing.

Then she sends the folder, with that line pasted into the message. The production desk can count to ten as well as she can, and now they don't have to. If a file goes astray on their side, the line says what left Halfmoon's building.

Notes on the listing.

expected and found both return a dictionary with the same kind of key: a tuple of the squeezed name and the suffix, as in chapter 86. That's the design. Two tables with matching keys can be compared by asking item in have, and neither table needs to know how the other spells things. In expected the value is a readable description for the MISSING line. In found it's the real path.

The first loop walks want, so the report comes in the order of your lists and a missing file leaves its line where you'd look for it. The second loop walks have for whatever nobody asked for. The .fea file in my stand-in folder is the kind of thing an export can leave beside a font, and a stranger is worth a line: it may be harmless, or it may be last week's file in this week's folder.

A file of size 0 counts as missing. That's chapter 111's lesson, kept.

missing += 1 counts as it goes, and the last line does one subtraction. Mira reads only that line on most days. If it ends 0 missing., she sends the folder.

The script doesn't create the folder. Chapter 111's script does that, and this one says so if the folder isn't there. One script that makes and one that checks is cleaner than two that both make.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Start from the folder that reports 0 missing. In it, rename one file so that its style is wrong: change GGPlum-Medium.otf to GGPlum-Meduim.otf. Run the script. Two lines change, and the summary with them:

  MISSING  GG Plum Medium .otf

  extra    otf/GGPlum-Meduim.otf
10 wanted, 9 there, 1 missing.

The script can't know those two lines are one mistake. It knows a wanted file is absent and an unwanted one is present, and it puts both in front of you. A check that tried to guess ("perhaps you meant Medium") would sooner or later guess wrong about a file going to a printer. Rename the file back.

Now the other direction. Add "Black" to STYLES and run. Two MISSING lines appear, one for each format, and the last line reads 12 wanted, 10 there, 2 missing. Plum has no Black: chapter 107 showed the axis stops at 700. The script believed the list because the list is all it has. STYLES has to say what the font can make, and exercise 3 takes it from the font so that it can't drift. Take "Black" out.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A loop inside a loop builds every combination of two lists, and its length is the product of theirs. To find what's missing you first write down what's expected, then compare two tables that share a kind of key. in on strings finds a part anywhere, so names that contain other names need a whole comparison, and squeezing both sides to letters and digits makes that comparison survive spaces and hyphens. rglob("*") reads a folder and everything under it, and relative_to shows where each file sits.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. The client adds web fonts. Put ".woff2" in FORMATS and run. How many files are wanted now, and how many lines did you have to change?
  2. Print the missing files again at the very end, after the summary line, so that a long report can't scroll them out of sight. Collect them in a list as you go.
  3. Replace the STYLES constant with the names of the font's own instances. Chapter 107's instance_records reads them. What should the script say when the font has no instances at all?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: One family is checked and sent. On the office server sits Oskar's archive: forty font files from before anybody at Halfmoon wrote a script. Chapter 113 opens each one, asks it a question, and closes it again without saving.

docs.title: 113. Open a folder of fonts
docs.text:
Wednesday of week twenty-two. A reseller wants to know which of Halfmoon's old families exist in more than one weight. Oskar's answer is a folder called archive. "Forty files," he says. "Fifteen years. I don't remember what's in half of them."

Every script so far worked on the font you had open. Today's script opens fonts itself, one after another, asks each a question, and closes it. Opening is the simple half. The closing needs care, because a script that closes fonts can close the wrong one, and it can throw work away without asking.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• FontLab 9 with Fly installed.
  • A folder of FontLab files to try it on. Three copies of Plum-practice under different names will do.
  • Chapter 95's try and finally, and chapter 112's rglob.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the script on a stand-in archive of forty invented files, with stand-ins for the two FontLab calls that open and close. Those two calls are used in the same way by one tested set of example scripts in FontLab's own collections, and that's all I have to go on for them.

docs.title: Step 1: Find the files
docs.text:
Chapter 112 walked a folder and everything below it with rglob("*"). The star stands for any name. Its smaller relation is glob, which looks in the one folder only, and both take a pattern:

from pathlib import Path

ARCHIVE = Path.home() / "Halfmoon" / "archive"
files = sorted(ARCHIVE.glob("*.vfc"))
print(len(files))

31

Path.home() is your own folder on this computer, whatever it's called. "*.vfc" means any name that ends in .vfc, FontLab's usual file type.

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
Thirty-one. Oskar said forty.

He might have miscounted. Before you tell him so, look at what the pattern can't see. It asks for names ending in .vfc in one folder, and that leaves out three kinds of file:

  • five files saved as .vfj, FontLab's other format, the one made of readable text;
  • four drafts in a subfolder called old;
  • and those four are named .VFC in capitals, by some older computer.

The pattern did what it was told. It counted the files that matched, and nothing in a count says what didn't match. Chapter 112 met the same thing from the other side: a test that's too loose finds too much, and one that's too tight finds too little, and neither complains.

So search everything, and decide in Python, where you can lower the case first:

KINDS = [".vfc", ".vfj"]


def font_files(folder):
    return [p for p in sorted(folder.rglob("*")) if p.suffix.lower() in KINDS]


print(len(font_files(ARCHIVE)))

40

Forty. The folder also holds a text file, a PDF and an exported .otf, and none of them is counted, because their suffixes aren't in KINDS.

docs.title: Step 3: Open one, and know which one you opened
docs.text:
Fly's pr is a way of asking FontLab to do things a person would do from the menus. You give it the name of a job and the details:

from fly import fl, pr

reply = pr.call("open_font", path=str(files[0]))
print(reply.get("status"))

ok

reply is a dictionary, and "status" is "ok" when the font opened. That's all it tells you that I can vouch for. It doesn't hand you the font.

So which font is it? You might reach for fl.CurrentFont(), on the guess that a font that opened a moment ago is the current one. Don't. It's a guess about what FontLab does with its windows, and if it's wrong, the "current font" is Plum-practice, with this morning's unsaved work in it.

Ask for the font by the one thing you know for certain about it, the file it came from:

def open_package(path):
    reply = pr.call("open_font", path=str(path))
    if reply.get("status") != "ok":
        return None
    for item in fl.flWorkspace.instance().packages():
        package = fl.flPackage(item)
        if package.path and Path(package.path).resolve() == path.resolve():
            return package
    return None

fl.flWorkspace.instance().packages() is every font FontLab has open, and fl.flPackage(item) turns each into the kind of package you've used since chapter 29. resolve() writes a path out in full, so two spellings of the same place compare as equal. The function returns the package whose file is the file you asked for, or None.

docs.title: Step 4: Close it, whatever happens
docs.text:
Closing is another job for pr:

pr.call("close_font", font_id=package.fgId, save=False)

package.fgId is the number FontLab knows this font by. save=False means close without saving and without asking. Read that again. No dialog appears. Whatever changed in that font since it was opened is gone.

For a font you opened to read, that's what you want. For any other font it's a disaster, which is why the last step mattered: the only package this script ever closes is one that open_package found by its path.

Two more precautions, and then the script.

First, the script never opens Oskar's files. It copies each into a scratch folder and opens the copy. If FontLab should change an old file on opening it, or if something I haven't foreseen goes wrong, the archive is as it was. shutil.copy(path, folder) copies a file into a folder and returns the new path. tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() makes a folder in the place your computer keeps for such things, and in a with block it removes the folder and everything in it when the block ends.

Second, the close goes in a finally. Chapter 95 used finally for work that must happen whether or not the lines above it failed. If reading a font's facts raises an error, the font is still closed.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Folder Report
# Opens a copy of each font file in a folder, notes a few facts,
# and closes the copy without saving. Changes no file in the folder.
import shutil
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from fly import fl, pr, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


ARCHIVE = Path.home() / "Halfmoon" / "archive"
KINDS = [".vfc", ".vfj"]
LIMIT = 3


def font_files(folder):
    return [p for p in sorted(folder.rglob("*")) if p.suffix.lower() in KINDS]


def open_package(path):
    reply = pr.call("open_font", path=str(path))
    if reply.get("status") != "ok":
        return None
    for item in fl.flWorkspace.instance().packages():
        package = fl.flPackage(item)
        if package.path and Path(package.path).resolve() == path.resolve():
            return package
    return None


def facts(package):
    info = package.info
    version = f"{info.versionMajor}.{info.versionMinor:03d}"
    masters = len(package.masters)
    return f"{info.familyName:<16}{version:>6}{masters:>3} masters"


def look_at(path, scratch):
    copy = Path(shutil.copy(path, scratch))
    package = open_package(copy)
    if package is None:
        return "DID NOT OPEN"
    try:
        return facts(package)
    finally:
        pr.call("close_font", font_id=package.fgId, save=False)


def main():
    if not ARCHIVE.exists():
        tell(f"No folder {ARCHIVE}.")
        return
    files = font_files(ARCHIVE)
    print(f"Font files in {ARCHIVE.name}: {len(files)}.")
    failed = 0
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as scratch:
        for path in files[:LIMIT]:
            line = look_at(path, scratch)
            if line == "DID NOT OPEN":
                failed += 1
            print(f"  {str(path.relative_to(ARCHIVE)):<26}{line}")
    looked = len(files[:LIMIT])
    print(f"Looked at {looked} of {len(files)}. Did not open: {failed}.")


main()

Save it as folder_report.py, point ARCHIVE at your folder, and save your own font before you run it. With Oskar's archive:

Font files in archive: 40.
  Bramble-2011-a.vfc        HM Bramble       2.006  2 masters
  Bramble-2013-c.vfc        HM Bramble       2.003  3 masters
  Bramble-2016-b.vfc        HM Bramble       2.005  2 masters
Looked at 3 of 40. Did not open: 0.

The names and numbers are mine, invented for the stand-in. Yours will be whatever your folder holds.

Three files, because LIMIT is 3. files[:LIMIT] is chapter 10's slice. Opening a font takes FontLab a moment, and forty moments is a while to wait for a script you haven't seen work. Watch three fonts open and close. Check in the Window menu that none of them stayed. Then raise LIMIT to 40:

Font files in archive: 40.
  Bramble-2011-a.vfc        HM Bramble       2.006  2 masters
  Bramble-2013-c.vfc        HM Bramble       2.003  3 masters
  Bramble-2016-b.vfc        HM Bramble       2.005  2 masters
  Bramble-2019-a.vfc        HM Bramble       2.000  1 masters
  Damson-2010-b.vfc         DID NOT OPEN
  Damson-2013-a.vfc         HM Damson        1.002  2 masters

and thirty-four more lines, ending:

  old/Sloe-draft-4.VFC      HM Sloe          2.006  3 masters
Looked at 40 of 40. Did not open: 1.

Notes on the listing.

look_at returns from inside the try. The finally still runs. Python works out the value to return, runs the finally, then hands the value back. So the font is closed before main prints its line.

A file that didn't open gets a line that says so, and the loop goes on. One bad file in forty shouldn't cost you the other thirty-nine. The script doesn't say why Damson-2010-b.vfc failed, because I don't know what the reply holds when a font doesn't open. Add print(reply) in open_package if you want to see for yourself. One case the script doesn't tell apart: if FontLab says ok but no open font has the copy's path, the line also reads DID NOT OPEN, and that font stays open. If the Window menu grows while the script runs, that's what happened, and you close those copies by hand without saving.

str(path.relative_to(ARCHIVE)) is chapter 112's relative path, turned into a string so that :<26 can pad it. The drafts show as old/Sloe-draft-4.VFC, folder and all.

"1 masters" is poor English, and exercise 1 mends it.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Prove the finally. In facts, change info.familyName to info.familyNam, set LIMIT back to 3, and run:

Font files in archive: 40.
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
AttributeError: ... has no attribute 'familyNam'

The script stopped at the first font. Now look in the Window menu. The copy of Bramble-2011-a.vfc isn't there. The error went up through look_at, and on its way the finally closed the font. Then it went up through the with, which removed the scratch folder. Both tidied up after a failure neither of them knew about.

Take the try and finally lines away, leave the close as an ordinary last line, and the same slip leaves a stray font open each time you run. That's a nuisance with three and a mess with forty. Put everything back.

docs.title: The line I won't have you run
docs.text:
One variant of this script circulates wherever people share snippets. It opens a file and then closes fl.CurrentFont(). On a good day the current font is the one it opened. On a bad day it's your own, and save=False does what it says. I've described it so that you'll know it when you meet it. This book's rule: a script closes only what it opened itself, found by path, and only copies.

FontLab's packages also have a close method of their own. The notes kept with FontLab's example scripts record that calling it from a script brought up a save dialog and crashed FontLab, so the book doesn't use it.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: glob and rglob find files by pattern, and a pattern that's too tight leaves files out without a word, so count against what a person expects. pr.call("open_font", path=...) opens a font and answers with a status, and you find the font it opened by comparing paths, never by assuming it's the current one. pr.call("close_font", font_id=..., save=False) closes without asking, which is safe only for a copy the script opened itself, and finally makes sure it happens. tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() and shutil.copy give a script a place to work that isn't the user's own files.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Mend "1 masters". Chapter 40's one-line if will do: "master" if masters == 1 else "masters".
  2. Oskar's question was which families have more than one weight. Have look_at return the family name and the master count as a tuple, tally the largest count for each family in a dictionary, and print the families where it's above 1.
  3. Add the year to each line. It's in the file name: path.stem.split("-")[1] for Bramble-2011-a.vfc. Which four files does that give no year for, and what should the script print for them?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The script can now go and look at fonts other than the one in front of you. Chapter 114 turns back to the one that's about to ship, and gathers everything that went wrong in the last release into a list of checks.

docs.title: 114. Check before you ship
docs.text:
Thursday of week twenty-two. Oskar puts a sheet of paper on Mira's desk. It isn't the old sheet of chores. This one is headed "Quince, 2019" and it has four lines:

  • A glyph in the Bold had one node too few. The in-between weights came out as scribble.
  • The seven was narrower than the other figures. Price lists didn't line up.
  • A kerning pair was missing in one master. The gap opened as the weight went up.
  • We sent a corrected font with the old version number. The client kept using the old one.

"Everything on there went out of the door," he says. "Each one cost a week."

You've already written a script for most of those lines. Chapter 100 put five checks of a single font into one list, and Part 6 has taught you what goes wrong between masters. Today the two meet: one script, nine checks, run before every export.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • preflight.py from chapter 100.
  • The exports folder from chapters 111 and 112.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the script in plain Python against a stand-in for the reader's font, with the kerning this book has made and the two export folders from this week.

docs.title: Step 1: Borrow the old checks
docs.text:
Chapter 100's five checks are good and you don't want a second copy of them. A copy is two things to mend when one changes. You've used import since chapter 4 to borrow from Fly. preflight.py is a Python file too, and it has a list named CHECKS.

Python has to be able to find it. Move preflight.py out of the Scripts folder and into the site-packages folder inside your user folder, the one where Fly lives. sys.path lists it. It'll leave FontLab's menu, and that's all right, because today's script does its job and more.

Then, in a new script:

import preflight

print(len(preflight.CHECKS))

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
Run those two lines:

Glyph names   274 looked at   ok
Unicode       235 looked at   ok
Features       35 looked at   ok
Font Info       5 looked at   ok
Metrics         8 looked at   ok
5 checks, 0 problems, 0 did not run.
Version 1.001: ready for the hand tests.
5

You asked for a list and got a whole report, and then the list.

import doesn't fetch names from a file. It runs the file, top to bottom, and keeps whatever names exist at the end. For a file that holds only def lines and constants you'd never see the difference, since running a def makes a function without calling it. But the last line of preflight.py is main(). Running the file runs the report.

Here it's a nuisance. In a script whose last line changes the font, it would be worse: importing the file would change the font.

Chapter 33 showed the cure in a side note and said you could leave it alone for now. Now you need it. Open preflight.py and change the last line from this:

main()

to this:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Python gives every file it runs a name, kept in __name__. A file that was imported gets its own name, "preflight". The file you ran directly gets the name "__main__". So the two lines say: call main if somebody ran this file, and not if somebody borrowed from it.

FontLab remembers a module once it's imported, as chapter 33 found, so the old preflight is still in its memory. For this one run, put chapter 33's reload under the import:

import importlib

import preflight

importlib.reload(preflight)
print(len(preflight.CHECKS))

5

One caution. I'm certain of how __name__ works in Python. I haven't seen what name FontLab gives a script when you run it from the Scripting panel or the menu. If it isn't "__main__", a guarded script run on its own would do nothing at all, silently. That's why today's script, which you run yourself, ends in a plain main(). Guard the files you import from. Leave the ones you run.

docs.title: Step 3: Four checks for the family
docs.text:
Each check keeps chapter 100's shape. It takes the font and the package, changes nothing, and returns a count of what it looked at and a list of sentences.

Oskar's first line is chapter 102. masters_model.check_glyph compares one glyph's contours, anchors and components across the masters:

def check_masters(font, package):
    masters = masters_model.master_order(package)
    looked = 0
    problems = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        fl_glyph = package.findName(glyph.name)
        signatures, ok, found = masters_model.check_glyph(fl_glyph, masters)
        if all([signatures[m] is None for m in signatures]):
            continue
        looked += 1
        if not ok:
            problems.append(f"{glyph.name}: {', '.join(found)} differ between masters")
    return looked, problems

The continue skips the glyphs FontLab builds itself, as chapter 102 did. Chapter 102 also printed where the difference was. A check gives one line a glyph, and compat_check.py is still there when you want the detail.

His second line is chapter 104, cut down to the ten figures. A set holds each width once, so a set with more than one member means the figures disagree:

def check_figures(font, package):
    masters = masters_model.master_order(package)
    problems = []
    for master in masters:
        widths = set()
        for name in TABULAR:
            glyph = package.findName(name)
            widths.add(dict(masters_model.widths(glyph, masters))[master])
        if len(widths) > 1:
            text = " and ".join([f"{w:.0f}" for w in sorted(widths)])
            problems.append(f"{master}: figures are {text} wide")
    return len(TABULAR), problems

His third is chapter 109's gaps, returning sentences. The fourth is new, and it's the one Halfmoon paid most for. Chapter 111 named each export folder with the version at the end. So the disk already knows which versions have gone out:

def check_new_version(font, package):
    info = package.info
    ending = f"-v{info.versionMajor}.{info.versionMinor:03d}"
    exports = Path(font.path).parent / "exports"
    problems = []
    if exports.exists():
        for folder in sorted(exports.iterdir()):
            if folder.name.endswith(ending) and list(folder.rglob("*.*")):
                problems.append(f"{folder.name} already holds files")
    return 1, problems

list(folder.rglob("*.*")) is every file under the folder with a dot in its name. An empty list counts as false, so an empty folder for this version is no problem. A folder with fonts in it is.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Ship Check
# Everything that went wrong last time, as checks: the five from
# preflight.py and four for the family. Read-only. Changes nothing.
from pathlib import Path

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.masters.inspect.model as masters_model
import preflight
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


TABULAR = ["zero", "one", "two", "three", "four",
           "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine"]


def check_masters(font, package):
    masters = masters_model.master_order(package)
    looked = 0
    problems = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        fl_glyph = package.findName(glyph.name)
        signatures, ok, found = masters_model.check_glyph(fl_glyph, masters)
        if all([signatures[m] is None for m in signatures]):
            continue
        looked += 1
        if not ok:
            problems.append(f"{glyph.name}: {', '.join(found)} differ between masters")
    return looked, problems


def check_figures(font, package):
    masters = masters_model.master_order(package)
    problems = []
    for master in masters:
        widths = set()
        for name in TABULAR:
            glyph = package.findName(name)
            widths.add(dict(masters_model.widths(glyph, masters))[master])
        if len(widths) > 1:
            text = " and ".join([f"{w:.0f}" for w in sorted(widths)])
            problems.append(f"{master}: figures are {text} wide")
    return len(TABULAR), problems


def check_kerning(font, package):
    masters = masters_model.master_order(package)
    tables = {m: scripting.kerning_pairs(package, m) for m in masters}
    everywhere = set()
    for master in masters:
        everywhere = everywhere | set(tables[master])
    problems = []
    for first, second in sorted(everywhere):
        absent = [m for m in masters if (first, second) not in tables[m]]
        if absent:
            problems.append(f"{first} {second}: no pair in {', '.join(absent)}")
    return len(everywhere), problems


def check_new_version(font, package):
    info = package.info
    ending = f"-v{info.versionMajor}.{info.versionMinor:03d}"
    exports = Path(font.path).parent / "exports"
    problems = []
    if exports.exists():
        for folder in sorted(exports.iterdir()):
            if folder.name.endswith(ending) and list(folder.rglob("*.*")):
                problems.append(f"{folder.name} already holds files")
    return 1, problems


CHECKS = preflight.CHECKS + [
    ("Masters", check_masters),
    ("Figures", check_figures),
    ("Kerning", check_kerning),
    ("New version", check_new_version),
]


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    total = 0
    broken = 0
    for label, check in CHECKS:
        try:
            looked, problems = check(font, package)
        except Exception as problem:
            broken += 1
            print(f"{label:<13}DID NOT RUN: {type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")
            continue
        total += len(problems)
        verdict = f"{len(problems)} problems" if problems else "ok"
        print(f"{label:<13}{looked:>4} looked at   {verdict}")
        for line in problems:
            print("   ", line)
    print(f"{len(CHECKS)} checks, {total} problems, {broken} did not run.")
    print("Ready to export." if total == 0 and broken == 0 else "Not ready.")


main()

Save it as ship_check.py and run it:

Glyph names   274 looked at   ok
Unicode       235 looked at   ok
Features       35 looked at   ok
Font Info       5 looked at   ok
Metrics         8 looked at   ok
Masters       201 looked at   ok
Figures        10 looked at   ok
Kerning       105 looked at   ok
New version     1 looked at   2 problems
    2026-12-07-v1.001 already holds files
    2026-12-08-v1.001 already holds files
9 checks, 2 problems, 0 did not run.
Not ready.

Your counts depend on what you kept from each chapter's exercises, and your folder names carry your own dates.

Eight checks pass, and the ninth has caught Halfmoon about to repeat the fourth line of Oskar's sheet. Version 1.001 went to the typesetter on Monday and to the publisher on Tuesday. Since then the font has been open on Mira's desk every day. She doesn't think she changed anything in it, and she can't show that she didn't. Anything exported today as 1.001 could be a different font under the same number, and nobody would know.

The mending is chapter 97's. Run bump_version.py for real, then run the check again:

New version     1 looked at   ok
9 checks, 0 problems, 0 did not run.
Ready to export.

Notes on the listing.

preflight.CHECKS + [...] joins two lists into a new one. The five old checks come first, so the report reads from the single font outward to the family. preflight.CHECKS itself isn't changed.

main is chapter 100's loop, almost word for word, and that's the reward for giving every check one shape. The loop doesn't know there are nine, or which file each came from.

The "looked at" column matters as much as the verdict. Masters says 201, which is the 274 glyphs less the 73 that FontLab builds itself. Had it said 0, the ok beside it would mean nothing, because a check that examined nothing can't find a problem. Read the count before you believe the word. If a number drops sharply between one Thursday and the next, something upstream of the check has changed, and that's worth five minutes even when every line says ok.

The last check knows less than it seems to. It reads one folder, exports, beside the font file. A font that somebody exported to the desktop and sent by email left no folder there, and the check will pass. It proves that this version number hasn't been used in the place where Halfmoon keeps its exports. That's a narrower claim than "nobody has this version", and it holds only as long as everyone exports through chapter 111's script.

No check here repairs anything. A check that mends things as it goes is a script you can't run on a whim. This one changes nothing, so the answer to "should I run it?" is always yes.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
A check that has only ever said ok hasn't been tested. Give each new one a fault to find, on a saved font.

Open the Bold e, delete one node on a straight stretch, and in the Bold's kerning delete the pair T ae. Then set the Bold seven to a width of 480. Run:

Masters       201 looked at   1 problems
    e: contours differ between masters
Figures        10 looked at   1 problems
    Bold: figures are 480 and 490 wide
Kerning       105 looked at   1 problems
    T ae: no pair in Bold
New version     1 looked at   ok
9 checks, 3 problems, 0 did not run.
Not ready.

Three faults in, three sentences out, and each says where to look. Those are the first three lines of the Quince sheet, caught on a Thursday afternoon and not by a client. Close the font without saving and open it again.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: import runs the whole file, so a file you borrow from must not do its work at the top level, and if __name__ == "__main__": keeps a file's last line for the times it's run directly. Lists join with +, so one script can take another's list of checks and add its own. A check for a mistake that already happened once is the cheapest check to justify, and the names of last week's export folders are a record a script can read.
