Checks that change nothing can be run at any moment, and each one should be seen to fail before you trust it to pass.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add the four signs from chapter 104 to a second list and check that they match the figures' width in each master.
  2. Write check_instances, using chapter 107's instance_records: a problem for every instance whose weight lies outside the masters.
  3. Oskar adds a fifth line to the sheet: "The Light had no copyright line." Which existing check already covers it, and how would you prove that without reading the code?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The font passes, and it has a new number. The client wants something no check can give: a sheet of paper with every glyph on it. Chapter 115 writes that sheet as a web page that uses the exported font.

docs.title: 115. A proof sheet
docs.text:
Friday of week twenty-two. The font is version 1.002 now. Mira ran bump_version.py yesterday, exported the five styles again, and export_family.py said 10 wanted, 10 there, 0 missing.

The publisher's art director writes: "Before I sign anything, send me a PDF with every glyph on it. Big. With the names."

FontLab can print glyph sheets, and for one font on one day that's the way to do it. Halfmoon will be asked for this sheet every time a font changes. So today a script writes the sheet as a web page. A browser shows it, and the browser's own Print command turns it into a PDF.

A point to settle first. The page doesn't show the font you have open in FontLab. It shows the exported file, the one the client will install. If the export went wrong, the page shows it going wrong, and that's what a proof is for.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • An export folder for the current version with the OTF files in it, from chapters 111 and 112.
  • A web browser.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9, and I haven't looked at the page in a browser with the real exported font. I ran the script in plain Python against a stand-in for the reader's font and an export folder of dummy files, and I read the page it wrote as text.

docs.title: Step 1: A page is text
docs.text:
A web page is a text file whose name ends in .html. You've written text files since chapter 26. Inside, the words are wrapped in tags, which are names in angle brackets. A tag opens, <h1>, and closes with a slash, </h1>:

from pathlib import Path

lines = ["<!DOCTYPE html>",
         "<html>",
         "<body>",
         "<h1>Hello from Halfmoon</h1>",
         "</body>",
         "</html>"]
target = Path.home() / "hello.html"
with open(target, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("\n".join(lines) + "\n")
print(target)

Run it, find hello.html in your home folder, and drag it into a browser window. You get a heading in large type. "\n".join(lines) is the join you've used since chapter 25, with a line break as the glue.

That's the whole method. The script builds a list of lines, joins them and writes them. Everything else today is deciding what the lines say.

docs.title: Step 2: Tell the page which font
docs.text:
A page names its font in a block of rules called a style sheet. Here's the one the script will use, kept in a constant:

CSS = """
@font-face { font-family: "Proof"; src: url("FONTFILE"); }
body { font-family: sans-serif; margin: 2em; }
.cell { display: inline-block; width: 6em; margin: 0.3em; text-align: center; }
.glyph { display: block; font-family: "Proof", monospace; font-size: 48px; }
.name, .code { display: block; font-size: 10px; color: #555; }
"""

The triple quotes are chapter 98's. This isn't Python inside them, it's the browser's language for looks, and you need to read only two lines of it.

The first says: there's a font I'll call "Proof", and its file is at FONTFILE. That word is a placeholder of mine. The script swaps it for the real address with chapter 30's replace. I could have used an f-string, but a style sheet is full of curly braces and every one would need doubling, as in chapter 88.

The fourth line says: anything marked glyph is set in "Proof" at 48 pixels, and if that fails, in monospace. The fallback is deliberate. A browser that can't load a font says nothing. It quietly uses another font, and you'd be looking at a handsome proof of the wrong typeface. Typewriter letters are an alarm you can't miss. They appear if the file didn't load, and also for any single character the font lacks.

The address is relative. The script writes the page into the export folder itself, so the font is at otf/GGPlum-Regular.otf from where the page sits. Send the whole folder and the page still works on the client's computer.

docs.title: Step 3: One cell for each glyph
docs.text:
Each glyph gets a small box: the character large, then its name and code.

import html


def cell(glyph):
    character = html.escape(chr(glyph.unicode))
    return (f'<div class="cell"><span class="glyph">{character}</span>'
            f'<span class="name">{glyph.name}</span>'
            f'<span class="code">U+{glyph.unicode:04X}</span></div>')

chr and :04X are chapter 23's: a number to a character, and a number to four hexadecimal digits. The strings use single quotes outside because the HTML has double quotes inside. Two strings side by side in brackets are joined by Python into one.

html.escape is new. Two of Plum's glyphs are less and ampersand, and their characters, < and &, mean something to a browser: the start of a tag and the start of a code. html.escape rewrites them as < and &, which a browser shows as the plain characters. Every other character passes through as it is. Browsers are forgiving about a stray <, but a proof shouldn't depend on forgiveness.

docs.title: Step 4: The mistake
docs.text:
Mira's first version looped like this:

cells = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    if glyph.unicode is not None:
        cells.append(cell(glyph))
print(f"{len(cells)} glyphs.")

235 glyphs.

The if has to be there, since chr(None) is an error. She printed the page to a PDF and sent it.

The reply took ten minutes. "Where are the small caps?"

The font has 274 glyphs. The page showed 235. The other 39 have no Unicode value: the small capitals, the ligatures, the slashed zero, the numerators. A page shows characters, and those glyphs have no character of their own. A reader reaches them through features.

The script wasn't wrong about any glyph it showed. It left some out, printed a count that sounded complete, and nobody compared 235 with 274. You've met this before, in chapter 113's pattern that found 31 files of 40. A filter needs two counts: what passed and what didn't.

So the leftovers go on the page too, by name, under their own heading, and the script prints both numbers. Showing them as shapes means switching features on in the page, which is exercise 3.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Proof HTML
# Writes a web page that shows every glyph of one exported font file.
# Reads the open font for names and codes. Changes nothing in the font.
import html
from pathlib import Path

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


STYLE = "Regular"
PAGE_NAME = "proof-glyphs.html"

CSS = """
@font-face { font-family: "Proof"; src: url("FONTFILE"); }
body { font-family: sans-serif; margin: 2em; }
.cell { display: inline-block; width: 6em; margin: 0.3em; text-align: center; }
.glyph { display: block; font-family: "Proof", monospace; font-size: 48px; }
.name, .code { display: block; font-size: 10px; color: #555; }
"""


def key(text):
    return "".join([c for c in text.lower() if c.isalnum()])


def latest_export(font, package):
    info = package.info
    ending = f"-v{info.versionMajor}.{info.versionMinor:03d}"
    exports = Path(font.path).parent / "exports"
    if not exports.exists():
        return None
    folders = [f for f in sorted(exports.iterdir()) if f.name.endswith(ending)]
    return folders[-1] if folders else None


def font_file(folder, family, style):
    for path in sorted(folder.rglob("*.otf")):
        if key(path.stem) == key(family + style):
            return path
    return None


def cell(glyph):
    character = html.escape(chr(glyph.unicode))
    return (f'<div class="cell"><span class="glyph">{character}</span>'
            f'<span class="name">{glyph.name}</span>'
            f'<span class="code">U+{glyph.unicode:04X}</span></div>')


def page(title, address, cells, leftovers):
    lines = ["<!DOCTYPE html>", '<html lang="en">', "<head>",
             '<meta charset="utf-8">', f"<title>{html.escape(title)}</title>",
             "<style>" + CSS.replace("FONTFILE", address) + "</style>",
             "</head>", "<body>", f"<h1>{html.escape(title)}</h1>"]
    lines += cells
    lines.append(f"<h2>No character of their own: {len(leftovers)}</h2>")
    lines.append("<p>" + " ".join(leftovers) + "</p>")
    lines += ["</body>", "</html>"]
    return "\n".join(lines) + "\n"


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    folder = latest_export(font, package)
    if folder is None:
        tell("No export folder for this version. Export first.")
        return
    source = font_file(folder, package.info.familyName, STYLE)
    if source is None:
        tell(f"No {STYLE} .otf in {folder.name}.")
        return
    cells = []
    leftovers = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        if glyph.unicode is None:
            leftovers.append(glyph.name)
        else:
            cells.append(cell(glyph))
    address = source.relative_to(folder).as_posix()
    text = page(f"{source.stem}, {folder.name}", address, cells, leftovers)
    target = folder / PAGE_NAME
    with open(target, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(text)
    print(f"Proof of {address}")
    print(f"{len(cells)} glyphs with a character, {len(leftovers)} without.")
    print(f"Wrote {target}")


main()

Save it as proof_html.py and run it:

Proof of otf/GGPlum-Regular.otf
235 glyphs with a character, 39 without.
Wrote /Users/mira/Halfmoon/exports/2026-12-10-v1.002/proof-glyphs.html

Your counts, file names and path will be your own. Drag the page into a browser. What you should see, and what I haven't seen: a heading, then rows of boxes, each with a large character in Plum and two small grey lines beneath it, then a second heading and a paragraph of names. To make the PDF, use the browser's Print command and choose to save as PDF.

Notes on the listing.

latest_export doesn't use today's date. The export was made yesterday, so chapter 111's folder for today doesn't exist. It gathers the folders whose names end in this version and takes the last. The names begin with the date written year first, so sorted order is date order. folders[-1] is the last item, by chapter 10's counting from the end.

font_file reuses chapter 112's key, which squeezes a name down to its letters and digits, so GGPlum-Regular and GG Plum plus Regular meet. I've copied key into this script so that it runs by itself. Chapter 114 said a copy is two things to mend, and that's fair, but a one-line copy is a small price.

as_posix() writes a path with forward slashes whatever the computer. Web addresses always use forward slashes, and on Windows a plain str of the path wouldn't.

<meta charset="utf-8"> tells the browser how the file's bytes spell characters. It matches the encoding="utf-8" in open. Leave either out and é may arrive as two characters of nonsense.

lines += cells adds every item of one list to another. It's chapter 114's + for lists, written short.

The space glyph gets a box with nothing visible in it. That's a true picture of a space.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Change STYLE to "Semi Bold", with a gap in the middle, and run. The first line reads Proof of otf/GGPlum-SemiBold.otf. key threw the gap away on both sides of the comparison, so the spelling didn't matter.

Now change it to "Black", a weight Plum doesn't have:

No Black .otf in 2026-12-10-v1.002.

The script stopped before writing anything. Set STYLE back to "Regular".

One more, and for this one I can only tell you what should happen. In the page function change "FONTFILE" to "FONTFIL", so the swap finds nothing and the page asks for a font file that isn't there. Run, and reload the page. By the rules of style sheets every large character should now be in typewriter letters. That's the alarm from Step 2. If your page looks like that when you haven't broken anything, the browser couldn't load the font, and the first thing to check is that the page is still inside the export folder. Put the name back.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A web page is a text file of tags, so a script can write one with a list of lines, a join and chapter 26's open. html.escape makes any text safe to put between tags, and a relative address written with as_posix() keeps a page and its font together when the folder moves. A proof must show the exported file and must make a failure to load it obvious, which is why the fallback font is an ugly one. A filter that drops items needs both counts printed, or 204 of 258 looks like everything.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add the family's version to the page's heading, read from package.info as in latest_export.
  2. Make a second page for the Bold by turning STYLE and PAGE_NAME into arguments of a function, and call it for every style in a list.
  3. A browser switches a feature on with a rule such as font-feature-settings: "smcp";. For each leftover whose name ends in .sc, add a cell that shows the letter before the dot with that rule in a style="..." attribute on the span. I haven't tested this. It works only if the features were compiled before the export, which chapter 93 left to a button.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Every glyph is on a page, one by one. Nobody reads a typeface one glyph at a time. Chapter 116 sets words and paragraphs at a ladder of sizes, and builds the page from a template.

docs.title: 116. Waterfalls and words
docs.text:
Monday of week twenty-three. The art director liked the glyph sheet. Her production editor has a different question. "The dictionary is set at 9 point. Does the Light hold up at 9? Send me text, not an alphabet."

Friday's page showed every glyph alone, and nobody reads a typeface that way. Today's page sets a word and a paragraph in each of the five styles, at a ladder of sizes from 9 point to 36. Type people call the ladder a waterfall.

That makes five styles, nine lines each, and every line is the same piece of HTML with three things changed. Building those with f-strings and plus signs, as chapter 115 did, would work, and you'd lose your place in the quote marks. Python has a tool for text with holes in it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The export folder for version 1.002 with five OTF files in it.
  • proof_html.py from chapter 115, to borrow from.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9, and I haven't seen the page in a browser with the real fonts. I ran the script in plain Python against a stand-in for the reader's font and a folder of dummy font files, and read the page it wrote as text.

docs.title: Step 1: A template
docs.text:
from string import Template

LINE = Template("$style at ${size}pt")
print(LINE.substitute(style="Light", size=9))
print(LINE.substitute(style="Bold", size=36))

Light at 9pt
Bold at 36pt

A Template is a string with named holes. A hole is a dollar sign and a name. substitute fills the holes from the names you give it and returns the finished text. The template itself doesn't change, so you can fill it as often as you like.

The braces in ${size}pt mark where the name ends. Without them Python would look for a hole called sizept.

Why not an f-string? An f-string is filled once, at the line where it's written. A template is written in one place and filled in another, many times. And a template doesn't care about curly braces, so a style sheet can sit inside one as it is, with none of chapter 88's doubling.

docs.title: Step 2: Borrow three functions from chapter 115
docs.text:
This script needs three functions you already have: key from chapter 112, and latest_export and font_file from chapter 115. Copy them in, unchanged, so this script runs by itself. They need Path, so the script's imports gain this line:

from pathlib import Path

And here are the three:

def key(text):
    return "".join([c for c in text.lower() if c.isalnum()])


def latest_export(font, package):
    info = package.info
    ending = f"-v{info.versionMajor}.{info.versionMinor:03d}"
    exports = Path(font.path).parent / "exports"
    if not exports.exists():
        return None
    folders = [f for f in sorted(exports.iterdir()) if f.name.endswith(ending)]
    return folders[-1] if folders else None


def font_file(folder, family, style):
    for path in sorted(folder.rglob("*.otf")):
        if key(path.stem) == key(family + style):
            return path
    return None

That makes three copies of key in three scripts. Chapter 114 said a copy is two things to mend. It is, but each script still runs on its own, and key is one line that hasn't changed since chapter 112.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Mira's first sample paragraph came from the publisher's own style guide:

TEXT = ("The dictionary is set in two columns on a page of 148 × 210 mm. "
        "Headwords are bold; senses are numbered 1, 2, 3; quotations "
        "follow in a lighter weight, with the author's name and a date.")

She made the page, printed the PDF and looked it over at arm's length. It was handsome. She sent it.

The production editor circled one character ten times: the × between 148 and 210, in typewriter letters, in every paragraph. Plum has no multiplication sign. The alarm from chapter 115 did its job, and it did it in front of the client.

The page can only show the fault after the fact. The script can know beforehand, because the open font knows which characters it has:

def absent(font, text):
    codes = {glyph.unicode for glyph in font.glyphs if glyph.unicode is not None}
    return sorted({c for c in text if ord(c) not in codes})

The first line is a set of every Unicode value in the font, built in the manner of chapter 37 with curly braces, which makes a set and not a list. The second walks the text one character at a time. ord is chapter 23's: the number behind a character. A character whose number isn't in the font goes into another set, so each is reported once however often it occurs.

With the × in the text:

The font has no glyph for: × (U+00D7). Change the text.

Now there's a decision. The script could draw the page anyway, or it could stop. It stops. A proof with a stranger's letters in it wastes the reader's attention on something that isn't the typeface. Mira changes the sign to the word "by". Whether Plum should have a multiplication sign is a fair question for another day, and exercise 3 keeps a note of it.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Proof Text
# Writes a web page that sets words and a paragraph in every exported
# style, at a ladder of sizes. Changes nothing in the font.
import html
from pathlib import Path
from string import Template

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


STYLES = ["Light", "Regular", "Medium", "SemiBold", "Bold"]
SIZES = [9, 10, 12, 14, 18, 24, 36]
READING = [9, 11]
WORDS = "Hamburgefonstiv 0123456789"
TEXT = ("The dictionary is set in two columns on a page of 148 by 210 mm. "
        "Headwords are bold; senses are numbered 1, 2, 3; quotations "
        "follow in a lighter weight, with the author's name and a date.")
PAGE_NAME = "proof-text.html"

FACE = Template('@font-face { font-family: "$family"; src: url("$address"); }')
LINE = Template('<p style="font-family: \'$family\', monospace; '
                'font-size: ${size}pt; margin: 0.2em 0">$text</p>')
PAGE = Template("""<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<title>$title</title>
<style>
$faces
body { font-family: sans-serif; margin: 2em; max-width: 40em; }
h2 { font-size: 10pt; color: #555; margin-top: 3em; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<h1>$title</h1>
$blocks
</body>
</html>
""")


def key(text):
    return "".join([c for c in text.lower() if c.isalnum()])


def latest_export(font, package):
    info = package.info
    ending = f"-v{info.versionMajor}.{info.versionMinor:03d}"
    exports = Path(font.path).parent / "exports"
    if not exports.exists():
        return None
    folders = [f for f in sorted(exports.iterdir()) if f.name.endswith(ending)]
    return folders[-1] if folders else None


def font_file(folder, family, style):
    for path in sorted(folder.rglob("*.otf")):
        if key(path.stem) == key(family + style):
            return path
    return None


def absent(font, text):
    codes = {glyph.unicode for glyph in font.glyphs if glyph.unicode is not None}
    return sorted({c for c in text if ord(c) not in codes})


def block(style, family):
    lines = [f"<h2>{style}</h2>"]
    for size in SIZES:
        lines.append(LINE.substitute(family=family, size=size,
                                     text=html.escape(WORDS)))
    for size in READING:
        lines.append(LINE.substitute(family=family, size=size,
                                     text=html.escape(TEXT)))
    return "\n".join(lines)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    lacking = absent(font, WORDS + TEXT)
    if lacking:
        listed = ", ".join([f"{c} (U+{ord(c):04X})" for c in lacking])
        tell(f"The font has no glyph for: {listed}. Change the text.")
        return
    folder = latest_export(font, package)
    if folder is None:
        tell("No export folder for this version. Export first.")
        return
    faces = []
    blocks = []
    for style in STYLES:
        source = font_file(folder, package.info.familyName, style)
        if source is None:
            print(f"No {style} .otf in {folder.name}. Left out.")
            continue
        family = f"Proof {style}"
        address = source.relative_to(folder).as_posix()
        faces.append(FACE.substitute(family=family, address=address))
        blocks.append(block(style, family))
    title = f"{package.info.familyName}, {folder.name}"
    text = PAGE.substitute(title=html.escape(title), faces="\n".join(faces),
                           blocks="\n".join(blocks))
    target = folder / PAGE_NAME
    with open(target, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(text)
    lines = len(blocks) * (len(SIZES) + len(READING))
    print(f"{len(blocks)} styles, {lines} lines of text.")
    print(f"Wrote {target}")


main()

Save it as proof_text.py and run it:

5 styles, 45 lines of text.
Wrote /Users/mira/Halfmoon/exports/2026-12-10-v1.002/proof-text.html

Open the page in a browser. What you should find, and what I haven't seen: five grey headings, and under each a word growing from small to large, then the paragraph twice.

Notes on the listing.

There are three templates, and each is one level of the page. FACE is one font rule. LINE is one line of type. PAGE is the whole page, with two holes, $faces and $blocks, that take many lines joined into one string. The page is built from the inside out: lines into blocks, blocks into the page. Look at PAGE and you can see the shape of the finished file, which chapter 115's list of little strings never let you do.

Each style gets a family name of its own, Proof Light, Proof Bold and so on, and its own @font-face rule. That's the plainest way to be sure which file a line is set in. LINE uses single quotes around the family name because the whole style="..." is in double quotes. The backslashes before them are there because the Python string itself is in single quotes. \' puts a quote mark in the text without ending the string.

A style whose file is missing is left out with a printed line, and the loop goes on, as chapter 113's did for a font that wouldn't open. The last line of output counts the styles that made it. If it says 4, read upward.

html.escape is applied to the sample text and the title, the things a person types. The template doesn't do it for you.

absent asks the open font, and the page shows the exported one. They should hold the same characters. If they don't, the typewriter letters are still there as the second line of defence.

docs.title: Reading the page
docs.text:
The sizes are in points, and a point on a screen isn't a point on paper. A browser's "9pt" depends on the screen and the zoom. For the production editor's question, print the page, or save the PDF and print that at full size, and read the 9 point paragraph on paper at the distance you'd hold a dictionary.

Then look at these things. In the waterfall, find the smallest size at which the Light's thin strokes still look continuous. In the paragraphs, compare the Light with the Regular at 9 point: the figures, the semicolons, the apostrophe in "author's". Check that Medium and SemiBold sit visibly between their neighbours. Chapter 106 worked their shapes out by arithmetic, and this is the first time anyone has read them.

The script can't answer the editor's question. It gives you a page on which a person can.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
In block, misspell a name in the first substitute: write sise=size. Run:

KeyError: 'size'

substitute insists that every hole is filled. The template has a hole called size, nothing by that name arrived, and Python refuses to write a page with ${size} printed in the middle of it. Put the name right.

Templates have a gentler method, safe_substitute, which leaves unfilled holes as they are. For a proof that goes to a client it's the wrong tool, since it turns a loud error into a quiet blemish.

One more. A dollar sign followed by a digit isn't a hole and isn't allowed either: Template("costs $9").substitute() stops with an error that begins ValueError: Invalid placeholder in string. In the template itself, write a real dollar as $$. In the text you pass in, a dollar is only a character, and you can write prices freely.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A Template is text with $name holes that substitute fills, and it can be filled many times, which suits a page made of repeating blocks. Templates nest by joining the small filled pieces and passing the result into a hole of the larger one. A script should check its sample text against the font's characters before it draws anything, because a missing character on a proof is seen by the client first. Sizes on a screen are not sizes on paper, so a question about 9 point is answered with a printed page and a pair of eyes.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a line of capitals and a line of figures with punctuation to each block, each from its own constant.
  2. Put the sample text in a file, proof-text.txt, beside the font, and read it with chapter 26's open when the file exists. Keep TEXT as the fallback.
  3. Have the script write the characters it found absent to wanted-glyphs.txt, one to a line with the code, before it stops. Over a few months that file becomes a list of what clients needed and Plum didn't have.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The client has seen the glyphs and read the text. Their next message is shorter: "What changed since the version you sent last week?" Chapter 117 opens two versions of a font and lists the differences.

docs.title: 117. What changed since last week?
docs.text:
Tuesday of week twenty-three. The production editor has two sets of files from Halfmoon now, version 1.001 from last Monday and version 1.002 from Thursday. She writes: "What changed between them? I need to know whether to reflow the sample pages."

Mira knows the answer from memory. Nothing changed but the number. She bumped the version because chapter 114's check found the 1.001 folders already in use.

She can't prove it. The note that bump_version.py writes says when each number was given, and says nothing of what was done to the font. And she has no copy of the font as it was last Monday. The exported files are there, but the file she works in has been saved over many times since.

So today has two results. One is a script that lists the differences between two open fonts. The other is a habit that makes sure there's a second font to open.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice.vfj open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • A few minutes to make a copy of the file, in Step 1.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the script in plain Python. The part that compares glyphs is Fly's own function, running for real on records I built from the shipped Plum. The part that reads two open fonts from FontLab is a stand-in.

docs.title: Step 1: Make a case whose answer you know
docs.text:
You don't have last Monday's font either. So build a comparison where you know what the script should say, the way chapter 42 tested a count on a glyph whose answer was known.

Save the font. In Finder or Explorer, copy Plum-practice.vfj and name the copy Plum-practice-before.vfj. Open the copy in FontLab too, so both are open. Then bring Plum-practice to the front and make three changes by hand, all in the Regular master:

  1. Make hyphen 10 units wider.
  2. Move the top anchor of H a few units to the right.
  3. In the Kerning panel, change the pair T ae from −48 to −40.

Write the three down. That list is the answer sheet.

docs.title: Step 2: Ask Fly what differs
docs.text:
Fly has a tool for this, made for its own comparison window. It works in two moves. capture reads one master of one open font into a snapshot, a frozen record of every glyph's width, outline, anchors and components. compare takes two snapshots and returns the differences.

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.fonts.revisions.model as revisions
from fly import fl

workspace = fl.flWorkspace.instance()
packages = [fl.flPackage(item) for item in workspace.packages()]
new = scripting.current_package()
old = [p for p in packages if scripting.font_id(p) != scripting.font_id(new)][0]

before = revisions.capture(workspace, scripting.font_id(old), "Regular")
after = revisions.capture(workspace, scripting.font_id(new), "Regular")
for difference in revisions.compare(before, after):
    print(difference.glyph, difference.fields)

The first two lines after the imports are chapter 99's: FontLab's list of open fonts, each turned into a package. scripting.font_id gives the number FontLab knows a font by. The font in front is the new one. The old one is whichever open font has a different number.

Each difference has four parts. glyph is a name. fields says which things differ, in Fly's words: advance, geometry, anchors, components, and a few more. left and right are the glyph's records from the two snapshots.

Mira ran this and got:

H ('anchors',)
n ('raw_node_state',)
hyphen ('advance',)

Two of her three, in a tuple each. The kerning pair isn't there, and a glyph she never touched is.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Start with n. Mira didn't change it. She had clicked one of its nodes that morning while looking at something else.

Fly's notes on compare say what that field is: the raw state of every node, and that includes whether the node is selected. A selected node in one font and not in the other counts as a difference. Fly keeps the field because its window lets a person switch it on and off. In a list for a client it's noise, and worse than noise. A client who reads "n changed" will ask what changed in the n.

A report of differences can be wrong in two directions. It can miss a change, and it can announce one that didn't happen. Each costs trust. So the script keeps a list of fields to pass over, and raw_node_state is on it:

QUIET = ["raw_node_state"]
fields = [f for f in difference.fields if f not in QUIET]

Now the pair. compare didn't miss it. Snapshots don't hold kerning at all. Fly's notes say it compares named fields and nothing more, and kerning, Unicode values, features and Font Info aren't among them. A tool that compares some things should say which, so the script's last line will name the rest.

docs.title: Step 4: Kerning, by set arithmetic
docs.text:
Kerning you can compare yourself. scripting.kerning_pairs(package, master) has given you a dict of pairs since chapter 69, and the keys of two dicts can be compared as sets, with chapter 25's signs:

was = scripting.kerning_pairs(old, "Regular")
now = scripting.kerning_pairs(new, "Regular")
print(len(set(was) - set(now)), "removed")
print(len(set(now) - set(was)), "added")
print(len(set(was) & set(now)), "in both")

0 removed
0 added
105 in both

set(was) is the set of a dict's keys. Minus gives the pairs in one and not the other, and it matters which side is which. & gives the pairs in both, and those are the only ones whose values you can compare. Three questions, three lines. That's the whole of a dict difference, and it works for any two dicts with the same kind of keys: widths by glyph name, Unicode values by name, files by size.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Font Diff
# Lists what differs between two open fonts, master by master: glyphs,
# widths, shapes, anchors and kerning. Changes nothing in either font.
from pathlib import Path

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.fonts.revisions.model as revisions
import fly.ap.masters.inspect.model as masters_model
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


QUIET = ["raw_node_state"]
WORDS = {"state": "layer", "advance": "width", "geometry": "shape",
         "anchors": "anchors", "components": "parts",
         "glyph_order": "glyph order", "master_presence": "master"}


def other_fonts(current):
    workspace = fl.flWorkspace.instance()
    packages = [fl.flPackage(item) for item in workspace.packages()]
    mine = scripting.font_id(current)
    return [p for p in packages if scripting.font_id(p) != mine]


def glyph_lines(old, new, master):
    workspace = fl.flWorkspace.instance()
    before = revisions.capture(workspace, scripting.font_id(old), master)
    after = revisions.capture(workspace, scripting.font_id(new), master)
    lines = []
    for difference in revisions.compare(before, after):
        name = difference.glyph or "(whole font)"
        fields = [f for f in difference.fields if f not in QUIET]
        if not fields:
            continue
        if "glyph_presence" in fields:
            word = "added" if difference.left is None else "removed"
            lines.append(f"{name}: {word}")
        elif fields == ["advance"]:
            was = round(difference.left.advance)
            now = round(difference.right.advance)
            lines.append(f"{name}: width {was} to {now}")
        else:
            lines.append(f"{name}: " + ", ".join([WORDS.get(f, f) for f in fields]))
    return lines


def kern_lines(old, new, master):
    was = scripting.kerning_pairs(old, master)
    now = scripting.kerning_pairs(new, master)
    lines = []
    for pair in sorted(set(was) - set(now)):
        lines.append(f"{pair[0]} {pair[1]}: kern removed, was {round(was[pair])}")
    for pair in sorted(set(now) - set(was)):
        lines.append(f"{pair[0]} {pair[1]}: kern added, {round(now[pair])}")
    for pair in sorted(set(was) & set(now)):
        if was[pair] != now[pair]:
            lines.append(f"{pair[0]} {pair[1]}: kern {round(was[pair])} "
                         f"to {round(now[pair])}")
    return lines


def main():
    if fl.CurrentFont() is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    new = scripting.current_package()
    others = other_fonts(new)
    if len(others) != 1:
        tell("Open two fonts, with the new one in front. "
                      f"{len(others) + 1} are open.")
        return
    old = others[0]
    print(f"Old: {Path(old.path).name}")
    print(f"New: {Path(new.path).name}")
    total = 0
    for master in masters_model.master_order(new):
        lines = glyph_lines(old, new, master) + kern_lines(old, new, master)
        total += len(lines)
        print(f"{master}: {len(lines)}")
        for line in lines:
            print(f"  {line}")
    print(f"{total} differences.")
    print("Not compared: Unicode values, features, Font Info.")


main()

Save it as font_diff.py. With Plum-practice in front, run it:

Old: Plum-practice-before.vfj
New: Plum-practice.vfj
Light: 0
Regular: 3
  H: anchors
  hyphen: width 348 to 358
  T ae: kern -48 to -40
Bold: 0
3 differences.
Not compared: Unicode values, features, Font Info.

Hold it against your answer sheet: three changes made, three found, and nothing invented. The widths are from my stand-in and yours will be your own. The glyph lines come in the font's glyph order, so they may be arranged differently.

Notes on the listing.

The first two printed lines name the files. In a comparison the direction is half the meaning, and a report that doesn't say which font it called old can't be checked.

difference.glyph or "(whole font)" is chapter 91's or between values. A few differences belong to the font and not to a glyph, such as a changed glyph order, and for those Fly leaves the name empty.

When a glyph is in only one font, Fly puts None on the side that lacks it, so difference.left is None means the old font didn't have it.

For a width the script prints both numbers, read from the records in left and right. For shapes and anchors it prints only the word. The records hold every coordinate, and you could dig them out. For a client, "H: anchors" is the right length. The person who needs the coordinates has both fonts open and can look.

WORDS turns Fly's field names into the studio's words. WORDS.get(f, f) is chapter 22's get with a fallback: a field the dict doesn't know is printed under Fly's name, so a field Fly adds next year still shows up.

capture reads every glyph twice, to be sure the font didn't change under it, and the script calls it for two fonts in each of three masters. On a large family, expect a pause.

docs.title: The habit
docs.text:
Close Plum-practice-before.vfj. Undo your three changes in Plum-practice, or keep them if you like them.

The script works, and it couldn't answer the editor's question, because there was no old font to open. The cure costs one line. Whenever files leave the building, a copy of the font goes into the export folder beside them, with chapter 113's shutil.copy. Then every version a client holds has a font you can open. Chapter 119's build will do it without being asked.

For today, Mira writes the editor the truth. "Between 1.001 and 1.002, only the version number changed. I can't show you a comparison for that pair. From the next version on, I'll send a change list with every release."

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Open both fonts again, with the three changes in place, and this time bring Plum-practice-before to the front. Run:

Old: Plum-practice.vfj
New: Plum-practice-before.vfj
Light: 0
Regular: 3
  H: anchors
  hyphen: width 358 to 348
  T ae: kern -40 to -48
Bold: 0
3 differences.
Not compared: Unicode values, features, Font Info.

Every number runs backward, and the count is the same. Nothing in the fonts tells the script which is older. It took your word, in the form of which window was in front. That's why the two file names are printed first.

Now open a third font, any font, and run:

Open two fonts, with the new one in front. 3 are open.

With three open, "the other font" has no meaning, and the script says so and stops. It would have been simple to take the first of the others and carry on. Then the report would compare Plum with a stranger, find hundreds of differences, and look like a disaster.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Fly's capture and compare list which glyphs differ between one master of two open fonts and in which respect, and they leave kerning, Unicode values, features and Font Info alone. Two dicts are compared with three set expressions on their keys: minus one way, minus the other way, and & for the keys whose values can be compared. A difference report has to keep quiet about things that aren't changes, such as a selected node, and has to say which font it took as the old one. None of it works without an old font, so a copy of the source belongs with every export.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Print the report's lines to a file, changes.txt, in the newest export folder, using a copy of latest_export from chapter 115.
  2. Add the master's count of unchanged kerning pairs to its heading line, so Regular: 3 becomes Regular: 3 (104 pairs the same).
  3. Font Info isn't compared. Chapter 99's sync_font_info.py reads Font Info fields from every open font with getattr. Read the same fields from the two packages here and add lines such as copyright: differs.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Everything so far has asked FontLab about the font. The client doesn't have FontLab. They have an OTF file. Chapter 118 opens that file with fontTools, a package that reads fonts with no font editor involved, and asks it the same questions.

docs.title: 118. A second opinion from fontTools
docs.text:
Wednesday of week twenty-three. The publisher's IT department runs every incoming font through a checking tool. Its report on Plum reaches Mira with one line marked: "237 characters. Your glyph sheet says 235. Which is it?"

Every number this book has printed came from FontLab, about the font as it sits in FontLab. The publisher doesn't have that font. They have five OTF files, and a file is what FontLab's export made of the font, which is a different thing. Mira has never looked inside one.

There's a Python package that reads font files with no font editor involved. It's called fontTools, and most of the type trade's checking tools are built on it, very likely the publisher's too. Today you open the exported files with it and hold what they say against what the open font says.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • The export folder for version 1.002 with five OTF files in it.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9, and I don't have files that FontLab exported. I built five small OTF files with fontTools itself, with the reader's glyph names, characters and features, and ran the script on those in plain Python. So the fontTools calls below ran for real. What FontLab's export puts in a file is the part I haven't seen.

docs.title: Step 1: Which fontTools
docs.text:
This is the first package in the book that Fly doesn't hand you, so the import needs a thought.

FontLab 9 ships a copy of fontTools for its own use, under the name fontlab_private.fontTools. A copy you install yourself goes by the plain name fontTools. The scripts I've read from FontLab's own people try one and fall back to the other, and so will yours:

try:
    from fontTools.ttLib import TTFont
except ImportError:
    from fontlab_private.fontTools.ttLib import TTFont

print(TTFont)

<class 'fontTools.ttLib.ttFont.TTFont'>

try and except are chapter 19's, and ImportError is the error chapter 4 showed you when a name couldn't be imported. Put together they say: use your own copy if there is one, and FontLab's if not. If you see fontlab_private in the printed line, you're on FontLab's copy, and that's fine for everything in this chapter.

Installing your own

FontLab's copy is an older one, kept for FontLab, and "private" is a fair warning that it may change. A newer copy goes into the site-packages folder in your user folder, where Fly lives (chapter 33), and the usual tool for that is pip, run in a terminal with its --target option pointing at that folder. I haven't done this with FontLab 9, so I'm not printing a command I can't vouch for. Nothing here needs it.

docs.title: Step 2: Open a file
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

path = Path("/Users/mira/Halfmoon/exports/2026-12-10-v1.002/otf/GGPlum-Regular.otf")
with TTFont(path) as ttfont:
    print(sorted(ttfont.keys()))

['CFF ', 'GPOS', 'GSUB', 'GlyphOrder', 'OS/2', 'cmap', 'head', 'hhea', 'hmtx', 'maxp', 'name', 'post']

Use your own path. with is chapter 26's: the file is open for the indented lines and closed after them.

A font file is a set of tables, each with a four-character name, and this is the list. Your file will have more of them than my small ones do. The ones worth knowing today:

  • name holds the texts: family name, style name, version, copyright.
  • cmap is the map from characters to glyphs. It's the file's form of every glyph's Unicode values.
  • CFF holds the outlines of an OTF as the curves you drew. A TTF has glyf in its place.
  • hmtx holds the widths.
  • GSUB holds the features that swap glyphs, such as liga and smcp. GPOS holds the ones that move them, such as kern.
  • GlyphOrder isn't a table. It's fontTools' own list of the glyph names.

Ask a few questions:

with TTFont(path) as ttfont:
    print(ttfont["name"].getDebugName(5))
    print(len(ttfont.getGlyphOrder()))
    print(len(ttfont.getBestCmap()))
    print(ttfont["head"].unitsPerEm)

Version 1.002
274
237
1000

Square brackets with a table's name give you the table. In the name table every text has a number, and 5 is the version. getBestCmap returns a dict from character number to glyph name, and its length is the IT department's 237.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Mira's first script compared each file's characters with the font's. For the font's side she took the line from chapter 116:

codes = {glyph.unicode for glyph in font.glyphs if glyph.unicode is not None}

and the script said, for every one of the five files:

GGPlum-Bold.otf       Version 1.002   274 glyphs  237 characters   9 features
  in the file only: U+00A0 U+00AD

It reported two characters in the file that the font doesn't have. That would be alarming, since an export shouldn't invent characters.

It didn't invent them. U+00A0 is the no-break space and U+00AD is the soft hyphen. You gave them to space and hyphen yourself in chapter 84, as second values. glyph.unicode is the first value only, and chapter 84 said to use glyph.unicodes, the list, when all of them matter.

So both counts were right. Plum has 235 glyphs that carry a character, and 237 characters, because two glyphs carry two each. The glyph sheet counted glyphs and the checking tool counted characters. Mira can write that back in one sentence.

The script's alarm was false, and the fault was in the script. When a file and a font disagree, there are three suspects: the export, the font, and the code that compared them. Look at the comparing code first, since it's the newest of the three and the least tested. The cure:

def font_codes(font):
    codes = set()
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        for code in glyph.unicodes:
            codes.add(code)
    return codes

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Inspect Export
# Opens every exported .otf of the current version with fontTools and
# holds what the file says against the open font. Changes nothing.
from pathlib import Path

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


try:
    from fontTools.ttLib import TTFont
except ImportError:
    from fontlab_private.fontTools.ttLib import TTFont


# Chapter 115's latest_export, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def latest_export(font, package):
    info = package.info
    ending = f"-v{info.versionMajor}.{info.versionMinor:03d}"
    exports = Path(font.path).parent / "exports"
    if not exports.exists():
        return None
    folders = [f for f in sorted(exports.iterdir()) if f.name.endswith(ending)]
    return folders[-1] if folders else None


def features(ttfont):
    tags = set()
    for tag in ["GSUB", "GPOS"]:
        if tag in ttfont:
            for record in ttfont[tag].table.FeatureList.FeatureRecord:
                tags.add(record.FeatureTag)
    return sorted(tags)


def read_file(path):
    with TTFont(path) as ttfont:
        return {"version": ttfont["name"].getDebugName(5),
                "glyphs": len(ttfont.getGlyphOrder()),
                "codes": set(ttfont.getBestCmap()),
                "curves": "CFF " in ttfont,
                "features": features(ttfont)}


def font_codes(font):
    codes = set()
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        for code in glyph.unicodes:
            codes.add(code)
    return codes


def code_list(codes):
    return " ".join([f"U+{code:04X}" for code in sorted(codes)])


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    package = scripting.current_package()
    folder = latest_export(font, package)
    if folder is None:
        tell("No export folder for this version. Export first.")
        return
    info = package.info
    wanted = f"Version {info.versionMajor}.{info.versionMinor:03d}"
    codes = font_codes(font)
    problems = 0
    shown = None
    files = sorted(folder.rglob("*.otf"))
    for path in files:
        try:
            said = read_file(path)
        except Exception as problem:
            print(f"{path.name}: DID NOT OPEN: {type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")
            problems += 1
            continue
        print(f"{path.name:<22}{said['version']:<15}{said['glyphs']:>4} glyphs"
              f"{len(said['codes']):>5} characters{len(said['features']):>4} features")
        shown = said["features"]
        if wanted not in said["version"]:
            print(f"  says {said['version']}, the font says {wanted}")
            problems += 1
        if not said["curves"]:
            print("  has no CFF table")
            problems += 1
        if codes - said["codes"]:
            print(f"  lost on the way out: {code_list(codes - said['codes'])}")
            problems += 1
        if said["codes"] - codes:
            print(f"  in the file only: {code_list(said['codes'] - codes)}")
            problems += 1
    print(f"{len(files)} files, {problems} problems.")
    if shown is not None:
        print("Features in the last file:", " ".join(shown))


main()

Save it as inspect_export.py and run it:

GGPlum-Bold.otf       Version 1.002   274 glyphs  237 characters   9 features
GGPlum-Light.otf      Version 1.002   274 glyphs  237 characters   9 features
GGPlum-Medium.otf     Version 1.002   274 glyphs  237 characters   9 features
GGPlum-Regular.otf    Version 1.002   274 glyphs  237 characters   9 features
GGPlum-SemiBold.otf   Version 1.002   274 glyphs  237 characters   9 features
5 files, 0 problems.
Features in the last file: cpsp dnom frac kern liga numr smcp ss01 zero

That's what my stand-in files gave. Yours are real exports, and I expect the first run to show you something I couldn't foresee. Read every line it prints as a question about the export, not as a verdict.

Notes on the listing.

read_file opens a file, takes five facts and closes it. Nothing from fontTools leaves the function. What comes out is a plain dict of text, numbers, a set and a list, which the rest of the script can use with the file long shut.

features is the one place that digs. Inside the GSUB and GPOS tables the features sit in a list of records, each with a FeatureTag. The same tag can occur several times, once for each script and language, which is why the tags go into a set. I counted nine: the eight features you wrote in Part 5, and kern. You never wrote a kern feature. An export builds it from the kerning pairs, so I've assumed FontLab's does. If your line shows eight, the kerning didn't reach the file, and that's worth a morning.

The two differences between sets are chapter 117's, pointing in two directions. A character the font has and the file doesn't was lost on the way out. A character only the file has came from somewhere, and you now know to suspect your own script first.

wanted not in said["version"] uses in and not ==, because some exports put more after the number, a build date or the name of the tool.

The loop keeps going when a file won't open, with chapter 100's except Exception and a line that says so. One bad file shouldn't hide the other four.

The script doesn't compare the glyph count with the font's. I don't know whether FontLab adds or drops glyphs at export, so there the script prints and leaves the judging to you.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
In read_file, take the space out of the table name, so it reads "CFF" in ttfont. Run:

GGPlum-Bold.otf       Version 1.002   274 glyphs  237 characters   9 features
  has no CFF table

and the same for every file, ending in 5 files, 5 problems. Table names have four characters, always. CFF has three letters, so its fourth character is a space, and the space is part of the name. Python doesn't complain about "CFF" in ttfont. It's a fair question with the answer no. Ask for the table itself, ttfont["CFF"], and you get KeyError: 'CFF'. Put the space back.

Now make a text file with three or four letters in it, name it GGPlum-Test.otf, and put it in the otf folder. Run:

GGPlum-Test.otf: DID NOT OPEN: TTLibError: Not a TrueType or OpenType font (not enough data)

The wording is from my copy of fontTools, and FontLab's older one may phrase it differently. A longer text file gets a different reason in the brackets, bad sfntVersion, because fontTools then has enough to read the first four characters and dislike them. The file name says OTF and the contents don't, and fontTools goes by the contents. The count at the end reads 6 files, 1 problems. Delete the test file before you forget it's there, or Friday's build will ship it.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A font file is a set of tables with four-character names, and fontTools opens it as something like a dict of them: name for the texts, cmap for the characters, CFF for the outlines, GSUB and GPOS for the features. A package Fly doesn't provide is imported with try and except ImportError, so the script works with your own copy or FontLab's. The exported file is a second witness to what the font holds, and it counts characters where FontLab's glyph list counts glyphs. When the file and the font disagree, check the code that compared them before blaming either.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Print the family name and the style name of each file. They're texts 1 and 2 in the name table. Does each file's style name match the last part of its file name?
  2. ttfont["hmtx"]["zero"] gives a pair, the width and the left sidebearing. Print the width of zero in each of the five files and hold the three masters' values against chapter 104's table.
  3. The folder has a ttf subfolder too. Make the script look at both kinds, and expect glyf where an OTF has CFF.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: There's a script to check, one to make the folder, two to proof, one to compare and one to inspect. On Friday somebody has to remember to run them, in the right order. Chapter 119 writes the script that remembers, and Oskar's sheet loses its last line.

docs.title: 119. The Friday build
docs.text:
Friday of week twenty-three. On Oskar's sheet one line is still open: Export the whole family to a dated folder every Friday.

Mira has every piece of it. ship_check.py says whether the font may go. export_family.py says whether ten files arrived. inspect_export.py reads them. Two scripts write proofs. bump_version.py gives the font its next number. Six scripts, and on a Friday afternoon she is the one who has to remember them, in order, and not carry on when one of them says no.

Remembering an order is work for a script. Today you write the one that calls the others.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9 and saved, with Fly installed.
  • The scripts from chapters 97, 112, 114, 115, 116 and 118.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran today's script and the six it calls in plain Python, with stand-ins for FontLab and with font files I built myself, through a whole Friday: a refusal, a first half, an export and a second half. Every block of output below comes from those runs.

docs.title: Step 1: A build has a hole in the middle
docs.text:
Nothing I've found lets a script press Export Font As with settings I can vouch for. Chapter 111 said so and nothing has changed. So the build can't be one run. It's two, with you in between:

  1. Check the font. Make today's folder. Stop.
  2. You export.
  3. Check the files, inspect them, write the proofs, keep a copy of the source, give the font its next number.

One script can do both halves if it can tell which one is due. It can, from the disk: if today's folder for this version holds no font files, it's the first half. If it holds some, the export has happened, and it's the second.

That's a better signal than a setting at the top of the script, because nobody has to remember to change it.

Two runs, with the export between them.

docs.title: Step 2: Teach six scripts to answer
docs.text:
Each of the six ends by printing. ship_check.py prints Not ready. and you read it and stop. A script that calls ship_check can't read. Printing tells a person. To tell another script, a function has to return something.

So make the same three changes to each of the six.

First, move it out of the Scripts folder to the site-packages folder where Fly lives, as chapter 114 did with preflight.py, so it can be imported.

Second, change its last line from main() to chapter 114's guard, so that importing it doesn't run it:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Third, add one line at the very end of its main, after the last print, indented four spaces so that it belongs to main and to nothing inside it:

Script Last line of main ship_check.py return total + broken export_family.py return missing inspect_export.py return problems proof_html.py return 0 proof_text.py return 0 bump_version.py return 0

The rule is the same for all six: main returns the number of things wrong, and 0 means go on. In inspect_export.py the return goes after the if shown is not None: block and not inside it.

Each of those main functions also has early exits, a bare return after "Open a font first." and the like. Leave them. A bare return gives back None, and you'll see in a minute why that's the right answer for them.

Once a script has moved, it's no longer in the Scripts menu. To run one alone, type two lines in the Scripting panel: import proof_text, then proof_text.main().

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Mira's first build called the steps in a loop and wrote down what each said:

def run_steps(steps):
    for label, step in steps:
        result = step()
        log(f"{label}: {result}")

She tried it on a folder where one file hadn't arrived, the Medium TTF:

>> Second half, for 2026-12-18-v1.003
  MISSING  GG Plum Medium .ttf
10 wanted, 9 there, 1 missing.
>> Files: 1
5 files, 0 problems.
Features in the last file: cpsp dnom frac kern liga numr smcp ss01 zero
>> Inspect: 0
Proof of otf/GGPlum-Regular.otf
235 glyphs with a character, 39 without.
Wrote /Users/mira/Halfmoon/exports/2026-12-18-v1.003/proof-glyphs.html
>> Glyph proof: 0
5 styles, 45 lines of text.
Wrote /Users/mira/Halfmoon/exports/2026-12-18-v1.003/proof-text.html
>> Text proof: 0
>> Source copy: 0
Version 1.003 -> Version 1.004
Note line for 3 masters: 2026-12-18: Version 1.004
6 fields changed.
>> Next version: 0
>> Build finished.

The second line says a file is missing. The fourth records it: Files: 1. And then the build carried on, wrote proofs into an incomplete folder, and gave the font its next number, which marks 1.003 as shipped. Build finished. is the last thing on the screen, and on a Friday afternoon the last line is the one that gets read.

She had made the steps answer and then not listened. A build has to stop at the first answer that isn't 0:

def run_steps(steps):
    for label, step in steps:
        result = step()
        if result != 0:
            log(f"{label}: stopped the build ({result})")
            return False
        log(f"{label}: ok")
    return True

run_steps now answers too: True when every step passed, False when one stopped it.

The test is != 0, not > 0, on purpose. A step that left through one of its early exits returns None. None isn't 0, so the build stops there too. A step that didn't say how it went is treated as one that went badly.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Friday Build
# Run it twice. The first run checks the font and makes today's folder.
# You export. The second run checks the files, writes the proofs, keeps
# a copy of the source and gives the font its next version number.
import shutil
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import bump_version
import export_family
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import inspect_export
import proof_html
import proof_text
import ship_check
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


LOG = []


def log(line):
    stamped = f"{datetime.now():%Y-%m-%d %H:%M} {line}"
    LOG.append(stamped)
    print(">>", line)


def keep_source():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    folder = export_family.export_folder(font, scripting.current_package())
    shutil.copy(font.path, folder / Path(font.path).name)
    return 0


BEFORE = [("Checks", ship_check.main)]
AFTER = [
    ("Files", export_family.main),
    ("Inspect", inspect_export.main),
    ("Glyph proof", proof_html.main),
    ("Text proof", proof_text.main),
    ("Source copy", keep_source),
    ("Next version", bump_version.main),
]


def run_steps(steps):
    for label, step in steps:
        try:
            result = step()
        except Exception as problem:
            log(f"{label}: DID NOT RUN: {type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")
            return False
        if result != 0:
            log(f"{label}: stopped the build ({result})")
            return False
        log(f"{label}: ok")
    return True


def font_files(folder):
    return [p for p in folder.rglob("*") if p.suffix.lower() in export_family.FORMATS]


def build(font, package):
    folder = export_family.export_folder(font, package)
    if not folder.exists() or not font_files(folder):
        log(f"First half, for {folder.name}")
        if not run_steps(BEFORE):
            return
        folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        log("Folder made. Waiting for the export.")
        print("Save the font. Then File > Export Font As, with chapter 112's")
        print(f"settings, into {folder}")
        print("Then run this script again.")
        return
    log(f"Second half, for {folder.name}")
    bump_version.DRY_RUN = False
    try:
        finished = run_steps(AFTER)
    finally:
        bump_version.DRY_RUN = True
    if finished:
        log("Build finished.")
        print("The font has its next number. Save it.")


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None or not font.path:
        tell("Open a saved font first.")
        return
    exports = Path(font.path).parent / "exports"
    exports.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    try:
        build(font, scripting.current_package())
    finally:
        with open(exports / "build-log.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            f.write("\n".join(LOG) + "\n")


main()

Save it as friday_build.py in the Scripts folder. This one you run yourself, so it ends in a plain main().

Notes on the listing, before the runs.

BEFORE and AFTER are lists of pairs, a label and a function. ship_check.main has no brackets after it. With brackets Python would call it on the spot, while the list is being made. Without them the list holds the function itself, to be called later by step(). Chapter 100's CHECKS worked the same way.

log does two things with one line. It prints it with >> in front, so the build's own lines stand out from what the six scripts print. And it keeps it in LOG with the date and time. datetime.now() is the moment it's called, and the part after the colon in the braces is a pattern for writing it: %Y the year, %m the month, %d the day, %H and %M the hour and minute.

main writes LOG to build-log.txt in a finally block, chapter 95's, so the file gets its lines when the build stops early and when something crashes. The "a" where you've always written "w" means append: add to the end of the file and keep what's there. A log that started fresh each run would lose the run that went wrong.

bump_version.DRY_RUN = False reaches into another module and sets its variable. The setting lasts as long as FontLab stays open, because a module is loaded once and kept. So the build puts the True back in a finally, whether the steps passed, stopped or crashed, and bump_version.main() run on its own afterwards still only rehearses. The build is the one place that has earned the real thing, since by that line everything else has passed.

keep_source does what chapter 117 asked for: a copy of the font file goes in beside the exports, so next month there's an old font to compare with. It copies the file as last saved. A script can't see changes you haven't saved, which is why the first half ends by telling you to save.

Python has a module called logging that does what log does and much more. I haven't seen how it behaves inside FontLab, where the screen it writes to isn't an ordinary one, so the book uses a few lines it can explain.

docs.title: A Friday, run by run
docs.text:
The font is at 1.002. Run the build:

>> First half, for 2026-12-18-v1.002
Glyph names   274 looked at   ok
Unicode       235 looked at   ok
Features       35 looked at   ok
Font Info       5 looked at   ok
Metrics         8 looked at   ok
Masters       201 looked at   ok

Not ready.

It stopped at its first step, and it was right to. Version 1.002 went to the publisher last week. Mira runs bump_version.main() by hand, with DRY_RUN off, for the last time. Then the build again:

>> First half, for 2026-12-18-v1.003

followed by nine lines of ok, and:

9 checks, 0 problems, 0 did not run.
Ready to export.
>> Checks: ok
>> Folder made. Waiting for the export.
Save the font. Then File > Export Font As, with chapter 112's
settings, into /Users/mira/Halfmoon/exports/2026-12-18-v1.003
Then run this script again.

She saves, exports, and runs it a third time. The folder holds font files now, so the script takes the other road:

>> Second half, for 2026-12-18-v1.003
  ok       otf/GGPlum-Light.otf

and nine more of those, then:

10 wanted, 10 there, 0 missing.
>> Files: ok

Then the five lines of inspect_export.py and >> Inspect: ok, the two proofs with an ok each, and the end:

>> Source copy: ok

Note line for 3 masters: 2026-12-18: Version 1.004
6 fields changed.
>> Next version: ok
>> Build finished.
The font has its next number. Save it.

The folder holds otf, ttf, Plum-practice.vfj and two proof pages. And build-log.txt, one level up, holds the day:

2026-12-18 15:40 First half, for 2026-12-18-v1.002
2026-12-18 15:40 Checks: stopped the build (1)
2026-12-18 15:40 First half, for 2026-12-18-v1.003
2026-12-18 15:40 Checks: ok
2026-12-18 15:40 Folder made. Waiting for the export.
2026-12-18 16:05 Second half, for 2026-12-18-v1.003
2026-12-18 16:05 Files: ok
2026-12-18 16:05 Inspect: ok
2026-12-18 16:05 Glyph proof: ok
2026-12-18 16:05 Text proof: ok
2026-12-18 16:05 Source copy: ok
2026-12-18 16:05 Next version: ok
2026-12-18 16:05 Build finished.

The times are my stand-in's. The counts are the reader's font as the book has built it, and yours will be your own.

The bump comes last, and that changes what the number on the font means. From today the font on the desk is always one number ahead of the last one shipped. Work done on Monday is done on 1.004, and next Friday's first run passes the version check with nobody thinking about it. Chapter 97 said the Friday build would call the bump. This is the call.

The second half doesn't run the checks again. It can't: the New version check would find today's own files and refuse.

Oskar takes the sheet off the wall and draws the eleventh line. He doesn't put it back.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Take return missing out of export_family.py again and run the second half on a complete folder:

10 wanted, 10 there, 0 missing.
>> Files: stopped the build (None)

Ten of ten, and the build stopped. main reached its end without a return, gave back None, and the build won't take silence for a yes. It's a nuisance and it's the right way round. The other way, a step you forgot to finish would pass every Friday. Put the line back. Because the module is already loaded, FontLab keeps the old one until you restart or use chapter 33's importlib.reload.

Now, in AFTER, misspell a function: proof_html.mian. Run:

AttributeError: module 'proof_html' has no attribute 'mian'

as the last line of a traceback, before any step ran. The list is built when the script is read, so a wrong name there fails at once. That's the good kind of failure. An error inside a step, while it runs, is caught by run_steps and becomes a DID NOT RUN line in the log, and the build stops there.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A function that prints tells a person and a function that returns tells a script, so a script that others will call needs a return with a meaning, and here it's the number of problems. A build is a list of labelled functions run in order that stops at the first answer other than 0, and treats no answer as a bad one. What can't be scripted, the export, sits between two runs, and the script decides which half is due from what's on the disk. A log file opened with "a" and written in finally keeps the record of the runs that failed, which are the ones you'll want to read.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. The second half is chosen by today's date in the folder name. Start a build at five to midnight, export after midnight, and say what the next run does. Then say what you'd do about it by hand.
  2. Add a step after "Source copy" that calls chapter 117's font_diff when a second font is open, and returns 0 either way.
  3. Run the build a fourth time, after Build finished. What does it make, and is it harmful?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Five weights are in the folder. The art director asked for nine, and chapter 107 said four of them lie outside what three masters can reach. Chapter 120 closes Part 6 with a release list written as code, and with an honest count of what shipped.

docs.title: 120. The family ships
docs.text:
Monday of week twenty-four. Friday's folder went to the publisher a little after four. This morning the art director's assistant writes: "Is this the release? Can we build the catalog on it?"

Mira starts typing yes and stops. The folder holds five weights. The art director asked for nine. Ines read the text proof on paper on Friday. Nobody has typed a line with the new files in the layout program the publisher uses. And nobody has told the art director in so many words that four weights aren't coming this year.

The build finished. That says the machine's part was done. A release is a claim made to a person, and it has parts no script can do. So the last script of Part 6 does no work on the font at all. It writes down what was asked for, what's in the folder, and what a person still owes, and it refuses to say "released" while anything is open.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Plum-practice open in FontLab 9, with Fly installed.
  • Friday's export folder from chapter 119, with the build's log beside it.

I couldn't run the code in FontLab 9. I ran the script in plain Python on a folder laid out like the one chapter 119's build leaves behind. Nothing here asks FontLab for more than the path of the open font, so this chapter leans on FontLab less than any other in the part.

docs.title: Step 1: Which folder?
docs.text:
The script needs the folder that was shipped. You have a function for that, latest_export from chapters 115 and 116. Here it is again, so these lines run by themselves:

from pathlib import Path

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl


def latest_export(font, package):
    info = package.info
    ending = f"-v{info.versionMajor}.{info.versionMinor:03d}"
    exports = Path(font.path).parent / "exports"
    if not exports.exists():
        return None
    folders = [f for f in sorted(exports.iterdir()) if f.name.endswith(ending)]
    return folders[-1] if folders else None


font = fl.CurrentFont()
print(latest_export(font, scripting.current_package()))

None

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
latest_export looks for the newest folder whose name ends in the font's version. Until Friday that was the right question. Since Friday it's the wrong one, and the reason is chapter 119's own rule: the build gives the font its next number as its last step. The font on Mira's desk says 1.004. The folder that went out says 1.003. There is no folder for 1.004, and there shouldn't be.

Nothing was broken. A function written for one moment was asked at another. The font's version used to mean "what I'm about to ship", and since Friday it means "what I'll ship next". Code that reads a value depends on what the value means, and a meaning can change with no line of that code changing.

So ask a question whose answer doesn't move: which is the newest folder that holds font files?

from pathlib import Path

FORMATS = [".otf", ".ttf"]


def shipped_folder(font):
    exports = Path(font.path).parent / "exports"
    if not exports.exists():
        return None
    found = None
    for folder in sorted(exports.iterdir()):
        if any([p.suffix.lower() in FORMATS for p in folder.rglob("*")]):
            found = folder
    return found

any with a list is chapter 44's. The folders are sorted by name, and the names start with a date, so the last one that passes is the newest. An empty folder doesn't pass. That matters: run Friday's build once too often and it makes an empty folder for 1.004, and the release must not land there. build-log.txt sits in exports too, and it's a file. Asking a file for the files inside it gives none, so it doesn't pass either.

docs.title: Step 3: Three kinds of line
docs.text:
Every item on a release list is in one of three states, and the list is only honest if it keeps them apart.

Shipped, or there. The script can see it: a weight with both its files, a proof page, the copy of the source font, the log saying the build finished.

Not yet. Asked for, not delivered, and everybody has agreed why. Thin and ExtraLight need a Thin master. ExtraBold and Black need a Black one. Chapter 107 worked that out and chapter 110 showed what three masters can and can't reach. These lines stay on the list, with their reason, and they don't block the release. Take them off and the list would read "5 of 5", which is true and misleading.

Open. Somebody still owes something. One open line and the script won't print "Released."

The third group includes things the script can't see at all. Whether Ines read the proof on paper isn't on the disk. So the script holds a short list of the hand jobs, each with a place for a name:

BY_HAND = [
    ("Text proof read on paper at 9 point", "Ines, 18 Dec"),
    ("Typed in the layout program", ""),
    ("Client told which weights are missing and why", ""),
]

An empty name means open. To close a line, a person types who did it and when, in the script, and runs it again. That's all the signing there is. The script can't check that the name is true. What it does is make the claim sit in a file with a name on it, and that's more than a "yes" in an email.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Release
# Reads the newest export folder that holds fonts and writes RELEASE.txt
# into it: what was asked for, what is there, and what a person still
# has to do. Changes nothing in the font.
from pathlib import Path

from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box

TITLE = "Halfmoon"


# Chapter 39's tell, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


# Chapter 112's key, written out again so this script runs by itself.
def key(text):
    return "".join([c for c in text.lower() if c.isalnum()])


FAMILY = "GG Plum"
FORMATS = [".otf", ".ttf"]
WANTED = ["Thin", "ExtraLight", "Light", "Regular", "Medium", "SemiBold",
          "Bold", "ExtraBold", "Black"]
NOT_YET = {
    "Thin": "needs a Thin master",
    "ExtraLight": "needs a Thin master",
    "ExtraBold": "needs a Black master",
    "Black": "needs a Black master",
}
PAPERS = ["proof-glyphs.html", "proof-text.html"]
BY_HAND = [
    ("Text proof read on paper at 9 point", "Ines, 18 Dec"),
    ("Typed in the layout program", ""),
    ("Client told which weights are missing and why", ""),
]


def shipped_folder(font):
    exports = Path(font.path).parent / "exports"
    if not exports.exists():
        return None
    found = None
    for folder in sorted(exports.iterdir()):
        if any([p.suffix.lower() in FORMATS for p in folder.rglob("*")]):
            found = folder
    return found


def weight_lines(folder):
    stems = {(key(p.stem), p.suffix.lower()) for p in folder.rglob("*")}
    lines, shipped, open_items = [], 0, 0
    for style in WANTED:
        there = [s for s in FORMATS if (key(FAMILY + style), s) in stems]
        if len(there) == len(FORMATS):
            lines.append(f"  shipped   {style}")
            shipped += 1
        elif style in NOT_YET and not there:
            lines.append(f"  not yet   {style}: {NOT_YET[style]}")
        else:
            lines.append(f"  OPEN      {style}: has {' '.join(there) or 'no files'}")
            open_items += 1
    return lines, shipped, open_items


def build_finished(folder):
    log = folder.parent / "build-log.txt"
    if not log.exists():
        return False
    with open(log, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        text = f.read()
    ours = False
    for line in text.splitlines():
        if "half, for" in line:
            ours = line.endswith(f"Second half, for {folder.name}")
        elif ours and line.endswith("Build finished."):
            return True
    return False


def paper_lines(folder, font):
    checks = [(name, (folder / name).exists()) for name in PAPERS]
    checks.append(("copy of the source font", (folder / Path(font.path).name).exists()))
    checks.append(("build finished, by the log", build_finished(folder)))
    lines, open_items = [], 0
