    for label, good in checks:
        lines.append(f"  {'there  ' if good else 'OPEN   '}   {label}")
        if not good:
            open_items += 1
    return lines, open_items


def hand_lines():
    lines, open_items = [], 0
    for label, who in BY_HAND:
        if who:
            lines.append(f"  done      {label} ({who})")
        else:
            lines.append(f"  OPEN      {label}")
            open_items += 1
    return lines, open_items


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None or not font.path:
        tell("Open a saved font first.")
        return
    folder = shipped_folder(font)
    if folder is None:
        tell("No export folder holds fonts yet. Run the Friday build.")
        return
    weights, shipped, open_weights = weight_lines(folder)
    papers, open_papers = paper_lines(folder, font)
    hand, open_hand = hand_lines()
    open_items = open_weights + open_papers + open_hand
    lines = [f"Release {folder.name}"]
    lines += [f"Weights: {shipped} of {len(WANTED)} asked for"] + weights
    lines += ["In the folder:"] + papers
    lines += ["By hand:"] + hand
    lines.append("Released." if open_items == 0 else f"Not released: {open_items} open.")
    for line in lines:
        print(line)
    with open(folder / "RELEASE.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write("\n".join(lines) + "\n")


main()

Save it as release.py and run it:

Release 2026-12-18-v1.003
Weights: 5 of 9 asked for
  not yet   Thin: needs a Thin master
  not yet   ExtraLight: needs a Thin master
  shipped   Light
  shipped   Regular
  shipped   Medium
  shipped   SemiBold
  shipped   Bold
  not yet   ExtraBold: needs a Black master
  not yet   Black: needs a Black master
In the folder:
  there     proof-glyphs.html
  there     proof-text.html
  there     copy of the source font
  there     build finished, by the log
By hand:
  done      Text proof read on paper at 9 point (Ines, 18 Dec)
  OPEN      Typed in the layout program
  OPEN      Client told which weights are missing and why
Not released: 2 open.

The same 21 lines are now in RELEASE.txt inside the export folder, where anyone who opens the folder finds them.

Notes on the listing.

Almost nothing in it is new, which is the point of a last chapter. Tuples in a list are chapter 36's. The pairs of name and suffix in weight_lines are chapter 112's way of matching file names, with key so that GGPlum-SemiBold and "GG Plum SemiBold" count as the same. ' '.join(there) or 'no files' is chapter 91's or between values. lines += [...] is chapter 115's. Reading the log is chapter 27's with open and chapter 87's splitlines.

Three functions return two or three things at once: the lines to print and a count of open items. weights, shipped, open_weights = weight_lines(folder) unpacks them, the way chapter 100 unpacked what each check returned. Each section counts its own open lines and main only adds them up. To add a section, write one more function of that shape.

weight_lines has three branches, one for each state. A weight is shipped when it has every format in FORMATS. It's "not yet" when it has a reason in NOT_YET and no files at all. Everything else is open, and that last branch catches two cases with one test: a wanted weight with a file missing, and a weight that's supposed to be absent turning up with a file.

build_finished reads the log as a story. It walks the lines and remembers, in ours, whether the last "half" line it passed was the second half for this folder. A Build finished. line counts only while ours is true. The log holds every build there ever was, and a finish that belongs to another folder says nothing about this one.

The script reads no font file and changes nothing in the font. Chapter 118's script inspects the files and chapter 114's checks the font, and Friday's build ran both. This one trusts the log for that, and says so in its line: "by the log".

docs.title: Mira's Monday
docs.text:
She opens the layout program, sets a paragraph in each of the five weights, and prints it. The Light holds at 9 point. She types her name into the second line.

Then she writes to the art director, not the assistant. "Five of the nine weights are in Friday's folder: Light, Regular, Medium, SemiBold and Bold. Thin, ExtraLight, ExtraBold and Black need two new drawings of the whole alphabet, one lighter than the Light and one heavier than the Bold. I can start on those in January. The list in the folder says the same."

She types her name into the third line and runs the script once more:

  done      Text proof read on paper at 9 point (Ines, 18 Dec)
  done      Typed in the layout program (Mira, 21 Dec)
  done      Client told which weights are missing and why (Mira, 21 Dec)
Released.

Then she answers the assistant. "Yes. Five weights, and RELEASE.txt in the folder says which."

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Go into Friday's folder and move GGPlum-Medium.ttf to the desktop. Run:

Weights: 4 of 9 asked for

and, further down:

  OPEN      Medium: has .otf

and the last line counts one more open item. The file was there on Friday, when the build checked. The release script looks again, because a folder can change after a build, and a release is a claim about the folder as it is now. Put the file back.

Now copy GGPlum-Light.otf, in the same otf folder, and name the copy GGPlum-Thin.otf. Run:

  OPEN      Thin: has .otf

Thin has a reason for being absent, and here it's present. The script could have counted that as good news. It doesn't, because a file nobody meant to ship is a problem of its own: the client would install a Thin that's a Light under another name. Delete the copy.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A release list has three kinds of line: what's there, what's agreed to be missing and why, and what somebody still owes. A script can check the first kind on the disk, can keep the second kind from being forgotten, and can only hold a place for the third, with a name in it. A function that reads a value depends on what the value means, so when the build began to bump the version, "the folder for the font's version" stopped being the shipped one. Putting a part together takes few new ideas: several functions that return their lines and a count, and a main that adds up.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a fourth hand job, "Old version removed from the client's server", and watch the count of open items change.
  2. Print, under the first line, the date of the release taken from the folder's name. The first ten characters of folder.name are the date.
  3. Move BY_HAND out of the script into a text file in the export folder, one job to a line, with the name after a |. Read it with chapter 27's loop and split("|"). Which is better kept in the script, and which beside the fonts?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Five weights are out, with a list that says so. Part 7 turns around and looks at the scripts themselves. Mira is one of two people at Halfmoon who can run them, and the other is on holiday. Chapter 121 gives a script a window with a button, so that somebody who has never opened the Scripting panel can use it.

docs.title: Part 7: Tools
docs.text:
A tool for somebody who wasn't there when you made it.

Mira makes tools for other people.

It's week twenty-four, the week before Christmas. Oskar is on holiday until January, Mira has a train to catch, and Ines is alone with a font and a folder of scripts she has never run. A script you wrote for yourself can assume you know what it needs. A tool for somebody else has to ask for it, in a window, and has to behave when she clicks the wrong thing.

The first six chapters build a window: a label, buttons that do something, a box for a number, a layout that holds when the window is stretched, a list to pick from. The sixth is the chapter on classes, which the book has put off until now. A window with more than three things in it needs one.

The next five make the window into a tool. It becomes a panel that stays open beside the font, follows the glyph you're looking at, remembers its settings in a file, shows progress on a long job, and puts each click into Edit > Undo as one step.

Two chapters deliver it: into FontLab's menus, and then into a folder with an installer, for a studio in Porto that has never seen your disk.

Then five chapters look outward. You draw numbers on the Glyph window's canvas. You read a script written for another font editor and find out how much of it runs here. You write a report that runs in more than one editor. You run the Friday build from the Terminal with FontLab as the server, and you have FontLab photograph its own windows for the release notes.

Chapter 139 tests your functions with FontLab closed. Chapter 140 is Oskar's first morning back, and the list Mira wrote for him.

Oskar's sheet has no lines left. The work in this part comes from the people who now use Mira's scripts: Ines, Rita in Porto, Tove with her other editor, and a friend with a script from somewhere else.

Two chapters break the rule that every sample imports through fly, and each says why: chapter 137's script runs outside FontLab, and chapter 138 calls a tool Fly has no name for.

You need the practice copy of Plum as Part 6 left it, and Fly installed in FontLab 9. I ran nothing in this part in FontLab 9. Windows, panels, menus and the canvas are the things I could check least, and each chapter says what was computed outside FontLab and what you'll be the first to see. Chapter 139 is the exception: all of its output is real.

docs.title: 121. A window of your own
docs.text:
Tuesday of week twenty-four. Oskar is on holiday until January, and Mira has a train to catch on Thursday. That leaves Ines alone with a font, a publisher and a folder of scripts she has never run.

"Show me once," Ines says, and Mira opens the Scripting panel. Ines looks at it for a while. "No. I'm not going to type into that. If you want me to change a number, give me a box with the number in it. If you want me to run something, give me a button."

It's a fair request. Everything you've written so far is driven by text: you edit a name at the top of a script, you run it, you read what it prints. Chapter 39 added small boxes that ask one question and go away. A tool for somebody else needs more than that. It needs a window that stays on the screen, shows something, and waits to be clicked.

This chapter makes the window. It shows three facts about the open font, and it has a button that does nothing yet.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open, Fly installed, and the Scripting panel. Nothing in the font changes.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9. I ran the script in plain Python with stand-in widgets that record what was asked of them, and with the real code of the Fly function that shows the window. So I can tell you what the script asks for and in which order. I can't tell you what the window looks like on your screen.

docs.title: Step 1: The smallest window
docs.text:
Type this and run it:

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import qt

def build(parent):
    label = qt.QtGui.QLabel("Hello, Ines.", parent)
    label.setWindowFlags(qt.QtCore.Qt.Tool)
    return label

scripting.show_script_dialog(build, "tools.hello")

A small window should appear over FontLab with the words Hello, Ines. in it. Click in the Font window behind it. Select a glyph. FontLab answers, and the small window is still there. That is the difference from chapter 39, where nothing else responded until you clicked OK. Close the small window with its close button when you've seen enough.

Now the words. The whole of what you see on the screen, with its windows and buttons and menus, is called a graphical user interface, or GUI. Each thing in it is a widget: a piece of text is a widget, a button is a widget, the box you type a number into is a widget, and a window is a widget that holds other widgets. A widget is an object, so it's one more wardrobe with drawers, like the glyph in chapter 6. You make one, and then you open its drawers to tell it how to look and what to say.

FontLab is built with a kit of widgets called Qt, and Fly hands you the same kit as qt. You met it in chapter 39 as qt.QtGui, the drawer where the widgets are. qt.QtGui.QLabel makes a label, a piece of text that the user can read and can't change. Every name in the kit starts with a capital Q.

The label gets two things: its text, and parent. A parent is the widget that a new widget belongs to. Here the parent is FontLab's main window, and you don't have to find it: show_script_dialog calls your build function and passes the main window in.

A widget with a parent is normally drawn inside that parent. You don't want your text painted in a corner of FontLab's main window, so the next line says otherwise. setWindowFlags(qt.QtCore.Qt.Tool) turns the label into a small window of its own that floats over its parent. Tool is Qt's word for a little helper window.

docs.title: Step 2: Who shows it, and who keeps it
docs.text:
Look at the last line again:

scripting.show_script_dialog(build, "tools.hello")

You wrote build, not build(). You're handing over the function, and Fly calls it when it's ready. Chapter 39 did this with the "recipe card" for the file box, and chapter 119 kept whole lists of functions that way.

show_script_dialog does four things with it. It calls build with FontLab's main window. It asks for the window you returned to stay in front of other windows. It shows it. And it writes the window down in a list that lives as long as FontLab is open, under the name you gave as the second thing, "tools.hello".

Your script ends a moment after the window appears. Python tidies up after a script, and a window that nothing refers to any more can be thrown away with the rest. The list is what keeps yours. Chapter 127 looks at this properly.

The name has a second use. Run the script again without closing the window. You don't get two windows. Fly finds the old one under "tools.hello", closes it, and opens the new one. In my stand-in run the list held one window after two runs.

docs.title: Step 3: A program that waits
docs.text:
Add one line to the end of the script and run it:

print("The script has ended. The window hasn't.")

The Output panel shows the sentence, and the window is on the screen at the same time.

The script has ended. The window hasn't.

Here is what is going on. FontLab spends nearly all of its time waiting. When you click, press a key or move the mouse, it wakes up, works out which widget that was meant for, lets that widget do its job, and goes back to waiting. This round of wait, wake, work, wait is called the event loop, and every program with windows has one.

Until now your scripts were one piece of work inside one turn of that loop. You pressed Run, FontLab ran your lines from top to bottom, and only then went back to waiting. That is why a script that takes a minute makes FontLab look dead for a minute.

A window changes the bargain. The script builds the window, hands it over and ends. The window then belongs to FontLab's loop like any other. FontLab draws it, moves it when you drag it, and closes it when you click the close button, and none of your lines are running while it does. Your code will run again only when somebody clicks something you have connected to a function. That is chapter 122.

One rule follows, and I'll state it once. You never start a loop of your own, and you never create an "application" object, whatever a Qt tutorial on the web tells you to do. FontLab already has both. You make widgets and hand them over.

docs.title: Step 4: More than one widget
docs.text:
A label alone is a poor window. To hold two widgets you need a third, plain one to put them in, and something that arranges them:

def build(parent):
    panel = gui.QWidget(parent)
    panel.setWindowFlags(core.Qt.Tool)
    layout = gui.QVBoxLayout(panel)
    layout.addWidget(gui.QLabel("GG Plum", panel))
    layout.addWidget(gui.QPushButton("Look again", panel))
    return panel

QWidget is the plainest widget there is: an empty rectangle. It's the window now, so it takes the Tool flag. QVBoxLayout is a layout. You don't see a layout. It stacks the widgets you give it from top to bottom (the V is for vertical) and works out their sizes, so you never write a position in pixels. QPushButton is a button with its text. The label and the button both name panel as their parent, because that is where they live.

gui and core are short names, set once at the top of the script:

core, gui = qt.QtCore, qt.QtGui

Two names get two values in one line, the way chapter 35 gave four names to the four parts of a row.

docs.title: Step 5: The mistake
docs.text:
Mira wants it to be clear which of the two things in the brackets is the parent, so she names it, as she has named encoding="utf-8" and allow_bases=True a hundred times:

layout.addWidget(gui.QLabel(font_text(), parent=panel))

No window appears. The Output panel has a traceback that ends in a ValueError, and the message ends with the words called slot does not support kwargs. I didn't see that message myself. Fly's notes on Qt record it from FontLab 9, for labels, buttons, layouts and a dozen other widgets.

"Kwargs" is short for keyword arguments, the name=value kind. FontLab's Qt kit doesn't accept them, anywhere. Every value goes in by position, in the order the kit expects: the text first, the parent last.

layout.addWidget(gui.QLabel(font_text(), panel))

This will catch you again, because the rest of Python has taught you that naming an argument is the careful thing to do. With Qt widgets inside FontLab it's the one thing that never works.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Save this as hello_window.py in your Scripts folder.

#FLM: Hello Window
# Opens a small window that says which font is open.
# The button doesn't do anything yet. Chapter 122 wires it up.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt

core, gui = qt.QtCore, qt.QtGui
KEY = "tools.hello"


def font_text():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        return "No font is open."
    package = scripting.current_package()
    info = package.info
    version = f"{info.versionMajor}.{info.versionMinor:03d}"
    lines = [
        info.familyName,
        f"Version {version}",
        f"{len(font.glyphs)} glyphs, {len(package.masters)} masters",
    ]
    return "\n".join(lines)


def build(parent):
    panel = gui.QWidget(parent)
    panel.setWindowFlags(core.Qt.Tool)
    panel.setWindowTitle("Halfmoon")
    panel.setAttribute(core.Qt.WA_DeleteOnClose)
    layout = gui.QVBoxLayout(panel)
    layout.addWidget(gui.QLabel(font_text(), panel))
    layout.addWidget(gui.QPushButton("Look again", panel))
    return panel


scripting.show_script_dialog(build, KEY)
print("The script has ended. The window hasn't.")

font_text has nothing to do with windows. It builds a string from things you know: the family name and version from chapter 95 and chapter 97, the glyph count from chapter 4, the masters from chapter 101. Keeping it apart from build means you can test it with print(font_text()) and no window at all.

Two lines in build are new. setWindowTitle puts a word in the window's title bar. setAttribute(core.Qt.WA_DeleteOnClose) decides what the close button means. Without it, closing a window only hides it, and it goes on existing where nobody can see it. With it, a closed window is gone.

KEY is the name the window is kept under. Give every tool its own. A good habit is your studio's name, a dot, and the tool's name.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
With Plum-practice open, the script asked my stand-in for a window titled Halfmoon holding this text and a button marked Look again:

GG Plum
Version 1.004
274 glyphs, 3 masters

The version is 1.004 because Friday's build raised it after shipping 1.003. Your glyph count may differ from mine if your practice font does.

Close every font and run it again. The window says No font is open. That is the early return in font_text. A tool for somebody else is run in all the situations you would never put yourself in, and the first of them is always "nothing is open".

Mira calls Ines over. Ines reads the three lines and clicks Look again. The button goes down and comes up, and nothing happens. She clicks it again.

"It's not connected to anything yet," says Mira.

"Then why is it there?"

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Delete the line return panel and run the script.

AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'setWindowFlags'

Chapter 24 showed that a function with no return hands back None. build made a perfectly good window and then kept it to itself. Fly got None, tried to open one of its drawers, and Python refused. The traceback points into Fly's file, not yours, which is unhelpful, so remember the shape of this one: 'NoneType' object has no attribute right after you call somebody else's function with a function of your own usually means your function forgot to return. Put the line back.

Now change KEY to "tools.hello2" and run the script without closing the window. You have two windows. Fly looked for an old window under the new name, found none, and left the first alone. Close both and change the name back.

Last, with the window open, open another font and bring it to the front. The window still says GG Plum. It read the font once, while build ran, and a label doesn't know where its text came from. This is what the button is for.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A window is a widget that holds other widgets, and a layout arranges them so that you never write a position. Your script builds the window, hands it to show_script_dialog and ends, and from then on FontLab's event loop looks after it. The name you pass keeps the window alive and replaces an older window of the same tool. Inside FontLab, Qt widgets take their values by position only, never as name=value.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a second label under the first that shows the name of the font's file. The path is font.path, and chapter 26's Path(...).name cuts the folder off. Decide what it should say when the font has never been saved.
  2. Change QVBoxLayout to QHBoxLayout and run it. Describe in one sentence what the H stands for.
  3. Put the button first and the label second. You only need to swap two lines, and you never touch a position.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Ines has a window and a button that does nothing. Chapter 122 connects the button to a function, so that a click reads the font again.

docs.title: 122. Buttons do things
docs.text:
Wednesday of week twenty-four. Ines opens the window from chapter 121, opens another font, and clicks Look again. The window still says GG Plum. She clicks harder.

"It's broken."

"It isn't connected to anything," Mira says. "It's a picture of a button."

A button is a widget that knows it was clicked. What it doesn't know is what you want done about it. This chapter tells it, and adds a second button that runs a small report: which glyphs have no character.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open, Fly installed, and hello_window.py from chapter 121 to copy from. Nothing in the font changes.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9. I ran the script in plain Python with stand-in widgets, where a stand-in button can be "clicked" from code and hands its function one value, as FontLab's buttons are documented to do. The label texts below are what the script wrote into the stand-in label, for a font with the glyphs yours should have after Part 5.

docs.title: Step 1: A function without its brackets
docs.text:
Type this and run it:

def greeting():
    return "Hello, Ines."

print(greeting())
print(greeting)

Hello, Ines.
<function greeting at 0x1298f4c20>

The digits at the end will differ on your machine. The first print has brackets after the name, so Python calls the function and prints what comes back. The second has none, so Python doesn't call anything. It prints the function itself, the way it would print a list or a number.

A function is a value. You can put it in a box, put it in a list, or hand it to another function. You've done all three without my making a fuss. Chapter 39 handed run_file_dialog a function it should call later. Chapter 119 put ship_check.main in a list, without brackets, so that the build could call it when its turn came. Chapter 121 handed build to show_script_dialog.

The pattern is the same every time: here is a function, call it when you're ready. A button needs that from you.

docs.title: Step 2: Connect
docs.text:
A button has a drawer called clicked. It isn't a number or a text. It's a signal: a thing that happens, with a list of functions to call when it does. The list starts empty, which is why Ines's button did nothing. You add to it with connect:

def on_again():
    label.setText(font_text())

again.clicked.connect(on_again)

These lines go inside build, after the label and the button are made. setText replaces what a label shows. on_again has no brackets in the last line, for the reason in Step 1: you aren't calling it now, you're handing it over. A function connected to a signal is called a slot.

Nothing in your script calls on_again. FontLab's event loop does, each time the button is clicked, long after your script has ended. That is the bargain from chapter 121: your lines run again only when somebody does something to a widget of yours.

on_again uses label, and nobody hands it one. It's written inside build, so it can see build's boxes, as change could see set_width's in chapter 49. That is also why label and again now have names of their own. In chapter 121 you made the widgets and added them to the layout in one line each, because nothing needed to find them later.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Run the script with those lines in, and click Look again. In my stand-in run the label didn't change, and this came out instead:

TypeError: build.<locals>.on_again() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given

I can't tell you where FontLab shows that message, or whether it shows it at all. Look in the Output panel.

Somebody gave on_again a value it didn't ask for. It was the button. A signal can carry facts about what happened, and clicked carries one: whether the button is now checked, for the kind of button that stays pressed in. Yours isn't that kind, so the fact is always False, and it's handed over anyway.

You could write def on_again(checked): and ignore checked. But other signals carry two facts, or none, and the book's rule for slots is simpler than learning each one:

def on_again(*args):
    label.setText(font_text())

The star is new. A parameter with a star in front takes however many values arrive, none or one or five, and collects them in a tuple. The name args is a habit, not a keyword. This slot never looks inside it. Write every slot with *args and this mistake can't happen to you again.

docs.title: Step 4: A slot must not fall over
docs.text:
Chapter 100 wrapped each check in try, so that one broken check couldn't stop the others. A slot needs the same care for a different reason. When a script fails, you're sitting in front of the Scripting panel and the traceback is under your nose. When a slot fails, the person in front of the window is Ines, the panel may be closed, and from where she sits a button has stopped working.

So the slot catches whatever goes wrong and says so in the window:

def show(make_text):
    try:
        label.setText(make_text())
    except Exception as problem:
        label.setText(f"Didn't work.\n{type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")

show takes a function, calls it, and puts the answer in the label. If the function fails, the label gets the name of the error and its message, the two pieces chapter 119 wrote into the build log. Both buttons use show, each handing it a different function. That is Step 1 again: show(font_text), without brackets.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Save it as button_report.py in your Scripts folder.

#FLM: Button Report
# A small window with two buttons. One reads the font again,
# the other counts the glyphs that have no character.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt

core, gui = qt.QtCore, qt.QtGui
KEY = "tools.report"
SHOWN = 8


def font_text():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        return "No font is open."
    package = scripting.current_package()
    info = package.info
    version = f"{info.versionMajor}.{info.versionMinor:03d}"
    lines = [
        info.familyName,
        f"Version {version}",
        f"{len(font.glyphs)} glyphs, {len(package.masters)} masters",
    ]
    return "\n".join(lines)


def bare_text():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        return "No font is open."
    names = [glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs if glyph.unicode is None]
    lines = [f"{len(names)} glyphs have no character."]
    lines += names[:SHOWN]
    if len(names) > SHOWN:
        lines += [f"and {len(names) - SHOWN} more"]
    return "\n".join(lines)


def build(parent):
    panel = gui.QWidget(parent)
    panel.setWindowFlags(core.Qt.Tool)
    panel.setWindowTitle("Halfmoon")
    panel.setAttribute(core.Qt.WA_DeleteOnClose)
    label = gui.QLabel(font_text(), panel)
    again = gui.QPushButton("Look again", panel)
    bare = gui.QPushButton("No character", panel)

    def show(make_text):
        try:
            label.setText(make_text())
        except Exception as problem:
            label.setText(f"Didn't work.\n{type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")

    def on_again(*args):
        show(font_text)

    def on_bare(*args):
        show(bare_text)

    again.clicked.connect(on_again)
    bare.clicked.connect(on_bare)
    layout = gui.QVBoxLayout(panel)
    layout.addWidget(label)
    layout.addWidget(again)
    layout.addWidget(bare)
    return panel


scripting.show_script_dialog(build, KEY)

bare_text is new, and there's nothing new in it. glyph.unicode is None is chapter 115's test for a glyph without a character. SHOWN caps the list, because a label that tries to show thirty-nine names is taller than Ines's screen. lines += names[:SHOWN] adds the first eight, with the slice from chapter 10.

The two slots are two lines each, and they look as if they could be one function. They can't yet. Each must remember which text to make, and a slot is called with a False and nothing else. Chapter 126 gives you a tidier place to keep such things.

The key is a new one, "tools.report". With chapter 121's key, running this script would close that chapter's window. With its own key, the two can be open side by side.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
The window opens with the three lines you know. Click No character:

39 glyphs have no character.
.notdef
a.sc
b.sc
c.sc
d.sc
e.sc
f.sc
g.sc
and 31 more

Now do what Ines did. Open another font and click Look again. For the second font, my stand-in played one of Oskar's:

Oskar Grotesk
Version 2.010
412 glyphs, 2 masters

Click No character again and the report is about that font:

3 glyphs have no character.
.notdef
f_i
f_l

Each click asks fl.CurrentFont() afresh. The window holds no font. It holds a label and two functions that go and look. Between the clicks it shows whatever the last click wrote, which is why, for a moment after you switched fonts, the label was about the wrong one. Chapter 128 deals with that.

Close every font and click Look again. The label says No font is open., because font_text checks before it reads, and the window stays up.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Put brackets where they don't belong:

again.clicked.connect(on_again())

Run the script. Now Python calls on_again on the spot, while the window is being built, and hands connect what came back, which is None. In my stand-in the window opened, and Look again was a picture of a button again. FontLab may refuse a None with an error instead; I haven't seen which. Either way the brackets turned "call this later" into "call this now". Take them out.

Then break the report. In bare_text, change glyph.unicode to glyph.unicod, run, and click No character:

Didn't work.
AttributeError: 'flGlyph' object has no attribute 'unicod'

The window is still there and Look again still works. The spelling of the object's type is my guess at what FontLab will print; the rest is from the run. Without the try in show, Ines would have seen nothing happen. Put the letter back.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A function's name without brackets is the function itself, a value you can hand to something that will call it later. A button's clicked is a signal, and connect adds a function to the list it calls on each click. A slot is written with *args, which accepts whatever the signal hands over. A slot catches its own errors and reports them in the window, because the person who clicked can't see a traceback.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a third button, Suffixes, that shows how many glyphs have a dot in their name, and the first eight of them. Write suffix_text, write on_suffix, connect it, add the button to the layout.
  2. Inside on_again, add print(args) as the first line. Click the button and read the Output panel. You should see a tuple with one False in it.
  3. Make No character count its own clicks. Put count = [0] in build, and in on_bare add one to count[0] and print it. Then try it with count = 0 and count += 1, and read the error. A function inside a function can read the outer boxes, and it can change what is in a list it finds there, but it can't put a new value in the box itself.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Ines can click. She still can't say how much. Chapter 123 puts a field for a number in the window, reads it when a button is clicked, and deals with what happens when the field holds something that isn't a number.

docs.title: 123. Ask for a number
docs.text:
Wednesday afternoon, week twenty-four. Ines has a page of the catalog on her screen, set in the Regular, and three letters on it look tight to her: n, o and H.

"Give them some air. Both sides."

"How much?"

"I don't know yet. Ten? Show me ten."

In Part 4 Mira would have opened set_sidebearings.py, changed two numbers at the top, and run it. Ines won't do that, and from tomorrow Mira isn't here. So the numbers have to move out of the script and into the window: a field for the glyph names, a field for each side, a tick box that says "don't change anything yet", and a button.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open with the Font window in front and the Regular master showing, Fly installed, and button_report.py from chapter 122 to copy from. This chapter changes sidebearings, so save the font first.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9. I ran the script in plain Python with stand-in widgets whose fields I could fill from code, and a stand-in font that holds Plum's sidebearings. The numbers below are Plum's Regular as it shipped. If Part 4 left yours different, your first three numbers on each line will differ and the sums will still hold.

docs.title: Step 1: A field, and what's in it
docs.text:
A field you can type in is a widget called QLineEdit. Take chapter 122's build, cut it down to one field, one button and one label, and make the button show what the field holds:

def read(owner, name):
    item = getattr(owner, name)
    return item() if callable(item) else item


def build(parent):
    panel = gui.QWidget(parent)
    amount = gui.QLineEdit("12", panel)
    go = gui.QPushButton("Shift", panel)
    label = gui.QLabel("", panel)

    def on_go(*args):
        label.setText(read(amount, "text"))

    go.clicked.connect(on_go)
    layout = gui.QVBoxLayout(panel)
    layout.addWidget(amount)
    layout.addWidget(go)
    layout.addWidget(label)
    return panel

The field opens with 12 in it, because that's the first thing handed to QLineEdit. Click Shift and the label says 12. Type 8 over it, click, and the label says 8.

The new piece is read. A field keeps what you typed under the name text. In some versions of the Qt that FontLab carries, amount.text is the text itself, and in others it's a function you call to get the text. read takes either. getattr, from chapter 95, fetches whatever sits under that name. callable is a built-in function that answers True when the thing you hand it can be called with brackets. If it can, read calls it, and if not, read hands it back as it is. The scripts that come with Fly carry the same four lines, and from here on so does every window in this book.

Notice when the reading happens: inside on_go. The field is read at the moment of the click, each time. If you read it once in build, you'd get 12 forever, because build runs before anybody has typed.

docs.title: Step 2: The mistake
docs.text:
Ten units on a width of 523. Change on_go to do the sum:

def on_go(*args):
    label.setText(str(523 + read(amount, "text")))

Click, and nothing happens. There's no try in this slot yet, so the error went wherever FontLab sends errors from slots, which I haven't seen. Chapter 122 said what to do about that. Wrap it:

def on_go(*args):
    try:
        label.setText(str(523 + read(amount, "text")))
    except Exception as problem:
        label.setText(f"{type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")

TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'

Chapter 23 used int to read text, and this is where you need it. What comes out of a field is text, always, even when every character in it is a digit. "12" is two characters. Had you written the sum the other way about, text plus text, Python would have said nothing and given you "1212".

int reads text as a whole number, so 523 + int(read(amount, "text")) gives 535. Then Ines types a lot:

ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'a lot'

The same for 12.5, and the same for a field with nothing in it. You could catch the ValueError and write a kinder message, as ask_factor did in chapter 68. But look at what you'd be doing: letting a person type anything, then telling them off for it. A field that can't hold anything but a whole number would be kinder still.

docs.title: Step 3: A field that only holds numbers
docs.text:
That widget is QSpinBox. It shows a number with two small arrows beside it. You can type digits into it or click the arrows, and it won't accept a letter.

left = gui.QSpinBox(panel)
left.setRange(-200, 200)

setRange says how far the number may go each way. A spin box keeps its number under the name value, and it's a number already:

def on_go(*args):
    label.setText(str(523 + read(left, "value")))

No int, no try for bad text, and nothing for Ines to get wrong. That's the idea to keep from this chapter: choose the widget so that the wrong answer can't be typed. Use a line edit when the answer is words, as it will be for the glyph names.

docs.title: Step 4: Yes or no
docs.text:
Every script in this book that changes a font has had a DRY_RUN line since chapter 31. In a window, that line is a tick box, a QCheckBox:

rehearse = gui.QCheckBox("Only show what would happen", panel)
rehearse.setChecked(True)

The text is its label, and setChecked(True) makes it open with the tick already in. It keeps its state under the name checked, and read(rehearse, "checked") gives True or False. Starting with the tick in means a first click shows numbers and changes nothing.

So three kinds of field give three kinds of value: text from a line edit, a whole number from a spin box, True or False from a tick box.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Save this in your Scripts folder as shift_dialog.py:

#FLM: Shift Dialog
# Adds to the sidebearings of the glyphs you name, or of the ones
# selected in the Font window, in the master that's showing.
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.metrics.panel.model as metrics
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

core, gui = qt.QtCore, qt.QtGui
KEY = "tools.shift"
LIMIT = 200
SHOWN = 8


def read(owner, name):
    item = getattr(owner, name)
    return item() if callable(item) else item


def plan_rows(font, master, names, left, right):
    rows = []
    for name in names:
        if font[name] is None:
            raise ValueError(f"No glyph called {name}.")
        rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
        old = (rich.getLSB(master), rich.getAdvance(master), rich.getRSB(master))
        new = (old[0] + left, old[1] + left + right, old[2] + right)
        rows.append((rich, layer_of(rich.fl, master), old, new))
    return rows


def shift(text, left, right, rehearse):
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        return "No font is open."
    package = scripting.current_package()
    master = package.master
    names = text.split()
    if not names:
        names = scripting.names_selected_names()
    if not names:
        return "Type some glyph names, or select glyphs in the Font window."
    rows = plan_rows(font, master, names, left, right)
    lines = [f"{rich.name}: {old[0]} {old[1]} {old[2]} to {new[0]} {new[1]} {new[2]}"
             for rich, layer, old, new in rows[:SHOWN]]
    if len(rows) > SHOWN:
        lines += [f"and {len(rows) - SHOWN} more"]
    if rehearse:
        return "\n".join(lines + [f"{master}: {len(rows)} would change."])

    def change():
        for rich, layer, old, new in rows:
            metrics.shift_and_set(layer, left, new[1])

    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    layers = [layer for rich, layer, old, new in rows]
    owners = [rich.fl for rich, layer, old, new in rows]
    history.commit("Shift sidebearings", layers, owners, change,
                   operation="geometry", facts=facts, allow_bases=True)
    return "\n".join(lines + [f"{master}: {len(rows)} changed."])


def build(parent):
    panel = gui.QWidget(parent)
    panel.setWindowFlags(core.Qt.Tool)
    panel.setWindowTitle("Shift")
    panel.setAttribute(core.Qt.WA_DeleteOnClose)
    names = gui.QLineEdit("", panel)
    left = gui.QSpinBox(panel)
    left.setRange(-LIMIT, LIMIT)
    right = gui.QSpinBox(panel)
    right.setRange(-LIMIT, LIMIT)
    rehearse = gui.QCheckBox("Only show what would happen", panel)
    rehearse.setChecked(True)
    go = gui.QPushButton("Shift", panel)
    label = gui.QLabel("", panel)

    def on_go(*args):
        try:
            label.setText(shift(read(names, "text"), read(left, "value"),
                                read(right, "value"), read(rehearse, "checked")))
        except Exception as problem:
            label.setText(f"Didn't work.\n{type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")

    go.clicked.connect(on_go)
    layout = gui.QVBoxLayout(panel)
    layout.addWidget(gui.QLabel("Glyphs", panel))
    layout.addWidget(names)
    layout.addWidget(gui.QLabel("Left", panel))
    layout.addWidget(left)
    layout.addWidget(gui.QLabel("Right", panel))
    layout.addWidget(right)
    layout.addWidget(rehearse)
    layout.addWidget(go)
    layout.addWidget(label)
    return panel


scripting.show_script_dialog(build, KEY)

It's the longest listing in a while, and most of it is old. Read it in three parts.

plan_rows is chapter 62's arithmetic. For each name it measures the three numbers, and works out the three new ones: the left side grows by left, the right by right, and the width by both. A name that isn't in the font stops everything with a raise, as in chapter 97.

shift knows nothing about windows. It takes text, two numbers and a yes-or-no, and gives back the text for the label. An empty names field means "use the glyphs selected in the Font window", which is chapter 15's names_selected_names. When nothing is selected there either, that helper falls back to the current glyph. package.master is the master that's showing, from chapter 101. The change itself is chapter 62's: shift_and_set moves the outline by left and sets the new width, inside one history.commit, with allow_bases=True for the reason chapter 55 gave. One click, one step in Edit > Undo.

build is the only part that knows about widgets. It makes them, and on_go reads all four at the moment of the click and hands plain values to shift. Keeping the two apart costs nothing now and pays in chapter 139, when you'll test plan_rows without a window or a font.

The small labels Glyphs, Left and Right are made inside addWidget, with no box to keep them in, because nothing will ever read them again.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Run the script. A window titled Shift opens: three fields stacked with their labels, a tick box, a button. Type n o H in the first field, set both numbers to 10, leave the tick in, and click Shift:

n: 70 523 66 to 80 543 76
o: 38 520 38 to 48 540 48
H: 76 672 70 to 86 692 80
Regular: 3 would change.

Each line reads left side, width, right side, before and after. Ines looks at the numbers, nods, takes the tick out, and clicks again. The last line now says Regular: 3 changed. She looks at her page. It's better. She clicks once more, by accident:

n: 80 543 76 to 90 563 86
o: 48 540 48 to 58 560 58
H: 86 692 80 to 96 712 90
Regular: 3 changed.

The window is still open and still armed, so a second click did the job a second time. Edit > Undo, once, takes back the second click, and the n is at 80, 543, 76 again. Each click was one step. Chapter 131 comes back to this: a tool that people use without reading should be harder to fire twice.

Now type n zz in the names field and click:

Didn't work.
ValueError: No glyph called zz.

Nothing changed, not even the n, because plan_rows reads every name before shift touches anything.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Delete the line left.setRange(-LIMIT, LIMIT) and run the script again. Try to type -10 into Left. The minus sign won't go in. A spin box that hasn't been told its range allows 0 to 99, so Ines could widen and never tighten. The other field still takes -10. Put the line back.

Then, in on_go, change read(left, "value") to read(left, "text"). A spin box has a text as well, the digits as it shows them. Set 10 and 10, type n o H, click:

Didn't work.
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'

It's Step 2's error, reached from a widget that was meant to make it impossible. The widget keeps letters out of the field, but the script still has to ask it for the number and not for the text. Change it back.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A line edit holds text, a spin box holds a whole number within a range, and a tick box holds True or False; read fetches each by name. A slot reads its fields at the moment of the click, never earlier. Pick the widget that can't hold a wrong answer, and you write less checking. Keep the function that does the work free of widgets, so that it takes plain values and gives back text.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a second tick box, Both sides the same. When it's ticked, on_go should hand shift the left number twice and ignore the right field.
  2. Make the last line of a rehearsal say how much wider the glyphs get in total: for the run above, Regular: 3 would change, 60 units wider.
  3. Type n n in the names field with the tick in, and read the two lines. Then decide what the tool should do about a name given twice, and make shift do it. A set, from chapter 25, loses the order; a loop that skips names it has seen keeps it.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The tool works, and it looks like a pile: label, field, label, field, a button as wide as the window. Ines says it's ugly, and she's the one who lays out pages for a living. Chapter 124 arranges it in rows and columns.

docs.title: 124. Lay it out
docs.text:
Thursday morning of week twenty-four. Mira's train leaves at noon. Ines has the Shift window open beside a page proof, and she's looking at the window the way she looks at a page somebody else set.

"Nine things in a column," she says. "The word Left has a whole line to itself. The button is as wide as a headline."

She takes a pencil and draws what she'd have made: the names field with its word beside it, the two numbers side by side, the tick box and the button sharing the bottom line, and the answer underneath.

"That," says Mira, "is three boxes inside a box. You've drawn the program."

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open with the Regular showing, Fly installed, and shift_dialog.py from chapter 123. The script does the same work as yesterday. Only the arrangement changes.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9. I ran the script in plain Python with stand-in widgets and stand-in layouts that record what was put into what, and the trees printed below come from those records. I can't show you how the window looks, and I won't describe pixels I haven't seen. The two warning texts in this chapter are Qt's own, written from memory.

docs.title: Step 1: Read the pencil sketch
docs.text:
Here is Ines's drawing, as an outline:

column
    form:  Glyphs + names field
    row:   Left, left box, Right, right box
    row:   tick box, Shift button
    answer label

A layout is an object that owns a strip of the window and decides where the things in it go. You met one in chapter 121: QVBoxLayout, where the V is for vertical. It stacks. Yesterday you gave it nine widgets and it stacked nine.

There are two more kinds in the sketch. QHBoxLayout, H for horizontal, puts things side by side. If you did chapter 121's second exercise, you've tried it. QFormLayout makes lines of a word and a field, with the words lined up on one edge.

The new idea is the indentation in the outline. A layout can hold widgets, and it can hold other layouts. You've seen this shape before. Chapter 35 put lists inside a list to make a table, and the outer list didn't care what its rows held. It's the same here: the column holds four things, and three of them happen to be layouts with things of their own.

docs.title: Step 2: One row
docs.text:
Open shift_dialog.py and find the end of build, where the layout is made. Change the part that adds the tick box and the button:

    bottom = gui.QHBoxLayout()
    bottom.addWidget(rehearse)
    bottom.addWidget(go)
    layout.addLayout(bottom)

Those four lines replace layout.addWidget(rehearse) and layout.addWidget(go). Run the script.

Look at the first line. Yesterday's layout was made with gui.QVBoxLayout(panel), and the panel in the brackets meant "you are this panel's layout". This one has empty brackets. It belongs to nobody yet. The last line gives it a home: addLayout puts a layout into a layout, as addWidget puts a widget into one.

In my stand-in, the record now reads:

VBox (column)
  Label 'Glyphs'
  LineEdit
  Label 'Left'
  SpinBox
  Label 'Right'
  SpinBox
  HBox (row)
    CheckBox 'Only show what would happen'
    PushButton 'Shift'
  Label ''

Seven things in the column where there were nine, and one of the seven is a row with two things in it.

docs.title: Step 3: A row and a form
docs.text:
Do the same for the two numbers. Their labels have to be made first, since a row can only hold what exists:

    sides = gui.QHBoxLayout()
    sides.addWidget(gui.QLabel("Left", panel))
    sides.addWidget(left)
    sides.addWidget(gui.QLabel("Right", panel))
    sides.addWidget(right)
    layout.addLayout(sides)

These replace the four lines that added Left, left, Right and right to the column.

The names field gets the third kind of layout:

    form = gui.QFormLayout()
    form.addRow("Glyphs", names)
    layout.addLayout(form)

addRow takes the word and the field together. You hand it plain text, and it makes the label for you and stands it beside the field. So the two lines that added a Glyphs label and names go, and no QLabel is written for this line at all. A form with one line may look like a lot of machinery. It earns its place when the tool grows a second field, since every word in a form lines up with the others, and a row of loose labels doesn't.

The order of the addLayout lines is the order down the window. Put the form first, then sides, then bottom, then the answer label.

docs.title: Step 4: The mistake
docs.text:
You'll write this one sooner or later, since it's one word of habit. Change the form's first line to match the way the column was made:

    form = gui.QFormLayout(panel)

Run it. My stand-in, which copies what Qt does here, prints the line below. I expect it in the Output panel, though I haven't seen where FontLab puts Qt's own complaints:

QLayout: Attempting to add QLayout "" to QWidget "", which already has a layout

Which layout is turned away depends on which was made first. In your script as it stands the column came first, so the form is the one refused, and I haven't seen what the window does with a refused form. In the finished script below the form is made before the column. There the form takes the panel and the column is refused, and my record showed a panel whose whole layout was this:

Form (form)
  'Glyphs' + LineEdit

One line in the window, and the rest of the widgets left with no place. Nothing stops, and no traceback appears. It's a warning, printed once, about a window that looks wrong.

A panel has one layout. That one is the outermost box of the sketch, and it's the only one that gets the panel in its brackets. Every other layout is made with empty brackets and is put into its parent with addLayout. Take panel out of the form's brackets again.

docs.title: Step 5: Give the arranging a function of its own
docs.text: build now does three jobs: it makes the widgets, it wires the button, and it arranges. The arranging is the part you'll change most often, each time somebody like Ines looks at the window. Move it into a function named for the job, and build gets shorter and the sketch gets one place to live.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Shift Dialog
# Adds to the sidebearings of the glyphs you name, or of the ones
# selected in the Font window, in the master that's showing.
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.metrics.panel.model as metrics
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

core, gui = qt.QtCore, qt.QtGui
KEY = "tools.shift"
LIMIT = 200
SHOWN = 8


def read(owner, name):
    item = getattr(owner, name)
    return item() if callable(item) else item


def plan_rows(font, master, names, left, right):
    rows = []
    for name in names:
        if font[name] is None:
            raise ValueError(f"No glyph called {name}.")
        rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
        old = (rich.getLSB(master), rich.getAdvance(master), rich.getRSB(master))
        new = (old[0] + left, old[1] + left + right, old[2] + right)
        rows.append((rich, layer_of(rich.fl, master), old, new))
    return rows


def shift(text, left, right, rehearse):
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        return "No font is open."
    package = scripting.current_package()
    master = package.master
    names = text.split()
    if not names:
        names = scripting.names_selected_names()
    if not names:
        return "Type some glyph names, or select glyphs in the Font window."
    rows = plan_rows(font, master, names, left, right)
    lines = [f"{rich.name}: {old[0]} {old[1]} {old[2]} to {new[0]} {new[1]} {new[2]}"
             for rich, layer, old, new in rows[:SHOWN]]
    if len(rows) > SHOWN:
        lines += [f"and {len(rows) - SHOWN} more"]
    if rehearse:
        return "\n".join(lines + [f"{master}: {len(rows)} would change."])

    def change():
        for rich, layer, old, new in rows:
            metrics.shift_and_set(layer, left, new[1])

    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    layers = [layer for rich, layer, old, new in rows]
    owners = [rich.fl for rich, layer, old, new in rows]
    history.commit("Shift sidebearings", layers, owners, change,
                   operation="geometry", facts=facts, allow_bases=True)
    return "\n".join(lines + [f"{master}: {len(rows)} changed."])


def arrange(panel, names, left, right, rehearse, go, label):
    form = gui.QFormLayout()
    form.addRow("Glyphs", names)

    sides = gui.QHBoxLayout()
    sides.addWidget(gui.QLabel("Left", panel))
    sides.addWidget(left)
    sides.addWidget(gui.QLabel("Right", panel))
    sides.addWidget(right)

    bottom = gui.QHBoxLayout()
    bottom.addWidget(rehearse)
    bottom.addWidget(go)

    outer = gui.QVBoxLayout(panel)
    outer.addLayout(form)
    outer.addLayout(sides)
    outer.addLayout(bottom)
    outer.addWidget(label)


def build(parent):
    panel = gui.QWidget(parent)
    panel.setWindowFlags(core.Qt.Tool)
    panel.setWindowTitle("Shift")
    panel.setAttribute(core.Qt.WA_DeleteOnClose)
    label = gui.QLabel("", panel)
    names = gui.QLineEdit("", panel)
    left = gui.QSpinBox(panel)
    left.setRange(-LIMIT, LIMIT)
    right = gui.QSpinBox(panel)
    right.setRange(-LIMIT, LIMIT)
    rehearse = gui.QCheckBox("Only show what would happen", panel)
    rehearse.setChecked(True)
    go = gui.QPushButton("Shift", panel)

    def on_go(*args):
        try:
            label.setText(shift(read(names, "text"), read(left, "value"),
                                read(right, "value"), read(rehearse, "checked")))
        except Exception as problem:
            label.setText(f"Didn't work.\n{type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")

    go.clicked.connect(on_go)
    arrange(panel, names, left, right, rehearse, go, label)
    return panel


scripting.show_script_dialog(build, KEY)

Save it. read, plan_rows and shift haven't changed by a character since chapter 123, which is what keeping them apart from the window bought you.

arrange reads like the pencil sketch, top to bottom: a form, a row, another row, and then the column that holds all three and the label. The inner layouts are made first, since the column can't be handed a row that doesn't exist yet. Only outer has panel in its brackets.

build makes the widgets, connects the button, and then calls arrange with all seven of them. Seven arguments is a long list, and you have to keep the order straight in two places. Leave it for now. Chapter 126 has a better home for a window's widgets than a line of arguments.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Run the script. My stand-in's record of the finished window:

VBox (column)
  Form (form)
    'Glyphs' + LineEdit
  HBox (row)
    Label 'Left'
    SpinBox
    Label 'Right'
    SpinBox
  HBox (row)
    CheckBox 'Only show what would happen'
    PushButton 'Shift'
  Label ''

Hold it against the outline in Step 1. Four things in the column, in Ines's order.

Type n o H in the names field, put 10 in both boxes, leave the tick in, and click Shift:

n: 70 523 66 to 80 543 76
o: 38 520 38 to 48 540 48
H: 76 672 70 to 86 692 80
Regular: 3 would change.

The same answer as yesterday, for a font in the state Plum ships in. The arrangement has nothing to do with the arithmetic.

Ines pulls the window wider by its corner and watches. What I'd expect, and haven't seen, is that the names field takes the extra room and the button doesn't. Try it and note what each widget does. A layout decides that as well, and it's the reason to use one instead of telling each widget where to sit.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
In arrange, add a line that puts the left box into the bottom row as well:

    bottom.addWidget(go)
    bottom.addWidget(left)

Run it. In my stand-in, which again copies Qt:

QLayout::addChildWidget: QSpinBox "" is already in a layout; moved to new layout

and the record shows what "moved" means:

  HBox (row)
    Label 'Left'
    Label 'Right'
    SpinBox
  HBox (row)
    CheckBox 'Only show what would happen'
    PushButton 'Shift'
    SpinBox

The left box has gone from its row and sits after the button. A widget is one thing in one place. Adding it a second time doesn't copy it. If you want two boxes, make two. Take the line out.

Then take out a different line: delete outer.addWidget(label), run, and click Shift. In my record the label is in no layout at all. It still exists and it still gets the answer, so what Qt does is draw it where a widget with no layout goes, in the panel's top corner, across whatever is there. I haven't seen how that looks in FontLab. When text turns up on top of a field, look for the widget you made and never added. Put the line back.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A layout owns part of a window and places what's in it: QVBoxLayout in a column, QHBoxLayout in a row, QFormLayout in lines of a word and a field. Layouts go inside layouts with addLayout, the way chapter 35's lists went inside a list, and a pencil sketch of boxes in boxes is the plan. A panel has one layout, the outermost, and only that one is made with the panel in its brackets. A widget lives in one layout, and one that's in none is drawn in the corner.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Swap the two rows so the tick box and the button come before the numbers. Before you run it, write the outline you expect, as in Step 1. It's two lines of arrange.
  2. Move Left and Right into the form: two more addRow lines, and sides goes. Count the layouts in the outline now. Decide which arrangement you'd give Ines, and why.
  3. Put the answer label beside the widgets and not under them. The panel's layout becomes a row, with two things in it: a column holding the form and the two rows, and the label. Remember which layout gets panel.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Ines is content with the window and not with the names field. She has typed n o H four times this morning and ncaron wrong twice. Chapter 125 takes some of the typing away: the window reads the font, finds the suffixes in its glyph names, and offers them in a list to pick from.

docs.title: 125. Lists and choices
docs.text:
Thursday, eleven o'clock. Mira's bag is by the door and her train is at noon. Ines has the Shift window open and is typing a.ss01 g.ss01 y.ss01 into the names field for the third time.

"Why am I telling it what's in the font? It has the font."

She's right. A field is for things only the person knows, like how many units to add. The glyph names are already in the file, and a window that makes you type them is asking you to do its reading for it. Today's window reads the font, works out which suffixes its glyph names carry, and offers them in a list to pick from. Pick one and it shows the glyphs that have it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open, Fly installed, and shift_dialog.py from chapter 124 to copy from. Today's script changes nothing in the font.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9. I ran the script in plain Python with stand-in widgets, for a font with the glyphs yours should have after Part 5. The two widgets that are new today are used the same way in the tools that come with Fly, so the calls are copied from working code, but I haven't watched them work.

docs.title: Step 1: Group the names
docs.text:
Before any window, the data. You want a dictionary with one key for each suffix, and under each key the list of glyph names that end in it. That's the grouping from chapter 100 again:

from fly import fl


def by_suffix(names):
    groups = {}
    for name in names:
        parts = name.split(".")
        if len(parts) < 2 or parts[0] == "":
            continue
        suffix = parts[-1]
        if suffix not in groups:
            groups[suffix] = []
        groups[suffix].append(name)
    return groups


font = fl.CurrentFont()
groups = by_suffix([glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs])
for suffix in sorted(groups):
    print(suffix, len(groups[suffix]))

dnom 10
numr 10
sc 10
ss01 4
zero 1

split(".") is from chapter 9. It cuts a.sc into ["a", "sc"], and it leaves a name without a dot in one piece, so len(parts) < 2 means "no suffix here". The second half of that line is for one glyph. .notdef splits into ["", "notdef"]: an empty piece, then the name. Its dot is at the front and belongs to the name, so the function skips it.

parts[-1] is the last piece, from chapter 10. A name can carry two suffixes, as A.ss01.alt would, and this script files the glyph under the last one.

Notice that by_suffix takes a list of names and gives back a dictionary. It doesn't know there's a font, and it will never know there's a window. That's the habit from chapter 123: the part that thinks stays apart from the part that shows.

docs.title: Step 2: Empty the box and fill it again
docs.text:
The window will need to do this more than once. Ines adds a glyph, clicks Look again, and the groups have to be rebuilt. The plain way to rebuild is groups = by_suffix(...), and inside build that won't work. The reason is a rule that chapter 122's third exercise ran into: a function inside a function can change what's in a box it finds outside, but it can't put a new box there.

So the script keeps one dictionary for the whole life of the window and changes what's in it. Two new methods do that:

groups = {"sc": ["a.sc", "b.sc"]}
groups.clear()
print(groups)
groups.update({"ss01": ["a.ss01"], "zero": ["zero.zero"]})
print(groups)

{}
{'ss01': ['a.ss01'], 'zero': ['zero.zero']}

clear takes everything out and leaves the same dictionary, empty. update takes another dictionary and copies each of its keys and values in. Together they say: empty the box, then fill it from this. You'll use the same two moves three times today, on the dictionary, on the list of choices and on the list of names, and every time in that order.

docs.title: Step 3: A box of choices
docs.text:
A QComboBox is the widget that shows one choice and drops open to show the rest when you click it. You fill it from a list of texts with addItems, and you ask what it's showing with currentText:

choice = gui.QComboBox(panel)
choice.addItems(sorted(groups))
print(read(choice, "currentText"))

dnom

That fragment belongs inside a build, where panel exists. sorted(groups) gives the dictionary's keys in order, as it has since chapter 43. The box shows the first one until somebody picks another. read is the small function from chapter 123, here because I can't tell you from source alone whether currentText is a value or a function in FontLab's Qt.

The point of this widget is what it can't do. A field lets Ines type ss1 or SS01 or .ss01, and then your script has to decide what she meant. A box of choices holds only what the font holds. You've stopped checking the answer and started limiting the question, which is the same thing the number box did for you in chapter 123.

docs.title: Step 4: The mistake
docs.text:
Now the function that fills the box, written the way I first wrote it:

def fill_choice():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    groups.clear()
    if font is not None:
        groups.update(by_suffix([glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs]))
    choice.addItems(sorted(groups))

It opens well: five suffixes. Click Look again and open the box:

dnom
numr
sc
ss01
zero
dnom
numr
sc
ss01
zero

Click again and there are fifteen. No error, no message, and each click makes it worse.

addItems adds. It does what its name says and has no idea that these are the same five as before. The dictionary got its clear and the box didn't. The cure is one line before the filling:

    choice.clear()
    choice.addItems(sorted(groups))

Whenever you fill a widget from data, ask what was in it before. If the answer isn't "nothing", empty it first.

docs.title: Step 5: The list, and the signal that fills it
docs.text:
The glyph names go in a QListWidget, a box of rows with a scroll bar when there are too many to show. It fills one row at a time, and each row is a small object of its own, a QListWidgetItem, made from the text:

def fill_list():
    names = groups.get(read(choice, "currentText"), [])
    listing.clear()
    for name in names:
        listing.addItem(gui.QListWidgetItem(name))
    label.setText(f"{len(names)} with this suffix.")

Empty, then fill, as before. groups.get(..., []) is chapter 22's careful lookup: if the box of choices is empty, its text is "", there's no such key, and you get an empty list back with no complaint.

What should call fill_list? Not a button. Ines has already said what she wants by picking, and a second click to confirm it would be the window being slow on purpose. The box of choices has a signal for this, currentIndexChanged, which fires whenever the choice it shows becomes a different one:

choice.currentIndexChanged.connect(on_pick)

It's chapter 122's connect with another signal's name in front. And here is something useful: filling the box also changes what it shows, from nothing to its first choice. So the signal fires when fill_choice runs, and the list fills itself. One function fills the choices, the choices fill the list, and nothing in the script has to remember to do both.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Suffix Picker
# Lists the suffixes in the font's glyph names and shows the glyphs
# that carry the one you pick. Changes nothing.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt

core, gui = qt.QtCore, qt.QtGui
KEY = "tools.suffixes"


def read(owner, name):
    item = getattr(owner, name)
    return item() if callable(item) else item


def by_suffix(names):
    groups = {}
    for name in names:
        parts = name.split(".")
        if len(parts) < 2 or parts[0] == "":
            continue
        suffix = parts[-1]
        if suffix not in groups:
            groups[suffix] = []
        groups[suffix].append(name)
    return groups


def build(parent):
    panel = gui.QWidget(parent)
    panel.setWindowFlags(core.Qt.Tool)
    panel.setWindowTitle("Suffixes")
    panel.setAttribute(core.Qt.WA_DeleteOnClose)
    groups = {}
    choice = gui.QComboBox(panel)
    listing = gui.QListWidget(panel)
    again = gui.QPushButton("Look again", panel)
    label = gui.QLabel("", panel)

    def safely(work):
        try:
            work()
        except Exception as problem:
            label.setText(f"Didn't work.\n{type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")

    def fill_list():
        names = groups.get(read(choice, "currentText"), [])
        listing.clear()
        for name in names:
            listing.addItem(gui.QListWidgetItem(name))
        label.setText(f"{len(names)} with this suffix.")

    def fill_choice():
        font = fl.CurrentFont()
        groups.clear()
        if font is not None:
            groups.update(by_suffix([glyph.name for glyph in font.glyphs]))
        choice.clear()
        choice.addItems(sorted(groups))
        if not groups:
            label.setText("No font is open, or its names have no suffixes.")

    def on_pick(*args):
        safely(fill_list)

    def on_again(*args):
        safely(fill_choice)

    choice.currentIndexChanged.connect(on_pick)
    again.clicked.connect(on_again)

    top = gui.QHBoxLayout()
    top.addWidget(gui.QLabel("Suffix", panel))
    top.addWidget(choice)
    top.addWidget(again)
    outer = gui.QVBoxLayout(panel)
    outer.addLayout(top)
    outer.addWidget(listing)
    outer.addWidget(label)
    fill_choice()
    return panel


scripting.show_script_dialog(build, KEY)

Save it as suffix_picker.py.

Three things in build are worth a second look. groups is made once, empty, near the top, and the functions below it share it. safely is chapter 122's show with a new job: it runs a function that does the work and writes any error into the label, so both slots are one line each. And fill_choice() is called on the last line before return, after the signal is connected, so that the first filling sets off the first list.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
The window opens with dnom in the box, ten names in the list from zero.dnom to nine.dnom, and under it:

10 with this suffix.

Pick sc. The list changes as soon as you let go: a.sc to h.sc, then one.sc and zero.sc, ten again. Pick ss01 and there are four, the three letters and ampersand.ss01. Pick zero and there's one, zero.zero, the slashed zero that chapter 89 wrote a feature for.

Now close the font, leave the window open, and click Look again:

No font is open, or its names have no suffixes.

The box and the list are both empty. Open the font, click once more, and they're back.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
In by_suffix, take out the second half of the test, so the line reads if len(parts) < 2:. Run it and open the box. There's a sixth choice, notdef, and picking it lists one glyph, .notdef. Nothing crashed. The window is now offering a suffix that isn't one, and Ines has no way to know that. Mistakes in the thinking part show up as wrong choices on the screen, which is a good reason to test that part alone, and chapter 139 will. Put the test back.

Then move the line choice.currentIndexChanged.connect(on_pick) down, to sit between fill_choice() and return panel. Run it. The box says dnom and the list is empty, with nothing in the label either. The first filling happened before anybody was listening. Pick sc and the window wakes up, because now the signal has a function to call. The order of lines in build hardly mattered until today. Once a widget's filling sets off a signal, connect first and fill afterward. Move the line back.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A widget that offers choices is filled from data, and the rule for filling is to empty it first, whether it's a dictionary (clear, then update), a QComboBox (clear, then addItems) or a QListWidget (clear, then addItem for each row). A box of choices can only answer with something that's in the font, so there's nothing to check afterward. Its currentIndexChanged signal fires when the choice changes, including when the box is first filled, so one filling can set off the next. The grouping itself lives in a function that knows nothing about windows.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Look again forgets what you'd picked and goes back to the first suffix. In fill_choice, read currentText into a variable before the clear. After addItems, if that text is in groups, find its place with sorted(groups).index(text) and hand the number to choice.setCurrentIndex. Pick sc, click Look again, and check it stays.
  2. Put the number of suffixes in the window's title: Suffixes (5). You'll need panel.setWindowTitle in fill_choice, and an f-string.
  3. Copy by_suffix and the box of choices into shift_dialog.py, next to the names field. When a suffix is picked, write its names into the field, joined by spaces, with names.setText. I haven't seen setText on a field in FontLab; it's the same call the label has. Now Ines can pick ss01, read the four names, take one out by hand, and click Shift.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Mira looks at the script from the door. build has four functions inside it, a dictionary they share, and five widgets they all reach for. It works, and nobody could say where the tool keeps its things. "You've been using objects for twenty-four weeks," she says. "Time you made one." Chapter 126 does: a class of your own.

docs.title: 126. Classes, at last
docs.text:
Thursday, twenty to twelve. Mira has her coat on. She scrolls through shift_dialog.py once more, top to bottom, and stops at the line that calls arrange with seven things in the brackets.

"That line is the tool telling you it wants to be one thing," she says. "It has a panel, two number boxes, a field, a tick box, a button and a label, and you're carrying them from function to function in your hands."

Since chapter 6 you've opened drawers in wardrobes other people built: a glyph has a name, a layer has shapes, a label has setText. Today you build a wardrobe. It's the last large piece of Python in this book.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open with the Regular showing, Fly installed, and shift_dialog.py from chapter 124. The tool does the same work as before and gains one small thing: it counts its own runs.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9. The small examples in the first three steps are plain Python, and I ran them as printed. The whole script ran against the stand-in widgets and the stand-in font from chapter 123.

docs.title: Step 1: A wardrobe with one drawer
docs.text:
Type this into the Scripting panel and run it:

class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0


first = Counter()
second = Counter()
first.count = 5
print(first.count, second.count)

5 0

class Counter: starts a class. A class is the drawing for a wardrobe: it says which drawers every wardrobe of this kind has. It isn't a wardrobe yet. Counter(), with brackets, builds one from the drawing, and you can build as many as you like. Each one is called an object, and the two here are separate pieces of furniture. Putting 5 in the first one's drawer does nothing to the second.

The function inside is where the drawers are made. Its name is __init__, with two underscores on each side, and Python calls it for you each time a wardrobe is built. You never call it yourself. Its one parameter, self, is the wardrobe being built. So self.count = 0 reads: in this new wardrobe, make a drawer labeled count and put 0 in it.

That's the same dot you've written since chapter 6. glyph.name opens a drawer in a wardrobe FontLab built. self.count opens one in a wardrobe you're building.

docs.title: Step 2: A wardrobe that does things
docs.text:
A drawer can hold a function. Add one to the class and run it again:

class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0

    def click(self):
        self.count += 1
        return self.count


first = Counter()
second = Counter()
print(first.click(), first.click(), second.click())
print(first.count, second.count)

1 2 1
2 1

A function that lives in a class is called a method. You've been calling methods for months: name.split("."), label.setText(...), groups.clear(). Now you know what they are.

Look at how click is written and how it's called. It's written with one parameter, self. It's called with nothing in the brackets. The object in front of the dot goes in as self. When you write first.click(), Python hands first to click, so inside it self.count is the first counter's drawer. With second.click() the same lines work on the second counter.

This settles the trouble from chapter 125, and from chapter 122's third exercise if you did it. count += 1 inside a nested function fails, because it tries to put a new box outside, and the way round is a list of one number. A method doesn't need the trick. self.count += 1 changes what's in a drawer of an object the method was handed, and that has always been allowed.

docs.title: Step 3: The mistake
docs.text:
Write a method the way you'd write any function that takes nothing:

class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0

    def click():
        self.count += 1
        return self.count


first = Counter()
print(first.click())

TypeError: Counter.click() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given

You gave it nothing, and Python says you gave it one. It's chapter 122's message, with the cause turned round. There the button handed over a value nobody asked for. Here Python does: the object in front of the dot always goes in first, and the method had no parameter to catch it.

Every method starts with self. When you see "takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given" and the function lives in a class, that's the first thing to check. Put self back.

docs.title: Step 4: The tool as one object
docs.text:
Now the Shift window. Three changes turn chapter 124's script into a class, and none of them changes what the tool does.

Every widget that was a box inside build becomes a drawer: left becomes self.left, label becomes self.label. They're made in __init__, since that's where drawers are made.
