arrange and on_go become methods. arrange loses its seven parameters and keeps one, self, because everything it needs is in the wardrobe it's handed.

And the button is connected to self.on_go. That's a method without its brackets, with its object attached. When the button calls it later, self is already filled in, and the button's own False lands in *args as before.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Shift Tool
# Adds to the sidebearings of the glyphs you name, or of the ones
# selected in the Font window, in the master that's showing.
import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.metrics.panel.model as metrics
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

core, gui = qt.QtCore, qt.QtGui
KEY = "tools.shift"
LIMIT = 200
SHOWN = 8


def read(owner, name):
    item = getattr(owner, name)
    return item() if callable(item) else item


def plan_rows(font, master, names, left, right):
    rows = []
    for name in names:
        if font[name] is None:
            raise ValueError(f"No glyph called {name}.")
        rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
        old = (rich.getLSB(master), rich.getAdvance(master), rich.getRSB(master))
        new = (old[0] + left, old[1] + left + right, old[2] + right)
        rows.append((rich, layer_of(rich.fl, master), old, new))
    return rows


def shift(text, left, right, rehearse):
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        return "No font is open."
    package = scripting.current_package()
    master = package.master
    names = text.split()
    if not names:
        names = scripting.names_selected_names()
    if not names:
        return "Type some glyph names, or select glyphs in the Font window."
    rows = plan_rows(font, master, names, left, right)
    lines = [f"{rich.name}: {old[0]} {old[1]} {old[2]} to {new[0]} {new[1]} {new[2]}"
             for rich, layer, old, new in rows[:SHOWN]]
    if len(rows) > SHOWN:
        lines += [f"and {len(rows) - SHOWN} more"]
    if rehearse:
        return "\n".join(lines + [f"{master}: {len(rows)} would change."])

    def change():
        for rich, layer, old, new in rows:
            metrics.shift_and_set(layer, left, new[1])

    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    layers = [layer for rich, layer, old, new in rows]
    owners = [rich.fl for rich, layer, old, new in rows]
    history.commit("Shift sidebearings", layers, owners, change,
                   operation="geometry", facts=facts, allow_bases=True)
    return "\n".join(lines + [f"{master}: {len(rows)} changed."])


class ShiftTool:
    def __init__(self, parent):
        self.panel = gui.QWidget(parent)
        self.panel.setWindowFlags(core.Qt.Tool)
        self.panel.setWindowTitle("Shift")
        self.panel.setAttribute(core.Qt.WA_DeleteOnClose)
        self.label = gui.QLabel("", self.panel)
        self.names = gui.QLineEdit("", self.panel)
        self.left = gui.QSpinBox(self.panel)
        self.left.setRange(-LIMIT, LIMIT)
        self.right = gui.QSpinBox(self.panel)
        self.right.setRange(-LIMIT, LIMIT)
        self.rehearse = gui.QCheckBox("Only show what would happen", self.panel)
        self.rehearse.setChecked(True)
        self.go = gui.QPushButton("Shift", self.panel)
        self.runs = 0
        self.go.clicked.connect(self.on_go)
        self.arrange()

    def arrange(self):
        form = gui.QFormLayout()
        form.addRow("Glyphs", self.names)

        sides = gui.QHBoxLayout()
        sides.addWidget(gui.QLabel("Left", self.panel))
        sides.addWidget(self.left)
        sides.addWidget(gui.QLabel("Right", self.panel))
        sides.addWidget(self.right)

        bottom = gui.QHBoxLayout()
        bottom.addWidget(self.rehearse)
        bottom.addWidget(self.go)

        outer = gui.QVBoxLayout(self.panel)
        outer.addLayout(form)
        outer.addLayout(sides)
        outer.addLayout(bottom)
        outer.addWidget(self.label)

    def on_go(self, *args):
        try:
            text = shift(read(self.names, "text"), read(self.left, "value"),
                         read(self.right, "value"), read(self.rehearse, "checked"))
            self.runs += 1
            self.label.setText(f"{text}\nRun {self.runs} in this window.")
        except Exception as problem:
            self.label.setText(f"Didn't work.\n{type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")


def build(parent):
    tool = ShiftTool(parent)
    return tool.panel


scripting.show_script_dialog(build, KEY)

Save it as shift_tool.py. read, plan_rows and shift are still plain functions above the class, unchanged since chapter 123. They don't need anything from the window, so they don't belong in it.

Read __init__ as a list of what the tool owns. Eight drawers: the panel, the answer label, the five widgets Ines works with, and runs. Anyone opening this file can now answer "what does this tool keep?" by reading one function.

Some names in the class have no self. in front: form, sides, bottom, outer, text. Those are ordinary boxes that live for the length of one method. The rule for choosing: if another method will need it, or the next click will, it's a drawer. If it's used up before the method ends, it's a box.

self.runs is the new thing the class makes cheap. The tool remembers how many times it has run since the window opened. With loose functions you'd have needed chapter 122's list of one number.

build has shrunk to two lines. show_script_dialog wants a function that takes the parent and returns a widget, so build makes the tool and returns its panel. The tool itself isn't the window. It owns the window, in the drawer panel.

One thing here I'm inferring. build ends, and its box tool goes with it. What keeps the tool from being thrown away is the button: it holds self.on_go, and that method holds its object. That's how Python works, and it held in my stand-in. Whether FontLab's Qt holds the method as firmly, I haven't seen. If your button goes dead a moment after the window opens, this is why, and chapter 127 keeps tools in a way that doesn't depend on it.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Type n o H, set both numbers to 10, leave the tick in, and click Shift:

n: 70 523 66 to 80 543 76
o: 38 520 38 to 48 540 48
H: 76 672 70 to 86 692 80
Regular: 3 would change.
Run 1 in this window.

Click again and the last line says Run 2 in this window. Type n zz and click:

Didn't work.
ValueError: No glyph called zz.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
In __init__, take self. off the front of one line, so it reads label = gui.QLabel("", self.panel). Run it:

AttributeError: 'ShiftTool' object has no attribute 'label'. Did you mean: 'panel'?

No window opens. label without self. is a box in __init__, gone when __init__ ends, and arrange went looking for a drawer that was never made. This is the commonest slip in a class, and the message names it plainly: this object has no such drawer. The suggestion at the end is Python guessing, and it's a wrong guess here. Put self. back.

Then change the connection to self.go.clicked.connect(on_go):

NameError: name 'on_go' is not defined

Inside a class there's no loose function called on_go. There's a drawer of that name in each tool, and you reach a drawer through its wardrobe: self.on_go. Change it back.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A class is the drawing for a kind of object, and calling it builds one, with __init__ run on the new object to make its drawers. A method is a function in a class; it's written with self first and called without it, because the object in front of the dot goes in as self. What a tool must keep between clicks goes in self. drawers, and what one method uses up stays in plain boxes. A window written as a class has one place that lists everything it owns, and its methods reach those things without being handed them.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a method reset(self) that sets both number boxes to 0 with setValue(0) and empties the label, and a Reset button connected to it. Remember *args.
  2. Add a drawer self.last = "" and store the names field's text in it after each run that works. When a run fails, show Last good run: n o H under the error.
  3. Turn chapter 125's suffix_picker.py into a class SuffixPicker. The dictionary groups becomes self.groups. Then look at fill_choice: now that it's a method, could it say self.groups = by_suffix(...) and do without clear and update? Try it, and say in one sentence why it works here and didn't in chapter 125.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Ines is on her own now. The first thing she does is drag the Shift window out of the way of the glyph she's looking at, and the second is lose it behind another window. Chapter 127 gives a tool a place in FontLab's own frame: a panel that docks at the side and stays.

docs.title: 127. A panel that stays open
docs.text:
Thursday afternoon. Mira is on a train and Ines is alone with the Light. She has the Shift window from chapter 126, and she has lost it twice: once behind the Glyph window, once behind FontLab itself. What she wants today is smaller than Shift and more constant. She wants to see a glyph's sidebearings while she looks at the glyph, without asking.

A thing you look at all day shouldn't float about. FontLab's own panels sit at the edge of its frame, and a script can ask for a place there. Getting the place takes one line. Keeping it is the lesson of this chapter: a script ends a moment after it starts, and anything the script made has to be held by something that lasts longer.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open with the Light showing, a Glyph window on n, Fly installed. The panel reads and changes nothing.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9. I ran the script against stand-in widgets and a stand-in panel maker that keeps a list of what was opened and closed. No script I could read calls Fly's panel maker the way this chapter does, so treat every sentence about what the panel looks like as a claim to check.

docs.title: Step 1: Three kinds of window
docs.text:
You've met two kinds already. Chapter 39's message box is the first kind: while it's up, nothing else in FontLab answers. You can't click a glyph, you can't open a menu, and the script itself waits on the line that showed the box. That kind is called modal. It's right for a question that must be answered before anything else happens.

The windows since chapter 121 are the second kind. They open, the script ends, and FontLab goes on working around them. That's why Ines could lose one.

The third kind is a panel: not a window of its own but a strip of FontLab's frame, with a title bar you can drag to another edge. It behaves like the second kind, in that nothing waits for it, and it has an address.

docs.title: Step 2: Ask Fly for a panel
docs.text:
Fly has a maker for panels. Put this in a new script:

from fly import ap, qt

gui = qt.QtGui


def build(content):
    layout = gui.QVBoxLayout(content)
    layout.addWidget(gui.QLabel("n in Light", content))


ap.FontLab().create_panel("Sidebearings", build, area="right")

Two things differ from show_script_dialog. There, your build made the panel and handed it back. Here, Fly has already made an empty widget inside the new strip, and build receives it as content and fills it. Nothing is returned from build.

And look at area="right". Since chapter 121 the rule has been: no named arguments. That rule is about Qt's calls, the ones on gui and core objects. create_panel is a Python function that Fly's authors wrote, and it insists on the name: the four areas are "left", "right", "top" and "bottom".

Run it. A strip titled Sidebearings should appear at the right edge with the one line in it. Fly's source says that when FontLab keeps its main frame hidden, the panel floats as a small window that stays on top instead. I can't tell you which of the two you'll see.

docs.title: Step 3: Run it again
docs.text:
Run the script a second time. In my stand-in, the list of open panels now reads:

panel 1 "Sidebearings" docked right
panel 2 "Sidebearings" docked right

Two panels, and a third if you run it again. show_script_dialog never did this, because it kept every window under its key and closed the old one before opening the new. create_panel doesn't swap an old panel for a new one. It hands back an object that owns the panel, and the script above dropped that object on the floor: no name was given to it, the script ended, and now your scripts have no way left to ask the first panel to close. You close it by hand, with the cross in its title bar.

So give it a name:

owner = ap.FontLab().create_panel("Sidebearings", build, area="right")

That's better for as long as the script runs, which is no time at all. Every run of a script starts with empty boxes. owner from the first run is gone before the second run starts, so the second run can't close what the first one opened.

Who is holding it?

Every object in Python lasts while something refers to it: a name, a list it sits in, another object's drawer. When the last reference goes, the object goes. A script's names all go when the script ends. That's the whole of the problem.

docs.title: Step 4: A place that outlasts the script
docs.text:
Something in FontLab does last longer than a script: every module Python has loaded. Chapter 33 showed that Python loads a module once and then hands every later import of it the same loaded module. sys is one of those. Python loaded it before your first script ran, and every script that says import sys gets that same module until FontLab quits. A dictionary put in one of its drawers lives as long.

Put these lines near the top of the script, after the imports:

import sys


def keep(key, things):
    kept = vars(sys).setdefault("kept_windows", {})
    if key in kept:
        kept[key][0].close()
    kept[key] = things

vars(sys) is the module's own dictionary of names, the one sys.path lives in. setdefault gives back the drawer kept_windows if it's there and puts an empty dictionary in it first if it isn't, so the first script to call keep makes the shelf and every later one finds it. keep takes a key and a list of things to hold. If the shelf has that key already, the first thing in the old list is asked to close, and then the new list takes the place. The object create_panel hands back has a close method, so it goes first in the list.

kept_windows is a name I chose. Python has no drawer by that name of its own, so nothing else will use it, and every script in this part that calls keep uses the same one. The end of the script becomes:

owner = ap.FontLab().create_panel("Sidebearings", build, area="right")
keep("tools.sidebearings", [owner])

Run it twice, and the stand-in's list reads:

panel 1 "Sidebearings" docked right
panel 2 "Sidebearings" docked right
panel 1 closed

One panel is open, and it's the new one.

docs.title: Step 5: The panel as a class
docs.text:
The panel needs a label, a button and two methods, which is a small wardrobe of the kind chapter 126 built. There's one new wrinkle. create_panel calls build, and build returns nothing, so how does the object made inside build get out to be kept? The same way exercise 3 of chapter 122 counted clicks from inside an inner function: a list that the outer function owns.

def main():
    made = []

    def build(content):
        made.append(SidebearingPanel(content))

    owner = ap.FontLab().create_panel(TITLE, build, area="right")
    keep(KEY, [owner, made[0]])

build drops the new SidebearingPanel into made. After create_panel comes back, made[0] is that object, and it goes on the shelf beside the owner. Chapter 126 guessed that a tool survives because its button holds one of its methods. Now it doesn't matter whether the guess is right: the shelf holds the tool by name.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Sidebearing Panel
# A panel at the side of FontLab that shows the sidebearings of the
# current glyph in the master that's showing. Changes nothing.
import sys

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import ap, fl, qt
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

gui = qt.QtGui
KEY = "tools.sidebearings"
TITLE = "Sidebearings"


def keep(key, things):
    kept = vars(sys).setdefault("kept_windows", {})
    if key in kept:
        kept[key][0].close()
    kept[key] = things


def glyph_text():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    glyph = fl.CurrentGlyph()
    if font is None or glyph is None:
        return "No glyph is showing."
    master = scripting.current_package().master
    rich = pGlyph(font, glyph)
    lines = [
        f"{rich.name} in {master}",
        f"Left {rich.getLSB(master)}",
        f"Width {rich.getAdvance(master)}",
        f"Right {rich.getRSB(master)}",
    ]
    return "\n".join(lines)


class SidebearingPanel:
    def __init__(self, content):
        self.label = gui.QLabel("", content)
        self.again = gui.QPushButton("Look again", content)
        self.again.clicked.connect(self.on_again)
        layout = gui.QVBoxLayout(content)
        layout.addWidget(self.label)
        layout.addWidget(self.again)
        self.refresh()

    def refresh(self):
        try:
            self.label.setText(glyph_text())
        except Exception as problem:
            self.label.setText(f"Didn't work.\n{type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")

    def on_again(self, *args):
        self.refresh()


def main():
    made = []

    def build(content):
        made.append(SidebearingPanel(content))

    owner = ap.FontLab().create_panel(TITLE, build, area="right")
    keep(KEY, [owner, made[0]])


main()

Save it as sidebearing_panel.py.

glyph_text is plain work with no window in it. It asks FontLab for the current font and the current glyph, wraps it in TypeRig's pGlyph, and reads the three numbers in the master that's showing. The class is two drawers and two methods. refresh fills the label and catches whatever goes wrong, as every slot since chapter 122 has. on_again is the slot, and all it does is call refresh; the split lets __init__ fill the label once without pretending to be a click.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
With n in the Glyph window and the Light showing, the panel reads:

n in Light
Left 84
Width 499
Right 80

Go to o in the Glyph window. The panel still says n. Click Look again:

o in Light
Left 50
Width 494
Right 50

Close every Glyph window, click a blank part of the Font window so that no glyph is current, and click Look again once more:

No glyph is showing.

I've used the Light because the Shift tool has been at work on the Regular since chapter 123, and your Regular's numbers depend on which of those clicks you undid.

Now drag the panel by its title bar to the left edge, or pull it loose so that it floats. FontLab does that part; your script has no say in it and needs none.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Change area="right" to area="middle" and run:

ValueError: Dock area must be left, right, top or bottom

That sentence is Fly's own, and it's a model of an error message: it says what was wrong and lists what would be right. No panel was made, so nothing needs closing. Put "right" back.

Next, take the name off: create_panel(TITLE, build, "right").

TypeError: FontLab.create_panel() takes from 2 to 3 positional arguments but 4 were given

The count includes self, as it did in chapter 126: self, the title and build make three, and your "right" was a fourth with nowhere to go. A function can demand that an argument be named, and this one does. Put area= back.

Last, in the Scripting panel, run import sys and then del sys.kept_windows while the panel is open, and then run the script again. Two panels. The first keep after the del found no shelf, made a new, empty one, and the panel that the old shelf held is on nobody's list. Close it by hand. A shelf is only as lasting as the drawer it sits in.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A modal window makes everything wait, a modeless one doesn't, and a panel is a modeless one with a place in FontLab's frame. An object lasts only while something refers to it, and a script's own names stop referring the moment the script ends. A dictionary in a drawer of a loaded module such as sys outlasts every script, so it can hold a panel's owner and close the old panel when a new one is asked for. A Python function can require an argument by name, which is a different matter from Qt's calls refusing names.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Open the panel at the bottom. One line changes. Then decide which edge suits a panel of four short lines, and say why.
  2. Add a fifth line that says how far apart the two sides are: Sides differ by 4 for the Light's n. Use abs, from chapter 36. A glyph with even sides should say Sides match.
  3. keep asks the old owner to close and trusts that it can. Print what close() gives back, run the script twice, and then close the panel by hand and run it once more. Write down the three answers. I expect True each time, and I haven't seen it.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The panel is in its place and Ines has stopped losing it. What she's lost instead is patience with the button: every time she moves to another glyph, the panel shows the one before until she clicks Look again. Chapter 128 takes the button away. The panel will look for itself, five times a second, and change its text only when there's something new to say.

docs.title: 128. Keep up with the font
docs.text:
Thursday, late in the afternoon. The Sidebearings panel sits at the right edge of FontLab and Ines has stopped losing it. She presses the key for the next glyph, the Glyph window shows o, and the panel still says n in Light. She clicks Look again. Next glyph, click. Next glyph, click. By the sixth glyph she has a name for the button, and it isn't printable.

A panel that shows the wrong glyph is worse than no panel, because sooner or later somebody believes it. Today the button goes. The panel will go and look for itself, often enough that nobody can catch it out, and it will hold its tongue when there's nothing new to say.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open with the Light showing, a Glyph window on n, Fly installed, and sidebearing_panel.py from chapter 127. The panel reads and changes nothing.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9. I ran the script against stand-in widgets and a stand-in timer that I could make tick as many times as I liked. The script follows an example in FontLab's collection of Python examples, live_glyph_panel.py, which watches the current glyph the same way.

docs.title: Step 1: Be told, or go and look
docs.text:
There are two ways to keep up with something that changes.

The first is to be told. That's what a button does. In chapter 122 you handed the button a function, on_again, and the button called it at each click. A function you hand over so that somebody else can call it later has a name: a callback. Every slot is one. So is build, which create_panel calls when the panel's inside is ready. You don't call a callback. You leave it at the desk and get on with your day.

So the tidy answer would be a signal that says "the user moved to another glyph", with a slot of yours connected to it. I looked for one and didn't find one I could check. FontLab does send signals when a glyph is edited, and none that I could verify for the moment somebody steps from n to o.

That leaves the second way: go and look. Ask "which glyph is it now?" again and again, and act when the answer changes. It sounds crude. It's how a great many working tools keep up, and at the pace of a person pressing keys it costs next to nothing, as you'll measure in step 4.

Going to look still needs somebody to say when. A script can't loop and wait, because while your loop runs, nothing else in FontLab can. What you need is something that calls you back at a steady beat.

docs.title: Step 2: A timer
docs.text:
Qt has that something, and it's a small object called a timer. Add these lines at the end of the panel's __init__, and add core beside gui at the top of the script, as in chapter 121:

self.timer = core.QTimer(content)
self.timer.setInterval(200)
self.timer.timeout.connect(self.on_again)

QTimer(content) makes a timer that belongs to the panel's inside, so when the panel goes, the timer goes with it. setInterval takes thousandths of a second, so 200 is a fifth of a second. timeout is the timer's signal, the way clicked is a button's, and you connect a slot to it in the same way: the function's name, no brackets.

Run the script. Step to o. The panel says n in Light.

Nothing is wrong with those three lines. One is missing. A timer that has been made and set is a clock with the pendulum held still. It needs a push:

self.timer.start()

Put that under the connect line and run the script again. Step to o, and the panel follows before you've looked across at it. Step to H, and it follows again. The button is still there, and nobody needs it.

A made timer is not a running timer. When a live tool sits there doing nothing and shows no error, look for the start.

docs.title: Step 3: Say nothing when nothing changed
docs.text:
The panel now writes its label five times a second, and almost every time it writes the text that was already there. In a minute that's 300 writes to say n in Light once.

Does it matter? For four short lines, you may never see the cost. For a tool that fills a list of 274 names, you would: the list would be rebuilt five times a second, and your place in it lost each time. The habit worth having is the one a good colleague has. Look as often as you like. Speak when you have news.

To know whether there's news, the panel must remember what it said last. That's a value that has to live between one tick and the next, which is the thing a drawer on self is for:

def on_tick(self, *args):
    text = self.look()
    if text == self.shown:
        return
    self.shown = text
    self.label.setText(text)

self.shown starts as None in __init__. The text for a glyph is never None, so the first tick always has news. After that, a tick that finds the same text leaves by the early return and touches nothing on screen.

Look at what counts as news. The comparison is on the whole text, so anything that changes any of the four lines is news: another glyph, another master, or a sidebearing that somebody has dragged. You didn't write a rule for each. You compared what you'd say with what you said.

self.look() is chapter 127's refresh with one change. It gives the text back, and leaves the writing to on_tick. It still catches whatever goes wrong and turns it into text. An error in a slot that runs at a click is one error. An error in a slot that runs five times a second is 300 a minute, and because an error message is also text, the comparison deals with that too: the panel writes it once and waits.

docs.title: Step 4: Count the looks
docs.text:
"It costs next to nothing" is a claim, and you have a panel to check it with. Give the object two more drawers, looks and writes, both starting at 0. Add one to looks at the top of every tick, add one to writes when there's news, and show both in a second, smaller label:

self.small.setText(f"Looks {self.looks}, writes {self.writes}")

That line goes after the early return, with the other write. If it sat above the return it would change the screen at every tick, and you'd have put back the chatter you took out.

So the line of counts only moves when the glyph text does. Between moves it shows the count as it stood at the last piece of news. That's the point of it: a big jump in looks beside a step of one in writes is the picture of a panel that looked a lot and said little.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
The button and its slot are gone. Save this as live_panel.py:

#FLM: Live Sidebearings
# A panel at the side of FontLab that shows the sidebearings of the
# current glyph and keeps up as you move about. Changes nothing.
import sys

import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import ap, fl, qt
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

core, gui = qt.QtCore, qt.QtGui
KEY = "tools.sidebearings"
TITLE = "Sidebearings"
EVERY = 200


def keep(key, things):
    kept = vars(sys).setdefault("kept_windows", {})
    if key in kept:
        kept[key][0].close()
    kept[key] = things


def glyph_text():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    glyph = fl.CurrentGlyph()
    if font is None or glyph is None:
        return "No glyph is showing."
    master = scripting.current_package().master
    rich = pGlyph(font, glyph)
    lines = [
        f"{rich.name} in {master}",
        f"Left {rich.getLSB(master)}",
        f"Width {rich.getAdvance(master)}",
        f"Right {rich.getRSB(master)}",
    ]
    return "\n".join(lines)


class LivePanel:
    def __init__(self, content):
        self.shown = None
        self.looks = 0
        self.writes = 0
        self.label = gui.QLabel("", content)
        self.small = gui.QLabel("", content)
        layout = gui.QVBoxLayout(content)
        layout.addWidget(self.label)
        layout.addWidget(self.small)
        self.timer = core.QTimer(content)
        self.timer.setInterval(EVERY)
        self.timer.timeout.connect(self.on_tick)
        self.timer.start()
        self.on_tick()

    def look(self):
        try:
            return glyph_text()
        except Exception as problem:
            return f"Didn't work.\n{type(problem).__name__}: {problem}"

    def on_tick(self, *args):
        self.looks += 1
        text = self.look()
        if text == self.shown:
            return
        self.shown = text
        self.writes += 1
        self.label.setText(text)
        self.small.setText(f"Looks {self.looks}, writes {self.writes}")


def main():
    made = []

    def build(content):
        made.append(LivePanel(content))

    owner = ap.FontLab().create_panel(TITLE, build, area="right")
    keep(KEY, [owner, made[0]])


main()

keep, glyph_text and main are chapter 127's, word for word, apart from the class name. The key is the same too, tools.sidebearings, and that's on purpose: keep finds the shelf that chapter 127's script made in sys, closes the panel with the button, if it's still open, and puts this one in its place.

EVERY is a name for the 200. A number that decides how a tool feels belongs at the top, where you'll find it when you want to change the feel.

The last line of __init__ calls self.on_tick() once by hand. Without it the panel would be empty for its first fifth of a second. A slot is a plain method, and you can call it yourself when that's useful.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
With n in the Glyph window and the Light showing, the panel opens with:

n in Light
Left 84
Width 499
Right 80
Looks 1, writes 1

Wait about five seconds, then step to o:

o in Light
Left 50
Width 494
Right 50
Looks 27, writes 2

Your count of looks will be whatever your five seconds came to. Mine was 27: one look when the panel opened, 25 that found nothing new, and the one that found o. Wait again and go to H:

H in Light
Left 88
Width 612
Right 84
Looks 52, writes 3

Now drag the left sidebearing of H a little way in the Glyph window. The numbers in the panel should follow the drag, a fifth of a second behind at most, and writes should climb with them. Use Edit > Undo to put the H back, and the panel should follow that too. Nobody wrote code for "a sidebearing was dragged" or for "Undo". The text changed, and the panel saw that it had.

Run the script a second time. The first panel closes and a second opens, with its counts back at 1. The first panel's timer went when its panel went, because you made it with QTimer(content). I haven't seen that happen in FontLab; in the stand-in, a closed panel's timer never ticks again. A panel's own cross may only hide it, and then its timer goes on ticking out of sight until you run the script again.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Take the news test out. Delete these two lines from on_tick:

if text == self.shown:
    return

Run the script, leave n showing, and wait about a minute. You'll see something near this:

Looks 300, writes 300

The label of counts is now busy all the time, and the panel has written n in Light some 300 times to an audience of one. Nothing looks broken. This kind of waste doesn't announce itself, which is the reason the counts are there. Put the two lines back.

Then make the panel lazy. Change the line at the top to EVERY = 5000 and run the script. Step from n to o. For up to five seconds the panel says n in Light above a glyph that is plainly an o, and it's chapter 127's panel again without even a button to press. Put 200 back.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A callback is a function you hand over for somebody else to call, and a timer calls yours at a steady beat once you've started it. When there's no signal for the change you care about, you can look for the change yourself, often. A live tool should remember what it last showed and write only when that differs. A slot that runs many times a second must never let an error out, and should count its own work so that you can see what it costs.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a tick box, Follow, that starts ticked. Connect its clicked signal to a slot that reads the box with chapter 123's read and calls self.timer.start() or self.timer.stop(). Untick it, step to another glyph, and watch the panel hold still.
  2. Add a line to the glyph text that gives the time of the last write, with datetime.now() from chapter 119. Put it in on_tick, where the write happens. Then work out what would go wrong if you put it in glyph_text instead.
  3. At one look every 200 thousandths of a second, how many looks is an eight-hour day? Work it out in the Scripting panel. Then try EVERY = 1000, use the panel for a few minutes, and decide which you'd give Ines.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The panel keeps up, and Ines has gone back to the Shift tool to open up the Light. Every time she opens it, the Left box says 0, and every time she types 12 into it. Chapter 129 gives a tool a memory that outlasts FontLab itself: a small file of settings, read when the tool opens and written when she clicks.

docs.title: 129. Remember my settings
docs.text:
Monday of week twenty-five, 28 December. The studio is half empty and Ines has the Light to herself. She opens the Shift tool, types 12 into Left, types 12 into Right, names three glyphs and clicks. She closes it to look at a proof. She opens it again, and both boxes say 0. By eleven she has typed 12 twenty times, and she has typed 21 once and not noticed until the H looked wrong.

A window forgets everything when it closes, and so does a script when it ends. Chapter 127 kept a panel alive in a drawer of sys, but that drawer empties when FontLab quits. The only thing that outlasts FontLab is a file. Today the Shift tool gets one: a few lines of JSON that it reads when it opens and writes when Ines clicks.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open with the Light showing, Fly installed, and shift_tool.py from chapter 126.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9. The settings functions are plain Python, and I ran them as printed against a folder of my own, with good files and damaged ones. The whole script ran against the stand-in widgets and the stand-in font from chapter 123. The one line I couldn't check is the one that asks FontLab where its data folder is.

docs.title: Step 1: Where the file lives
docs.text:
A settings file needs a home that isn't the font's folder (the settings belong to Ines, not to Plum) and isn't the Scripts folder (which chapter 133 will replace wholesale). FontLab keeps a folder of its own for each person who uses it, and Fly knows where it is. In shift_tool.py, make sure the top has import json and that ap is among the names on the from fly import line, and then add:

def settings_path():
    return ap.app.paths.userDataFolder / "tool-settings.json"

userDataFolder is a Path, and the / joins a file name to it, as it did in chapter 112. On a Mac I'd expect FontLab/FontLab 9 inside your own Library/Application Support, though a FontLab preference can put it elsewhere. Print ap.app.paths.userDataFolder once in the Scripting panel, after from fly import ap, so that you know where to look.

One file will do for every tool you write. Inside, each tool has its own drawer, under the key it already has:

{
    "tools.shift": {
        "left": 12,
        "right": 12
    }
}

That's a dictionary of dictionaries, the shape family-info.json had in chapter 99, one level deeper.

docs.title: Step 2: Read it, and the mistake
docs.text:
The first version writes itself:

def load_settings(key):
    with open(settings_path(), encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return json.load(f)[key]

Call it from the tool and the tool doesn't open at all. The Output panel says:

FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/Users/ines/Library/Application Support/FontLab/FontLab 9/tool-settings.json'

There is no file yet. Nobody has clicked, so nothing has been saved, and a tool that can't open until it has been used can never be used. This is the mistake that every settings reader makes once: it treats the file as something the script owns. The script doesn't own it. The file can be missing, because this is the first run or a new computer. It can be half written, because the laptop lid closed at the wrong moment. A person can have opened it in a text editor and changed 12 to "12". It can be a perfectly good file with no drawer for this tool in it.

So a settings reader has one rule: the file may suggest, and the script decides. Whatever happens, the tool opens.

docs.title: Step 3: Defaults first
docs.text:
The way to keep that rule is to start from values the script trusts and let the file replace them one at a time. In the tool:

DEFAULTS = {"left": 0, "right": 0}

And beside settings_path, in the same script:

def read_settings_file():
    try:
        with open(settings_path(), encoding="utf-8") as f:
            stored = json.load(f)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return {}
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return {}
    if not isinstance(stored, dict):
        return {}
    return stored


def load_settings(key, defaults):
    values = dict(defaults)
    mine = read_settings_file().get(key)
    if not isinstance(mine, dict):
        return values
    for name in defaults:
        if name in mine and type(mine[name]) == type(defaults[name]):
            values[name] = mine[name]
    return values

read_settings_file has three ways to give up, and each one gives back an empty dictionary: no file, a file that isn't JSON, and a file that is JSON but isn't a dictionary. The two except lines are the pair from chapter 99. There, a damaged file stopped the script with a message, because the script was about to write into a font. Here it only costs Ines a 12, so the script shrugs and carries on.

load_settings copies the defaults with dict(defaults), which does for a dictionary what list(caps) did for a list in chapter 51, so that the tool's own DEFAULTS is never touched. Then it walks the names in the defaults, not the names in the file. That direction matters. A name in the file that the tool doesn't know is ignored without any code to ignore it. A name the tool knows and the file lacks keeps its default.

The last test is type(mine[name]) == type(defaults[name]). The default for left is 0, a whole number, so the stored value has to be a whole number too. Text like "12" is refused, and so is 12.5, and so is true. The defaults do double duty: they say what the value is when nothing is stored, and what kind of thing it has to be when something is.

docs.title: Step 4: Write it
docs.text:
def save_settings(key, values):
    stored = read_settings_file()
    stored[key] = values
    with open(settings_path(), "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(stored, f, indent=4, ensure_ascii=False)

Saving reads the file first. One file serves every tool, so the Shift tool has to put its drawer back among the others, not replace the whole file with its own two numbers. Read everything, change one key, write everything.

Two decisions go into the tool, and neither is about Python. When to save: after a click that worked. A click that raised an error saves nothing. A click the tool turned down with a sentence of its own still saves the boxes. And what to save: the two numbers, and not the tick box. A tool that remembers being armed opens armed. Only show what would happen starts ticked every time, whatever happened yesterday. The glyph names aren't saved either. They change with every click, and a field that fills itself with last week's names invites a click on the wrong glyphs.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Shift Tool
# Adds to the sidebearings of the glyphs you name, or of the ones
# selected in the Font window, in the master that's showing.
import json

import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.metrics.panel.model as metrics
from fly import ap, fl, qt
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

core, gui = qt.QtCore, qt.QtGui
KEY = "tools.shift"
LIMIT = 200
SHOWN = 8
DEFAULTS = {"left": 0, "right": 0}


def settings_path():
    return ap.app.paths.userDataFolder / "tool-settings.json"


def read_settings_file():
    try:
        with open(settings_path(), encoding="utf-8") as f:
            stored = json.load(f)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return {}
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return {}
    if not isinstance(stored, dict):
        return {}
    return stored


def load_settings(key, defaults):
    values = dict(defaults)
    mine = read_settings_file().get(key)
    if not isinstance(mine, dict):
        return values
    for name in defaults:
        if name in mine and type(mine[name]) == type(defaults[name]):
            values[name] = mine[name]
    return values


def save_settings(key, values):
    stored = read_settings_file()
    stored[key] = values
    with open(settings_path(), "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(stored, f, indent=4, ensure_ascii=False)


def read(owner, name):
    item = getattr(owner, name)
    return item() if callable(item) else item


def plan_rows(font, master, names, left, right):
    rows = []
    for name in names:
        if font[name] is None:
            raise ValueError(f"No glyph called {name}.")
        rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
        old = (rich.getLSB(master), rich.getAdvance(master), rich.getRSB(master))
        new = (old[0] + left, old[1] + left + right, old[2] + right)
        rows.append((rich, layer_of(rich.fl, master), old, new))
    return rows


def shift(text, left, right, rehearse):
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        return "No font is open."
    package = scripting.current_package()
    master = package.master
    names = text.split()
    if not names:
        names = scripting.names_selected_names()
    if not names:
        return "Type some glyph names, or select glyphs in the Font window."
    rows = plan_rows(font, master, names, left, right)
    lines = [f"{rich.name}: {old[0]} {old[1]} {old[2]} to {new[0]} {new[1]} {new[2]}"
             for rich, layer, old, new in rows[:SHOWN]]
    if len(rows) > SHOWN:
        lines += [f"and {len(rows) - SHOWN} more"]
    if rehearse:
        return "\n".join(lines + [f"{master}: {len(rows)} would change."])

    def change():
        for rich, layer, old, new in rows:
            metrics.shift_and_set(layer, left, new[1])

    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    layers = [layer for rich, layer, old, new in rows]
    owners = [rich.fl for rich, layer, old, new in rows]
    history.commit("Shift sidebearings", layers, owners, change,
                   operation="geometry", facts=facts, allow_bases=True)
    return "\n".join(lines + [f"{master}: {len(rows)} changed."])


class ShiftTool:
    def __init__(self, parent):
        self.panel = gui.QWidget(parent)
        self.panel.setWindowFlags(core.Qt.Tool)
        self.panel.setWindowTitle("Shift")
        self.panel.setAttribute(core.Qt.WA_DeleteOnClose)
        self.label = gui.QLabel("", self.panel)
        self.names = gui.QLineEdit("", self.panel)
        self.left = gui.QSpinBox(self.panel)
        self.left.setRange(-LIMIT, LIMIT)
        self.right = gui.QSpinBox(self.panel)
        self.right.setRange(-LIMIT, LIMIT)
        saved = load_settings(KEY, DEFAULTS)
        self.left.setValue(saved["left"])
        self.right.setValue(saved["right"])
        self.rehearse = gui.QCheckBox("Only show what would happen", self.panel)
        self.rehearse.setChecked(True)
        self.go = gui.QPushButton("Shift", self.panel)
        self.runs = 0
        self.go.clicked.connect(self.on_go)
        self.arrange()

    def arrange(self):
        form = gui.QFormLayout()
        form.addRow("Glyphs", self.names)

        sides = gui.QHBoxLayout()
        sides.addWidget(gui.QLabel("Left", self.panel))
        sides.addWidget(self.left)
        sides.addWidget(gui.QLabel("Right", self.panel))
        sides.addWidget(self.right)

        bottom = gui.QHBoxLayout()
        bottom.addWidget(self.rehearse)
        bottom.addWidget(self.go)

        outer = gui.QVBoxLayout(self.panel)
        outer.addLayout(form)
        outer.addLayout(sides)
        outer.addLayout(bottom)
        outer.addWidget(self.label)

    def on_go(self, *args):
        try:
            left = read(self.left, "value")
            right = read(self.right, "value")
            text = shift(read(self.names, "text"), left, right,
                         read(self.rehearse, "checked"))
            save_settings(KEY, {"left": left, "right": right})
            self.runs += 1
            self.label.setText(f"{text}\nRun {self.runs} in this window.")
        except Exception as problem:
            self.label.setText(f"Didn't work.\n{type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")


def build(parent):
    tool = ShiftTool(parent)
    return tool.panel


scripting.show_script_dialog(build, KEY)

Save it over shift_tool.py. Next to chapter 126's version, four places changed. import json is new, and ap joins the from fly import line. DEFAULTS is new, with the four settings functions from steps 1 to 4 under it. __init__ asks load_settings for the saved values and puts them in the two boxes with setValue, after setRange, so that the box already knows its limits when the number arrives. And on_go reads the two numbers into names of their own, because it now needs them twice: once for shift and once for save_settings, which sits after shift and so is skipped when shift raises.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Open the tool. Both boxes say 0, since there's no file. Type n o H, set both boxes to 12 and click Shift:

n: 84 499 80 to 96 523 92
o: 50 494 50 to 62 518 62
H: 88 612 84 to 100 636 96
Light: 3 would change.
Run 1 in this window.

That was a rehearsal, and it saved all the same: the numbers are what Ines chose, whether or not she has used them yet. Look in the folder from step 1. tool-settings.json is there, with the six lines shown above.

Close the tool. Run the script again. Both boxes say 12, the tick box is ticked, the names field is empty. Quit FontLab, start it, open the font, run the script: 12 and 12.

Then try a name that isn't in the font, with 30 in Left:

Didn't work.
ValueError: No glyph called zz.

Open the tool again and the box says 12. The 30 went nowhere, so it wasn't kept.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
The file is yours to damage. Open tool-settings.json in a text editor and put quotation marks round the first number and a silly value in the second:

{
    "tools.shift": {
        "left": "12",
        "right": 5000
    }
}

Run the script. Left says 0: "12" is text, the default is a number, and the type test turned it away. Right says 200. The number 5000 passed the test, because it is a whole number, and then the spin box cut it down to the top of its own range. The settings code checks the kind of value and the widget checks the size, and between them a wrong file can't put a wrong number in the box.

Now delete the last three lines of the file, so that it stops in the middle, and run the script again. Both boxes say 0. Inside read_settings_file, json.load raised JSONDecodeError: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes, the second except caught it, and the tool opened on its defaults. Click Shift once and look at the file: it's whole again, written fresh. Notice what that cost. If other tools had drawers in the damaged file, they're gone, because the save started from an empty dictionary. For a file of spin-box numbers that's a fair price. For anything you'd mind losing, a reader should stop and say so, as chapter 99's did.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A tool remembers across sessions by writing a small JSON file in FontLab's user data folder, one file for all your tools with one dictionary per tool. Reading starts from defaults the script trusts and takes from the file only the names it knows, with values of the right type, so a missing, broken or edited file can never stop the tool opening. Saving reads the whole file, changes one key and writes it all back, and it happens only after a run that worked. What to remember is a design decision: the numbers, yes; the tick box that makes the tool safe, no.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a Forget button that saves DEFAULTS and sets both boxes back to 0. Which of the functions you already have does all the work?
  2. Give the Sidebearings panel from chapter 128 a drawer of its own under its key, tools.sidebearings, holding the number of milliseconds between looks. Change it in the file by hand, run the panel, and check with EVERY printed that it took. What should the panel do with 0?
  3. Change the 12 in the file to true and run the tool. The box says 0. Now change the test in load_settings to isinstance(mine[name], type(defaults[name])) and run it again. What does the box say, and what does that tell you about True and whole numbers?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: With the numbers remembered, Ines grows bolder: she empties the names field, selects every glyph in the Font window, and clicks. FontLab stops answering for most of a minute, and she can't tell whether it's working or stuck. Chapter 130 shows her how far along it is, and gives her a way to say stop.

docs.title: 130. Progress and patience
docs.text:
Monday afternoon, 28 December. Ines emptied the names field, selected every glyph in the Font window, and clicked Shift. The button stayed pressed in. The window wouldn't move. She clicked again, and a third time, and then sat with her hands in her lap for most of a minute, wondering whether to force FontLab to quit and lose the morning's work. Then the label filled in, three times over.

Nothing had gone wrong. The tool was busy, and a busy tool that says nothing looks the same as a dead one. Today's script does a long job the polite way: it shows how far it has got, it lets you stop it, and FontLab stays awake the whole time.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open and Fly installed. The script only measures. It changes nothing in the font, so you can run it, stop it and break it as often as you like.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9. The whole script ran against stand-in widgets, a stand-in timer that I ticked by hand, and a stand-in font with the 274 glyph names yours should have by now. The slice counts below come from that run. How long anything takes, and what a frozen window looks like on your machine, I haven't seen.

docs.title: Step 1: Why the window froze
docs.text:
Chapter 121 described the event loop: FontLab goes round and round, and on each turn it repaints what needs repainting, notices clicks, and calls the slots that are owed a call. The loop does one thing at a time. While it's inside your slot, it isn't repainting and it isn't noticing clicks. It gets back to that work when your slot returns.

A slot that takes a hundredth of a second is invisible. A slot that walks 274 glyphs in three masters and measures each one is 822 pieces of work in a single turn of the loop, and for as long as that takes, FontLab can't draw so much as a pressed button popping back up. Ines's second and third clicks weren't lost, either. They waited in a queue, and the loop delivered them when it came round again, which is why the job ran three times.

So the cure isn't to work faster. It's to return sooner.

docs.title: Step 2: A bar, and the mistake
docs.text:
Qt has a window made for this, QProgressDialog: a line of text, a bar, and a Cancel button. You give it the text, the button's word, the two ends of the bar, and a parent:

dialog = gui.QProgressDialog("Measuring...", "Cancel", 0, len(jobs), parent)

dialog.setValue(n) moves the bar to n. The obvious thing to do with that is this:

def on_go(*args):
    rows = []
    for name, master in jobs:
        rows.append(measure(font, name, master))
        dialog.setValue(len(rows))

It reads well and it does nothing useful. setValue changes a number inside the dialog and asks for a repaint, and the repaint happens on the next turn of the loop. There is no next turn until on_go returns. The bar is told 822 things and gets to show the last of them, when it's all over. Cancel is as dead as every other button. This is the mistake nearly everybody makes with their first progress bar, and it's worth making once on purpose to see it.

Some people get out of it by calling a Qt function in the middle of the loop that forces a turn of the event loop from inside the slot. I'm not going to teach that. It lets a second click start a second job in the middle of the first, and the tools this book learned from don't do it.

docs.title: Step 3: Slices
docs.text:
What works is to cut the job into slices and do one slice per turn of the loop. Chapter 128 gave you the machinery: a timer calls a method, the method does a little and returns. There, the timer fired five times a second. Here its interval is zero, which doesn't mean "never" or "all at once". It means "as soon as the loop has nothing else to do". Repainting and clicks come first, and your slice gets every turn that's left.

The job has to remember where it was between slices, and that's what a class is for. The rows measured so far are the bookmark:

def on_tick(self, *args):
    start = len(self.rows)
    for name, master in self.jobs[start:start + SLICE]:
        self.rows.append(measure(self.font, name, master))
    self.dialog.setValue(len(self.rows))

You've cut the front off a list before, with names[:SHOWN]. A slice with a number on each side of the colon takes the middle: jobs[25:50] is the items numbered 25 up to, but not including, 50. Near the end, jobs[800:825] asks for more than the list has and gets the 22 that are left, without complaint. That saves a line of arithmetic.

SLICE is 25. Too small, and the job spends its time going round the loop. Too large, and each turn takes long enough that the window stutters. Twenty-five glyph layers is a guess that's kind to a slow machine, and it's a name at the top of the script so that you can change it.

docs.title: Step 4: Stop, and stop once
docs.text:
Three things can end the job: it runs out of work, the person clicks Cancel, or something raises an error. All three want the same handful of actions, so there's one method for them:

def finish(self, text):
    self.over = True
    self.timer.stop()
    self.dialog.setLabelText(text)
    self.dialog.setCancelButtonText("Close")
    print(text)

self.timer.stop() is the line that matters most, and Break it shows why. The button changes its word because, once the job is over, there's nothing left to cancel. But it's still the same button, and it still sends the same signal, canceled. (Qt spells it with one l.) So the slot for that signal has to know whether the job is already over:

def on_cancel(self, *args):
    if not self.over:
        self.finish(f"Stopped. {len(self.rows)} of {len(self.jobs)} layers measured.")
    core.QTimer.singleShot(0, self.dialog.close)

I left self.over out of my first version. The job ran to the end and said "Done", I clicked Close, and the Output panel got a second line: "Stopped. 822 of 822 layers measured." A tool that tells you it stopped a job it finished isn't one you'd trust with a font.

The last line is there because of what Qt does with this button. As far as I know from Qt's own documents, a click on it hides the dialog at once, whatever the button says. A hidden window isn't a closed one: it's still there, out of sight, and so is its timer. So the slot closes it properly. QTimer.singleShot(0, ...) means "call this once, the next time the loop comes round", which is a polite way to close a window from inside one of its own signals. It also means the sentence in the label is on show while the job runs and after Done, but a Stopped sentence is only ever read in the Output panel, where finish prints it.

Cancelling doesn't throw anything away. The rows measured before the click are still in self.rows, and for a job that only reads, half an answer is a fine thing to be left with.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Long Job
# Measures every glyph in every master, a slice at a time, behind a
# progress window with a Cancel button. Changes nothing.
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

core, gui = qt.QtCore, qt.QtGui
KEY = "tools.longjob"
SLICE = 25
SHOWN = 6
TITLE = "Long Job"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def measure(font, name, master):
    rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
    return (name, master, rich.getLSB(master), rich.getAdvance(master), rich.getRSB(master))


class LongJob:
    def __init__(self, parent, font, jobs):
        self.font = font
        self.jobs = jobs
        self.rows = []
        self.looks = 0
        self.over = False
        self.dialog = gui.QProgressDialog("Measuring...", "Cancel", 0, len(jobs), parent)
        self.dialog.setWindowTitle("Long Job")
        self.dialog.setMinimumDuration(0)
        self.dialog.setAutoReset(False)
        self.dialog.setAutoClose(False)
        self.dialog.setAttribute(core.Qt.WA_DeleteOnClose)
        self.dialog.canceled.connect(self.on_cancel)
        self.timer = core.QTimer(self.dialog)
        self.timer.timeout.connect(self.on_tick)
        self.timer.start(0)

    def finish(self, text):
        self.over = True
        self.timer.stop()
        self.dialog.setLabelText(text)
        self.dialog.setCancelButtonText("Close")
        print(text)
        for row in self.rows[:SHOWN]:
            print(row)

    def on_tick(self, *args):
        self.looks += 1
        try:
            start = len(self.rows)
            for name, master in self.jobs[start:start + SLICE]:
                self.rows.append(measure(self.font, name, master))
            self.dialog.setValue(len(self.rows))
            if len(self.rows) == len(self.jobs):
                self.finish(f"Done. {len(self.rows)} layers measured in {self.looks} slices.")
        except Exception as problem:
            self.finish(f"Didn't work.\n{type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")

    def on_cancel(self, *args):
        if not self.over:
            self.finish(f"Stopped. {len(self.rows)} of {len(self.jobs)} layers measured.")
        core.QTimer.singleShot(0, self.dialog.close)


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        tell("Open a font first.")
        return
    masters = scripting.current_package().masters
    jobs = []
    for glyph in font.glyphs:
        for master in masters:
            jobs.append((glyph.name, master))

    def build(parent):
        job = LongJob(parent, font, jobs)
        return job.dialog

    scripting.show_script_dialog(build, KEY)


main()

Save it as long_job.py.

main makes the list of jobs before any window opens: one pair, a glyph name and a master name, for every glyph in every master. That's the cheap part, a list of 822 pairs of words. measure is the expensive part, and it's the same three calls the Sidebearings panel made in chapter 127.

Three lines set the dialog up, and each one switches off something a QProgressDialog would otherwise do by itself. setMinimumDuration(0) shows it at once (left alone, it waits four seconds to see whether the job is worth a window). setAutoReset(False) and setAutoClose(False) keep it from emptying its bar and vanishing the moment the bar is full, which would hide the word "Done" before anybody read it.

The timer is made with the dialog as its parent, so when the dialog goes, the timer goes with it. And build hands back job.dialog and lets go of job, as chapter 126's build did: the dialog and the timer hold self.on_cancel and self.on_tick, and those methods hold the job.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Run the script with Plum-practice open. A small window appears with a bar that fills from left to right, and while it fills you can drag the window about. When it's full, the label and the Output panel say this, with my stand-in's numbers in the rows:

Done. 822 layers measured in 33 slices.
('.notdef', 'Light', 0, 500, 0)
('.notdef', 'Regular', 0, 500, 0)
('.notdef', 'Bold', 0, 500, 0)
('A', 'Light', 22, 554, 22)
('A', 'Regular', 13, 596, 11)
('A', 'Bold', 3, 596, -33)

Thirty-three slices: 32 of 25, and one of the 22 that were left. The six rows are the first of the 822, there to show that the job did measure something. Click Close, and the window goes.

Run it again, and this time click Cancel while the bar is under way. The window goes, and the Output panel says where the job had got to. I stopped my stand-in after 14 slices:

Stopped. 350 of 822 layers measured.

followed by the same six rows. Your number will be whatever the bar had reached, and always a multiple of 25: Cancel is a click, a click waits for the loop, and the loop comes round between slices, never in the middle of one. If the bar is full before you can reach the button, your machine is quick. Set SLICE = 1 and try again.

One more thing, for tools that change the font. Don't put a commit in each slice, or one job would leave 33 steps in Edit > Undo. Do the slow part in slices, the measuring and planning, and make the change in one commit at the end. Chapter 131 does this to the Shift tool.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Delete self.timer.stop() from finish and run the script. The bar fills and the label says "Done", and it all looks right. Then look at the Output panel:

Done. 822 layers measured in 34 slices.
Done. 822 layers measured in 35 slices.
Done. 822 layers measured in 36 slices.

and on and on, each with its six rows, as fast as FontLab can print them. The timer is still firing. Every tick finds an empty slice, sees that the rows are all there, and finishes again. A zero-interval timer that nobody stops is a job that never ends. Click Close to kill it (closing the dialog takes its child, the timer, with it), and put the line back.

Now set SLICE = 822 and run it:

Done. 822 layers measured in 1 slices.

One slice, one turn of the loop, and the bar never shows a middle. That's Ines's freeze, with a progress window that had no chance to appear. The machinery is all there, and it's the size of the slice that makes it work. Set SLICE back to 25.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: FontLab's event loop does one thing at a time, so a slot that doesn't return leaves the whole program unable to repaint or to notice a click. A long job stays polite by doing a slice of its work each time a zero-interval timer fires, and keeping its place in an object between slices. A QProgressDialog shows the bar and sends canceled when its button is clicked, and one finish method, guarded so that it runs once, serves for done, stopped and failed alike. A tool that changes the font plans in slices and commits once.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Make the label say how far the job has got, as in Measuring... 350 of 822, by calling setLabelText in on_tick. Then change it to say which glyph is being measured. Which of the two would you rather watch?
  2. After a Cancel the window is gone, and the sentence about where the job stopped is in a panel Ines may not have open. Use the script's tell, chapter 39's message box, to say it in a message box as well. Where does the call go so that it appears once, and only after a Cancel?
  3. Give finish one more line of output: how many of the measured rows have a negative number on either side. Use the bracketed list from chapter 37 with an if.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Ines can see that a long job is alive, and she can stop it. That leaves her three clicks, which shifted every glyph in the Light three times. Chapter 131 makes the Shift tool one that deserves to be clicked by somebody who doesn't read scripts: one click, one Undo, a button that can't be pressed twice, and messages that say what to do.

docs.title: 131. A tool people can trust
docs.text:
Tuesday, 29 December. Ines took yesterday's three clicks back with three trips to Edit > Undo, which worked, and then she wrote Mira an email with three numbered complaints.

One: the window stays armed after a real change, so a second click does the change again. Two: she typed n ncaron, the label said Didn't work. and something about an auto layer, and she could not tell whether her n had moved. Three: she typed two names wrong, and the tool told her about the first one only.

Mira answered from her mother's kitchen in four words: "She's right. Fix it." Today's script is the Shift tool from chapter 129, hardened. Every change it makes is still one step in Edit > Undo. What's new is everything around that step: what the tool checks before it, what it says, and the state it leaves the window in.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open with the Font window in front, Fly installed, and shift_tool.py from chapter 129, with its settings functions.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9. The whole script ran against the stand-in widgets and the stand-in font from chapter 123, with a stand-in for Fly's commit that can be told to refuse or to fail half-way. The refusal texts are copied from Fly's source; the text of a write that failed half-way is built the way Fly's source builds it, around an error I made up.

docs.title: Step 1: Ask the cheap questions first
docs.text:
Read chapter 129's shift from the top and count how much work it does before it finds out that there's nothing to do. It measures every glyph and builds every line, and only then does the commit discover a problem. A careful tool turns that round. It asks the questions that cost nothing, in order, and leaves at the first bad answer:

def shift(text, left, right, rehearse):
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        return "Open a font first.", False
    if left == 0 and right == 0:
        return "Left and Right are both 0, so there's nothing to do.", False

Two things changed here. The first message used to be No font is open. That states a fact and leaves the person to work out the remedy. Open a font first. is the remedy. When you write a message, write the next thing the person should do.

The second change is the comma. shift now gives back two values: the text for the label, and True or False for "did the font change?" A return with a comma gives back a tuple, as functions have done since chapter 42, and the caller takes it apart in one line: text, changed = shift(...). The window needs that second value in step 4.

Complaint three is the next question. Chapter 123's plan_rows raised an error at the first name it couldn't find. Collect them all instead:

font_names = ["n", "o", "H"]
names = ["n", "zz", "o", "qq"]
missing = [name for name in names if name not in font_names]
print(f"Not in this font: {' '.join(missing)}.")

Not in this font: zz qq.

In the script the test is font[name] is None, as it has been since chapter 51. One sentence, every bad name, and Ines fixes both in one go.

docs.title: Step 2: Ask Fly what it would refuse
docs.text:
Complaint two. ncaron was built in chapter 56 from n and caron, and its layers are auto layers: FontLab rebuilds them from the parts. Fly refuses to commit an edit to one, because touching it would make FontLab rebuild every auto layer in the font. The refusal is correct. What's wrong is finding out about it from an error, after the click.

Fly will tell you in advance. The facts you've been passing to history.commit since chapter 55 can be asked directly:

facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
refused = history.refusals(facts, names, "geometry", allow_bases=True)
print(refused)

{'ncaron': 'has auto layers'}

refusals takes the facts, the names, the kind of edit and the same allow_bases you'd give the commit, and returns a dictionary: each name Fly would refuse, with the reason. An empty dictionary means every name is welcome.

Now the tool has a choice, and it's a design choice more than a Python one. It could refuse the whole click. Or it could leave ncaron alone, change the rest, and say so. For sidebearings the second is right: when n gets wider, ncaron follows by itself, which is the point of an auto layer. So the script plans rows only for the names that aren't in refused, and adds a line for each one that is:

lines += [f"Left alone: {name} ({refused[name]})" for name in refused]

Looping over a dictionary gives its keys, as in chapter 22.

One more question belongs here, because it needs the plan. A big negative number can ask for a glyph narrower than nothing. Any row whose new width is under zero stops the click, with the names.

docs.title: Step 3: Two kinds of going wrong
docs.text:
Here's the slot every tool has had since chapter 122, and it's today's mistake:

def on_go(self, *args):
    try:
        self.label.setText(self.work())
    except Exception as problem:
        self.label.setText(f"Didn't work.\n{type(problem).__name__}: {problem}")

It catches everything, which was the right first lesson. But Didn't work. covers two very different days. On one, Fly looked at the request, refused it, and the font is untouched. On the other, the change began and something broke in the middle. Ines's question, "did my n move?", has a different answer on each, and one message for both answers neither.

Fly keeps them apart for you. When it refuses before writing, it raises a ValueError. When a write has started and can't be finished or checked, it raises a RuntimeError, and its message says that changes may remain. Chapter 99 used two except lines under one try. Do that here. These are the last five lines of on_go, under its try:

except ValueError as problem:
    self.label.setText(f"{problem}\n{UNTOUCHED}")
except Exception as problem:
    self.label.setText(f"Stopped part-way: {problem}")

UNTOUCHED is the sentence Nothing was changed., kept in one constant so that the tool always says it the same way. Python tries the except lines from the top and takes the first that fits. A ValueError fits the first. Anything else falls to the second, which admits what it doesn't know. It doesn't need to say what to do about it, because Fly's error for a write that stopped half-way ends with that advice.

The type name is gone from both messages. ValueError: helped you while you were writing the tool. It tells Ines nothing.

docs.title: Step 4: Leave the window safe
docs.text:
Complaint one, and the reason for the second value. After a real change, the slot ticks Only show what would happen again:

            if changed:
                save_settings(KEY, {"left": left, "right": right})
                self.runs += 1
                self.rehearse.setChecked(True)
                text += f"\nChange {self.runs} from this window. Edit > Undo takes it back."

The next click, meant or not, is a rehearsal. To change the font a second time, Ines has to untick the box a second time, and that small chore is the whole safety. You might think of greying the button out while the tool works. It wouldn't help: as chapter 130 showed, clicks made while a slot runs wait in the queue, and they arrive after the slot has finished and the button is live again. What protects the font is the state the slot leaves behind.

The settings are now saved only after a real change, and the run counter counts only real changes, so the label can call it by its right name.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Shift Tool
# Adds to the sidebearings of the glyphs you name, or of the ones
# selected in the Font window, in the master that's showing.
# One click is one Undo step, and the tick box comes back after it.
import json

import fly.ap.core.history.glyphs as history
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import fly.ap.metrics.panel.model as metrics
from fly import ap, fl, qt
from fly.pens import layer_of
from fly.tr.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import pGlyph

core, gui = qt.QtCore, qt.QtGui
KEY = "tools.shift"
LIMIT = 200
SHOWN = 8
DEFAULTS = {"left": 0, "right": 0}


def settings_path():
    return ap.app.paths.userDataFolder / "tool-settings.json"


def read_settings_file():
    try:
        with open(settings_path(), encoding="utf-8") as f:
            stored = json.load(f)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return {}
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return {}
    if not isinstance(stored, dict):
        return {}
    return stored


def load_settings(key, defaults):
    values = dict(defaults)
    mine = read_settings_file().get(key)
    if not isinstance(mine, dict):
        return values
    for name in defaults:
        if name in mine and type(mine[name]) == type(defaults[name]):
            values[name] = mine[name]
    return values


def save_settings(key, values):
    stored = read_settings_file()
    stored[key] = values
    with open(settings_path(), "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(stored, f, indent=4, ensure_ascii=False)
UNTOUCHED = "Nothing was changed."


def read(owner, name):
    item = getattr(owner, name)
    return item() if callable(item) else item


def unique(names):
    found = []
    for name in names:
        if name not in found:
            found.append(name)
    return found


def plan_rows(font, master, names, left, right):
    rows = []
    for name in names:
        rich = pGlyph(font, font[name])
        old = (rich.getLSB(master), rich.getAdvance(master), rich.getRSB(master))
        new = (old[0] + left, old[1] + left + right, old[2] + right)
        rows.append((rich, layer_of(rich.fl, master), old, new))
    return rows


def shift(text, left, right, rehearse):
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None:
        return "Open a font first.", False
    if left == 0 and right == 0:
        return "Left and Right are both 0, so there's nothing to do.", False
    names = unique(text.split())
    if not names:
        names = scripting.names_selected_names()
    if not names:
        return "Type some glyph names, or select glyphs in the Font window.", False
    missing = [name for name in names if font[name] is None]
    if missing:
        return f"Not in this font: {' '.join(missing)}.\nCheck the spelling. {UNTOUCHED}", False

    package = scripting.current_package()
    master = package.master
    facts = history.scan_auto_facts(package)
    refused = history.refusals(facts, names, "geometry", allow_bases=True)
    rows = plan_rows(font, master, [name for name in names if name not in refused],
                     left, right)
    thin = [rich.name for rich, layer, old, new in rows if new[1] < 0]
    if thin:
        return f"Too far: {' '.join(thin)} would be narrower than nothing.\n{UNTOUCHED}", False

    lines = [f"{rich.name}: {old[0]} {old[1]} {old[2]} to {new[0]} {new[1]} {new[2]}"
             for rich, layer, old, new in rows[:SHOWN]]
    if len(rows) > SHOWN:
        lines += [f"and {len(rows) - SHOWN} more"]
    lines += [f"Left alone: {name} ({refused[name]})" for name in refused]
    if not rows:
        return "\n".join(lines + [UNTOUCHED]), False
    if rehearse:
        return "\n".join(lines + [f"{master}: {len(rows)} would change."]), False

    def change():
        for rich, layer, old, new in rows:
            metrics.shift_and_set(layer, left, new[1])

    layers = [layer for rich, layer, old, new in rows]
    owners = [rich.fl for rich, layer, old, new in rows]
    history.commit("Shift sidebearings", layers, owners, change,
                   operation="geometry", facts=facts, allow_bases=True)
    return "\n".join(lines + [f"{master}: {len(rows)} changed."]), True


class ShiftTool:
    def __init__(self, parent):
        self.panel = gui.QWidget(parent)
        self.panel.setWindowFlags(core.Qt.Tool)
        self.panel.setWindowTitle("Shift")
        self.panel.setAttribute(core.Qt.WA_DeleteOnClose)
        self.label = gui.QLabel("", self.panel)
        self.names = gui.QLineEdit("", self.panel)
        self.left = gui.QSpinBox(self.panel)
        self.left.setRange(-LIMIT, LIMIT)
        self.right = gui.QSpinBox(self.panel)
        self.right.setRange(-LIMIT, LIMIT)
        saved = load_settings(KEY, DEFAULTS)
        self.left.setValue(saved["left"])
        self.right.setValue(saved["right"])
        self.rehearse = gui.QCheckBox("Only show what would happen", self.panel)
        self.rehearse.setChecked(True)
        self.go = gui.QPushButton("Shift", self.panel)
        self.runs = 0
        self.go.clicked.connect(self.on_go)
        self.arrange()

    def arrange(self):
        form = gui.QFormLayout()
        form.addRow("Glyphs", self.names)

        sides = gui.QHBoxLayout()
        sides.addWidget(gui.QLabel("Left", self.panel))
        sides.addWidget(self.left)
        sides.addWidget(gui.QLabel("Right", self.panel))
        sides.addWidget(self.right)

        bottom = gui.QHBoxLayout()
        bottom.addWidget(self.rehearse)
        bottom.addWidget(self.go)

        outer = gui.QVBoxLayout(self.panel)
        outer.addLayout(form)
        outer.addLayout(sides)
        outer.addLayout(bottom)
        outer.addWidget(self.label)

    def on_go(self, *args):
        try:
            left = read(self.left, "value")
            right = read(self.right, "value")
            text, changed = shift(read(self.names, "text"), left, right,
                                  read(self.rehearse, "checked"))
            if changed:
                save_settings(KEY, {"left": left, "right": right})
                self.runs += 1
                self.rehearse.setChecked(True)
                text += f"\nChange {self.runs} from this window. Edit > Undo takes it back."
            self.label.setText(text)
        except ValueError as problem:
            self.label.setText(f"{problem}\n{UNTOUCHED}")
        except Exception as problem:
            self.label.setText(f"Stopped part-way: {problem}")


def build(parent):
    tool = ShiftTool(parent)
    return tool.panel


scripting.show_script_dialog(build, KEY)

Save it over shift_tool.py. unique drops a name given twice and keeps the order, which was exercise 3 in chapter 123. plan_rows lost its raise, because shift has already checked every name before calling it. Every early return carries False. Only the last line, after the commit, carries True.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Type n ncaron n, set both boxes to 10, and click Shift with the box ticked:

n: 70 523 66 to 80 543 76
Left alone: ncaron (has auto layers)
Regular: 1 would change.
