One n, though you typed two. Untick the box and click:

n: 70 523 66 to 80 543 76
Left alone: ncaron (has auto layers)
Regular: 1 changed.
Change 1 from this window. Edit > Undo takes it back.

The box is ticked again. Click once more without touching it, and the label ends Regular: 1 would change. with the numbers starting from 80. Nothing moved. Choose Edit > Undo once and the n is at 70, 523, 66.

Now the three kinds of "no". Type n zz qq:

Not in this font: zz qq.
Check the spelling. Nothing was changed.

Type hyphen, set both boxes to −200:

Too far: hyphen would be narrower than nothing.
Nothing was changed.

Set both boxes to 0 and the tool says there's nothing to do. Each of these returns before the plan is used, so none of them can have touched the font, and the tool says which.

The third kind I can only show from the stand-in. Told to fail half-way, it printed the tool's two words and then a sentence of the shape Fly builds: the name of the commit, what went wrong, and what to do. The middle part here is my stand-in's invention:

Stopped part-way: Shift sidebearings did not finish: the stand-in was told to fail. Native changes may remain; use Edit > Undo.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Delete the line self.rehearse.setChecked(True). Untick the box and click twice. The label says Change 2 from this window. and the n has moved twice: chapter 123's accident is back. One line stood between Ines and that.

Put the line back. Now swap the two except blocks, so that except Exception comes first. Open a Glyph window, so that it's in front, untick the box and click. Fly refuses to commit from there, with a ValueError. But Exception fits every error, it comes first, and Python never reaches the second block. The label says Stopped part-way, and the sentence Nothing was changed. is gone. Nothing was written, yet Ines is told the opposite, and if she reaches for Undo it takes back whatever she did before. That's a worse fault than the one the message was written for. Order the except lines from the narrowest to the widest, always.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A tool earns trust by asking its cheap questions first and leaving at the first bad answer, with a message that says what to do next. history.refusals tells you before the click what the commit would refuse, so a refusal becomes a line in the report. Two except lines keep "nothing was changed" apart from "something may have changed", and the narrow one goes first. After a real change, the slot puts the window back in its safe state.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. When the names field is empty, the tool uses the selection without saying so. Add a line to the label for that case, such as Using the 12 selected glyphs.
  2. Give the tool a limit: with more than 40 rows and the box unticked, return a message that asks for a rehearsal first, and False. Decide how the tool should know that a rehearsal has happened.
  3. Change shift so that a refused name stops the whole click. Run n ncaron both ways and write down which behaviour you'd want for sidebearings, and which for a script that deletes contours.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The tool is fit to hand over. Ines still starts it by opening the Scripting panel, finding the file and pressing Run, and she has said what she thinks of that. Chapter 132 puts the tools where the rest of FontLab's commands live: in the Scripts menu, sorted, under names she'd recognise.

docs.title: 132. Into the menu
docs.text:
Wednesday, 30 December. Ines has written out how she starts the Shift tool, step by step, and pinned it to the studio board: open the Scripting panel, open a file, look for shift_tool.py among forty others, press Run. Underneath, in red: "Four steps to start one tool."

She's right. A tool you have to hunt for is a tool you'll stop using. Today the Shift tool moves into the Scripts menu under a name she'd say aloud, the Halfmoon tools get one tidy place there, and the tool gets a key. The key takes more work than you'd hope, and I'll show you where the limit is.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
FontLab 9 with Fly installed, and shift_tool.py from chapter 131. No font has to be open to follow the steps.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9. I ran the three files in plain Python against stand-ins for the windows and for FontLab's menu bar. What the real menu shows, and whether the key works on your keyboard, are things I haven't seen.

docs.title: Step 1: Two folders, two jobs
docs.text:
You've used two folders since chapter 33, and it's time to say plainly what each is for.

The Scripts folder is FontLab's. Chapter 18 put your first file there. Every .py file in it becomes a line in the Scripts menu, a folder inside it becomes a submenu, and the #FLM: line at the top of a file is the name the menu shows. FontLab reads the folder when it starts and when you choose Scripts > Refresh Scripts.

The module folder is Python's. It's the site-packages folder you found in chapter 33. Python looks there when a script says import. FontLab's menu never looks there.

So a file in the Scripts folder can be started and can't be borrowed from. A file in the module folder can be borrowed from and can't be started from the menu. Chapter 114 moved preflight.py from one to the other for that reason, and it left the menu when it went.

The Shift tool has to be both. Ines wants to start it from the menu, and in step 4 a second script will need to borrow it. One file can't live in two folders. Two files can.

docs.title: Step 2: The tool becomes a module
docs.text:
Move shift_tool.py out of the Scripts folder and into the module folder. Then change its last line. It was this:

scripting.show_script_dialog(build, KEY)

Make it this:

def open_tool():
    scripting.show_script_dialog(build, KEY)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    open_tool()

The window-opening line now has a name, open_tool, so that other files can ask for it. The last two lines are chapter 114's guard: they open the window when you run the file from the Scripting panel, and do nothing when another file imports it. You can still work on the tool the way you have all month.

The first line of the file was #FLM: Shift Tool. A module isn't in the menu, so that line now says nothing to anybody. Change it to a plain comment, such as # shift_tool.py: the Shift tool, as a module other scripts import.

docs.title: Step 3: A launcher with a good name
docs.text:
In the Scripts folder you have a folder named Halfmoon, from chapter 18. Make a new file in it, Shift Sidebearings.py:

#FLM: Shift Sidebearings
import shift_tool

shift_tool.open_tool()

That's the whole file. It's called a launcher: it owns nothing and decides nothing. It finds the tool and starts it. Choose Scripts > Refresh Scripts, and the menu has Scripts > Halfmoon > Shift Sidebearings. Ines's four steps are two clicks.

The launcher is three lines for a reason. When you mend the tool, you mend shift_tool.py, in one place, and the menu line never needs touching. The name in the menu and the code that does the work can now change without each other.

That leaves the naming, which is most of what makes a menu pleasant. Three rules have served the studio:

  • Name the job, not the code. Shift Sidebearings says what will happen to the font. shift_tool says what the file is. The first belongs in the menu and the second in the module folder.
  • Start with the verb. Shift Sidebearings, Copy Sidebearings, Open Up Bold. A menu is a list of things to do, and a verb first lets the eye run down it.
  • One folder for one studio. Everything Halfmoon wrote goes in Halfmoon. If that grows past a dozen lines, sort by what the tools work on, with the folder names in title case: Halfmoon Spacing, Halfmoon Checks. Keep it one folder deep. I've seen FontLab's own script collections go one level down and no further, and I haven't seen what the menu does with a folder inside a folder.

docs.title: Step 4: A key for the tool
docs.text:
Now the hard part. Ines wants a key: one press, and the window is there.

Here is what I can tell you honestly. I searched Fly, the helpers under it and FontLab's scripting names for a way to give a line in the Scripts menu a keyboard shortcut from a script, and found none. FontLab has its own place for shortcuts in its settings, and whether Scripts-menu lines appear there is something to look for in your copy; I haven't seen it.

What a script can do is add a menu of its own, and that menu's lines can have keys. Fly has a helper for it, OwnedMenus. "Owned" means the helper remembers every line it added, so that it can take them all away again:

from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.qt.menus import OwnedMenus


def report(error, owner):
    print(f"Halfmoon menu: {type(error).__name__}: {error}")


menus = OwnedMenus(qt, fl, error_sink=report, owned_title="Halfmoon")

OwnedMenus is Fly's own Python, so keyword arguments are fine here; the no-keywords rule from chapter 121 is for Qt's widgets. error_sink is a function you hand over, as you handed slots to buttons in chapter 122. When a menu line's work raises an error, Fly calls report with it, and the error goes to the Output panel. owned_title is the name of the new menu in FontLab's menu bar.

A line goes in with add_action, which wants the menu's name, the line's text, and the function to call:

token = menus.add_action("Halfmoon", "Shift Sidebearings", shift_tool.open_tool)

Here is the mistake that's waiting. It's the one from chapter 122, in new clothes. Write shift_tool.open_tool() with brackets and Python calls the function there and then: the Shift window opens while the menu is being built, and what the menu line receives is None, the nothing that open_tool returns. In the stand-in, choosing the line then prints this:

Halfmoon menu: TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable

No brackets. You're handing over the function, to be called later.

add_action gives back a number, a token, that stands for the new line. Ask for the line by its token and give it a key:

menus.action(token).setShortcut(qt.QtGui.QKeySequence("Ctrl+Alt+Shift+S"))

The key is written as text, with the modifier keys spelled out and joined by +. On a Mac, Qt reads Ctrl as the Command key. Three modifiers is a mouthful, and that's deliberate: FontLab already uses most of the short combinations, and a script that takes one of them over has made an enemy.

One thing remains. menus is an object, and chapter 126 showed what happens to an object nobody holds: Python throws it away, and its menu lines go dead. keep from chapter 127 holds it, and it is in the script again, word for word, so that the script runs by itself. And keep closes whatever it held before under the same key, which here means that running the script twice gives you one Halfmoon menu, with the old one taken out first.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Halfmoon Menu
# Adds a Halfmoon menu to FontLab's menu bar, with a shortcut
# for the Shift tool. The menu lasts until FontLab closes.
import sys

import shift_tool
from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.qt.menus import OwnedMenus

KEY = "tools.menu"
MENU = "Halfmoon"
SHORTCUT = "Ctrl+Alt+Shift+S"


def keep(key, things):
    kept = vars(sys).setdefault("kept_windows", {})
    if key in kept:
        kept[key][0].close()
    kept[key] = things


def report(error, owner):
    print(f"Halfmoon menu: {type(error).__name__}: {error}")


def main():
    menus = OwnedMenus(qt, fl, error_sink=report, owned_title=MENU)
    keep(KEY, [menus])
    token = menus.add_action(MENU, "Shift Sidebearings", shift_tool.open_tool)
    menus.action(token).setShortcut(qt.QtGui.QKeySequence(SHORTCUT))
    print(f"{MENU} menu added. {SHORTCUT} opens the Shift tool.")


main()

Save it as Halfmoon Menu.py in Scripts/Halfmoon. Notice the order inside main. keep comes straight after the menus object is made and before any line is added, so the old menu is gone before the new one is filled. Do it the other way round and, for a moment, two menus named Halfmoon exist, and add_action may put the new line in the old one.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Refresh the menu and choose Scripts > Halfmoon > Halfmoon Menu. The Output panel says:

Halfmoon menu added. Ctrl+Alt+Shift+S opens the Shift tool.

In the stand-in, the menu bar gained one menu, Halfmoon, with one line, and pressing the key opened one Shift window. Running the script a second time closed the first menu and left one.

The menu lasts until FontLab closes. Tomorrow it's gone, and Ines chooses Halfmoon Menu once to get it back. That's one click a day for a key that works all day, and she has agreed to it, with a look. FontLab can run a script of yours every time it starts, and that would spare her the click. I haven't seen it work for a script like this one, so the book leaves it there and Ines keeps her click.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Forget the guard. In shift_tool.py, replace the last two lines with a bare open_tool(). Restart FontLab, so that Python reads the module afresh, and choose Halfmoon Menu. A Shift window opens, though nobody asked for one: the import shift_tool line at the top of the menu script ran the whole file, and the whole file now ends by opening a window. An import should give you names and do nothing else. Put the guard back.

Leave the tool in the wrong folder. Move shift_tool.py back into the Scripts folder and restart FontLab. Choose Shift Sidebearings:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'shift_tool'

The launcher asked Python for a module, and Python looked only where it looks. The file is in plain sight in the menu's folder and invisible to import. Move it back.

Both breaks needed a restart, and so will every change you make to shift_tool.py from now on, because Python reads a module once. While you're working on it, run the file itself from the Scripting panel, which the guard allows, or use importlib.reload from chapter 33.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: The Scripts folder is for files you start, and the module folder is for files other scripts borrow from, so a tool that needs both becomes a module plus a three-line launcher. A menu name says the job, starts with a verb, and lives in one folder per studio. A script can't give a Scripts-menu line a key by any route I could find, but it can add its own menu with OwnedMenus, and those lines take keys. Whatever adds things to FontLab's menu bar must be kept, and must clear away the old before adding the new.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Give the Suffix Picker from chapter 125 the same treatment: a module with an open_tool function and a guard, a launcher named for the job, and a second line in the Halfmoon menu with its own key.
  2. The live panel from chapter 128 has a main function and no window key. Decide what its open_tool should be, and add it to the menu without a shortcut. What does the menu script have to import?
  3. Add a third line to the Halfmoon menu, Remove This Menu, whose function closes the menu. You'll need a small function of your own that calls menus.close(), and you'll need to think about where menus has to be for that function to see it.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The studio's tools now sit in two folders on one computer, put there by hand, file by file. Then Oskar's cousin rings from her studio in Porto: could she have them too? Chapter 133 packs the Halfmoon tools so that one file puts everything where it belongs, on any computer.

docs.title: 133. Pack it up
docs.text:
Thursday, 31 December. The studio shuts at one. At ten Oskar's cousin Rita rings again from Porto: she has FontLab 9, she has two people who space type all day, and she would like the Shift tool and the Suffix Picker before the year is out. Ines starts writing her an email. It has eleven steps by the time she stops: find this folder, make that folder, copy these two files here and those two there, mind the capital letters.

Eleven steps is eleven places to go wrong, and Rita will go wrong at step three, as anyone would. Today you put the tools in one folder, laid out so that one file in it can do all eleven steps. Then you write a short script that checks the folder before it leaves the building.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
shift_tool.py and the two launchers from chapter 132, and suffix_picker.py with its launcher, from chapter 132's first exercise. If you skipped that exercise, leave those two files out, and your output will have no Suffix Picker lines. You also need Instamix 1.0.9 or newer, installed as in chapter 4. It will generate the current install.vfpy for this folder.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9. The checking script is plain Python and I ran it as printed, on a folder built the way this chapter describes. The check below reads the project with Instamix's parser, without installing it. These checks do not establish that the windows and menus work in FontLab.

docs.title: Step 1: What the installer wants
docs.text:
install.vfpy is a generated entry point. You don't edit it. Instamix writes the current shared bootstrap into your folder; it reads what to do from a second file beside it, pyproject.toml. Older copies can have different bootstrap checks, so generate a new one for a new delivery.

Open it in FontLab 9 (double-click it, or drop it on FontLab's window) and it does this, all inside FontLab's own data folder:

  • It puts each package you list where Python looks for modules, the site-packages folder from chapter 33.
  • It copies everything in your folder's Scripts folder into FontLab's Scripts folder, keeping the folders, so Scripts/Halfmoon/Shift Sidebearings.py lands in the Halfmoon submenu.
  • It records the deployed files in its ownership ledger and adds list and uninstall commands under Scripts > Instamix. The extension payload stays under Extensions/Library; scripts run from their normal deployed locations.

Then it asks for a restart. So the folder you send needs four things in it:

spacing-tools/
    install.vfpy
    pyproject.toml
    spacing_tools/
        __init__.py
        shift_tool.py
        suffix_picker.py
    Scripts/
        Halfmoon/
            Shift Sidebearings.py
            Suffix Picker.py

Two of those are new to you: the folder called spacing_tools with a file called __init__.py, and pyproject.toml. The names say what's inside: tools for spacing. The folder you send has a hyphen in its name, like a file name; the package inside has an underscore, because the package's name is what a script writes after import, and Python reads a hyphen there as a minus sign.

docs.title: Step 2: A module that is a folder
docs.text:
The installer doesn't place loose .py files where Python looks. It places packages. A package is a folder that Python treats as a module, and what makes a folder a package is one file inside it with a fixed name: __init__.py, with two underscores each side.

When a script says import spacing_tools, Python searches its folders for spacing_tools.py or for a folder spacing_tools that holds an __init__.py. If it finds the folder, it runs __init__.py, and what that file defines is what spacing_tools. followed by a name reaches. Your tools don't need anything defined there. Each of them carries its own helpers, so the file only has to exist. One line saying what the package is will do. Here is all of __init__.py:

"""Halfmoon Type's spacing tools: the Shift tool and the Suffix Picker."""

A string on a line of its own at the top of a file is a docstring. Python keeps it as the module's description and does nothing else with it. So the move is small:

  1. Make a folder spacing_tools inside spacing-tools.
  2. Save that one line in it as __init__.py.
  3. Copy shift_tool.py and suffix_picker.py in beside it.

The two modules now live inside the package, and a module inside a package is reached through it:

#FLM: Shift Sidebearings
from spacing_tools import shift_tool

shift_tool.open_tool()

That's the launcher from chapter 132 with one line changed: import shift_tool has become from spacing_tools import shift_tool. The Suffix Picker's launcher changes the same way:

#FLM: Suffix Picker
from spacing_tools import suffix_picker

suffix_picker.open_tool()

Nothing inside shift_tool.py or suffix_picker.py changes. Save both launchers into spacing-tools/Scripts/Halfmoon.

One thing to do on your own machine first. Your loose shift_tool.py and suffix_picker.py are still in site-packages, and a loose shift_tool.py left in that folder is what import shift_tool finds, so an old launcher would go on running the old one. Move them somewhere safe before you try the installer yourself. Rita's machine has neither, so she has nothing to move.

docs.title: Step 3: The file that says what's what
docs.text:
pyproject.toml is a settings file that Python tools agree to read. The format is called TOML. It looks like the JSON of chapter 129 with the brackets taken off: names in square brackets start a table, and under each one come lines of name = value.

[project]
name = "spacing-tools"
version = "1.0.0"
dependencies = ["fontlab-fly>=1.3.0"]

[tool.fontlab-install]
id = "com.example.spacing-tools"
packages = ["spacing_tools"]

[project] holds the distribution name, this delivery's version and the distribution requirements. Here the tools need Fly 1.3.0 or later. [tool.fontlab-install] is the installer's own table. Its id is how FontLab's data folder will tell your tools from everyone else's, so it has to be yours alone, and the custom is to write it backwards from the general to the particular, with dots: kind of outfit, its name, the thing. com.example is the stand-in this book uses; put your own studio's web address there, backwards. Small letters, digits and hyphens only. packages lists the package folders. There's no line for the Scripts folder, because the installer looks for a folder called Scripts, with that capital, by itself.

Python can read TOML with a module that comes with it:

import tomllib

text = """
[project]
name = "spacing-tools"
version = "1.0.0"
dependencies = ["fontlab-fly>=1.3.0"]

[tool.fontlab-install]
id = "com.example.spacing-tools"
packages = ["spacing_tools"]
"""
project = tomllib.loads(text)
print(project["tool"]["fontlab-install"]["packages"])

['spacing_tools']

tomllib.loads takes text and gives a dictionary, as json.load gave you one from a file. A table is a dictionary, and the dot in [tool.fontlab-install] makes one inside another, so you go down through three keys to reach the list.

Now generate the installer from a terminal where Instamix is available:

uvx --from "fontlab-python-instamix>=1.0.9" fontlab-instamix stub spacing-tools

Run that command from the folder containing spacing-tools. It writes spacing-tools/install.vfpy. If a previous installer is there, inspect it first; add --force only when you intend to replace that file. The generated bootstrap checks the provider's migration and rollback capabilities before deploying the project.

docs.title: Step 4: The mistake that looks like a tidy-up
docs.text:
Here's the one I'd have made. The folder spacing_tools holds three files, and one of them has an odd name, holds one line that does nothing and looks like clutter. Delete __init__.py, and send the folder.

Your launchers import a package you no longer sent. Rita would write back "it doesn't work", and you'd be guessing from another country. Catch that missing file before sending anything, in a sentence that says which file and why. The check below reads Instamix's actual project contract, then checks the package and menu files you intend to deliver.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Check Package
# Reads a folder of tools and says whether install.vfpy has what it
# needs. Changes nothing.
from pathlib import Path

from fontlab_instamix.bootstrap import BootstrapError, read_project

FOLDER = Path.home() / "spacing-tools"


def launchers(folder):
    found = []
    scripts = folder / "Scripts"
    if not scripts.is_dir():
        return found
    for category in sorted(scripts.iterdir()):
        if not category.is_dir():
            continue
        for path in sorted(category.iterdir()):
            if path.suffix == ".py":
                found.append(path)
    return found


def check(folder):
    problems = []
    for name in ["pyproject.toml", "install.vfpy"]:
        if not (folder / name).is_file():
            problems.append(f"{name} is missing.")
    if problems:
        return [], problems

    try:
        project = read_project(folder)
    except BootstrapError as error:
        return [], [str(error)]

    lines = []
    for name in project.packages:
        if (folder / name / "__init__.py").is_file():
            lines.append(f"package   {name}")
        else:
            problems.append(f"{name}/__init__.py is missing, so {name} isn't a package.")
    for path in launchers(folder):
        first = path.read_text().splitlines()[:1]
        if first and first[0].startswith("#FLM:"):
            lines.append(f"menu      {path.parent.name} > {first[0][5:].strip()}")
        else:
            problems.append(f"{path.name} has no #FLM line at the top.")
    return lines, problems


def main():
    lines, problems = check(FOLDER)
    print(FOLDER.name)
    for line in lines:
        print(f"  {line}")
    for problem in problems:
        print(f"  PROBLEM   {problem}")
    if problems:
        print(f"{len(problems)} to fix before you send it.")
    else:
        print("Ready to send.")


main()

Save it as check_package.py, and set FOLDER to where your spacing-tools is.

check asks the cheap questions first, as chapter 131's tool did: if either of the two files is missing there's nothing to read, so it says so and stops. read_text() is new: it opens the file, reads it all and closes it, the three lines of chapter 27 in one. is_dir() is the sibling of chapter 111's is_file(), true for a folder. read_project reads the same metadata the installer will use. It returns facts about the package without deploying any files. A malformed TOML file still raises Python's TOMLDecodeError.

BootstrapError describes a missing or unusable installer table, including an invalid reverse-domain id. The check reports that message instead of maintaining its own, slightly different rule for ids.

launchers walks the Scripts folder two levels down, a loop inside a loop, because that's how deep the menu goes: categories, then scripts. For each launcher, check reads the first line and looks for #FLM:. splitlines()[:1] gives a list holding the first line, or an empty list for an empty file, so the test can't trip over a file with nothing in it. path.parent is the folder a path sits in, and .name of that is the category.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
spacing-tools
  package   spacing_tools
  menu      Halfmoon > Shift Sidebearings
  menu      Halfmoon > Suffix Picker
Ready to send.

Three lines say what Rita will get: one module to import and two lines in her menu. Read them as she would. If a tool you meant to send isn't in the list, it isn't in the folder.

Now zip the folder and send it, with a note of three lines, not eleven:

1. Install Fly first, from its own folder, the same way.
2. Unzip spacing-tools and double-click install.vfpy.
3. Restart FontLab. The tools are in Scripts > Halfmoon.

Line one makes the dependency explicit for Rita. The metadata also declares fontlab-fly>=1.3.0. Instamix can use a compatible sibling checkout or ask uv to resolve a distribution requirement; it refuses an incompatible source instead of silently changing it. Check the release instructions for any version not yet available from PyPI.

For a plain unzipped source folder, Instamix copies the package into FontLab's data folder. Rita's tools stay at the version you sent. A Git checkout can be installed editably, so its folder must stay in place. This example declares version 1.0.0; increase it for the next delivery. Other projects can derive a version from their build metadata or Git history. There is no universal 0.0.0 rule.

docs.title: A source project or a ready extension?
docs.text:
This chapter sends a source project with pyproject.toml. Instamix also installs ready extensions: a reverse-domain folder such as com.example.spacing-tools.fontlabext, with manifest.fontlabextj at its root. A .fontlabextz is a ZIP containing one or more whole .fontlabext folders, including their folder names. Its download filename does not define their identities; each manifest id must match its enclosing folder.

For a single script, Instamix can build that second form without running the script:

fontlab-instamix wrap width_report.py --out dist --id com.example.width-report --name "Width Report" --version 1.0.0 --zip

That creates a manifest and a script deployment rule. It does not package the imported spacing_tools module automatically: send this chapter's complete source project when its launchers need that package. For several ready extensions, fontlab-instamix pack puts their whole folders into one .fontlabextz. Inside FontLab, fontlab_instamix.gui.install_selected() can select archives or manifests; folder=True selects an extension folder.

An upgrade can refuse an owner-edited or unowned conflicting path. Keep the files it names; do not delete them merely to make the installer green. Instamix 1.0.9 restores the project's earlier deployed files and receipts on failure. Separately installed dependencies can remain. If restoration fails, keep the recovery directory named in the error. A timeout is an unknown outcome, so inspect the installation before retrying.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Make the tidy-up from step 4: delete spacing_tools/__init__.py, and run the check.

spacing-tools
  menu      Halfmoon > Shift Sidebearings
  menu      Halfmoon > Suffix Picker
  PROBLEM   spacing_tools/__init__.py is missing, so spacing_tools isn't a package.
1 to fix before you send it.

The same fault, caught on your side, in a sentence that says which file and why. Put it back.

Then change the id line to id = "Spacing Tools":

  PROBLEM   [tool.fontlab-install] id must be a reverse-DNS id like com.example.tool

This is the installer's own metadata error, caught by the check before deployment. Put it right. Last, delete the closing bracket of the packages line:

TOMLDecodeError: Unclosed array (at end of document)

That one isn't caught, and the script stops with Python's own error. It's readable enough for you, and you're the only one who runs this script, so I've left it. The rule from chapter 131 was about messages for people who didn't write the tool.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A package is a folder with an __init__.py in it, and Python imports it by the folder's name. install.vfpy reads pyproject.toml beside it, places the packages where Python looks, copies the Scripts folder into FontLab's menu, and records ownership so that removal can preserve edited files. TOML is tables of name = value, and tomllib.loads turns it into dictionaries. Before you send tools to someone who can't ask you questions, run the checks that their machine would run, and word the answers yourself.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add live_panel.py from chapter 128 to the package and give it a launcher. The check should show three menu lines.
  2. Make check complain when a launcher imports a module that isn't in the package. Reading the launcher's second line and looking for the word after import is enough for launchers shaped like yours.
  3. Add a file README.txt to the folder with the three-line note in it, and make check report a problem when it's missing. Rita's colleagues will open the folder without the email.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Rita's reply comes at ten to one: both tools are in her menu. Mira, back on Monday, has left a request of her own on the board: she wants to see the sidebearing numbers in the Glyph window itself, beside the glyph, without a panel at all. Chapter 134 writes a function that FontLab calls each time it draws a glyph.

docs.title: 134. Drawing on the canvas
docs.text:
It's Monday 4 January. Mira is back, the package went to Porto on Thursday, and she has spent the morning with the sidebearing panel from chapter 128 docked at the right. By eleven she has an opinion about it.

"It's correct," she says, "and it's in the wrong place. I'm looking at the n. The numbers are over there. Can't they sit under the glyph, where the space is?"

They can. This chapter puts two numbers and a line into the Glyph window, drawn by FontLab every time it draws the glyph. You won't open a window, connect a button or start a timer. You'll write one small class, put it in a folder with a particular name, and FontLab will find it and call it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open, Fly installed at version 1.3.0 or later, and Fontlabapp 1.2.31 or newer. This is the minimum for the lowercase bundle suffixes used here. You need chapter 126 for classes and chapter 128 for the word callback. No helpers from earlier chapters are used today.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9. I loaded the finished folder with the same loader FontLab uses at start, and I called the class on hand-made glyph measurements in plain Python; the numbers below come from that. What I have not seen is the drawing itself: the line and the numbers appearing in a real Glyph window. The people who wrote the plugin system say the same about their own reporters, so treat the picture as the part to check first.

docs.title: Step 1: A class built on another class
docs.text:
Every class you have written so far started from nothing. A class can also start from another class and change only what differs:

class Tool:
    title = "Tool"

    def describe(self):
        return f"{self.title} is ready."


class ShiftTool(Tool):
    title = "Shift"


print(Tool().describe())
print(ShiftTool().describe())

Tool is ready.
Shift is ready.

Two things are new. The name in brackets after ShiftTool says "start with everything Tool has". ShiftTool has no describe of its own, so it uses Tool's. And title sits in the class body, outside any method, with no self. in front: it belongs to the class, and every object made from the class sees it through self.title. ShiftTool replaces that one value, and describe, which it never wrote, picks up the new one.

In chapter 126's picture, a class was a wardrobe you built yourself. This is a wardrobe bought ready-made, where you swap one drawer.

That's how a plugin works. Somebody else wrote a class called Reporter that knows how to live in the Glyph window: how to be listed, switched on and off, and handed a glyph at the right moment. You build on it and supply the one thing it can't know, which is what to draw.

docs.title: Step 2: The function FontLab calls
docs.text:
A reporter has one method to write, compute. Here is the smallest reporter that draws anything:

from fly.ap.plugins.reporter import Mark, Reporter


class Sidebearings(Reporter):
    name = "spacing_sidebearings"
    title = "Halfmoon Sidebearings"

    def compute(self, snapshot):
        return [Mark("text", ((0, 0),), text="here")]

name is how FontLab remembers the reporter and title is what it shows in its list. compute is a callback, like the timer's on_tick in chapter 128, with a different caller: FontLab calls it whenever it draws a glyph while the reporter is switched on. It hands over a snapshot, which is a set of measurements of the glyph taken a moment ago, and it expects a list of marks back.

A Mark is a note saying "draw this, here". The first value is the kind: "text", "line", and a few more. The second is a tuple of points in font units, the units of chapter 43, so (0, 0) is the glyph's origin on the baseline. A text mark has one point and so the tuple has one pair in it, which is why there's a comma before the closing bracket. After those come the colour and, by name, the text.

Notice what compute doesn't do. It doesn't draw. It returns a list, and FontLab draws what's on it. That split is the same one you made in chapter 123, when plan_rows worked out the numbers and something else used them, and it pays in the same way: a method that only returns a list can be called in plain Python, with no window anywhere, to see what it would draw.

Mark is an ordinary Python class, so naming a value, as in text="here", is fine. The rule against names inside brackets from chapter 121 was about Qt's own widgets.

docs.title: Step 3: Read the snapshot
docs.text:
The snapshot carries what you need. snapshot.advance is the glyph's width. snapshot.bounds, when the reporter asks for it, is the box around the outline as four numbers: left, bottom, right, top. snapshot.metrics holds the font's vertical measures, with ascender and descender among them.

From chapter 61, the left sidebearing is the distance from zero to the left edge of the outline, and the right sidebearing is the distance from the right edge to the width. So one small function is enough:

def edges(snapshot):
    if snapshot.bounds is not None:
        left, bottom, right, top = snapshot.bounds
        return left, right
    xs = []
    for contour in snapshot.contours:
        for node in contour.nodes:
            if node.on_curve:
                xs.append(node.x)
    if not xs:
        return None
    return min(xs), max(xs)

It has three ways out. If the box is there, it gives the box's two sides. If not, it collects the x of every on-curve node and gives the least and the greatest; that's a fair second best, a little off for a round glyph whose curve bulges past its nodes. If there are no nodes at all, the glyph is empty and it gives None. Whoever calls it has one thing to check.

The box is only there if you ask. A reporter asks with one more line in the class body, needs_bounds = True. FontLab doesn't measure what no reporter wants, because all of this happens while it draws, many times a second when you drag a node.

That's the rule for a callback of this kind: be quick, and change nothing. compute gets measurements, not the glyph, so it couldn't change the font if it tried. Keep it that way in spirit too. Don't open files in it, don't print in it, and don't loop over the font.

docs.title: Step 4: Leave out self
docs.text:
Here is the mistake to make once. You write compute the way you'd write a loose function:

from fly.ap.plugins.reporter import Mark, Reporter


class Sidebearings(Reporter):
    name = "spacing_sidebearings"
    title = "Halfmoon Sidebearings"

    def compute(snapshot):
        return [Mark("text", ((0, 0),), text="here")]

Called by hand, it says:

TypeError: Sidebearings.compute() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given

You gave one value and Python counts two, because the object itself always arrives first. Chapter 126 met this error from the other side. Put self back.

In FontLab you wouldn't see a traceback in your face. Reporter wraps every call to compute in a try, for the reason your slots have caught their own errors since chapter 122: an error that escapes while a window is being drawn can take more than your plugin down with it. The reporter draws nothing and reports the error once, not once for every redraw. So when a reporter is switched on and the canvas stays bare, the first thing to do is call compute yourself, in plain Python, and read what it says.

docs.title: Step 5: A folder FontLab finds
docs.text:
A reporter isn't run from the Scripts menu. It lives in a folder, called a bundle, inside FontLab's user data folder, the one chapter 129 wrote the settings file into:

Extensions/
    reporters/
        Sidebearings.fontlabreporter/
            plugin.json
            sidebearings.py

The folder's name ends in .fontlabreporter and sits in reporters; both say what kind of plugin this is. sidebearings.py holds the class. plugin.json is a JSON file, the format from chapter 99, that introduces it:

{
  "id": "spacing_sidebearings",
  "name": "Halfmoon Sidebearings",
  "kind": "reporter",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "entry": "sidebearings:Sidebearings",
  "min_app_version": "1.2.31"
}

entry is the file's name without .py, a colon, and the class's name. id must equal the class's name, and name must equal its title. Saying the same thing in two places looks wasteful, and it's there on purpose: FontLab can read the JSON and list the plugin without running any of your Python, and when it does run it, a mismatch tells it the two files have drifted apart.

Use lowercase suffixes for every new bundle: .fontlabreporter, .fontlabfilter, .fontlabtool, .fontlabpalette and .fontlabgeneral. App 1.2.31 also accepts the former title-case suffixes so existing tools remain discoverable. Do not install both spellings as separate copies.

Instamix can wrap this draft for delivery after you have saved sidebearings.py:

fontlab-instamix wrap sidebearings.py --out dist --id com.example.sidebearings --name "Halfmoon Sidebearings" --version 1.0.0 --kind reporter --plugin-id spacing_sidebearings --entry sidebearings:Sidebearings --min-app-version 1.2.31 --zip

The wrapper validates this metadata without importing the draft. It puts the canonical reporter bundle inside a .fontlabext with a manifest, then packs the whole extension folder into .fontlabextz. It does not prove that the reporter draws correctly; the Glyph-window check below is still needed.

FontLab looks for bundles when it starts. Make the folders, save the two files, and restart.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Save this as sidebearings.py in the bundle folder:

# Shows a glyph's sidebearings in the Glyph window. Changes nothing.
from fly.ap.plugins.reporter import Mark, Reporter

BLUE = (80, 145, 190)
GAP = 7


def edges(snapshot):
    if snapshot.bounds is not None:
        left, bottom, right, top = snapshot.bounds
        return left, right
    xs = []
    for contour in snapshot.contours:
        for node in contour.nodes:
            if node.on_curve:
                xs.append(node.x)
    if not xs:
        return None
    return min(xs), max(xs)


class Sidebearings(Reporter):
    name = "spacing_sidebearings"
    title = "Halfmoon Sidebearings"
    layer = "background"
    needs_bounds = True

    def compute(self, snapshot):
        found = edges(snapshot)
        if found is None:
            return []
        left, right = found
        low = snapshot.metrics.descender
        high = snapshot.metrics.ascender
        width = snapshot.advance
        return [
            Mark("line", ((width, low), (width, high)), BLUE),
            Mark("text", ((0, low),), BLUE, text=f"{left:g}"),
            Mark("text", ((width + GAP, low),), BLUE, text=f"{width - right:g}"),
        ]

There's no #FLM line, because this file never appears in the Scripts menu.

The class body has four lines of facts before any method. layer = "background" asks for the marks to go behind the outline, so they don't cover the nodes Mira is dragging. needs_bounds = True is the request from step 3.

compute asks edges for the two sides and returns an empty list for an empty glyph: nothing to say, nothing drawn. Otherwise it makes three marks. The line stands at the glyph's width and runs from the font's descender to its ascender. The left number sits at zero and the right number a little past the line, both at the descender, which puts them under the glyph in the space they describe. GAP keeps the right number from touching the line.

The right sidebearing is width - right. The :g in the two f-strings, which you used in chapter 107, prints 70.0 as 70 and leaves 50.5 alone.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
You can check the class before FontLab ever sees it. With a snapshot for an n as Plum ships it in the Regular, where the width is 523 and the outline runs from 70 to 457, compute returns three marks:

line   at x 523, descender to ascender
text   "70"  at x 0
text   "66"  at x 530

Left 70, width 523, right 66. If you kept the shift from chapter 123, your own n is ten wider on each side, and your numbers will be 80 and 76. For the shipped o, both texts say 38. For space, which has no outline, the list is empty.

Then restart FontLab, open the n in a Glyph window, and choose View > Reporters. Halfmoon Sidebearings should be in the list. Switch it on. What I expect, and haven't seen, is a blue line at the right edge of the glyph's width and two blue numbers under the glyph. Drag the whole outline ten units to the right and, as you let go, the left number should go up by ten and the right one down by ten. Then choose Edit > Undo. Nobody clicked anything, and no timer is running: FontLab drew the glyph again, so it called compute again.

Mira switches it on and closes the docked panel.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Open plugin.json and change "name" to "Sidebearings". Restart. The reporter isn't in the list. The loader refused the bundle:

ValueError: manifest id/name/kind must match the entry class

It refused before running any drawing code, and it went on to load everything else. A bundle with a mistake in it is skipped and logged, and the others load. Put the name back.

Now, in sidebearings.py, delete the two lines in compute that test found is None. Call compute with an empty glyph:

TypeError: cannot unpack non-iterable NoneType object

edges gave None and the next line tried to split it into two names. In the Glyph window this would be the quiet failure from step 4: nothing drawn for space, one report, and every other glyph fine. A plugin is called for every glyph the user opens, including the ones you didn't think of. Put the test back.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: A class can be built on another class, keeping all of it and replacing a value or a method. A plugin is such a class in a folder FontLab searches at start, with a small JSON file that introduces it. Its one method is a callback that FontLab calls on every draw, so it must be quick, change nothing, and return a list of marks for FontLab to draw. And because it only returns a list, you can call it in plain Python and read the answer before you trust it on the canvas.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a fourth mark: the width, as text, at the top of the line. Use snapshot.metrics.ascender for the height.
  2. Mira wants a warning when the two sides of a round glyph differ. Give the two numbers a red colour, (220, 50, 45), when they differ by more than 4, and keep them blue otherwise. Check with the o, and then with a made-up snapshot where they differ by 10.
  3. Make a second bundle, with its own folder, id and class, that draws one line at half the glyph's width. Work out which of the six values in plugin.json must change, and which may stay.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: On Tuesday a friend of Mira's sends her a script that finds glyphs with stray single points. It was written for another font editor, and its first line imports a module FontLab doesn't have. Chapter 135 reads a script from somewhere else, and finds out how much of it runs here.

docs.title: 135. Scripts from other apps
docs.text:
It's Tuesday 5 January. A friend of Mira's, who draws type in Glyphs, has sent her a file called Find Stray Points.py with a one-line message: "This saved me last month. Does it run in yours?"

A stray point is a path with a single node. It prints as nothing, and it can turn up later as a dot in somebody's PDF. Mira would like to know whether Plum has any. She opens the file, sees from GlyphsApp import Glyphs on line six, and passes it across the desk to you.

Today you read a script written for another program, ask a tool what it needs before you run it, and then run it without changing a character of it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open and Fly installed. Type the friend's script from step 1 and save it as Find Stray Points.py in your Downloads folder. That's where a file somebody sends you lands.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9. The part that reads the friend's script without running it works outside FontLab, and I ran it as printed: the reports below are what it said. I also ran the friend's script, unchanged, through the same translating layer on the small test font that layer ships with, which has one glyph. What I haven't seen is that script walking Plum inside FontLab.

docs.title: Step 1: Read it before you run it
docs.text:
Here is the whole of what arrived:

#MenuTitle: Find Stray Points
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
__doc__ = """
Lists glyphs that have a path with a single node.
"""
from GlyphsApp import Glyphs

font = Glyphs.font
found = []
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    for layer in glyph.layers:
        for path in layer.paths:
            if len(path.nodes) == 1:
                found.append((glyph.name, layer.name))

Glyphs.clearLog()
for name, layer_name in found:
    print("%s (%s)" % (name, layer_name))
print("%d stray points." % len(found))
Glyphs.showMacroWindow()

You have never seen this dialect, and you can read most of it anyway. That's worth noticing: after 134 chapters, an unfamiliar script is mostly familiar.

Go through it the way chapter 38 went through a traceback, one line at a time, sorting each into "I know this", "I can guess this" and "I must look this up".

The first line is a comment that plays the part of your #FLM line: the name for the other program's menu. The second is a note about the file's text encoding, left over from older Pythons. __doc__ is a name holding a description; the three quote marks start a string that may run over several lines. None of these three does anything when the script runs.

The middle you know. An empty list, three loops one inside the next, a test with len, and a tuple appended for each hit. font.glyphs you've used since chapter 7. A layer that has paths, and a path that has nodes, are a guess you'd get right.

Two lines near the end look odd:

name, layer_name = "A", "Regular"
print("%s (%s)" % (name, layer_name))
print("%d stray points." % 3)

A (Regular)
3 stray points.

This is how Python filled strings before f-strings. Each %s is a gap for a value and %d is a gap for a whole number; the values come after the lone %, in a tuple when there's more than one. You'd write f"{name} ({layer_name})". You don't need to write the old form, only to recognise it, because a great many scripts in the world still use it.

That leaves the lines to look up: the import, and the three things asked of Glyphs. Glyphs.font must be the current font, the other program's fl.CurrentFont(). clearLog and showMacroWindow sound like emptying and showing its Output panel.

So you can say what this script does before running it. It reads every layer of every glyph, changes nothing, and prints a list. That's the first question to ask of any script from somewhere else, and you answer it by reading.

docs.title: Step 2: Why it can't run, and what an adapter is
docs.text:
Paste it into the Scripting panel and it stops at line six. FontLab has no module called GlyphsApp.

You could translate it by hand. Glyphs.font becomes fl.CurrentFont(), the layers and paths become whatever FontLab calls them, and in half an hour you'd have your own version. Then the friend fixes a mistake in hers, and you have two scripts that have drifted apart.

The other way is an adapter. A travel adapter doesn't change your charger or the wall; it sits between them with one shape on each face. A software adapter is a module with the names one program expects on its front and calls to another program at its back. Chapter 4 listed one in the toolbag and left it there: Glyport, gp in Fly. It supplies a GlyphsApp module whose Glyphs.font is FontLab's current font, wearing the other program's names.

Its own documents are blunt about the edges, and you should be too. It covers the common model: fonts, glyphs, layers, paths, nodes, anchors, components. It doesn't claim to be the other program. Scripts that build that program's own kind of dialog, or that paint in its edit view, or ask an instance for a ready-made interpolated font, are refused with an error that names what was missing. A refusal is the adapter working as it should; one that guessed would be worse.

docs.title: Step 3: Ask what it needs
docs.text:
Before running a stranger's script, you can have Glyport read it:

from pathlib import Path

from fly.gp import inspect_source

SCRIPT = Path.home() / "Downloads" / "Find Stray Points.py"

report = inspect_source(str(SCRIPT))
print(report.required_capabilities)
for item in report.dependencies:
    print(item.line, item.module)

('glyphs:model',)
6 GlyphsApp

inspect_source opens the file as text. It doesn't run it. It finds the imports and works out which parts of the adapter the script would lean on. Here the answer is one: the model, which is the part Glyport covers. dependencies lists each import with its line.

The report also carries diagnostics, which are notes with a severity of "info", "warning" or "error", and a message. For this script there's a warning that nothing in the file says which version of the other program it was written for, so Glyport will assume the newest.

docs.title: Step 4: Believe the report too much
docs.text:
Here is the mistake. The report said glyphs:model and nothing else, so you conclude the script will work. To see why that's too much, add a line to the end of the friend's script that asks for one of the refused things:

shown = font.instances[0].interpolatedFont

Inspect it again:

('glyphs:model',)
6 GlyphsApp

The report hasn't changed. The inspector reads imports and broad areas; it doesn't follow every name on every line, and it can't know what a font will hold when the script meets it. Glyport's own report says so in a note of its own: "Imports and capabilities are observations; runtime behavior is unexecuted."

It's chapter 93 again. There, "the features compile" didn't mean "the features are right". Here, "nothing it needs is missing" doesn't mean "it runs". An inspection can tell you no. It can't tell you yes. Only a run can, and for a script that changes things, only a run on a copy. Take the extra line out again.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Try A Glyphs Script
# Reads a script written for Glyphs, says what it needs, and runs it
# through Glyport if you agree. What the other script does is its business.
from pathlib import Path

from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from fly.gp import inspect_source, run_script

SCRIPT = Path.home() / "Downloads" / "Find Stray Points.py"
KNOWN = ["glyphs:model"]
TITLE = "Try A Glyphs Script"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def ask(question):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    answer = run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, question, "Question", box.Yes | box.No)
    return answer == box.Yes


def findings(report):
    lines = []
    for item in report.dependencies:
        lines.append(f"line {item.line}: imports {item.module}")
    for item in report.diagnostics:
        if item.severity != "info":
            lines.append(f"{item.severity}: {item.message}")
    return lines


def unknown(report):
    return [name for name in report.required_capabilities if name not in KNOWN]


def stops(report):
    return [item.message for item in report.diagnostics if item.severity == "error"]


def main():
    if not SCRIPT.is_file():
        tell(f"There's no file at {SCRIPT}.")
        return
    report = inspect_source(str(SCRIPT))
    print(SCRIPT.name)
    for line in findings(report):
        print(line)
    print("needs:", ", ".join(report.required_capabilities))

    if stops(report):
        print("Python can't read it. Not run.")
        return
    extra = unknown(report)
    if extra:
        print(f"Needs something this script doesn't know: {', '.join(extra)}. Not run.")
        return
    if not ask(f"Run {SCRIPT.name} on the current font?"):
        return
    handle = run_script(str(SCRIPT))
    print("Ran.")
    handle.close()


main()

Save it as try_script.py.

Three small functions read the report and main decides. findings turns imports and any note above "info" into lines for the Output panel. unknown lists what the script needs beyond KNOWN, the short list of things you have decided you trust the adapter with. stops collects the messages of errors, which mean Python couldn't read the file at all.

tell and ask are chapter 39's message boxes, here again so that the script runs by itself. main has four ways to stop before running anything: no file, a file Python can't read, a need outside KNOWN, and you saying no. Only then does it call run_script, which runs the friend's file through the adapter as she wrote it, character for character. run_script runs the file and gives back a handle, an object that stands for that one run. close() tells Glyport you're done with it, so that whatever the other script held is let go. Glyport's own introduction shows the handle in a with block. The code doesn't support that, so the script calls close() itself.

The question in the prompt is plain on purpose. You've read this script and know it only reads. The next one somebody sends may not, and try_script.py can't tell the difference. The person who reads the script decides.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Find Stray Points.py
line 6: imports GlyphsApp
warning: No generation-specific evidence; runtime defaults to glyphs4 unless a profile is specified explicitly.
needs: glyphs:model

Then the prompt. Say yes, and the friend's script runs. On the one-glyph test font I ran it on, it printed:

A (Regular)
1 stray points.
Ran.

On Plum I expect a longer wait, since it visits every layer of 274 glyphs, and with luck a count of zero. I can't print Plum's answer, because I haven't seen it. "1 stray points" is the friend's grammar, and it stays, because the file is hers.

Mira reads the Output panel, then goes to look at the one glyph it names in her own font. That's the right order: the script points, and a person looks.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
In the friend's script, add a line under the import:

import vanilla

vanilla is the kit the other program's scripts build windows with. Run try_script.py:

line 6: imports GlyphsApp
line 7: imports vanilla
needs: glyphs:model, ui:vanilla
Needs something this script doesn't know: ui:vanilla. Not run.

The inspector saw the import, named the area, and your script refused, because ui:vanilla isn't in KNOWN. Glyport does have an answer for some of those windows. Whether to trust it is a decision to make script by script, with the file open in front of you, and a short KNOWN list is how you make it on purpose. Take the line out.

Now change the friend's last print to the form Python 2 used, with no brackets:

print "%d stray points." % len(found)

error: Missing parentheses in call to 'print'. Did you mean print(...)? (Find Stray Points.py, line 19)
warning: Python 2 syntax suggests glyphs2; this is an era heuristic, not a declared app version.
needs:
Python can't read it. Not run.

Old scripts look like this. The report is empty after needs: because a file Python can't read has no imports to find. Glyport has a tool for adapting such files, and that's beyond this chapter. Put the brackets back.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: You can read a script in a dialect you've never used by sorting its lines into known, guessable and to be looked up, and you should, before anything else, to learn whether it changes the font. An adapter puts one program's names in front of another program's objects, so a script can run unchanged and stay the same file its author maintains. An inspection that reads the file without running it can rule a script out, and can't rule it in. And an adapter that refuses what it can't do, by name, is one you can build on.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a count to findings: one line saying how many lines the friend's script has. SCRIPT.read_text() from chapter 133 and splitlines from chapter 87 are enough.
  2. Translate the friend's two odd print and % lines into f-strings in a copy of her file, and check that the copy prints the same. Then decide which file you'd keep, and why.
  3. Make try_script.py take a list of scripts and print the short report for each, running none. Which of the four stops still make sense?

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The friend's script runs here because an adapter speaks her program's dialect. There's a wider agreement than that: a shared set of names, called fontParts, that several font editors accept. Chapter 136 writes one report that should run in more than one of them, and uses Fly's other adapter, fp, to run it in FontLab.

docs.title: 136. One script, several editors
docs.text:
It's Wednesday 6 January. Mira's friend Tove got her answer about stray points, and has written back with a request of her own. "That font summary you print before a release, with the counts. Could I have it? I'm in RoboFont, mind."

Every script you've written starts with from fly import. Tove's editor has no Fly. You could write her a second version, and from then on every change would have to be made twice.

Today you write the summary once, in a way that doesn't care which editor it's in, and give each editor a three-line script that hands it a font.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open and Fly installed. Chapter 135 for the idea of an adapter, chapter 95 for a function that returns a dictionary, and chapter 33 for importing a module of your own.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9, and I haven't run it in RoboFont. What I did is closer to the point of the chapter than either: I ran plum_report.py on a small seven-glyph test font through two different sets of fontParts objects, outside any editor. One was the reference set that the fontParts project ships. The other was Fontport's, the objects Fly's fp gives you, working on a font in memory. Both printed the same six lines, which are below. FontLab's side of the three-line launcher is unseen.

docs.title: Step 1: The agreement
docs.text:
In chapter 135 an adapter made FontLab answer to one other program's names. That works for one pair of programs at a time.

fontParts is a different kind of thing. It's a written list of names: a font has info and kerning, and you can loop over it to get glyphs; a glyph has name, width, unicode, and so on for a few hundred names. Nobody's editor is described by it. It's an agreement that several editors have each undertaken to answer to, whatever their own objects are called underneath. Programmers call such a list an interface. The wall socket is one: the kettle doesn't know which power station is behind it.

You've been on the other side of an interface already. In chapter 134, FontLab's part was to call compute with a snapshot and yours was to return marks. Neither side knew more about the other than that.

Fly's fp, Fontport, is FontLab's way of keeping its side of the fontParts agreement. It was in the toolbag in chapter 4.

docs.title: Step 2: A function that takes a font
docs.text:
The trick to writing for several editors is small. The part of your script that does the work must never go looking for the font. It's handed one:

def glyph_count(font):
    return len(font)

There's no fl.CurrentFont() in it and no import at all. Whoever calls it has to bring a font, and the function will work with anything that answers to len. You've written functions like this since chapter 29. What's new is noticing that such a function has no idea where it is.

Getting the font is the one thing every editor does differently, so it goes in a separate, tiny script for each editor. For FontLab:

from fly.fp.world import FontWorld

font = FontWorld().CurrentFont()

FontWorld is Fontport's front desk. Its CurrentFont gives the font in front, wearing fontParts names, or None when no font is open. Its glyphs are FontLab's own glyphs. Nothing is copied; a change made through these names would be a change to your font, which is why today's script only reads.

docs.title: Step 3: Use only what's on the list
docs.text:
Now the summary, with fontParts names:

def summary(font):
    without = []
    for glyph in font:
        if glyph.unicode is None:
            without.append(glyph.name)
    return {"glyphs": len(font), "without": without}

Looping over the font gives glyphs. glyph.unicode is the glyph's character code as a number, or None when it has none. len(glyph) counts its contours and glyph.components lists its components, so a glyph with neither has nothing drawn in it. font.kerning behaves like a dictionary of pairs, so len of it counts them. font.info.familyName and font.info.styleName are the two halves of the font's name.

Some of these are spelled the way you know from Fly and some aren't. Don't guess from Fly. The agreement has its own documentation, and the rule for a portable script is that every name on a font or glyph comes from there.

docs.title: Step 4: Trust the order
docs.text:
Here is the mistake, and it's the one that makes two editors disagree about the same font. This version collects the glyphs with nothing drawn, in the order the loop meets them:

def empty_names(font):
    empty = []
    for glyph in font:
        if len(glyph) == 0 and len(glyph.components) == 0:
            empty.append(glyph.name)
    return empty

On my test font, which has two empty glyphs, one set of fontParts objects printed:

Nothing drawn     2  nbspace, space

and the other:

Nothing drawn     2  space, nbspace

It's the same font and the same function. The agreement says that looping over a font gives you every glyph. It doesn't say in what order, and the two disagree. One follows the font's glyph order; the other follows the order of its own storage.

You would never have found this in FontLab alone. A script that runs in one place can lean on a hundred habits of that place without knowing it. The cure costs one word: return sorted(empty). Whenever a portable script shows a list, it puts the list in an order of its own choosing.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
There are three files today. The first does the work. Save it as plum_report.py in the site-packages folder from chapter 33, where Python looks when a script says import:

# A font report that uses only fontParts names, so it can run in any
# editor that speaks fontParts. It reads the font and changes nothing.


def summary(font):
    without = []
    empty = []
    widest = None
    for glyph in font:
        if glyph.unicode is None:
            without.append(glyph.name)
        if len(glyph) == 0 and len(glyph.components) == 0:
            empty.append(glyph.name)
        if widest is None or glyph.width > widest.width:
            widest = glyph
    return {
        "glyphs": len(font),
        "without": sorted(without),
        "empty": sorted(empty),
        "widest": widest,
        "pairs": len(font.kerning),
    }


def lines(font):
    facts = summary(font)
    out = [f"{font.info.familyName} {font.info.styleName}"]
    out.append(f"Glyphs            {facts['glyphs']}")
    out.append(f"No character      {len(facts['without'])}")
    out.append(f"Nothing drawn     {len(facts['empty'])}  {', '.join(facts['empty'])}")
    widest = facts["widest"]
    if widest is not None:
        out.append(f"Widest            {widest.name} at {widest.width:g}")
    out.append(f"Kerning pairs     {facts['pairs']}")
    return out


def report(font):
    if font is None:
        print("Open a font first.")
        return
    for line in lines(font):
        print(line)

It has no #FLM line and no import. It doesn't use Fly or anything you wrote in earlier chapters, because Tove has neither. That's the price of a portable file: it can lean on Python and on the agreement, and on nothing of yours.

summary gathers the facts into a dictionary, as the functions of chapter 95 did. lines turns the facts into text. report prints, and deals with there being no font. Keeping them apart means the part that reads the font can be checked without printing anything, which chapter 139 will use.

widest starts as None and is replaced by any glyph wider than the one held so far. It's the glyph itself that's kept, so lines can ask it for both its name and its width.

The second file is FontLab's launcher. Save it as plum_report_fontlab.py:

#FLM: Plum Report
from fly.fp.world import FontWorld

import plum_report

plum_report.report(FontWorld().CurrentFont())

The third is for Tove. Hers starts from the agreement's own front door, which her editor fills in:

from fontParts.world import CurrentFont

import plum_report

plum_report.report(CurrentFont())

The two launchers differ in one import. Everything that could need fixing next month is in the file they share.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
On the seven-glyph test font, through both sets of objects:

Plum Regular
Glyphs            7
No character      1
Nothing drawn     2  nbspace, space
Widest            m at 790
Kerning pairs     2

In FontLab, with Plum-practice in front, I expect the first number to be 274, the count chapter 114's check prints, "No character" to be 39, since that check finds 235 glyphs with one, and 105 kerning pairs, as chapter 109 left them. Which glyphs it finds with nothing drawn, and which is widest, you'll see before I do. If your first two numbers differ from chapter 114's, believe chapter 114 and tell me.

One thing to watch for. A fontParts font is one master. FontLab's Plum has three, and which of them CurrentFont hands over through Fontport, I haven't seen. The style name on the first line will tell you.

Mira sends Tove two files and a line: "Put them in the same folder. Run the short one."

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Add a line to summary, inside the loop:

        if glyph.selected:
            print(glyph.name)

selected is on the agreement's list: a glyph can say whether it's selected. Run the report. Through Fontport, on the first glyph:

UnsupportedCapability: RGlyph.<lambda>: No native primitive implements this FontParts operation

And through the reference objects, which have no window to select anything in:

NotImplementedError: The RGlyph subclass does not implement this method.

A name being on the list means every editor knows what you're asking. It doesn't mean every editor can answer. Fontport's documents say plainly that selection is one of the things it doesn't carry, along with a few kinds of change it refuses because FontLab stores the thing differently, such as kerning values with a fraction. As in chapter 135, a refusal that names the missing piece is the honest behaviour.

So "portable" is a claim you test, editor by editor. The way to know that a report runs in two places is to run it in two places. Take the two lines out.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: An interface is a list of names that several programs agree to answer to. A script becomes portable when the working part is a function that's handed its font, uses only names from the agreement, and leans on nothing of yours; fetching the font goes in a separate few lines for each editor. The agreement leaves things unsaid, such as the order of glyphs, so a portable script chooses its own order. And being on the list isn't the same as being supported, so you run the script in each place before you say it works there.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add a line to the report for the narrowest glyph that has something drawn. Decide what to do when two glyphs tie, and make sure both editors would name the same one.
  2. glyph.leftMargin is the left sidebearing, and None for a glyph with nothing drawn. Add a count of glyphs whose left and right margins are equal. Mind the None.
  3. Write a third launcher that doesn't use the current font at all. It asks FontWorld().AllFonts() for every open font and prints a report for each, with a blank line between.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Friday's build still starts with somebody opening FontLab, finding the Scripts menu and clicking twice. Ines would like to type one line in a terminal window and go for coffee. Chapter 137 drives FontLab from outside, and finds out how long a job it will accept that way.

docs.title: 137. Drive FontLab from outside
docs.text:
It's Thursday 7 January, and tomorrow is a Friday. Ines has run the Friday build more than once now, and each time it began the same way: find FontLab among the open windows, open the Scripts menu, find Halfmoon, click.

"I have a terminal window open all day," she says. "I type one line and things happen. Can the build be one line?"

Some of it can. Today a Python script that isn't inside FontLab asks FontLab to do things and reads the answers. You'll also find the limit: FontLab gives a job from outside five seconds, and the Friday build was never a five-second job.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
FontLab open with Plum-practice in front. The Friday scripts from chapters 114 to 119, where FontLab can import them. uv from chapter 4, and a copy of Remopy, which comes as a folder called fontlab-remopy from the same place as Fly.

Two things about today are different from every other chapter, and I'd like them said before any code.

The script you write today doesn't run in FontLab. It runs in the Terminal, in an ordinary Python that has never heard of FontLab. So it can't start with from fly import, and it doesn't: it's the one script in this book that imports another package by name. The rule since chapter 4 was about scripts inside FontLab, and that rule stands.

And I have run less of this chapter than of any other. I ran friday.py against a stand-in that answers the way Remopy's own code says FontLab answers: a value and the printed text on success, an error with a type and a message on failure, and no answer at all when time runs out. The lines friday.py prints are from those runs. I haven't seen it talk to a real FontLab. How long each Friday step takes on Plum, which decides whether this chapter works for you, I can't tell you.

docs.title: Step 1: Two programs
docs.text:
Until now there was one program. Your script ran inside FontLab, as a guest in its house, and could touch anything.

Today there are two. FontLab is one. The other is a plain Python started from the Terminal. They don't share names, modules or memory. All that passes between them is text: one sends a request, the other sends back an answer.

The usual words are client and server. The server is the program that waits to be asked, and here that's FontLab. The client is the one that asks. A waiter and a kitchen work this way. The waiter can't cook and can't see the stove; he hands in a slip and gets back a plate, or a message that the fish is off.

FontLab has to agree to be asked. It's a preference, which Remopy's documents call mcp.enabled, that lets programs outside FontLab send it requests. Remopy can switch it on for you. In the Terminal, in the folder that holds fontlab-remopy:

uv run --with ./fontlab-remopy fontlab-remopy setup

uv run --with means "run this with that package available, for this one run". Nothing is installed for good.

docs.title: Step 2: Ask one question
docs.text:
Save this as ask.py, beside the fontlab-remopy folder:

from fontlab_remopy import FontLab

with FontLab() as app:
    print(app.eval("1 + 1"))

And run it from the Terminal:

uv run --with ./fontlab-remopy ask.py

2

That's an unimpressive result with a strange history. The text 1 + 1 went from your script to FontLab; FontLab's Python worked it out; the answer came back as text and was turned into a number again. FontLab() in a with block opens the line and closes it when the block ends.

eval is for one expression. For several lines there's run, which takes a whole piece of Python as a string. Whatever that code puts in a variable called result comes back to you:

from fontlab_remopy import FontLab

CODE = """
from fly import fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
print("counting")
result = len(font.glyphs)
"""

with FontLab() as app:
    done = app.run(CODE)
    print(done.value)
    print(done.stdout)

The code in the string is a FontLab script, and it does start with from fly import, because it runs in there. What comes back has two parts you'll use: done.value is what result held, and done.stdout is everything the code printed. Its print didn't go to FontLab's Output panel. It was caught and sent back to you.

The value must be something that survives being written down as text: a number, a string, True, None, a list or dictionary of those. A glyph can't cross. You can't bring the font to the Terminal, only facts about it.

docs.title: Step 3: One call for the whole build
docs.text:
Here is the tempting version, and the mistake. The Friday build is a function, so ask for it:

from fontlab_remopy import FontLab

with FontLab() as app:
    app.run("import friday_build\nfriday_build.main()")

Two things go wrong, and neither is your code's fault.

First, there are two clocks. FontLab stops any code sent from outside after five seconds; that limit is FontLab's, and Remopy can't raise it. Remopy has a patience of its own, thirty seconds unless you ask for another number, after which it stops waiting and raises TimeoutError. I haven't seen what comes back when FontLab's five seconds run out: it may be an error with FontLab's own wording, or an answer Remopy can't read. The second half of the build writes two proofs and reads ten font files. I'd be surprised if that fits.

Second, and worse, is what you know afterwards. When the time runs out, the client gets no answer. No answer isn't "it failed". The work may have stopped half-way, or finished a moment after the line went quiet. Remopy's documents put it plainly: the outcome is unknown, so check FontLab before repeating.

This is new. Inside FontLab, a script that failed told you so. Between two programs there are three results: yes, no, and silence. Silence has to be treated as "go and look".

That changes how you cut the work up. Each request should be short, so that it fits. And a request whose silence would be dangerous shouldn't be sent at all. Chapter 119's last step gives the font its next version number. If that call went silent, you wouldn't know whether Plum is at 1.004 or 1.005, and running it again might make it 1.006. So that step stays inside FontLab, where the answer appears in front of you and Edit > Undo is one keystroke away. The steps that only read and report are safe to repeat, and those are the ones to drive from outside.

There's a third trap in the same call. friday_build.main opens a small window when no font is open, and so does any script that uses chapter 39's ask or tell. A window waits for a click. Nobody is there to click, and the call ends without a useful answer. Code you send from outside mustn't ask questions.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
# Runs the Friday build's checks in FontLab from a terminal window.
# FontLab must be open, with the font in front.
#     uv run --with ./fontlab-remopy friday.py
# This file runs outside FontLab, so it can't import fly.
from fontlab_remopy import FontLab, NativeExecutionError, ResultTransportError

WHICH_HALF = """
import export_family
import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
import friday_build
from fly import fl

result = "none"
font = fl.CurrentFont()
if font is not None and font.path:
    folder = export_family.export_folder(font, scripting.current_package())
    result = "before"
    if folder.exists() and friday_build.font_files(folder):
        result = "after"
"""

HALVES = {
    "before": [("Checks", "ship_check", "main")],
    "after": [
        ("Files", "export_family", "main"),
        ("Inspect", "inspect_export", "main"),
        ("Glyph proof", "proof_html", "main"),
