        ("Text proof", "proof_text", "main"),
        ("Source copy", "friday_build", "keep_source"),
    ],
}


def code_for(module, function):
    return f"import {module}\nresult = {module}.{function}()"


def run_step(app, label, module, function):
    try:
        done = app.run(code_for(module, function))
    except NativeExecutionError as problem:
        error = problem.payload.get("error")
        if type(error) is dict:
            print(f"{label}: DID NOT RUN: {error['type']}: {error['message']}")
        else:
            print(f"{label}: DID NOT RUN: {problem}")
        return False
    except (TimeoutError, ResultTransportError):
        print(f"{label}: no answer. It may or may not have run. Look in FontLab.")
        return False
    if done.stdout:
        print(done.stdout.strip())
    if done.value != 0:
        print(f"{label}: stopped the build ({done.value})")
        return False
    print(f"{label}: ok")
    return True


def main():
    with FontLab() as app:
        half = app.run(WHICH_HALF).value
        if half == "none":
            print("Open a saved font in FontLab first.")
            return
        print(f"{half.capitalize()} the export.")
        for label, module, function in HALVES[half]:
            if not run_step(app, label, module, function):
                return
    if half == "before":
        print("Checks passed. Run Friday Build in FontLab, export, then run this again.")
    else:
        print("Files checked. Friday Build in FontLab gives the font its next number.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Save it as friday.py, beside ask.py.

WHICH_HALF is a FontLab script kept in a string, in the triple quotes of chapter 98. It's chapter 119's own test, moved: no saved font gives "none", a folder with font files in it gives "after", and anything else gives "before". It answers with a word and opens no window.

HALVES lists the steps for each half as a label, a module and a function. They're chapter 119's lists with two differences. Each step is named in text, because the functions themselves live in FontLab and can't be mentioned out here. And "Next version" is missing, for the reason in step 3.

code_for writes the two-line script for one step. Chapter 119 arranged for every one of these functions to return its count of problems, and that count is what crosses back as done.value.

run_step has the three results in it. An error inside FontLab arrives as NativeExecutionError, whose payload carries the type and message of what went wrong in there. When FontLab's wording isn't the usual pair of type and message, the script prints whatever the error says of itself. type(error) is dict is chapter 11's type put to work: is this thing a dictionary? Silence arrives as TimeoutError, or as ResultTransportError when something came back that Remopy couldn't read, and the line it prints says the one true thing about both. The brackets after except hold two kinds of error for one block, as in chapter 99. Otherwise there's an answer: the step's own printed lines are shown, and anything but zero stops the build, as in chapter 119.

After a silence, main stops. It doesn't try the next step, and Remopy wouldn't let it: once a call has timed out, the line is closed until you open a new one.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Before the export:

uv run --with ./fontlab-remopy friday.py

Before the export.
...
Checks: ok
Checks passed. Run Friday Build in FontLab, export, then run this again.

Where I've put three dots you'll see the lines ship_check.py prints, the table from chapter 114. They were printed inside FontLab and carried out to your Terminal.

Ines still has to go to FontLab once, and that isn't new: chapter 119 already had a manual step in the middle, because the export is hers to do. After the export, the same line again:

After the export.
...
Files: ok
...
Inspect: ok
...
Glyph proof: ok
...
Text proof: ok
Source copy: ok
Files checked. Friday Build in FontLab gives the font its next number.

If one of those steps takes longer than five seconds on your machine, I expect one of two lines in its place, and the run ends there. Either a DID NOT RUN line carrying FontLab's words, or this:

Glyph proof: no answer. It may or may not have run. Look in FontLab.

Then look. If the proof file is in today's folder with the right time on it, the step ran. And tell me which step it was. A step that can't fit has to be cut smaller inside its own script, and that's a change to chapter 116 or 117.

Ines gets most of what she asked for. It's one line, typed twice, with one visit to FontLab between and one after.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
In HALVES, change "ship_check" to "ship_chek" and run it:

Before the export.
Checks: DID NOT RUN: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'ship_chek'

The error happened in FontLab. Its type and its message travelled back as text and your script printed them. That's the "no" of the three results, and it's as clear as an error inside FontLab ever was. Put the name back.

Now close FontLab and run it again. I can't show you these lines, because my stand-in is never closed. Remopy looks for FontLab's side of the line and, depending on what it finds, raises FileNotFoundError or times out on the first call, the one that asks which half. Notice that main has no try around that call. Add one in exercise 2.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Two programs that can't see inside each other can still work together by passing text: a client asks and a server answers. What crosses is plain data, so you send code as a string and get numbers, words and printed lines back. A request can end in yes, in no, or in silence, and silence means the outcome is unknown. So work driven from outside is cut into short requests, opens no windows, and leaves out any step that would be dangerous to repeat.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Write count.py, which prints the number of glyphs in the current font and the font's family name, using one run and a dictionary as the result.
  2. Wrap the WHICH_HALF call in main so that a TimeoutError or FileNotFoundError prints "FontLab isn't answering. Is it open?" and ends the script.
  3. Before the steps of either half, print the font's version number, so the Terminal shows which build this is. Chapter 96 has the name to ask for. Send it as code and bring the answer back as result.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The release notes for 1.004 need pictures: the specimen line, and the n with its new sidebearing numbers under it. Mira has been taking them by hand, cropping each one. Chapter 138 has FontLab take its own pictures.

docs.title: 138. Pictures of your work
docs.text:
It's Friday 8 January. The build ran this morning, at the second attempt, from Ines's terminal and then from the Scripts menu, and there's a folder called 2027-01-08-v1.004 with ten fonts in it.

The release notes want two pictures: the specimen word, and the n with Mira's sidebearing numbers under it. Last time she took them by hand. Press the keys, drag a rectangle, miss by a few pixels, drag again, find the file on the desktop, rename it, move it. Two pictures took ten minutes, and the two rectangles weren't the same size.

Somebody has already written a tool that photographs FontLab's windows. Today your script calls it, keeps the two files it needs out of the eight it's given, and puts them where the release lives.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open, and an export folder with fonts in it, from chapter 119. And GrabLab, which comes as a folder called fontlab-grablab from the same place as Fly. It has an install.vfpy of the kind you met in chapter 133: drag it onto FontLab, then restart.

GrabLab isn't in Fly's toolbag, so today's script imports it by its own name, grablab. That makes it the second and last exception to the rule from chapter 4, after yesterday's. Yesterday's script ran outside FontLab. This one runs inside, and the reason is plainer: Fly has no alias for it.

I haven't run this chapter in FontLab 9, and a chapter about pictures is the one where that matters most, because I have no picture to show you. I read GrabLab's code to learn what it's called with and what it hands back, and ran release_shots.py against a stand-in that makes empty files with the names GrabLab's code builds. The printed lines below are from those runs. What the pictures look like, you'll see and I haven't.

docs.title: Step 1: Ask for pictures
docs.text:
Open two Glyph windows. In one, the n, with chapter 134's Sidebearings reporter switched on. In the other, type the specimen word.

Then, in the Scripting panel:

from grablab import Grab

grab = Grab()
grab.newGrab()
paths = grab.grabGlyphWindows()
print(len(paths))

Grab() makes a grabber. newGrab starts a new set of pictures: it makes a folder for them, named with the date and time, inside a folder called GrabLab in your Pictures folder. grabGlyphWindows photographs every Glyph window that's showing and returns a list of the files it wrote.

Leave out the second line and you get the first mistake most people make with this tool:

AttributeError: 'Grab' object has no attribute 'grab_folder'

The message is true and no help. It's GrabLab's own inside showing: the folder is set up by newGrab, and nothing has set it. When somebody else's tool gives you an AttributeError about a name you never typed, the usual cause is a step you skipped. Their README lists the steps in order.

docs.title: Step 2: Count what came back
docs.text:
With two Glyph windows open, I expect print(len(paths)) to say:

8

You asked for two pictures. GrabLab was written for people who document software, and it's generous. For each window it takes the drawing area alone and then the whole window with its title bar and toolbars, and it saves each of those as a PNG picture and as an SVG drawing. That's two windows, two views and two formats.

Print the names to see the pattern:

from pathlib import Path

for path in paths:
    print(Path(path).name)

Each name starts with fl_, then two letters for what was photographed: gv for a Glyph window's drawing area, gw for the whole window. Then come the window's title, the time, and the font's name. If your FontLab is set to its dark look, the letters get a d: gvd and gwd.

This is what calling another tool is like. Inside your own module you decided what every function returns. Here somebody else decided, for their reasons, and the names of the files are the only description you get. So you write a small function that says what you want out of what you're given.

docs.title: Step 3: Keep two of eight
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

KEEP = ["fl_gv_", "fl_gvd_"]


def wanted(paths):
    found = []
    for path in paths:
        path = Path(path)
        if path.suffix == ".png" and any([path.name.startswith(kind) for kind in KEEP]):
            found.append(path)
    return sorted(found)

Path(path) is a precaution. GrabLab's code hands back Path objects today, but its documents only say "file paths", and wrapping a Path in Path costs nothing. any with a list is chapter 44's, and startswith is chapter 9's.

The list comes back sorted for the reason chapter 136 gave: the order windows are photographed in is GrabLab's business, and the order of your release pictures should be yours.

You can also ask for less in the first place. Grab takes settings by name, and Grab(grab_svg=False) makes a grabber that doesn't write the SVG drawings. That halves the eight. I haven't seen whether the choice outlasts the script and changes what GrabLab's own menu commands write. The filter stays, because the whole-window pictures still come.

docs.title: Step 4: Borrow the folder
docs.text:
The pictures belong in the release folder. Chapter 120's release.py has a function that finds it, shipped_folder, and the natural line is import release.

Try it and the release summary prints, all 21 lines, and RELEASE.txt is written again. release.py ends with a bare main(), so importing it runs it. You've met this three times, in chapters 114, 119 and 132. And there's a second cost that you'll meet in chapter 139: a script that borrows from another script breaks when somebody changes that one.

shipped_folder is eight lines. Copy it, with the FORMATS list it reads, into today's script:

FORMATS = [".otf", ".ttf"]


def shipped_folder(font):
    exports = Path(font.path).parent / "exports"
    if not exports.exists():
        return None
    found = None
    for folder in sorted(exports.iterdir()):
        if any([p.suffix.lower() in FORMATS for p in folder.rglob("*")]):
            found = folder
    return found

It's chapter 120's function, word for word. Now release_shots.py runs by itself, and nothing in release.py has to change. Today's script ends with the guard all the same:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

It runs when it's run and keeps quiet when it's borrowed. A script somebody may one day borrow from should end this way from the start.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
#FLM: Release Shots
# Photographs every open Glyph window and copies the pictures into the
# newest export folder, in a subfolder called shots.
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

from fly import fl, qt
from fly.ap.ui.dialogs import run_standard_message_box
from grablab import Grab

KEEP = ["fl_gv_", "fl_gvd_"]
FORMATS = [".otf", ".ttf"]
TITLE = "Release Shots"


def tell(text):
    box = qt.QtGui.QMessageBox
    run_standard_message_box(qt, fl.MainWindow(), TITLE, text, "Information", box.Ok)


def shipped_folder(font):
    exports = Path(font.path).parent / "exports"
    if not exports.exists():
        return None
    found = None
    for folder in sorted(exports.iterdir()):
        if any([p.suffix.lower() in FORMATS for p in folder.rglob("*")]):
            found = folder
    return found


def wanted(paths):
    found = []
    for path in paths:
        path = Path(path)
        if path.suffix == ".png" and any([path.name.startswith(kind) for kind in KEEP]):
            found.append(path)
    return sorted(found)


def copy_shots(shots, folder):
    target = folder / "shots"
    target.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    number = len(list(target.glob("*.png")))
    copied = []
    for shot in shots:
        number += 1
        copy = target / f"{folder.name}-shot{number}.png"
        shutil.copy(shot, copy)
        copied.append(copy)
    return copied


def main():
    font = fl.CurrentFont()
    if font is None or not font.path:
        tell("Open a saved font first.")
        return 1
    folder = shipped_folder(font)
    if folder is None:
        tell("No export folder holds fonts yet. Run the Friday build.")
        return 1
    grab = Grab(grab_svg=False)
    grab.newGrab()
    shots = wanted(grab.grabGlyphWindows())
    if not shots:
        print("No Glyph window to photograph. Open one and run this again.")
        return 1
    for copy in copy_shots(shots, folder):
        print(copy.name)
    print(f"{len(shots)} pictures in {folder.name}/shots")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Save it as release_shots.py in your Scripts folder. tell is chapter 39's message box and shipped_folder is chapter 120's, both here again so that the script runs by itself.

copy_shots copies; it doesn't move. GrabLab's originals stay in Pictures, with their sidecar files beside them. Each picture GrabLab takes has two small text files with the same name that record sizes and what was photographed. Leave them where they are.

The copies get names of your choosing: the folder's name, then shot1, shot2. The count starts from the number of PNG files already in shots, so a second run adds shot3 and shot4 and replaces nothing. GrabLab itself never writes over a file, and it's a good habit to copy from it along with the pictures.

main returns 1 for "didn't happen" and 0 for "done", as the Friday scripts have since chapter 119, so this one can join a list of steps later.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
With the two Glyph windows open:

2027-01-08-v1.004-shot1.png
2027-01-08-v1.004-shot2.png
2 pictures in 2027-01-08-v1.004/shots

Open the shots folder and look at them. Which window became shot1 depends on how the two window titles sort, which I haven't seen. I expect the drawing area and nothing else, with the reporter's numbers under the n if the reporter was on.

Then check two things I can't check for you. Is the picture sharp enough for the notes? On a high-resolution screen a picture has twice as many pixels each way as the window's size suggests. And did the grab leave your windows as it found them? GrabLab changes a few display settings while it works and puts them back. If anything looks different afterwards, tell me.

Run it a second time:

2027-01-08-v1.004-shot3.png
2027-01-08-v1.004-shot4.png
2 pictures in 2027-01-08-v1.004/shots

Mira has four pictures and wants two, so she deletes the first pair, where the n was too small. The second pair goes into the notes. Both were taken the same way and are the same kind of picture, and it took a few seconds.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Close both Glyph windows, so that only the Font window is open, and run the script:

No Glyph window to photograph. Open one and run this again.

grabGlyphWindows didn't complain. It photographed every Glyph window, there were none, and it returned an empty list. An empty list from somebody else's tool is a result your script has to expect. Without the if not shots: lines the script would have made an empty shots folder and printed "0 pictures", which looks like success.

Now a quieter break. In KEEP, delete "fl_gvd_", switch FontLab to its dark look, open a Glyph window and run it. You get the same "No Glyph window" line, with a window open in front of you. The files were written, under names your filter no longer knows. A filter on names is a guess about somebody else's naming. When it finds nothing, print one of the names it was given and read it. Put the entry back.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: Calling another person's tool means working with their choices: their order of steps, their folder, their file names, and more results than you asked for. You read their documents for the steps, look at what comes back before you trust it, and write one small function that keeps what you need. An empty answer is an answer and needs its own message. A script you might borrow from should guard its main(). When your script copies files for people to read, it gives them names you chose and doesn't write over what's there.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Add "fl_gw_" and "fl_gwd_" to a second list, and make the script copy whole-window pictures into a subfolder called windows.
  2. grab.grabFontWindows() photographs Font windows. Add one picture of the Font window to the shots, and decide what it should be called.
  3. Add "Pictures" to chapter 137's HALVES, after "Text proof". Then think about whether it belongs there: what did step 3 of that chapter say about jobs with a time limit, and how long does a photograph take? Time it before you decide.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: This morning's build stopped the first time through, at the glyph proof. Days earlier somebody had changed one small function in the glyph proof's script, the proof stopped finding a font, and nobody knew until today. Chapter 139 writes down what your functions are supposed to do, in a form Python can check in two seconds, without opening FontLab.

docs.title: 139. Test your tools
docs.text:
It's Monday 11 January. On Friday the build stopped at "Glyph proof" the first time through, and it took twenty minutes to find out why.

The week before, Mira had tidied proof_html.py, chapter 115's glyph proof. One of the things she tidied was its copy of key, the small function from chapter 112 that makes two spellings of a name comparable. She took out .lower(), because the names she was looking at were all in the same capitals anyway. They weren't, for one weight. The proof uses key to find font files, and it stopped finding one.

The change was one word, the build broke, and nobody knew for four days. Today you write down what your functions are supposed to do, in a form Python can check in a second, in the Terminal, with FontLab closed.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
uv from chapter 4 and the Terminal from chapter 137. The spacing-tools folder from chapter 133, with copies of chapter 115's proof_html.py and chapter 136's plum_report.py put inside it, next to pyproject.toml. No FontLab at all.

This is the one chapter where I can say the opposite of what I usually say. I ran all of it. Every block of Terminal output below is copied from a real run on my machine, including the failures. Your version numbers and timings will differ.

docs.title: Step 1: A claim Python can check
docs.text:
You have checked your work all through this book by running a script and reading what it printed. That works, and it has two costs. You have to be there. And you have to remember what the right answer looked like.

assert is a Python word that does the reading for you:

assert 2 + 2 == 4
assert len("Plum") == 4

assert is followed by something that should be true. If it is, nothing happens at all, and the script goes on. If it isn't, the script stops with an AssertionError. A line of assert is a claim, written where Python can hold you to it.

A test is a function that makes a few such claims about one of your functions:

def key(text):
    return "".join([c for c in text.lower() if c.isalnum()])


def test_key_ignores_capitals_and_punctuation():
    assert key("Plum-SemiBold") == key("plum semibold")

The test's name says what's being claimed, in words, and starts with test_. That start matters, as you'll see in a moment.

Notice what the test doesn't say. It doesn't say how key works. It says what must come out for something that goes in. Mira could rewrite key from top to bottom tomorrow, and as long as those two spellings still come out equal, the test has no complaint. A test fixes the behaviour and leaves the code free.

docs.title: Step 2: Something to run them
docs.text:
You could call each test function yourself. There's a tool that does it for you, and it's the one nearly everybody uses: pytest. It looks in the folder for files whose names start with test_, runs every function in them whose name starts with test_, and reports.

It isn't installed, and it doesn't need to be. In the Terminal, in the spacing-tools folder:

uv run --no-project --with pytest --with fontParts pytest -q

The -q at the end asks pytest for its short report. This is chapter 137's --with again: run pytest, with pytest and fontParts available for this one run. You'll need fontParts in step 4. --no-project is new. uv sees the pyproject.toml that chapter 133 wrote for FontLab's installer and takes the folder for a project of its own kind, which it isn't: without those two words it stops and complains that the file has no version.

docs.title: Step 3: A file you can't import
docs.text:
Here is the natural first test file, and the mistake. Save it as test_proof.py in spacing-tools:

from proof_html import key


def test_key_ignores_capitals_and_punctuation():
    assert key("Plum-SemiBold") == key("plum semibold")

Run pytest:

test_proof.py:1: in <module>
    from proof_html import key
proof_html.py:7: in <module>
    import fly.ap.core.scripting as scripting
E   ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'fly'

The test never ran. key needs nothing from FontLab; it takes a string and returns a string. But it lives in a file whose imports need FontLab, and importing one function means importing its whole file. The last line of pytest's report says Interrupted: 1 error during collection: it gave up before running any test in any file.

Delete test_proof.py. As long as it's in the folder, pytest stops there and runs nothing else.

The cure is to sort your functions by what they need. The plain functions can't stay in a script that starts by importing Fly, because Python runs those imports before it lets you have anything else from the file. They need a package of their own, of the kind chapter 133 made. In spacing-tools, make a folder plain beside the folder spacing_tools, and in it a file __init__.py:

# Small functions that need nothing from FontLab, so that tests can
# import them anywhere. FontLab scripts borrow them from here.


def key(text):
    return "".join([c for c in text.lower() if c.isalnum()])

Then, in proof_html.py, delete def key and its line, and put this line with the other imports:

from plain import key

The rest of proof_html.py still says key(...), so nothing else in it has to change. key is now a borrowed name, and the function itself lives where a test can reach it. Copy the changed proof_html.py back over the one FontLab runs.

FontLab has to be able to find plain too, or the glyph proof stops with No module named 'plain'. In pyproject.toml, the line chapter 133 wrote becomes:

packages = ["spacing_tools", "plain"]

When the tests pass, run chapter 133's Check Package, run install.vfpy again and restart FontLab. I haven't seen that second install run.

This is the lasting idea of the chapter, more than assert or pytest. A function that works something out from plain values can be tested anywhere. A function that reaches into FontLab can only be tested in FontLab, by hand. So keep the working-out apart from the reaching-in. You did this in chapter 136 without being told why: summary and lines are handed a font and print nothing.

docs.title: Step 4: A font for the tests
docs.text:
plum_report.summary needs a font. There isn't one in the Terminal.

Chapter 136 solves this too. summary uses only names from the fontParts agreement, and the fontParts project ships plain objects that keep that agreement with no editor behind them. A test can build a tiny font from those in a dozen lines, with glyphs whose every number you chose:

from fontParts.fontshell import RFont

font = RFont(showInterface=False)
glyph = font.newGlyph("n")
glyph.unicode = 0x6E
glyph.width = 600
print(len(font))

RFont(showInterface=False) makes an empty font and no window. newGlyph adds a glyph and hands it back. 0x6E is the code for n, written the way chapter 6 showed.

Because you built the font, you know the right answers before the report runs. That's what makes a claim possible. You can't write assert facts["glyphs"] == 274 about Plum and trust it next month, when Plum has 280. You can write == 4 about a font you made with four glyphs, and it stays true.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
# Tests for the functions that don't need FontLab. Run them in the
# Terminal:  uv run --no-project --with pytest --with fontParts pytest -q
from fontParts.fontshell import RFont

import plain
import plum_report


def small_font():
    font = RFont(showInterface=False)
    font.info.familyName = "Test"
    font.info.styleName = "Regular"
    for name, code, width in [("n", 0x6E, 600), ("m", 0x6D, 900), ("space", 0x20, 250)]:
        glyph = font.newGlyph(name)
        glyph.unicode = code
        glyph.width = width
        if name != "space":
            pen = glyph.getPen()
            pen.moveTo((50, 0))
            pen.lineTo((width - 50, 0))
            pen.lineTo((width - 50, 500))
            pen.closePath()
    font.newGlyph("n.alt").width = 620
    font.kerning[("n", "m")] = -10
    return font


def test_key_ignores_capitals_and_punctuation():
    assert plain.key("Plum-SemiBold") == plain.key("plum semibold")


def test_key_keeps_digits():
    assert plain.key("Plum v1.004") == "plumv1004"


def test_summary_counts_glyphs_and_pairs():
    facts = plum_report.summary(small_font())
    assert facts["glyphs"] == 4
    assert facts["pairs"] == 1


def test_summary_lists_glyphs_without_a_character():
    facts = plum_report.summary(small_font())
    assert facts["without"] == ["n.alt"]


def test_summary_sorts_the_empty_glyphs():
    facts = plum_report.summary(small_font())
    assert facts["empty"] == ["n.alt", "space"]


def test_summary_finds_the_widest():
    facts = plum_report.summary(small_font())
    assert facts["widest"].name == "m"


def test_lines_for_an_empty_font():
    font = RFont(showInterface=False)
    font.info.familyName = "Test"
    font.info.styleName = "Regular"
    assert plum_report.lines(font) == [
        "Test Regular",
        "Glyphs            0",
        "No character      0",
        "Nothing drawn     0",
        "Kerning pairs     0",
    ]

Save it as test_tools.py in spacing-tools, beside the plain folder and plum_report.py.

small_font builds the font: n and m with a triangle drawn in each, a space with nothing drawn, an n.alt with no character and nothing drawn, and one kerning pair. The pen lines are chapter 46's. Every test that wants a font calls small_font() and gets a fresh one, so no test can spoil the font for the next.

Each test makes one claim, or two that belong together. When one fails, its name tells you what's wrong before you read any code.

Two tests are there because of things this book already got wrong once. test_key_ignores_capitals_and_punctuation pins down what Mira's tidying broke. test_summary_sorts_the_empty_glyphs pins down chapter 136's mistake, the order that differed between editors. A good time to write a test is right after a bug: you know what went wrong, and the test keeps it from coming back unnoticed.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
uv run --no-project --with pytest --with fontParts pytest -q

Six dots and an F:

......F                                                                  [100%]
    def test_lines_for_an_empty_font():
        font = RFont(showInterface=False)
        font.info.familyName = "Test"
        font.info.styleName = "Regular"
>       assert plum_report.lines(font) == [
            "Test Regular",
            "Glyphs            0",
            "No character      0",
            "Nothing drawn     0",
            "Kerning pairs     0",
        ]
E       AssertionError: assert ['Test Regula... pairs     0'] == ['Test Regula... pairs     0']
E
E         At index 3 diff: 'Nothing drawn     0  ' != 'Nothing drawn     0'

1 failed, 6 passed in 0.46s

I didn't plant that. I wrote the last test expecting it to pass, and it found a flaw in chapter 136's script that neither of us saw. Read the line that starts At index 3. When no glyph is empty, the report's fourth line ends in two spaces: the gap before a list of names that isn't there. Nobody sees two spaces at the end of a line in the Output panel, but a program reading the report would.

A dot is a test that passed, an F one that failed. For a failure pytest shows the test, marks the line with >, and on the E lines shows both sides of the == and where they part. That's more than a bare assert would tell you.

The fix is in plum_report.py, in lines. Replace the "Nothing drawn" line with these two:

empty = f"Nothing drawn     {len(facts['empty'])}  {', '.join(facts['empty'])}"
out.append(empty.strip())

strip is chapter 27's. Keep the indentation of the line you replaced. Run pytest again:

.......                                                                  [100%]
7 passed in 0.06s

It took six hundredths of a second. Send Tove the new file. And since you fixed the copy in spacing-tools, copy it over the plum_report.py that FontLab runs.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Do what Mira did. In plain/__init__.py, change text.lower() to text and run pytest:

>       assert plain.key("Plum-SemiBold") == plain.key("plum semibold")
E       AssertionError: assert 'PlumSemiBold' == 'plumsemibold'

>       assert plain.key("Plum v1.004") == "plumv1004"
E       AssertionError: assert 'Plumv1004' == 'plumv1004'

FAILED test_tools.py::test_key_ignores_capitals_and_punctuation - AssertionEr...
FAILED test_tools.py::test_key_keeps_digits - AssertionError: assert 'Plumv10...
2 failed, 5 passed in 0.07s

That's the bug from the top of the chapter, found in seven hundredths of a second where Friday took four days. The names of the two failed tests say what key no longer does. Put .lower() back and run it once more to see seven dots.

Now be clear about what the seven dots mean. They mean that seven claims about two files hold. They say nothing about shift_tool, about Undo, about the export, or about anything else that touches FontLab. Those are still checked the old way, by running them and looking. Tests cover the working-out, and they're one more reason to move as much of each script as you can into working-out.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text: assert states something that should be true and stops the script when it isn't. A test is a function of such claims, named for what it claims. pytest finds the files and functions that start with test_, runs them all, and shows where a failed claim parted from the truth. Only functions that can be imported without FontLab can be tested this way, so they live in a file of their own. A test needs data whose right answers you know, which means data you built. And passing tests are a statement about what they cover and nothing else.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Write test_key_of_an_empty_string. Decide what key("") should give before you run it.
  2. Add a glyph to small_font that's wider than m. Run pytest and read which tests fail. Then decide for each whether the test or the font should change.
  3. Find one more function in any script from Part 6 that takes plain values and returns plain values. Move it to plain/__init__.py, import it back into the script, and write two tests for it.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Oskar's holiday ends next week. In July he left a sheet with eleven lines on it and a folder called chores. The last chapter is his first morning back in the new year: what he finds, what's on the new list, and where you go from here.

docs.title: 140. Oskar comes back
docs.text:
It's Monday 18 January, and Oskar is back from his holiday.

The wall over Mira's desk is bare. The sheet he left there in July had its eleventh line drawn through in December, and he took it down himself. There's a Halfmoon folder in the Scripts menu that wasn't there when he first went away, and a Halfmoon menu beside it. He opens the Scripts menu, reads down it, and runs the Friday Build on a Monday to see what happens. It runs its checks, then tells him to save, export and come back.

"Who wrote that?"

"I did," Mira says. "Ines made me put it in the menu."

On his keyboard there's one sheet of paper. It's in Mira's handwriting, and it has five lines.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Plum-practice open, with a glyph in a Glyph window. Nothing new to install.

This chapter has one short script. I ran its plain-Python parts, and the outputs marked as such below are real. What it prints for a FontLab glyph I haven't seen, because I haven't run anything in FontLab 9, and this last time that's the point of the script: it's the one you run to find out what I couldn't tell you.

docs.title: The new list
docs.text:
Here's what Mira wrote:

  1. The variable font the publisher wants next.
  2. Greek, properly: spacing and kerning for the freelancer's glyphs.
  3. Rita wants the Shift tool in Portuguese.
  4. Tests for accentkit.
  5. Bold ellipsis: third dot outside the glyph.

The fifth is the pencil line from chapter 49, still waiting. The fourth you could start this afternoon, with chapter 139 open beside you. The other three have something in common: this book doesn't cover them. There's no chapter on exporting a variable font, none that kerns a script Mira can't read, and nowhere did I show how a tool's labels change language.

That's how it will be from here. The list never ends, and the book does. So the last thing to learn is how to work on a line that nobody has written a chapter for. There are four moves, and you've made each of them already without its name.

docs.title: Step 1: Ask the object
docs.text:
Every chapter told you which drawers an object has: glyph.width, glyph.name. I knew because I'd read the documents. Python lets you ask the object itself.

names = dir("Plum")
print(len(names))
print(names[-3:])

dir takes any object and returns a list of every name you can put after its dot. For a string, in the Python that FontLab 9 carries, I get:

81
['translate', 'upper', 'zfill']

That's real output, and I ran it because I wasn't sure of the number. What I remember about an object and what the object says can differ, and the object is right.

Many of the 81 names start with an underscore. Those are the object's own plumbing, and by a convention every Python programmer keeps, a name that starts with an underscore says "not for you". Leave them out and a string has 47.

dir gives names and nothing more. To learn what one of them does, ask for its note:

help("Plum".strip)

Help on built-in function strip:

strip(chars=None, /) method of builtins.str instance
    Return a copy of the string with leading and trailing whitespace removed.

    If chars is given and not None, remove characters in chars instead.

That's real output. Notice there are no brackets after strip: you hand help the function itself and don't call it. Whoever wrote the function wrote that note, in triple quotes as its first line, the way chapter 135's script had one at its top.

Two cautions for FontLab's own objects. I expect dir to work on them, since it works on everything, but I haven't seen what it lists. And FontLab's objects were written in another language, so many will have short notes or none. For the helpers that Fly routes to, which are written in Python, the notes are there. I read them to write this book.

docs.title: Step 2: Read what somebody else wrote
docs.text:
Chapter 135 was a reading lesson: twenty lines by a stranger, taken a line at a time. That skill is now worth more to you than any single helper, because the fastest way to do something new in FontLab is to find a script that does something near it.

You have more to read than you may think. Everything Fly routes to is Python, in files on your disk, in the folder chapter 4 had you make. The fontlab-fontlabapp folder alone holds the code behind most of the helpers you've called since chapter 7. When a chapter said that tell wraps a helper, run_standard_message_box, the helper is in there, and you can open it.

Read as chapter 135 did. First the imports, which say what the script depends on. Then the bottom, which says where it starts. Then follow one call inward, and stop as soon as you know what you came to learn. You don't have to understand a file to borrow one idea from it.

docs.title: Step 3: Look before you build
docs.text:
Chapter 133's installer, chapter 136's fontParts and chapter 138's GrabLab all came from other people. Before you start on a line of the new list, spend ten minutes finding out whether part of it exists. These are the pieces I know of around Fly, by the names of their folders:

Folder What it is fontlab-fly The toolbag: short names for the packages below. fontlab-fontlabapp Helpers for fonts, windows and dialogs: ap. TypeRig Geometry and glyph tools, with its own panels: tr. fontlab-python-pens Pens: fly.pens. (inside FontLab) FontLab's own Qt, behind every window since chapter 121: qt. pythonqtside For code written for PySide: qs. This book doesn't use it. fontlab-glyport Runs scripts written for Glyphs: gp. fontlab-fontport fontParts objects on FontLab's fonts: fp. fontlab-python-plugmix Ready-made plugins, among them reporters like chapter 134's. fontlab-python-scriptmix A couple of hundred Scripts-menu scripts, sorted into folders. fontlab-python-examples Example scripts and lessons. fontlab-remopy FontLab driven from outside, as in chapter 137. fontlab-grablab Pictures of windows and panels, as in chapter 138. vfjLib Reads and writes FontLab's VFJ files without FontLab.

I have to be straight about this table. You downloaded Fly and its seven neighbors in chapter 4. When I wrote this, several of the other names weren't yet published where anybody can download them, and I can't tell you which are as you read it. If one isn't where you found Fly, ask on the forum from step 4, and don't trust a download of the same name from somewhere else.

For Mira's third line, start in fontlab-python-scriptmix. Among a couple of hundred scripts, somebody may have needed labels in two languages before her.

docs.title: Step 4: Ask a person
docs.text:
When the object, the code and the folders haven't answered, ask people. FontLab has a forum at forum.fontlab.com with a section for scripting, and the people who wrote the tools in the table read it.

A question gets answered when it's cheap to answer. Chapter 38 taught you to read a traceback; now you write for somebody who'll read yours. Send four things:

  1. What you wanted, in one sentence.
  2. The smallest script that shows the trouble. Cut yours down until removing one more line makes the trouble go away. Half the time you find the answer while cutting.
  3. What happened: the last lines of the traceback, copied, never retyped.
  4. Your FontLab version, and whether Fly is installed.

Oskar's rule for the studio is shorter: "Don't ask me until you can show me ten lines."

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text:
Steps 1 and 2 in a form you can keep in the Scripts menu:

#FLM: What's In It
# Lists what an object offers: the names you can put after its dot.
# It reads and prints, and changes nothing.
from fly import fl


def public(thing):
    return [name for name in dir(thing) if not name.startswith("_")]


def matching(thing, word):
    return [name for name in public(thing) if word.lower() in name.lower()]


def show(thing, word=""):
    names = matching(thing, word)
    print(f"{type(thing).__name__}: {len(names)} of {len(public(thing))} names")
    for name in names:
        kind = "does" if callable(getattr(thing, name, None)) else "is"
        print(f"  {kind:<6}{name}")


def main():
    glyph = fl.CurrentGlyph()
    if glyph is None:
        print("Open a glyph first.")
        return
    show(glyph, "width")


main()

Save it as whats_in.py.

public is dir without the underscore names. matching keeps the names that contain a word, in either case. show prints them with one word in front: does for a name you call with brackets, is for a drawer you read. callable and getattr are chapter 123's and chapter 95's. word="" is a parameter with a start value, as in chapter 34, and since an empty string is inside every string, leaving it out shows everything.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
On a string and a number, in plain Python, show("Plum", "strip") and show(596.0) print:

str: 3 of 47 names
  does  lstrip
  does  rstrip
  does  strip
float: 7 of 7 names
  does  as_integer_ratio
  does  conjugate
  does  fromhex
  does  hex
  is    imag
  does  is_integer
  is    real

That's real. The script as saved asks the current glyph about "width", and here I can only say what I expect: a first line that starts with the kind of object a glyph is, then a handful of names with width among them. Run it, then change "width" to "layer", then to "".

Read the long list slowly. You'll meet names from all through this book, and many more that it never used. Each of those is something a glyph can tell you or do that I didn't have room for. Some of them are the start of a line on your own list.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Ask for the note on a name that isn't there:

help("Plum".nope)

AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'nope'

help never ran. Python has to fetch "Plum".nope before it can hand it over, and the fetch fails. It's chapter 6's error, and you get it for a wrong guess. whats_in.py exists so that you don't have to guess.

Now the other mistake, the one that gives no error:

print("Plum".upper)

<built-in method upper of str object at 0x10487ce30>

That's a function, printed without being called. The number at the end will differ on your machine. Whenever you see angle brackets where you expected a value, you've left off the ().

And one caution that has no error message at all. dir tells you a name exists. It doesn't tell you whether calling it is safe. Among a glyph's names are some that change the glyph, and a few, as chapter 110 found, that make loose objects FontLab doesn't want held. Before you call a name you found by asking, read its note, look for a script that uses it, and try it on a copy of the font. That has been the rule since chapter 14, and it matters more now that nobody is checking the names for you.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
dir lists what an object offers and help prints the note its author left. A leading underscore means "not for you". The code behind the helpers is on your disk and can be read the way chapter 135 read a stranger's script. Before building, look at what exists. Before asking, cut the trouble down to ten lines. A name you found yourself is tried on a copy first.

Across the whole book, you learned to hand a computer the part of your work that needs no talent, and to check what it did.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Run show on fl.CurrentFont(), with "kern" as the word. Compare what you find with what chapters 69 to 80 used.
  2. Pick one name from a glyph's list that this book never used. Find its note with help. Then search the folders from step 3 for a script that calls it.
  3. Take a sheet of paper. Write down the job in your own week that takes an afternoon, needs no talent and comes back every time something changes. Then write the questions the script has to answer, as chapter 20 did, before you write a line of code.

docs.title: The sheet
docs.text:
Oskar reads Mira's five lines twice. He takes a pencil and writes three words next to the first one. They aren't the three words from July.

Ask the font.

Then he pins the sheet to the wall, where the old one was, and goes to make coffee.
